A game which fulfills some of that metroidvania itch without being complicated or costing any moolah. There's a distinct lack of music so you may want some 8-bit chiptunes playing in the background. :)
This game will also remind others of super meat boy in it's structure. You can spend hundreds of lives at a specific point, but there are many checkpoints and unlimited lives (in normal mode). These allow you to become comfortable with the controls and gameplay, not to mention giving an endorphin rush for getting to the next bell after a particularly challenging section. One small downside I noticed is that the cling power-up has some issues on moving platforms, but those areas that necessitate it are few and far between.
I would easily pay at least $5.00 for games which provide a similar experience, and that's saying something because I'm an extreme cheapskate.  I say you should totally grab it for the current price of $0.00 because it is a really good game. I also will highly recommend you support the creator because it's not often that one can find a quality product provided with no strings attached like this.

Lilli, the girl who hardly rabbits at all.
The Good:
* Charmingly minimalistic characters and backdrops
* Psychotically twisted, mute, protagonist is amusingly succinct
* Narration is occasionally effective and supplies the odd good joke
* Cleverly sidesteps gory visuals with fantastic delusions
* Right click skips the long speeches
* Space reveals click points
* Above average voice work works well.
* Despite the dark humour doesn't devolve into swearwords or crudity
* Easily 8 hours of fun
The Bad:
* Often overly wordy, has you skipping the text with right clicks
* Some quests are simple, others obtuse and some seriously hard
* Most locations you can only click on useful objects limiting choices
* Sound/music is nothing special
* Third Act feels rather messy and is the weakest
* A very so-so ending
* Not much replay value, hardly unexpected
Background: played several game by this company and wanted to give this one a try
Impressions: While the visuals sometimes feel cheap and flash like the game shines in it's humour and range of jokes it attempts in the dialogue, mostly delivered by the dryly spoken narrator. The quests are typical of the genre apart from one of final ones that's interesting but under explained. The best part is when edna is on screen and when the narrator gets to put his twist on describing the scenes in funny and obtuse ways.
Recommended for: Mature point and click fans who like rye twisted humour that hints at the dark in a chripily cheerful voice.
Conclusion: 6/10. Not for kids but those who like some black comedy and silliness.

I haven't played the first Edna and Harvey game so was somewhat skeptical of picking this up as other Deadilic titles while excellent storywise really put me off with the voice acting, however I'm really pleased I grabbed this in a sale as it's one of the best point and clicks I've played in a long time. While not overly hard, it's enough to make you think on how to proceed without ever having to refer to a walkthrough, and the story is pretty damn good, although I was a little disappointed at the ending which seemed rather abrupt. You could probably complete this in a single sitting if you wanted however expect to spend a good couple of hours straight at it. I completed it over a weekend just playing a couple of hours at a time each day.
There were a couple of bugs that kept popping up now and again, mainly with the interface, but nothing that crashed the game or stopped you proceeding.
There is an intelligent story here hidden behind the cute fluffyness, I urge you to give this a go if you like a good story and a good point and click adventure game... They are so rare nowadays!

**Please scroll down for UPDATE EDIT 26.06.2015**
I would've loved to have given this a thumb's up, but I can't and I won't...
I really like the oddity of the story, as much as I got into it (a couple hours gameplay on 1st and 2nd install before I realised the achievements were broken)...the artwork is whimsical, the music is nice. There's a kind of twistedness to it, to Lilly's character that makes it disturbingly sweet. And unlike some others who have played this, I like the puzzles and the narrator's babble.
However, as this is a review for the game bought on Steam, it fails. I scoured the internet and countless forums for help on fixing the 'broken' achievement problem, tiny bugs - I've tried everything that I found, but all to no avail. Some of the fixes, well, the game simply wouldn't let me even try them out...
Some have said disable Steam Cloud, I did.. some have said delete save games and uninstall, reinstall, I did - nothing. One poster even said turning off Subtitles and exiting/ restarting did the trick for them - must be nice for them because when I try this, the main menu freezes forcing me to hard shut the game down every time - and guess what? The **** Subtitles option is always checked (even the ONE time I managed to exit the game properly and come back in, the Subtitles were activated).
After vainly trying this, my 3rd time, I have decided to shelve it indefinitely on my Steam shelf and let it collect dust. Some may think it silly to not play a game simply because the achievements aren't working, but we all have our quirks. Not to mention, the main menu settings have some serious issues with being touched, freezing up the game in protest - this alone is severely annoying for me.
But the main reason I will not recommend E&H:HNE is because during my fruitless search for solutions, I discovered that Deadalic are not very catering to their paying public. Many places claimed the devs had stopped supporting some of their games on Steam altogether - I dunno, whatever that drama may be doesn't interest me so much. What I do know is that the achievement issue spans back more than two years. I received this game as a gift not even a month ago, and the problems are still present - despite some Spring-ish update only this year they claimed fixed this problem.
Regardless, I will not buy Deponia now because of this experience, and probably nothing else Daedalic spins out. I have Journey of a Roach due to Koboldgames being on board - as things are going all right with that game, I suspect Daedalic mainly stuck to the publishing side of things - yay...
It is an exceedingly rare thing for me to have a bad experience with a game - when it happens, I'm unforgiving...
-1/10
**UPDATE EDIT 26.06.2015**
So, I got a new pc and have been in the process of re-downloading many games to try it out. Scanning my library, my eyes were caught by Edna & Harvey - this game has always been a bit of a constant fingernail scratch on the back of my neck... annoying and teasing. I was attracted to the story, art and gameplay from the start - but the hoop-jumping to find answers and the devs', largely, disinterest in taking part in Steam forums for their games and their standoffish attitude toward their playerbase was a turn-off.
I did some searching again and found
which cures the Steam achievement issues. I would like to add that I did try something along these lines the last time I gave it a chance but it did not work (perhaps there were some remnants of the game left after numerous uninstall-/ re-installments to try to fix the problem and as this is a new pc...). So, I installed it, made sure Steam Cloud was off, ran it, chose English language, saw my version was 1.3.4.390, exited the game, rechecked to verify that Steam Cloud was still unselected, restarted the game, saw my version was now showing v. 2.0.4.0395, began a game and the achievements have been rolling in.
The game on its own has always been about a 9/10 for me, but I won't alter my recommendation because my feelings about Daedalic haven't changed. The jury's still out on if I'll ever purchase another game developed by them - it's the principal of a thing, it's principalities ;-)
Look at the Edna & Harvey Steam forum... there are numerous broken achievement posts on the first page alone, THIS MONTH - why can't the devs sticky the link above and be done with it? It's crazy.
And for any gamers who think other gamers throwing a stink about broken achievements are silly or whiney: Steam is an app for gamers with incentives to thoroughly explore most games and obtain rewards for doing so via achievements and perfect game stats - this is a game in and of itself.
This review was and remains for Edna & Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes, the STEAM version.

Quite honestly one of the best roguelike RPG's i've played.
There's a character creation system with a variety of classes, perks and appearances. Most need to be unlocked but there's quite a lot to get.
The movement and battles are turn-based and the unique flavor to this particular game is a encroaching wall of darkness from the left that closes in each time you do something.(Move, attack, etc) This means you have to keep a eye on the darkness and consider wether to go on or maybe try to clear that one dungeon or pick up that one item in time.
This creates a sense of pressure that makes for a fun atmosphere.
There is a online aspect to the game in the form of death/milestone messages from other players in the same world that show up in the upper left of the screen.
The worlds are randomly generated but there are specific types that have special quests or certain restrictions. There is also the ability to share world ID's with others so they can play the same world.
For a fairly cheap price this is a great game to pick up.

This game has a few cons i'd like to get out of the way right off. Like any team based multiplayer game, expect some people to get mad at you for not knowing how to play...or just because you're alive. Also not only is the learning curve pretty tough, most of the people you're up against have been playing for more than a couple years so you will lose fights. a lot. The last negative thing that I can think of is that it can sometimes be hard to find a game. Either the server for your area is full and you have to wait, or its comepletely empty and you have to wait in an empty server and end up getting whooped in a 1v2 by people playing like their life is on the line.
If you can get past that, it is incredibly fun and rewarding when you DO get that victory. Hell, i've had losses that have been more fun than an hour of playing Fallout 4 or somethin.
Get this game if you like competitive games that can be punishing but rewarding.

Honestly a fantastic game that I can play for hours on end. I believe this is honestly the best game in the franchise, despite a few things here and there. I'll just get right to the pros and cons of the game so you can move on with you're day :)
Pros+
+Easy to run :D (Helpful with my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ computer)
+Different every time you play
+Plethora of Civilizations to play as, from Rome to the Songhai Empire (DLC required for some unfortunately)
+Great setup options for games (via Advanced Setup)
+All DLC at a fairly cheap price (Like $29.99 USD I believe, but understandable considering how old the game is)
+Endless hours of singleplayer gameplay
+Incorporates strategy in ways you don't see in many games today
+Not just your everyday RTS, you have to control many things such as:
-Happiness and Unhappiness (Counter eachother, with happiness being good obviously)
-Culture, which is used to spawn great people and grow your empire
-Science, which is used to research Technology
-Gold, which is used to purchase and provide maintenance Units and Buildings, to trade with other Civilizations, and to use as gifts to City-States
-Faith, which is used to spread your religion via units and buildings (i.e. Missionaries and Great Prophets)
-Food, used to feed your people, which in turn grows your empire's borders(rate depends on amount of food)
-Production, which is used to build units, buildings and wonders, the more you have, the quicker they are built
+Great Community
+Great Modding Community, hundreds of Mods on the Workshop
+Pretty good graphics for its time, not a bad game to look at
Cons-
-In Multiplayer, Diplomacy with other players and Civilizations does not work like it does in SinglePlayer
-Minor bugs here and there, such as units causing visual tearing, however it only lasts about a second and doesn't occur often

Overall, I honestly give this game a solid 10/10. However, this game will definitely not be for everybody. Even though you can change the speed of the game (change the average amount of turns it takes to do things/progress), it is still at its core a game of patience. Personally, I have great patience for this game, but I know not everybody is like that. Anyways, I 100% recommend this game, as it is one of my favorites of all time and I certainly will be playing it for a while.

(This review contains some spoilers.)
isn't so much a "quirky" RPG as it is unrelentingly grim and depressing. It's also one of the best indie RPGs made in a long, long time.
Coming off as the love child of
and
,
puts players into the shoes of a man who has been beaten down so thoroughly that he has virtually nothing left, but still perseveres in order to rescue the only woman in the world. More than any other game in a while,
forces you to weigh the consequences of your actions and continue on in the face of nonstop tragedy and tough decisions. Make no mistake - this game
leave you drained by the end of it.
may not be the flashiest RPG out there, but it is a masterwork on how to effectively build tension and uncertainty while utilizing various gameplay elements to the fullest. Every step feels like it could be your last. Enemies will routinely wreck your party, even with planning. Sleeping at a campfire runs the risk of a permanent injury, or worse, one of your companions bailing on you. There is no loyalty between anyone, not even between Brad and Buddy. A choice between chopping your arm off or permanently sacrificing a companion is one of the easier decisions forced upon you. Give something to an innocuous pair of NPCs and an entire village could be wiped out.
Somewhere between the game insinuating that a major character was molested and a decision where I had to choose between sacrificing my current party members or chopping off a minor body part, I had to put the game down and step away for a while. The subject matter is unrelentingly dark, and even the few moments of levity the plot and characters provide aren't really balanced with the grim nature of the world Brad and everyone else inhabit.
The game will flip between moods on a dime - one minute, you're taking part in Russian Roulette that can (and will) cause permadeath for your companions, and the next you're in a village where an amateur magician is asking you to find some playing cards for him. You go from a hilarious wrestling sidequest that riffs on the WWF to a pair of decisions that easily qualify as the darkest moment in the game.
Still,
does have moments of humor and amusement. The various companions you meet throughout the world all have quirky backstories and interesting little comments after battles (which makes it all the more difficult at the end of the game, during a certain cutscene). There are interesting and funny little notes written throughout the world, and some of the ambient locations you run across (like a McDonalds parody, where fast food meals are gifted from the "heavens" above) are quite unique.
The battles are pretty straightforward, but do rely on a lot of strategy, especially if you're playing in "Pain Mode" (where you can only use savepoints once). There is a definite degree of strategy, and even with overleveled characters, you still have to figure out the weaknesses of bosses and attempt to counter them. The game also does a great job of encouraging replayability through multiple endings, alternate choices and different party configurations.
Also, there's a really great fast-travel system that allows you to get to one of the main hubs instantly. It's always something I harp on about longer RPGs not having, but it was pulled off very well here.
If there's anything I didn't like in the game, it's the fact that a certain character that administers the decisions comes off as a bit too "deus ex machina" for my tastes, and some of the bosses either force you to grind or counter them with a really-overpowered companion. I also didn't feel that many of the companions warranted being part of my active party, and they don't do much of consequence after being recruited.
Still, I was more than satisfied after a single playthrough of the game.
is a title that will leave you emotionally drained and weighing the consequences of everything that leads up to that final, nihilistic ending.
And I wouldn't have it any other way. Highly recommended.

This game is brillianlty written. LISA combines great humor and a good, dark, deep story into a great game. LISA touches on subjects such as: abuse, struggles of woman being used, the struggles of being a parent, drug addiction, and loss. LISA is about a man named Brad who loses his sister, was bullied as a child, and abused by his father. Not being able to grasp the loss of his sister, he resorts to using "joy"(a drug thats suppose to make you happy) to try to forget about his sister's death. Brad also has a deep hate for his abusing father and can never forgive him for all the pain and suffering he has caused him. LISA can be a very funny game as it makes many great jokes, but at some points it turns serious and can probaby make your heart feel weak.
LISA is a turn base RPG that make you want to play it over and over again after completing. . Their are 30 companions (all being great chracters) that can join you on your adventure through the weird world of LISA. Another excellent Saints game.  Not as good as 3, but still fun. Graphics for the most part look the same as 3 which isn't a bad thing.
Game gets off to a fast start as usual, but the Saints are now in the White House and The Boss is the President of the USA. On the way to a public speaking, the White House is attacked by aliens at which point, after a good battle, the alien leader, Zinyak captures you (The President), and sticks you in a simulation of Steelport. circa 1950's. Kinzie, your computer hacker is able to contact you and continues to help you try to break the simulation and escape and eventually take you back to a newer version of steelport.
Along the way, you gain super powers and special weapons as you continue to beat challenges and collect clusters to help you continue to save the other Saints as you make your way to your final battle with Zinyak himself.

Bloodlines is a great rpg, it has a very awkward tutorial that does a poor job of introducing the game to you and it can be quite a turn off for newcomers but the tutorial does not represent the game well at all. Once you are left to explore the first area of the game after the tutorial you start to see the strengths of the game and you start to understand why this game has such a cult following. It has an interesting story and world, interesting lore and interesting characters with also very surprisingly great voice acting. I absolutely loved exploring the open world hub areas without the burden of objective markers, soaking in the world and atmosphere from just talking to npcs and discovering side missions which by the way are very well done and tell great stories on their own and end up being very memorable. The ideologies of the different vampire factions I found very intriguing in particular. The main missions offer up nice variety with the visuals and locations you are visiting and you can tell the developers tried to make an effort to make each mission feel different from each other so the game doesn’t get repetitive. However you can tell the developers ran out of either time or money because the level design in the later stages become really generic and repetitive especially compared to the early missions like the amazing ocean house hotel. The rpg mechanics are implemented to the game very well, I appreciated the amount of options in the character creation and the leveling up system. I really liked the morality system with the humanity and being faithful to the masquerade, it’s well integrated with the main and side missions in particular. I appreciated all the different ways you can tackle an objective even though I always ended up just going in guns blazing. Speaking of the combat I enjoyed it overall I don’t think it’s horrible like some people claim, it does it’s job perfectly fine in my opinion and it can be pretty fun at times. The end game can be very brutal if you haven’t leveled up your character in a few certain ways which does restrict the freedom you have with your character. I recommend installing the fan made unofficial patch of the game because without it it’s almost unplayable with all the bugs, crashes and lack of high resolution options.

Spoiler-free recommendation:
Well deserving of its “flawed masterpiece” label; it’s definately both.
If you like role-playing games, first-person-shooters, horror, vampires, and B-movies ... this game is an absolute must in your library; it contains all of those elements (albeit clumsily executed). Unfortunately, the game lives up to its reputation of being riddled with bugs, unfinished content, and its at best serviceable gameplay mechanics.
The thing that saves this poor, neglected project, however, is the story. It’s rich, deep, interesting, and will draw you in. The characters are unique and memorable. For example: you know how in games like Skyrim there are so many forgettable NPCs? The quest-givers all interact with you so similarily? Most of the citizens have no character? Well, in Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines, every NPC is memorable, even the quest-givers. Each character feels like they have their own world going on around them and your dialogue counts; if you say the wrong thing at the wrong time they might react totally different instead of trying over and over to shove a quest into your hands. They’re not just standing there waiting for you to accept their quest. How you talk to them, and what you’ve done in the story previously, determines how they react to you — if at all.
Nothing is really handed to you, as if you are some walking god and everyone believes in you or you’re the chosen or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ Really, they did a good job of painting the picture of being an isolated being in modern L.A. You kind of have to discover everything on your own and earn rewards — much as you would in any similar situation.
And again, the story is interesting and mysterious enough to really draw you in. The character’s conversations are fun and organic so you always feel like there’s something “new” to experience.
However, it may be a bit of a trial to get over some of the downright ugly animations. Facial expressions are nowhere near what is possible with the Source engine (though its obvious a legitimate effort was made), and a lot of movements look stilted and unnatural. Heh, or maybe “supernatural”?
Combat is frustrating, yet oddly satisfying — especially melee. I’m not sure why. It rather reminds me of Diablo click-fest mixed with mouse-view. But keep levelling your character and it gets easier, and make sure you use your powers.
But despite all its flaws, I found I just could not help booting the game up over and over again to see where the story would lead me next. If you like Deus Ex, or really any story-rich experience, this game borrows heavily from all the classics and indeed adds its own flare. I highly recommend this game because it is at its best moments a timeless experience, and at its worst a guilty pleasure. And for me, I liked it.

Lisa: The Painful RPG is an interesting game which I do indeed reccomend playing, though there are quite a few odd, bothersome problems that prevent it from reaching the level of what I would consider really great. I wish Steam had an "in the middle" option to rate things, because I would probably use it in this case.
Lisa takes place in a post-apocalyptic world where females have been wiped out, leaving the direction of the world up to a large collection of sweaty, perverted, screwed up middle aged men to inherit the Earth.  The only known remaining female is Buddy, a little girl being cared for by a man named Brad. When Buddy is kidnapped, Brad goes off to hunt her down. Truth be told, this plot isn't actually really focused on in any real intense way. The plot isn't bad, though truthfully it's not really focused on until the last quarter of the game or so; most of what you do has little relation to the main plot and mainly consists of Brad interacting with people in the wasteland.
Lisa is funny; surprisingly such. It's got a very irreverent, bizarre sense of humor that is hard not to chuckle about. Unfortunately, it suffers from a horrible case of tonal schizophrenia. It never seems to know when to be serious and when to try and make you laugh. For example, there's an area where you're forced to play god with the lives of people in your party. Immediately preceding this is a scene where a strange bald man is attacked by a tiny spider while trying to defecate in the middle of a field. There's no real consistency to what it's trying to do, and this in turn causes everything to have less impact than it could have, both humor-wise and emotional-wise.
The gameplay itself is a mixed bag. The battle system is very plain, though I feel it to be pretty fun. It's your average turn-based RPG system, but characters have a myriad of different systems to how they use their skills, and said skills often interact with others in strange ways. There's a massive amount of characters in the game, sort of reminding me of Chrono Cross; you go around the world finding a bunch of crazy weirdos who don't really have much (or any) plot or character development to their name, but all look cool and do cool things. This means that there are many, many possible party combinations if you ever feel the need to do subsequent playthroughs to mix things up.
What drags the gameplay down is navigating the world, which seems to be intentionally designed to be as slow and cumbersome as possible. The world of Lisa is a very vertically-oriented thing; getting around more or less anywhere requires a lot of hopping up and down cliffs, scaling and going down rope, etc. There is also fall damage if you drop just a little too far, as well as bottomless pits that scattered all over that will give you game overs if you aren't careful. This wasn't much of a problem at first, but by the end of things, I was thoroughly tired of the hassle it was to get anywhere and find anything. This is redoubled by the fact that depending on how you play the game, something that you do might make using ropes even SLOWER!
Overall, I'd reccomend Lisa. It's a very interesting, special little game that's trying to tell an interesting, special story. I think the beginning of the game, for the first two or three hours, is probably the strongest section of it. However, the many (perhaps intentionally?) strange and cumbersome design choices and the unfortunate handling of the pacing of the plot kept me from enjoying it as much as I really wanted to.

Normally the idea of a "1st person platformer" should fill most gamers with horror, but A Story About My Uncle manages to make it not as unpleasant as it sounds. But it's still not good.
The Gameplay is simple: Think 1st Person Bionic Commando. You will Jump from platform to platform, using a grappling hook to swing or catapult you onto various floating platforms to progress through the level. You are resctricted to using the grapple once, twice, or thrice as you progress. And... that's it. You gain an ability to , for lack of a better word, "double jump" as well but it only adds just a little more to the experience.
This sort of mechanic can be fun, but not in the challenges they've constructed. This is the kind of thing I can see working well in an open world style game, like some of the older Spiderman games. But alone it gets repetetive. They try to keep things interesting by changing scenery, adding moving obstacles, but you're still just jumping from platform to platform. There are only rare moments where combining a series of swings and mid air jumps has that satisfying "Nailed it!" feeling.
It's not particularly challenging, and it is challenging it does so in an unfair way. For example, some surfaces you can grapple, and some you can't. The graphical quality is so poor, and environments so dark you'll have a hard time guessing what you can latch on to and what you can't. Later in the game you'll be able to "recharge" your grapple mid air by clicking on Blue Crystals. But the hit box is so narrow you'll miss clicking it completely and plunge to yorur death as you accidentally use your last grapple charge on a piece of rock (you need at least one charge to recharge oddly enough).
One of the most frustrating parts is when your grapple is just out of range of your intended target and you will frantically click on the surface in question so you can just grab it before it falls away from you again, only to find you've quickly expended 2-3 charges on one surface.
Understandably some of the above are 'skill based' problems. That maybe so, but it's also not very fun.
Graphically the game is something roughly equivalent to Xbox and Xbox 360 hardware. It's very dated with lots of polyons. Environments generally features lots of contrast, but are also too dark even on recommended brightness setting.
There is some kind of story here, but it's really all a McGuffin. The whole idea of the game is you're chasing afer your Uncle? Why? It's not really explained. The narrator's blasse tone has all the suspense of an airport announcer.
With 3 strikes in gameplay, story, and presentation I can't recommend this game enough.

The story behind Divide by Sheep is total whimsy. Death is a lonely little soul with a sheep fetish (maybe he’s from Buxton, I don’t know), he just loves those wooly little ruminants. Being an anthropomorphic personification of the slide into decrepitude and the inevitable surcease of life, he can only be friendly with dead things. As a result and in a leap of somewhat startlingly stark logic, he decides to kill everything. In a flood. Old Testament style. Sploosh.
Now this is where you come in, it’s your task to float the little darlings on to rafts and rescue them from his bony clutches. So far so simple, but wait, they are on islands, and some islands only hold so many sheep. If you get them to jump from an island that can hold, say seven sheep onto one holding only four, three of them will drown and spent eternity as the grim reapers fluffy playthings! Ah well, them’s the breaks. Of course, just like islands, some rafts can only hold so many sheep, so you will have to strategically drown some of them anyway just to get to the end of the level.
And so it goes, sheep drown, sheep live, and as the game progresses you get to slice them in half with lasers (they get duct taped back together on the raft, don’t worry), bounce them off trampolines, and feed them to wolves. Of course, wolves need rescuing too, so them too get to bounce about like little black motes of soot. A fed wolf can’t bounce as that would cause nasty vomitory complications so they just sit there looking happy while the raft floats off into the sunset. While you tax your brain trying to work out how to meet all three victory conditions for the level or at least one of them so you can move on and see what devilry has been set in store for you next.
Visually, this game screams out what it is, a mobile game that has come to Steam. With blocky, voxel style graphics, cutesy sounds and music, and a user interface that screams out “I was on an iPhone” in a loud squeaky voice.
None of this detracts from the inherent addictiveness of flinging sheep at laser beams, fences and the occasional kraken however, in fact it enhances the dark comedic nature of the game and has you giggling at the animated cut-scenes that explain the latest twist to the game play with visuals of bisected ruminants, flying ungulates, and snapping canidae.
On the whole, Divide by Sheep is a cute, enjoyable, darkly comedic time sucker of a game. It has a real “one more level” appeal to it that has had me sit to play it, and then wonder why my freshly made coffee is now cold on more than one occasion. tinyBUILD have made a bit of a corker here, and it’s well worth the 4 quid it costs on Steam

Rating 9/10
What is it?
This is a turn based rogue game that has an isometric perspective. You have to constantly keep moving to the right because a darkness keeps creeping in from the left.
The Good
+ 8 Classes to fit your play style. Knight, sword master, hunter etc.  Obviously each one has their own unique strengths and weakness  along with their own stat growth rate.
+ Different modes offer players interesting new dynamics to the world. I.e Better weapons but harder enemies
+Different levels of difficulty. The easiest difficulty level stops at a certain distance, however the later difficulties can be much longer.
+ Lots of secrets to find out, giving the game a lot more depth than it appears to
+ Randomized Levels
The Bad
- The game can be frustrating, especially if you get a bad world generated.
Conclusion
This game is surprisingly addicting. At first it doesn't look like much but the more you play it the more it grows on you. You quickly realize that strategy is involved depending on the class your playing. The fact that you are forced to keep moving means you are going to have to make some tough decisions. Given the price point, this is probably one of the better deals you will find.
This is a great point and click game, with a dark sense of humor and great writing. If you are a fan of the genre, you should get it.

One Way Heroics has a certain whimsical charm to it, and not just with its 8-bit graphics. The soundtrack is absolutely
. Every time I open this game, I stop for about 10 minutes just to listen to the title screen's music. The mechanics of the game are fantastic, despite the somewhat steep learning curve, and is simplistic enough for a casual session but is also surprisingly deep enough for a major time investment.
The story isn't exactly an enchanting epic, but you can do with it as you like. Either fill in for them or just ignore it. Some great darkness is consuming the world, which is the left most part of the screen, and you have to escape that darkness by going to the right, hence the title of the game. Along the way, you'll encounter beasts, animals, dungeons, and dodgy terrain; all of which you must face in order to prepare for the advent of the Demon Lord.
Your journey is defined by you. It can turn from a simple stroll across the meadow to a desperate struggle to survive. It can be simple, it can be deep. Overall, One Way Heroics is a great adventure RPG that can't hurt your wallet.

I could give you an actual review of the game with reasoning behind why I like it so much, but instead I think I'll let you read through the story of one of my playthroughs and see for yourself.
Once upon a time, there was a ship, appropriately titled "The Loser." The Loser really sucked at doing just about anything, but was given an extremely important mission for the Federation nonetheless, as the bureaucrats at the top wanted to save money. They were to go to the far end of the galaxy and stop the evil rebel armada. Among The Loser's grand crew was the captain, Lousy, who made the worst decisions possible. There was also Stupid, an Engi, who did nothing except what Lousy told him too, and then managed to mess everything up anyway. He liked to play in fire. Then there was his brother, Fred, the engineer. Fred was the only person who didn't suck at his job.
Moments after leaving the station, The Loser encountered a rebel ship, armed to the teeth with heavy weaponry. Lousy, being the lousy captain he was, decided to attack the ship. After a quick three minutes of "battling" (devoting all time to hull breach repairs and attempting to put out fires) Lousy ran away from the battle, jumping into warp, and, despite the ship still being on fire, decided to answer a distress call form a nearby space station. The station was being attacked by giant spiders, so Lousy happily sent in his battered crew to take care of them. However, it turned out that Giant Spiders were, well, giant. Running and screaming for their lives, the crew almost made it to their ship, though Fred did take the opportunity to distract the giant spiders by throwing Lousy to be feasted upon by them. Lousy died as he lived: screaming and running from a bad decision he made.
Now alone, Stupid took it upon himself to claim the position of captain, much to Fred's dismay. Despite having taken heavy damage, Stupid opted not to go into a store for repairs, and instead went inside a giant nebula, whereupon they were taken by surprise by slavers. The slavers demanded one of their crewman as a slave, and, though Stupid clearly wanted to fight their 10x bigger ship, Fred was more than happy to offer up Stupid as a slave. Stupid initially refused, but, upon being told there was candy on the slave ship, eagerly agreed. Fred never saw Stupid again.
Happy with the new peace and quiet, Fred took the opportunity to make some smart decisions. He flew the ship into a store and had it repaired. Realizing he had no money left, Fred took the nearby planets, asking if anybody needed some mercenary work done. One small group asked them to destroy a rebel scout that had been harassing a space station nearby. Though he was initially going to deny the job, remembering how well their last Rebel encounter had went, the pay was too good. He made it to the outpost and, though careful strategy and manipulation of ion blasters and drones, managed to take out the enemy ship. He then immediately spent all his money on a scrap recovery arm, thinking it would be a great long-term investment.
Feeling good about himself, he took up a couple of other jobs that were fairly easy, and accumulated many resources. Realizing he had to make it to the next system before it was too late, he decided that he's done enough mercenary work for now, and flew full-speed to the next system, just before the rebels took over the one he left.  Choosing between a Mantis-controlled system and a Mantis-controlled system, he chose the Mantis-controlled system. Stopping at a store, he considered buying a cloning chamber, but then shuddered at the thought of more Lousys and Stupids running around and opted just to get fuel. All was quiet for a while, Halfway across the system he found an abandoned rebel ship and stripped it of resources. He fought off a rebel scout quite easily, and, on a whim, decided to check out a distress signal from another space station. Their message came through; they'd also been overrun by giant spiders. Immediately Fred turned tail and left. There was no way he was going down the same way as the not-dearly departed Lousy.
As he left, he suddenly read a signal on his console; there was an intruder on deck! Arming himself with a laser, he cautiously made his way out into the main hallway, where he found a mantis begging for sanctuary from a pirate ship that he had just escaped from. Moments later, the pirate ship itself appeared, offering up a bounty for the Mantis's return. Fred contemplated, and realized that, while it would be smarter to return the Mantis, he WAS getting rather lonely, and imaginary friends could only do for so long.  Besides, he had been able to handle every ship thus far with a few simple strategies. He responded by firing upon the pirate ship.
But it was a trap! The Mantis tore out his shields, leaving him unshielded and crippled before teleporting back onto the ship. Several drones came out of the pirate ship, protecting it from anything Fred launched. Fred immediately threw his own drones at them in hope  of doing some damage, but they were reduced to scrap heaps in seconds. With his back against the wall, Fred decided that he had no choice but to get out of there, desperately firing Ion charges at their weapons while he powered up his engines. He couldn't fix that now; he just kept powering the ship's engines, hoping to get away in time. The oxygen system broke, and slowly the air grew thinner. It became nearly impossible to breathe. The rebels won.

LISA is a post-apocalyptic RPG. I find it good but not very fun, and I will try to explain why.
I will start with what got me into playing the game: the graphics are simple, but the art style is rich and very evocative (special mention to all the different monstrously mutated humans). It translates into the scenes visited: a lot of variation, twisted stories, but with a simple delivery and charm. This is mostly what kept me going, knowing that each area would reveal new characters and stories with their own personality that bring something new to the experience. While it is impressive that all these scenes can hint at much more depth while being so short, it also disappointed me that there was little follow-through to any of these stories and characters. Especially regarding all the many players that can be recruited to the party of the player. Only a little bit more follow-through for the main quest, but new elements that concern it are so far from each other that it feels disconnected from the experience. At least there are moments with terrible choices to make, and some of those will stick to the player's mind even after the game has been closed!
While I appreciated the variety in locations, I found it very hard to appreciate the core gameplay that would get me from one place to the other. The game looks like a platformer, but there is no way to jump so moving up requires cords. There are many platforms to climb, so exploring is both tedious and dangerous as falling in a pit can lead to a game over. And the framerate can occasionally tank so much that navigating the levels becomes even more painful. I would have stopped the game after a few minutes if there wasn't quickly a bicycle to move faster, but even then navigating these mountains and having a hard time remembering where each door among many goes really put me off. And that is where I could also see that despite its limitations the game was well designed, as backgrounds were hugely different for each place, or sometimes annoying enemies would serve as a way to remind the player which direction had not been explored yet.
Talking about combat, this game is similar to a jRPG as the player chooses the different attacks, and then everyone attacks in turn with no movement involved. There are some moments with surprise encounters, but thankfully very rare or it would have convinced me to stop the game as well. It is not really necessary to grind either, so the usual reasons as to why I hate jRPGs are largely mitigated here. And even if I do not like jRPG combat logic (why can my character heal during a battle but not outside?), the combat system was not a complete bore due to the original attacks and effects (can make someone feel weird, cry, trip and so on). So not especially enjoyable, but not too taxing while having depth and enough variety in the enemies encountered to prevent too much repetition.
Another question is: are the save locations frequent enough to prevent frustration? I would say that it is alright, there are enough save points to not have to walk long distance over and over. However, the rest camps can be quite annoying as there are high chances to treat the player very unfairly by kidnapping a party member, poisoning the group, stealing the in-game currency. I get it, Lisa's world is harsh and it has to be painful for the player as well, but I would just load the save and try over and over until my party has been healed. And waste my time. Because I don't want to waste my time looking around for a kidnapped party member, or having to grind experience to upgrade a new one if the previous one decided to abandon me.
In Lisa, every design decision makes sense and has been well thought. The game could have been so horrible to play if the developer didn't know what he was doing! But as it is, playing is alright. Not fun, but with enough variety to push me to seek the next deviant scene I will encounter and yearn for more. And the music kicks♥♥♥♥♥ I do not know if I can recommend Lisa as I did not enjoy most of my time with it, but I still find it a good and interesting game with a lot of depth under its simple appearance.

The tagline of this game couldn't be more accurate.  LISA: The Painful RPG isn't afraid to delve into territories most consumers will likely be turned off by: childhood sexual abuse, drug addiction, lots of violence.  The journey of the main character, Brad, is a downward spiral into a world of pessimistic nihilism, where the motto "Anything that can go wrong, will go wrong" is an inescapable reality.
The story:
We're introduced to Brad Armstrong at a very young age; us waiting very little time before witnessing his abusive relationship with his father; the neglectful state of the home he lives in; and, of course, his little sister, Lisa.
Cut to many years later, soon after an unexplained event that killed off the female population -- the world has been driven into a sort of Fallout/Borderlands/Mad Max state of chaos, where societies have broken down into roaming, violent gangs.  This is the last age of humanity, as there is no way to reproduce, and very little hope for the world remains.
That is, until, Brad -- now aged and addicted to a drug called "joy" -- stumbles upon a baby in the middle of nowhere...  A baby girl.
And without knowing how she got there, or why, he takes it upon himself to raise her as his own, vowing to keep her identity a secret from the world, for fear that if she was ever discovered, she would be subjected to the same abuse he and his little sister were subjected to as children.
However, despite his careful attempts to conceal her gender, she is one day discovered and kidnapped.  And so Brad vows to undergo a dangerous journey to save her from a fate worse than death.
...
LISA is not a happy game, despite the plentiful amount of Borderlands/Fallout-style post-apocalyptic humor thrown in.  It is a game not only about sacrificing parts of Brad's body, but also his humanity; what little remains that makes him a good person -- all for a small, slim hope.
I have to say, the last thirty or so minutes of the game were so gutwrenching and expertly handled, I had to stop and just think for like ten minutes after the credits began to roll.  Seriously, it was masterful.
Gameplay:
LISA plays very much like a side-scrolling Earthbound, with unlockable attacks, different party members and first-person-style turned-based combat.  It's pretty fun, and provides a pretty decent challenge -- although sometimes the difficulty can spike when you least expect it, providing sort of an uneven curve.  Not a huge deal though.
The primary complaints I have are with the interface, especially when trying to use the shops.  For some reason, whenever I am looking at weapons I potentially want to buy, I am unable to compare them to anyone else but my immediate party.  Which means I have to leave the shop, run over to a gang sign, switch my party out, and then go back to the shop.  It's strange because this isn't an issue when I'm buying from an armor shop.  In addition, many pieces of equipment will affect multiple stats (like agility, luck, etc), but, when comparing your equipment in the shops, I am only able to see the attack comparison for weapons, and the defense comparison for armor.  So there are times when I have spent a ton of mags on an "upgrade" when the item is actually a downgrade, simply because I was unable to see all of the stat changes prior to my purchase.  I guess it's possible that I'm an idiot and am doing something horribly wrong, but, after almost 30 hours of playing, I'm decently confident that I've tried everything.
Overall, despite some of those aforementioned, minor complaints, LISA is a fantastic and criminally underrated game.
Oh, and the music is freaking awesome, too.
So go play it!
Final Verdict:
A solid 9/10.

This is one of the best RPGs in terms of interesting and memorable NPCs. Nearly every single person you meet has strong and unique personalities. Even an insignificant shopkeeper could be funny as hell. And when I say funny, I mean HILARIOUS - this game has some of the funniest lines I've ever seen in a game. I'd say it's worth the price just for the jokes (make sure you listen to all the radio programs). The writing of this game is simply brilliant. And the voice acting is SO GOOD I can't believe it's a game made in 2004. While the main story is mostly linear, and the choices in the game is relatively lacking, the game still has an excellent replayability and offers a great role-playing experience - the dialogs have lots of variations in details depending on your gender, race and previous actions, which really adds to the roleplay and makes the conversations feel more natural. Side quests are often more non-linear and open-ended than the main quests (although they are not Fallout level non-linear). They are really interesting quests too. Very few side quests are generic fetch quests. One thing that impressed me is that if you fail a quest (for example, by killing a quest NPC), the game actually tells you how you failed the quest and why it is failed in a seperate "failed quests" category of the quest log. I've tried killing quest NPC at different stages of a quest, and to my surprise, the game actually recognized the difference and had different discription on how the quest failed, even making sarcastic jokes on me since I failed it in such nonsensical ways. (You can't kill main quest NPCs though, which is understandable.)
The atmosphere of the game is fantastic. You really feel like being a vampire roaming the night streets of Los Angeles. The story is focused on the Kindred's secret society and its social structure, complicated politics and conspiracies. You will also meet other creatures of the night as well, and learn about their relationship with vampires. The lore of the game is fascinating. Learning about the various clans of Kindred and their unique traits and powers, the mythologies circulating in Kindred society, the different sects and their history, there are enough to keep you interested while not dumping too much information at the same time.
My main gripe about the game (after properly patched) is the inventory UI is cluncky and clumsy. There is not even an indication of how many items you can carry before your inventory is full. Speaking of which, this game does not have an equipment pannel, but you can collect talismans that you only need to keep in inventory to take effect, which I really like. It's strangely satisfying to look at all the little trinkets I've collected on me. Another complaint is that the stats system is a bit too complicated while not deep enough at the same time. There are too many stats, but a lot of them are not really very useful. Also there are some effects of attributes that do not really make sense to me (why would intellegence increase intimidation, and wits increase defense?). I don't know anything about the VtM pen&paper game. I feel the general idea of this stat system is perfect - there is "attributes" that represents your body's inherent capabilities, and there is "abilities" that represents your prowess in things you learn and practice, and it's the combination of these two that determines the number outcome of your various skills. I also like the idea that skill books and NPCs can only increase your abilities but not attributes, so sometimes you may want to save more XP to increase the latter, but attributes are more expensive to increase than abilities, so there is a trade-off here. In a word, I really like the general idea of the system, but the execution leaves a little more to be desired and ends up a little unbalanced. But again, sometimes it's the unbalance that brings fun. The old Fallouts was much more unbalanced than the newer ones, but there is a certain charm in the lack of balance.
As for the combat, I do not really have much complaint as a lot of people seem to do. Maybe it's because I play a Tremere and the blood magic is hella fun (at least for me). The stealth play is implemented pretty well too. There are active skills (called "disciplines") that is very helpful in stealth, like Trance in the Dominate discipline that incapacitates a guard for a period of time, while not making him feel anything suspicious happened to him when he wakes up. The brightness affects the odds of being seen a great deal when sneaking so you always want to stick to the shadows and turn off lights when possible. You can stealth kill enemies. You can distract guards by throwing things. The stealth in this game actually plays like a proper stealth game unlike most RPGs.
All in all, VtMB is truly a gem in the RPG genre. It's definitely worth picking up for any RPG fan.

As a huge fan of the VTM tabletop game, I'll admit, I was skeptical when I first bought this.  Sometimes adapting one media into another (be it book to movie, game to movie or, in this case, one type of game to another), it either loses something or gains WAY too much to be enjoyable to longtime fans of whatever the previous media was.  So, yeah, I had my doubts -- but let me tell you, they were entirely unfounded.  This has become one of my favorite (if not absolute favorite) RPGs of all time.  Not only does it stay true to the source, which was a big selling point for me, but it is so incredibly easy to become immersed in the world you're presented.  The atmosphere is wonderful, especially for an older game when creating those elements is a bit more limited than it is now; maybe it's just me, but while wandering around Santa Monica, L.A., and the rest, I definitely do get that feeling of 'city by night'.  Lots of memorable NPCs scattered about, and the combat system is..fair, I think.  A little wonky here and there, but for the most part, it's pretty smooth.  That your decisions/dialogue affect some aspects of gameplay is always a neat element, too,  and as an added bonus:  no sparkly, wussy vampires.  That goes along with 'staying true to the source', yes, but for anyone who can't help but roll their eyes upon seeing 'vampire', it's worth calling attention to this.
Really, I can only find two major downfalls for this game:  first and foremost would be the graphics.  While again, it is a beautiful game, especially for its age, it certainly could benefit from some better visuals, especially where player characters and NPCs are concerned.  This isn't super important to me or anything, as it doesn't take...well, anything, away from the game, but it is worth mentioning.  Second would be the fact that there is no fast travel while in a zone.  It DOES help with immersion, I'll admit, and it's not like the zones are HUGE, by any means, but sometimes it does seem tedious to have to run from point A to point B.
All in all, thought, this game is absolutely fantastic.  It's hardly perfect, but for anyone who enjoys RPGs, I cannot possibly recommend this one enough.  This is just one of those games where, every time someone mentions it, someone else will just HAVE to reinstall it.
It's just THAT good.

I'd like to preface this review the fact that I played with the Unofficial Patch v9.7, which, as far as I'm concerned, is how the game needs to be played. It was kneecapped by several issues during the development cycle and suffered severely as a result - the patch seeks to change that.
So, I was bored and wanted to see what all the fuss was about - "best RPG ever" and "nothing comes close" were words I saw tossed around a lot - it's said that whenever you mention "Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines" on the internet, someone reinstalls it. And after playing it, I'm hardly surprised.
As a game, it's not the most exciting - the combat is mediocre at best, though not unenjoyable. The stealth works, which is more than you can say for a lot of games nowadays. There are a few weapons available, but only a handful. You will have your favourites like your .50 Desert Eagle or your Dirty Harry hand cannon (albeit the .44 magnum in the game is a Colt Anaconda and not a S&W Model 29) as well as more original items like a crossbow and a fully automatic shotgun. The combat does become increasingly important as you progress through the game - do not underestimate that.
In terms of aesthetic, it was released in 2004, but with the patch's retexture, it's far from unbearable. If you can play vanilla Fallout 3/New Vegas, you won't mind the characters/modelling here. In fact, the facial expressions are the best I've seen in a game. It is dated, though. Throughout my playthrough, I had no bugs, texture glitches, physics glitches or crashes, though that probably makes me lucky (or Luckee) rather than the it making the game stable. The atmosphere the art style creates is amazing, as well as the music, which is the best soundtrack in a game I've heard, bar Mass Effect.
Where this game is virtually unparalleled is its top notch writing. Throughout the game, all 35 hours in a single playthrough, there was one 15 minute quest I did not enjoy as well as a brief period where the level design frustrated me to no end (anyone who's played will agree and probably knows what I'm talking about). This meant 2.86% of my playtime was not enjoyed whereas everything else was pretty much flawless. Like I said, the atmosphere is amazing. The writing is almost perfect: all of the characters are interesting, distinct and you want to know more about them. This game does not spoon feed you. There is no map, no marker, no detailed quest descriptions. It's just you. The story builds up in scale over time, and maintains its edge even after its explosive beginning. I still felt as invested in it at the end as at the beginning, if not more. The dialogue is always brilliant. It's made me laugh a lot, and the skill checks are a welcome sight in any game.
The actual role-playing elements are great. Doing harder tasks and more quests is rewarded with copious amounts of XP (and more importantly, $$$) and these can be spent on your clan abilities or your skills. Your clan can really affect your entire game. My first playthrough was as a Toreador (I say first because there will undoubtedly be a second), and that meant I really upped my speech skills. But those playing as a Nosferatu, good luck, no silver tongue will save that face, and if you're playing as a Malkavian, I wish you luck in understanding your speech options, let alone the other people. The options are entirely changed as a Malkavian, as a result of your inherent madness, and you'll be in for some great conversations (particularly with street signs). Nosferatu cannot blend into normal society because they look more like the product of an industrial meat grinder than a human being, so have to sneak and use tunnels. You also get bonus abilities depending on your clan. The way Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines handles introducing you to the World of Darkness format is exceptional, and you'll pick it up with no difficulty. The way you can play your own character and handle situations in your own way is second to none until the last hour and a half or so of the game. But this is negligible in what is otherwise an almost perfect game.
So, deliberate no longer. Buy this game. Play this game. I warn you, however, as nothing you play from thenceforth will truly live up to it.

TL;DR: A game making the point that you cannot make a game unless you devote a big chunk of your time to actually do it.

There, I spoiled it for you. But then again,
has very few actual gameplay features. It advertises that it's a game about
for a week. The problem is, it's not really a game about that. It's hardly a game at all.
The concept sounds awesome. What do you have to do to make it through the week as an indie developer, to push for that deadline? Maybe you'd have to make a timetable and try to manage your time between game development, designing, art work, writing, sound design and also free time and relaxing. Require the player to put that into the right order to come up with the game. Perhaps even require keeping your hunger, exhaustion and focus at bay. Throw in a couple of events you need to take into account, like a birthday party or some special holiday. Voilà! So how's the execution of that anticipation in this game?
It's poor. It's outright appalling. It's the bare bones of what I expected with fluff all over it. In the game, every day you have a choice of basically two options: either use the time for developing the game or goofing around.
There are eight kinds of goofing around. Choosing any shows you a video of the developer goofing around: e.g. playing with his cat, being at a party or playing poker with his friends, with no gameplay whatsoever. Then the night comes and you get to see videos of weird dreams. They are potentially epilepsy inducing with all the flashing lights. All in all, no games were developed that day.
I found these videos to be "artsy", in that bad way where you get bored and awkward and feel tempted to skip but cannot in case you miss something interesting. There's some angsty, varying music on the backgrounds of the videos. It varies from heavy metal to eerie ambience to some experimental stuff and unfortunately I liked none of it. At least every video grants you an achievement.
If you instead choose to develop your game, like you probably should, you get a taunty hint of how meager your attempt is and then get to play a tedious game of "developing". It's the same game every day, just more difficult and more tedious every time because of the horrible music and varying background that camouflages the game pieces you are trying to identify. A cringing sound plays in the background making the experience agonizing (it made me take off my headphones). That seems to be the whole point too: the game developer's life is hard and boring work.
I watched all the videos and played the game through to its two different endings ("bad" and "good" one) in 40 minutes and still have to idle it to get the trading cards if I care enough. It costs just 1 € so you don't lose much anything but time for it. Fortunately, its Store Page itself warns you not to take the game too seriously. My warning is this: it is
a game developing simulator. In fact, there's no game here to begin with.

Divide by Sheep is a nice logical game with elements of brutality towards animals.
Death was lonely. Who wouldn't be (I know thousands of people die every day. But really - people are boring)? So he decides to have some animals dead to have some friends.
Players goal is to deliver exact amount of animals (Sheeps, Wolves or Pigs) to the raft. To do it, player has to move groups of animals between islands, increasing or decreasing (mostly by drowning) groups to make them fit into the raft. There are many types of islands, eg. ones that swap places of groups without them killing each other, there are lasers that work only on sheeps - they cut them in half, so you need two squares per helf of the sheep, and you need to deliver any 2 parts of the sheep to the raft. There are few more blocks, but these are just examples.
Each animal have different relationship towards the others - Wolves eat sheep, pigs always kick their groups amount of animals from the island they land on and so on.
Later in game there are more raft types; not only you have to deliver few animal types, but you have also ones that require you to kill specified amount of any animal, or deliver exact amount of any animals to the giant squid.
Overally, this is a good game. Sure it gets hard sometines, but that's the charm of all logical games. With 150 levels aviable, it's a lot you get for 5 euro.

Normally the idea of a "1st person platformer" should fill most gamers with horror, but A Story About My Uncle manages to make it not as unpleasant as it sounds. But it's still not good.
The Gameplay is simple: Think 1st Person Bionic Commando. You will Jump from platform to platform, using a grappling hook to swing or catapult you onto various floating platforms to progress through the level. You are resctricted to using the grapple once, twice, or thrice as you progress. And... that's it. You gain an ability to , for lack of a better word, "double jump" as well but it only adds just a little more to the experience.
This sort of mechanic can be fun, but not in the challenges they've constructed. This is the kind of thing I can see working well in an open world style game, like some of the older Spiderman games. But alone it gets repetetive. They try to keep things interesting by changing scenery, adding moving obstacles, but you're still just jumping from platform to platform. There are only rare moments where combining a series of swings and mid air jumps has that satisfying "Nailed it!" feeling.
It's not particularly challenging, and it is challenging it does so in an unfair way. For example, some surfaces you can grapple, and some you can't. The graphical quality is so poor, and environments so dark you'll have a hard time guessing what you can latch on to and what you can't. Later in the game you'll be able to "recharge" your grapple mid air by clicking on Blue Crystals. But the hit box is so narrow you'll miss clicking it completely and plunge to yorur death as you accidentally use your last grapple charge on a piece of rock (you need at least one charge to recharge oddly enough).
One of the most frustrating parts is when your grapple is just out of range of your intended target and you will frantically click on the surface in question so you can just grab it before it falls away from you again, only to find you've quickly expended 2-3 charges on one surface.
Understandably some of the above are 'skill based' problems. That maybe so, but it's also not very fun.
Graphically the game is something roughly equivalent to Xbox and Xbox 360 hardware. It's very dated with lots of polyons. Environments generally features lots of contrast, but are also too dark even on recommended brightness setting.
There is some kind of story here, but it's really all a McGuffin. The whole idea of the game is you're chasing afer your Uncle? Why? It's not really explained. The narrator's blasse tone has all the suspense of an airport announcer.
With 3 strikes in gameplay, story, and presentation I can't recommend this game enough.

If that is the case and your goal is to collect achievements over game play, then be wary purchasing and playing this game. The story is humorous and slightly dark, the puzzles are fun, it is a good length and it has the simple art style that initially attracted me to the first game. In fact the graphics are slightly more polished. The control system is slightly more streamlined as well. One thing that did disappoint me was that despite being called Edna and Harvey, they have been demoted to supporting cast. The eccentric humour of Edna had Harvey have has been replaced by Lilly a small girl who says pretty much nothing and the fairly deadpan humour of the narrator. The game is still funny just different. Another disappointment was the achievements. The first game's achievements made you explore more of the game but the achievements here are for repeatedly clicking arbitrary things. These are fairly minor complaints, this is overall a very good point and click adventure.

Edna & Harvey: Harvey's New Eyes is a mildly dark and twisted point & click adventure that feels a lot like Sam & Max style adventure games. Interestingly enough, you don't play as either Edna or Harvey, instead playing the role of the young innocent schoolgirl, Lilli. But Lilli doesn't speak too much, and most of her dialog is filled by a narrator that loves to hear himself talk. Even though his voice acting is good, he all too often comes off as being melodramatic when it usually isn't necessary. The result is a game that tries to be funny all of the time, but only succeeds some of the time. The narrator makes every effort to lighten the mood, but his delivery is often dry and humorless and the intended humor often can't compete with the game's dark themes.
The puzzles were pretty straightforward. There were only a handful of places where it wasn't obvious what the next move was. Graphical drawings are nicely done and the story is well written.
Steam achievements are broken. I finished the entire game without a single achievement unlocking.
Overall, Harvey's New Eyes is a reasonably well done point & click adventure that doesn't leave any lasting impressions.

A fun, but repetitive game, that will quickly grow old.
The game is essentially a roguelike 'lite', as there actually isn't much randomization when you get down to it. A handful of terrain types, a handful of dungeon layouts, a handful of enemy types. After a few playthroughs, you'll have seen everything in the game, so it's only a question of what order you'll encounter them.
Many of the perks are of miniscule use at best, such as improving your swimming skill. The classes generally aren't too different from each other in practice, outside of their own gimmick. The Force User, for example, can learn spells at any time by exchanging levels. But most of the spells aren't worth the cost, so you'll find yourself using your basic attack spell while saving up experience. Since most skills have a significant cost restriction, you'll find yourself using basic attacks and relying on position for most of the game, rather than unique skills.
That being said, for $4, you're getting your money's worth. A few hours of fun, maybe more if you really want to stretch the challenge, and it is very fun for those few hours. It might be a game that you enjoy for an afternoon, then forget about for a few months, only to come back and enjoy it again. Maybe it'll be a game you only enjoy for a day, even if you never play it again. All in all, worth checking out if it appeals to you, but don't expect it to be exceptionally memorable.

This is by the far the best single vampire game in existence.
There have been countless vampire games through the years.  Some focus on the monster, some focus on the romance,  Most you don't particularly have to think about all the consequences of becoming one.  This game will immerse you in a seductive and dangerous world of vampirism the likes of which has not been replicated to this degree in a game.  And when I say you, I mean you.  It is a deeply personal affair in which you can take a personal journey or a journey of any character you wish, with whatever depth you wish.
Do you want to be the outcasts of society?  Do you want to be the Hollywood monster that people avert their gaze from?  Do you want to be the Anne Rice version of a vampire?  Smart, seductive, ruthless.  Do you want to be utterly insane?  So many ways to make yourself your own, so many ways to interact with the myriad of story lines in the dark, urban nightlife of Cali.
The music is also phenomenal.  Utterly fantastic.  The soundtrack feels dark and gritty while you're wandering the streets, diving in sewers and popping in night clubs seducing and making your way.
Modding is REQUIRED.  I say again, R E Q U I R E D.  Don't think about playing this without extensive research on the must have mods.  The story of this title is infamous, go read if you want to know why it requires so much rework and how passionate this community around it is.  I did the unofficial patch and a few graphic overall mods myself, your mileage may vary.
Writing this review makes me want to install it again and play...
If you have any interest of vampires whatsoever, pick it up!

The atmosphere is dark, seedy, erotic, and exactly what I wanted from a game about vampires.
The story is excellent, detailing the embrace and subsequent activities and moral quandaries of a fledgling vampire. There are seven vampire Clans that you can choose from, each rich with lore and personality. Speaking of which, the characters are unforgettable, ranging from chillingly inhuman to warm and charismatic. The voice acting is sublime, making this one of the few games where I don't skip through characters' dialogue after having heard it thousands of times through my numerous playthroughs.
Of course, this is a 2004 game that is full of bugs and other issues. But, the Unofficial Patch by Wesp takes care of most of these and makes the game the experience it should be.
I technically play 4 different versions of this game, hence my relatively low playtime of, at the time of this review, 80 hours (Steam only records the vanilla game's playtime) I've put 80 hours into vanilla game (with the unofficial patch). I also play the Clan Quest Mod version, the Antitribu Mod, and The Final Nights Mod. Each of these versions makes it into a different enough experience that replayablility isn't an issue. New Clans, disciplines, characters, enemies, environments, bosses, mechanics, etc. I would complete at least one playthrough of the vanilla game before playing the mods, in order to highlight the differences and make for a more interesting experience.
If ever you've been a fan of vampire literature, or really any medium involving vampires, I consider this game a must-play.

This is a really interesting RPG, so I'll just start off by listing some of the aspects of the game that liked and disliked. The dialogue choices and writing are superb, and you could just go on and on listening to what NPC's have to say. I really liked the different choices available throughout the game and the various ways that you could complete quests. The setting and lore was what really kept me hooked. It really made the atmosphere feel great. The gameplay as whole was good, but I felt that the combat was clunky. Fighting enemies ranged from somewhat fun to frustrating. It's really just mashing left click and popping your magic on every now and then. Stealth is also broken, and you can really cheese enemies this way. In addition, the game seems to be rushed towards then end, and your character build starts to matter less since you're forced into stealth or fighting sequences. With that said, I would HIGHLY recommend installing the unofficial patch. It restores a lot of the content missing from the game and fixes numerous bugs. With the patch installed, VtM:B is an excellent game that you will enjoy from beginning to end. Multiple playthroughs are definitely worth it since each clan plays very differently and there are many ways to do quests. Buy it when you get the chance.

the graphics are quite solid,

Ignore all positive reviews for this game. The devs have clearly given up with no patches coming out for 3 whole years.  The game resembles a WW2 strategy/management game, but has more in common with a tower defense game. Firstly, you get a factory to build either: A) Spitfires and Hurricanes, B) Airfields, C) RADAR, D) Other Factories, and E) AA Guns. Thats it. You place the building wherever you want, intercept German bombers with the fighters, get taxes from cities that haven't been bombed by the Germans to supply the factory(ies) to build more resources in a game that becomes bland and unfun in LESS THAN 2 HOURS. The combat is just awful. In real life, the Brits employed a tactic called 'The Big Wing' where a massive amount of British planes flew together to compensate for the overwealming German numbers. In this game, you get a max of 8 planes who can face up to 20 German bombers AND fighters. Bombers have this weird attack, going head-on with your fighters, which cripple your own, but the bomber comes out just fine, with it's one machine gun destroying your plane while your eight seem to have no effect. A dogfight in this game is just 2 fighters flying in a circle trying to shoot each-other. Thats it. Often, your pilots get shot down, and you need to babysit the 'Bail Out' button, because you have less than a second to bail one or more of your pilots out, or else they die. They simply cannot bail out themselves, for reasons unknown, so you need to stare intently on the list of pilots you have, waiting for that red button to appear. The game has no sense of actual skill involved, so you start using your precious planes like how the Russians did because that seems to be the only tactic to work, rushing them.
Theres only one good thing to come out of the game, and it isnt even a part of the gameplay itself, its the awesome, rare background for your steam profile, which I use alot and will continue to do so because the artstyle rocks.
But in conclusion, this game sucks, horrendously. It isn't even worth 3 bucks to be honest, and I can't understand why people preach of how good this game is. It's on the bottom of the steam store for a reason, and it should stay that way.

has received a LOT of negative comment since its release on April 1st (ahum) of this year. The description on the Steam Store page explicitly asks not to take it too seriously, and so people have mostly jumped in expecting some fun and entertainment. Which the game ... does not provide.
At its core, this is a (slightly) interactive story, which "teaches" the player how to succeed or - more likely - fail at becoming a developer of Indie games. During one week you're every morning presented with a choice: to work on your game, or rather do something else. If you work on the game enough, and you succeed at the fairly stupid but not that easy clicker-mini-game, then you finish a game and it may be published. Goal accomplished.
If you choose to other things, you're presented with one out of eight different full-motion video's, which feel like being directed by a decent amateur cinematograph (or first-year student) and are shot in Russia. They contain some nice images, but are mostly unsettling in their vagueness. There's no interaction at all in this part of the game: you just watch and wait (or skip and proceed to the next day, quickly getting all the achievements, but that would completely beside the point).
Now, based on these all-too-meagre contents, it could be a straightforward affair, and I could dismiss this little "game" as  an utter failure. But the game has stirred something inside me while playing, something I've been thinking about. Maybe there is a "deeper" meaning to it, such as: if you do what you're expected to do (working every day on your project, in order to succeed), life is boring as hell. Which, to me, makes sense, and not at the same time. It all depends if you can put something of yourself, of your dreams maybe, into your work. But if you choose not to focus, and to do whatever you feel like doing on a given day, life becomes unsettled, even upsetting. That's where the nightmares come in: every night, there's a short but disturbing dream. Nothing spooky or horror-like, no, just unsettling. It's difficult to describe it so I suggest you just pay the dollar or euro, and go and watch (play) this.
Try to do it with an open mind, not expecting some quick fun, and maybe you'll get the same feeling as I had: that this game wants to tell us something, about life, about dreams; surely in a clumsy and unpolished way, but stll: I feel there is more to it than just "a game not to be taken seriously".
