I'm very fond of HSL, so I wish I could recommend this game more highly. Its appealingly nostalgic looking, fairly accessible, and charmingly simple - cutting back on a lot of roguelike conventions without losing the main idea. Looting and getting stronger is predictably addictive.
Unfortunately it still feels unpolished and balanced poorly, and the worst offender is the fact that there are just relatively few meaningful actions for the player to consider and take throughout a playthrough. Questions a player faces are two: whether or not to engage, or whether or not to equip - and the answers to those questions are often strikingly obvious. I also haven't found a single practical reason yet to focus on melee over ranged weaponry. That fact combined with a relatively common boost makes the experience very simple to game.
In some was HSL feels like an iOS casual game, with a veneer of hardcore trappings, minus the in-app purchases. But I am fond of it, and will keep playing a bit.

There are two major features that differ from typical rogeulikes in HSL.
First, the usual character progression and management is absent.  No experience or levels are gained, your power relies entirely on gear and enchantments.
Second, instead of one or more large, random dungeons, HSL offers several themed quests with varying environments and dangers.  It's like a "puzzle roguelike," since they feel different and benefit from different tactics.
Character progression relies a bit too much on chance, and many attempts end quickly when I spawn surrounded by enemies or just can't find any good loot.  It can be frustrating, but it's fun if you stick with it.

I was rather surprised by the relatively high number of negative reviews for a game I find so fun, so I thought I'd add my two cents:
This game is a rather unforgiving but fun look at the Battle of Britain. First I'll look at the pros and cons, and then I'll give some tips that I've found helpful to ease the pain in the beginning of the game, because if you screw up in the beginning it can make the game pretty much impossible going forward.
Pros:
-The strategic and tactical gameplay are both challenging, but fun. On the strategic level, you can manage war production, which includes buying airfields, AA guns, factories, radar towers, airplanes, and the pilots. The money you earn is enough to buy the necessities for defense, but not enough to make the game easy. You're always having to prioritize, which I find fun and rewarding when done right. Even when done wrong, defeat never feels cheap, and you always feel as if it was more of a learning experience than a punishment.
-The tactical gameplay is mosty fun (the parts that weren't so fun will be in the cons), and, for me at least, I never get tired of downing Jerries. Call me odd, but it gives me a strange sense of satisfaction when I shoot down German bombers, as if I'm saving the lives of actual civilians.
-The stats are set up in a helpful way, helping you to keep track of your most experienced squadrons and even most experienced single pilots. This can be crucial. After all, if a huge stack of fighters and bombers is approaching, do you want to send out your veterans or untried rookies? On the other hand, you can send rookie squadrons to take out small stacks of enemies, giving them relatively easy experience points.
Cons:
-Certain elements of tactical combat can be frustrating. In particular, a high amount of micromanaging is required. This is normally not so bad, since you only control 8 fighters at a time. But when your fighters are engaged in a sprawling dogfight with enemy fighters, your own fighters are often slow to react without your direct intervention. This can lead to several of your fighters being shot down in a row before you have time to react, which is incredibly frustrating. Also, when they're tangled up in a dogfight, your own fighters and the German fighters look very similar, which adds an unnecessary layer of difficulty to fights.
-When your fighters get to a certain level of health, they're given the option to parachute. But the health requirement for this is very low, so low that you'll often have less than a second to react before the airplane is destroyed and the pilot killed. Fortunately, you have the option to pause the combat at any time, but given how fast the planes can be destroyed, you have to have some good reflexes on that pause button.
-On the strategic level, if you are on the ropes and German airplanes are pouring over the countryside, you're pretty much done for, since the bombers will almost always target your airfields. This can be frustrating since the bombers can destroy your planes faster than you can get them in the air, which wastes a lot of money and is just plain not fun. Even strafing runs by fighters can take out most of your planes and pilots on the ground.
Overall, even though this game isn't perfect, it's still a tense, rewarding, and very fun rendition of the Battle of Britain. For 8 dollars, I definitely recommend it.
Tips:
-Always make sure to have at least two squadrons, and have at least one of them on the ground while the others are in the air. You might feel inclined to get as many fighters as you can airborne to patrol, and in the very earliest stages you can usually get away with this. However, if all of your squadrons are in the air at one time, then this means that they'll all be refuelling at the same time as well. So if bombers suddenly come to your airfields while you're refuelling, you may not get your fighters airborne in time to prevent them from being destroyed on the ground. So always have at least one squadron on standby to respond to threats like this.
-Your fighters' guns have a longer range than the rear gunners on bombers, so feel free to attack them from behind, as long as you turn away before you get in range of the rear gunners. This can get you some easy experience points for rookies, assuming you've dealt with the enemy fighters first.
-Get enough radar stations to monitor the southern English coast, but not so many that they overlap. This will allow you to wait to launch your planes until the enemy is actually coming without costing you too much money. What else should you spend that money on, you ask? Well, I'll tell you:
-Buy plenty of AA guns. These can weaken tough units, and enemies will also try to fly around AA guns if they can, making their movements more predictable. Also, AA guns can actualy shoot down whole stacks of enemy fighters, letting the game deal with one of the most frustrating enemies so you don't have to.
I'm sure there are other things you'll learn along the way, but I think the tips above will help ease you into the game withouth too much frustration. But still, some things can't be taught and have to be experienced. Or maybe I'm just feeling too lazy to keep typing. In any case, I hope more people will give this game a chance, and if my review convinces someone on the fence to do just that, then I'll be content.

If Earthbound was reading a love-letter to childhood while realizing the darker details, then LISA the Painful curbstomps your childhood amidst laughter and a world with little remorse.The Painful will put you into a juxtaposition of emotions: Depression, laughter, guilt, fear and emptiness. It manages all its mature themes with a dark, quirky sense of humor.
As well as telling a good story, the game also learns from its inspiration, Earthbound, on how to not be a boring JRPG.
If you think this game will be a grindfest with plenty of Phoenix Downs and a non-interactive battle-system, you are mistaken. The Painful goes against many old RPGs.
For starters, your experience is shaped by misfortunes you can and cannot control. Party members can be taken away (sometimes permanently) as well as your items (dirty mags, the currency, and equipment items and other loot) and your abilities. Second, there is also a heavy incentive against grinding. There are a limited amount of bosses/enemies on the overworld. The areas that have random encounters, either in the dark or in the tall grass, yield almost no items or experience.
The only way you're going to beat this game is toughen up, smarten' up with your team, and, with a little luck and foresight, you will make do however you can.
In battle, some characters have a combo attack system to keep you engaged like the protagonist, Brad Armstrong. The way it works is you can chain together attacks (freestyle mode) to do a special attack. Or you can do the special attack.  The benefit is that by working your way up you'll do more damage, and the special attack is a finisher. All combos can be viewed in battle, so you don't need to memorize them.
Only a handful of the 30 party members use this system to not wear its novelty far too soon. Each character's also posseses their own strengths and weaknesses. For example, making a party that are all addicted to Joy (a sparse drug; not too infrequent) can be a hassle when all your characters suffer withdrawal. If you give them Joy, they do critical damage for several turns before they have another withdrawl.
One last and very important distinction for an RPG: The choices are just as brutal as the story and gameplay. There is no "right answer." Sacrifices will be made and those decisions will fall on you.
In short, this game does not screw around, and neither should you. Yet you can still have fun!
As mentioned before, the combo system keeps you engaged in the gameplay. Another reason for enduring LISA's psychological masochism is the world Olathe. It uses both exploration and the dark humor to keep your spirts up.
Unlike most RPG Maker games, the game is a 2D world that feels as complex as a 3D world. Each Area, which there are four total (3 you can revisit anytime; one point of no return), is a laybrinthlike puzzle. It works because secrets, items and even hidden party members can be found by exploration.
Also, because there is little to no random-encounters, you have more time to explore the overworld, which can yield to some secret stashes or minibosses for XP. You will have more fun for less grinding.
Not only is exploring the world a joy, the world is the most interesting character. The creator came up with the world through asking himself, "What would a world of burly dudes be like with no women?" The answer to that question touches on the biological necessity for men to be needed and their alternatives (cross-dressing and gay sex, suicide, violence, drugs, nostalgia.)
The humor, in my interpretation, adds commentary on men's issues by how often they are belittled or laughed at. I won't say it's the game's intentions, but the game can make you think about the topic. Scenes like the prostitution one, which is played for laughs, might have a different emotional effect on you.
The personalities you find and dialogue are very failthful to the deadpan humor of Earthbound. However, it's only when you combine every character, their plights and quirks, with Olathe do you really find the real starring character, the world itself.
I won't say the cast of characters (Brad, the NPCs and your party) are underdeveloped. They're more comedic tropes given one personality to play. Everyone is given a cliche name for achievements: The American Guy, The Rooster Guy, The Drunk Guy.
Brad's story also doesn't set anything new for a redemption story. However, the emphasis on your choices through the gameplay does make the story something special. For example, if you can go through the game with no Joy for Brad, you'll unlock a secret ending.
Despite my glowing praise, I do have some nitpicks.
As with many RPG Maker games, there are technical problems. There is a Q&A forum for some useful fixes that try to solve everything. I can't really fault the devs as they have been adamant on resolving these issues; t's more of a fault with RPG Maker itself. Rebindable keys/joystick are also available, which I would recommend playing with a directional-pad or keyboard. You will fall off ledges less with more precise controls.
However, my biggest grievance is that enemies do not have a visible life-bar. Unless you have played the game, some enemies will have larger health-bars than you would think. Not having that vital information doesn't add challenge. It adds to needless deaths, then replaying cutscenes with no skip option.
And as far as being able to cheat at the game, I think it's fixed by the one-use save points for Pain Mode. It's time-consuming to save-scum for perfection, but you can lessen the challenge as an optional alternative. Permadeath, as much as it may instill fear into players, is so scarce and unimportant towards the ending that if it ever happens you shouldn't feel disheartened. Only a handlful of enemies that can kill your party members, most of the time they're optional bosses. If you lose all your HP in normal battles you just faint like usual.
In the end, you'll probably find that having 30 characters, admittedly with a lot of similarities to each other in their combat styles, is far too much to manage. I would say that a huge cast offers some replay value but you can mitigate a lot of bad decisions with your party by replaying the game knowing what to expect.
Lastly, I don't think the reward for going out of your way to beat the game with zero Joy on the hardest setting is worth the effort. The cutscene/voice-overs become addressed in the sequel/expansion, the Joyful.
None of these issues ruin this masterpiece. The Painful RPG sets out to leave you smiling while walking a bloody trail of tears, asking yourself, "Why?" The only question you should ask your friends who haven't played is, "Why haven't you played this already?"

"Mafia 2" is the sequel to the (mostly) unkown "Mafia: The City of Lost Heaven". It's a third-person shooter sandbox game. But, at the same time, it isn't.
Unlike the "Grand Theft Auto"s or the "Saints Row"s, "Mafia 2" has a strong focus on storytelling: you play as a WW2 veteran who comes back to his home in Empire Bay, and starts his journey inside the italian mob, trying to reach the top. The story is brilliantly written, and strongly resembles movies like "The Godfather" and "Goodfellas" in the best way possible.
At the beginning of each chapter, you wake up, answer the telephone, get dressed, and go where you have to go. So, the only moment when you are free is when you've left the house, before going where you have to go. However, there isn't that much to do in the city. There were going to be side missions, but they were left out to focus more on the story, and it shows. You can drink at bars, buy guns and clothes or go on a mindless rampage where you rob every store.
The songs on the radio are all great (but that's cause I like this era) and the gunplay feels really good, with pistols, rifles, shotguns, grenades, molotovs but no melee weapons.
Overall, this is a great game for storytelling and atmosphere, but it lacks in the sandbox department. For an experience more similar to GTA, you should buy the DLCs Jimmy Vendetta's or Joe's Adventure.

I bought this game on sale for $0.87, and I feel a little bad for doing so because this game is worth much more than its full price.
One Way Heroics is, as you probably already know, a scrolling roguelike in which if you get stuck in the darkness, it's game over.
I can't speak much to the mechanics here - they are standard roguelike mechanics and, while there are a few imaginative additions (pills of teleportation, buddy tablets, etc), the game plays essentially like the standard roguelike. The gameplay is solid, and outperforms many other well-recognized roguelikes, but doesn't attempt to re-invent the genre.
The charm of the game is in how well it is built. I enjoy the music and the look and feel of the world, as well as the characters (most of whom only have a few lines of dialogue). The world feels varied and interesting thanks to a variety of enemies and enemy modifiers, multiple area types (such as mountainous regions that force careful movement planning or deserts that drain energy), and NPC encounters. The fact that the game will generate a world based on an alphanumeric codeword is also a plus, since it can make every run different.
To sum up: Aside from the scrolling mechanic, the game doesn't do anything new or different. But it doesn't really have to. It's well put-together, carries its own brand of charm, and it's definitely worth the $3 pricetag.

Being a big fan of Anime, turn based RPG's and rogue-like games, I was very curious with One Way Heroics, having an accessible price, I decided to risk buying it and check it out, truth be told I would never thought I'd love this game so much as I do, it completely caught me by surprise.
The mechanics are quite simple, you're forced to go eastwards in an 8 character string world (that is randomly generated each play-through) in order to avoid a mysterious mist that is covering the planet.
Each decision you take being a dialogue option, attacking, defending, healing, equipping and so on, will be counted as a turn, each turn you do the mist will also do his in parallel so you'll have to make sure to not fall behind or your play-through will be over, so you'll have to have special attention to which decisions or paths you should take, sometimes you'll feel compelled to explore a dungeon and find new items but the mist can prove to be too risky since you'll always have that constant threat looming next to you.
You have different ways of ending one play-through depending of the difficulty and the game mode you're playing, you can achieve victory by killing the demon king, by reaching the end of the world, by killing a secret boss and so on, in order to spice it up the developers decided to make some random events, cities and quests to make the game more interesting and more unique in each play-through.
The game UI is quite simple and it does well its job, the game soundtracks are fun and memorable but they can get a bit repetitive after a while, the art style ain't phenomenal by any means but overall it has an interesting and unique presentation to it.
The game is very affordable and full of content, it has great replay value, so I'd like to recommend to all of you who is thinking about getting this underrated gem, you'll love it!

TL;DR: This is a good game, defenitely recommend it! Does however require the expansion factions to play for a longer time, so buy it on sale or from a third-party seller.
So I come hear from time to time and read the reviews, and later on this game has gotten a lot of hate. Some is justified, such as the extensive DLC spam from the creators, some is debatable as whether the new loot system is good or bad, and other matters likely comes from individual experiences and cannot be said for the entire community.
So, is this a good game? Yes, yes it is. If we start looking purely at gameplay, I would say that this game is top-tier, or very very close.
1.The graphics are good, for a 2013 game. If you come from some game released this year and expect the graphics to be on the same level, I cant promise that you will be satisfied. It is an improvement from COH1 I think. What stunned me when I started playing was the details of the game. You can zoom in really really far and observe the details closer which I really liked. However, the game requires a heavy computer and will warn you if it doesn't meet the standards for a good experience. The camera is also adjustable, meaning you can play the game like you would play chess, or you can go for an FPS-ish view. I haven't found that option in any other game yet.
2. The sound effects are really good (Some of them even makes you waste and ability just to hear the sound of it), and the voices for your units are really good and sometimes quite funny, and I believe they capture the mood of a common soldier fairly good. They are made with empathy, which makes the game immersive. The sound is also changing to how close you are to battle, meaning that you only will hear a distant thunder if your camera is on the other side of the map of the battle, and break your ears if your camera is centered on it.
3. The environment is adaptable (?) meaning that you can for instance blow hole through iced lakes or mow down trees with your tanks (not all,mind you) and so on. This has led to some spectacular surprise attacks. The original maps are kinda dull when you've played them for a while, but then the awesome community comes with hundreds upon hundreds of new  and creative maps from the workshop. The best thing with this is that Relic actually promotes this by adding recommendations of maps in the main menu, and posting about it on their facebook page, and actually adding user created content to multiplayer (When you search for a game, you can also play on maps other than the ones Relic made). This is what makes the game replayable IMO.
4. The factions are good and fairly balanced in my opinion, and they let you explore your type of playstyle with fair historic accuracy. If you want to blitzkrieg your opponents down, play the Germans. If you want to flood your opponents with human waves, play the Soviets. If you want to fortify positions and destroy your enemy with artillery, play the British ,etc. It comes down to you. The commanders and their abilities add to this, and let you further decide your playstyle. Before each game starts you can pick 3 commanders, each with 6 (I think) abilities that decides your style of play. When the game starts you can only choose 1 of these, thus setting you up with this specific commanders abilities. This is a very good way of ensuring unique games for you. However, for this game to be enjoyed for a much longer time you will have to buy the DLC factions Britan, Germany 2 and USA. They are worth the money on sales, maybe a little pricey without. I recommend you to buy the basegame first and then see if you like the game enough and buy the other factions.
5. The campaign and missions are something more on the side that you get for free, with additional purchases available. The campaign has an okay story where you play through the eyes of a Soviet officer in Gulag as he tells his war stories to his former superior officer, and each chapter lets you live through these stories. Its quite interesting, with a tad of plot-twist at the end. Don't count on it, however. The side missions (theatre of wars) are okay too, a thing to pass your time if you're bored I suppose. Dont count on them either.
(6). The war spoils, or loot system, is a way for you to get skins, commanders etc. without paying for it, only by playing the game. Up until some time ago, this was entirely random and there was a drop chance for each game you finished. This was good, but it wasnt frequent enough for (at least) me to care. So they introduced a new system where you get points for each game finished, up to a cap. When you reach that point you get a free drop. Some players hate this, because the game turns into a "grind-fest", some like it because more free stuff. I don't really mind it, I play because the game is fun.
Now, I dont think anyone wholeheartedly disagrees with me, so time to adress the issues. Relic is somewhere between EA and Paradox, or at least they were. The prices are a bit too high for a 2013 game and there is a tad too many DLC's and expansions. The game also became a bit of pay-to-win as those who would pay money for better commanders would have a bigger chance of winning as their abilities was generally better (It is however a skill game and the best player usually wins). I did, for the record, not see many people who paid for more commanders. Also, some players complain over the main menu where they promote the DLC's, wanting you to buy them. I never heeded this, let alone did I get annoyed by it. But they do not only promote their DLC's, but also the user-created maps, guides and most recently, streams on Twitch. This I like really much. During the recent half year or so, I really feel that Relic took on all the complaints and improved the game. There hasnt been an overpriced expansion since September 2015, and even that one is'nt so soul-crushingly expensive. I bought it, and I loved it. The only expansion I can say is not even near worth it is the Ardennes Assault, read the reviews there for more information. Furthermore, Relic is, in recent time,a really good developer. They care, as said, for their community by promoting user-created content and hosting tournaments with live commentary on Twitch, etc.
So, to end it all, if you're reading this on a sale, buy it. If you like RTS you like this game.

CoH2 is a WW2-era RTS game focused on small-scale skirmishes rather than battles with hundreds and thousands of soldiers. It is a deeply tactical game, where good positioning and a good mix of troops is more important than building the perfect economy or rushing out at your opponent as soon as you can. A normal skirmish or mp match will start with you sending out some basic infantry and trying to conquer territory points, which then generate resources for better units. Depending on your faction, there is a little base building to do, but it never gets more complicated than just unlocking the next building and placing one in your command territory. CoH2 offers a nice variety of units ranging from normal and elite infantry to light vehicles, field guns and tanks. The different factions vary in their play style, for example: where the Soviets are good at swarming and hitting the enemy early, they lack elite units and their heavy artillery is not really precise (though devastating) - and their tanks are heavy and well armed but really slow. The CW and OKW are good at defending, OKW is strong in early game because of fast access to light vehicles, CW more in the late game when they have their heavy tanks, etc.
To get used to the game and learn how to control your units you can play the campaign (which is well done and tells some nice war stories, but does not reach the quality of a Blizzard RTS campaign) and some matches against the AI. The game's focus however is on multiplayer, and it does a good job there, the balancing is okay (there is always something to improve with balancing in every game :D), matches range from quick and action-packed skirmishes to long lasting materiel battles, and each one plays different. In direct comparison to the first installment of the series, CoH2 improves on gameplay with their sightlines and cold mechanics as well as AI, while inheriting a lot of CoH1's strengths and weaknesses, pathfinding to be named as example for the­ latter.
Beyond the basic game, CoH2 offers a lot of customization in almost all aspects of the game, with maps, commanders (~CoH1 doctrines), unit buffs, individual skins and designs - some of which can be found on the workshop or earned through playing the game - and of course gameplay mods, which are also supported by the workshop and add a lof of fun to an already good game. One thing that really disappoints though is SEGA's dlc policy - buying a game only to be greeted by the newest items on the in-game (real currency) shop on the main menu and realizing that if you really want to play the full game, at least buying the army packs for US, CW and OKW is almost mandatory is frustrating and really bad style imho.
Tl;dr: If you liked CoH1, you will like CoH2 even more - if you played BKMod or sth. similar in CoH1, you will want to play CoH2 with Wikinger or Realism Mod. If you're into RTS games in general, CoH2 offers many hours of thrilling sp and mp gameplay to you. BUT: Do NOT buy for normal price. Wait for a sale. Do NOT support this f2p-microtransaction-bs in a normal priced AAA-game.

I have waited a decade and change to play this game. I still have an ancient Bradygames walkthrough guide along with written notes in it to deal with each clan character. But in the end, perhaps it was a blessing in disguise to wait this long, where I can now play the game with all the bugs fixed. Due to that, I can say, without a doubt, that Bloodlines is one of the most underrated, underappreciated RPGs you have never heard of.
Your beginning is straightforward enough. In Los Angeles, you are changed into a vampire against your will, which♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥the local vampiric powers-that-be enough to kill them outright. You, on the other hand, are spared with the understanding that you will contribute to Kindred (as these vampires call themselves) society or else. From there, it becomes a tangled web of politics, competing agendas and choices that are eventually going to♥♥♥♥♥♥SOMEBODY off enough to take a shot at you.
Prior to this intro, you get to create your character from scratch with the aid of a simplified but true-to-the-source White Wolf character sheet. Picking one of seven clans will likely have the biggest effect on your gameplay, as each has their own unique strengths and weaknesses. After that, though, anything goes. Just be careful to note violate the Masquerade (an honor system where you do nothing too stupid too often to tip off the mortal herd that vampires are real) and you can be whatever kind of character you want: brawler, socialite, hacker, thief, assassin, gunfighter. Just always account for the fact that sooner or later, you're going to have to fight and you'll find unique playthroughs each time you pick a different clan.
One other important note: getting the latest fan-made patch for this game (9.7 at the time of this writing) is an absolute MUST or you're going to have the dubious joys of running into all those bugs the original game came with. But with that accomplished, have fun!

Divide by Sheep is (perhaps surprisingly) fun, even if math isn't your strongest suit. It is, at its core, a puzzle/logic game. Don't let the mathiness intimidate you, if you are wont to be intimidated by mathiness. Players are able to engage in unlimited trial and error to sort out each level, as needed. Nevertheless, there have been 2 times (so far) that I've resorted to YouTube'ing a level to complete it (that's 2xs out of 100+?). So, in my opinion, Divide by Sheep is well balanced; the difficulty increases at an acceptable, steady rate which maximizes fun and minimizes frustration.
It *does* get a little repetitive at times, but Divide by Sheep is the sort of game that you can spend a couple of days away from yet come back to again (as opposed to taking a couple days off and forgetting the game exists) because the game really IS fun. Beyond the gameplay, the graphics are another positive point. The design/concepts are pleasantly ironic; there is a certain (and non-morbid) amount of satisfactory stress relief in killing sheep. Well. Not killing. Delivering them to the reaper. *cough* The cuteness of the graphics provides the perfect offset and absurdity level for what you will need to do in order to complete the levels of the game, i.e. kill sheep.
One (albeit obscure) criticism is that the comic strip-like stills between levels, which sometimes appear to "explain" new features added to an upcoming level, are often rather opaque in the sense that they can be very difficult to make sense of. Thankfully, Divide by Sheep is highly forgiving - you can reset any given level after experimenting to learn about a new platform "The Hard (but still amusing) Way". Because of this the, at times confusing, explanatory stills do not pose a significant problem. Consider it a pet peeve.
One of the things I found very helpful (even if I didn't often avail myself of the feature because I am a stubborn completionist who will try and try again until I must YouTube because all of the stars) was the ability to wave a surrender flag if/when I was stuck. I appreciated that this was possible even if I did not take advantage of it.This feature would, in theory and practice, allow me to progress through the game (without needing to cheat YouTube walkthroughs) despite only being able to complete one or two out of three deliveries in a given level. The flag waving prevents stuck-ness and provides a lack of gated-ness that many modern puzzle games lack. This feature made Divide by Sheep more inviting and took the pressure off for a not-really-particularly-skilled-at-mental-math sort of person like me. (I'm better with theory. I swear.)
I 100% recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a well-made puzzle game and to anyone who is more pedestrian about puzzlers as well. Divide by Sheep IS solidly organized, thought out, and skillfully crafted, yet it remains pleasing for those who are slightly less particular about puzzlers.  There is no game snobbery here. If you insist upon elitism in gaming or consider "gamer" as a status symbol, Divide by Sheep isn't for you, probably. This game is pure egalitarian entertainment with logic, fried sheep, half sheep, sheep souls, wolves, TNT, sticky platforms, pigs, YOU NAME IT.
PS: As a professional educator, I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the educational value of the game - whether for young math learners, older folks warding off the brain fog that comes with aging (I probably qualify for this category), or an ice breaker for ESL students (linguistic demand is low). Divide by Sheep has much potential as a classroom/educational/mental flexibility tool while still being fun enough to not feel like a tool.

Bloodlines was a game ahead of its time with a fairly complex & in-depth storyline full of both drama & dark humor oriented to a more mature-audience. It contained a plethora of (sometimes hidden) content & alternatives dependant upon your chosen character's build/evolution (skills & abilities) as well as roleplaying actions & dialogue choices, revealing possibilities for more diverse interactions with non-player characters, finding items (Magical Swords to Flaemthrowers), unlocking additional story/quest options & finaly determining which alternate ending you experience. Even selecting a different clan offered unique additional alternatives & possibilities for added replay value (admittedly some clans offered much more additional content and a far more unique experience: Clan Malkavian).
Unfortunately, when Bloodlines was released, it masqueraded as a rushed & bug-ridden mess, often frustrating at best & unplayable (literally) at worst. It took years of hard work by devoted fans who looked beneath the original facade to discover an actual treasure and reveal it to the rest of the world, carefully removing the bugs & even unlocking lost content the original programers created but left unfinished, yet hidden within. Years later it emerged in an updated version, cleansed, even improved, with lost/unfinished content restored & to this date, numerous player-made mods still being created by an active community fanbase.
The original advertising along with some of the more overt tragically (pseudo) hip stereotypes & soap-opera cliche's, often straight from the origianl pen & papper/live-action roleplaying books, didn't do anything to help entice the more mature audience the game was originally aiming for; however, the machiavellian plotlines, diverse characters from both ancient times to the modern nights, & the dark but fascinating merging of real-world history with the supernatural entities, timeless conspiracies & endless Jihad of the World of Darkness made this into the lasting classic it has become.

There isn't much I can say about this game that hasn't already been said, but since this has become one of my top five favorite games of all time, I have to leave a review.
There are very few RPGs that have this level of depth. Fantastic atmosphere with fleshed out NPCs. Excellent writing is complimented by voice acting. The clan you choose and the choices you make have a direct effect on how the world responds to you and on how the story unfolds, which has become increasingly rare in modern games. Your choices have consequences that open and close doors. There's a lot of replay value just in exploring the "what ifs".
That being said, it is an unfinished game, and the gameplay leaves something to be desired. You /have/ to install a fanmade patch in order to be able to even complete the game, which is why I have so few hours logged since I forgot to have it launch via Steam. Even with it intalled there are some bugs that I needed to fix with the console. Combat is clunky and the unavoidable camera change in melee is annoying. Some skills become very unviable in late game. However, I do like the perk system and how there is a real feel of progression. Obviously the graphics are going to be dated since it's a thirteen year old game, but I think they hold up pretty well and it's not a deal breaker for me, especially since I don't own a powerful gaming PC.
Overall, Bloodline's succesions highly outweight its shortcomings. If Troika hadn't been rushed and had time to fully develop and complete this game, I have no doubt it would be considered one of the greatest RPGs of all time.

I was rather disappointed with Mafia 2.
I am unsure how much of my review of this game is based upon Grand Theft Auto as opposed to why I am not the fondest of this game. Grand Theft Auto is a very good crime-life series of games. With a great sandbox, good enough story, difficult enough, and it makes use of the entire game world. I feel like Mafia 2 is a game with a more or less basic crime drama story, quite easy gameplay aside from the ridiculous damage you take from enemies, awful sandbox and doesn't really make use of the entire world.
Starting with the story, the story focuses around the character you play named Vito. You follow him on his journey to becoming a "made man" through his crime-life. Him and his best friend Joe are in this together to fulfill their dreams of power.
The story I found is really forgettable. For a game that relies completely on following story-driven objective only without any side-questing, the combat and the story had to be up to par, and they weren't. To me anyways. The story and the cast of characters I found it in to be extremely forgettable. There was only 3 characters in the entire game I liked, and their appearances were spotty as hell. One is in it for 3 chapters and another pops in and out and is gone. And the the other was in it for one chapter and a few seconds at the end. Every other character in the game that I didn't like was really boring, shallow, and had the most deepest voice 2 daily doses of testosterone could provide. Really throughout the entire game, nothing really surprised me or got me interested in the story, it was just onto the next mission of just killing people cause I was told to. Which made sense because Vito felt the same way at the end of the game more or less. But really, just about everyone in the story minds as well have just had a sign that said "you're going to kill me later in the game or beat the living hell out of me."
It was annoying that really the only characters I actually liked weren't really in the game save for one person. But ultimately the cast was ruled by a boring cast.
And inside the story there was of course, combat. And for a game centered around combat. It was passable. But for relying on combat and story to carry the game, it was bad. The enemies in this game deal ridiculous damage and I played on normal. I mean I could literally get shot by 3 bullets from a enemy and it's just over. Done. Restart the checkpoint. But I said the combat was easy, doesn't dying easily all the time hard? Normally, yeah I suppose so. Really you're not poking your head out of cover unless it's to shoot someone obviously. So really you just had to quick-kill people with each zoom in. I takes roughly 2-3 shots to get the job done most times with really any gun except the tommy-gun. The magnum was an exception since it's a slow firing gun. But with a really simple crosshair and gun accuracy system. You could kill enemies quickly and pick them off one-by-one like a piece of cake. And it wasn't even satisfying either. In GTA it feels good when you get a guy down, with whatever gun you're using. In this game they just fall down and your gun is just whatever. Reload and continuing firing I guess. Most of the time whenever I got killed in this game is because the bullets clip my characters ENORMOUS hitbox. It was so hard to hide from bullets most of the time in this game. I felt like I was always being hit and throughout my let's play all I could hear was that annoying heartbeat sound all the time. Also grenades and molotovs have the most ridiculous AOE (area-of-effect) i've ever seen in my life. I could still take near death damage from a molotov a good few paces away. Far enough to say I shouldn't have taken any damage, especially behind cover.
For me, all combat missions where I just run in and out of cover. Wasn't satisfying. It felt like I was just playing through to finish a mission.
And the missions don't make use of the entire world. The world in this game, is incredibly small. Compared to GTA 4, the game world is roughly 3/4's as big as the starting island of GTA 4. Which is just awful. And the game doesn't even make use of the world like GTA. GTA re-hashes their missions so cleverly around these islands that it felt like a new experience every time. In Mafia 2 it felt boring and I visited the same locations so many times in an obvious way. At the same time, there is so many places they could spin-off of and make the game fun. But it wasn't like that.
That said, the art design of the game is nice but feels stiff. The game doesn't feel flowing and smooth. Even with the music it just felt like a game where the cogs and gears were too easy to see and not refined in a pleasing way that'd really make the city feel alive.  Even with the designs, there were a ton of stores and places to visit. But I never found myself short on cash and so I never robbed stores or visited any of the stores for guns. Any gun they could ever give me I could find with full ammunition in really any chapter. There was a lot of interesting aspects to how you spend your money in this game. Even for buying gas for your car. But I never spent money on anything once except to buy a suit for a mission and to buy a trenchcoat-like suit for my own pleasure.
This game as a sandbox is disappointing. There isn't anything interesting or particularly fun you can do. The idea of fighting off hordes of policemen in this game isn't pleasing or a pleasing thought. The game is simply too stiff and really doesn't allow for any craziness or particularly creativity in anyway. Cars aren't fun, messing with the NPC isn't fun, the environment isn't fun. There is absolutely nothing to do outside of the story-driven mission. And would you really want to? This game is so boring when not playing the on-rails story that you can't help how colorless and bland this game really is. It's not fun at all when doing your own thing.
That said, when I beat the game. I was really surprised it didn't go into sandbox mode. The game ended and when I tried to load up again it was just the final fight again (which was extremely easy mind you and not a "special end-game fight" It was more random than anything to me.)
I guess i'm not really surprised since this game doesn't have a day - night system. The time changes whenever you finish a mission. So if you wanted to play at early morning or late night world. You'll have to load up a certain chapter and play the missions until it's dark.
Just. So much stuff about this game is just really disappointing to me.
Do I think it's a bad game though? No. Most certainly not and not by any stretch of the word. But would I recommend it? No, I mean if you want a pretty okay game and nice cruise through a game. Yeah, it's fine. You're probably only going to play it one more time though. Because there's much better games out there and have much more amounts of replayablitity.
In short, if you want an decent game and a good fair just one or two playthroughs with nothing too crazy or anything. Just a good, run-of-the-mill crime-drama video game. Sure, why not. It's not bad and it's a good enough time to just sit down and play it once or twice and have finished your fun. But as a game for more than that? I'm afraid not, there's much better choices out there for crime-drama games with vasts amount of replayablility and creativity.
Anyway, thank you for reading. I hope you found this review helpful enough to consider while pondering your decision to purchase this game or not.

I've had my heart broken several times in my life. Once, on Christmas Day 1989, I eagerly ran downstairs and gasped at the sight of what was clearly a crudely but lovingly wrapped skateboard. A skateboard that I had wanted ever since I had seen Marty McFly cruise through the streets of Hill Valley as a stowaway behind an unsuspecting SUV driver. A skateboard with a custom deck, with artwork that would cause my fellow skaters to shout "rad". A skateboard whose wheels would send me gliding across the streets as I headed for the nearest half-pipe. A skateboard of majestical proportion.
I grabbed it, and with shaking hands and a heart beating against my chest, I tore that festive wrapping as hard as I could. Through an intricate web of sticky tape, ribbon and ever expanding wrapping paper, I dug through. Years later, I wondered that this is what Andy in The Shawshank Rdemption must have felt like as he dragged hinself through the tunnels. My own redemption was in sight. My prize was near. Finally, the last shred of packaging fell away to the floor. And there it was... a plastic skateboard from the local store. With stiff plastic wheels. And a picture of a clown on the deck.
That's what playing Mafia 2 felt like.

So the game hits on a lot of nostalgia for me.  With the very retro RPG look, and the handling of an old school adventure RPG, it's already got a lot going for it.
The game play is basically a "Run from the wall of death" style game reminicent of old side scrollers, where if the Death Wall (the Darkness in this case) gets you, you die, while at the same time, all of your resources are limited and nothing is infinite.  This makes the game heavy on the two major elements of game play:  Risk/Reward and Resourse Management.  Do I want to venture into that dungeon?  Will I get more out of it then I use to go in?  Will I die?
The other big element of gameplay is multiple play throughs.  You do a dimention, and either win or die.  All characters are "one and done."  On each subsequent play through, you make new characters, allowing you knowledge of what your characters are good and bad at, and giving you control over HOW you'll play each adventure.  After each adventure, you get points that you can use to unlock stronger abilities (perks), new classes, and expand the "Dimentional Box" which allows you to carry a limited number of items over to new adventures, or to merely store them for future difficult adventures.
The final big element of the game is the randomly genereated dimentions.  Each play through you can go to a new random dimention (with differing base parameters), replay old dimentions (same base parameters but different world layout), or do any of the current special dimentions with descriptions of what's special about them.  Alternately, you can input dimention codes manually to have a similar experience as friends, to find dimentions that spawn things you might want (finding codes online), or just to do your own variety of random.
Pros:
- That price!
- Lots of replay value
- Enough customization options
- Very rewarding gameplay
Cons:
- Some dimentions can be surprisingly difficult even on the easiest mode
- Can be grind intensive
Tips:
- I have a coveted "Lumberjack Battleaxe" which is just the best at breaking walls.
- Nice easy dimention:  RVOFGTKI

I remember browsing some cheap games on the Summer Sale when I came across this One Way Heroics, for only 75 cents at that time I didn't really expected it to be that good. A couple of days later I bought it and was quite suprised of how good it was.
The concept is pretty simple: With every move you make the screen scolls to the right, when you get too far to the left you die. During the time you need to escape from the Darkness you have to fight enemies, find treasure, buy gear and get ready to fight the big boss, The Demon Lord, who is trying to destroy the world.
Before you do that though you've got to choose a class, perks and (the most interesting part of this game) a dimension. Dimensions are randomly generated worlds which will most of the time be different from another one, if you want to you can even create a dimension name of your own. This is also the way the game introduces some sort of semi-multiplayer, people can be in the same dimension and you can see the progress other players are making, everyday there will be a special dimensions created where people can play alongside others.
Of course dying is also part of the game, while this game is mostly a Roguelike, some of the things you did will be carried over to your next playthough. When you die you get Hero Points based on how well you did, these will be saved and you can buy things with them, Classes, Perks and spaces for the Dimensional Vault. the Dimensional vault is basicly a chest where you can put your treasure and gear you collected and will be openable on every run, allowing you to use that gear in your next run.
While this game might not seem that good at first i'd say that as a fan of both Pixel graphics and Roguelikes this game is really good for it's price and will keep you entertained for a long time. I'd rate it a 9.7/10

is a casual point-and-click adventure/puzzler by
. It’s light in style, yet dark in humor.  It is silly, funny, doesn't frustrate, and has some fun and challenging puzzles.  It is the kind of game that true fans of the genre will adore, casual fans of the genre should enjoy, and indifferent fans of the genre may welcome.
I find myself saying the following about many of
adventure games: what really gives the game a quality above the par is the atmosphere of the game.  The music, the art style, the characters, the dialogue, the humor, the game mechanics... it all blends together into a charming, unique, and very enjoyable experience.
The game plays with classic point-and-click mechanics.  It is a strongly story-driven experience with a lot of dialogue.  There are inventory based puzzles, dialogue based puzzles, and minigame style puzzles that must be solved to progress the game.  Some of the puzzles are pretty challenging because the solutions don't really make sense logically— but they make sense within the confines of the twisted reality of the game.  While a feature like that can be frustrating at times for adventure gamers, I think it fits in perfectly with this game.
As I alluded to, there's a real lot of dark humor in this game and it fits the atmosphere perfectly. It isn't a kid's adventure game.  Even as someone who truly enjoys adventure games, I sometimes find myself bored with their trivial, childish storylines; with
though, I truly enjoyed the hilarious story from beginning to end.
Simply put: what makes this game great is the way it perfectly blends classic, nostalgia-inducing, childish adventure gameplay with adult themes and dry, dark humor.  If you are an adult that enjoys adventure games, and are craving a good experience, then you should check this game out.  And if you have been on the fence about trying an adventure game, this is a pretty good one to play to get a taste of what the genre can offer.

After the cluttered, nonsensical, and unlikeable mess that was Deponia, I wouldn't have ever touched another game from this studio if it weren't for being in a Humble Bundle.  It would have been my loss, because this was everything Deponia wasn't: puzzles that made sense and had a logical progression, likeable characters, and a deep interesting story.  Of course, it suffers from a buggy UI, once that was so game-breaking I had to reload an earlier game because loading at that point didn't fix it.  And it had several localization oversights, reverting to German in the middle of conversations.  The mental-block mechanic could have had some potential, but ended up being simply annoying.  If you were ever halted by a mental block, you'd simply switch modes and try again.  Those are relatively minor issues, though.
It was still a worthwhile play for the price I paid, and about 10 hours (making it comparitively lengthy) time well spent.

However, while some others praise the voice acting, that was actually my least favorite thing about the game. While I didn't dislike the story, the voice acting was so annoying to me that I thought about simply turning it off. The only reason I didn't is because some things happen in the game where you need to hear him explain the situation to know what's going on. I honestly believe that the main voice actor doesn't know English as a first language, since native English speakers just don't talk like he does. It sounded like he was reading off of a piece of paper, without understanding how sentance structure works. Some of the lines even had blatant grammar errors that I honestly cannot believe the devs didn't catch. It didn't sound natural at all.
Other than that, I really enjoyed my experience with this game. This is an excellent platformer with fantastic visuals and a great original gameplay mechanic, and it runs really well even on medium/low end systems. I just wish the main voice actor spoke his lines better than he did, then this game would have been pretty much perfect.

The first Edna & Harvey game was in my opinion one of the best recent point & click adventure games. Harvey's new eyes unfortunately doesn't share all of the best aspects of the first game. In particular puzzles are much easier and less creative and too easy for my taste and it doesn't have unique responses to almost every action you might attempt as the first game did.
What it does share with the first game is the dark humour and the appealing and very apropriate cartoon visuals. This is the main strength of the game, the darkly humorous story. Lily is a great main character, at the same time adorable and scary. The appeal of the story comes to a large part from the contrast between Lily's innocent appearance and the disastrous consequences of her actions. The general crazyness inherent in the details of the game world, e.g. there is a meat-eating plant in mother superiors office and there is a hamster equipped with night vision goggles who appears more than once to steal Lily's things, also helps keep the game entertaining as does the sarcastic narration. The unique style of the graphics are entirely appropriate and I don't think the game would have worked nearly as well with more "serious" graphics.
Sound effects are adequate but no more than that and voice acting is average. The music is fairly good but not exceptional.
All in all this is a very entertaining adventure game, although too easy for experience players and lacking the extreme attention to detail of the first Edna & Harvey game. I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys adventure games and dark humour.

You'll have to upgrade your ship and train your crew to get to your fleet because every sector will be harder than the previous one. And never gets repetitive because every game is randomized.

So, after a few years with this game gathering dust in my library, and a recent Humble Bundle purchase, I decided to try and give this game a second chance. I already wrote a review about it once, and it was also negative. But I admittedly hadn't put much thought into my negativity towards this game, other than its completely stupid campaign plot for the Soviet Campaign. But really, there's more to this game that makes me dislike it, so let me try again, and be more in-depth about it.
So, let's start with the gameplay. Actually, it's not as bad as I initially thought it was. I had to get used to the different Commander system, but I can at the very least appreciate how you can mix and match your "loadouts", to get a faction that you personally play best with in either way. They made a lot of little tweaks here and there that make the game more playable vs. CoH1, like the ability for units to vault over terrain, and to deliberately choose to move a tank backwards, as opposed to micro-clicking behind the tank to get it to do that. Units can fight while capping points, scenery works better as cover. It ultimately has what I loved about Company of Heroes 1, gameplay wise. The newer factions, like Americans and English, seem to be easier to micromanage, as there's no real base building anymore, and frankly, I certainly hope people are done pretending base building added anything. Does it really matter *where* the support infantry barracks is placed? Come on, don't kid yourself. There's also some blatantly gimmicky stuff like winter maps where soldiers can freeze to death.
Graphics don't have much to talk about. I mean, they're great! Textures look marvelous, each model is super-detailed, down to the badges on their uniforms. Snow on the High setting has neat, Assassin's Creed III style, permanent deep footprints trailing behind anyone moving through it. You could practically feel your feet getting cold and wet just looking at the men running through it. Ice looks good, weather effects are convincing. Not much to say, though, aside from that. Game looks good.
So, it looks good, and plays good, and yet I *don't* like this game. It's now time for me to elaborate why that is.
Let's start with single playability. I'm a huge, anti-social dork, so yes, single player experiences matter a lot to me, even in RTS games. Apparently liking single player in RTSes makes me a big weirdo, for some reason, but I digress. The Russian campaign is, as famously pointed out by YouTuber BadComedian, a stupidly written story rife with offensive russophobic cliches. We've all seen the cutscene where a Comissar executes a dude for saving Captain Ibrahmovich's life, because he missed rolecall in-so-doing. There's really not much to say about it, other than that. Missions are forgettable, one mission was literally just a copy-paste of Carentan and Carentan Counter-attack from CoH1, so that seemed pretty lazy to me. The only parts I do remember are the stupid ones, like the mission where you set buildings on fire with civillians inside of them (truly a Company of *HEROES*), or the mission where you besiege a German town and go all Bitter Springs on the civillians trying to escape. What the ♥♥♥♥? Why did Relic make a game where we play as cartoonishly evil a-holes?
There's also the Ardennes Forest (aka The Battle of the Bulge) campaign that I tried for a little bit. It looked fun in the trailers. The map reminded me of Dawn of War Dark Crusade, a game with a fascinating SP campaign. But no, it actually wasn't even close to being as interesting as Dark Crusade. Just a bunch of scenarios with poorly implemented campaign features like Company Strength and requisition to try and fool you into thinking you weren't just playing a bunch of random scenarios and maps with the same units over and over again. Nothing from Dark Crusade like Territory Garisons, or defensive missions against the Germans, or turn-based requisition gains, or special territory bonuses. I didn't even finish it, I grew bored very quickly.
I'm sure some of you are saying "singleplayer doesn't matter in RTSes", but forget that. Tell that to Homeworld, or Company of Heroes 1, or Dawn of War 1 and 2, or Age of Mythology. If you can't craft a memorable singleplayer experience then that's a strike against you in my book. If you wanted to make what is essentially the Red Orchestra of RTSes, why even bother *having* a campaign then? I'm getting distracted again though, so on to my next point.
Now for the final thing -- the thing that made me uninstall this game again, for good this time. The thing that makes me regret that I am far, far past the deadline for a re-fund. The multiplayer system. As I said before, I'm not big into the multiplayer games of RTSes, but hey, "when in rome", right? So I got into it. I saw that there were a bunch of unlockables. Commanders, skins, faceplates, and it didn't bother me too much because two of those three things are 100% pointless and you can just ignore them. So I play like 5 games in multiplayer, and I get my first loot crate. 500 "Supplies". So I mosey on over to the store, figuring I could buy a commander or something. One commander -- that's one commander out of like, 20 -- costed 15,000 Supplies. I don't even want to do the math, because I would just get angrier. Oh, but don't worry, guys! Just pay $3 bucks and you can get it now!
The first comparisson that comes to mind is Freemium phone games, but even that's better than this despicable system. At least you didn't ALREADY PAY $60 for flipping Candy Crush! So, not only do you pay full price for Company of Heroes, but then Relic tries to swindle you out of even more money with this awful, Skinner Box "war loot" feature. That's disgusting, revolting, and insulting. It's not even like you can ignore it, like with Team Fortress 2, because there are commanders in game that give you an objective advantage over others. So, the game is rewarding those who would pay more money for better commanders. It's pay to win, but it's *not* free to play. That's unforgiveable.
This can't be the same Relic that made Homeworld and the first Company of Heroes. I don't know what happened, but I don't know Relic anymore.
This game fails as a single player and multiplayer experience. Play something else, something that respects you a little more, because this game is disrespectful to anyone who gives it their time.

Bloodlines was a game ahead of its time with a fairly complex & in-depth storyline full of both drama & dark humor oriented to a more mature-audience. It contained a plethora of (sometimes hidden) content & alternatives dependant upon your chosen character's build/evolution (skills & abilities) as well as roleplaying actions & dialogue choices, revealing possibilities for more diverse interactions with non-player characters, finding items (Magical Swords to Flaemthrowers), unlocking additional story/quest options & finaly determining which alternate ending you experience. Even selecting a different clan offered unique additional alternatives & possibilities for added replay value (admittedly some clans offered much more additional content and a far more unique experience: Clan Malkavian).
Unfortunately, when Bloodlines was released, it masqueraded as a rushed & bug-ridden mess, often frustrating at best & unplayable (literally) at worst. It took years of hard work by devoted fans who looked beneath the original facade to discover an actual treasure and reveal it to the rest of the world, carefully removing the bugs & even unlocking lost content the original programers created but left unfinished, yet hidden within. Years later it emerged in an updated version, cleansed, even improved, with lost/unfinished content restored & to this date, numerous player-made mods still being created by an active community fanbase.
The original advertising along with some of the more overt tragically (pseudo) hip stereotypes & soap-opera cliche's, often straight from the origianl pen & papper/live-action roleplaying books, didn't do anything to help entice the more mature audience the game was originally aiming for; however, the machiavellian plotlines, diverse characters from both ancient times to the modern nights, & the dark but fascinating merging of real-world history with the supernatural entities, timeless conspiracies & endless Jihad of the World of Darkness made this into the lasting classic it has become.

There isn't much I can say about this game that hasn't already been said, but since this has become one of my top five favorite games of all time, I have to leave a review.
There are very few RPGs that have this level of depth. Fantastic atmosphere with fleshed out NPCs. Excellent writing is complimented by voice acting. The clan you choose and the choices you make have a direct effect on how the world responds to you and on how the story unfolds, which has become increasingly rare in modern games. Your choices have consequences that open and close doors. There's a lot of replay value just in exploring the "what ifs".
That being said, it is an unfinished game, and the gameplay leaves something to be desired. You /have/ to install a fanmade patch in order to be able to even complete the game, which is why I have so few hours logged since I forgot to have it launch via Steam. Even with it intalled there are some bugs that I needed to fix with the console. Combat is clunky and the unavoidable camera change in melee is annoying. Some skills become very unviable in late game. However, I do like the perk system and how there is a real feel of progression. Obviously the graphics are going to be dated since it's a thirteen year old game, but I think they hold up pretty well and it's not a deal breaker for me, especially since I don't own a powerful gaming PC.
Overall, Bloodline's succesions highly outweight its shortcomings. If Troika hadn't been rushed and had time to fully develop and complete this game, I have no doubt it would be considered one of the greatest RPGs of all time.

Fantatsic little strategy game for less than £6. Its a smart but simple take on the Battle of Britain where you take on the task of defending Britain from the Luftwaffe in 1940. The game is essentially in two parts, the strategic map where you purchase and place factories, AA, airstrips, order planes and recruit pilots. You also direct you squadrons on sorties on this map in pausable real time. But when a squadron meets an enemy squadron, the map swaps to a tactical view, where you can control planes by "drawing " their flight route. As pilot become more expirienced they are more accurate and need less micromanaging (actually performing better than I could if in direct control). You need to try and save your pilots as training takes time, and the loss of experince can be devistatinging to your war effort, so the bail out button should be at your fingertips - just dont bail out over the sea! If you do well, you get more cash to spend on replacing planes, and expanding your defences. If you let your cities get bombed your income drops. Love the ability to edit the pilot names, which makes it sadder when they go down in flames (or even sadder when they are bombed/strafed when still on the runway!) Any bugs that may have existed once have been resolved, as far as I could see, having just finished the short "Blitz" 10 day campaign. Ready to see if I can survive the 50 day one now.....

As it stands I heavily advise AGAINST buying this game for several reasons.
1 - You can lose all of the pilots in a squadron simply because they're too terminally stupid to make the decision to bail out themselves and it's often an impossible task to hit the bail out button the game gives you in the *tiny* window of time available to you to do so while the pilot's plane is under fire.
2 - Withdrawing is not an option, say your pilots have stripped away the fighter cover for a flight of bombers but are in no shape to carry on the fight? Tough. It's very much the stalinist approach of victory or death, if you go back to the map you're left at the tender mercies of the auto-resolve system (which will happily let four bombers wipe out a squadron) or you're forced to fight on and risk losing all of your pilots to problem #1. (Yeah having to tell your guys to bail out is irritating.)
3 - No big wings. The 'big wing' was a tactic in which several RAF squadrons would group together to engage enemy attacks together, it took time to set up but it helped even out the numbers against massive German formations. This game does not let you do that and instead expects you to fight off dozens of planes with just eight of your own which leaves you at the mercy of problem #2 wherein you cannot withdraw should carrying on the fight become foolish which is particularly infuriating if you have another squadron or two nearby that could take over.
4 - The voiceacting is terrible, I had to turn off the audio for the tutorial guy just because I couldn't stand the sound of the mans voice.
5 - If you accidentally create a squadron at your airfield when that airfields squadron is in the air, tough luck. Doesn't matter that this new ghost squadron has no planes, you can't delete it, move it or do anything with it and you now have as many as eight rather expensive flying machines in the air that can't land because the airfield 'is full'. Despite the ghost squadron again, having no planes.
If you have your heart set on this game wait a few weeks or even a month or two for some patches to come in, otherwise you're setting yourself up for an absolute pain in the rear.

Those reviews that call this game addicting are right on the money. Those that state it is challenging are also right. I've played 7 campaigns so far and have lost all but 1.
There are many, many frustrating elements to this game. It demands heavy micro-management of your aircraft. For a game whose central theme is air combat, air combat is pretty clumsy. Your pilots will be slaughtered mercilessly by the Luftwaffe's BF-109s.  In a one-on-one fight, your AI pilots will fly around in circles chasing a 109, spraying bullets at empty sky until their guns go dry or you break the endless loop. If you break the loop, your pilot will be immediately shot down. You can take the short route and auto-resolve air battles, but if you do so then 100% of your lost pilots will be KIA - that's right, they won't think to bail out unless you tell them. Managing your fighters in combat vs bombers and Ju-87s is usually doable, but against the nimble Bf-109s it's just impossible because the scale is too small and the means of control too clumsy. Against the 109s I will auto-resolve...but this usually results in the loss of 75% of that squadron's pilots due to the aforementioned inability to bail out. Historically, the RAF didn't do this badly vs German fighters.
Speaking of those 109s again...the designers do not seem aware of the severe range restrictions on German fighters during this era. They had no drop tanks, and generally had only about 20 minutes loiter time around London. I am seeing Bf-109s roaming over Lincoln and northern Wales...unless they had an aircraft carrier (they didn't) all those 109s would crash before they made it home.
You are also limited to only 8 aircraft of your own per air battle. No Big Wings with multiple squadrons intercepting the German mass raids - coordinated attacks are impossible. The Germans have no such limitations, so when the Luftwaffe sends 16+ twin engine bombers and 8+ fighters, you must attack them piecemeal with two or three of your (hopefully) 8 plane squadrons. Expect the first two squadrons to be wiped out due to fighting outnumbered, and because the German Bf-109s will kill 2 or 3 of your fighters for each that they lose. In fact, the numerical disparity gives the Germans such an advantage that an 8 Spitfire RAF squadron attacking 16 German Bombers escorted by 12 Bf-109s, is likely to be wiped out without killing a single German aircraft. This has happened repeatedly. You might even win against this raid, but it won't matter because another one is coming loooooong before you can train and rebuild the lost squadrons. If you avoid battle, then they will blast your airfield to bits and you'll lose the planes because they can't land anywhere.
I like the strategic management aspect of building and placing airfields, radar, AA guns etc. However you only get to start with one factory, 1-2 airfields, and ZERO radar stations and AA guns. I would have liked to have seen a little more inventory at the start of the game. Playing a game about the Battle of Britain, where the RAF starts with no radar is a little silly. Radar was a cornerstone of the British air defense network. Southern England was laden with AA guns and barrage balloons, but you don't have them. New airfields, AA guns, and radar are crazy expensive, and your economy builds very slowly. You have the option to choose between Hurricanes and Spitfires in production, but I cannot discern any difference or advantage of one over the other. In this battle of attrition, the Germans will simply out-resource you in 4-5 days.
Squadrons won't land at an airfield if it is "full". So let's say you have two squadrons based at 2 airfields. One squadron was in combat and lost a few planes, with a pilot or two bailing out safely. The remaining aircraft return to base. At the same time your second squadron is also airborne, and the pilots who bailed out from the OTHER squadron start returning to your SECOND squadron's airfield. Now when squadron 2 returns to land, they CAN'T, because squadron 1's bailed out pilots have gone to squadron 2's base, and it is now too full to land at. That means you lose ALL of squadron 2's planes and pilots because they run out of fuel and crash, because two or three pilots WITH NO PLANES are apparently occupying the entire runway!
I fully realise that a simulation of the Battle of Britain should be nail-biting, edge-of-your-seat tense, and certainly not a "milk run." But this game goes a bit too far, to the point where it's almost mathematically impossible to win.
The game menu, instructions, and all written material are rife with spelling and grammatical errors. For example, your daily commander's review may state "We are loosing this battle." "Restart the campagin." Due to the prevalence of Czech and Polish squadrons in the game, I assume that the game was developed in Poland or the Czech Republic by people who did not speak English as their native tongue. If not, WTH? Have someone proofread your material!
Despite all the above criticisms, I am giving the game a thumbs up, because it IS an addictive game that keeps me coming back. But it's also frustrating as hell, and I may not come back much longer. I definitely hope some updates and patches are coming...

This is an extremely engaging game with simple mechanics that work well for it. If you are a fan of JRPGs or loot snagging in general, you'll have a great time.
Despite this being a procedurally generated roguelike game, it does manage to squeeze in some story and interesting characters. The unique bit is that, the generation is based off of whatever you want to type in. If you die in the dimension you entered if you want to revisit that dimension, the map generated will be the same (from what I've seen). This means that you can try to learn aspects of a specific dimension and plan around it.
Don't worry about the random generation screwing you over too hard either. On each character run you are always given 15 free turns that you can use in bundles of 3 whenever you want. So if you see a long stretch of unavoidable mountains, you could in theory use all 15 turns to pass them if it was really that bad/unavoidable.
The combat is simplistic, but deep enough that strategy actually matters since your positioning will often determine the outcome of a fight if more than one opponent is present. The game has a fair number of weapons and weapon types, some of which offer longer ranges and others which are really great at busting down terrain (Yes, you can break down walls of a house to talk to the people inside).
If you love optimization, NPC party building, pretending you actually have friends or are just looking for a fun game with a wonderful soundtrack, I'd spend the 83 cents to play this. I believe the regular asking price is $3, which is more than fair. Had I not only found this thanks to the steam sale, I would have gladly paid the $3.

Lily is without a doubt one of the most awesome characters ever. She looks innocent, she barely speaks, sports a cute bow on her head and is a raging psychopath on the inside. I thought the story of the game was interesting as it has such a weird concept. It's not really something you can predict along the way and it also has multiple endings depending on what you choose. Most of the characters throughout the game, even those that don't have a lot of screentime, have very good and detailed personalities. It makes it fun to interact with them as they all treat Lily individually. It also adds to making Lilys character feel real.
I didn't like the the artstyle of the game. I guess it's a matter of personal taste. Everything looks sloppily drawn and some characters just look weird when they talk.
I am glad there was an option to skip out on the mini game puzzles in the game. I don't think I had the patience to sit through a single one of them. Most of them relied on being able to remember things and it's difficult for me having high functioning autism.
I thought the voice acting was quite good (especially for a Deadelic game). I can't recall any actor that was outstanding, but there also wasn't anyone that was terrible. The only problem with the voice-acting is the narrator that just has too much dialogue when Lily uses items. There are some bugs in the games, such as the achievements are at the time not working at all. Sometimes the inventory would lock and refuse to open, but simply walking to another room or reloading helped fix the problem.
Overall I enjoyed this game. It has a good sense of humor, great character interaction and there is also a sense of deep character development depending on how you chose to end the game.
