Published by: Dingaling Productions, LLC
Developed by: Dingaling
Genre: Adventure, Indie, RPG
Release Date: 15 Dec, 2014
Completionist Gameplay: 50+ Hours
DISCLAIMER: I’ll be honest here. This game didn’t really do anything for me at all and I barely put any time at all into it (probably the reason why I didn’t enjoy it as much as others seem to have), but I can certainly see why so many people loved it. I tried my best to review this as objectively as possible and have used that to decide that this game deserves a “recommended” review.
LISA is set in a post-apocalyptic setting about a man called Brad who stumbles upon the last girl on earth. After keeping her safe from the rest of the men on the planet for many years while raising her as his own daughter, the secret is out and leagues of pervy men arrive to kidnap her. While the story is interesting enough, it never really caught my attention. It’s sarcastic humour and meta jokes combined with the depressing, hopeless and sometimes boring background story or characters left a bad taste in my mouth, though I can certainly see how it could be equally as amazing for another person.
This game doesn’t really bring anything new to the table, but it doesn’t do too many things wrong either. It’s an average, 2D-plane, occasional platformer with turn-based combat. While I like the added depth of special combo’s Brad and the other members of his party can use to inflict extra damage on their enemies if the player can remember the right combinations, as the game progresses you don’t get to do anything new. One thing I really dislike about the combat system is that there isn’t an enemy health bar at all. This can cause issues when in a particularly difficult and long fight, leaving you to feel like it might never end.It’s very vanilla and seems to be modelled after the classic model RPG, so if you’re into that, this game is for you! The platforming is mostly there to flesh out the scenery or reveal a little comedic scene. If you’re not careful though, you’ll continue on a cliff to the side of the screen, only to discover that it ended without any warning and you’ve just lost 500 HP.
One thing I really liked about this game are the choices it makes you take as you play. These choices will alter how you play the game, and definitely personalize the whole experience. For example, you could bribe an enemy instead of fighting him, sacrifice party members instead of your own arm, or even partake in optional mini-games (like russian roulette) that could either make or break your gaming experience. These choices really help the player realize exactly how hopeless and desolate this world is.
The art style and music choices of this game were very clever. The scenes and backgrounds are very beautiful, colourful and vibrant, and the music is invigorating and upbeat yet somehow do not clash with the macabre feeling of the story
Overall, I can see why this game is as loved by many as it is. There’s nothing fundamentally wrong with the game, the story is interesting, the game is playable, the art style is both beautiful and yet depressing and it certainly has enough gameplay hours for the price of it. If you’re a fan of RPG’s and hopeless efforts, I would recommend this for you as long as you’re sure that it’s something that you’ll love.

A Post-Apocalyptic Turn-Based RPG with old school graphics, LISA provides a unique experience and creativity on a level that I haven't enjoyed in some time. The game puts you in the role of Brad Armstrong, a washed up martial-artist living in a bizarre, often comical (but very dark) wasteland in which women have seemingly ceased to exist with the collapse of society. Coming across a female baby, Brad adopts the child (naming her Buddy) and devotes himself to trying to "protect" her from all of the potential dangers and abuses the world would dish out onto the last remaining human female on Earth. The game follows this primary motivation as you're faced with decisions that call on Brad to sacrifice more and more for the sake of saving Buddy from the various antagonists, often to the detriment of Brad himself and ease of gameplay and while learning more about Brad's own deeply flawed personality. You can also recruit a colorful cast of party members to assist you throughout the game, all bringing their own combat styles to compliment Brad's own martial arts arsenal. As mentioned, LISA is somehow able to blend extremely silly and humorous content with an overall bleak and dark story and setting, managing to make the player laugh and feel at the same time. The "Joyful" DLC picks up where the "Painful" original installment of the game leaves off, and offers closure to the story. The music is also top notch. Even further, it's all very impressive when you consider it was originally conceived as an RPG-Maker game. LISA has been one of the most enjoyable gaming experiences I've had in a while, and felt more or less fresh the whole way through. I highly recommend it.

Vampire the Masquerade: Bloodlines isn't the best RPG you'll ever play, not even close. But it has a heck of a lot going for it, largely due to it's interesting story which has twists even I didn't see coming, as well as characters which are evocative and also quite original.

Recently, I picked this game up in a Humble Weekly Sale, and I greatly enjoyed it.  It should be noted that it is a sequel; as a result, many parts of it will make little to no sense without playing the previous game: "Edna and Harvey: the Breakout."  I, being cheap, chose to watch a playthrough on youtube rather than buy the twenty dollar game, so that I might have context for this game.  I also have a few warnings about this game.  For starters, do not be fooled by the innocent exterior, this game is dark, extremely dark.  It may also screw with your mind to some degree or another, especially the ending.  The ending can be a no-win situation, unless you count the somewhat secret ending.  I'll leave it to you to figure out how to get to that ending.  This game differs from its predecessor in as much as there is a secret ending which can be considered somewhat good.  Despite the darkness and tendency to mess with the head, or perhaps because of it, the story is very good and well written.  This game is more than just a game, it is a story (in fact "Edna and Harvey: the Breakout" was originally a German university project on the topic of "The Computer Game as a Non-Linear Narrative Form."  In my opinion, both games accomplish the goal of proving the computer game as a storytelling medium very well.)  I know that most games need a story of some sort, but point-and-click adventure games depend heavily on the story, bringing it to the forefront, as opposed to FPS games, for example, where story can and often does take a backseat to the gameplay of shooting things.  As a result, this genre of games must be judged on storytelling more so than others.  Also, being a point-and-click adventure game, it requires the usual application of combined genius and madness to figure out the circuitous solutions to the puzzles.  While it is very good for what it is, I wouldn't recommend it to anyone who dislikes the genre.  If your prior experiences with point-and-clicks range from "meh" to bad, I doubt this will change your opinion of them.  All of the above also goes for this game's predecessor, which I also recommend.  Finally, I would like to bring up price.  I have seven hours logged on this game by Steam, and I've beaten it.  So I would say 20 dollars is a tad bit steep, and would suggest waiting for this game to go on sale, if it ever does.  I enjoyed it, but I don't think 20 dollars is worth it, especially since point-and-click adventure games have almost no replay value.  There are other games for the same price or less that you could probably get more playtime out of.  So, to sum up the pros and cons of this game, it is a very solid point-and-click with a good, if dark and confusing, story, generally clever, if contrived and circuitous, puzzles, that, while generally fun, probably isn't worth 20 dollars.

Published by: Dingaling Productions, LLC
Developed by: Dingaling
Genre: Adventure, Indie, RPG
Release Date: 15 Dec, 2014
Completionist Gameplay: 50+ Hours
DISCLAIMER: I’ll be honest here. This game didn’t really do anything for me at all and I barely put any time at all into it (probably the reason why I didn’t enjoy it as much as others seem to have), but I can certainly see why so many people loved it. I tried my best to review this as objectively as possible and have used that to decide that this game deserves a “recommended” review.
LISA is set in a post-apocalyptic setting about a man called Brad who stumbles upon the last girl on earth. After keeping her safe from the rest of the men on the planet for many years while raising her as his own daughter, the secret is out and leagues of pervy men arrive to kidnap her. While the story is interesting enough, it never really caught my attention. It’s sarcastic humour and meta jokes combined with the depressing, hopeless and sometimes boring background story or characters left a bad taste in my mouth, though I can certainly see how it could be equally as amazing for another person.
This game doesn’t really bring anything new to the table, but it doesn’t do too many things wrong either. It’s an average, 2D-plane, occasional platformer with turn-based combat. While I like the added depth of special combo’s Brad and the other members of his party can use to inflict extra damage on their enemies if the player can remember the right combinations, as the game progresses you don’t get to do anything new. One thing I really dislike about the combat system is that there isn’t an enemy health bar at all. This can cause issues when in a particularly difficult and long fight, leaving you to feel like it might never end.It’s very vanilla and seems to be modelled after the classic model RPG, so if you’re into that, this game is for you! The platforming is mostly there to flesh out the scenery or reveal a little comedic scene. If you’re not careful though, you’ll continue on a cliff to the side of the screen, only to discover that it ended without any warning and you’ve just lost 500 HP.
One thing I really liked about this game are the choices it makes you take as you play. These choices will alter how you play the game, and definitely personalize the whole experience. For example, you could bribe an enemy instead of fighting him, sacrifice party members instead of your own arm, or even partake in optional mini-games (like russian roulette) that could either make or break your gaming experience. These choices really help the player realize exactly how hopeless and desolate this world is.
The art style and music choices of this game were very clever. The scenes and backgrounds are very beautiful, colourful and vibrant, and the music is invigorating and upbeat yet somehow do not clash with the macabre feeling of the story
Overall, I can see why this game is as loved by many as it is. A Post-Apocalyptic Turn-Based RPG with old school graphics, LISA provides a unique experience and creativity on a level that I haven't enjoyed in some time. The game puts you in the role of Brad Armstrong, a washed up martial-artist living in a bizarre, often comical (but very dark) wasteland in which women have seemingly ceased to exist with the collapse of society. Coming across a female baby, Brad adopts the child (naming her Buddy) and devotes himself to trying to "protect" her from all of the potential dangers and abuses the world would dish out onto the last remaining human female on Earth. The game follows this primary motivation as you're faced with decisions that call on Brad to sacrifice more and more for the sake of saving Buddy from the various antagonists, often to the detriment of Brad himself and ease of gameplay and while learning more about Brad's own deeply flawed personality. You can also recruit a colorful cast of party members to assist you throughout the game, all bringing their own combat styles to compliment Brad's own martial arts arsenal. As mentioned, LISA is somehow able to blend extremely silly and humorous content with an overall bleak and dark story and setting, managing to make the player laugh and feel at the same time. The "Joyful" DLC picks up where the "Painful" original installment of the game leaves off, and offers closure to the story. The music is also top notch. Even further, it's all very impressive when you consider it was originally conceived as an RPG-Maker game. LISA has been one of the most enjoyable gaming experiences I've had in a while, and felt more or less fresh the whole way through. I highly recommend it.

- Attention to detail is off the charts.

Cons:

The game that gives you post-traumatic stress to whistling.
For those of you who don’t want to read the whole review I’ll just say it here, the game is good, great even. And if you think you have the emotionally strength to play the game then.
1: You’re wrong.
2: It is definitely worth your money and time.
But on to the more meaty review.
Other people have already pointed out the story and the savage feels of the game so I’ll only cover the basics. You play as Brad Armstrong, a drugged up ex karate teacher in a post-apocalyptic world where all women have mysteriously vanished in an event known simply as the White Flash. Brad’s built a small family for himself here but still suffers from the memories and guilt of his abusive father and his younger sister’s suicide. However one day Brad comes across of all things, a baby, a baby girl at that. Knowing what will happen to her as the “last female” in the world Brad decides to adopt her and keep her a secret, seeing her as his second chance to make up for his sister. However eventually as the child gets older and word gets out an all out war is started over the girl.
Like I said others have gone into greater and better detail over the story so I’ll just give those basics to the beginning and just say its horribly heart wrenching but magnificently written. Well worth the money just for it alone.
Now for gameplay its your pretty basic turn based RPG. Very very Earthbound in style with its main “stand out” mechanic being that party members can be permanently killed by certain enemies. Its not overly hard if you know what you are doing in an RPG even in Pain Mode but still enjoyable enough, the party members are all unique and varied enough to come up with some fun strategies. (I ran Bo, Fly and Buckets myself and managed to defeat Mike without any deaths).
The game also has a big thing for forcing you to make choices/decisions, but again other people have already covered this and for the sake of saving time I’ll just say its interesting but sometimes down right terrible.
However as much as I love the game there are a few downsides I need to point out, none of them are game breaking but something to consider if you are thinking of making your own RPG.
-My main one is with the “Withdrawal” system, now I have nothing with the idea itself infact I think it blends story and gameplay brilliantly. However my main complaint is that it can take effect during cut scenes of all things. Now walking around I understand but since you have no control over cut scenes it’s a bit unfair that it can randomly kick in during them especially if its before a boss fight.
-This is mainly with Pain Mode however the fact that there is no way to quick save the game. I don’t mean the F9 save at any moment quick save I mean the older kind where you can make a temporary save and turn the game off if you don’t have time to get to a regular save point. Now in normal mode this is just an annoyance but in Pain Mode (which deletes save points once you use them) this means you need to make sure you have time to play a decent chunk in the game in one go.
-While the before (tho I will admit vaguely) Decisions are important to the game, they are also really easy to cheat in a few cases. For example, the first one the game throws at you is either give up all your items or lose your first party member. However if you don’t pick up any items before this you are free to go back after this event and get them costing you barely nothing other than 10 minutes of back tracking.
-This one just may be personal, but you run out of things to do before the fun wears off. I had done literally everything in the game and I still wanted to mess around before the last boss but there is nothing to do in the game once you complete everything, even just grinding there is very little of. And while Pain Mode does offer some replay incentive it doesn’t actually add much more content to the game.
-The Achievements for the game are very boring, which is odd considering how intelligent and thought out the rest of the game is. But almost all of them are the most basic form of “achievements” get a party member, get so far in the story, get a certain ending, etc. I don’t want to get achievements just for playing the game I want them to be something special you work for. Plus you need to beat the game 3 times to get all of them and there are only 2 play modes so atleast one time is just going to be a repeat playthrough which is something a lot of people don’t like.
But still, these are mild complaints next to the amazing masterpiece that is LISA the Painful. The story is perfect, the music is awesome and captures every moment perfectly. It knows just when to be giggling silly to life crushing horrible. It’s certainly not a “happy” experience. But it sure is a Joyful one.

LISA is a messed up game. You play a messed up character who had a messed up childhood in a messed up world... but then, that's exactly why this game makes sense, because LISA is a subtle reflection of the twisted reality that we actually live in. Sure, we might not exist in a post-apocalyptic world, where no women are left alive and dirty magazines are used as currency - but we do live in a world where abused kids grow up with scars, where drugs are the easy way out, and where a broken man might sacrifice everyone in his way in his personal quest for redemption.
LISA is a game of black humor and wretched humanity, dressed in old-school game mechanics that are entertaining enough to keep you going. It paints the tale of a desperate protagonist, succeeding in twisting your emotions where games like "The Last of Us" arguably failed. It's not for everyone, but if you can stomach bleak situations spattered with jokes that range from the silly to the perverse... well. Good luck.

This game is probably the most worthwhile purchase I've made on Steam thus far. I bought it for $0.87 during the summer sale and definitely didn't expect to get as much mileage out of it as I am.
One Way Heroics starts with a pretty simple plot and concept, but there's a lot lurking beneath the surface. What starts off as a simple JRPG excuse plot-- the encroaching darkness that you have to defeat-- actually serves as an interesting and challenging game mechanic. Since you're constantly advancing and trying to stay as far ahead of the Darkness as possible, you're basically forced to make decisions about where you go, who you fight, and what dungeons and towns are worth investigating. Add the class/perk character customization system, and you can pretty much play this game in any way you choose (once you unlock the classes and perks with Hero Points, anyway).
I liked the fact that after you die the results screen actually gives you an evaluation and advice on how to succeed in your next run. The Hero Point/Dimensional Vault system is also pretty interesting; having your previous runs contribute to your next feels a lot more satisfying than just having your saves wiped whenever you die. Despite these concessions and the save system that allows you to savescum if you want to, the game is still challenging and fun to play.
If you like roguelikes, you really can't go wrong with this one, especially for the price (even when it's not on sale!). I've played way too much of this game and don't plan to stop anytime soon. Not until I reach 10,000 km!

I managed to snag this game for one dollar, and even at it's worst it is a couple bucks. And quite frankly it feels like I'm robbing the developers. I've been pretty hooked the last few days on it and expect to push through until I get full completion.
It is a rogue-like game, meaning that it has perma death and randomly generated worlds. You make a character, you pick from some classes and perks, and you push that character as far as it can go. A darkness on the left side of the screen keeps you moving ever forward in your attempt to get as much gear and power before your inevitable death or the death of the endboss. When you die, you gain some points that you can use to unlock more bonuses to choose from and slowly amass a constant storage between characters so you can save some epic items.
There is no real multiplayer other than a Dark Souls-like feature where you encounter the ghosts of players on the same server that benefit you slightly and that you can compete with.
The sound is cute and retro, nothing astounding. The visuals are about Final Fantasy 1 quality but are pretty enough to get you through. The gameplay really hooks me. For some people, you will spend many hours through many characters striving to do better and unlock everything. For others, you'll play for an hour or two. And for the price you pay, you really can't go wrong.

I can definitely recommend this game to anyone that like either Rogue-like games (or games that are random and different every play through) or the classic JRPG using stats like STR and the like.
If you like either of those types of games, give it a try. If you like both, have fun :)
This games has a few strong points to it:
* Limitless Replay Value - Several classes, perks and endings!
* Class Diversity - Each class has it own strengths and weaknesses, choose to overcome weaknesses or play to strengths.
* Few Difficulties - One really predictable difficulty (easy), and the rest start to push your limits and actually challenge you.
* Challenge "Dimesions" - Preset dimesions or worlds with special setting to make the playthough a bit tougher.
As well as its downsides:
* Tends to kill you in the most unexpected and sudden ways.
* Can and probably will make you snap a keyboard or two in half.
* If you can't tell already, these downsides are actually jokes because there are no downsides I can see.
Overall I've found it to be quite enjoyable. With each adventure being a new experience, and several character to play around with.. It's definitely a game I'd recommend.
Considering it goes on sale for less than a dollar often, and even at it's full 3.49 price, it's a fair price to pay for a game that has this much replay value to it. At the price, if you try it and hate it.. you're not out much. Compared to a larger title, you're not paying much and honestly won't regret it as much.

I always welcome new strategy games based on the Battle of Britain or WW2 air combat in general. Unfortunately The Few is disappointing in the end.  I found myself craving more of a simulation than a casual game.
I really disliked the air to air combat portions of the game. It's real time, and without heavy micro-management of your aircraft, you'll often send your pilots in to be slaughtered mercilessly by the Luftwaffe's BF-109s.  Rookie pilots seem to vary in skill between Top Gun and Full Retard.  I've watched several times as pilots will fly around in circles chasing a 109, spraying bullets at empty sky until their guns go dry or you break the endless loop.
You are also limited to only 8 aircraft of your own per air battle.  No Big Wings with multiple squadrons intercepting the German mass raids.  So good luck to you when the Luftwaffe sends 16+ twin engine bombers and 8+ fighters.
The map screen is where the most interest for me is at.  I like the aspect of building and placing airfields, radar, AA guns etc.  However you only get to start with one factory, 1-2 airfields, and ZERO radar stations and AA guns.  I would have liked to have seen a little more inventory at the start of the game.  Playing a game about the Battle of Britain, where the RAF starts with no radar is a little silly.
One annoyance of the game is that squadrons won't land at an airfield if it is "full".  So let's say you have two squadrons based at 2 airfields.  One squadron was in combat and lost a few planes, with a pilot or two bailing out safely.  The remaining aircraft return to base. At the same time your second squadron is also airborne, and the pilots who bailed out from the OTHER squadron start returning to your SECOND squadron's airfield.  Now when squadron 2 returns to land, they CAN'T, because squadron 1's bailed out pilots have gone to squadron 2's base, and it is now too full to land at. That means you lose ALL of squadron 2's planes and pilots because they run out of fuel and crash.  It is flip the table frustrating.
Overall I was disappointed with The Few.  A few little fixes or changes could improve the game, but not enough for me personally to want to spend more time with it.

The game's singleplayer component has four "parts": a tutorial, save the princess, sandbox mode, and challenges. The tutorial does a good enough job of teaching you some basics. It does not, however, prepare you for multiplayer, but more on that later.
Save the princess is the closest thing to a campaign this game has. There is an opening crawl of text I couldn't remember as soon as it finished going by, because it just doesn't matter and isn't all that interesting. You go through an incredibly small number of levels, going from the left side of the area to the right side of the area, until you come across a necromancer and the princess you're supposed to rescue. From what I can tell, you cannot switch classes on levels that don't feature class-switching rooms, and the final level did not have a class-switching room that I could find, so I was stuck with an archer. No matter how many times I tried, the necromancer repeatedly killed me due to seeking spells, and sneaking past him won't let you rescue the princess from her room, either. Finally, I figured maybe I could exit that game mode and load it up again, and maybe I could be a different class. That just set me back to the beginning of the entire Save the Princess "campaign." It wasn't fun the first time, so I wasn't going to play through it again.
Challenge mode seemed to be an endless series of brief levels in which you either have to get from the left side of the area to the right side, kill everything in sight, or a few other objectives. In most of the modes, if you die once (which can be very easy to do), you go to a different map and don't get to try that challenge again. I beat a few of these, and they were okay, but nothing I really had fun with, though.
Sandbox mode just throws you into a map by yourself and you build just for the sake of building, because there don't seem to be enemies or really anything to "do." You just build stuff, from what I can tell. The singleplayer content is very limited.
Multiplayer seems to be the main focus and point of interest for players in regard to this game. There do appear to be a significant number of people playing, and the people I played with seemed to know what they were doing. I asked what I could do to help out on more than one occasion in the 35-40 minute two-team capture the flag mode, which has teams prepare for a few minutes then battle for half an hour, trying to take the other team's flag away (of course).
Most everyone seemed to be building things and mining, though I wasn't sure what I needed to mine or build, and asking didn't help. I had no interest in doing Internet research to know enough to play a 2D 8-bit-looking game, so I figured being a combatant might fare better. I went with playing as an archer and I think I may have gotten one kill in the entire round. Approaching the enemy's base can be deadly, though navigating the weird base layout my own team built got me killed several times when I slipped and fell from atop structures, trying to get down to find something to
to help out. Building amidst everyone else's structures could♥♥♥♥♥♥people off, as I know all too well from people in Sanctum 2 who put towers in stupid places. ;p The second round I played in ended in a tie with neither team even engaging the other in a full-on battle, which is really lame when you spend about 40 minutes playing. =/  The best that happened were little skirmishes where I was a "bad team mate" and ran out into battle like an idiot, getting slaughtered for no good reason.
I wish the tutorial covered more stuff, to help prepare players for that experience. I'm not a big competitive multiplayer fan as it is, so it certainly wouldn't have made me love the game, but I was clueless in multiplayer, because the only builder class stuff the tutorial teaches you is how to use a catapult that's already built, how to build a ladder, and how to build a bridge. I saw people running around with big buzz saw looking things, placing glowy blocks that allow passage for one team but not the other, and more, whilst scampering about in multiplayer, and the tutorial doesn't cover this. The multiplayer is not very newbie-friendly (even less so than other multiplayer games), and though the other players didn't seem to be jerks or anything, they offered no assistance while I was politely asking what I should work on before finally giving up out of being useless in the game.

Background: I have been playing Real Time Strategy since the original Command & Conquer.  WWII is my favorite Theatre of War.  I am also a bit of a history nut when it comes to authenticity.
The Many Faces of PVP:  COH2 has gone through many changes in PVP from the War Spoils Hack to Farming being defined in strange ways by the Dev Team.  Just reading through COH2 Forums there is a cross section of people on both sides of each new Initiative by the Devs (Who by the way are Active and Do Respond on the Forums).  No change goes unnoticed. Units can be a Hard or Soft Counter to other units which is a determination of their effectiveness against any given unit.
Factions:  As of this writing there are a healthy number of Factions and Playstyles.  Playstyles here is a bit different from other RTS Games like C&C. So you choose a Faction (US, Russia, Early Germany, Late Oberk Germany, Britain) You then choose 3 commanders (only using 1 per battle) to further specialize your army or make up for its shortcomings. Some Armies like Oberk Germany are Late Game Powered where as Russia and US are Early Game Rushers.
PvE Campaigns/Theatres/Scenarios: First things first the Ardennes Campaign Pre sale that included the 4th Ranger Battalion that makes the campaign much easier was a mistake and if you delve enough into the forums you'll find a immense number of upset individuals.    Bypassing that There is a huge variety of Scenarios available that the game really needed to help you understand the armies at your disposal.  The Russians and US have a campaign that immerses you into how their armies work but Germany did no so the Scenarios help you grasp how their armies function and ultimately how to Win. Right now the only exception is Britain who does not have a campaign so it is all self learning.
The Code (Realism): So every game has its take on Realism. COH2 uses a series of variables to determine Hit% for units like glancing tank shots off Armor, weapon accuracy, and a Cover system to modify certain values.
Social: This game's community is active and there is a built in function to connect to Twitch.TV in the User interface. Tournaments are held every so often so even though it has been out a while, there is still events to be part of.
Final Thoughts: While not perfect even with all the DLC and changes to PVP,  COH2 is a great game of strategy that is ever evolving with the community and it is worth buying.
As always be sure to watch gameplay videos before buying!

A deep RPG whose strengths are able to overcome its various flaws.
You start by picking one of seven vampire clans, which have their own advantages and disadvantages, slightly different starting stat upgrade choices, and 3 different special powers (some of which are unique to certain clans, others can be found among multiple clans).  Dialogue choices and NPC dialogue can change depending upon the clan you choose.  Especially interesting is the freakish looking Nosferatu clan who are suppose to stay in the shadows.  If you choose them, some NPCS will refuse to speak to you and may even freak out if you attempt to, others will comment on how hideous looking you are.  There're even unique events that happen if you choose the Nosferatu.  Sorry old woman working at the diner...
As a vampire living in a normal society, you have to keep your existence hidden.  If you start sucking blood out on the main streets or use certain special powers, people will notice and you'll get 'masquerade' violations.  As you start getting more and more, vampire hunters will randomly show up to kill you.  If you get too many violations, you'll be executed by the vampire clans.
You earn experience by completing quests and use that experience to choose how to upgrade your character.  You can choose to spread experience around or focus in certain areas.  How you build your character will change how you'll be able to complete quests.  You can choose to focus on social skills, which will make it easier to talk, seduce, or intimidate your way into certain areas.  You could focus on stealth, lockpicking, and hacking to make your way around.  Or you could just beat the crap out of everyone in your way.
The dialogue choices in the game are deep, and there're plenty of interesting & likeable characters throughout the game who will react to you based on how you talk to them.  If you insult some enough, they won't bother talking to you anymore or give you their sidequests.  The game also has several different endings, some of which will only be available if you've stayed friendly with certain major characters.
The game has four major areas you can travel between and freely explore or ignore.  The game finds a sweet point on area size.  Areas are large enough that there're plenty of unique places that you'll want to explore.  However, areas are never so large that you feel like it'll take forever to find/complete all the quests and they can all be completely traversed within a minute or two.
On the downside, the game has several bugs even with the "Unofficial Patch" installed.  I didn't run into anything game breaking, but there was a time or two where I had to change up my choices so the game wouldn't get stuck.  Stealth isn't the game's strongsuit.  Sometimes enemies won't notice you even if you're right in front of them.  Sometimes if they see you or hear you, they'll get stuck in search mode and just stand staring at a spot you need to walk through to get by.  Sometimes you can get them out of being stuck, other times you can't.  For the most part, combat is alright, but don't expect to be blown away.
I went into the game worried that it might be overhyped and not that good.  Was very pleasantly surprised by how much I ended up enjoying it.  If you like deep RPGs, you'll like this game.

This isn't a game as such, it has interactive elements but they are more of an allegory for the development process than an actual game itself.
I think people are under appreciating what this actually is. It's an artistic expression representing the life a an indie developer. Working on the game option is how you come to a "good ending" but alternatively you can chose to witness 7 days of activities, normal things like watching your cat or listening to the rain. Things that might make you stop and daydream for a while. After each day however, the night ensues bringing with it the obscure fragments of discorded sounds and a malaise of out of focus images. Taking influences from every day activities is a ways of formulating ideas. Drawing from everyday life and dreams is how fantastic creations are made, be it works of art, music or games.
It's an important reminder of the developers who have the skills to create but the agony of translating the realms of imagination into a format people can enjoy as a playable game.
Don't be too quick to judge Make it Indie! Try to enjoy it for what it is.

This game on the other hand managed to fix almost all of those problems. The UI still wasn't that great but an improvement nonetheless.
The puzzles were mostly easy and logical, but occasionally I had to roam around the areas looking for the missing items. I had to resort to a walkthrough on one occassion when I couldn't find an item anywhere and I thought I had tried everything. I thought I had already done what I was supposed to do and that the game had told me, that I couldn't do that. After that part it was smooth sailing again.
The game also had a few mini-games, of which some were just logic puzzles. They weren't all that interactive and if you had troubles solving them, you could skip them. I didn't find them that hard, but two of them were a bit more challenging.

Of course the achievements are completely optional, but I don't really see the point in having achievements in point-and-click games in the first place. If they require you to do something completely useless, they just distract you from the story and for story-driven games that's not a good thing.

Once upon a time, the harbingers of divine provenance known as "Kickstarter" and "Greenlight" descended to grace our earth. As the light of their infinite potential shone upon us all, a hundred nerds realized they could make a game exactly like that unique SNES RPG they always loved, EarthBound, and people would pay them for it! (Others thought the same thing about Secret of Mana, but that's off topic.) They did so. And people paid them for it. And all was well in the land of RPG nostalgia.
Except that off to the side, another faction of jaded RPG fans wished those developers been a little more creative, since the very source of EarthBound's brilliance was that it set itself apart from every other RPG at the time with its modern-day setting and overtly humorous tone. For a game to slavishly copy EarthBound is a willful rejection of this. A declaration that indulging in nostalgia, and nothing but, is of greater worth than forging one's own path. (Much the same could be said of all the 'lo-fi surreal horror' RPG/adventure games trailing in the shadow of Yume Nikki, but that's also off topic.)
Thanks to this dismal outlook of mine, I was genuinely taken aback when I gave LISA a chance, and it proved itself different from anything that's come before. This makes it a more worthy successor to EarthBound than any other latter-day game, but there's no need to even call it a successor. LISA stands on its own.
LISA does not conceal its sources of inspiration. But instead of illustrating the same idyllic and urban landscapes as EarthBound or the same endless surreal realms as Yume Nikki, it fuses elements of both into a setting equally unexplored by RPGs, a post-apocalyptic wasteland colored by its observer's insanity and reminiscent of Borderlands or Mad Max. The unhinged individuals you meet in LISA are not (merely) sources of momentary amusement, but hints that something is horribly wrong with the world, driving some to the brink of sanity and others far past it. The mutated horrors you do battle with are not fleeting intruders from the creator's twisted psyche, but creatures dreadfully at home within the setting and the story. And yet that story is not about horror. It's a story about trying to do the right thing.
(As an aside, LISA is a sequel of sorts to a 2012 RPG Maker game by the same creator, retitled as "LISA: The First" to distinguish it from this one. Though it hews far closer to Yume Nikki than its successor, considering that it does have a message and it was made and released for free, I bear no grudge against its existence. It's worth playing if you like that kind of game, but by no means is it essential to enjoy or understand this one.)
Add to that an expansive world which rewards careful exploration and a battle system that also takes after EarthBound, but which has a surprising amount of tactical depth exceeding that of its source of inspiration (and honestly most SNES RPGs) and you've got yourself an RPG well worth playing despite its modest length (befitting of its equally modest price.)
The game has its flaws, many as a result of being (originally) made in RPG Maker. Most settings besides the controls, such as window size, can only be configured via command-line launch options. There are a few areas where the game becomes distractingly choppy, in particular all of the zones containing football players (probably a coincidence.) It's easy to accidentally walk off a cliff when the game is only displaying at a few FPS, resulting in an instant game over, and there could stand to be less 'easy' accidental deaths in consideration of performance issues like these. Or in consideration of 'pain mode,' which can force you to go a long time without saving.
Also, I seem to be in the minority in this, but I wasn't impressed with the music. It makes heavy use of a leitmotif which, to be blunt, failed to make me think anything besides "Oh, it's that melody again... and it still sounds like something I myself would noodle out on the piano while not really trying." Other tunes are forgettable, pure ambiance, or annoying due to their use of obnoxious samples; there's probably only two or three tracks I genuinely enjoyed. Still, I can't say any of it's unfitting for the atmosphere of the game, and it's a small blemish on an otherwise solid and cohesive aesthetic.
And that's all there is to it. Play this game.

A fun and challenging rogue-like with perma-death where you captain your own ship and must use it to cross a dangerous and unforgiving galaxy. You carry information vital to the remnants of the Federation, and have to run from a massive Rebel fleet sweeping the galaxy for your ship. Every time you warp to a new star system the Rebels will take over more of the map, with the goal for each of the eight sectors being an exit beacon. You'll also need to explore as many star systems as possible on the way in order to get enough money to upgrade your ship and buy better weapons. Get it right and you'll have to face a massive boss in the final sector, who will force you to use everything you've learned in the game to defeat.
As you explore these randomly generated galaxies you'll encounter distress calls, slavers, space pirates, supergiant stars and maybe end up on a few side quests along the way. Being more of a management game the combat encounters aren't dogfights, instead you issue the orders, targeting important systems on the enemy ship whilst they try and do the same to you. These fights can get very hectic later on, especially when the enemy start beaming over to your ship. You'll need to manage system power, organise resistance against the boarders (or even depressurise the parts they're occupying) and battle their vessel all at once.
Thankfully, the game allows and even encourages you to pause when giving orders, aiming weapons and even opening airlocks. Potentially game ending situations may have solutions if you study the carnage carefully. Perhaps that massive fire could be extinguished by draining the oxygen from that whole area? Maybe you could lure those dangerous Mantis boarders to your medbay for an unfair advantage? If you de-power life support momentarily, perhaps you could then give your engines a little extra kick to dodge that missile? Maybe you could use the hacking module to make the enemy medbay malfunction and finish off the retreating and injured intruders? Overcoming these tricky situations are some of the games best moments, where you manage to come back from the brink with all your crew still alive - even if your ship took a battering along the way.
FTL isn't without problems - While the RNG factor isn't as high as most new players would think, it can occasionally throw something very tough your way when you aren't ready. The randomness also means you'll be seeing the same events fairly often after a few sessions. On your tenth run or so you'll be tired of hearing distress calls about giant alien spiders and Zoltan scientists wanting to study your crew. It's also a bit lengthy for a game that features perma-death, with most sessions taking roughly an hour to clear the game. Dying to the final boss after such an investment into your ship and crew only to be forced to start over can feel pretty harsh. Luckily FTL is such an addictive game that you'll most likely be happy to hit the restart button and see what this version of the galaxy has waiting for you.
Whatever it is, it'll probably feature giant spiders at some point.
If you want to play a game where you can run your own starship then this is the game for you. You'll feel just like Captain Picard if he was an incompetent bum and a danger to all who serve under him. And you'll probably love every minute of it.

Mafia II is an open world, action, third person shooter game. Where you play as Vito Scalletta, you follow the life of Vito starting out with being caught in a crime and being sent to fight the war, upon his return he finds himself getting wrapped up with his old buddy "Joe", doing more daring and daunting heists.

You are Vito Scalletta, an immigrant from Sicily. You start out with your friend Joe Barbaro pulling small time jobs, eventually escalating to the point where they join a Mafia family and get themselves really twisted up in some crazy adventure.
I found myself often times questioning the ethics of this game, but I found it reassuring to see that some of the characters found themselves questioning their very own actions. It's very easy for a game to paint some glamorous "mob glory days" picture of crime, which I personally would disagree with, but the characters seemed quite genuine in what they said and how they acted.
I don't want to give away any of the story, but let me just say the game doesn't make the "jobs" super easy and make it seem like something you could do in real life. The consequences from various actions where quite believable and made me appreciate, respect, and enjoy the story and this game all that much more.
One more note about the story, there are radio announcers which will respond to dynamic events that happen throughout the game, I reacted differently to different scenarios the second time playing through and the radio announcers also had different things to say about the event. I think that's really cool!
Don't jump into this game like it's a FPS, it doesn't play like one at all. I started the game on Medium difficulty (I thought I was ready for what was to come... I played Just Cause 2, so I wasn't new to 3rd person shooters... not quite.) Here's the tip: Get used to ducking behind cover, towards the end of the game you can only take a few shots before you die.
Movement is quite natural, as always; I use a keyboard and mouse for my play style, you duck behind cover, and there isn't much complication with other buttons, unless you're trying to adjust the radio station in the car (I did that often, once I stopped crashing into stuff).
Vehicle controls: Atratzu hates driving in video games, he has it as a taboo, but he tolerated it while playing this game... and he begrudgingly admits that he's now somewhat "okay" at driving around in this world. Fair warning: there is A LOT of driving around in this game, you drive down to your house, then drive to see Joe, then drive with Joe to meet up with another friend, then drive to pick up a truck, then drive that truck to sell something, then drive back home and go to bed. etc, etc, etc.
Driving isn't that bad, but if you already know you're bad at driving in video games (like me), you might want to consider giving this game a skip.... or walk! but walking would take forever, so I don't suggest walking, just crash into stuff and hide from the cops when they see you fail-driving like me! :D

The achievements are standard for most games, but there are a lot of DLC achievements that I won't be able to get because I don't own the DLC. Achievements are: "Beat the game", "Beat the game on hard difficulty", "Do this neat thing while on this chapter of the game", "Do this neat thing sometime in the game", "Do something you wouldn't have thought to do", and a few grindy "do this again enough times until we give you the achievement".
Mafia II costs $29.99 I spent 25 hours in the game (09/11/14), I still haven't gotten the last few achievements that aren't linked with the DLC, so I'll probably put in enough time to average the game out at 30 hours. so the quality of the game is definitely good. I would recommend buying the game with the DLC, or getting it from a humble bundle (which is where I got mine).

I enjoyed the game, it was slow going, because I didn't like driving, but once I got the hang of it, I stopped following traffic rules and would dart around cars and get to my story location in very good time.
I would recommend this game to someone who enjoys crime-type-games already. It's difficult for me to think of a standard demographic to recommend this game for because it has a big mix in it, you need to drive, shoot, duck behind cover, run, and like hearing a story. If you like some or all of those this game is for you.
To recap:  The story was excellent, The game play was straight forward, driving kicked my butt,  achievements aren't really note worthy, if you want 100% get the dlc, the price was fair for the time I spent. I recommend this game.

I hesitantly recommend Mafia 2. It is a good game at its core, with many problems hindering enjoyment to an extent. Unfortunately.
If we'll start with the postivite, Mafia 2 is a game with enjoyable gameplay and solid gameplay mechanics. It is set in the very nicely rendered Empire Bay, which is quite nice to drive around it. I also liked the characters in this game.
As stated before, I think Mafia 2 has quite a lot of problems, or rather, things I found negative - of which two were indeed major. Story and "open world". Mafia 2 fails as an open world game, it's that simple. The world is only there to allow you to freely drive between and in missions. There is literally nothing else of substance; if you don't consider crunching cars or looking for wanted posters enjoyable. The story in Mafia 2 - while not bad per say, just feels like a put together of every mafia story cliché imaginable. I wish it would have been more original, considering the game becomes very story driven, due a large part to the empty open world.
Furthermore, the game was too easy even on hard - apart from the odd firefight were I felt like I should have brought an automatic weapon and a frustrating and unforgiving fighting system which caused death several times. And it holds your hand too much - oh god how I hate that, though it is probably a consequense of the state of games today. Definitely not specific to Mafia 2.
And oh, don't expect any problems from the police in this game. Honestly, it's quite pathetic. Driving around a corner will lose the cops most of the time.
All in all, if you love mafia stories and like the sound of a story-driven mafia game, don't mind the clichés and it actually being quite linear, you will probably like Mafia 2. It certainly seems most do. And I did too, well mostly anyway.

Mafia II is an action-adventure video game developed by 2K Czech and published by 2K Games. The game is the direct sequel to 2002's Mafia: The City of Lost Heaven. Set within the fictional Empire Bay (based on New York City, Chicago, Los Angeles, Boston and Detroit, the story follows a gangster and his efforts to climb through the ranks of the Mafia crime families. The game is played from a third-person perspective and its world is navigated on-foot or by vehicle. You take control Vito Scaletta, a war veteran who becomes caught up with the Mafia when trying to pay back his father's debts.
The game is set in the 1940s - early 1950s era of Empire Bay, a fictional city based on New York City, Chicago, Los Angeles, Boston and Detroit. There are 30-40 vehicles in the game (45 with downloadable content) as well as licensed music from the era. Many firearms from the previous game return, such as the Thompson submachine gun and Colt 1911, as well as a pump-action shotgun. New World War II-era weapons like the MP 40, the M3 submachine gun, the MG 42 and the Beretta Model 38 also appear in the game. Interacting with objects in the environment involves two action buttons- a standard action and a "violent" action (for example, when stealing a car, the player may choose to either pick its lock or break the window glass), used in context-sensitive situations.
A map is included as in the original Mafia game, but the checkpoint system has been completely overhauled New controls include a cover system that allows you to take cover behind objects (such as generators, walls and large crates) and shoot enemies, rather than just entering an arbitrary crouch pose behind them. The game's cutscenes are created by the game engine in real-time. For example, if you're riding in a car and a cut scene starts, you will be driving the same car with the same condition (damaged or intact) and you will also be wearing the same clothes.
This game is just phenomenal both of the main characters are well fleshed-out and memorable, and the story just comes to an end in an original but shocking manner. Overall I think Mafia II really is a huge improvement over the first game. I highly recommend this game it is just absolutely fantastic there is just so much you can do in the game that you will never get bored. The story is very interesting and fun to play through, the world of Empire Bay is very detailed and has a realistic feel to it. If you're a fan of The Godfather, I am 100% sure that you will love Mafia II just as much!.

One of my favorite games on Steam and the gateway drug into my obsession with tanks.
I'm not gonna lie. As much as I personally love Company of Heroes 2, I realize there's plenty of flaws.
-The DLC/Add ons- To have all the content in this game gets really pricey, even when it's on sale. Unlocking commanders (access to certain abilities and units) takes a lot of grinding, pure luck, or spending real money.
-Unrealistic damage models- In most cases it is likely just the inevitable side effect of game balancing. But there are many things in CoH2 that would make a WWII historian or tank expert raise an eyebrow .
-Similar to the previous mention, due to balancing or plain ignorance, some things in CoH2 are historically inaccurate to varying degrees and it might drive someone crazy (e.g. British Infantry Tank Valentine IX in-game looks like it's doing 25mph when in real life it only went at 15) I'm not super nitpicky about this but I can see that if someone wants a more authentic WWII RTS experience, they might not like CoH2.
-A lot of people already mentioned the Soviet portrayal controversey so I won't go into detail. Again, it's something historians would debate against.
-A do kinda wish the German units would actually speak in German rather than English in an accent with a few German words here and there.
-There's a lot more units to use in CoH2 than in the original game, but I wish there were as many units as in the Europe at War mod for Coh1. Also as of now Japan's army is still not present.
-There's not a large amount of active players these days, at least from what I can tell.
Despite this list of things that might turn people away from this game, I still think CoH2 is a solid game for what it is.
+Great to play with friends- communicate for teamwork and dominate your enemy!
+Pretty good graphics for it's time, though it's arguably demanding...
+Great sound- a big improvement from the first game. Much more accurate sounding weapons and vehicles
+Steam Workshop gives access to many more maps to play on, vehicle skins to use, mods, etc. Expands the game significantly
+Many strategic options and tactics to use which makes each match unique
+Dynamic environment and infantry cover system adds to the micromanagement aspect
+Intense matches- many can end in a clutch victory and scrambling all your forces for the last minute effort to turn the game around will make plenty of memorable matches.
I realize not everyone will like CoH2 as much as I do. Still, I think it's a game worth trying if you like WWII and/or RTS games. Starting with the British Forces standalone game when it's on sale is a good way to try out the game since it's the cheapest one.

The only game where you can sacrifice sheep, cut them in half, put them back together and still win! Divide by Sheep has one of the easiest concepts for a puzzle game but yet still manages to make your brain explode whilst still making you want to keep playing more and more. Although, I can definitely recommend buying this as it is really fun, it still has a few things which could be improved which I will explain in my Pros and Cons.
Pros:
♦ Great Gameplay that really makes you think without making you want to rage quit and never play again (There is the right balance here which makes it fun. It's one of those puzzles you just pick up and want to complete that no matter how frustrating it can be at times you never want to put it down until it's solved)
♦ Decent number of Worlds and Levels (5 worlds, 30 levels a world, this is a good balanced number as it's not too few levels or too many. It doesn't leave you wanting more levels or make you feel like it's just dragging on and on becoming repetitive)
♦ Awesome Cartoon Styled Graphics (This adds a nice edge to the style of the game)
♦ Sound that just fits (Music and Sounds that can be listened to over and over again without sounding repetitive and annoying)
♦ Decent Tutorials and Tutorial style (These are set of graphics/images before the level happens. They are well designed and detailed enough to understand what is going on which is awesome)
♦ Not Repetitive (Each World looks graphically different from the last and incorporates aspects from the previous but adds something new. Also each level is scaled on from the last making each level a unique puzzle in its own. This makes the game fun and not repetitive)
♦ Achievements are easy to get by just playing the game (Really easy to 100% if you can 100% all the puzzles)
♦ Star incentive to keep trying a level until you 100% it (This is a nifty way to draw people into keep them playing a level until they 100% it and get all 3 stars for the level)
♦ Awesome Graphical Story involving the Grim Reaper (For the minimal story in the game, it works)
♦ Decent looking Steam Trading Cards, Emoticons and Backgrounds (Really well designed)
♦ Controls just work (This is because the only thing you have to use is the mouse)
♦ Worth the Price of $5 (At a $1 a world or $1 per 30 levels, you will definitely get your moneys worth)
Cons:
♦ Don’t have to rescue/kill all the sheep, pigs or wolves (I found this part a weird concept as it felt like I was completing a Jigsaw Puzzle for example without using all the pieces).
♦ Ported from Mobile without 100% checking that everything is consistent for the PC version. (I say this as it says "Rate this App" in one of the tabs. This should say something like "Review this Game" and shows the Devs didn't bother checking it/changing it for pc)
♦ Can't skip some cut scenes (Such as Intro Scene)
♦ Some aspects seem randomly introduced such as Pigs (One second you’re just playing with Sheep & Wolves and the next you know you have Pigs. I just felt they could have introduced them better in my opinion)
♦ Menu looks like Mobile still (This isn't a major issue as the game works fine, it would just be nice to have the menu looking more like a PC games to make it look more PC orientated then straight ported from Mobile)
♦ No Graphics or Resolution options (This is annoying if you want to play in different size resolutions or change from FullScreen to Windowed Mode as this is the type of game that would suit Windowed Mode)
Side Note:
♦ Most people complain that this is a mobile port. In some aspects like the menus and options it is. However, if you can look past that fact, it is a really, really well made puzzle game that shouldn't fully be criticised on the fact that the Devs didn't fully change it for PC. With this said unlike some Mobile Ports, the Devs have made full use of the majority of Steam Features such as Achievements and Steam Trading Cards. Therefore, it's not just a straight Mobile Port in all aspects and the gameplay 100% works.
Overall, even though there are a couple of cons, they are only minor things which could improve the game slightly. Therefore, as the game just works, has good graphics, a decent storyline, isn't repetitive and has a decent amount of levels, worlds and content that will keep you thinking and thinking... I recommend you buy this. You'll definitely get multiple fun hours out of this if you are into puzzle games or just want to sacrifice sheep... So buy this and sacrifice a sheep today!

You start by picking one of seven vampire clans, which have their own advantages and disadvantages, slightly different starting stat upgrade choices, and 3 different special powers (some of which are unique to certain clans, others can be found among multiple clans).  Dialogue choices and NPC dialogue can change depending upon the clan you choose.  Especially interesting is the freakish looking Nosferatu clan who are suppose to stay in the shadows.  If you choose them, some NPCS will refuse to speak to you and may even freak out if you attempt to, others will comment on how hideous looking you are.  There're even unique events that happen if you choose the Nosferatu.  Sorry old woman working at the diner...
As a vampire living in a normal society, you have to keep your existence hidden.  If you start sucking blood out on the main streets or use certain special powers, people will notice and you'll get 'masquerade' violations.  As you start getting more and more, vampire hunters will randomly show up to kill you.  If you get too many violations, you'll be executed by the vampire clans.
You earn experience by completing quests and use that experience to choose how to upgrade your character.  You can choose to spread experience around or focus in certain areas.  How you build your character will change how you'll be able to complete quests.  You can choose to focus on social skills, which will make it easier to talk, seduce, or intimidate your way into certain areas.  You could focus on stealth, lockpicking, and hacking to make your way around.  Or you could just beat the crap out of everyone in your way.
The dialogue choices in the game are deep, and there're plenty of interesting & likeable characters throughout the game who will react to you based on how you talk to them.  If you insult some enough, they won't bother talking to you anymore or give you their sidequests.  The game also has several different endings, some of which will only be available if you've stayed friendly with certain major characters.
The game has four major areas you can travel between and freely explore or ignore.  The game finds a sweet point on area size.  Areas are large enough that there're plenty of unique places that you'll want to explore.  However, areas are never so large that you feel like it'll take forever to find/complete all the quests and they can all be completely traversed within a minute or two.
On the downside, the game has several bugs even with the "Unofficial Patch" installed.  I didn't run into anything game breaking, but there was a time or two where I had to change up my choices so the game wouldn't get stuck.  Stealth isn't the game's strongsuit.  Sometimes enemies won't notice you even if you're right in front of them.  Sometimes if they see you or hear you, they'll get stuck in search mode and just stand staring at a spot you need to walk through to get by.  Sometimes you can get them out of being stuck, other times you can't.  For the most part, combat is alright, but don't expect to be blown away.
I went into the game worried that it might be overhyped and not that good.  Was very pleasantly surprised by how much I ended up enjoying it.  If you like deep RPGs, you'll like this game.

Bloodlines is another one of those games I have where it is really difficult to decide whether to say yes or no to a recommendation. Sure it's quite dated by now but even when it was released it wasn't a marvel of first person role-playing games by any means (in fact it barely worked back then). Since its release many, MANY patches have been released by the fan community which almost make it a good game but it falls short because, at its core, it is flawed. You can't fix a games core mechanics.
Combat is awful. It wouldn't be as big of a deal if you could talk your way or sneak your way through all of the game but you can't. There are some missions which force you to fight and if you didn't put enough stats into combat for your Ventrue super-persuadertron sex machine, you will have to start the game over. The ranged weapons don't have any punch to them and melee combat basically involves exchanging blows and hoping your enemy runs out of health before you do. Make sure you put enough points into soak and dodge or you won't make it very far.
Like a lot of the action rpg's of the era, the world is lifeless and hollow which is surprising considering this is the company that made Arcanum. That is more of a technological limitation I suppose but if you look at, say, Deus Ex... they managed to make the world in that game feel alive and active with even less hardware power. Part of it could be that they built the game in the old Half-Life 2 Source Engine which really wasn't made for role playing games... but then you look at Dark Messiah which by no means is a real RPG but they nailed melee combat so much better than Vampire does.
Visually it's not bad for when it was made and there are new texture packs that update it a bit. The hub cities kind of look like 20 different people designed a different part of it and then they sewed it together at the end. Interior areas aren't bad. Sparsely furnished and not very immersive (you're telling me 4 people go to the only club on town on the weekend?) but, again, that's just a sign of the times.
The different dialog choices are where this game shines and you can tell they put a lot of time into mapping out different paths you could take with every major NPC. The script and voice acting are garbagebag, unfortunately, but video games didn't start hiring Keifer Sutherland and Patrick Stewart until later. Listening to a low-talent white actor try to portray a black hoodlum is epic cringe so I guess there's some merit there.
The inventory system is atrocious but like I said, Source wasn't really built for RPG's. Switching weapons mid-combat is dangerous and time consuming. The weapon choices are pretty uninspiring and don't really have much of a variety in what they do. You have guns which all do pretty much the same thing and melee weapons with which if you have the strength for the better one, it's always the one you're going to use.
The variety in dialogue based on which clan you are, your humanity rating, and your skills as well as the variety in quests are really what make this game shine for me. It is fun to play at times... experimenting with what different dialogue choices or actions will do... but it just doesn't have much of a payoff gameplay-wise.
When it's difficult for me to say yes or no to a game it comes down to am I going to have the patience to finish the game. I really doubt it with this one. I've owned it for almost a decade and I've never gotten past the second hub because it's so boring and broken. I know there are a ton of fanboys out there who will disagree and probably give this review tons of "unhelpful" ratings (if anyone even sees it, this game is old AF) but, you know... fanboys are always wrong.

This is one of the many extremely cheap games I got during the Summer Sales (2014).  I got it simply because I knew the trading cards would make up or at least almost make up for the 74 cents I spent.  I launched it, and was ready to let it sit and run for cards, but then, the music started.  The music was wonderful to listen to.  After sitting on the menu just listening to the music for about 30-/+ minutes, I decided I'd actually give the game a try.
I see a menu allowing me to choose my name, class, and additional perks.  Each of the characters has different standard perks, abilities, and gear.  Though it looks like you're going in extremely weak, you get random perks for leveling up and for exchanging levels with the Goddess statues that you find throughout the worlds.  If you choose the right combination of perks for a class, you can be very well set late-game.
The mechanics are simple; Z to attack, X to open the inventory menu, and C to open the grid view so you can aim without moving your character.  You progress to the right of the screen to escape the darkness that's consuming the land.  If you touch the left end of the screen, you die.  There's a boss to fight, and if you kill him, you win (though you will not kill him without leveled gear and good stats).  You can climb mountains and swim in water in exchange for turns and stamina.  You find items scattered about, there are merchants, dungeons, and random villages (of which usually have a person that allows you to save your progress).  It's pretty much a standard turn-based exploration RPG, but is very clever in which they execute certain aspects.
The first game I thought of while playing this game was one of my favorites for the GBA- Pokemon Mystery Dungeon: Red Rescue Team.  The moving mechanics, the menus, the navigation, and the soundtrack all are similar, and very well executed.  This game renewed the genre for me.

-The game has a very high replay value due to the randomly generated worlds and limitless perk combinations.
-The game is very cheap, and is well worth the money.
-The soundtrack alone is worth the cost of the game.  The game is almost just a bonus.
-It's very well set up, with little to no bugs (I have yet to find one)

-People wanting to experience another classic RPG with a twist.
-People that enjoyed the Pokemon Mystery Dungeon series and games similar to it.
-People with limited funds.
-People that just want a game to play that is unlike many of the games here on Steam.
-People unwilling to pay the minute price.
-Idiots.

Story:
There's really not much of a story. You play as a pig and you kill waves and waves of wolves that are after him for god knows what. But this game is really not about the story. Gameplay:

Graphics:

Bottom line:
You really can't go wrong with this game. It's free, can get highly additive and is great fun for anyone looking to kill a few minutes before going somewhere. I say overall i would give it a download and is fun for any type of gamer looking for a fun quick game to play.

-The DLC/Add ons- To have all the content in this game gets really pricey, even when it's on sale. Unlocking commanders (access to certain abilities and units) takes a lot of grinding, pure luck, or spending real money.
-Unrealistic damage models- In most cases it is likely just the inevitable side effect of game balancing. But there are many things in CoH2 that would make a WWII historian or tank expert raise an eyebrow .
-Similar to the previous mention, due to balancing or plain ignorance, some things in CoH2 are historically inaccurate to varying degrees and it might drive someone crazy (e.g. British Infantry Tank Valentine IX in-game looks like it's doing 25mph when in real life it only went at 15) I'm not super nitpicky about this but I can see that if someone wants a more authentic WWII RTS experience, they might not like CoH2.
-A lot of people already mentioned the Soviet portrayal controversey so I won't go into detail. Again, it's something historians would debate against.
-A do kinda wish the German units would actually speak in German rather than English in an accent with a few German words here and there.
-There's a lot more units to use in CoH2 than in the original game, but I wish there were as many units as in the Europe at War mod for Coh1. Also as of now Japan's army is still not present.
-There's not a large amount of active players these days, at least from what I can tell.
Despite this list of things that might turn people away from this game, I still think CoH2 is a solid game for what it is.
+Great to play with friends- communicate for teamwork and dominate your enemy!
+Pretty good graphics for it's time, though it's arguably demanding...
+Great sound- a big improvement from the first game. Much more accurate sounding weapons and vehicles
+Steam Workshop gives access to many more maps to play on, vehicle skins to use, mods, etc. Expands the game significantly
+Many strategic options and tactics to use which makes each match unique
+Dynamic environment and infantry cover system adds to the micromanagement aspect
+Intense matches- many can end in a clutch victory and scrambling all your forces for the last minute effort to turn the game around will make plenty of memorable matches.
I realize not everyone will like CoH2 as much as I do. Still, I think it's a game worth trying if you like WWII and/or RTS games. Starting with the British Forces standalone game when it's on sale is a good way to try out the game since it's the cheapest one.

Divide by Sheep is a wonderfully crafted puzzle game, sporting a beautiful artstyle, well paced  difficulty increases with new feature introductions woven in, and a lovely dose of black humor.
+Art: LOVELY modern-retro isometric style with great and vivid color choices.
+Gameplay: Clever use of "division" makes for a smooth and fun puzzle experience.
+Humor: The concept of the game alone is pure gold, even if the humor is black.
+Difficulty: New features and difficulty both come at a good pace, although there is sometimes inconsistency in said difficulty.
+Sound: The audio design is pretty good, and there are no problems that stand out.
-"Tutorial": The briefing for new features through the use of a single picture can make instructions a little murky at times.
-The menu is slightly awkward to navigate with a mouse.
-Nobody likes it when the "Rate this app!" page stays on a mobile port, but this isn't a huge deal.
+/- It would be cool if there were even more options for how to divide the sheep.
Welcome to the wonderful world of Divide by Sheep, a fun puzzle game where it is your job to fling livestock from platform to platform to ensure the correct amount get to the end.
Divide by Sheep is a puzzle game through and through. There's no run and gun, there's no portals, there's no incentive to click as fast as you can, there's no minigames or leveling up. All there is, is a collection of levels with simple mechanics used in very clever ways, and a goal. That's right, it's just you and your brain. You can take as much time as you need, and retry at any time, but be prepared to do it a lot if you intend to complete every level perfectly.
Never before has it been more difficult to simply kill one sheep, or feed a few dogs. In your quest to (sometimes literally) extract these cute animals, you will have to systematically divide, subtract, and add to the groups of critters. You have various tools at your disposal for doing so, including incineration, lazers that split individuals in half, drowning, replacing (and still drowning,) jump pads that split your group up and send them in specific directions, platforms that swap with each other, etc.
Sacrifice is the name of the game, here, and it's never been more cute or fun. Divide by Sheep starts off relatively easy, and with great pacing gradually introduces more features and difficulty, although sometimes a level or two might be easier or significantly harder than previous ones. All of the puzzles are completely solvable and require experimentaiton or calculation, but never abstraction; you will never have that moment where you have to look up a solution to a puzzle and then go "How was I supposed to know that's what I was supposed to do?" The design of the levels is brilliantly clever and you will find yourself feeling increasingly satisfied with figuring out how to beat them with a perfect score. Get ready, it's really addicting!
The graphics in Divide by Sheep are pretty simple, but very effective. It has a classic isometric style with modern design, with an almost vector art aesthetic. The menu transitions and navigation are smooth and simple, and I love how the UI stays almost completely out of the way, however, I will fault it slightly for clearly being intended for touch devices, and for having a rate this app page. There is also no option to change resolution. There is, however, a button to make the gameplay more child-friendly, which is really cool, and considerate of the developers, because this would be a great mental workout for any kid who can understand the mechanics.
If you've looked at the screenshots or trailers, then you know most of what you need to know about the game's graphics.
So there's not a whole lot to say about the audio in Divide by Sheep, except that I like the music, and surprisingly at no point found myself getting tired of it or completely tuning it out. The sounds are pleasant enough, and there's good audible feedback for actions and navigation. There are also no problems with the quality of the sound itself.
Divide by Sheep is an exceptional puzzle game that will keep you busy for quite a while. It is challenging and engaging but never unfair. The content to price ratio is very good, and I am entirely comfortable recommending the game at full price...in fact, they could have charged more and I would still recommend it at full price. Seriously, treat yourself.
