I adored this game when I played it and consider it the best Daedalic adventure game I've played.  The concept and execution of the story and how you are pushed through the events was wonderful to watch and experience alongside the protagonist.
The premise is a simple one, you are a good little girl at a Catholic school who never speaks or gets the opportunity to speak who is always disciplined harshly and ignored.  The narrator, guides you - the player - through the story by telling you - the protagonist - what to do as a voice in her disturbed head.  Then someone tests a mind control device on her, putting more voices in her head commanding her to do and not do things.  The story grabs you right from the beginning and keeps you playing just to see either what will happen and how Lilli will reconcile all the voices in her head telling her to do this, not do that, argue with each other and make Lilli figure out how to shut everyone up.  It remains rather light hearted and veers into the dark without actually crossing the line.  I'd put it at the level of a Tim Burton film as far as how the story is written.
The voice acting, sound, and artwork are very well done.  Everything has improved since The Breakout.  The characters are all well done, the voice acting in the English localization is spot on.  The translation from German doesn't have so much Germanglish as the Deponia series did.  The art style contributes to the feeling of how messed up Lilli is, right down to the little gnomes censoring all the gore and dismemberment from her multiple murder spree and the narrator explaining it all away as coincidence or happenstance.  The scenery in Lilli's mind in the parts where she tries to break her conditioning are also out there, well done, and develop Lilly and the people around her.
One interesting thing about the puzzles in this game are the mental blocks Lilli has in her head.  As she breaks them, she break one of the rules at a time.  Which rule she is has broken plays a role in solving puzzles during the later parts of the game.
One thing to note, achievements are wonky.  You may or may not get them during your playthrough.  If that is something you find important, there may be workarounds but it's not something I dug into too far.
This is a fun little game about a mentally disturbed girl off on an adventure to help out a friend and clear out the mess in her head.  It's good fun and probably my favorite game in Daedalic's library.

Yes on recommending but you must be very sure in understanding what your walking into.
Lisa is a 2d side screen scroller adventure with a rpg style of combat. Your
character is attempting to rescue your adopted daughter. The interface of the game is simplistic and sleek. You gain companions as you progress, and each has their own classes and skills. You chose the movements your players make, whether it be attack, use a skill, or guard. Save points in the game become more spread out the further you go into the game, and you spend a lot of time getting back to where you died, losing much of your play time or progression.
The game does start to feel grindy, as you are aware of where the enemies respawn, as opposed to jrpg games where the spawns are random. As the level of difficulties continue to climb, you are forced to go back to these spawn points and repeatedly grind out battles in order to get to a point where you can progress. In this, the game does not respect your time. In addition, the combat is repetitive, and you must be sure you like the style of combat or it will get old fast. You do feel as though you are gaining strength, but the enemies require you to put in more and more time farming areas you have already cleared in order to be strong enough to face later zones.

The opening story is very strong, and gives you an emotional connection to your character, and reason for fighting. The music sets the atmosphere beautifully aswell. Unfortunately, with the increasing need for grinding, this game requires a large amount of time to complete. Based on the  story, I can recommend this game, but if you don't have a lot of time to devote to grinding through levels, and are not sure about the combat then I would say to look for other games to enjoy.

FTL is the best semi-roguelike spaceship sim I've ever played. Especially after the Advanced Edition update. It has a great blend of exploration, combat, strategy, simulation, and a strong emphasis on randomness - all of which gives it great replayability. The ever-present enemy fleet pushes you forward, but in doing so it makes you think very tactically about your path and the choices you make. The scrap system is great and likewise forces you to make tough decisions when it comes to system upgrades, purchases, and repairs.
There's a variety of interesting ships and races, and managing your crew is just as rewarding and challenging as managing your weapons and power usage. A good crewmember can bolster your effectiveness, but you have to protect them from dangers such as enemy crewmembers beaming in, hull breaches (and low oxygen situations in general), shipboard fires, and foolhardy choices during random encounters. Likewise there are cases where you can wipe out the enemy crew and defeat them from within even if you can't overwhelm their ship's defenses from the outside - just don't try that on an unmanned vessel. Different ships have their own strengths which you can work to bolster, and weaknesses which you can attempt to mitigate. Your success depends on many factors, including your flexibility and ability to work with what you have. A bit of luck and careful decision-making can make any ship into a powerful force.
The hilarious and well-written random encounters are one of my favorite elements. They help to bring the universe and the various factions within (friend and foe alike) to life. There's great rewards to be had, but often also great risk. However even those risky encounters, if you have the right crewmember and/or ship component available, you can often avoid danger entirely while getting rewarded. There's often more than one possible solution so during the course of your journey you may find yourself seeking a well-balanced ship. Many encounters end in a fight, but if you're confident in your ship and abilities, there's scrap to be had.
It has multiple difficulty levels, I prefer to play on Hard but the choices available gives everyone a good challenge from new crewmembers to old hands. There's a little something for every gamer in FTL. Even the music is fantastic, and always seems to be just right to set the mood. The sheer randomness means no two trips through the galaxy will be alike - but although the game has a large random element, you still are in charge of choosing your path through the galaxy. It's a perfect balance of unpredictability and player choice. The only terrible thing is that there's no plans for a true sequel. I can only hope some day someone will create an even larger game in the same vein as FTL.

This is one of the few games I would recommend to anyone.  A fantastic little puzzler with a simple premise and an execution polished to a mirror sheen.  It's got cute colors and a catchy tune while also undercutting that overbearing sweetness with some violence and a quirky, dark story (simply and unobtrusively told through the occasional quick slide show).
The puzzles escalate beautifully and, while never holding your hand, the game starts you off extremely simply and takes you through increasingly complicated scenarios until, by the end of the game, you have a complete understanding of everything and are able to utilize the game's weird toolset to your advantage.  The puzzles get quite clever and what may be an obstacle to work around in one level will be made into a vital asset in another, simply as an emergent property of the interaction of simple rulesets.
Simply a great puzzle game.

this has to be the BEST point-and-click adventure game i have played thus far.  despite it's childish presentation, Harvey's New Eyes manages to create an expirience of pure comedy and tragedy.  Despite being a sequel to the first game, its able to keep everything in order, meaning even if you don't get the relation or references to the first game it doesn't truly damage the experience.  And no matter what happens, you will find you can never hate your character, Lilli, because she seems so lovable and innocent, even when she does thing that make her seem...dislikable.  The narrarator's voice perfectly fits anything the game offers and retains a comedy style that is simple but amused me on many levels,  all the while showing small bits of just how dark the story really is.  How dark IS the story, you ask?  Play it and find out.

By the time of the third act (and, arguably, the second) the great concept has fallen to the wayside and even the very charming art and sound design are starting to wear thin. Worse, it starts to gain things that are death knells for any good adventure game - bizarre, tedious puzzles and characters that are boring if not completely unlikable.
The game's great sense of humor in its genuinely clever first act means that it's still worth your time, so this is still a recommendation - but it's a tentative one, and it's flaws are enough that you should consider them before you make a purchase.

Yes on recommending but you must be very sure in understanding what your walking into.
Lisa is a 2d side screen scroller adventure with a rpg style of combat. Your
character is attempting to rescue your adopted daughter. The interface of the game is simplistic and sleek. You gain companions as you progress, and each has their own classes and skills. You chose the movements your players make, whether it be attack, use a skill, or guard. Save points in the game become more spread out the further you go into the game, and you spend a lot of time getting back to where you died, losing much of your play time or progression.
The game does start to feel grindy, as you are aware of where the enemies respawn, as opposed to jrpg games where the spawns are random. As the level of difficulties continue to climb, you are forced to go back to these spawn points and repeatedly grind out battles in order to get to a point where you can progress. In this, the game does not respect your time. In addition, the combat is repetitive, and you must be sure you like the style of combat or it will get old fast. You do feel as though you are gaining strength, but the enemies require you to put in more and more time farming areas you have already cleared in order to be strong enough to face later zones.

The opening story is very strong, and gives you an emotional connection to your character, and reason for fighting. The music sets the atmosphere beautifully aswell. Unfortunately, with the increasing need for grinding, this game requires a large amount of time to complete. Based on the  story, I can recommend this game, but if you don't have a lot of time to devote to grinding through levels, and are not sure about the combat then I would say to look for other games to enjoy.

FTL is the best semi-roguelike spaceship sim I've ever played. Especially after the Advanced Edition update. It has a great blend of exploration, combat, strategy, simulation, and a strong emphasis on randomness - all of which gives it great replayability. The ever-present enemy fleet pushes you forward, but in doing so it makes you think very tactically about your path and the choices you make. The scrap system is great and likewise forces you to make tough decisions when it comes to system upgrades, purchases, and repairs.
There's a variety of interesting ships and races, and managing your crew is just as rewarding and challenging as managing your weapons and power usage. A good crewmember can bolster your effectiveness, but you have to protect them from dangers such as enemy crewmembers beaming in, hull breaches (and low oxygen situations in general), shipboard fires, and foolhardy choices during random encounters. Likewise there are cases where you can wipe out the enemy crew and defeat them from within even if you can't overwhelm their ship's defenses from the outside - just don't try that on an unmanned vessel. Different ships have their own strengths which you can work to bolster, and weaknesses which you can attempt to mitigate. Your success depends on many factors, including your flexibility and ability to work with what you have. A bit of luck and careful decision-making can make any ship into a powerful force.
The hilarious and well-written random encounters are one of my favorite elements. They help to bring the universe and the various factions within (friend and foe alike) to life. There's great rewards to be had, but often also great risk. However even those risky encounters, if you have the right crewmember and/or ship component available, you can often avoid danger entirely while getting rewarded. There's often more than one possible solution so during the course of your journey you may find yourself seeking a well-balanced ship. Many encounters end in a fight, but if you're confident in your ship and abilities, there's scrap to be had.
It has multiple difficulty levels, I prefer to play on Hard but the choices available gives everyone a good challenge from new crewmembers to old hands. There's a little something for every gamer in FTL. Even the music is fantastic, and always seems to be just right to set the mood. The sheer randomness means no two trips through the galaxy will be alike - but although the game has a large random element, you still are in charge of choosing your path through the galaxy. It's a perfect balance of unpredictability and player choice. The only terrible thing is that there's no plans for a true sequel. I can only hope some day someone will create an even larger game in the same vein as FTL.

Iron Snout is a free game with colorful and cute graphics, goofy sound effects, and a simple yet addicting game concept.
When I first saw this game, I saw the intro video and fell in love with its simple and cute artwork. Soon after, I installed the game mainly to hear the hilarious sound effects and to throw a few wolves around. About 10 minutes in, I knew that I was going to be spending a lot more time on this game than I had planned.
This game offers a short and helpful tutorial at the beginning that you can play over and over until you master the controls. The controls that this game requires are used only by the arrow buttons. By hitting the arrows in a certain order, you can punch/kick (left and right attack) and spin to attack (upper and lower attack) as well as jump over(dodge) the wolves that are coming at you. After getting used to the controls, you can start to get fancy by grabbing the weapons from the wolves and turn around and use them to defend yourself or to kill them.
As you play, on the upper right of the screen, the game will keep track of how many wolves you killed in that match. After you lose all of your lives (displayed by pieces of bacon on the upper left of the screen), there will be a new screen that appears on the right that will display your match stats. It will display your length of the match, how many strikes you had, how many hits you had, your best combo, your number of weapon kills, your projectile kills, projectiles dodged, items you caught, and most importantly…the number of heads you knocked off.
Iron Snout is both comical and satisfying. I highly suggest giving it a try, especially because it is free! It is for gamers of all ages. Kids will enjoy the simplistic concept as well as the goofiness of the game. Older gamers will enjoy the ability to collect a variety of in game achievements as well as competitively aim for high combo kills. After a long day at work, this game is just what you want to play to unwind. You may even find yourself laughing to yourself and addicted just as I found myself.

This game, for me, is so hard to review, I've struggled for days to find the words. There are some some short bits that are easy to talk about, like it being a short game (1 hour max), it having a beautiful soundtrack, or that the developer is very active and will quickly respond to contact, on Facebook for example, but that's about it. To call it a game just about teenage angst or depression would be wrong and to call it just an 'aesthetic/artsy game' even more so. I think it's two things: it is what it is, with it being a game in which each level (or dimension) represents a dream of the sole maker, from which we can piece certain parts of his mentality and life; but it's also a game with such different experiences that at least one dimension will probably resonate with any player. If this explanation is confusing, I apologize, but it really is what I think of the game. Part just about the maker and his dreams, part about ourselves experiencing it and from it experiencing other things or relieving our own life. It's not a flawless game, for example the controls feel floaty, but it adds to the total experience of being in various dreams, but even disregarding the fact that it was made by one person, it's still a much more enjoyable game than others, partly due to it hitting so close to the player during a playthrough. My personal favorite dimensions were the frame one (would love to play a full puzzle game with that mechanic),; the sabotage level, due to the beautiful music playing, the dimension itself, the eerie tone and the narration; and the let her go level, due to its meaning, the way it was all presented and the music playing. All in all, definitely recommend it to all those who don't just want meaningless action in a game

CoH2 is undoubtedly a solid RTS game set in an exciting period of history. However, as a conciencious gamer I cannot recommend this game to anyone, due to the lack of content in the base game and the seriously insulting amount of DLC and microtransactions that have been crowbarred unethically into this game. Relic Entertainment have lost the plot, and I am sure that we will see more of this behaviour with their future releases (i.e. Dawn of War 3 - get ready for the pre-order bonus, DLC spam and microtransaction triple threat).
Relic Entertainment are a strange company. On one hand, they make solid games with an interesting take on the RTS genre. On the other hand, their business model is an absolute disgrace and they should be ashamed at their efforts to consistently rip their customers off by releasing unfathomable amounts of DLC (which - let's be honest - almost always features content that should have been in the base game). The base game single player missions will be over in all-too-few hours, and they don't offer a great deal of replayability once completed. Sure - the major DLCs add extra missions, but considering the short duration of the original missions its fair to say that they should have been a part of the game from day 1.
The microtransactions that have been added to the online aspect of the game are disgusting and will remind many gamers of ten-a-penny mobile games like Candy Crush. I find it insulting that Relic expect gamers to part with their money for tacky cosmetic items that probably took them all of 5 mins to create, and which certainly should have been in the game from day 1.
Yes, the game is a decent RTS in terms of mechanics and action, but as gamers we need to ask whether we want to encourage disgraceful practices like the overabundance of DLC (featuring content that should have been in the game), tasteless and unnecessary microtransactions and an overall lack of value in the games we buy. I feel that Relic Entertainment are a tainted company and they won't realise the error of their ways until gamers start putting their money where their mouths are.

One of the best video games of all time and one of my eternal favorites.
The world, story and atmosphere are unparalelled.
In contrast to other known Vampire fictions, this one happens in modern day Los Angeles where by luck (bad or good) a steamy night of wild debauchery drains all of your bodily fluids and thrusts you into the world of the undead.
Even though the stiffs are divided between faux-regality and anarchists, they all follow rules of the Masquerade - as a bearded man once said "Sheep need not know that the wolf is here". And by all of them i mean those who are not hairy beasts or necromantic golems of stolen flesh. But that's another story.
A choice of 7 clans offers gameplay more diverse than any class choice in any other game ever could.
You're not just picking your skills and appearance here. You're picking your unlife.
For instance, as a diabolic Tremere you will often find yourself using the blood magic exclusive to your clan to explode your enemies from inside out.
As a deformed Nosferatu, your non-human appearance will force you to live and travel through the sewers, as any human who sees you will surely get a goddamn heart attack triggering 6 GTA Police stars.
Meanwhile as my favorite - an insane Malkavian, you will be a spoiler spewing machine who encounters events exclusive to those not of sound mind and all of your dialogue choices will represent your twisted psyche - in a hilarious way.

First impression:a casual puzzle game requiring arithmetic in a non-obvious way, but  ultimately boring
I'm going to go against the flow of 96% positive reviews here and not recommend this, because after 30 levels I felt bored by it and wasn't motivated to continue. But then I'm no fan of match-3 games either.
The one nice thing it does is that it lets you literally divide sheep in half (you can set the amount of gore from the main menu). Other than that, it's a straight-up puzzler that I think of as a "labyrinth" game: figure out the correct sequence of actions to reach your goal. Some levels have multiple ways to achieve that, but there's no reward for choosing one over the  other. I should also mention that the difficulty ramps up nice and even over the first 30 levels (of 150), and that new mechanics are introduced with little more than a picture hint and an opportunity for the player to research what they do in the next level (that's good).
A small nigle
I hold against it is that the game seems to favor playing by trial and error: when I want to do it perfectly and figure out a master plan before starting to move the sheep around, the game slows me down by making me do each hop (and animation) separately instead of doing broad sweeps: I wish I could swipe a group of sheep over several hops at once, or maybe swipe a circle on a group of islands and have every group make a hop to the neighboring island. Instead it is hop-wait-hop-wait, and precisely because the game avoids such grander mechanics, it's casual. Oh, and if you didn't turn the music off after 10 minutes I admire your patience. [There's more information on the music in the comments.]
I don't regret paying 0.99 for this game (it is 80% off), but I had hoped for something more memorable which it ultimately isn't. Try this one out if you get it in a bundle.

Well, this game is a bit special. I did like it, the concept and all, but it's way too short, with very little replay values. Also, it's quite repetitive, if you actually decide to work on "your" indie game. Just like in real life. Just to say, it took me 15 minutes to get everything, and I spent the rest of the total time waiting for Steam Trading Cards.
It's a really simple game. You have a week, a total of 7 actions, which consist pretty much as "Work on your indie game" or "Do not work on your indie game". Obviously, it's not /that/ obvious, but with little to no thinking, it's almost as obvious.
If you decide to work, you get a little puzzle game that's quite simple at first, getting harder day after day. While, if you decide to have fun, you get treated to a short video.
Basically, it's "video or logic game". You also get to see a video every night.
Thought, I do have to give the game some points, since it gives a great moral lesson: "You can do everything you want, if you actually spend time towards your goals."
Even if it's repetitive, boring, uninspiring, if you work toward what you want to do, if you work to do what you want, you only need to invest time in it, and eventually, you'll do it. Maybe not in a weekend.
You can actually finish the game in 5 minutes, since the author thought about making a skip video button, which is sometimes a real time saver.
This game is quite original, there's some place for improvements, but it gets bland and repetitive way too soon.
If you're an achievement hunter or someone who wants a really cheap game on steam, this is the game for that.

First of all, this game is unforgiving. If this statment puts a bad taste in your mouth, then this game is not for you. However, if what I just said doesn't bother you at all, then you just might have found a gem worth keeping.
This game is a rougelike, so don't expect to have all the pieces of the puzzle when you first begin. (Google "Rougelike" if you don't know what that term means, trust me it helps.) Your first dozen (or few dozen, depending on your luck) playthroughs are more than likely going to end in failure, and the world will be doomed without you. However, as you discover strategies that work (and ones that don't) things will start to turn around. Still, odds are you will die more times than you will reach that happy ending. But that's the thing, the game doesn't stop at the ending. Multiple endings add to replay value, as do multiple objectives that you don't even know exist when the game begins. Add in the fact that worlds are randomly generated, and you will never have two playthroughs that are quite the same (aside from multiple deaths, as that is always a possibility).
In short, this game will give you back everything that you put into it. If you don't give it a chance, you will have wasted your money. Fight through the first dozen deaths and learn from your mistakes, and this game will leave you addicted like it has done for me.
You see all these indie-like games on Steam. This is one of the few that are good.

One Way Heroics is an open-world roguelike.  You explore the world from left to right, running away from the darkness that will literally kill you, so be afraid of the dark.  This is a good feature as it prioritizes movement (such as if that chest behind me is worth getting) rather than just attacking.  Combined with terrain effects, like evasion rising in forests, this is a must-have for such a low price (on sale for 87 cents).  I have only seen movement set up in such importance in those grid-based strategy rpg's like Final Fantasy Tactics.  The random story loading up during the first load is an excellent idea too, and it is pretty decent.
You have various classes to try out for replay value.  The only issue I have with this game is that hotkeying isn't really mentioned.  I would prefer to have a hotkey for a few items or skills, but that isn't a big deal.  Neither are the tiny graphics because it can immerse you on your very first play.

Good roguelike for less than $1.  More replayability than many AAA titles.  Some may call it the second coming of christ, but in the interest of not offending any Jews, I'll just settle with calling it GOTYAY.

After playing KaG for a about 20 hours here's what I think. KaG is a great mixture between a medieval strategy game and Terraria. Though I do think my favorite part of KaG is watching a good defense crumble.
The community on the other hand is quite small. It's not small enough to make the game dead, since there is always a hectic battle to join with around 8 or more players, I just think it could really get some more people in there playing it.
Also the battles themselves are not for people with little time. They can last anywhere from 5 minutes to 3 hours depending on how good the builders are.
All and all KaG is a game you should totally but if you love medieval warfare or are a fan of building games.

I recommend this game to any fans of the RTS genre. It is very fast paced yet requires complex thinking and strategy. It differs from Star craft and Dawn of wars "blob" ( massed infantry attacks ) style of play with the ability to cover, and garrison units. Microing your untis effictively while simultaneously teching up the production trees enables you to live out your WW2 tactical fantasies; smashing back your opponents advances with well placed troops , vehicles and fortifications instills a sense of pride as you capture points to secure more resources and further advance the battlefield and up the command ladder to access passive buffs, special skills or the ability to call in special units. There are many diffrent commanders to choose from, and unlock. As well as unique camoflauge skins for vehicles and passive buffs for your army. There is an In-game store to purchase some but, everything can be earned by competing in matches against players or the computer ( requires an internet connection to earn XP{ loot pts}) *** THIS IS NOT A PAY TO WIN GAME*** Although there are up to three passive buffs called intel that you can equip at a time. The advantages they give are slight , and many people stack all three on one unit type effectively limiting their ability to gain subtle bonuses across the board in favor of getting a bonus on one unit type- they are now reliant on to make the most of. In short choose your bulletins and commanders wisely. The starting ones are pretty good. This game is still being updated and patched as of writing this review. There are lots of tournaments and plenty of active players to keep it competitive and interesting. If you dont like the multiplayer scene ; there are various scenarios and mission sets to do solo or with a friend or Computer ally , and purchasable ones as well. The only thing missing from this game is the japanese or Italians but I think they will add another AXIS faction to match the Allies 3. Check this game out , you wont be disapointed.

I can't even begin to talk about LISA: The Painful RPG and how amazing it is. No game ever existed has leaved me with such emotional devastations. While I have never cried watching/playing a work of fiction, LISA got damn ♥♥♥♥ing close.
The game starts off with Brad Armstrong, a formal martial arts teacher and now a drug addict. This is a world where a certain incident known as The Flash has wiped all women on Olathe(the name's from a real city in Colorado and pronounced 'o-layth-uh'), and has turned it into a wasteland. Brad and his buddies finds the only baby girl in the world, and while Brad's buddies think it's good to bring her to Rando, the most powerful warlord in Olathe, Brad sees her as his 'second chance', as he had an abusive father and a little sister called... well, Lisa. And she killed herself and all that, so Brad feels guilty. Brad names the girl 'Buddy' and starts raising her. Events transpire and Rando eventually gets ahold of Buddy. This is where Brad starts his journey.
The world of Olathe is surreal. Really surreal. The surrealism in this game is out there, and to the max. There's a character that just says 'I like big butts... They never lie.' and serves no other purpose whatsoever. There are so many great moments in LISA that happens because of this surrealism. LISA really is heavily inspired by EarthBound in this aspect, and its turn-based gameplay. Only thing that this isn't inspired of by EarthBound is its much more mature humour, and the absence of the rolling HP thing.
LISA isn't all fun though. It's called The Painful RPG for a reason. Throughout the game, you will be given harsh choices like A. Get ♥♥♥♥ed in the♥♥♥♥♥ B. Get ♥♥♥♥ed in the mouth. C. ♥♥♥♥ yoursef. What's better? Well, C seems better, but it actually just gives you both A and B, or just gives you a game over. Than B sounds better, but it only SOUNDS better. Having your arm chopped off definitely SOUNDS better then killing off one of your party members, but it still ♥♥♥♥ing sucks. LISA transits this moment of surrealism and 'wat just happned m8' to 'oh... ♥♥♥♥...♥♥♥♥♥♥.. that was... oh god' pretty well. You can never tell if the game is trying too hard.
The best part of LISA, bar none, is its storytelling. It's a RPG Maker game, yet it still tells its story in a way that lives such impact. The game does such a great job at telling a story by not telling. It never forces the story on you, instead you see it and understand it. There are many 'battles' that are just meant to be something where the game will try to tell something to you, but it just tells it in a turn-based RPG battle. THIS is how you tell a story. Take advantage that it's a video game. Push narrative into the gameplay.
An example. Brad suffers from drug addiction, more specifically to 'Joy'. It's a drug that 'makes you feel nothing'. Because of this, Brad suffers from the 'Withdrawl' status effect now and then, which decreases all of his stats tremendously. ...does the game ever tell you this fact? "Brad suffers from Joy addiction! You better take some Joy, ♥♥♥♥♥!"? No. It does say 'Brad took some Joy.'. Does it tell you what it is? It tells you that it's a drug. But the way it emphasizes that Brad is indeed ADDICTED by it by telling it in a gameplay-form, and forces you to take them yourself was done perfect.(you shouldn't take them though... why? just don't.)
There are about 30 party members in this game. ♥♥♥♥ing 30. All of them have their advantages and their weaknesses, and sure as hell are funny. You can meet Harvy Alibastor, a Fishman lawyer, or Nern Guan, a self-proclaimed 'historian'. There are some OP characters(psst psst birdie psst), but trying out different combinations of them are definetely very fun. This aspect you could say was inpired by Chrono Cross, where there are also many party members that just says 3 or 4 lines then joins your party. Like Chrono Cross, most of these party members are completely optional.
Oh God the soundtrack. Don't even get me STARTED on it. Just buy it.
. 8 bucks. BUY IT. ♥♥♥♥ING DO IT. Two hours worth of just amazing pieces. It keeps on tone with the whole surrealism theme, but has diversity as well. 'Brawlin'' is a hip-hop sounding track, while 'Burning Sunset' is a classic RPG Maker-style 8-bit electronic track. Then there's 'Die! Die! Die!', 'Boy Oh Boy' and 'Work Harder' and their surreal-sounding tunes, and 'Praise Wally' and 'Blood for Sex' for some creepy♥♥♥♥♥shit. My personal favorite is 'Goodbye Baby' and 'Goodbye'. 'Goodbye' is a much darker-sounding remix of 'Goodbye Baby', though both conveys the entire tone of the game well.
Are there even anything bad about LISA? Kinda. The game is two-dimensional outside of battle, and of course, you get to climb many many ropes. But those many ropes are often placed right near a cliff where you can fall into a pitch blue 'GAME OVER' screen. This♥♥♥♥♥♥is definetely annoying in the 'Pain Mode', where you can only save at checkpoints once. You also move pretty slow without your Bicycle, which you get probably about 2 hours into the game. A lot of people were put off by this.
The game is pretty open-world. At least for a JRPG inspired game. There are four 'main-areas', with them having mandatory 2-3 other 'side-areas' and 3-4 optional side-areas, with the exception of the the final one which is pretty linear(the game also gets really dark at that point). Because of this, there is never a sense of direction, and while I though that was cool, people who are pretty bad at directions were kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off by this. You also get to backtrack sometimes to get optional party members and events, which just confuses them even more. Also, if you're not fond of RPGs in general, the gameplay can get really repetitive.
Lastly, this game is made on RPG Maker. RPG Maker games are kinda notorious for being really easy to make, and for being pretty bad. And by that, I mean♥♥♥♥♥♥ The technical limitations were pretty bad here. The fullscreen support is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥, and in general, the game squeezed out everything that the RPG Maker had. Austin Jorgenson(AKA Dingaling. also goes by the alias of Widdly 2 Diddly), the sole creator of LISA, has 8000 ♥♥♥♥ing hours on RPG Maker VX Ace on his Steam profile. This man over-worked, I can tell you that.
The real theme of LISA is abuse, addiction, and "Did I do the right thing?". The story of this game will be stuck on your mind for good few weeks. If you weren't satisfied by this adventure, LISA: The Joyful, a sequel/DLC is a must buy. It follows Buddy after the events of The Painful RPG and explains many of the plot holes and such.
LISA is a hell of a journey. Literally, it's a 'hell-hole RPG', as Austin puts it. This game is in my opinion, the game that shows how far come we've come for storytelling in video games, and in fiction in general. It will live a bitter taste in your mouth, but you will still laugh along with it in many other parts anyways.
This game is a MUST BUY for anyone who can tolerate this kind of surreal and kinda offensive type of humour. Watch the trailers, and maybe a bit of gameplay and also on EarthBound, and you can get a feel for this game. If you look like you can tolerate it, just buy it.

One Way Heroics is a fun and easy to understand approach to RPG rogue-likes with features to help the player extend his own gameplay from a single playthrough.
We choose from a variety of classes with pickable perks and go on a random adventure.
Encountered by enemies and time itself, we wander across endless open plains and underneath mountain ranges, find dungeons with lots of danger and treasure, find cities to sell our useless stuff to NPCs and head further east.
This gameplay routine might sound boring and stale but is actuallly a really fun activity the more you play.
The charm lies in the different classes and the different approach of each class.
You can "level up" your class globally in a way and earn Hero points at the end of each game (regardless of victory or death) and put these points to good use by buying additional perks or classes and more slots of a globally shared item storage that all your future characters have access to. Give yourself a headstart if you start to struggle.

Gameplay is nothing special, but it's functional. You can stealth, speech, shoot and melee your way through any situation. It's pretty varied. I'm not going to say you can use any of these in any situation, but the flexibility reminded me of DeusEx, and that's always a good thing.
The writing, however, is what makes this game into something really special. Dialogue options that only like 5% of the playerbase would ever get to see on one playthrough are actually the norm here - yes, the writers were actually that dedicated.
Every character is incredibly interesting, there's a lot of funny, bizarre and unique situations in every hub and overall it's just been a while since i've found a game that made me forgive it's general mediocrity because it nailed a few aspects so well. You need patience if you're going to buy this game. It's worth it. I'm really hoping they revisit the Vampire: The Masquerade universe at some point; maybe with the new world of darkness?

King Arthur's Gold is another sad story of an independently developed game that had the potential to become a staple in everyone's library: a resource-lite multiplayer game that was easy to pick up and learn in less than an hour (but master after a few hundred) with a very simple goal and addicting gameplay... yet relegated to obscurity due to a multitude of bad developer decisions that stemmed from lack of experience and arrogance.
After convincing a multitude of complete strangers to join a community restricted server and playing just for fun, I found many people enamored with just how simple and straightforward the game was. There were a number of complaints as to how the game usually flowed and cries for balance, but that's just typical for a strictly multiplayer game.
But then they scrapped the original engine for the one you see in this commercial release.
It wouldn't have been so bad, but the best way I can describe transitioning between the old and newer engine is how it felt switching from Melee to Brawl: one felt tight and responsive, the other felt floaty and imprecise.
Despite community outcries for changing how the entire game felt, they refused to listen and had the gall to say the knew what's best for everyone, while snarkily insulting anyone who thought otherwise. Many people felt cheated, as they bought the game for what it originally was and instead got a different final product.
And so people left.
The community was already divided in two before the engine switch. With the engine update, Premiums decided to move onto the newer game, taking the same servers F2Ps played on with them. And with no place to play on, a huge portion of the community died.
My advice? Don't buy this game, even on sale. There's no worse multiplayer game than one with a dead community. Thanks Geti.

Problems:
BALANCE:
The germans are much better.

PRICE:
Even if the game is on sale the value propostion is very bad. Buying the game is really only buying one quarter of the game. It will take 100 to 120 dollars to get your desired faction and all the commanders you need to be competitive.
PAY TO WIN:
Any game that holds gameplay affecting elements behind a pay wall is pay to win. This game locks all the best commanders behind a paywall, and you must buy them to play as well as someone with them. These commanders almost never drop, but the system is there to give the appearance of a fair game.
COH1 IS BETTER:
pay to win is still in COH1 but it is far less significant. Also, the balance is better, and the value proposition is much better.

Space fans prepare yourself for another great game! FTL is a 2D, space adventure game where you carry information that is vital for the Federation. Your mission is to survive and travel to the Federation base and pass on the info before you die. On your journey you encounter pirates, rebels, mercernaries, slave traders, shops, and various races of aliens as well as the common humans. You can outfit your ship with different systems and technology that have different uses and provide different strategies. E.g ion weapons disable sytems for a short time, beam weapons damage multiple targets and rockets/bombs ignore shields. Different races have advantages too, so choose ones that suit you, some have exceptional engineering skills, others have better combat skills. All in all, the game is great fun and even if you're not into space games give it a chance. It'll surprise you, you'll be determined to make it to the end and unlock all of the ships. As a bonus it has a free DLC that comes with it so be sure to give it a try. 10 out of 10 would shoot lasers again and also 10 out of 10 would watch Star Wars again. :D

FTL: Faster Than Light. Is perhaps a very intriguing space game. It has a simple premise yet it's
far more than just "reaching the finish line" you take charge of a ship and crew (which by the way you can customize and outfit to your specific wants and needs. As you try to outrun a galatic meance and reach the federation. Simple right? Well that's the beauty of it. As the gameplay shows you have a lot of RPG elements
To clarify on what exactly on those RPG elements:
You can make choices such as saving a ship coming under attack by a pirate. or investgating a planet. Be warn however, some of these choices can backfire and/or have major consequences. You can name your crew, ship and customize your ship to whatever suits your wants and needs. Do you decide to stay and get valuable cargo? Or jump to the next sector. Staying in a sector when the "enemy threat" decides to consume the sector ramps of the diffculty from "okay having fun?" to "Okay having fun? Good!....now time to die".
Also what's amazing about this game is just the small details. Like for example, if your fighting
against an enemy ship in an asteriod field. The asteriods play an effect. That both helps and hindersyour chances of winning. And as the game progresses forward the game get's harder as you go deeper and deeper into each sector.
I want to really tell all about this game. But to simply put. If you love a simple space game with RPG elements mixed with tactical combat. This game is for you.

If you would've told me a day ago that I was going to play a game all about math, division, and adorable little animals being cut in half, I would've called you crazy. Even more so for saying I was actually going to ENJOY it, of all things. That was yesterday. Today we have Divide by Sheep, a hilarious little puzzle game that is full of charm and some very challenging puzzles.
Now I feel before we move any further, we should really note something. This title is extremely App friendly in design. If you are somebody who gets easily bugged by that type of thing, you are going to grind your teeth as you gain 3 stars and see a complete lack of options menu. With that aside, I love Divide by Sheep. The game is disguised beautifully, but its all about math and putting numbers in the proper order to get the outcome you want. Using sheep, pigs, wolves, lasers and more, you will send the adorable little animals on their voyage to the hands of Death.
That's right, Death is lonely and wants a friend, but I mean Death is adorable, who wouldn't want to be his friend?
Small plot aside, the aesthetics and charm of Divide by Sheep is what got me hooked. This is incredibly important aspect to the game, otherwise it's just a math puzzle game. The dark humor is what kept me smiling, even when I got frustrated. So much so as a matter of fact, that if you are not a fan of math, you may not enjoy this title as much. You must bounce sheep or an assortment of animals to a raft that requires a specific number. Sometimes it's easy and sometimes it can be incredibly complicated. The difficulty scales rapidly and there have been more than a few times that Divide by Sheep has made me scratch my head and made my eyes go cross. More elements are introduced to complicate matters, such as limited number platforms, wolves that eat sheep, laser grids that divide sheep hilariously in half, and bouncing platforms that send your helpless animals flying.
That isn't to say that Divide by Sheep is too hard to beat or play though. If you can match just one of the numbers you are allowed to progress to the next level. Getting stuck is never an issue, and the challenge is one you set on yourself. Go for three stars or just say screw it and come back to it later, just like a real math test. Divide by Sheep has a large assortment of levels all with the 3 star challenge. The aesthetic of the levels does change from grassy halls to frozen tundras but for the most part, level design is always the same. Some floating platforms, which is your puzzle, and a raft to put X number of animals on.
On occasion after beating a number of levels, you are rewarded with an adorable piece of art, that usually explains a new up coming element in some manner.
It really is hard to find a fault with Divide by Sheep, because it's a very simplistic game. That in itself may be an issue though, because sometimes lets face it, math sucks. Mind you, this is why I'm a writer instead of a Architect or something that actually pays. But I digress. The point is, if Divide by Sheep had a fault it would be that it's a one trick pony. It doesn't exactly claim to be anything else than what it is, so this isn't a fault to the game. You should be more than aware what you're getting into if you buy this game. Aside from that and the App like nature of Divide by Sheep, it's bug free and is very fun to play. The replay value comes from trying to get 3 stars on every level, which unless you're very clever, is going to be long and challenging.
The options menu for the most part is non-existent, however there are parental controls if you wanted to leave the messy parts of the game out, like sheep being cut in half and leaving bloody messes. This feature while not incredibly important, is rather nice to be included and makes this game also a great learning tool. The music and soundtrack of Divide by Sheep are absolutely adorable and jaunty, matching the games almost carefree tone. It never really got grating on my ears or did any painful repeats. The music changes from area to area of the game thankfully so there is always something new to listen to around the corner.
I have played plenty of puzzle games but none that actually made math fun for me. I am not huge fan of Sudoku or other games of its nature. That in itself is an incredible compliment to the games level design. After being stuck on a level for a while and finally beating it, you get the "aha!" feeling that is quite addictive. Divide by Sheep may not be incredibly innovative but I haven't seen many games like it.
There are some areas that Divide by Sheep could've added a little bit more to make the game user friendly. There is no hint button or any hand holding whatsoever, so if you bang your head against the wall, you are heading to Youtube or a forum for help. While there is a quick start over button, a undo last move button would've been very nice for some of the more complicated puzzles that involved many steps. While these puzzles are rare they do happen, and having to start completely over again left me a little wanting.
Divide by Sheep is available on Steam and mobile markets, the price is representative of that fact at $4.99. This makes it an absolutely steal if you love puzzle games, plus hey, Steam achievements are always fun. You can always nab this game for on the go at $2.99 on the iTunes store. This game makes a great traveling companion. So if you are in the market for an incredibly adorable puzzle game that is going to give you plenty of bang for your buck and more than likely make you scratch your head, I can't think of a better game than Divide by Sheep.

I have never played another game that's been quite as immersive as FTL. If you haven't played it, you might dismiss it as some overly complex 2d strategy game that you'll never get the hang of and quit in frustration. Trust me, it's more than that.
You assume the role of captain on your very own starship, which you're able to build on and customize as you go. Sounds easy enough, right? Nope. After travelling through beautiful and randomly generated galaxies with your loyal crew, the soundtrack will permeate your soul and appeal to your adventureous side just a tad too much. You'll make a command blunder and lose part or all of your crew who, by this point, feel like family. You'll be lucky to escape with anyone at all. You'll lie awake at night, kicking yourself for your moment of indescretion. You'll run through all the options that you could have taken but failed to do so. Eventually, you'll come to terms with your grief and return to the game to start over. Maybe things will go better for you this time. In time, you'll become a battle-hardened leader with a strategy and a passion for victory.
Being a fan of Star Trek, nothing else has better helped me to feel the pressures and uncertainties faced by Kirk and Picard. This game practically generates Star Trek plots for you to tell your friends (and perhaps embellish the truth to make you look like you knew what you were doing facing those Mantis instead of fleeing). This is my favorite game and it's a true masterpiece. I highly recommend it.

What is funny is as you begin this game you REALLY don't know what you are getting yourself into. The swell of emotions you get from this game is almost overwhelming, so I decided to summarize what I believe this story means.
WARNING: THIS POST CONTAINS SPOILERS
This game was a beautiful example of how most people perceive life, ranging from a sunshiny walk on the beach to a scary backstage haunted by a ghost and a music box with legs. Steven Harmon took his most vivid dreams and made a beautiful game displaying the beauties and stresses of long adult life. as the story begins, we have the first five levels of seemingly normal memories, transformed into dreams. as you get farther into the game, Steven's real heart reveals itself. he starts to paint darker pictures, starting with the level 'Nobody Wins' (Witch I believe it's level 7?) where he explains his dislike for Bull Fighting by saying "The people get mauled, and the Bulls get shot". After that it spirals down where he expresses his felling loss, sabotage, and anger. One of the levels that really got to me was Self-Destructive Portrait where he describes what it feels like to be angry at the world for throwing criticism at people who work so hard, and honestly, I cried while watching the video for the first time.
But out of all of this, my favorite part was when the DLC pack was released and the game was updated, when on the final level a second doorway appeared (witch BTW, took half an hour to get to XD) and it led to a final level, not accessible from the level page. it was snapshots of steam reviews of people criticizing him, even in the good posts. ahead of you you are faced with a giant wall, too tall to see with a giant doorway. as you pass through the doorway everything turns bright white and you see flashes of all the people that have supported Steven Harmon throughout this whole thing. Ahead of you is a glowing door, and it sends you to the cutscene that the "Last Level" would have if you got to the other door.
What I take from this ending is,
You will do things in life,
And people will criticize you.
But if you put your heart an soul into your work,
You will find your supporters outnumber them 10 to 1.
So do what you love
Do what makes you happy
Keep Dreaming.
Steven, if you read this, I love your game and i implore you to never give up on your work. you will have supporters in whatever you do next, I'm sure of it.

EDIT: Living in the shadow of bigger games, my hours played didn't go that high. But it's like homemade food. You always go back to it and it always makes you smile. I bought the DLC today and I am definitely gonna give it another go.
To the team who made this game: I wish I could shake your hands. This is just great. Just great.
Now, to the rest of the people, who want to know if they should buy the game. YES. DEFINITELY YES!
The price is ridiculously low. I got this game by selling trading cards.
The graphics are "fine". I don't know the engine this game was made on, but if I had to guess, I would say RPG Maker VX Ace (I use that engine for my works, and the graphics are pretty close) with a loooooot of custom scripting. Another reason this game is so good. A lot of work has been put on it, and I can see it.
So yeah, the graphics. They match the gameplay perfectly and they don't "try too hard" to impress. They are pretty, they are simple and they are great.
The music is pretty good too. Again, the music matches the gameplay and the whole atmosphere.
The story. Well, WHICH one? I mean, every player, has their own experience. YOU choose your path. YOU choose what to do with the guy or girl you are controlling. YOU can go around and kill everyone. Or YOU can be the hero and kill the Demon Lord. And on top of all, it's Rogue-like. That means, that everytime you play, even if you try to do exactly the same things, you will have a different experience.
This game has humor. When you "socialize" with your "companion", a smile on your face is guaranteed.
The only thing that I kinda hoped I could change, is the speed the darkness advances. The speed is perfect, don't get me wrong, but I would love to mess around a bit.
All in all, great game, I bought it for 0,74 euros and I would buy it even if it was 7 euros.

This game is a racing platformer. You use a racecar to traverse platforms. You get a boost ability, and wings (I think?) to slow your descent. The appeal is the challenge. You can't just recklessly use the boost meter. You have to conserve your fuel until the next checkpoint (where you get more fuel) and make sure you're not going too fast or too slow. The game's levels get increasingly harder as you progress the game, and this is perfect as you become familiar with the game.
There's around 25 platforming levels, but there's also time trials where you try to complete these in a certain amount of time which are another 25 levels. These are lighter on the platforming, and more about racing through a track as fast as you can.
Not much to say about the game, but it's genuinely fun.

Speaking as someone who has had this game on their trusty iPod Touch since 2009, I can definately say that this port is well worth buying. In fact calling it a "port" from a mobile game from 8 years ago would be an insult, and that's the last thing I want to do to these developers.
If you don't know what Jet Car Stunts is, the best way to describe it is that it's like Super Meat Boy mixed with Mario Kart, if all the levels in Mario Kart were Rainbow Road and you're alone and the only items and obstacles are physics. The main part of the game focuses on getting your jet powered car to the end of a course in the sky, complete with loops, jumps, hoops and all sorts of things you have to pilot your car through. It's this simple game mechanic that makes it so addictive, mixed with the rewarding controls and physics, which I'll get onto. Some of these levels are taken from the mobile game while a lot of them are new or sort of "refurbished" maps. If you're like me though, you'll often restart in a semi-perfectionist-rage as soon as you crash or fall out for a complete gold record, which I do and have been doing since I played it on my iPod.
You will pick up the controls and the physics incredibly fast, although I've known the physics of the game for a while so that might just be me, as I feel they have given a few tweaks to them. However it was a learning curve to understand how this game controls on an Xbox controller. Not to say that's bad, as mapping the boost and the air brake to the triggers (very important features to controlling your car while airborne) is ingenious and something I didn't know I wanted until I tried it. In the mobile version you had on screen buttons to control them, and now they're set to the triggers, it allows you to finely control how much of your precious afterburner you use, or just using enough of your airbrake to slow you down just enough or if you're on the ground you can use it for some high-speed-brakingu dorifto (drifting feels waaaaay too nice in this)
The visuals get an overhaul too, now they have a sort of cartoon-y artstyle, which I like. It looks better than it did on the mobile versions. While it's more subtle and doesn't impact the look of the game that much compared to its older version, it looks good enough. It also has a few more sounds thrown in compared to the older versions, which are nice too.
The only gripe I've got with this is that the camera is a bit too close to the car, making it hard to aim yourself into the parts of the course at times.
Other than that the game is flawless and deserves you're attention, sale or not.

TL;DR: Get this game if you enjoy Trackmania, F-Zero X/GX, Burnout, throwing your controller in a fit of childish rage, or the batmobile chace sequence from Batman Begins.
Jet Car Stunts is not a traditional racing game. It's a test of patience, skill, and anger management. There is no such thing as 'easy' here. The difficulty starts at 'Intermediate' and quickly proceeds to 'melting your face off'. Yeah, I know the game says 'very easy' in the menus, but it's not. I'm reminded of F-Zero GX in terms of difficulty, and to some extent gameplay. Whomever coded the physics engine knew exactly what they were doing. The physics are solid and consistant. The car initiates a drift seamlessly and predictably every time you expect it to. Driving this car makes me feel like an unholy fusion of Batman and Fujiwara Takumi. Flying this car makes me feel like a bullet fired out of a gun, at least until I hit a floating cube or the side of a mid-air hoop and disintegrate, muttering darkly as I restart the entire level from the beginning. That said, starting the level over is actually extremely quick and painless, moreso than restarting from checkpoint. Not only is there no loading screen to start over, but you don't have to wait for the countdown. It's more of a suggestion, really. just hit the gas to bypass the starting countdown and you are Drifting with delight in mere seconds.
This game does have its flaws however, with little content,little reason to ever restart form a checkpoint, and stark level designs. But my biggest issue is how timing and replays were handled. Sure, the timer functions and is reliable, but it does nothing else. It would be nice to be able to see by exactly how much you are ahead or behind the actual ghosts you are at each checkpoint. You may only view a replay upon conclusion of a stage, and only until you exit the menu. after that, the replay is lost forever. Moreover, you may only keep your single best ghost for each stage. This means, that if I actually manage to do some cool jet car 'stunts' on a level, I have no way of storing that sick run if it is not my fastest on the stage. I would also like the ability to choose to race one of my friend's ghosts instead of some random stranger. Finally, the medal times on the stages are far too slow and they don't have actual ghosts representing them.
All in all, jet car stunts for PC retains the casual 'pick up and play' attitude from the mobile release, but gives you the option of an actual controller. This is a rare combination  of arcade racer and 3D platformer that actually works. the game is by no means flawless, but its positives outweigh the negitives  by a wide margin.

There's a really good chance you'll give up on Jet Car Stunts with a sour taste in your mouth. It's difficult, yes, very difficult. I've had several short burts of frustration and enjoyment in the near 3.5h I played it before writting this review. As such, you either need to be looking for this kind of game or be in the right mood to play it - if that's the case, I can recommend Jet Car Stunts, especially with the sale price.
There's just one car (+1 in Collector mode) , and a good amount of levels, and 3 game modes, and hard to master controls. The jet + air brake mechanics are good (just that).
As it's often the case in games that focus on time trials and speedrunning, it's the player's drive for improvement that determines how replayable Jet Car Stunts is - if all you want is to get through each track once and in a single game mode, you may feel it's short, while I feel it offers a lot of content.
Each level has check points, such that if you destroy your car or get off the track you don't have to restart from the beginning. This is a smart decision by the devs. due to the nature of the game (a difficult driving platformer), as it eases your way to the finish line and given it can feel like a chore when you get stuck on a platforming section. Some players would prefer to respawn exactly where they crashed, but with that you would not have to successfully complete each stunt, so I'm happy with checkpoints.
You can complete the game faster and with less repetition because of the check points, but of course if you want to improve your time and/or get gold medals you have to go through the tracks without retries.
In Platforming mode, you get gold medals for completing the course without retries. In Time Trial mode you get gold medals for finishing 5 laps within the required time. In Collector mode there are no medals, you just collect stars that are in hard to reach locations.
The gameplay is quite different in Collector mode when compared to Platforming and Time Trial - your boost regenerates automatically and you have more air control. It takes time to adjust, and this is by far the least enjoyable game mode, particularly because my feel is it's too difficult to consistently and repeatedly pull off the stunts.
Overall I like it, and for me it was a steal at the sale price, but going back to the initial paragraph in my review I recommend it if you are looking for this type of game and/or you are in the mood for playing a challenging game that will kill you a lot.

It has it all when it comes to WW2 infantry RTS and is EXCEPTIONAL.

Resource limits - except enemy AI
Resource income dependent on map control - except for enemy AI
Buildings produce 1 unit at a time - except enemy AI

AI knows when his infantry have been clicked for bombardment by your field guns (so no warning smoke flares) and will move its units away.
AI British infantry squad will nearly always kill a combat engineer with their first shot - your British infantry couldn't kill a combat engineer in a million f*****g years.

Decent game.  No fundamental flaws but nothing that's amazingly outstanding either.  The voice acting was really good, as was the dialogue, though I thought the story was cliched to hell and back - I can't tell if its meant to be an homage to the old Mafia movies we grew up with, or if its blatantly copying from them, but personally it felt like the latter.  For most though that's probably perfectly fine, I still have a full stomach of this type of fiction from my teenage years - that's partially where "Consigliere" comes from - and as such, a lot of the story elements felt cheap, in lack of a better term. It was also very, very predictable, there's a lot of Scorsese storytelling going on which is great but I feel like I've seen this movie a hundred times. It even basically ends the same way as all gangster fiction does, "I got into this life to get rich and powerful but in the end it cost me more than it was worth" type situation, which is probably faithful to reality but again, I've seen it a hundred times.  At least it wasn't a dopey revenge tale like so many of these games tend to be.
I do think the Mafia games possibly have the most intelligent wanted level system I've ever seen for an open-world crime game, its basically the same system from the first game's where the car you're driving can be wanted, but if the police don't have your description (ie haven't seen you outside of the vehicle), you can switch cars and the wanted level is instantly gone no matter how high it is.  If they HAVE seen you, all it takes is a change of clothes, or for situations where that isn't plausible, you have a couple of ways to bribe your way out, but its expensive.  Or, there is a chance where a cop sees you commit a crime but isn't able to get your description OR your plate number, in which case all you have to do is outrun him for a short period of time.  All in all I like how that works, it makes logical sense and practical sense, not just one or the other like in, say, Grand Theft Auto. The Police AI is a crapload better than the first game too, cops will actually stop crimes committed by NPCs now (or attempt to).  It was really kinda bad in the first game, as I remember it.
ts still not perfect, I can get fined for speeding or crashing into cars, but I can drive on the sidewalk and run redlights and cops don't give a flying ♥♥♥♥; if you're going to implement traffic laws then go all the way, or just leave it out (which would've been my preference).  You also can run out of gas, and there are gas stations to refill at, but I never once ran out of fuel except when trying to do a specific achievement and even if I had I would've just stolen another ride, so that's another mechanic I could do without.  I remember there being a licensed Godfather game for the PS2, I feel like this game could've copied some of the gameplay tropes from it, such as territory wars, or extorting individual businesses, etc would've benefitted it greatly, but it also admittedly would've distracted from the "cinematic experience", which is something this series is all about having (moreso the first game though). Also despite the presence of public transportation, there's no means of fast travel, that disappointed me.
I got this as a part of the Humble Bundle, the 2K bundle that several of us partook in (and honestly had no expectation that I'd ever pick this up before that sale, I liked the first game in its time but that time was long ago); having paid around $8 for all those games, I think this is a good (not great) experience.  If I'd paid $60 or even $30, however, I think I'd be a lot more critical; perhaps that's the best review I could give, in that sentence.

A fantastic first-person plaformer. If you liked Mirror's Edge and Cloudbuilt, you'd love this game.
This game is essentially a jujitsu simulator cause it's all about grappling. This is a fantastic first-person platformer. Unlike most other platformer that emphasize, well, the platforms, A Story About My Uncle is a platformer that emphasizes aerial movement. Your character's primary method of getting around involves grappling onto floating and moving objects and getting swinging incredible distances.
And what really stands out about this game is the ability to play as you want. There aren't many artificial restrictions (invisible walls) and there are multiple ways to solve a challenge. If you want to try a crazy way to get over an obstacle, the game encourages it and doesn't punish you (infinite lives, checkpoints everywhere so you don't lose progress). Instead of feeling like you're following a line on the ground, it really makes you feel like you're exploring a world.
A bonus for this game is it's imersiveness. At one point, I fell off a location high up off the ground and I actually got cold sweats cause I felt like I was actually falling. I'd love to see this game in VR as it would be quite the experience.

Abiding memory begets a tale.
I was strolling out of the boss's office in Hollywood. Yet another errand for yet another bigwig I couldn't care less about. But I'm new to this Kindred business and I need to ingratiate myself to my "betters" if I'm going to survive.
I'm only still alive because one of them spared me. I'm the child of an unauthorized embrace, and as such should have been killed, along with the one who turned me. Though his sentence was death, mine was a chance to prove myself. A chance granted as a cheap political maneuver by a self-serving pencil-neck, but a chance nonetheless.
As this plays on my mind, strolling down the street, I am fast approached by a woman I don't recognize. She screams with disbelief. She knows me. From before, when I was human.
She and her friends were so worried. They have no idea where I went that night. Was I kidnapped? Was I drugged? Am I alright? It seems she was with me the night I was embraced. Indeed, she may be the last one to see me when I was still human. Questions fly from her mouth in a frenzy. Her concern is genuine.
I collect myself, trying to explain to her that, yes, I'm fine, no, I'm not in trouble, but her concern is appreciated. She is not swayed. She insists on finding help for me.
She says, "It's going to be okay."
For the first time, I panic. Legitimately. I'm afraid for this woman, because she doesn't know what she's doing, and her desire to help me is genuine. She can't be dissuaded. I try to talk her out of it. She starts walking toward a payphone. All because she recognized me, and cares.
I don't want to kill her, but I may have to, in order to protect the Masquerade. I don't want to screw up, give the higher-ups even more reason to despise, doubt, or distrust me. But I want to hold on to my last shreds of humanity, refusing to succumb to the darkness that was forced upon me. If there's to be any justice in this, I can't fall any further.
She can't make that phone call.
"It's going to be okay."
No, it's not.
Finally, as she's within arms reach of the phone, I remember the powers I wield. I use them to disorient her. She regains consciousness after a few seconds and walks past and then away from the phone, and me. She seems to remember nothing of our conversation.
My relief is overwhelming. I think about talking to her again, just to make sure it worked, but I don't dare.
Instead, I run.
This experience is a throw-away bit around the midpoint of Bloodlines, but represents the hallmark of a game that truly involves the player. If I weren't so involved in the role-playing experience, I wouldn't care about any of the systems that punish me for being a monster or betraying the Kindred. I certainly wouldn't care about an NPC I've never met. But I'm invested deeply, and so I care deeply.
What a masterful game this is.

This game continues to be amazing over a decade after its original release, arguably even more amazing as a result of fan-patching that actually fixes many issues and even reenables some cut content.  The game benefits from being set in a well-established world; the "World of Darkness" from White Wolf's pen & paper rpg Vampire: The Masquerade is the result of over a decade's worth of refinement that provides an excellent setting for a player-driven story heavy RPG.
Worthy of special mention is the "Malkavian" player class.  A number of RPGs have a quiz to suggest a particular class to the indecisive or uninformed player.  Never before or since have I ever been as satisfied by the result of such a quiz as when I was presented with the Malkavian class by Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines' integrated quiz.  Playing as a character class whose dialogue choices are incredibly roundabout and esoteric in addition to being filled with veiled spoilers due to your character being canonically insane is a surreal experience to say the least.  If you listen carefully enough you can actually hear the voices in your head dropping hints about things mid-conversation.

Can't recommend this enough, by far one of my favorite games and for many good reasons. To give you an example, I had this on PS3, went plat, and I just got it again on PC, intending on going 100% again, cause I'll be damned if it's not worth it
To begin with, this game does what other open world games don't: exploring the genre in a whacky way, and make us want to explore everything and have fun from start, ALL the way to 100% completion. I stress this because I usually hate going 100%, as most games make it a chore and involve at least a few very time comnsuming actions needed for completion (lifeless farming or chasing hidden tiny stuff that are not even cleverly obscured, or require actual skill to reach). Not Saints Row, I legit had the most fun actually trying to do all the achievments and made me come back again and again, and I was in fact sad to find out I did all the little challenges!
Now, be warned this game actually does take itself VERY seriously, by not taking itself seriously. The storyline for example is at least ridiculous and cheesy, but all intended and where it shines is when it reproduces iconic scenes for you to be part in. Riding that rocket while Aerosmith is playing in the background the ONLY song that could be played in that scene -all as soon as you start no less- is not only memorable, awesome and hilarious just for being there, it also prepares you on what to espect in the best of ways
The gameplay itself could not be more fun. The physics and mechanics are very well thought out, and they execute really smooth. I found myself just running to my favorite ingame song and deciding to jump and wallride in specific parts. It felt like boss. I still do it, just run around and rythmically jump and climb, so simple yet so satisfying
I recommend it especially to people who have not played any Saints Row, and are kind of bored of exploring vast realistic open world games, although the best route would be to play SRTT first as SRIV is taking the game on a different spectrum. This game is definitely not as detailed as GTA, not nearly as realistic, but this is exactly it's point: being it's own game, exploring whatever GTA does not.

I've been playing games for a very long time. I do play video games a lot, as my main hobby since approximatively 15 years now. And this game is one of the best games I ever played.
No 3D, no cinematics, no super duper ultra realistic graphics, no incredible sound effects, no voice acting. But trust me. This game, (and it's extension The Joyful), is a masterpiece.
It is dark, but has really funny moments and a lot of references that make it an emotionnal rollercaster. The story and the characters are not perfect : they are human.  You are no hero. You are no god. You are human. Sometimes happy and funny events occur, you are going to laugh a lot. Sometimes things are going to suck, and you are going to cry.
The game will not hold your hand thought. There is a lot of sh*t going on, and if you want to figure out the whole story you will have to pay attention to a lot of things : what people say, what items you get, what choices you make. There are a lot of "secret" areas that can give you more hints about the story, but you will have to find those yourself. You can go throught this game missing out a lot of things since it is surprisingly big.
The music totally fits the atmosphere of the game, it is perfect.
IMO, saying anything more than that would spoil it. Why haven't you bought the game already ?
