LISA is one of the best games I have ever played, though if I were to elaborate on that it would take away from your first-time experience playing.  I'd highly recommend bringing some friends over, sitting down together, and going through this game, as all of you are going to need emotional support by the end.
If you are debating whether or not to buy this and you're totally on the fence, your opinion of this will sway you one way or the other:
Also, there is no greater lie on this green earth than "I did not save-scum for Buckets." You'll see what I mean soon enough.

Buy this game. Buy it now.
Complex characters, a story which isn't spoon fed to you, mature subject matter, dark humor, amazing soundtrack, and an ending which will tear you apart.
Brad is a man dealing with the aftermath of his sister's suicide (Lisa), who killed herself due to their father's abuse. He finds a baby girl, in a world where women had gone extinct, and swears to protect her. This is his chance to make things right, but at what cost?
For myself, the most impressive part of this game was the DLC, as well as final installment to the series, "Lisa: The Joyful". Buddy is refreshingly well developed character. On the surface she may seem like just a psychotic killer, but as a woman, she is the victim of abuse and is fed up with being told what to do with her body (the latter being a frustration many women may find they relate with). This is a perfect contrast with Lisa's character in the first game, who ultimately was driven mad by her father's abuse. Lisa had no control over what happened to her, but Buddy is taking that control back.
For this reason Lisa is an incredibly empowering, as well as I dare say "feminist", videogame which is not only entertaining but important. I hope this dear indie game is inspiring for developers when writing female characters in the future because honestly, Dingaling nailed it. Buddy isn't a victim, nor is she some moral hero - she's just sick of peoples' ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t and is reclaiming her body as her own.
Lisa has something for everyone, in humor, story, character development, and even gameplay. It is well paced with multiple endings. I would only warn those with histories of abuse to be wary for (as previously mentioned) this series does deal quite heavily with abuse and its aftermath. I look forward to anything Dingaling puts out in the future. I cannot recall a time I have been equally impressed by a videogame, and it has easily taken its place among my all time favourites.
Pros:

- Well placed dark humor which isn't forced, "edgy", or gimmicky
- Some of the design is very interesting, especially the mutants
- Multiple endings i.e., replay value.
- Well written characters
- Moral ambiguity
Cons:
- I honestly can't think of any. In my opinion this game is pretty close to perfect.
- Actually, when looking at the game as a trilogy, the first game (Lisa: The First) is only good because of the games which followed (The Painful and The Joyful). Alone, it is basically another Yume Nikki clone. However, originally I don't think Dingaling was planning on a second or third game, which can be seen by the vast change in style between the first and second, so this can be forgiven. What would be interesting is if the first game was redone to make it stand apart from a regular Yume Nikki clone with some added parts to foreshadow the following games, although I don't think this is likely to happen. Regardless, this would be my single qualm with the trilogy, and I don't consider it a very big one.
Finally, I think I should include some trigger warnings for the game considering its content.

Decent game.  No fundamental flaws but nothing that's amazingly outstanding either.  The voice acting was really good, as was the dialogue, though I thought the story was cliched to hell and back - I can't tell if its meant to be an homage to the old Mafia movies we grew up with, or if its blatantly copying from them, but personally it felt like the latter.  For most though that's probably perfectly fine, I still have a full stomach of this type of fiction from my teenage years - that's partially where "Consigliere" comes from - and as such, a lot of the story elements felt cheap, in lack of a better term. It was also very, very predictable, there's a lot of Scorsese storytelling going on which is great but I feel like I've seen this movie a hundred times. It even basically ends the same way as all gangster fiction does, "I got into this life to get rich and powerful but in the end it cost me more than it was worth" type situation, which is probably faithful to reality but again, I've seen it a hundred times.  At least it wasn't a dopey revenge tale like so many of these games tend to be.
I do think the Mafia games possibly have the most intelligent wanted level system I've ever seen for an open-world crime game, its basically the same system from the first game's where the car you're driving can be wanted, but if the police don't have your description (ie haven't seen you outside of the vehicle), you can switch cars and the wanted level is instantly gone no matter how high it is.  If they HAVE seen you, all it takes is a change of clothes, or for situations where that isn't plausible, you have a couple of ways to bribe your way out, but its expensive.  Or, there is a chance where a cop sees you commit a crime but isn't able to get your description OR your plate number, in which case all you have to do is outrun him for a short period of time.  All in all I like how that works, it makes logical sense and practical sense, not just one or the other like in, say, Grand Theft Auto. The Police AI is a crapload better than the first game too, cops will actually stop crimes committed by NPCs now (or attempt to).  It was really kinda bad in the first game, as I remember it.
ts still not perfect, I can get fined for speeding or crashing into cars, but I can drive on the sidewalk and run redlights and cops don't give a flying ♥♥♥♥; if you're going to implement traffic laws then go all the way, or just leave it out (which would've been my preference).  You also can run out of gas, and there are gas stations to refill at, but I never once ran out of fuel except when trying to do a specific achievement and even if I had I would've just stolen another ride, so that's another mechanic I could do without.  I remember there being a licensed Godfather game for the PS2, I feel like this game could've copied some of the gameplay tropes from it, such as territory wars, or extorting individual businesses, etc would've benefitted it greatly, but it also admittedly would've distracted from the "cinematic experience", which is something this series is all about having (moreso the first game though). Also despite the presence of public transportation, there's no means of fast travel, that disappointed me.
I got this as a part of the Humble Bundle, the 2K bundle that several of us partook in (and honestly had no expectation that I'd ever pick this up before that sale, I liked the first game in its time but that time was long ago); having paid around $8 for all those games, I think this is a good (not great) experience.  If I'd paid $60 or even $30, however, I think I'd be a lot more critical; perhaps that's the best review I could give, in that sentence.

There isn’t much of a game here.  You watch videos based on your selection and the only interactive parts are choosing what to do and the simplistic game (click on the quadrant of a circle that is in every shape) that you play in order to ‘develop’ your indie game.
You can choose to develop your game or other activities like listening to music, play with your cat or go for a walk.  The videos are on the whole fairly well done with good framing and lighting.  The best videos are the Creative Commons licensed ones that play whilst you are developing the game.  The music consists of many Russian bands/acts that you wouldn’t have heard of unless you are a native.  The game has a quirky sense of humour which tends to fall flat.  Fortunately, all the videos can be skipped, which is a good metaphor for the game.
You will unlock almost all of the achievements on your first time playing - all of them if you get the good ending.  Within half-an-hour you will have seen everything the game has to offer, and there is really no point in playing it again, unless you want the trading cards.  In the information about the game in the Steam store, the developer/publisher asks you to “Don't take this game too seriously!”  I was sent a key for the game; if you want to pay for it, bear in mind that there is not much game here, seriously.

I will mention these issues later, however here they are grouped together.
Yeah, this game starts out pretty well, however it does become a bit of a slog halfway through. That's not to say it's not enjoyable, however it can be painfully boring. There are two sections in fact where you literally have to do nothing but hold in a button constantly for about 2 minutes while the developer speaks, the second one actually resetting the timer if you let go of the button. I'd compare the experience to a less polished version of "The Beginner's Guide" as that is what it quite reminds me of, especially later into the game. It's still a pretty decent experience though, and it is free.

I find this game rather confusing, as it doesn’t seem to have much in the way of cohesion. In the beginning of the game, it’s about the developer’s dreams, and while they are confusing, they are interesting and pretty fun to explore. They also don’t overstay their welcome. The game then changes into a “rejected staring artist” narrative. It is actually pretty relatable, though forced.

Update, the developer explained that these aren't views of others but rather his own.
The game then changes to an interesting sort of “The Beginner’s Guide” sort of experience for a bit, and that was also pretty good. Again, my only major issue with it is that the three major sections to this game are pretty...disconnected.
Now, for some technical stuff as well that you may care about. This game suffers from severe screen tearing in certain areas, and it also has so very trippy effects in certain other places, like in some doors. This is notable as for me and some of the people who watch my videos it causes a bit of nausea, so you may want to watch out if you suffer from more severe motion or simulator sickness. This was on the highest quality settings at 60fps. The game does however run very smoothly otherwise, as typical with decent programming on the Unity engine. Using a gamepad, however, despite the game giving instructions for it appears to be pointless, as many of the inputs do not seem to be properly set up.
While the music is great, the audio is very poorly optimized in a areas, especially where there is speech. I had extreme difficulty hearing him at certain points, specifically this one point where there is a loud piano playing at the same volume as the speech, making it almost impossible to hear it without turning up your volume to painful levels.

Are you up for a race against the clock where it's more about using your thrust and gliding through the air than it is about racing? That's Jet Car Stunts in a nutshell, a game that's about the challenge and precision as you fly your stunt car from platform to platform hovering high in the sky. Its clean aesthetic makes it appealing to play and the game does ease you into challenges before it becomes too difficult. There's a sense of joy to make it through a course on your last try, but be certain this is a game for a select few that enjoy the genre.
Even if your car looks like a red tank on four wheels, its light, which lets the thrust take you flying through the air. When you're gliding through the air, you can tilt your spoiler to control your movement in the slightest way. Other than those two things, it plays similar to a lot of other arcade games that put you behind the wheel and it is easy to control with the keyboard or a 360 controller. You have buttons for forward, reverse, thrust and air brake. When I say air brake I mean the sides of your stunt car go out and you can slow yourself down in the air. Its an interesting mechanic and it does work well to counteract the thrust. There are optional and brief tutorial courses that get you skilled to the game's tricks.
The boost feels good to use and it gives your car a sense of speed more than almost any other game with nitrous. Maybe you need that speed to lift off into the air. You can also adjust the options to turn off the sense of speed. Even on the ground it feels much faster. Well I say on the ground, even though everything is in the air.
There are three modes and the main mode is platforming. You have ten tries to make it through each course and there are five difficulties each with five courses. These courses are open circuits, so anything can happen from course to course. One course can be like an upward hill that's floating thousands of meters off the ground. Another course can have you going in a loop, then jump down through rings. Having the courses suspended in mid air does open up a lot of opportunity for imaginative, creative courses. It also allows for a budget, minimal design of colored blocks rather than trees.
Your objective is to make it to the gate at the end. Even if there's a minuet amount of space after the goal, you can still plow through and drive off and its still a victory. If you fall into the abyss below or slam into something at top speed, you will respawn at the last checkpoint. You only get a checkpoint if you drive through its triangular gate, so if you fly over it, then you missed your opportunity. Crossing through a checkpoint refills your boost completely.
You need to time your boosts and spare your thrust for later sections. Even if you recharge your boost at checkpoints, you can still run out and be forced to respawn at the cost of time. This makes some courses feel like trial and error that you need to get accustom to before you make it through. Other times, there are blind jumps guided by an arrow block that keeps you from over jumping, because you're aiming for rings that you'll never see until you jump. The earlier courses show you the rings before you jump, but its the later courses you need to be wary of.
Time Trial mode lets you race the same courses, but more like a closed circuit where you do laps. So imagine the same tough course that you have to do five times. It does get easier as you do it more often. At the end of each lap, there's a fog bank that puts you back at the start so seamless that you maintain your speed. Its a nice touch. Time Trial more for endurance and it gets dull. A challenge is one thing, racing a ghost or yourself is another.
There are optional ghosts in the game and I enjoy them being here, because it makes the game feel more alive. Otherwise it feels vacant. I realize that its just white tiles that I'm driving on and without competition, I feel less motivation to exceed and keep playing. These ghosts make mistakes and I have a feeling they are human recordings for the most part. After each successful drive, you get a gold, silver or bronze medal and you get a rank based on an unseen online leader board. My best runs earned around #500 while my worst runs ranked me at #700 - #1,500. I have a feeling there's a player drop off as the game gets more difficult.
The final mode is the toughest of them all and that's the Collector. This mode has you collecting five stars on only eight of the same twenty-five tracks. You need to search high and low for these stars in places that its questionable how you can get to them, but its mostly extreme precision. After trying a few times on the first level, I assume that you need all five stars, before the goal lets you in. I gave up and ran away. It seemed too overwhelming from the start to even get into it, but that's why this is the third mode rather than the first.
As for unlockables, I never encountered any hint of any other than completing all five courses on one difficulty level unlocks the courses of the next difficulty level. I would like to play as other vehicles to see a difference in their weight and how they perform, but with this being a challenge and precision based game, that may throw things off.
In terms of sound and music, its minimal. There is no music during the game itself, just air and light engine sounds. I suppose music would get in the way of anything that takes focus to accomplish. The menus are where the music is and its nothing special.
I'm on the fence about this game really. I had fun for a brief while. The challenges are engaging before they get too difficult for me. The clean look certainly helps it stand out from other games and a lot of times a game boils down to its graphics to sell you. I want to like it and maybe I do, its just tough to recommend to others. It was more challenging and a bit tedious than it was fun. It feels one dimensional, even if it makes good use of that one dimension across twenty-five courses. It should add or have more facets to keep it interesting and engaging. Even having more to unlock would have kept me interested longer.
As always, the choice is yours, but I feel like even the price is a bit too high, but well there are always sales.

This game is essentialy a multiplayer game. There is a singleplayer mode, but ultimately it's just a little gimmick without any real value, and the true juices of the game can only be found in it's multiplayer. Is it a good game? Yes. So what's the problem?
The game is very fun, it offers three classes all with completely different roles, used in order to combat the other team. Well, it can be fun...
When it comes to games that offer a compelling storyline or an amazing sandbox for singleplayer, multiplayer might not be such a big problem, and so servers aren't that big of a deal. But seeing as how this game focuses on multiplayer, there should be a few official servers for a few regions like EU, US, Aus, etc. But when you open up the server list there's only one (or maybe two at most) servers from one gamemode. The rest are either completely empty or from another region meaning the ping is rediculously high and so unplayable. You can play on modded servers, but I'm talking about the official servers. I get it's not that big of a game but I still find it to be a problem.
But then again, this isn't as big of a problem. What is perhaps this game's major downfall is the community. Again, if a game has a worthy singleplayer, then the community might not be an issue at all. But as you will most likely spend all your time in this game with other players it becomes an issue. A rather large one. You mightn't find any major issues with the community at first but as you play on it becomes more apparent. One issue is the community's dislike of 'noobs' or new players in general. They will often get kicked for mistakes evidently made because they are new, and on the topic of getting kicked, you will often times get kicked for the dumbest of reasons. Disagree with how a base is being built and try to change a bit? Get kicked for griefing. Start a chat with a teammate? Get kicked for spamming. And so on, so forth. The players often tend to be racist and intolerant if you disagree with them, again, sometimes ending up with you being kicked.
To summarize, should you get the game?
If you don't mind sitting around in singleplayer playing around with options and mechanics clearly designed for multiplayer, then go for it!
Don't find the above issues a problem? Then go for it!
Otherwise, no.
You might be able to pump some hours into it but you will either love it or absolutely despise it.
Now, this is coming from a person who has played this game pre-steam, in other words before it was released on Steam, so I would have played this game a lot more in the past.

'You Have to Win the Game' is a non-scrolling 2D platformer that urges the player to explore a maze-like map to recover various artifacts. These objects allow the player to access new parts of the map and give the protagonist abilities like wall-jumping or double jump. As the adventure unfolds, the game proposes a riddle to the player, before the end, he or she must give answer to one question: "What is the magic word?".
The most important part of the game, since it doesn't have a narrative to speak of.
, which means a lot of exploration and backtracking (that is, if you don't download the map from google).
, you can recover a few objects that enhance your movement, but they solely affect the jumping mechanics. This means you cannot attack enemies, they kill you in one hit and you can only avoid them.
I really enjoyed the exploration and backtracking needed to advance, because
in my opinion and there are plenty of collectibles to look for. Some sections are really tough, but
, which are located wisely to not interrupt the progress of the player.
So the platforming and the exploration are solid, but what about the riddle part? Well, it's difficult for me to evaluate the quality of a riddle, but I think this one is fine. The first time I finished the game, I found the hints necessary to solve it, but I couldn't get the solution. The second time I surrendered and looked it up on a steam guide (the flesh is weak). I repent myself for doing it, because I think I could have figured it out if I had dedicated it enough time. It's not explicit nor too complex either (once you find the hints).
I really liked the looks of this game,
for the most part. And maybe it doesn't have a story, but the designs of some of the screens, the names they have and the general aesthetic of it all, are very suggestive and prompt me to imagine the past history of some of the places you visit (even if that history is pretty much surreal or nonsensical).
The sound department is pretty empty,
. I personally didn't mind the absence of music since the gameplay is so satisfying and I think the silence helps set an eerie mood that fits the visuals. A minor nitpick would be that some rooms of the map, the ones where there's an enemy shooting proyectiles, can be a bit nerve-racking, because each of those proyectiles makes its own sound, sometimes resulting in a confusing cacophony.
: If you don't like the silence, you can always play some 'Metroid' music in the background, which I think fits perfectly (Nine Inch Nails would be an alternative).
I'd say the first time I played the game, took me around 2 hours to beat it, without looking any guides or walkthroughs, so it's a short game. Still, the game has various modes in case you want to put your platforming skills to the test.

I don't usually write reviews for any game, but LISA simply blew me away. It gripped me throughout the entire Playthrough and didn't let down a single time.
LISA is a 2D-sidescrolling, turn-based RPG, set in a post-apocalyptic wasteland, where the human race is facing extinction due to the lack of women. You take over the role of Brad Armstrong, who happened to find a stray baby, who is also the only girl. Aware of the importance of her exisence, he keeps her and raises her in secret as if she were his own daughter.
One day, Brad finds his home ambushed and the girl missing, at which point he sets off on a pilgrimage to reclaim the girl, at all and any costs.
Despite looking wacky and somewhat lighthearted, the game and the tone of it can be grim and dark, even depressing. But the coexistence of both the comedic and tragic elements emphasizes and quite underline one and the other. The tragic elements seem darker and sadder and the comedic elemtents will appear all the funnier.
The combat system, like already mentioned, is a turn-based RPG, somewhat remniscient of classics like Earthbound.
The player controls Brad as well as 3 additional party members which can recruited at various points in the game. Unlike most RPGs, party members can permanently die and there is no way to retrieve them. The combat system is sometimes used to depict crucial moments of the game for an odd but still effective and decent delivery.
The game will often force the player to make a crucial decision, which will significantly alter the progression of the game.
Not only that but it will leave the player asking if he or she has done the right thing.

One Way Heroics is a Mystery Dungeon-style roguelike (that is, similar to Pokemon Mystery Dungeon, Chocobo's Dungeon, Shiren, Izuna, etc) with an open world that constantly scrolls to the right, meaning you have limited time to spend in each place and you have to keep moving forward to avoid death by screen edge.
Gameplay is standard Mystery Dungeon-style roguelike fare; you have an attack button, inventory with weight limit, three pieces of equipment, some basic stats, everything is turn-based, the usual stuff. Unlike other Mystery Dungeons the world is open (though you can't go back, obviously) with mini-towns and dungeons spread throughout the map. Objective of the game is to level up and get good items to defeat the Demon Lord.
Items can be passed to future characters after your run, and you get a score in points which you can use to unlock classes, unlock perks or expand your item storage. Character creation is limited to picking a class and a bunch of simple perks. Various difficulty levels, and a 'Maniac mode' makes the game harder by disabling the item storage. Unfortunately there are perma-saves with no mode for a no-save run; not saving is entirely optional and only gets you a few extra points.
Definitely worth it for the really low price.

Excellent game. There are only two real flaws that I've found. First, the darkness not only moves at its own pace/round, but it also is always at the edge of your screen. Meaning you can't run forward to get some extra time in town or in a dungeon. Understandable, but not necessary.  Second, this game is based heavily on luck. I played 3/4 of the way through on one character, then desperately needed a shrine to trade in levels for buffs and a town for selling and buying. I went 50-100 km without finding either of those, and was taken down halfway into the boss because I was trying to limit my movement to conserve energy. The next game I played, I walked not 30km out of the starting area before getting killed in 3 hits by an "infamous harpy" that threw fireballs at me. Then the next game I played, I got a holy sword and saved up all my gear and buffs and destroyed the boss in about 5 rounds, dealing about 389 damage a hit.
The thing about death in this game is that it's supposed to be both tragic and amusing. Amusing, when you run out and instantly get stuck in a house and devoured by darkness or destroyed by a devil-harpy, and tragic when you run 200km and get torn to bits by a fire-breathing bear. This game set a goal to be a certain type of RPG, and succeeded. It's not a super-powered-loot-fest, and it's not ungodly difficult. It's both, and in a way that works.

As a first person adventure game, this game fails to tell you a compelling and moving story like most conventional games do. You fall asleep, and you found a series of unreasonable "dreams", and you wake up. That's it.
As a piece of art, however, this piece tries to investigate how unreasonable, or sometimes realistic, seldomly too realistic, small pieces of dreams can be, and how uncorrelated a series of them can be. Just like the real dreams you usually have when you are sleeping, you will find yourself in a place, sometimes so weird, sometimes so real, but you will never know you're dreaming. Then, without any telltale signs or logical transitions, you will find yourself blinked into another place, and again, sometimes so weird, sometimes so real. These illogical transitions between many bits of dreams always happen when we dream, and will go on and on until our biological clock or a physical alarm clock alarms us to wake up.
This piece also tries to emulate that weird feeling you never had when you are dreaming. When you are dreaming, you will never realise that the situation around you is just a dream, no matter how weird it has become. Your brain will make you believe you are living in the real world, although there are many different details from the real world you know very well. When we are awake playing this game, we will be aware of the situation since we are awake and playing with all the consciousness, a luxury you would not have when you are sleeping and unconscious.
Luckily, this is a piece of art, not a game. A piece of art freely available, just like in a public art gallery. The soundtracks are also great, too.

You jump your sheep across islands that can only fit a certain amount of Sheep, if your sheep can't fit then they fall off to their death which may be nessesary. Like I said there are a tonne of mechanics that change the way you think and play.

This game is very fun and easy to learn and I highly recommend picking up the game. I give it a 9/10 for being, fun, addictive and just awesome.

I write this review from the perspective of someone with a couple world records and generally rank 5-50 on everything else. The game is overall fine and worth your time if it intrigues you, but it's not without potentially game-ruining problems depending on what you want from it.
This game offers an interesting platform for arcade-style-racing speedrunning, although you can play 2 of the 3 modes without being forced to be fast. The closest comparison I can draw would be time trials from Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed and Trackmania. The mechanics present other than steering are, 1) A turbo boost, of which you get a fixed allotment per checkpoint, and 2) Mid-air aerodynamic manipulation, for lack of better words. Properly managing your boost, when and how long for, are key to being fast. Proper manipulation of your flight path and alignment are key to taking the shortest flight from point-to-point while avoiding obstacles and landing without losing speed.
This is all fun and makes for a pretty decent game, however the developers have left out some of the most basic things. You can't see any leaderboards and there is no way to see your current rank after it's shown on the results screen. You'll never see it again unless you beat your current time record, and then you'll only see your new rank. The only way I can confirm my world records are still #1 is by playing the map and making sure my ghost still beats the other ghost of the #2 player. This prevented any form of competitive community before it even had a chance to exist. All you're ever going to find is the ghost of the person 1 rank above you, or below if you're #1, unless you starting searching names and friending players.
I have to recommend Sonic & All-Stars Racing Transformed much more than this game to anyone seeking time trial competition, or even just a better skill-based Mario Kart. It's surprisingly deep. Trackmania is also another fine choice.
I also want to point out that the trailer shows a bunch of "cool jumps" that miss checkpoints and basically mean game over, and "cool techniques" that actually slow you down. Makes it look more compelling than it really is.

I got this game at launch and didn't bother playing it other than the campaign but picked it back up last year. This is a review of the game in its present and near future state. This game is good for the multiplayer, and the expasions. The game wasn't great when it came out, but updates and add-ons have changed that.
Gameplay: Players build and control units of soldiers and battle them in order to destroy the enemy and win the game. Standard RTS. COH2 has a directional cover system that makes map awareness critical. Players have a wide variety of units to select that compliment each other. This isn't starcraft and you can't just blob one unit and hope to win. MGs suppress infantry but don't do much damage while mortars do high damage over large distance but are vulnerable to direct fire. Tanks can bully infantry but anti-tank guns and even anti-tank small arms like panzerfausts and AT rifles can easily crush tanks. You need some kind of balance to win. Buildings can be garrisoned by infantry, making them much harder to kill. You can kill them out, or blow up the building.
You have 3 resources: Manpower, Munitions, and Fuel. All resources increase at set rates. Manpower is the primary resource, being used to produce all units. Fuel is a secondary resource, but it is critical. All the cool things require manpower and fuel to be built. Mosts games feature intense fights over fuel points. Munitions is last, and is used to upgrade units with better weapons or call in airstrikes from commander abilities (more on this later). Resource control is a critical aspect of COH, just like an RTS.
Gameplay is 9/10 in my opinion.
Graphics: Not great but its an RTS so it doesn't matter that much. The explosions look great and thats what I like. 7/10
Voice acting: 10/10. This game has great voice acting. The voice actors are good, have plenty of lines so you don't hear the same thing all game and fit their roles respectively. The only, only issue is that the roles they were given were a little stereotypical at times (The German machine gunner is a complete sociopath, American engineers are lazy conspiracy theorists, conscripts embrace the thought of being cannon fodder too openly). The wehrmact talks like hardened veterans in a really bad situation. The Russians talk like young men conscripted suddenly. Americans talk just like the A**holes that we are. And if you pay attention the voice acting really makes this game feel like a bloody, horrifying wargame. Tough guy americans scream "I don't wanna die" when supressed. If a German Grenadier squad takes a casaulty and starts to move you can hear someone frantically screaming "Don't leave me!". Relic did good on the voice acting.
Campaign: Don't bother with the base campaign. Play ardennes offensive for some rage inducing difficult gameplay. Ardennes is 10/10, base campaign is 6/10
Multiplayer: The bread and butter.
Gametypes: Two gametypes. Destroy the enemy base, or hold victory points until you drain the enemy of points. I only play the latter because it makes for intense battles.
Maps: A huge variety of maps are present and they all have a huge impact on how the game runs. Placement of resource locations, available cover, line of sight etc.
Gameplay: Currently there are 5 armies, the Soviets, Americans, British, Wehrmacht, and Oberkommando West. These are split into Axis versus Allies. Each has a distinct play style that keeps the game intersting, as well as commanders. Commanders can be selected during a game and unlock unique units and abilties to call in. Commanders get let you call in support like offmap artillery barrages, recon flights or airstrikes. They can give your units unique abilities like the ability to camoflage or throw certain grenades. They can also be use for special units like Guard Rifle infantry or the legendary Tiger Ace. Some commanders are less useful, and even less distinct than others, but there's enough to keep it intersting.
Balance: Its alright. Updates change the balance so the game doesn't become static but I really think the brits are OP, just because all their stuff is significantly cheaper than it should be.
Overall: Great game with good replayablity, inspite of the poor launch. The game has aged well and I recommend you pick it up. 8.5/10

I don't get the people on these bad reviews. I like this game. Here's why:
The graphics are lovely, and the scenery combined with the music is awesome.
(this does not imply that a game needs to have good graphics, it's just that the graphics here are wonderful, it wouldn't look the same if they weren't good)
The story was nice.
The gameplay is so much fun, and there is a variation of methods you use to proceed, from rocket boots, to a grappling hook, to being able to jump really high, and run and jump in order to jump further distances.
However, the story was short (which is perfectly fine, to make it longer they would have to fill it in with extra/side mission bullcrap that would make the game worse), but there is a good reason to still keep on playing the game, and that is time trial mode. What it does is lets you try to speedrun the levels and get the best time, so if you have friends that play this, good times can be bragging rights, but it's also just fun in general to try and do it as fast as possible.
TL;DR I'd give it a 10/10. I seriously have no reason to dislike this game.
Just buy it at a sale.

So I nominated LISA for the "I'm not crying, there's something in my eye," award. I am nearly incapable of actually crying, but I experienced very worthwhile emotions throughout playing this game. It was such an unexpected, awesome videogaming serendipity. I saw it one day after work on a steam sale, was very intrigued, bought it and did not stop playing for about a week straight. This game is the singlemost enthralling experience I've had in about 5 years. I liked its unique setting, extremely imaginative, charming characters, a beautiful if intensely dark storyline/dialogue. In short, I highly recommend LISA to RPG enthusiasts. I will at some point refine my review, but I'd like to at least have some thoughts posted as to why I nominated this title for the award I chose. There isn't much I disliked about LISA. The beginning grind and harshness can turn some away, but it's very much worthwhile to push through, farm some experience a bit here and there and progress.

Therefore, on a whole, I finished this completely by getting all achievements in 11 minutes and the only reason anyone would play longer is if they wanted the Steam Trading Cards. Company of heroes 2 is, overall a good game. It has a lot of improvements from its predecessor but it also has some diminishing features. The base game gives access to story mode and also access to two factions, soviets and werhmact while three other factions the british, oberkommando west and United state forces are unlockable by buying their respective dlc's.
Pro's
-Fun online gameplay.
-Lots of mods and skins.
-Many different commanders and tactics to try for each faction.
-New loot system so all commanders can be bought with ingame currency or dropped in after match loot.
-Game has balance updates every month with hotfixes coming every now and then.
Con's
-Factions are unbalanced in certain aspects such as USF.
-Story mode isn't so much fun and the story itself is quite boring.
-Tank pathing is quite annoying and sometimes tanks are loss due to this.
-Online auto download sometimes doesn't start. (Very random)

Now I last played Iron Snout whilst it was still in development however the gameplay really hasn’t changed all too much since then. It’s One Finger Death Punch but not as you know it.
Iron Snout allows you to fulfil your Kung Fu fantasies with the push of a button. With simple controls it’s about as arcade as it gets. Build up combos while dodging every attack, all the while giggling at the wolves as they escalate their vendetta against your porky self. And that’s about it. It’s incredibly simple and great time killer.
The lack of different game types can’t really be complained about since the game is ultimately free, this includes the wonder if the game will ever be added on. It certainly would be nice if some customisation to your piggy character could be added or even if you could fight in different backdrops but alas, what you see is really what you get in this arcade beat ‘em up.

Anyway, if you're looking for over-the-top fun and gameplay like in GTA or Saints Row, you won't get it here. This game's main focus is the story and the characters. You'll more often than not feel like you're playing a movie and waiting for another cutscene. Mafia 2 takes place during and after the 2nd world war and follows the story of Vito Scalleta and his best friend Joe Barbaro as they get involved with the Mafia. Without spoiling too much, the game takes some inspiration from the classic mafia movies, like The Godfather and The Goodfellas. I must also admit that I shed some tears on more than one occasion throughout the game. If you played the first Mafia, you'll also find a nod to the main character in one chapter, which recreates a certain event that happened in the first one.
Most of the Mafia II takes place in the fictional city of Empire Bay, which I think is based on New York and is fully explorable by the player. You are able to go pretty much anywhere with your vast collection of classic cars. The gunplay consists of using the cover-system and a variety of authentic weapons from that era, like MP40s, Thompsons and many more. The melee combat, while not on par with Sleeping Dogs or Batman games, is pretty good and challenging.
While the game is athmospheric and recreates the 40s and 50s very well, I must say that I'm dissapointed with the inconsistencies regarding the texture quality, most of it is good, but some things look considerably worse and can sometimes break the immersion. The game also suffers from some pretty noticable object pop-in. But, this game is one of the few, that does the depth of field right, I usually don't like DOF, but in this game it was very pretty. Also, the first part of the game takes place during the winter and the second part is during the summer, so It freshens up the game a bit.
If you're planing on buying it, you can safely purchase the base game without the DLC, which is more or less the cosmetic stuff. There are 2 'expansions', one of them has no story whatsoever and is very arcady (Jimmy's Vendetta) and the other one (Joe's Adventures) only has 1 mission which ties in to the main story.
In conclusion, if you like story rich games, like The Last of Us, Grand Theft Auto IV, Wolfenstein The New Order and so on,
or if you like classic movies about the Mafia and awesome Italian accents, then by all means, get this game. You will not be disapointed. But if you're the type that skips all the cutscenes and doesn't care about the plot, then this game is not for you.
(By the way, don't be fooled by my playtime, I've beat this game 2 or 3 times, before I was into "supporting the developers" thing, if you know what I mean. Once I got it for 'free' on my PS+, I didn't feel the need to buy it again on Steam, so I pirated on PC. For that I'm deeply ashamed and will probably buy Mafia III as soon as it comes out.)

The on-foot gameplay is great, the shooting feels nice and tight. The story is the real reason to play this though. If you're a fan of "Goodfellas" or "The Godfather" this is a must-play.

Mafia II is not an open-world game like GTA or Saints Row, as some may expect. It is more of an interactive movie.
That's not a bad thing. To have your sandbox for mayhem and destruction, there are other games. Mafia II is more about atmosphere, history and a good story. And that's what it does well.
You accompany and move the protagonist through several years, starting with his service in the army, then his way through the ranks (and intrigues) of the Mafia. Elaborate cutscenes and voiceovers allow for fleshed-out characters and plot, and the missions are both subordinate to the plot as well as versatile. No grinding in this game (unless you really want to).
It's not much of a shooter, even though you have some shootouts. Many fistfights, yes; but it is not a boxing game, either. If any of the gameplay aspects is predominant, it's driving cars. Different cars from different decades, different motors and chassis... different handling, and different goals - fast & reckless, inconspicuous, tailing somebody, or just getting somewhere. Most of the time, you are driving to get somewhere.
A good amount of work seems to have gone into the cars, making them look right for the period with lots of details. The clothing isn't bad either, and the interiors of buildings range from OK to really good. The civilian and enemy AI is so-so, doing its job.
I'd need to revisit the game to have a closer look at the city and judge it - the game keeps you closely tied to the storyline  (not much open world/sandbox, see).
And the story is good. Of course you will encounter many Mafia tropes - probably because the reality had its defining aspects, some of which carry over better to a game than others.
So, if an interactive mafia movie is something you might be interested in, I can recommend Mafia II.
If you want a sandbox for mayhem, look elsewhere (like Saints Row).
Either way, have fun!

I was sadly too late to throw in some money to the kickstarter for LISA, because if I had known the game would be this incredible I would have pushed what funds I could spare. To put it short: LISA is a true underrated gem of a game.
You play as Brad Armstrong, a former martial arts teacher who after an apocalyptic event now wallows in a miserable existence of self-hatred and pain-relieving drugs; tethered to his traumatic childhood at the hands of his abusive father Marty, as well as the loss of his younger sister Lisa. However, by chance he stumbles over an orphaned baby girl left alone. Realizing he has a chance to turn his life around, Brad attempts to raise the baby as his own daughter. But after several years, Brad returns home one day to find it spattered with blood and bodies; a dying friend telling him his daughter has been taken away by a local warlord named Rando. And thus, Brad's journey begins.
LISA's mechanics stay fresh and fun throughout the game. While most of the characters just use a standard command to attack, certain characters like Brad use the ASWD keys to string about four different moves. Combos are a common tactic to use in this case, especially since some of them activate special moves. Thus, you'll find yourself pulling these combos off to activate them rather than just selecting it separately. I found this to be a dynamic and enjoyable choice in design.
The story itself is a damn good rollercoster of emotions. Dingaling balances the dark and confronting themes of his game with off-the-wall absurdist humor, body horror that would make David Cronenberg proud, and post-apocalyptic badassery. This game was brilliant at making me laugh my head off one minute, and sending a cold chill down my spine the second.
The game choices in LISA, unlike most other RPGs, really do matter to the game. One very notable change is whether or not Brad has any of his limbs cut off: not only is your strength greatly diminished, the the keys used to string combos are reduced down to just ASD, or worse just taken out entirely. I can't remember the last time a game's choices affected the mechanics of the game, or if ever.
Though despite LISA's delivered promise of a cruel and brutal experience (one I respect, and held no grudges against), there were a few moments I felt were legitimately frustrating. Your introduction to the Russian Roulette mini-game, for example, is one I found to be rather nasty given the chance that it can wipe out half of your party.
The soundtrack is one of the best you'll ever listen to, and I highly recommend getting the Deluxe Edition just for it. Like the story, it has it's own variety and all the songs strike at the right cords. "Men's Hair Club" is a personal favorite of mine.
Overall, I highly recommend this game if you're a fan of indie RPGs with good stories and steep learning curves. LISA is a game I will never forget, and it's one I will champion for many months to come.

Too frustrating for me once I got late into the game. I stuck with this game until Area 3 but then it just started to feel like it was not a fun way to spend my time. I don't have loads of free time so I really care about making the most of it, but if you're willing to put up with that aspect I think you might still want to try this game for the unique experience it provides.
You'll likely encounter many spots where you lose lots of progress due to the placement of save points. You'll find yourself frequently backtracking just so you can save because you never know what's up ahead and if it might kill you. Especially as you get farther in the game, you get into situations where, no matter how well you use your characters, you'll lose if you don't grind. I don't find grinding to be a fun way to spend my free time. Neither do I enjoy doing the same part of a game like this over several times. There's annoying spider enemies that are easy to beat but just waste your time and don't give you any XP. There's annoying mechanics where you will just outright lose characters without much warning when you sleep at a fire, or your whole party will get poisoned. People who play this game say that the solution to those is to backtrack to earlier camps that you know are safe or that don't have a high chance of those bad things happening. How is that fun at all? You just have to spend time backtracking to something just so you can avoid these events - there's no challenge or anything, it's just asking for you to be bored so you can keep playing.
If it weren't for the frustrating gameplay, I would wholeheartedly recommend this game - the writing, art, music, etc... are all really original and entertaining in the same way that Earthbound was. Unfortunately, while you may find yourself drawn into the game in the earlier parts because of the relatively forgiving gameplay, it's all preparation for a slap in the face as you get to the later areas and realize you aren't really having fun with the game. Even then, the earlier parts of the game aren't without the same sort of frustrating design decisions that detract from the experience. I think it would've been possible to achieve what it seems this game was trying to achieve without having all these frustrating gameplay elements.
Either way, if you're just looking to have consistent fun and don't want to deal with something really frustrating or occasionally boring, don't get this game. If you're willing to put up with that and don't mind spending your free time doing things like grinding, backtracking just so you can save your game or find a safe campfire or switch party memebers or buy stuff at a shop, getting a game over because you're underleveled, or other gameplay elements like that that have been fixed in other modern games, you owe it to yourself to play this game for the unique experience it provides.

If you are considering buying LISA: THE PAINFUL, do so. Buy it right now and the expansion LISA: THE JOYFUL. Go play and beat both.
If you aren't thinking about buying LISA then read on.
LISA is a drug. LISA is about drugs. LISA is about sadness.
LISA will make you unhappy. It is PAINFUL to play, yet you can't and must not stop. Be yourself when you make decisions. Play on Pain Mode. Don't savescum. Learn from what you've done. Learn when it is right to forgive. Hate yourself, your actions, and everything around you. Then finally learn how to be happy.

A wasteland of Joy, mutants and desperate fiends. A tale of love, abuse and loyalty.
You play the part of Brad, a broken man known as an accomplished martial arts instructor, deeply tormented by grief and abuse.
Your life changes the day one of your drugged up afternoons are interrupted by a baby girl lying on the ground in front of you - a seemingly impossible event in a ruined world inhabited solely freaks and deranged men. The future of humanity is now literally in your hands and you will be forced to go to great length and make crushing choices to protect it.
Who will you be at the end of all of this?
The story, writing and soundtrack are the absolute highlights of this tale. Many of the tracks from the soundtrack stand on their own, even outside of the context of the game. The dialogue is impressive, moving from pitch black darkness to absolute hilarity with ease. The disturbing visuals adds greatly to the experience. The aesthetic looks like something Ralph Steadman would conjure up if he was less talented and into pixel art.
It is not without flaws, however. The game has some mechanical issues of major proportions and the limitations of the game engine are often apparent. It's not bad enough to detract from an incredible experience but one can't help but wonder what the game would play like with a bigger budget and a custom engine.
LISA is definitely not for everyone. If it is for you however - and if you read this far it quite possibly is - you will laugh, be disgusted, get angry and maybe even shed a tear or two when you experience this piece of art. It will make you feel something and that's a rare thing in gaming.
Seriously recommended.

I'm going to assume you guys know the basic premise of the game, so I'll skip the explanation and tell you guys how I feel about it.
This game provides very niche game play not seen in many other games. It gives you a fresh breather from the cookie cutter FPS games and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ly simple and repetitive indie puzzle-platformers that flood steam. The satisfaction you get from watching multiple enemies die in succession to a simple spiked pit trap of yours is immense. Spamming arrows down onto your enemies from afar is sadistically cathartic. Blitzing with your fellow Knights into enemy territory, whether it be above ground or covertly through a tunnel, is exciting and chaotic. This game puts a whole new spin on PvP action. It's a great way to spend an hour or two listlessly clicking away at gory little pixels on your screen for fun. And it is fun.
This game is actually deceptively hard to master. And maybe not in a good way. The controls feel very clumsy and sluggish, like you're wrestling a cow while wearing a straitjacket with the left side of your body completely paralyzed. Mining is a sluggish "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ I didn't mean to break THAT!" wonky ♥♥♥♥ fest that somehow fails to be an effective point-and-click system that will inevitably result in you accidently destorying your team mate's projects and uselessly digging up dirt from time to time. The Builder must also deal with extremely agitating buidling mechanics. It takes practice to build the simplest walls and traps with ease. PvP as Knight and Archer are perhaps less broken but it can still be a little confusing to tell where you are aiming sometimes. Navigation is also a ♥♥♥♥♥ as the battlefield quickly deteriorates and begins to look more and more like Marvel's Apocalypse went to town on the map. Craters form and intricatel defenses crumble, leaving a messy nightmare-scape that is near impossible to traverse at times.
Besides that there is the community. It can be best described as a senior citizen on life support. And not the cool senior citizen either, I mean the one that tries to guilt the nurses into ♥♥♥♥ing him before he dies and yelling at his care takers for giving him the wrong flavored pudding. The game's player base is very small and the few people you DO encounter can be VERY toxic and harsh towards new players; descending into frothing, seething fits of rage because "yer breakin muh meta". I'd say they're even worse than CSGO. You will get vote kicked a lot for simply exploring the game's mechanics and learning.

Achievements: All possible.  Frankly, they're quite easy.  They don't even require beating the whole game.
Pros/Cons:
+ The art is adorable and wacky.  It's got a lot of charm.
+ The songs are good.  They're all catchy with good rhythm.
+ Even to get an S rank, there was an allowance for mistakes, which was nice.  It was a little forgiving.
+ It's only $4.99.  While I didn't get a ton of playtime out of it, it is a rhythm game and replayability is a huge factor.  It's not a bad deal.
+/- This is the sort of rhythm game that's very metronomic.  Button presses never stray away from the underlying beat, nevermind what the rest of the music is doing.
+/- Much of the game's difficulty came from distractions thrown in to disrupt the player's concentration on the button prompts.  I, personally, don't enjoy that type of challenge in a rhythm game, but others might.
- It's really short.  There's only seven stages.
- There's no tutorial to speak of.  The game just plops you into a level with no real instruction.  Given that the level ends if you do poorly enough, it's a little frustrating.
- Button prompts cannot be changed.  They'll always be playstation buttons.  Even with it being a ported game, it's still annoying when playing with a keyboard or different type of controller.
- The timing for a few of the songs felt a tad... off.  Not enough to completely ruin the game, but enough to be frustrating to compensate for.  That said, not everyone seems to have this problem.
- Controls cannot be edited.
Overall:
Superstar Dance Club was alright.  As a lover of rhythm games, I did find some enjoyment out of it.  However, the wonkiness in the timing paired with the shortness and lack of button customization really hold this game back.  I know it was ported from the PS1, but that does not excuse the absence of a tutorial.  I really loved the art and the crazy looking dancers, but that alone cannot redeem this game for me.
Pick this up if you are feeling particularly nostalgic.  Otherwise, I'd suggest passing it up.

tl;dr this game is worth the dollar just so you can marvel at how horrible it is. I have no way to explain the positive reviews. If this game was your childhood, you were seriously starved for video games to play.
From my very first glance at the little cover image when this game popped onto my screen as a Steam gift, my impression of Superstar Dance Club was that it had to be a Dadaist statement, not an actual game. The ridiculous title and hideous art style suggested that the creator was either an utterly talentless "indie developer" trying to be ironic, or a colorblind virgin with an art style primarily influenced by Astro Boy and Mew Mew Kissy Cutie Black.
To get this out of the way: the gameplay of Superstar Dance Club has two different sequences of buttons at the top of the screen, and the game tells you at the last second which sequence comes next. The two sequences do not change over the duration of the song, and buttons are always pressed rhythmically on the downbeat. So it's a really stupid and boring system, but don't get me wrong, Bust a Groove had an even stupider core mechanic and Bust a Groove was awesome. The difference is that Bust a Groove is full of personality and has great music. Thanks to the simple enjoyment of tactile interaction with catchy songs, rhythm games almost can't help but be entertaining for at least a little while.
As for Superstar Dance Club...
... well.
The first song in Superstar Dance Club is one sickeningly cheerful measure of blaring synthesizer looped eight times. It's 30 seconds long, tops.
I was a little curious about the rest of the songs--surely some of them would mix it up with different instrument voices or something--but the sync is so far off (and/or the timing is so strict) that I was not equal to the challenge of pressing the X button four times to make the lazily drawn waifu on the screen cycle between her five frames of "animation." So I said screw it and uninstalled.
When I say that this game seems like a Dadaist statement, I mean that I could imagine someone creating this game as a way to sneer at people who think that the objective of game development is to create something that players enjoy. Superstar Dance Club is bad in a way that's much more than a lack of good qualities: what we have here is the Sweet Bro and Hella Jeff of rhythm games. It is a nega-game that finds creative ways to be unpleasant.
Go ahead and buy it, I guess. Perhaps you will gain something from the experience.

Superstar Dance Club is a rhythm game originally released as a budget title on PlayStation in the early '00s. There's quite a bit of interesting history surrounding it that Wikipedia won't tell you, actually.
In Japan it was originally a Simple 1500 game known as "Love Para: Lovely Tokyo Para-Para Musume", developed by Warashi and published by Media Rings in 2001, with XS games localising and releasing it in North America in 2002, and Europe in 2003. It's existence is mainly to cash in on the Para-Para dancing fad in Japan at the time. A lot of that cultural significance was understandably lost in XS Games' localisation, which is what this Steam version is based on, but you can still see elements of early '00s Japanese culture in the game's visuals.
Youtuber Vysethedetermined2 explains this game's history in more detail in this video's description. You can also see what the game looks like running on original hardware.
But as for the game itself, I'm coming into this from a 2015 perspective, as I hadn't even heard of it beforehand. So, as a 2015 release, it actually stands up quite well! The graphics are charming and have aged well despite the low resolution, the music is catchy Eurobeat-inspired tunes, and the gameplay hold up well too! It's not too complicated, you just press the buttons to the beat, and occasionally the button prompts change positions on the screen to keep you on your toes. It starts out easy, but gets very challenging in the later stages! There are 7 stages in all, and each have three difficulty levels, so it's not a particularly long game, but at its original price of ¥1500, or indeed $5 USD on Steam, it's good value for the content you're getting.
On the technical side, like all of Console Classics' PlayStation rereleases, this release runs in a PS1 emulator with no enhancements, so it's exactly how it was back in 2001 for better or for worse. Since it's a 2D game, raising the internal resolution would only introduce graphical issues anyway. To make the game more presentable on modern systems, it comes with its own launcher with a bunch of preset graphical and sound settings, and control profiles for a variety of controllers. It even adds Steam Achievements. Unfortunately, you can't remap the controls to your liking, so Xbox 360 controller users are stuck using the analog stick to navigate the menus, but it also supports the PS3 controller without requiring it to be remapped to XInput controls, so that's a plus if you want to play with the original control layout.
While the presentation is a bit bare bones and could stand for some more customisation, the game itself is very well preserved, and for retro games I feel preserving exactly how they were is important, so I'm pretty happy with this release.
Do I recommend it? Absolutely. If you like rhythm games, this one may be simple, but it's great value and definitely fun and charming.

One of, if not the, best 2D platformers I've ever played.
People who will enjoy this game are ones who are looking for a challenging retro 2D platformer that takes both skill and a bit of luck.  The game has multiple modes (Infinite Lives (respawn at checkpoints), SIngle Life (failure deletes save), and 9 Lives (Play as a kitty cat!) and 2 campaigns derived from the same map (Normal and Extra Spicy).  Both have a completely different feel to them as each has a different progression and abilities are obtained in a different order.
My only gripes are the lack of a soundtrack (kinda wish they had something like K.O.L.M had but then again, there's always youtube and neither gameplay nor immersion are affected by this) and the lack of some kind of minimap (backtracking in this game is an absolute pain and relies on the memory of the player.  This is especially noticeable when coming off of another game such as VVVVVV, which shares a similar map style).
It's free and an easy game to become obsessed with, so you have no excuse to at least give it a look.

Most importantly, you get all this good to great gameplay for free. If this was a 10 euro game I wouldn't recommend it because of lack of content. 5 Euros? Still dangerous. 2 Euros? If you like jump and runs of the cat mario (but much, much, much less punishing and frustrating) type you will enjoy this game and I recommend it to you.

I understand why this game could be appealing for some people. I do. But it's certainly not appealing to me!
Pinstripe is a "stylish" platformer where you move in a dreamy world populated by very strange non-playing characters with which you can barely interact. There are a few things that you can do, most of all jumping and shooting with a sling, although the game does veeeeeeeeeeery little to tell you what to do or how to do it. There are puzzle elements which are hard to find but most of the time not hard to solve (mostly they are annoying skill games in which you must push the spacebar repeatedly to switch on several lights at the same time).
Initially I was just annoyed, especially because in order to proceed you basically need to find what in any game would be just secret areas, and here it is something that you must find out unavoidably if you want to proceed further (for instance, without getting to all the areas of the first part, you will hardly accumulate the 300 frozen drops needed for the trip to Red Wash). But ok, thanks to a couple of walkthrough I was able to find my way to the final part of the world.
Still annoyed, but on board, let's see if the conclusion of the game is better than the beginning... and then I got stuck in a glitch (continuously respawning in the middle of the screen and falling down outside the screen). That was it for me, I didn't find the game compelling enough to bother to finish it and having to stand not only its gameplay, but also its glitches.
Both the music and the voice acting are good, though. And the graphic style can be appealing. To me, the killer is the boring gameplay and the inexplicably convoluted world building. What's even more inexplicable to me is that it seems that many people find pleasure in finishing the game repeatedly to get all the achievements... I suppose that there is a cup of tea for everyone!
It was a fun game though the gameplay mechanics could of used some work.

This may be my first review, and to be honest I know that probably no one will read this. HOWEVER! My thoughts on this game after playing it for about an hour.
Holy.♥♥♥♥♥♥ Balls. My first thought was "This game is going to be the exact reason why Trackmania doesn't have rockets" but after playing through the tutorial and being amazed at the easy and intuitive controls my thoughts were "Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥? Why dopesnt Trackmania have rockets?!"
So yes, that is what this game essentially is. It is Trackmania with rockets. This is not in any way negative as Trackmania is arguably one of the most visually pleasing and intuitive racing games out there.
The only negatives that come to mind, or simply things I feel the game is missing are:
- The graphics leave a bit to be desired. I understand this is an indi game, and for an indi game they are amazing. But I think if they were a bit better this game would be insane.
- Get the community involved more than just ghosts! Let us race each other, crash into each other in lap races, race against each other in real time in time attack. Add in a track editor that we can build tracks and share with other players.
- I feel like I should be able to control each air brake individually, at least each side, purely for more control in mid air.
That's it. If these things were implemented I think this game could easily be as big as Trackmania at it's peak. I am THOROUGHLY enjoying this game.

Side-scrolling action meets team-based gameplay. What's not to love?
Don't let the pixel graphics fool you. This game is actually a lot of fun, especially when you're playing with a full server, and both teams are giving it their all. Battles can go on for an hour, or only for a few minutes depending on the gamemode, as well as how well your team constructs your base. Mid-field bunkers and towers change hands constantly, or are brought down under a rain of bomb arrows and ballistae bolts. Arrows rain down from the battlements as your team rushes for that one small opening in the enemy base...The action can get pretty intense, especially when a well-laid plan works out.
The game is fairly simple to understand, and its various gamemodes (some of which are more popular than others at certain times of day) allow you to play short or long games easily. Controls are simple as well, which is a plus.
For the most part, the community is pretty chill. If you're on the Austrailian or EU servers. US servers, unfortunately, tend to be filled with salty players or trolls looking to mess with people. This is especially bad around night-time, when most admins and mods are offline, and nobody is there to enforce the rules. You'd be shocked at how many people freely throw around derogatory terms and names. It's almost like walking into a room of 12-year old CoD players getting salty with each other.
BUT. The game itself, when everything is going smoothly, and players are focusing on the game (instead of on their egos), is VERY solid. Everything is balanced. No team gets any special treatment, your K/D is not important at all, and your skill is ultimately what wins or loses you the game.
Basically:
Great game. Balanced gameplay. US servers are fairly toxic sometimes. I give it 4 triple-arrow shotgun blasts out of 5.

I like the theme in this game of the preciousness and also objectification men can treat women with. It caught me off guard, I dismissed this game and it had to win me over and it did. I was opposed to the art style of cute little caricature of a tough guy with a big head, but it won me over. It's called dark and painful, and I also dismissed it thinking it was just going to be cynical and sardonic, but I don't think it is. It feels like a singular vision and not a story by committee, and it feels rich and deep. Technical aspects like not being able to skip the opening, accidentally selecting pain mode 3 times in a row, falling off cliffs constantly, I find easy to overlook personally. I celebrate these sorts of unique and singular flavors that are quite rare, even amoung independentally developed games, which still largly think inside the box in terms of story telling. I also dismissed this as an RPG maker game, why would I pay for it? I ended up buying it twice. Plus the DLC and soundtrack.

This game...is rough. Not in a diffuculty sense, unless you play Pain Mode, but in an emotional sense.
In a story standard, better have a box of tissues nearby. This game will not hold back on the feels, because this deals with some heavy stuff. It would be best if you would play LISA: The First before any of this to understand the storyline. Then play this game, then Pain Mode, then the Joyful DLC. Or you could just...watch it on YouTube.
In a gameplay standard, it's amazing! Even though it's just an RPG, it's one of the most original ones I've encountered. Instead of an open world, you're limited to a 2D platformer, such as ones like Mario or Megaman. And with that 2D feature, there's different depths, adding to that platforming aspect. This world is very large; and if you don't know what you're doing, you're bound to get lost. With that open world comes a wacky cast of helpers, some serious, other just...weird. The fighting system is just like any other RPG, except, sometimes, your basic attack can input combos, which can lead to special moves!
The music is fantastic, too! It helps set the mood for whatever is happening in the game, and does it really well!
This game also requires patience. There's a lot of ways to die. And I mean A LOT. Brad moves kinda slow, but you'll get some faster way of transportation pretty early on.
Overall, buy this game, the soundtrack, the artbook, and the DLC. It is worth it.

similar to Company of Heroes , but very complex , you can control groups and squads , or you can control single units , even control acuratly with mouse aiming and arrow key movements.
for example say you have 1 tank unit , and 2 infantry soldiers , you can have the 2 infantry soldiers fight as a group or fight as single units(1soldier). you can use cover and environment to hide during combat.
say an enemy tank arrives facing your own tank unit , you can either let the tank engage automaticaly or you can take control of it, then use mouse for accurate aiming , each vehicle parts with different resistance or weakness.
you may decide to only destroy the vehicle tracks , or turret , to disable it depending on the situation , without completely destroying the vehicle , wich you can later repair and use for your own soldiers.
use the arrow key to control tank movements all while controlling the camera and turret targetting. or simply left click for move orders and let the AI control itself.
each single soldier or vehicle have its own inventory and can rearm from dead bodies or pickup helmets from fallen soldiers , after a long battle you can find alot of weapons ,helmets and grenades that might be better then your current equipment. items are found on fallen bodies or may be dropped on the ground.
the environment is destroyable so you can drive a tank into objects or fire explosive rounds to clear a path for your infantry , for example as a defending team you may want to shell the area you will be shooting at so that the invading enemies do not have any cover to protect themselfs.
you can also create very customised squads with machineguns , antitank weapons , grenades, by changing the inventory of each individual soldiers live on the battlefield.
the game does not give you a tutorial but simply information messages poping up as you play. it is hard to learn . but you learn from your mistakes , you click and read everything , and it becomes much easier after a few missions.
you can also control game speed , with 6 different speeds , slow down when you need to think or control large number of units in a short time.
you can also scavange for ammo and weapons on dead bodies and rearm your veterans so they can continue fighting. each individual unit has its own inventory and grenades , ammo , etc...
i personaly enjoy this more then company of heroes (not that company of heroes was bad , i did post a positive review for both game. lol) , Men Of War is more difficult, more advanced, and much more fun for people looking for a tactical strategy game.

I originally wrote a review back in 2013, and much has changed since then. However, I still cannot recommend this game, despite having played it for so much. I will keep things brief. Because much of the development is focused on multiplayer, I will mainly discuss that.
The balance for the units is variable, but tends towards being good enough to the point where I cannot complain about that alone. However, it has always been the case that German tanks absolutely destroy all other units in the game. This could be offset by AT guns, which are readily available. However, that will never happen as your teammates will likely build blobs of infantry, rather than a good force capable of dealing with a variety of situations. In my three years of playing this game, I have rarely had a teammate who bothered to build anti-tank guns. Similarly, I have been on teams that seemed to be absolutely convinced that taking the fuel objective will assure victory, despite their inablilty to form any cohesive plan beyond typing obscenities into chat and throwing fits when they don't get their way. Since the game has absolutely no punishment for such behavior, these people tend to infest the game, while all the polite players tend to move on.
From a technical view, this game is barely functional. The game freezes and drops players constantly, and often crashes during mode changes. Sound effects and music will freqently continue playing at incorrect times, and will often overlap and become very distracting. Had the "battle servers" not been implemented, the game would be an even bigger waste of time, but at least it does not frameskip and lag constantly when it actually "works". Loading takes forever due to the hardware limitiations of some players' computers, causing matchmaking to take anywhere from five to fifteen minutes. You are waiting far more than you are playing. This makes people impatient, and auses them to drop out. Frankly, I don't blame them. Frequently, the solution I hear is to play with friends, to which I reply that other people generally have schedules, family, relationships, jobs and a host of other real-life issues that make this practical to those groups whom have no responsibilities or lives. Things are not much better design-wise.
Battles usually consist of blobs going against each other, with the bigger and better armed blob winning. This will typically take time as WWII rifles were clearly about as accurate as an uncrumpled napkin thrown against the wind. Since the AI is awful at pathfinding, it will often retreat down the worst possible path, and will happily run through a minefield. Weapons team frequently get stuck in deployment, making redeployment impossible, unless the member holding the weapon is killed. Engineers will happily corner themselves in a spot with barbed wire, and it is impossible to free them at times. Even ordering squads behind cover is a chore, as they seem to prefer vaulting in front of it and get shot. Overall, the AI requires a large amount of babysitting.
The only reason I continue playing this game is because the marketplace is far more concerned with anime graphic novels, Trump campaign cash-ins and an endless parade of reboots rather than making a decent squad-based RTS.
