This game is beautiful, moving, and fun to play.  It's relatively simple platforming-style gameplay with some puzzle-solving elements and shooting an occasional enemy.  It's not a difficult game, which I find perfectly fitting for the mood of the game, and which I personally prefer.  But if you're the type of person who wants to be crying in the shower over how hard a video game is, this one's not for you.
You are navigating through hell to find your kidnapped daughter, while unveiling a mystery behind the story.  Normally I hate when games make me go back & forth between screens I've already visited, but I didn't mind it in this game at all.  The scenery and music was so pleasant, and at the points where you were heading backwards it was to uncover many new things, so it felt fresh - you're not walking back ten screens just to pick up one thing that is newly unlocked, like some other games do.  Plus, your character moves pretty fast.
There are a lot of small, quirky details in this game that made me smile.  And I found myself genuinely moved at the end when the full story is revealed.
I felt the ending had just the right mix of satisfaction and open-endedness.
A couple very minor gripes (in case the developer is reading):
- The game is only in widescreen, which was not made clear initially.  The default setting is fit-to-screen, so on my fullscreen monitor the edges were being cut off.  As I was playing, and my character was walking off-screen for a bit before actually advancing to the next scene, I suspected that the aspect ratio was off but it didn't seem significant.  It wasn't until I got impossibly stuck at one part in the game and looked up a video walkthrough that I discovered a VERY significant portion was being cut off - including the items I needed to interact with for that puzzle.  Had to quit back out to the menu and change the display to a fixed aspect ratio so I could see everything.
- One puzzle-type moment where you are trying to open the door to Pinstripe's house was unfairly difficult and I found I was only able to accomplish it with keyboard smashing as fast as I was physically able.  (Although considering how angry I got about it, the keyboard smashing was a somewhat satisfying outlet.)  There were two similar door locks in a previous area that weren't AS impossible, where it was more within the range of being a satisfying challenge.  But that final one was just infuriating because it felt like no amount of skill or finessing was going to help you - it was only pound space/enter at top speed until you get lucky.
- As other reviewers have complained about - the fact that you need 300 drops for the lift ticket and you're only capable of collecting just barely that many if you've gotten every single drop up to that point is rather frustrating.  It would have been nice to have a little more wiggle room on that, so you're not totally locked out if you've missed a handful.
ANYWAY, those small complaints aside, this game is beautiful and wonderful.  A quick play (about 2-3 hours), but it still felt satisfying.  I'm not one to whine about price vs gameplay time as long as the game is well-made and a good experience, which Pinstripe absolutely is.  Plus the short length lends it to being easily replayable for achievement completion and the secrets that can only be unlocked on a second playthrough.  I definitely recommend it if you're a fan of light indie games with an emotionally-involving story.  As a Kickstarter backer (full disclosure?), I'm very pleased with my investment!

I personally didn't like how the save system worked; it made it difficult to replay and do the secret stuff since it provides a save station, yet you're not in complete control of it. I expected the usual "if you load, it brings you right to where you were when you saved" dealie, but this game does ninja secret saves which kinda defeat the purpose of the save points. It would've been okay if it pulled a Skyrim and had a list of saves and a separate slot for autosave to load from, but it doesn't, so that was pretty inconvenient.
*START OF SPOLIERS I GUESS*
I only got super stuck a couple of times: getting to the ice minigame in Edge Wood and putting the numbers in to get to Red Wash. However, I feel like it was just my fault for not realizing the solutions. I mean, the Edge Wood one seems a bit "okay, c'mon now; how could you expect me to do that, there, at that time, using only what I know up until that point?" but it's also kinda iffy to decide on since the solution is somewhat indicated, meaning I might've just been temporarily dumber than the majority, so I'll just be safe and say I was being dumb. The Red Wash one was litterally me just being dumb though. The numbers were clearly indicated (and glowing) at the top, and I just happened to think I couldn't interact with them.

Art is crazy great to look at and beautiful, characters are fun and alive, voice acting is awesome, music really fits the moment and gets you into it, story is basic but very enjoyable; it's definitely a game I would recommend to everyone. It's also fairly short, so it's ideal for those who don't have a lot of free time. I litterally played through 6 times.
All in all, yes, it has its small kinks, but I can tell you one thing for certain: this game has lots of heart in it, and it really shows. Please play it; you won't be disappointed. :D

This game is fun and CoH1 used to be a revolutionary invention of a strategy game. Matches can be exciting until the very end since you can recover from heavy blows if done right. There is a ton of micro managing involved and less macro, and what makes this game different from other strategy games is that there is action and battle all game long, hardly room to breathe, and aggressive playstyle is heavily encouraged. Also, no base building.
The game should be enjoyed in a not overly competitive setting (ranked is fine, but don't play it for money) and here is why: while most is based on raw skill and finesse of a player, the realism aspect (no perfect 100% accuracy etc.) can completely turn the tide of battle based on mostly luck. Example: I was bombarding an occupied building with a mortar. It was about to collapse so the squad abandoned it. Right as they left the building, before they could even spread out, my mortar round actually missed the building and hit the entire squad and wiped them out in an instant. Another example: tanks make an extreme difference in this game but sometimes whether they get destroyed or not depends on rng - does the AT gun hit the last shot before the heavy tank can retreat? Does it miss my tank so it can escape to safety? Those can be game deciding factors. There are some community tournaments taking place but other than that there is no competitive scene for this game, which is partially due to the random element this game has to it. I just wanted to mention this. For me it's neither a negative nor a positive aspect.
However, I cannot support the decisions they made when they created and published this game. Which is a bummer because otherwise this game would be WAY more popular. It currently has a decent playerbase/count, but the numbers keep falling steadily. Back to what I dont like about this game.
3 out of 5 playable factions are DLC. Balance issues take too long to be addressed so DLC factions often stay overpowered for quite some time - right now the balance is in a decent place, though, I'm happy at last. Campaigns are DLC. And the game, a game you pay full price for, has microtransactions for items which heavily define and support your ability and playstyle in matches, so that lacking said items would put you at a large disadvantage. I don't like calling it pay to win since with enough time investment, you can buy those items yourself (ingame currency and random loot), but...it is close to p2w. I'm sad about it and I hope if they ever release a CoH3, they show that they learned their lesson. IF they do it better next time, I'll be here - playing the game a crap ton and recommending it to everyone because then it has the potential to become big.

Absolutely loving this game and I'm never going to stop playing it. The mechanics are easy to understand and work with right from the start. The story is tidy and doesn't get in the way, but gives you a focus. The gameplay is wonderful. The soundtrack is pleasing and adds depth without being annoying. The artwork is delightfully detailed but elegantly simple. Soooooo many wonderful things to say about this game.
It's extremely challenging, even on easy, and forces you to consider alternative solutions to combat, travel, weapons, personnel, everything. For example, you may have enough "money" to upgrade your ship with protection from ion bursts, but you instead purchase something else. Next thing you know, you're running into a bunch of situations where the ion protection would have been very helpful. Now you have to find some other way to deal with the enemy while repairing damages from ion bursts.
I like that the game is never the same twice which gets the brain going too. You may play one scenario where where lots of drones would have made the difference, but you die anyway. So you start a new game, start grabbing drones like crazy and the next thing you know they're useless in this scenario.
I have caught myself playing this game for hours straight with hardly a break. The only other games that have caught my attention like this are Civilization (all of them), Borderlands and Skyrim. The only real critique I have is in regards to the store system. It would be nice to be able to sell anything I have on the ship like missiles, ship systems, etc. Then again, I could see how that might allow a player to OP their ship and may take away some of the other gameplay aspects of the game. I agree with The Mighty Griggles: Giant space spiders are an instant rage quit.
*** Edit ***
Over one year now and this is still one of my favorite games ever. I easily waste hours each time I start it up. The mod community is fantastic and the mods add so much more life to the game. I can not recommend this game any more than I already do.

Rogue-like slasher with rpg elements. Nice quick convenient "die and build up" your character aspect. Essentially every time you die in trying to beat the game, you get better and better equips you can store in your "dimensional" storage which allows you to use it for the next play-through. The catch is that every time you replace previous items you can only use items from that particular play-through. This in turn gets you to use unique classes specifically to collect up amazing gear way later and then die off, use that gear from the beginning and in turn collect up better gear. Eventually you'll get so epic with unlocked perks and such that the game will be a breeze. It's a fun challenge. 5 hour marker beat it but there is harder modes to play and some replay value involved with different classes and whatnot. :)
Update:I have played it a good bit more and there is in total, three ways to beat the game. The first is the most obvious, the other two.. quite a bit of a challenge. More game-play to it than I thought. more than 15 hours in, and still not quite to those other two endings yet :P

Heart and Soul one like me always wished to see within a commercial RPG Maker game. The game takes example from the Mother series (Earthbound) in making a simple turn based rpg that focuses on personality and charm and expands on that concept the way only this specific developer could. Soma Spirit is a unique experience that takes inspiration from multiple greats. If classic Rareware made an rpg, I'm not even sure they could match the amount of quirkiness shown in this one. Ultimately the game is a satisfying experience that any JRPG or non JRPG fan can enjoy. It is a pleasant place to be where the player has the choice to shift the direction of the story via cruicial choices. I am proud to say that I highly recommend this one.

Tl;dr: A good game that is worthy of a look at by any RPG or Indie enthusiast.
If you are a fan of good RPG Maker games, this is a 100% must buy.
While by no means perfect, this game certainly has the heart and soul put into it with a wonderfully delightful style reminiscent of the Mario and Luigi RPG's (Two characters with both being usefull), A Link to the Past (Light and Dark World) and even a unique battle system that makes each battle a chess match. With branching stories and a difficulty setting, this game ozzes replayability.
Have I mentoined the charm? The charcters of this world are so interesting and fun to be around, and while the story isn't a shakespearean masterpiece, the characters and idea alone are certainly more and enough for an Indie Title.
It would be a crime to not mention the awesome soundtrack. Developer Torch 60 really served up one spicy soundtrack, with soothing, chraming beats in the light world, and fast, electric pieces in the dark world. It's a soundtrack so good, they even have a music player in game for you to listen to them all! Thanks Torch 60!
Overall, this game is worthy of a look at by any RPG or Indie enthusiast. It's a great game to play on those long weekends, and I hope to see a sequel, or even a new game, from this dev team in the future.

So far I've really been enjoying the game. The music has been wonderful, and the plot shows a branching storyline that you will be introduced to early. You'll know which world you are in at any given time by the music, and whether anything in the world (minus your player characters) are monochrome and sad, or colorful and happy. I would reccomend this at full price for someone looking for a neat, casual, RPG experience.

This is a rather short RPGMaker game.
You have 2 parties with 4 members each. At the end both are united. Now this party still has 4 members and you can only
choose 2 of them (the others don't get any experience).
The world is real small with only a few dungeons. You see your enemies and can avoid them (most times) but some are
so fast that you can't do anything but fight. Later there is one annoying blue orb that you can't fight but is real real fast
and follows you...if hit you lose hitpoints till you die.
Running or sailing the open world there are a few encounters. You don't see the enemies beforehand but the encounters
are allways at the same spot...once triggered you must go to town or a dungeon before you can fight them again.
There are some hidden locations with chests but you must bump into walls or walk certain spaces to find them.
The balancing of the game is not the best. Most times its special skills against everything. And your best friend are
magic points refill potions.
The story has big potential but is wasted. The end is crap and total unlogical.
Going back to already played towns/dungeons can trigger funny effects like your choosen party disbanded and now you have the original party till you can get to the only point were you can choose your partymembers.
Its not a total loss but nothing you must play. So if you can get it cheap try it.

This game even though Aldorlea you make great games, I personally can't recommend this game.  The balancing in this game just isn't that well made.  And I was playing on normal.
I actually thoroughly enjoyed this game up until the final dungeon.  At that point though this game like Moonchild just drug to an absolute crawl.  Part of the problem is the final dungeon is split into 3 very big and VERY open areas which makes it feel as if no matter what you do you make very little progress, plus its the only dungeon to have traps that suck your health, and end up dying rather quickly.
But what really put a sword through this was the final boss fight.  Did you playtests this at ALL?  I was lv 30!  With the way this game is designed I doubt that unless you abuse the 2x exp relics that most people would be lv 22-24 by the time they reach Raven III.  The problem is that this game does 2 boss fights in a row, and the second unless you are prepared can insta-KO you in a couple of rounds due to one of the good/bad things about this game's combat system. Alright you maggots, are you ready to get involved in possibly the greatest war second only to THE Great War? , well too bad.
Yeah if you came here looking for a historical look at WWII through the eyes of the Soviet Union or even the United States, you'd be a fool. You'd also be a fool to buy this game at full price like I did, and it's DLC, for full price like I did, trust me boys and girls and everything inbetween it's better you just buy this and everything for it when it's in a Summer / Winter sale.
Now hold on don't go let me give you the review so for anyone looking for a number I give this game a 6/10 slightly above average / average.
Alright to the real review!
Graphics: The graphics are overall pleasing, I feel like some of the textures could've been higher and to be really honest, the Animations are only really decent, they hardly went all out on them, after all if you pay close attention to a soldier reloading his fingers don't move and the ammo he's reloading sort of just clips into the gun. But otherwise they're still nice, and in fact if you play it as intended, zoomed out a little and flying like the all seeing eye the game looks rather great, trees and foliage need a little more work but I've seen very few games make them adequate in my eyes. Also I personally would give this warning, Do NOT play this game if you do not have a high end / upgraded PC you will have a very hard time playing it, the graphics on my PC are pretty good and even then I have some problems.
Sound design: Oh I must admit I looove the sound design it's really good, and the voice acting for the characters and vehicle drivers is probably my favorite bit of this game, but it is CRIMINAL to not mention if you want to hear a better bit of the sound design you should have a unit engage then pan to the edge of the map and listen to the far off echo of the gunfire. That was a lovely little touch and I wish it was more a part of the game since it comes off as "just ambiet noise" and it's not, it's still lovely to listen to a .50 cal firing a quarter mile away.
Gameplay: The gameplay to CoH II is actually very fluid for the most part, infantry combat can go either way and generally speaking it comes down to which faction you're playing, how experienced you are with counters , cover, and concentration but that's really only going to be important in multiplayer, Skirmish is a blast though in my opinion, here's a quick rundown of unit types for those of you fanatics out there like me who wanted to see what they tossed into this game to make it interesting, let's just throw some Soviet units out there : Basic infantry - Conscripts, Engineers, Penal Battalions. Weapon Teams - Maxim Machine Gun Teams, 81mm Mortar Teams, 76mm Anti Tank Gun Teams, Light Vehicles - American Lend Lease Armored Car, American Lend Lease Half Track, Russian T-60 Light Tank (37mm gun). Medium Tanks And Light Artillery - SU-76 SPG / Tank Destroyer, T-34 Medium Tank, SU-85 Tank Destroyer, Last but not least the favorite of any tank fan , Heavy Tanks - The IS-2, KV-1, And KV-8 (A KV-1 with a flamethrower and 47mm short barrel gun.)
Overall the list isn't too shabby, but obviously there are going to be problems with people's expectations and what you get, but I think the unit list isn't too bad.
Now I won't talk about the Campaign much I'll just say this, it's not great, in fact I'd say if you played it for the story, if you have Russian Lineage that served in The Great Patriotic War, you'd probably be offended by it, but to be fair, this was a Canadian look at the Russians,
Long story short I think the game is getting a lot of negativity without it being brought on about the game itself, I'll agree the price tag is outrageous, I'd call it a 20 dollar game at that but the DLC chopping is pretty bad too.. there are a whole 3 factions in the DLC waiting to be brought back to the game, and one of them (The Oberkommando West) was both uneccessary, and clearly not balanced well enough, even to this day it's hardly a finished faction so many problems are brought up with that faction, for instance they have such a vastly superior group of infantry that the Russians practically can't fight them without Shock Troops or without massive blobs of Conscripts but the problem isn't just in their infantry it's their ability to be the faction with the fastest "tank" roll out in the game, by that I mean they can start building and have built a tank by about a 4-8 minute lead on the other factions, and it's just utterly moronic to have to deal with it if the person controlling it knows what they're doing. Personally I wish they had added literally anything other than ANOTHER German faction, sure putting the Italians in there would've been hard to do what with their lack of armor, but look at what they did to the poor U.S. , the U.S. has a massive arsenal to choose from and they put a Tank Destroyer in the main Tank building that wasn't even mass produced, they don't even put the Hellcat in there, they put a Jackson in there though!, what!?
Arrgh now that I think about it this game is a bit irritating, but only really in Multiplayer, the story is trite but no one should buy it for the story. Skirmish is fun though, and the community is busy making maps so it's always a fresh new bit of gameplay to try a map you've never seen before.
Hopefully this small essay didn't turn anyone away from the game without at least looking up some gameplay on YouTube of it to see if it's your thing.

This little thing is a gem in the rough; I bought it for a dollar, and haven't regretted a single thing. This game has an adorable level of attention payed to it, from the helmets of the soldiers to the magnificent armor warfare system. Everything about your squads must be managed--from their health to their ammo supply--but if you click the right settings they'll do alot of the basic healing stuff on their own.
What is great about the game:
You can use captured weaponry and fight awesome battles with memorable moments; I remember watching a German tank slip into an icy stream, its crew bailing out and swimming to shore before being gunned down by my Soviet troops. The tank selection is great, the artillery mechanics are great..oh, and did I mention that you can go First Person too (well more third person, but same concept)? In one mission, I had my men crawl on their bellies, sniping enemy units as they went, to capture a broken T-34 tank. Once mine, I personally drove it about, shooting every Nazi fanatic I could see.
This game is also very realistic, as my T-34 rampage was ended by a single German soldier's hand held anti-tank grenade...although to be fair I ran my tank over several trenches into the middle of several infantry companies. From fire suppression tactics to Hulk episodes in a tank, this game has everything to make a fun WW2 experience (minus the Russian winter of starvation and other bad things...). Everything is also very destructible, and for the game's age, the graphics are actually quite nice.
What is not so great about the game;
No game is perfect, however awesome it may be, and this one does have a few flaws. I've been following the development of Pinstripe since its Kickstarter campaign. The story behind its creation is as inspiring as the game itself – there is a ton of heart put into it and it shows. Pinstripe's strong points are of course its stunning art and music direction. The world is vivid, colourful and imaginative, the characters are quirky, the voice acting is entertaining, and the soundtrack sets a solemn and tranquil tone (the soundtrack is also just a great listen on its own). There is a really nice balance between a sort of dark underlying plotline contrasted against a consistent dose of light humour and general silliness, which prevents the story from ever getting too heavy. Pinstripe isn't a particularly long game, but for a casual gamer like myself, this is actually preferable. Plus, there is a clever design element that will leave anyone with even a hint of curiosity in their bones unable to resist at least second playthrough, if not a third or fourth. Highly recommended to anyone who enjoys the puzzle adventure genre!

Addicting little game that you start over and over again "just one more time" to see if you can beat your own score. The game starts out with some basic moves to defend against the incoming wolves. Soon you begin to notice that you can disarm beaten wolves as well, which allows you to fight back using their weapons. This is where a tactical layer of the game comes into play: Should I try to catch the incoming cleaver out of the air or should I duck below it, so it hits the wolf on the other side? Should I throw the cleaver into the wolf wielding the chainsaw or should I let it come close so I got a chance to grab the chainsaw for myself?
The more you play, the better you get at finding the best solutions for the different combinations of enemies the game throws at you and soon you will find yourself escaping from seemingly impossible situations with ease.
Since the game is free & small in filesize there is no reason not to try it. Unless you are a wolf.

is a strategy game taking place in WW2, where the player can fight for the Soviets, Germans or Allies. Players command infantry and tanks to win the battle at hand and progress through the campaign of each faction.
This game is really good and fun, though as players progress through the campaigns the battles become increasingly difficult to achieve without stuffing up either one thing or getting everyone killed, often fighting against uneven odds to outright one-sided battles. Never the less, this game was really enjoyable and is one that I am fond of remembering.
The graphics are quite good, from the enviroment to individual soldiers.
While not memorable, the theme whenever a battle is about to/currently happening makes the battle flow nicely.
Aside from introductions to campaigns (the Soviet campaign in particular), they don't appear that often to make any significance. The art used is the same for the graphics.
Aside from the Soviet campaign, the story is derived mainly from historical-ish settings (probably).
For a total of 19 missions altogether and the difficulty of such missions, this game should at least last players for a day (assuming the player has the time to play this for the day).
Other than the short-cut keys, the controls for this strategy game is pretty easy.
The main attraction to this game. Featuring realistic accuracy, items and damage. Players may face overwhelming enemies and are placed with only a few infantry available.
While there's not much of a story to follow, the battles are engaging and fun on EASY alone. Experience this game yourself to enjoy this epic game.

Trials looks simple, but it's pretty dificult if you want to truly master it. Getting only Gold medals is going to take you a long, long time. I'd gladly recommend Trials. It's a game anyone can enjoy, even if it's for just a few tracks.

This game touches on a lot of issues that artists and creators of all sorts come across, making it relatable and therefore potentially enjoyable for those who can relate to those feelings. However, at the risk of sounding heartless, just because it displays those issues in a personal and emotional way doesn't necessarily mean that it makes this game exempt from criticism. Self-realising that one's own games are difficult to navigate and confusing in purpose isn't something to glorify through means of performance art, and especially doesn't work in a game medium.
I am not aware of the history of this game creator, so this review is one written outside full context (which should be expected if you're willing to put out your work). I can say it must be very hard to deal with criticism and being told that your creation is unworthy and not good enough. However, the fact that the progression through the game, both mechanically and narratively speaking, is stilted and 'awkward' -- however self-realised and/or purposeful this is -- means that it makes it very hard for there to be a reliable connection between authorship and the consumer. In writing, there's a rule about 'show, don't tell', and that applies to this game too: this game does a lot of blunt telling, but has a difficult time creating a setting where the one playing can feel as though they're discovering this situation/circumstance/emotion that the creator is feeling, because it's being literally spoken or shown up in text in their face.
There are things I like about this game, and there are some areas that have a lot of potential. The typographical leading from the 'campfire' section is some very interesting wayfinding, the part where you had to hold down the mouse button and messages are conveyed through audio, and, on a slightly pettier note, the fact that it has Liszt's "Liebestraum no. 3" in the final level, since it is a beautiful song. However, I believe it falls short in a lot of ways; the fact that there needs to be a function to skip levels included in the UI speaks volumes about how there could be ways to better tinker with the game.
Don't get me wrong, all art is self-indulgent, and as an artist I'm not going to make myself an exception. But the strength and heavy-handedness that is put behind the meaning to this game is not backed up mechanically or narratively, both of these areas being fairly unrealised and underdeveloped, from what I can tell. I would highly recommend looking at games like The Beginner's Guide, Gone Home, or maybe even a game like Presentable Liberty for evocative narratives with interesting mechanics and dynamics.

FTL will change you forever.

Alright. I bought this game when it was on sale, a long time ago. It was 2,60 at that time (just like right now) and I thought. Well, it looks decent, so why not? To my surprise, the game actually was really good. The graphics were nice to the eye, which is important for some people. But the story is what really hooked me in. I will give my Pro's and Cons down below:
- An beautiful story you can easily immerse yourself into.
- (For me) Good graphics, but this may differ for others.
- Well-created maps, that give you enough of a challenge qua parkour. They're also very beautiful.
- The Voice Over is good, they chose the right people for the right characters, in my opinion.
- Very smooth gameplay, the mechanics work really well and I had perfect performance with NO issues.
- Very short story, it can be finished in under 3 hours if you actually rush it through. But the price makes up for that.
(It's just the fact that such an good story like this has to be SO short!)
- The NPC's in certain villages may look derpy, to the point they (hilariously) look ridiculous.
- I've only glitched once in this game, when I grappled something I went through a wall. Shouldn't affect gameplay much whatsoever.
That's about it. The game really is worth it especially for the price it is currently at. It was a hidden gem, and I am very glad I picked it up.

Full disclosure: I backed it on Kickstarter
Overall, a good game.
It's atmospheric: the art and atmosphere are sweet and dark, and I found myself lost in the soundtrack on multiple occasions.
Mechanically, it's basic, harldy straying from conventional 2-D puzzle platformers everyone knows and many consider stale, but it's solid. The physics didn't confuse me: it's very responsive, with no floaty movements or delayed jumps. It's polished in a way I'd never expect from a one-man studio, and Thomas Brush definitely seems to have squashed all the bugs.
There aren't many puzzles, and I've certainly encountered tougher ones than I did in Pinstripe, but they weren't all 'easy'.
My biggest concern with the game is its length - I don't mind having spent money on what amounts to a three hour experience, but if you're someone who wants an hour of gameplay per unit currency, you may not see its worth. The new game plus content is hardly different from the base game, though I'm enjoying my time going through at a slower pace with the differences.
The game is mostly story-based and atmospheric, and while it doesn't have the most complex writing I've seen in a game, it's heartwarming and kept me playing through to a satisfying end sequence. It's a fine balance of tragic and joyous.
In all, I recommend the game to anyone who thinks a short indie adventure is worth €15. It's a nice experience and a great start to Atmos Games'/Thomas Brush's full-time career as an indie developer. Thumbs up, but it's certainly not without its criticisms.

I watched the Game Grumps play the demo of this game back and 2016, and once I saw it had come out I knew I was going to buy it. And I have no regrets.
What is there to say about this game? The art style is minimalist but gorgeous, and goes perfectly with the soundtrack. The music switches between eerie, heartbreaking, and beautiful with a flawlessness I have yet to see matched by another indie game. Immersion is important in any game, and Pinstripe pulls that off wonderfully. I became invested in Ted, and really, actually wanted to get Bo back.
Gameplay wise, the physics surprised me on how good it was. I found the puzzles logical and an interesting kind of hard, as opposed to just frustrating. The 'find the difference' puzzles were by far my favorite; challenging as well as simply lovely to look at.
The NPCs you interact with run the whole gamut, from creepy to hilarious, and it was the voice acting that made that possible. All the voices in this game are absolutely stellar in their own right, and I commend the voice actors for doing a fantastic job. The characters add another layer of story and atmosphere to the game, again in a manner I haven't seen done so well very often.
All in all, I truly enjoyed this game. Fifteen dollars is a bit pricey, but personally I would say that it is absolutely worth it. This game was a five year long labor of love, and it shows how much work was put into it. I reccomend buying this game to people who are interested in a game that will make them completely immersed in an experience.

This entry in the long-running, legendary series of turn-based strategy games had big shoes to fill after the vastly-successful and well-received Civilization IV. At first, it didn't measure up. But with the two major expansions and additional scenarios and civilizations added with DLC, this now-complete game is a masterful and worthy entry in the series. The at-the-time-revolutionary hex system and inability to stack units will require a change in thinking that will at first frustrate you if you're not used to it. But it will inspire you to think of new strategies and techniques you'd never otherwise have imagined. The Religion & Culture systems added by the expansions are brilliant and fun. With all the DLC, the number of different civilization choices for the player is immense and varied. This is worth your money if you are at all interested in historical turn-based strategy games. Build your own civilization to stand the test of time!

A game that obviously takes a lot of insperation from the Mother series still remains to be so wickedly dark and charming in its own way. The game itself looks so simple at times, yet there are times where it uses this simple art style to show these insane and honestly disturbing images of a world that has long since lost the idea of "Normal."
The game itself starts off rather slow, and not really picking up until you enter Area 2, yet I don't think it suffers for this. This slow start allows players to get hints at the overall world they will be diving into, hinting at a much darker story then what is originally presented in the first 20-30 min.
The story itself pulls no punches: You play Brad Armstrong, a washed up druggie who used to be a martial arts instructor to make up for his inability to protect those he cared for. From the get go we are given this flawed and down right un-likable character who is every bit as human as the world is completely lost. You can tell he has long since lost the ability to feel pain, and does everything he can to run from the scars his past has left.
But don't worry...
Funny, twisted, crazy, goofy, creepy and sad. Buy this game.

This is a cute lil RPG set in a post apocalyptic world and it follows the middle aged man named Brad in his quest to redeem himself.
Brad is (in my eyes, but I know not everyone agrees) a very loveable character with a rather narrow mindset. At the beginning of the game we are introduced to brad in his childhood as we are given a peek of his troubled life, his abusive father and as a result of that, his alcohol addiction and his addiction to the drug called Joy.
Brad now lives in a world that is seemingly devoid of wimen. Just walking through this land and seeing how the male population is coping with the lack of females is hilarious (DRAGQUEEN ALERT!) and sad, both at the same time.
Brad however has a secret, he found a baby.
A female baby.
The last female on earth.
And he will do ANYTHING to protect her from a world filled with sex-depraved males, but is it really that simple?
What is the difference between a man protecting the last female on earth from a bunch of sex-driven maniacs and a damanged middle aged drug addict keeping the last female on earth locked up in his cellar to keep her away from people who just want to save humanity?
What do you think? Buy the game and find out...

Obscenity is hard. Obscenity can get bogged down in being too stupid, too shocking, too crass. In order to make obscenity into something meaningful, it needs coherence. Enough coherence to counterbalance the revulsion of the content. LISA, remarkably, navigates this balance beam.
It offers plenty of strange, dirty, cruel content, but all with context. The comedy's juxtaposition with the tragedy isn't just for contrast, it's works thematically as well. The lighthearted fantasy alongside cutthroat survival, both in world building and in gameplay, mesh entirely with the narrative's ultimate goals.
But this isn't a visual novel or something, it's a game too. And it's a fun, surprisingly balanced game, especially considering the single-man production. There are a ton of party members, and most of them feel distinct in theme as well as in gameplay. You can set up a team with lots of fun, powerful combinations, and there aren't too many ways to go wrong. Equipment upgrades are infrequent and expensive enough to feel meaningful. Resources both feel tight because of scarcity, and loose because of anticipated demise. Other than the occasional dark cave or grassy field, all battles are satisfyingly non-random. This kind of gameplay balance is tough for bigger games to manage, so it's a bit wondrous how well it works in LISA.
I waited to buy LISA on sale, because we all have a backlog of games now. But I put it at the top of my que, and it was worth the favoritism. LISA was well developed enough, meaningful enough, and satisfying enough that I'd freely recommend it at the full $10 price tag. I have spent $10 more poorly many, many times.

Every player on the team plays a certain role similar to the ship structure in Homeworld. For an unadvertised indie game this very simplistic space shooter has a lot of potential if it can attract a crowd. This is one of the very first games I'm writing a review for, and I'll tell you why.
This game has a frankly STUPID amount of potential.
-With a couple tweeks on ship speed and size (as there tends to be a gulf between ships sizes and the weapons provided) [Specifically the gulf between Frigates and Corvettes {My complaint being with the corvettes just being heavy fighters, with rotating, singular turrets}] this game would perform very very well.
--A couple things to be taken in to account (game dev, and potential players):--
-Slamming full speed into a meteor should kill you (depending on ship size, speed and shield) [It currently does not]
Speed for some of the larger ships needs to be improved, especially the maneuverability (turn speed) of the Corvette and the Frigates
-Potential option for not displaying location of enemy ships until they are in Line Of Sight (Allowing for Corvettes to possibly display locations of ships to whole team, adding a strategic advantage to them.)
-Please please, please, game developer gods, add a spectator cam.
-Add a speech box
-Allow for team speak/world speak
-Do not make someone leave the game the SECOND they die.
-More complex explosion for larger ships
-Deadly shrapnel from exploded ships (Could block weapons, provide covered approach. [Would work based on size/speed {Bottom=DroneDebris/FighterDebris/CorvetteDebris/FrigateDebris/DestroyerDebris/CapitalShipDebris=Top}])
-A tutorial, and sensible controls
-Flying into a larger ship's engines should slowly kill you.
-Port and Starboard mounted cannons that slightly swivel
Other than that, it functions great as a quick, fun game with decent ship interplay. I highly suggest you bring a group of friends into this, especially if you can get enough friends to fill a server.

Exactly what it says on the tin. 20 minutes of JRPG from start to end credits. Some setup, some voiced dialogue (Charming amateur work.), some nice art, and one boss fight. It's all quite easy.
Just turn off active time battle. You don't know these characters so you'll have to check their skills.
You can change two party members, so you might want to replay to see what different plot there is.
Still, the whole thing is incredibly trivial. A lot of effort went into the art, voice work, etc, and everything is certainly workmanlike, but there's nothing all that interesting here. Fun enough for a freebie though.
In reflection, though, I think that is actually something profound. Look how rare it is for a game to have the monster ACTUALLY BE A MONSTER that must die. How rare it is for the heroes to actually save the day from a monster. There's no twist where you were the monster all along. No stupid navel gazing about two so gray so grimdark factions and having to pick blah blah.
When you get down to that, a game that promises heroes slaying a monster and saving the day and delivers exactly that... that is kinda rare these days, isn't it?

So far I have played roughly an hour, and I am enjoying it a lot. It takes a lot from his previous game - coma - at least inasmuch it is a dark, atmospheric game with an emotional charge and a sense of loss. It carries the same interests too; body noises, mushrooms and dark goo mix with an interesting early 1900s nightmare before christmas aesthetic.
While coma was an entertaining distraction, however, with puzzles that required very little thought (except for one bizarrely taxing musical test at the end) this game has vastly better puzzling credentials. Thus far the puzzles have been both satisfying and not obscure, ramping up in difficulty and neatly interlocking with and drawing attention to the thematic elements of the game (for example; a pill bottle used to treat an illness is linked with a childish note about treasure with tragic implications...)
The acoustic soundtrack is particularly worth picking out; his last game had an exceptional soundtrack, with redwind field in particular being wonderful, and this game continues that, veering between eerie and soothing as the situation demands.
If I have any major criticism is it that the tone of the writing is variable, and a couple of guest voices that are, ahem, out of place.
For those interested in off-kilter games with a strong aesthetic and tone this is well worth your time. It is exceptional, and for the price doubly so!

Im going to point out first, Whilst I recommend this game, this review will be a hotspot for me to get something off my chest which I'll explain later. For now though, I'll focus on the good things and why It's so bloody good. Before asking about my playtime, I own this on Xbox One, and the reason for low playtime here is I was streaming this Co-operatively with another streamer. When another friend asked me to play, I ended up on my Alternate account with steam share enabled so I didnt overwrite saves. To put it out there, this is the first saints row I ever felt the dying need to finish, with good and bad focus in mind.
Everything in this game, simply put, Is beautiful. Graphically you can see it cut a few corners when zoomed in, but its actually very pretty. the Ragdoll physics are still better than GTA and are way more fun, Customisation on everything is still a personal favourite, and progression isnt shy in that sense either. You do feel your progression. I think the main thing that got me the most was Character Creation. I love it when I can push out a character I can adjust everything on. (To be honest, Most characters end up being female when given the choice, then I play around making cute/hot characters. No need to guess why, eh?). I truly felt attatched to my character, in a game where I make it my own,  for the first time. the appearance was something I could die for, and the attitude was just great to watch and listen to. SR4 will hold a place in me for this, as I used to think all the sliders and options were just merely a gimmick. Im actually a huge fan of the animations in this game too, as it shows how the movement of your characters and other peoples actions show how the overall vivbe of the game changes. I liked them alot, and found the movements on this to be much more human like than GTA, which felt dull in comparison. the only negative think visually that got me was the glitchy effect, when either wandering around or when collecting clusters. whilst It was within reason, maybe a little overboard?
Ripping through Steelport at 100m/s whilst jumping and gliding 100's of feet in the air, was stupidly fun. No need for cars or planes, really, but what makes this game fun is how everything is kept in there too. meaning you can pilot a plane, drive a car or bike, but you dont really have to. the exploration is insane to put it simple, theres a lot to aim for to complete this game, and that just gives me even more reason to play it. It ran really well on my Rig (i7-3770K @ 4.1Ghz, GTX 1060, 16GB Ram) staying 55fps or above whilst streaming whilst maxing out to around 110fps. Off stream even more on Avg. Superb!
Overall, the game Is HIGHLY recommend, its so bloody fun, and I wouldnt see why for £15 for all the DLC you would give this a pass. solo is fun, co-op is even better. I know some wont like the more serious side of SR being tainted, but this game was too much fun to put on a miss list. However, I kind of feel weird at this one thing. Please, if you intend to play the game, do not read beyond this point as spoilers are inbound.
The story, for my liking, seems to have just gone mad. now some would argue that with SR making a different approach after 3 means its just natural, but some of the events were just that insane that I just felt a bit robbed. I loved the "you became the president, Aliens invade and you're captures in a simulation". I loved how you build bonds with your crew and sometimes get a little "woo-woo" in there too, whilst also learning each characters weakness via nightmares. but I wasn't a big fan of bringing back Johnny Gat. Ill point this out if I dont make it clear enough on my profile, Liking anime has meant ive seen some pretty funky story lines, and I dont let stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥slide in that, but even on SR4's scale of weirdness, I couldnt bring myself to enjoy it either. this is a personal thing though, and I would say that writing it out here has got it off my chest way easier than I thought, but It will still Irk me for a long time, maybe for ever, Who knows? The game ends in a way that I expected. After the events of the story just 2-3 missions in, you cant really see anything happening except for what Is spelt for you.

LISA is a Kickstarter RPGMaker game by Austin "Dingaling" Jorgensen, and it fargoes typical RPG gameplay and presentation.  You play Brad Armstrong, a drug addicted ex-martial arts teacher who finds the last female on the planet in the form of a baby girl.  Years pass and she gets kidnapped by raiders, who are going to "use" her to save the human race. So it's up to Brad and the 27 party members who you can recruit (and lose) to find Buddy and bring her home.
I've played a lot of RPGs and LISA brings a lot to the table for me, a lot of people point out the obvious influence of Earthbound had on this game, in terms of the graphics and silly humor and it really adds to the charm of the game for me as both of them contrast the darker parts of this game so much. The pacing and delivery of the story in this game are both expertly done, the story really kept me invested for the whole ride, the story takes many twists and turns, and makes you question if you really ARE the good guy in this story. The presentation is great as well, the music is strange, bizarre, and great, the soundtrack is one of my favorite things in this game, and all the party members have their own quirks and unique sidequests to unlock them, my favorite being entering a wrestling league with the "Shocklord", based on Fred Ottoman from the WWE, who is a wrestler famed for screwing up his dramatic entrance every time. All the other enemies and characters have charm of their own, such as the Karate Masters hidden throughout the game, and a group of Power Ranger cosplayers.
The gameplay is somewhat reminiscient of Barkley, Shut Up and Slam: Gaiden, it has a similar combo system for some characters, you can use the WASD keys in certain combinations to use various basic attacks, followed by the respective move, all these moves are easily viewable at any time by going to skills, as it will show you the combination to use, other characters use abilities by just selecting the ability, should they not have combos. On top of combos, party members can have TP, which regenerates as they take and deal damage, or addiction, which requires you to feed their addiction of Joy or else their stats are reduced. The fights flow very well and there isn't any need for grinding, which is a real breath of fresh air, there are only 4 areas in the game with random encounters, and the mobs there aren't worth grinding, the way fights are handeled is very similar to Chrono Trigger, you're able to see the enemies, and fight them as such.  It's a very streamlined, polished way of handeling encounters in general.
As for complaints, I don't have much, the party members are reduced to one-note in terms of personality, like "The Guy Who Talks A Lot" and "The Football Player".  The humor can be a bit disjointed as well, for instance, you find a man trying to poop, but is terrified by a spider, then right after that, you're forced to choose between chopping your arm off and saving a party member's life, and then, again, right after that, you get attacked by a man with no eyes, making eye puns to the death. But as far as complaints go, that's it, I really enjoy this game, and I'd recommend it to RPG fans, or just people looking for a great story.

LISA's messed up story was so enjoyable to me.  The ending is a little vague or I'm a little slow, I wasn't quite sure what happened, but otherwise it's a janky journey with some very interesting encounters.

i started lisa in january and dropped it for like, seven months before i picked it up again and safe to say i'm glad i did eventually finish it
lisa is really atmospheric and immersive, of course everyone likens it to earthbound and it definitely is an accurate comparison not only in terms of the setting but also enemy design and out-of-battle gameplay. further to that i feel like the developer dingaling had a really clear understanding of what he wanted his game to be and the limitations of its game engine, lisa's fortes are its plot, its characters and its tone, all of which are beyond sufficiently interesting and disturbing, while the gameplay is very standard adventuring and turn-based fights, with which every person on the planet is acutely familiar. that isn't to suggest the gameplay is necessarily bad in essence, but it's maybe just a tad lacking for the player experience. can't exactly blame the dev for including a fundamental property of rpg gameplay in an rpg though so it's not a major issue
one thing i do wanna give lisa special credit for is its diversity in practically every sense of the word's application, this game is really ♥♥♥♥ing refreshing for the post-apocalyptic genre because it exhibits so much more than 'survivors' and 'zombies' which has been done since the ♥♥♥♥ing dawn of time, it shows that a game set in dystopia can not only serve its ultimate purpose of being sinister but also maintain different varities of morbidity in its settings, characters, humour and even music (standout examples for me were the Wally's area and the power rangers' subplot). it's not so common that a modern game nails an attempt at creating a plethora of differing characters and having nearly every single one of them distinctly memorable but dingaling made it happen so big props to him for that
as for the bit where i ramble about the game with complete and blatant partiality, there's these like two songs in the game which are ♥♥♥♥ing awesome and i love them so much, one of them plays whenever you're sailing and it starts off with a steel drum melody which is then taken over by brass and when i first heard it it made me so ♥♥♥♥ing emotional cause it was near the end of the game and it felt intensely sentimental, the other song plays in this place called seesaw village and it's this ♥♥♥♥ing goofy, upbeat, undeniably happy song which uses sound effects that remind me distinctly of ape escape so it was super nostalgic hearing it. both of these songs pretty much singlehandedly cemented lisa as a memorable game not just because they were so good but more importantly because they acted as such a stark but optimistic contrast in a game whose main focuses included depression, suicide and hopelessness
overall lisa is pretty standout in the current rpg/indie genre, probably could've used a little more length but most of that is me wanting to see more of the world lisa is set in, not for the faint of heart but if you can handle an overwhelming sensation of pessimism and periodic horror elements then it's well worth your time, 8/10

If you ever wanted to play Homeworld 2 as an FPS, then "Code Name: Rogue Fleet" will revive that daydream as a mere daydream. This game is your textbook example of a true alpha-stage game.
There is only a skeleton of a game here, but it is a complete skeleton; very bony, unappealing, the joints need lubrication, yet the presence of cartilage tissue is a pleasant surprise.
Gameplay: very slow, very forgiving, marginally satisfying to learn.
Graphics: Unity graphics, so it is decent. Asteroid surfaces are only textures. Note: The sun glare is horrible.
Learning Curve: On par with stepping on a Lego while wearing thick socks; sharp, unfriendly to humans, yet simple.
HUD Interface: Stupidly transparent; easy to understand once your eyes adjust.
Menu Navigation: Stupidly transparent, odd font sizes, odd naming of buttons; your eyes never adjust, easily the worst part.
Aesthetic: Plain, but but satisfying; it sits on the "less is more" peak of visual appeal.
Conclusion:  This game is worth exactly $0.05 of emotional investment! Recommended to download for tracking development!

The hours we have on log is pretty much the time it took us to finish the game, but needless to say we are looking forward to seeing what else this game has in store. I've played the other games from this dev, Prison Run and Gun and Hot Guns, and I've loved both.  This one plays very similarly to both but the level design is sort of a medium between the two.  Prison Run and Gun was a find-the-widget-to-unlock-exit style of sidescolling puzzle game.  Hot Guns was a shoot-through-several-sub-levels-to-beat-a-world kind of game.  Cash Island has the shorter style of level like Prison Run and Gun but with the more sidescroller/platformer type of level design of Hot Guns.  It's a really happy middle gound.  The game itself is very true to the trailers.  If they look like something you'll enjoy, you probably will.  The controls are very tight and the music is excellnt (kind of a late 80's/early 90's funk and synth rock vibe).  Overall, the gameplay falls into the very delicate balance of being fun yet challenging, with repeated deaths usually evoking laughter instead of frustration.  I hope this dev keeps up the amazing work.  All three of these games bring me right back to the joy and comfort of the warm glowing CRT television that was my usual afterschool companion so many decades ago.

I played this after finishing its own follow-up, Super Win the Game, and really enjoying it.  It's essentially the same thing, just sandwiched into a singular long dungeon rather than multiple shorter ones, and skips the fluff to get right to the point: a fun metroid-like platformer.
And that's exactly what it is, a PLATFORMER.  No weapons, no way to harm enemies, just run, jump and dodge.  There are upgrades, but they serve only to reveal new platforms or increase your ability to jump even more.  The presentation is, unlike its NES-inspired succesor, based on DOS games of the 80s, complete with CGA graphics by default (and EGA optional).  Also like Super, you get this awesomely well-done CRT monitor overlay, which isn't quite as detailed or with as many options as Super but is much easier on the eyes by default.  These options can be changed in the GAME menu in the options, rather than Video; took me a bit to figure that out.  The sound is... fine, for the period it's emulating.  There is NO music, however, just like most real DOS games, so come prepared with your own.
This game is quite fun, offering a good couple hours (or a bit more, depending on your skill at platforming, exploring, finding and deciphering simple clues) of solid gameplay for absolutely FREE. Thomas Brush had the opportunity to be the ever-rare video game auteur. Every creative choice was his to make, all the way down to the music, which is unheard of in games.
The result is a short (around 2 hours, perfect length for what the game tries to do) puzzle-platformer with mild combat. But what's more impressive is the tight story, impeccable visual design and the sublime music.
Very mild spoilers here, but I was anticipating the story to go down the easy
route and it never did. That element of the story was just a backdrop to hang the main character's arc on, and I have immense respect for that.
I would say that this game didn't
strike me with that feeling of "awe" that I'm always seeking in video games, but I have a ton of artistic respect for Brush in making all of the components of his game come together in a cohesive vision. And I'm eagerly awaiting whatever he makes next!

The Good: The art style is consistent and amazing. The voice acting is perfect. The puzzles are mildly brain-bendy but not impossible. The story unfolds nicely. Choices you make lightly impact the closing scene.
The Bad: No ability to change volume control in-game. No ability to change controller settings.
The Meh: The climax event felt short. And if you have certain items, it's no different than any other combat. There wasn't a huge payoff for success. NG+ is not made more difficult, nor does any of the story change. (I haven't been able to get through to Vintage Mode and likely will attempt to do so at a later date.)
Pinstripe is nicely done and well presented, though it left me wanting more.

You play as Teddy, an ex-minister. At the start of the game his young daughter Bo is kidnapped by the sinister, bowler-hatted, glowing-eyed Pinstripe, and taken down into the depths of Hell. Teddy ventures down into the underworld in search of Bo, meeting and chatting to new characters, solving puzzles and minigames to open up new areas for exploration. His main tool for solving these challenges is a catapult (or slingshot, if you're American) which can be shot accurately and/or rapidly to break things, activate objects in sequence or destroy enemies. It makes a satisfying THWACK! noise that never gets old.
You can play with keyboard/mouse but the controller configuration is very good, movements are easy and intuitive. I played with a Steam controller and the right touchpad suits the game nicely, although at times it can be frustrating to target things quickly. There is a minigame at one point where you have to shoot balloons as they appear. I tried in vain for ages to beat it with the controller, then I discovered the mouse option and beat it straight away. Silly me.
As you progress through the game you pick up 'Frozen Drops' which are added to your wallet and can eventually be used to purchase special items. The items cost huge numbers of drops, so you won't get them all on the first playthrough - they essentially provide motivation to replay the game. You must also collect the 9 clues that are needed to complete the game and solve some of the main area-opening puzzles.
After your first playthrough you enter ADVENTURE PLUS! mode where you have the same world and repeat the same storyline with some modifications, but this time there are extra doorways and areas to explore, which were previously locked, and you should also amass enough Frozen Drops to purchase further special items such as clothing and weapons. I'm even more excited to play the second time as I was the first!
The whole thing is beautifully hand drawn in a very distinctive style - everyone has long spindly limbs and comical facial features. Colourful explosions and exquisite lighting add to the wow factor - the 3D clue items collected in your inventory can be spun around and catch the light wonderfully. I spent a fair amount of time just sitting there spinning these things around and admiring them.
The music throughout the game is extra special, and occasionally you find old-fashioned gramophones which you can activate to play some more lovely tunes - cool, haunting melodies that are well worth stopping for a while to appreciate in full.
The voice acting is second to none, done by professional and celebrity actors. I'm pretty sure the childish voice of Bo is done by the actress who played the Red Queen in the Resident Evil movies. Awesome.
Medium challenge. There's enough brainwork needed to make it interesting but it's never difficult to the point of frustration. Many of the puzzles involve shooting stuff with the slingshot but there are many different puzzle types, all of them engaging and gorgeous to look at. This is a game that constantly distracts you from your objectives with its sheer beauty and your urge to shoot everything in sight, just for the hell of it (see what I did there?)
It's possible to die, if you get hit by too many projectiles. It says 'Game Over' but it's not - you just respawn without any loss of progress or Frozen Drops.
Trading cards, 12 achievements which are hard to get - at the end of my first playthrough I had one. ONE. Steam Cloud, which is particularly useful for fully cross-platform games like this which, attract dual-booters like myself who appreciate being able to continue their game whichever OS they happen to be using at the time.
It is a comparatively short game. Others have said their first playthrough took 2-3 hours, and it can be speed-run in under an hour (there's an achievement for this). I'm not ashamed to say that I savoured my first game at a leisurely pace for 10 hours, loved every wonderful minute, and am looking forward to further playthroughs. The top quality of every aspect of the game gives me no hesitation to recommend this at full price. It's a must-buy.
Most good games are strong in one or two particular areas, for example many puzzlers I play are strong in challenge but weak in background music. Pinstripe stands out for me as a game that has been to the gym every day and honed every muscle - it didn't skip leg day. The result is a game that feels like a privilege to play. Totally absorbing. A hot candidate for my GOTY.

I’ve often found that indie games are so much more emotional and heart driven than AAA games, and Pinstripe is certainly no exception to this fact. Every aspect of the game is perfectly cohesive and immersive from the beginning to the end and I loved every minute of it. Everything about Pinstripe flows together so well to create a hauntingly beautiful and story-driven game. Each element from the graphics, to the music, to the voice acting was extremely well done. The only problem in the game I had was a tiny bit of lag every now and then while jumping. The only other issue is the price point. The game is short and at $15 it’s a bit on the pricey side, but I’m happy to be supporting the talented developer behind the game.

"Just a few hit points on the hull, and these are the final moments of FTL. My sweaty hands press sweaty buttons as the flagship bears down upon the S.S. A-Hole. If only my Mom could see me now."
Let’s start off with the basics — FTL is a Rogue-LITE. There’s permadeath, but that’s about the only thing that really connects it to the classic concept of a rogue-like game. In fact, I think FTL is basically its own classification. I’ve never really played anything quite like it before, and it was refreshing to see a new concept on the market.
Let’s talk about the pros.
FTL’s gameplay is super solid. So far, I’ve come across no bugs at all, everything works as it should. The tutorial correctly explains each mechanic, and they’re each so simple that I thought at first the game would be a dud. Oh boy, how I was wrong. These simple mechanics scale into a huge atmosphere of strategy, where each move you make could decide your life or death in the final battle with the flagship.
Just like in XCOM, you get attached to your crew super quickly, and when one dies it’s almost enough to rage quit. Each race manages to bring a different component to your crew, which again adds to the overall strategy.
The combat relies on your micromanagement of different weapons, and your outfit in general. It’s satisfying to find a weapons strategy that destroys the enemy. Thankfully, there isn’t just ONE strategy to choose from, although they all revolve around your opponent’s shields.
"One by one, my crew members are dead. The shields are down, the weapons turn orange, this is the end. But I know I just need a one more shot. I can do this."
Them cons tho.
FTL does fall short in a few instances, and none bigger than the lore. If FTL could create a real world around it’s fantastic gameplay, the game would be SO MUCH BETTER. Also, the text-heavy encounters try to be physiologically difficult to decide on, but honestly it’s super easy to figure them out.
Another large shortcoming is the lack of weapon variety and quest variety. Even with the expanded universe I find quests that I’ve already done and are super easy to do again with my foreknowledge. I just can’t see myself replaying this with so little variety.
"One second. The weapon is charged, but so is his. They both fire."
It's really good, it's hard but unforgiving. Most of the negative reviews reflect that. It's easily worth the price.

I bought the PC prequel to this game, Trials 2, in a Steam sale years ago and it was one of the most dangerous purchases I have ever made. It is in my nature to get addicted to incredibly hard and frustrating skill games and it is one of the best. I have very little bad to say about that game.
The sequel moved to 360, which was really sad and upsetting that they ditched the fan base that supported them. After a few years, they announced the return to PC which was good news! It uses Uplay which is fine but I would prefer that it didn't. I would prefer full integration with Steam friends.
Then it arrived. I started playing it. I got addicted again. I was 100% most of the game. I hated the game but couldn't stop playing it. Most of this came down to the horrible bugginess of the game. It would have huge FPS drops and jitter. The black and white level is almost unplayable. In a game that requires accurate timing, the bugs required me to mess up over and over again. The replays were also useless and didn't work properly.
I will move away from the bugs to the actual gameplay.
I much prefer playing on keyboard. Some of the harder levels with really steep inclines clearly were more designed for a controller but are possible with keyboard after pain staking trial and error.
The dynamic camera in the game is frustrating, I much preferred Trials 2 static side on camera. In this game, it is common to have blind jumps that you have to memorize.
The one level that is 18 minutes long (If I remember rightly), is horrible. I don't like having to repeat a level that long.
Otherwise, this game is amazing. The level designs are great. Controls feel satisfying. 100% this game is incredibly hard and equally satisfying and I did get very addicted.
I will say I do recommend this game but it is a gamble with the bugs. If you have an older graphics card, I imagine the gamble is higher.

A story-driven JRPG-ish game about a withdrawn, addicted and kinda tortured middle-aged man trying to save a young girl he had once found abandoned in the barren land and raised with a few friends of his in secret for some years. That secret got out though, and since the world knows no women anymore everyone tries to get his hands on her, either to sate sexual urges or to make sure she'll be used to breed children and thus save humanity from the otherwise inevitable extinction.
LISA's world is kinda post-apocalyptic. Could be America, could be not - not much is said here. Sometimes memories of the past flicker in front of the eyes of some characters showing a world that was once intact. Since there are no women around anymore most men apparently saw no reason to take proper care of what we would regard as civilized: Many people sleep in tents, caves or other derelict make-shift-ishy structures; gangs roam the area, people fight each other over gasoline, "dirty magazines" (which is the world's currency) or other stuff; joy is - for example - being found in playing Russian roulette, abusing drugs (most favorably a blue pill called "Joy", which the protagonist consumes as well), or reliving old sports and habits like overly-dramatic wrestling. Unless people still find more to their lives than hanging around aimlessly, that is.
The protagonist, Bradley Armstrong, follows a pretty violent path. In the old world he used to teach martial arts, and he doesn't hesitate to use his skills against others. His father never having been very caring towards him adds to it (and is shown in the very powerful, subtle introduction cinematic). A few people leave him a choice, many others do not. It's not seldom that you need to run down rather helpless and apathic people or nutcases who merely block your way. The game tosses pathetic weaklings or overpowered, unbeatable foes at you if it serves the story. Antagonizing Brad and relativizing the evilness of your opponents is quite an important topic in this game even it may be a little behind it's true potential because you are rarely having any true choice, for the worse or better your path in the story is narrow and tight.
At specific points you're forced to make critical choices which have bad outcomes one way or another. You'll often either lose items, get Brad mutilated or his gang members permanently killed. These are individual characters with very short stories of theirs. They have skills and stats according to what they are, used to be or would love to be (drunk, playboy, wrestler, casanova, cross-dresser, ...) and losing them can feel like a genuine loss, but there are plenty of them joining you along the way, you pick them up during all kinds of situations. Sleeping at open places can even result in some of them getting kidnapped by local gangs or abandoning you "just like that". They will level up through combat, four of them are battling at a time in a very classic, turn-based JRPG-ish manner. New members have a level depending on which part during the game they are recruited. Focusing on leveling up the same four people too much and losing them to some circumstances could be grave mid-/late-game. I never had such issues because there are just so many gang members and because I grinded a bit around the middle. Most battle encounters are fixed, some enemies can be "seen" before you actually fight them, plenty jump you by surprise, some can be escaped from (story-relevant ones apparently not). A few areas have generic enemies randomly attack you endlessly if you're willing to stick around, allowing to grind.
What makes this game very special is it's morbid, dry, crude humor. It's quirky, full of subtleties and manages to capture a sense of constant wonder what to expect around the next corner. The situations under which Brad and his gang ge  captured and threatened can feel forced at times, and earlier in the game I had a few moments of light frustration when I tripped over the edges of cliffs into sudden "game over"s forcing me to load back to one of the fixed saving points in the world nullyfing some of the battles or item-grabbings I had done along the way. But that could very well be intended to create suspense, to punish too much carelessness and to actually give you some feel of depression and hopelessness in a mostly barren, dry world. I think the game does well in creating an ambiance of this kind. It has some strong, heartrending moments too and doesn't shy away from making fun of the world and it's characters at times. Even I, the player, felt mocked on several occasions. These were funny parts and they add to the strong charme and cleverness of this game. Everything seems thoughtful, like all would serve a proper purpose and nothing was wasted during development. I don't think there are too many games that have this kind of precision in design.
The music is pretty great too. It can feel dry, odd, crazy, pumping, serene - it's really all there and hits the themes, the style and visuals of the game on the spot.
A little on the negative side: The game had a prequel. Some things can be confusing/are left unanswered (like what the crazy mutated creatures you sometimes encounter exactly are, and how women came to disappear in the first place, or what world this is at all - apparently it's a fictional one inspired by America or American lifestyle, but I'm not sure) and some references that are made are apparently directed at that earlier game. This isn't clear to anyone who doesn't look a little deeper. It's still a very strong game in it's own accord but this could catch some people off-guard.
Sometimes I had visual glitches. Like models of story characters I had met earlier appearing in one place or another for no purpose. They didn't move, they didn't react, they did nothing, nor did my character react to them anyhow. One guy just floated a few spaces in thin air. Later he was gone from there again. The game doesn't seem to have any graphical options even if it scaled fittingly to my screen when going from windowed to fullscreen. In combat some characters allow you inputs to execute certain moves in a row, but even when using my XBox controller the game is showing me   the control hints as if I was using my keyboard ("WASD" instead of "XYAB"). These are rather trivial aspects as far as I'm concerned but I don't want them left unmentioned.

This is still the best Men of War game made. The graphics may not be the best, and the voice acting is♥♥♥♥♥♥(hilariously), but this still trumps the other games by far. The only other game that is comparable is Faces of War, which was the game that came before MoW. MoW: Red Tide at least tried to stay close to it's roots, but suffered massively from the huge difficulty spike (compared to the original MoW) and the lack of any sort of Multiplayer (I mainly play single player games, but MoW was my exception). MoW: AS and MoW: AS2 completely changed the way the games were played previously. Changing it to more of a 'capture the flag' type game mode. Gone were the interesting characters, story, and missions. Instead you just get to play a bunch of scenario type maps that continually open up as you capture more 'flags'. That is not the MoW I enjoyed. Lastly, 1C decided to milk the series with a bunch of terrible spin-offs that I hope no one ever has to experience. The two most prominent ones being MoW: Vietnam (♥♥♥♥ing terrible game), and MoW: Condemned Heroes (which I never played, but have seen playthroughs of...it is terrible as well). They have also started to use the engine to allow a bunch of indie/small developers to make some MoW-lite games based in other periods (such as WW1, Civil War, and Modern times). None of these, however, have been able to stack up to the original Men of War. I don't understand why 1C decided to waste the success of Men of War on all these stupid spin-offs. They could have made a Men of War 2, just using the Modern engine, and with the same kind of experience MoW 1 had. But no, they'll just keep wasting the potential that Men of War had on these stupid games that are completely different from what Men of War originally was.
Overall, I'd give this game a solid 8.5/10. It isn't perfect, and has many issues, but it is still the best game that the 'series' has come up with. It's just a shame that this will never see a proper sequel that will live up to it's name-sake.

I found out that another game called "Caves!", which seems to be EXACTLY the same game as this, has been released. I'll not change the review of this product, but I would like to warn people: buy this, buy the other, buy none of them. But please don't buy both of them.
As a neutral judgement I must say that "No lights" is better due to the improved light effects that do not seem to be present in "Caves!".
REVIEW:
Well, I found a couple of symbologies hidden in this VERY simple game. Maybe it's exactly this simplicity that made me look for "meaning"... and the great and unsettling soundtrack, repeated "ad infinitum", made the rest.
INFINITE, PROCEDURALLY GENERATED LEVELS WITH NO GOALS OR VICTORY CONDITIONS:
In this infinite and uncaring universe there is no "higher" purpose for our lives except the purpose WE choose.
LIGHT AND DARKNESS:
The game is called "No Lights" because, if you pay a little attention, you'll discover that gathering and extinguishing the light sources scattered through the levels is important in order to locate the exit torch. You'll need darkness to see the feeble, shaky light of the exit. Thus darkness is knowledge, light is ignorance.
Overall, No Lights it's a nice experience, deeper than I thought. Longevity isn't obviously the objective the devs had in mind while developing the game, but that's ok for the price tag (I got the game with a coupon). I value the most the feelings and thoughts that this experience evoked.

Starts out with only 2 available classes. More classes are unlockable. Basic Strength Agility Vitality Intellect Willpower Charisma type stat set up.
