If your Stamina decreases below zero you begin to lose Health. Just living makes your Energy decrease so I look at it as a Hunger bar. There is food you can eat to keep these numbers to an acceptable level.
You apparently always start with a plant that constantly grows Healing Herbs so don't forget to pick them. After a playthrough you get Hero Points and you can spend those on unlocking perks, classes, or slots in a Dimensional Vault that will allow you to keep items after you die, so you may use them in other playthroughs.
The Darkness never stops. If you get consumed by it, you die. Game over, man. Luckily for you, this is a Turn- Based game. So you'll have plenty of time to see what's in front of you, check your inventory, and plan your moves. It's funny because you might see a merchant NPC and you'll do some trading and then continue to run from the darkness and the NPC will scream as he gets swallowed up.
Get. This. Game.

OWH lets you pick a few items to carry on your next run via a Dimensional Vault. This means you can get stronger on subsequent runs. You put items in that box after your run is over and when you start a new game you can pull them out of the Dimensional Box and power up your character.
Gameplay: 9/10
Sometimes you will get annoyed with how things turn out, but as with many roguelikes, the next run is usually better than the previous. There is also plenty of things to unlock such as more classes and stat perks can be chosen to further customize your character. There are save points like a traditional JRPG, if you find a town you can save your progress. If you just can't let go of that one run, then just fire up the previous save.
Graphics: 8/10
Classic 16-bit RPG style. One caveat: The game will go fullscreen mode, but there is no way to change the resolution. Compared to the rest of the game, this is a minor gripe.
Soundtrack: 8/10
Great! At times I was reminded of greats like Chrono Trigger. It's not that good, but its a very solid soundtrack. Fits the adventuring motif perfectly.
Replayability: 10/10

An okay platforming game that unfortunately grows tiresome quickly.
Pros:
+ Some visually stunning enviroments make platforming exhilirating.
+ The way you progress with some of the features is pretty neat, gaining the ability to use your grappling hook more often and other abilities like boosting through the air.
+ There are some interesting challenges throughout the game, like making it past certain parts without using your grappling hook.
Cons:
- The platforming gets repetitive fairly easily.
- Some parts are made extraordinarily difficult due to infuriating placement of checkpoints, which sometimes can even make it confusing to tell how much progress you've made due to similar looking scenery in areas of different checkpoints.
- The story is pretty boring, made worse by the fact that the alien girl who tags along with you is incredibly annoying. The framing device used throughout the game is the protagonist narrating it as a bedtime story to his daughter. I hope it worked, because I would've fallen asleep if I were her.
- The writing and voice acting both suffer from the fact that seemingly neither the writer or the voice actors are native English speakers; the dialogue (which, in its own right, is pretty terrible, with plenty of unintentionally funny parts) is riddled with grammatical errors, and the mostly mediocre voice acting is more of an annoyance than something you'll actually be interested in hearing.
- While some parts of the game use interesting mechanics like a monster that will essentially kill you if it sees you moving, other parts serve to confuse you; there are some rooms with layouts that give barely any indication of where you're supposed to go, which is a huge problem when there are moving platforms that require you to think fast to navigate them.
- Though the environments of the game are generally visually appealing, the design of the alien race you interact with is strange, unintentionally creepy, and outdated; the aliens wouldn't look out of place in a PlayStation 2 game.
As I'm writing this, it's on sale for $2.59; at that price, I would get it, but when the sale ends, skip this.

I backed this game on Kickstarter, and I am very glad I did.  It's a game about a father's journey through Hell to rescue his daughter from the clutches of the sinister Mr. Pinstripe.  Thomas Brush has a more surreal vision of Hell than the typical fire and brimstone, choosing more moody and eerie landscapes (with beautifully appropriate music to match) to convey the atmosphere.
It's not all doom and gloom, though, as there are other characters that will help you on your quest, and there is a fair amount of humor present in the dialogue.  The voice acting is excellent as well, and the "guest" YouTuber voice actors felt like a natural part of the cast and never out-of-place.  Richard Terhune (Mr. Pinstripe) and Dan Avidan (Daniel the Monster) especially did an amazing job of sending shivers down my spine.
The puzzles are fun and light, and never feel obtuse or frustrating.  And while the game is short, it has replayability value in its Adventure Plus mode, with buying new items, visiting areas that were blocked to you before, and uncovering other hidden secrets.
In short, if you're looking for a game that stays in your imagination long after you've beaten it, definitely get Pinstripe.  It's the most pleasant road through Hell that you're ever likely to walk.

This game immediately earns a 10/10 from me, and I would most definitely recommend anybody even remotely interested in this title to pick it up; you won't regret it.

When I first saw Pinstripe in its early stages on Steam Train, I was incredibly excited. To think that this beautiful game was to be made by one person, all on their own... needless to say I felt compelled to back the project.
I am glad to say I am absolutely glad I was able to contribute to the making of this game. A good number of people say the game is too short. It certainly is shorter than most other indie games out there, but considering the scope of the project, the fact that the cells, animation and details have all been hand-illustrated, and all of this is  being done by ONE person, I'd say I'm still very impressed with the final result. Would I have liked a longer game? Sure, but I see this as a gateway to hopefully even more games from this creator in the future.
The gameplay itself is familiar and easy to follow, with a good few mind-bending puzzles scattered throughout. There's also quite a few hidden details and areas you can really find only after playing the game a couple of times. I found the story to be truly unique, and told in such a way that it feels satisfactory and "mind-blowing" when you put the pieces all together. Not to mention the ending... absolutely beautiful. The visual details, atmosphere, the music and the voice acting all come together so wonderfully, I can't help but recommend this for others to play.
Again, however, if you are looking for a game that lasts for hours, then this may not be for you. However, if you aren't too concerned with the length of gameplay, and are looking for a new, interactive and story-driven adventure, then this is the game for you!

Very happy to have supported this game, and look forward to anything else from Atmos in the future.

I checked it out based purely on the fact that some of the cameo voice actors (Dan from NSP, and JackSepticEye) retweeted the announcement of the release of the game on Twitter. From there, I just bought it on a whim to surprise myself, having no idea whether or not I'd like it. Have to say, I loved it.
The gameplay itself is very basic, it's mostly walking around and interacting with the many NPC's, who provide you with the help to get you from point A to point B, or just to give you a chuckle. Humour is subjective, but I think the game does it quite well with the characters it has, albeit it is a little odd to have the antagonist - who seems so feirce and horrifying at first - calling you childish names. It's an interesting mix between creepy as all Hell, but ridiculously stupid - and I love it. The game takes itself seriously, whilst not at the same time.
The premise is that your daughter has been kidnapped by Pinstripe, a man/spirit thing who intends to adopt Bo and make her his own daughter. Why? It's never really explained. No idea what his grudge is against our player character Ted, but we'll ignore that for now. But he seems like a terrifying entity of pure evil, but then a little bit into the game, he'll call you something silly like a "freakishly looking♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" or something. It might put some people off to take you out of the immersiveness a bit for a silly insult, and even other NPC characters who fart while they talk, but it's all down to personal taste, and I think adds to the games charm and keeps it from just being drab and dull the whole time for the sake of a gritty story.
The voice acting matches the writing, and is brilliantly done by all involved. Lines are delivered with just the right amount of care where needed, as well as the right amount of sass and sarcasm.
The gameplay, stated by the dev himself, isn't very much to look at -- the game is mostly about the story. But I did find it fun wandering through the environments trying to find what secrets I could, some were easily missable if you're just running through not paying attention. The game is mostly exploring the maps, but it combines a slingshot early on for use in those maps, and it's how you progress through most of the game. The inventory system is a bunch of clues you find along your way to help with various puzzles later down the road, all of which are easily solved by examining the clues correctly (which I got stuck on one time), and it never seems to hard, or too easy. Sprinkled in are a few cool mini-games, which serve as a nice distraction for a simple reward like frozen oil drops, these include timed lock mechanisms, a flappy bird kind of game, and spot the difference - all of which don't take long at all to complete and don't completely intrude on the game.
All in all, really fun game. There's more I've yet to explore, such as playing through using the meaner responses (as you can respond to some NPC's with specifically story-based "nice" or "mean" responses, which may or may not effect your ending -- haven't tested that yet), and exploring the games few golden padlock doors. There's also various items you can acquire in the game with the frozen drops that you can't get on your first playthrough, and I definitely want to try and grab them if I can.
I definitely recommend the game. It takes around 2hrs or so to beat for your first time, so I do wish it was a bit cheaper, but I'm still happy I got it. It's a fun experience to go on, and if you're in to story games, it's a nice little story about a father and the search for his daughter that'll be sure to brighten your spirits with its charming characters. And maybe weird you out a little too. Sack juice, anyone?

Mafia 2 is the second installment of the Mafia series, which got started with "Mafia: The City of Lost Haven" a long while back, which I consider a classic, good game. Mafia 1 was my alternative to GTA 3, which had a more linear (and shorter) storyline, with darker and more realistic themes. Mafia games seem to always nail it when it comes to story and atmosphere, as Mafia 2's story, atmosphere and the player experiences it offers match and in most cases surpass the original Mafia game. Pair that with beautiful graphics, awesome gameplay mechanics and a more open world and Mafia 2 truly takes the series a big step forward.
Vito Scaletta, the main character of the game, is present in many "Top 5 protagonists in video games" and he is often accompanied in those top 5s by his friend Joe, who is probably my favorite supporting character in a game to date.
Many games which resemble movies and have awesome stories might fall short on their gameplay (I'm looking at you, Remember Me!) but Mafia 2 certainly does not. As you are exploring the immersive city of Empire Bay, you will meet different organized crime syndicates, some of them Italian-American (which Vito & Joe may join) and some of them Chinese, Irish, etc. In the game, you will get to experience the "American dream".. while also inevitably misery, family problems, corruption, among other things. The game is immersive, serious and well-written, with comic relief from Joe and other characters which really gives you a couple of good laughs on your first playthrough.
The atmosphere is great, the gameplay is great, the graphics are great alongside the destruction effects of the engine, the story is immersive, the characters are rich and interesting, and the game also has a fair share of replayability. The only shortcomings of the game I may think of is the lack of a real open world (which might be intended, a linear game does not by any means translate to a bad game), the length (It's not that short, and as you might see I've managed to put a lot of time into it, but for people who want to do everything as fast as possible, it might end fast too)
All in all, I definitely recommend Mafia 2 for anyone. A great take on American organized crime which many might recognize to be inspired by Goodfellas, among other things. Just my opinion, but it is definitely a more enjoyable and immersive experience compared to GTA IV and some others, a must-buy!

Lisa is a fantastic game. On its own, the spoon-fed plot is enjoyable, but the real joy comes from exploring the world and putting story elements together. The dialogue alone makes Lisa a game worth purchasing. It shifts wildly between the poles of childish light-hearted toilet humor and poignant dark psychology. There is an entire area in the middle of horrific violence that is completely dedicated to professional wrestling memes. It is wonderful. The music is heavily atmospheric and has neat tie-ins with the story (especially whenever you hear a horn). The combat system is one that's been done before (kind of a mix of Xenogears and Earthbound), but battles aren't tedious as they are in other RPGs. More attention is given to exploration and dialogue than combat, so getting into constant fights and grinding is never a worry. There are a few areas (five in total throughout the entire game) that have infinitely-spawning random encounters, but the time spent in them is short enough to not become repetitive. The remaining fights are all either scripted or completely avoidable based on choices.
The character development is somewhat lacking for certain party members in the game. For Brad, Buddy, certain party members, and the main antagonists of the game, character development is strong - especially if information on them is sought out by the player. For other recruitable characters, it isn't as much. While this is to be expected from a game that both relies on its humor for character recruiting and one with a large recruitable roster, there should be a little more backstory for certain party members and enemies. Information on a lot of them is available through the artbook, but it's not in the game itself. In pain mode, there are some added enemies that don't really add anything to the plot, but who one would think would be important.
The rest of the gripes are fairly minor. Navigating menus can be somewhat tedious. If Brad uses a bottle of soup on a character, it exits the menu to display text that the bottle is now empty and it is necessary to navigate back to the item menu again. That could probably be streamlined better.
The combat UI can be buggy at times. There are times when a party member will receive a status ailment and the text on the screen will never disappear. Sometimes enemies will just disappear from view. They are still there, and reappear when they're selected, but their sprites will just vanish momentarily.
The UI to set controls is awful. Thankfully the game defaults to controller settings that are present in most console RPGs, but trying to set up custom controls is very difficult unless the player is very familiar with the game beforehand.
Most of the characters are useful in their own ways save a few. The Joy withdrawal mechanic on Brad can be annoying, but it isn't game-breaking; however, a significant portion of the recruitable party members are also Joy addicts, and withdrawal symptoms happen so often that keeping Joy addicts in your party is a significant liability. Some really interesting recruits rarely see use because their Joy addiction is such an annoyance that other non-addicted party members are much more preferable.
The stengths of Lisa far outweigh the weaknesses. It is a hilarious and emotional journey that encourages exploration and strengthens its storytelling through gameplay. It is wholeheartedly recommended.

I've been sitting here for 30 minutes trying to think what to say for this review but...I don't know if I can aptly describe this game. I'll certainly try though. It's really unlike any other game I've played. LISA is intensely surreal and weird. Often featuring disturbing imagery followed by laugh-out-loud lines. Very unsettling.
The world of LISA is cold and ruthless. Most games tout "your choices will affect the game." I'm not sure I've seen a more extreme case of this actually happening than in LISA. Every choice that it presents you with is a lose-lose proposition. There are no right choices in this game. While brutal, it is also very refreshing to see a real no holds barred attitude to this type of game design.
The actual mechanics of the game are very straight forward, you basically can move left and right and jump. The battle system is your typical turn-based RPG affair albeit with LISA's dark humor for the flavor texts. I found the game to be pretty unforgiving early, but as you find more party members, I found it to get much more bearable. Truthfully, the battles were just a vehicle for the story which is where the meat of this game is at. Thankfully there are very few random encounters, so the pacing is strong and doesn't get bogged down.
I have zero problems recommending LISA. I am eager to play the free prequel as well as the sequel coming later this year. Behind The Witcher 3, this is probably the best game I've played in 2015.
One of the greatest RPGs ever.

I picked this up expecting something like World in Conflict or Company of Heroes. Instead, I found a game that required so much micro management that just getting a group of men to walk across a field required at least three button commands and constant attention.
On some level, I can appreciate the attempt to model some of the complexity of real war - tanks have individual sections that can be damaged for different effects, all units have limited ammo for you to keep track of, enemies have angles of vision that you can exploit for flanking attacks, etc. But  the control interface and the AI of your units is so poor that constant micromanagement is necessary to keep your troops from getting slaughtered.
The tank you get command of in the very first mission is a terribly powerful weapon, but mine got destroyed over and over because it wouldn't turn to attack targets I commanded it to hit. You captured the farm house and lost all your tanks, mind you, it's only about 10% of the map. That took you an hour. Some people would rage quit, but not you  You have half a dozen riflemen an assault squad leader. You take the point and mission objective tells you that you must now defend the farm house with what you have. The countdown begins, naturally, they are almost there. They are 3:00 minutes away. You try to repair your tankette, instruct two of your riflemen to move the machine gun towards the bushes and rifle through enemy casulties. You pick up a Panzerfaust and hide in the farm house.
The enemy force come in and its a tank and a couple of squads. You are outnumbered and outgunned. You ran out of AT grenades and all you have is a Panzerfaust. Some people would rage quit, but not you. You take out a fifth of their forces, but most of your men are pinned. The tank is edging closer and closer. Its near the range of the AT infantry, you instruct your AT to take out the tank. Of course this is too important of a task to assign to the AI so you take personal control of the infantry. He jumps out of hiding he fumbles for his panzer. (Did you forget to put away your rifle before blowing your cover?) Your infantry takes the panzer out, loads it up and... gets gunned down by the tanks nachine gunner. Some people would rage quit, but not you.
You lose the battle. You declare defeat.
If you are the person who thinks how they can improve, likes a challenge and have the time this game is for you. If you'd quit because things didn't go your way, this is not for you. The story and kind of game you have is a sort of RTS epic that you will be hard pressed to find elsewhere.

Lamia Must Die is a game of adventure wherein you are not just one person but rather four people. You can change two of your party members and their styles are definitely unique. You adventure into a dungeon and skip all the trash tier monsters completely. The only game play is a big epic boss battle.
The graphics are not that good, but it's excuseable. This game runs mainly on artwork and pictures anyway and it's played through various GUI's, which all look and feel rather fluid and work well. The artwork itself is rather nice and sometimes kind of mediocre, though certainly better than I could care to draw. I'm not completely convinced that some of the pictures of the characters drawn were drawn by the creators of the game or anyone they hired. I don't think they were commissions and rather just something free. If they were drawn by the creators then I ask why there is no consistency in the art work. Some of it looks great while others look like it was drawn by a complete ametuer who had way too much interest in♥♥♥♥♥♥ I of course refer primarily to Lamia.
The story is pretty alright. I give it a 6/10. Basically, there is a snake-lady (Naga?) monster attacking the village and eating their children. Many people have tried to slay this foul, big ♥♥♥♥♥♥d beast but all of the soldiers were eaten. They probably couldn't tear their eyes away from her♥♥♥♥♥♥ So now you and your vagabond party of adventurers/heroes/whatever-the-f*cks embark on a perilous journey to which you get little to no part in as far as interaction goes to venture into Lamia's cave and slay the bodacious reptilian babe. A bit sexist, if you ask me. No one's asking me so now we continue. It gives a campfire scene and talks about what they're going to do and how they're going to get to Lamia. This kind of bugs me because "You" say that it's not as easy as just getting to the big bad monster, but it skips any gameplay that could have happened anyway. You're treated to a dialogue between yourself(s) and Lamia to which you learn a little more about her and then combat is engaged in. Overall, it's a fairly "meh" storyline.
What I do like is the characters. They all have their reasons for being there, whether that be royal responsibility or just straight up revenge. They have different personalities and lives, as you would be able to see if you beat the game. The outro for each character is different depending on if they died or not. Try and find them all! I found myself at least a little bit drawn into their characters and those characters' lives, despite how little I'm told about them and how little exposure I get.
The sounds are what you'd expect from a game like this. For the most part, generic. Though they are satisfying to some extent. You've likely heard most of the sound effects before. Something nice is that they voiced the character's themselves. My favourite is the Male Paladin, as he does the best job. I also quite enjoyed the narrator's voice and I'd encourage them to dub anime or something as they have fantastic voices. Unfortunately, most of the women don't seem to be so gifted and they seem to be trying a bit too hard to sound Fantasy-esque and it just doesn't end up working for them, though I wouldn't say they're terrible. Just average at best.
The music, while I'm unsure if it's stock music or composed music, was fitting to the theme and sounded good. I didn't find myself getting bored of it at all. That being said I've only played about an hour and a half so far.
The gameplay consists of nothing other than a big, epic boss battle. I use the word epic and I mean it. It's challenging - hard as my♥♥♥♥♥♥ in fact - and leaves you seething just enough to be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at Lamia for kicking your♥♥♥♥♥time and time again but not enough to make you rage quit. Pinstripe is an atmospheric puzzle platformer that tells the story of a preacher's search for his daughter.  The art is stylish and atmospheric, and the art style is the main reason to check out the game.  Also, the characters and the voice acting are quite strong.
There are puzzle, platforming, and combat elements.  The level of challenge of the puzzles and combat are medium.  I was never stuck for too long on any one puzzle or combat sequence.
The game only took a couple of evenings for me to complete the game for the first time.  I enjoyed it enough to play it through twice, to see what I missed the first time around.

My favourite part about Pinstripe aside from the art/sound design that others have mentioned is that the puzzles always mades sense to me. They weren't obvious or too easy, but when you did reach the conclusion, it made sense. I tend to get frustrated with the logic in adventure game puzzles, but Pinstripe feels like a completely different type of game, shaking off the inventory puzzles that have bogged down adventure games since Monkey Island.

This review is written after one playthrough on the medium difficulty without any DLC.
I played the game primarily for the story, and the story didn't disappoint. Most of the dialogue was both well-written and well performed (the animation wasn't as good in the cut-scenes at times, but over-all it was pretty good). Of course the characters usually seemed oblivious to the fact that pretty much every firefight involved 20 enemy enemies, but this oddity is usually present in this kind of game, and easily overshadowed over the joy of gunning down 20 mobster with a Tommy Gun. The firefights are fun, if sometimes a bit repetitive, and the difficulty is fair, if sometimes unforgiving - an itchy trigger finger is a good thing, when an enemy with a shotgun comes at you, it's spray-and-pray or die. The combat is largely cover-based, with a fairly big selection of different weapons. There's also a melee combat system, but it's mostly used at particular situations, making it almost akin to a mini-game. Some tasks require a lot of driving, which gets tedious at times.
I thought the graphics were pretty good, and the music impressed me - both the ambient music in cut-scenes and the radio music when driving around. The graphics and soundtrack succeed at creating an atmosphere that helps immerse one into the game, and make those long drives a bit less annoying.
All in all I'd recommend this game for people who like action games with good stories - it's not an extremely long game, but it still takes a lot longer than the first Max Payne game. Get it when it's on sale some time, the 30 euro it costs now, is a bit much.

Not just one of the best games I've played in years, but one of the best games I've played period. LISA is a turn-based RPG in the style of Earthbound, set in a post-apocalyptic world in which women, and by extension, humanity, are on the verge of extincition. The story follows Bradley Armstrong, a gruff, bearded man, who, in spite of his appearance, is not some typical action hero, but a deeply troubled and unstable individual. Finding a baby abandoned in the wastes, Brad finds himself faced with deciding between his own desperate need for redemption in caring for her, and the potential salvation of humanity in the hands of others.
No matter what decisions you make, it's a tragic narrative, and as such, moments of humor are often present between major story beats so as to keep it from becoming too depressing. It pulls off this balancing act stunningly, simultaneously poignant, and hilarious. All while immersing you in a deep, rich world, better realized in 2 Dimensions than many other games' are in 3. With a huge cast of memorable characters and a fantastic soundtrack,  LISA stands out among it's peers as a both a bold new IP, and a love letter to a handful of existing ones. I couldn't recommend it more.
10/10

I normally don't make any reviews of games on Steam, but in this case I feel that it's only proper to make an exception, so bear with me.
Lisa is a sidescrolling RPG which tells the story of Brad, a down-on-his-luck former martial artist with a very unfortunate past. Brad sets out on a dangerous journey to find a girl who may prove to be crucial to the survival of the species.
Plot, in my opinion, is the strongest point of the game. It makes one think and consider various options, as well as theories. One could say that it provides some serious food for thought, and this wouldn't be an exaggeration. Choices that one makes on the way affect the gameplay and the game world in a few different ways. After all, this is a post-apocalyptic wasteland, you never know what lurks around the corner. The story is very dark, but there are also plenty of wacky, downright comical moments in the game.
What is more, this game has a pretty unique art style. It is very charming in its own way. Pretty much every character looks different and has personality. It reminds me of Earthbound (and rightfully so - supposedly, Earthbound was one of the dev's biggest inspirations). The soundtrack is also excellent - it features both quirky and serene pieces, and so everyone will find some appealing songs in it.
All things considered, I think that this is one of the strongest indie titles from 2014. A sequel/DLC is due in 10 days, so hopefully it will wrap-up certain characters arcs. I can sincerely recommend this game, it is definitely worth the asking price.
So, what are you waiting for? Step into the world of Olathe and have fun. :)

Is LISA game of the year? Maybe not, but it's absolutely the Indie of the year for myself.
Quick backstory. I first heard about this game through a friend, who tried to tell me how phenomenal it was. I glanced at the pictures and wrote it off as a simplistic and boring RPG. The amount of regret I have for that instant judgement is unbelieveable.
Fast forward a few weeks, the same friend buys LISA and gifts it too me out of the kindness of his heart. I play it for 20 minutes, and I'm hooked. The game has an amazing draw in capability, sucking me into the story right away. A couple days of heart wrenching, laughter filled, sad days later I beat it. Everything about this game is phenomenal, so let me break it down for you.
Sound/Music: Amazing. For a tiny studio, that originated with a RPG Maker game, the sounds and music are phenomenal. They fit the tone of the game amazingly, and there are still songs I regularly listen to because of how great they are.
Gameplay: Not what I was expecting. Turn based RPGs generally bore me to death these days, so for this game to pull me in being turn based is a feat in its own. The combat is excellently done, with things like Brad flying across the screen, to Terry falling over for your entire journey, I was never bored watching the combat play out, or playing it. The overworld sections are also equally well designed, with only one minor flaw that we'll come back to. The world itself is fantastically designed to have minimal backtrack, and when there is some, it's meaningful, or done in such a way it isn't boring. Just exploring around is a good time. Unfortunately, it's marred but on slight thing, which are the cliffs. They have a way of sneaking up on you, and walking off one sends you straight to the gameover screen, forcing a restart from the last save. That's alright, unless your on Pain Mode, or haven't saved in ages, then it's just rage inducing. Other then that, the gameplay is phenomenal.
Story: The best. Ever. Seriously, the story is the biggest drive of this game, and it's equal parts funny and horribly depressing. It sucked me in so well, I spent hours looking into every ounce of the LISA universe lore. The one major thing is, if you care even a tiny bit about the story, DO NOT spoil it for yourself by googling it. There are so many twists and turns and moments that my jaw dropped that reading it on a wiki wouldn't do justice to. After you've cleared the game, read away, it's more then worth it, even if it is an insanely sad world.
Overall, LISA will most likely be my personal game of the year, beating out Fallout 4, and any other upcoming games, just due to how well it sucked me in. I have no doubt there will be plenty of excellent games realeasing until 2016, but I highly doubt anything will suck me in quite like LISA: The Painful RPG did.

3) Knowedge that it is free - if you are not on a restrictive download amount.
THE MINI GUIDE
Honestly you should not need a guide for this as each room - for lack of better description - Has limited game mechanics that will take at most 120 seconds to learn.
To complete each room you simply have to do one or more of the following:
Walk through an open door
Look for something out of place
Interact with something
Exploit the room game mechanic
Avoid something
Stopping to read & listen to the audio can provide additional infomation as to waht you are ment to be doing.
TO THE CREATOR
Making art - regardless of which from it takes - should be done to make yourself happy, If said art makes others happy -  then congratulations - if not then ask yourself the following:
Is it valid criticism which could help you improve next time ?
Is it someone trying to put you down to make themselves feel bigger ?
The answer to the first question is worth thinking about but the second is not worth your time.

The game is quite short, about 10-15 minutes, depending on how you strategize against Lamia, the one and only battle of the game. While I beat it on my first try, I'm sure others will try once or twice depending on how you go about the battle.
I understand that this was originally a standalone game, so I can see why you'd want to focus mostly on the boss battle itself. The battle system itself was definitely the star of the game, seeing as how it was more active than turn-based, which required more strategy and quick-thinking on the players' part. I did like the fact that you could choose different party members, for a different type of experience and ending depending on who you chose.
The voice acting, while it was nice, did feel a bit hammy and even forced on some lines. The characters themselves also would be nice to have some improvement on - while they had their own little backstory and endings, they did feel a bit generic. Perhaps some characterization work could be worked into the main battle itself?
Overall, a short, but good and potential-worthy game.

I really like the idea of 150+ hours of gameplay being compressed down to a single boss fight. But you're at a significant disadvantage from the start by not knowing the characters and skills. After a few tries though the battle is pretty straight forward. It took me 3 tries to beat Lamia and I have to admit I was a little disappointed that she didn't have multiple forms.
Some cons: I hate the button input sequences for the spells; I was using a controller and had to keep switching back and forth between that and my keyboard. It's also pretty devestating when you miss a input and waste your turn. I also experienced a significant amount of slow down even with the lower resolution. I have a pretty powerful setup so I know that wasn't what the problem is. My last nitpick is that I wish the meters and status effects for the characters where displayed more clearly and the turn reticle/circle thing was bigger.
Definitely worth a try if you're an old school rpg veteran, I mean you have nothing to lose (except time I guess) because it's free. I hope there's a sequel.

This review is written after one playthrough on the medium difficulty without any DLC.
I played the game primarily for the story, and the story didn't disappoint. Most of the dialogue was both well-written and well performed (the animation wasn't as good in the cut-scenes at times, but over-all it was pretty good). Of course the characters usually seemed oblivious to the fact that pretty much every firefight involved 20 enemy enemies, but this oddity is usually present in this kind of game, and easily overshadowed over the joy of gunning down 20 mobster with a Tommy Gun. The firefights are fun, if sometimes a bit repetitive, and the difficulty is fair, if sometimes unforgiving - an itchy trigger finger is a good thing, when an enemy with a shotgun comes at you, it's spray-and-pray or die. The combat is largely cover-based, with a fairly big selection of different weapons. There's also a melee combat system, but it's mostly used at particular situations, making it almost akin to a mini-game. Some tasks require a lot of driving, which gets tedious at times.
I thought the graphics were pretty good, and the music impressed me - both the ambient music in cut-scenes and the radio music when driving around. The graphics and soundtrack succeed at creating an atmosphere that helps immerse one into the game, and make those long drives a bit less annoying.
All in all I'd recommend this game for people who like action games with good stories - it's not an extremely long game, but it still takes a lot longer than the first Max Payne game. Get it when it's on sale some time, the 30 euro it costs now, is a bit much.

One of the only RTS games that cuts out the worker/economy management borefest and focuses on the battlefield tactics. This game is fantastic the graphics and explosions are very well done and the terrain is altered throughout the battle, craters from explosions in battle cause craters that your infantry can take cover in, buildings can be destroyed, rivers, snow and ice all have to be taken into account, the maps in this game just feel very alive and the map is completely different by the end of match, you feel like battle really happened there opposed to many other RTS titles where the map is squeaky clean at the end of the match.
The game also has asymmetrical armies and maps which makes every match different depending on which side of the map you spawned on and what the enemy army is, you must adjust your strategy and be careful in selecting the appropriate commander that best fits the situation. You can also construct things like machine gun emplacements, barbed wire and tank traps anywhere on the map which can change the way battles are fought in that area.
The multiplayer is where this game truly shines in my opinion but if you just want to play vs some AI in a skirmish match the game even has matchmaking for that. Automatch vs AI will match you up with other players and you will take on the AI together. You can also select custom match and set AI as your allies or play a 1v1. There is also a custom match lobby ingame which lets you join other peoples custom lobbies which may have mods that automatically download so you don't have to go searching for the mod to be able to play with them. I definitely recommend grabbing the master collection when it's on sale if you're interested in buying this game.

A nice game made in a retro style, which seems to take inspiration from VVVVVV, being challenging but not unforgiving. The aesthethic is very simple as you can see from the screenshots; and it emulates being played on an old monitor. Even then, you can disable that effect, and add colour if you like.
So, let's go to gameplay. It's a pretty simple platformer, but, like I mentioned above, it's challenging. It also has a metroidvania style, meaning that there's no clear path when you start, but you still need to unlock certain abilities in order to progress. Most of the levels offer a different puzzle, and while some might seem hard at first, once you figure out how to solve them, they can be quite easy. Even then, there's a few that relay on fast reflexes, which increases the difficulty a bit, but, as I said, the game is forgiving, meaning you'll always have a checkpoint nearby whenever a tough puzzle comes up.
The game also offers three different gamemodes: normal, with unlimited lives; cat mode, with 9 lives (but keeps checkpoints); and YOLO mode, which disables checkpoints entirely, meaning that if you die, you've got to restart from the beginning. Even then, when you come to know the game, YOLO mode adds a nice challenge. Besides the different gamemodes, the game offers two campaigns, the original campaign, and the "Extra Spicy" one, which changes most of the levels, making them more difficult.
I don't think I have a lot more to say about this game, other than I enjoyed it. If you like platformers like VVVVVV, or Super Meat Boy, I think you'll enjoy this game.

Is LISA game of the year? Maybe not, but it's absolutely the Indie of the year for myself.
Quick backstory. I first heard about this game through a friend, who tried to tell me how phenomenal it was. I glanced at the pictures and wrote it off as a simplistic and boring RPG. The amount of regret I have for that instant judgement is unbelieveable.
Fast forward a few weeks, the same friend buys LISA and gifts it too me out of the kindness of his heart. I play it for 20 minutes, and I'm hooked. The game has an amazing draw in capability, sucking me into the story right away. A couple days of heart wrenching, laughter filled, sad days later I beat it. Everything about this game is phenomenal, so let me break it down for you.
Sound/Music: Amazing. For a tiny studio, that originated with a RPG Maker game, the sounds and music are phenomenal. They fit the tone of the game amazingly, and there are still songs I regularly listen to because of how great they are.
Gameplay: Not what I was expecting. Turn based RPGs generally bore me to death these days, so for this game to pull me in being turn based is a feat in its own. The combat is excellently done, with things like Brad flying across the screen, to Terry falling over for your entire journey, I was never bored watching the combat play out, or playing it. The overworld sections are also equally well designed, with only one minor flaw that we'll come back to. The world itself is fantastically designed to have minimal backtrack, and when there is some, it's meaningful, or done in such a way it isn't boring. Just exploring around is a good time. Unfortunately, it's marred but on slight thing, which are the cliffs. They have a way of sneaking up on you, and walking off one sends you straight to the gameover screen, forcing a restart from the last save. That's alright, unless your on Pain Mode, or haven't saved in ages, then it's just rage inducing. Other then that, the gameplay is phenomenal.
Story: The best. Ever. Seriously, the story is the biggest drive of this game, and it's equal parts funny and horribly depressing. It sucked me in so well, I spent hours looking into every ounce of the LISA universe lore. The one major thing is, if you care even a tiny bit about the story, DO NOT spoil it for yourself by googling it. There are so many twists and turns and moments that my jaw dropped that reading it on a wiki wouldn't do justice to. After you've cleared the game, read away, it's more then worth it, even if it is an insanely sad world.
Overall, LISA will most likely be my personal game of the year, beating out Fallout 4, and any other upcoming games, just due to how well it sucked me in. I have no doubt there will be plenty of excellent games realeasing until 2016, but I highly doubt anything will suck me in quite like LISA: The Painful RPG did.

I absolutely loved this game. I did play it on the lowest difficulty, so my experience may be a bit different from the standard. This game has a compelling story with believable characters that actually made me care. I think this game has a very good balance of horror (well actually less real horror and more just creepy stuff), which I tend to dislike but I enjoyed immesely in this game; action, which can be hectic and very challenging, but is also extremely exciting, with many heart-pounding moments where I almost felt like I was actually in the game; and intrigue in the form of the Dark Ones, which I found to be very interesting. I had goosebumps throughout what had to have been a third of the game, which is always a sign that the game I am playing is interesting. I think that the hallucinations with the Dark Ones are extremely well-done, because they don't happen so frequently that I can tell when they're coming and get bored of them, but they happen just often enough to keep me guessing. The only problem I have with this game is the level design, which is occasionally confusing and hard to find where to go, but that is only in 2 or 3 levels and is somewhat bearable. It certaintly doesn't ruin the game and most of the levels are fabulous.

An atmospheric stealth shooter with survival elements that has always and will always stand above the rest. My recent playthrough is the first time I've expericed the Redux edition and honestly all of the changes are postive. The game drips with immersion by using beautfiul lighting, audio and realism. One audio complaint however, would be that the children sound like thirty-year-old-women.
The gameplay itself is pretty standard for an fps save for the addition of gasmasks and such, It is best experienced on Ranger mode to make it feel more survival based and make the player really consider resource management as you will no longer heal outside of combat and a few other things. A cool feature of the harder modes is that they don't simply make enemies bullet sponges, both Artyom(MC) and the enemies die in a headshot or a few body shots.
The story is of course considerbly better than most games as it is based off of a renowned novel.
Not much more I can say without spoiling or ruining the gameplay experience so hey try it if you want, it drops to £3 on sale but is still worth the non-sale price.
Oh and notable technical aspects would be that it is well optimised for pc(not amazingly but very good) and there are a few bugs, my gas mask filters vanished once and I died.

First, the issues. The game lacks balancing the ammo you find with the weapons you have and gives less explanation to it's mechanics than it should, especially with the damage of the guns and the availability of ammo in the game. You should basically stick to just some of the guns (Revolver, Shotgun and Assault Rifle) to find more ammo that fits into your guns.
The gamma ajustment is also misleading and the game works best with less lighting, making the stealth more immersive and intuitive.
Also, the scope rendering for magnified scopes sucks, zooming the whole screen.
With that being said, the game excels at ambientation, with a good enough plot and pacing. It balances well the stealth, and the immersion shines the most on Ranger mode. It is also flexible and can be played as a more conventional shooter, but I would not recommend the game for those looking for these kind of games.
It is a recommendation for those looking for the ambientation and a more unique linear experience.

This is a wonderful game. The storyline is wonderful and creative. As I am writing this review, I have not read the book. I will add an edit to this review when I read the Metro books and compare the games to the books. I have played through the game twice. Once in English and once in Russian with English subtitles. The voice acting of the game is great. Sometimes the game does desynch with the audio (might just be my computer) and there are a few bugs in the game as well. My recomendation is that you keep your eyes wide open and collect all the ammo you can. Use stealth to your advantage and rarely use bullets. I made that mistake by using to much ammo and running out of ammo by  the end. I had to switch to millitary ammo (used as currency) in the end. In my case it wasn't as bad because I was at the end of the game, but you don't want this to happen to you in the middle of the game. I have not played all of the difficulties, but I can say that the two I did play was a fun ride. The game is also very beautiful at times. Metro 2033 usualy stays at its dark musky color of the metro stations, or the gray/white color of overworld Moscow, but the menus and the ending and colorful and well detailed. On the topic of the menu, it is full with activity. Not activity that clutters your screen, but activity that adds to the atmosphere of the game. It has the hustle and bustle of the Metro underground and you are in the center of it. The game is worth the full price, but I recomend that you wait for a major Steam Sale and purchase the bundle pack of 2033 and Last Light together. I will add another edit to this review after I have finished Last Light and compare them. From what I have read, you should play this game first because it offers more background story that Last Light does. Edits to this review (originally written on 4 December 2018) will come once I have finished Last Light (I will also write a seperate review for that game) and once I have finished reading Metro 2033. That is all I have to say for now. Edits to come soon.

The world is ending, what do you do? Go out and kick the crap out of a demon lord. But in all seriousness this is a very good game. At its core it's a JRPG but has roguelike mechanics. You start off with 2 classes and a few minor perks(which are optional) and you'll unlock more as you meet certain requirements. Each class can equip basically any type of equipment(which has durability), with each class having their own unique passive ability. For example the hunter has longer range with bows or the knight being able to defend against more attacks. As you travel through the world fighting monsters and visiting towns you'll probably notice the big wall of death to your left. That's pretty much what your trying to stop. Pushing forward while leveling and gearing up seems to be your only option. Eventually you'll make it to the demon lord(hopefully powerful enough to stop him). Died to him, the wilderness, nature, and/or the big wall of looming death? No problem. There's a carry over feature. Every playthrough allows you the chance to purchase perks and transfer items with your hero points(how much you gain depends on your performance). All in all it's a solid game(especially considering the price(even more so during the summer sale)).

I had the pleasure of beta testing this game and this gave me an interesting perspective on the game; while some changes from the initial beta to the final release I wouldn't agree with (but were based on the feedback of other beta testers, such as making the puzzles and boss battle easier), overall the game is still a beautiful experience.
This game has a solid playtime and holds up wonderfully to multiple playthroughs - certain areas and features are only accesible on a second or third playthrough. Little clues throughout the game call you back in to discover different secrets, like Film Strips and a gun seen hanging up in the final area of the game.
Gameplay is relatively simple, and is sure to please fans of 2D platforming. Along with the platforming, there are also several moments of unique minigames that switch up the gameplay to keep things fresh.
My favorite thing about the game is the story and the characters in it. The characters are fun and fresh, and the big YouTuber cameos are unintrusive if you're there for the game and not Jacksepticeye or the Game Grumps. But most of all, the story: what is really going on is never really spelled out to you. As the credits roll, all of the pieces came together in my mind to form a beautiful, heartbreaking story.

I actually have some pretty polarizing thoughts on this game. Here's a quick summary before I go more in depth:
Pros
+ Authentic portrayal of the late 40's/early 50's
+ Well optimized; very few bugs encountered
+ Great graphics, though character models are notably aged
+ A story ripped straight out of the mobster movie genre
+ Literally the best collectible item I've ever seen in a game ever (Playboy magazines)
Cons
- Terrible open world
- A.I. is wonky most of the time
- Nvidia Physx
The game actually has very few cons, but the cons that it does have seriously hurt.
Let's talk open world, first. To put it simply, Grand Theft Auto 4 is still fun to play after beating the story, Saints Row 3 is still fun to play after beating the story, Mafia 2 is NOT fun to play after beating it. The only reason you'll want to play is for the story, and once it's done there's not really anything else going for it, unless you want all the collectibles, but you can just load up individual chapters from the main menu to do that. Most open world games have fast travel, Mafia 2 DOES NOT. This is horribly, horribly annoying. You literally drive MORE than you shoot at bad guys or experience the story. And get this, driving isn't fun. At all. It's at least somewhat realistic, but it doesn't have a sophisticated damage system so you'll always see the same pre-canned scratches and dents, cops seem to literally spawn around your character constantly and it's very easy to die whilst driving. If there was a fast travel system the time it would take to beat Mafia 2 would be cut in half. Seriously.
In most open world games it's fun to cut loose and wreak havoc. Mafia 2 does not want you to do that. It encourages you to act like a civil person. There are no crazy weapons like an RPG, tank or even a sniper rifle and cops in this game are EVERYWHERE. They literally do spawn around your character, ESPECIALLY when you're wanted. I've watched cop cars (they show up on your minimap) appear right next to me, just around a corner or behind me. They actually do spawn like this, it's very annoying.
A lot of crime oriented open world games have side missions or little activities to do on the side. Mafia 2 does not. Its world feels empty. This makes up most of the reason why it's simply not fun to play after beating Mafia 2.
Now time to talk story. Mafia 2's story isn't the most original thing on the planet. It draws very heavily from mobster movies and while that is intentional the plot itself is fairly contrived, the writers did not try to do anything crazy or ambitious to try and blow your mind, they just made a coherent mafia-themed story set in the late 40's/early 50's. While this is all true, I still found myself wanting to see how the story ended, and what twists would occur. There were twists, there were moments of excitement and I did enjoy the story. Until the ending.
*SPOILERS*
*SPOILERS*
Stop reading if you don't want spoilers.
The ending of Mafia 2 is really bad. I'm not joking. It's downright terrible. You kill the big bad guy once all is said and done, there are some revelations and you're feeling the climax approaching. A happy ending is literally set up, but then that's thrown way out the window and your partner the entire game is killed for no reason. The developers just shoe-horned that classic "oh he made it but at WHAT COST!?!" ending when it didn't even belong. It seriously was very, very unnecessary and actually made me mad as I liked Joe a lot (certainly more than Roman from GTA IV).
Something interesting to note about this game: it may be called Mafia 2, but for the majority of the game you're doing things non-mafia related or doing things FOR the mafia, but never really doing things AS the mafia.
Onto the subject of Nvidia and Physx. This game looks GREAT wtih Apex Physx. Combat is enhanced greatly, slick cloth physics are dangling everywhere, particle effects are flying all over the place, it really is something to behold. HOWEVER, because Nvidia is a greedy company, they deny access to this technology to anyone that doesn't have an Nvidia graphics card. Because of this unfair gimmick, I am placing it as a con and I really hope that one day video games can be experienced AS THE DEVELOPERS INTENDED, and NOT AS GREEDY COMPANIES INTENTED.
So, in short, I can't NOT Recommend this game. It's a well made video game, but what's inside of that video game isn't always good. Play it for the story and collectibles, then shelf it. If you're a fan of the mobster genre and/or the 40's/50's aesthetic this game will be perfect for your tastes.
There's just better open world games out there, most of them blow Mafia 2 out of the water, but for its unique ties to the mobster genre and its time period, I'd say it's still worth it.

This isn't a bad game per say. In fact I found it quite entertaining, if a little rough around the edges. The problem isn't that the game is bad, but the developers. Had they continued to push out content and updates, this game could have been great. I could have dumped hours and hours into it. However, less than a week from the official release, the developers went radio silent. They even promised a new update way back on May 18th, slated for May 25th. It is now August 23rd at the time I write this review, and there has not been a word, or an update since that post.
Now, I normally don't write reviews about this kind of thing.♥♥♥♥♥♥happens, people have lives. A small group of indie devs can have things come up. But it's been three full months. The dev's haven't posted or replied to anything on the forums in that time. They also gave absolutely no indication they were going on hiatus. They just took the money and ran.
Apparently this developer group has a history of abbandoning games. Their last couple hotel simulator games were abbandoned and left incomplete. This is just one more on the list.
Is it a bad game? No. Is it worth the money? Honestly, the $8.00 asking price is quite reasonable for what you get.
Should you buy it?
I wouldn't, the game needs work, and it doesn't look like its ever going to get it. If the game had any future prospect I would probably recommend it, but right now, while it isn't a bad game, you can do better with your $8.00.
Developers shouldn't be encouraged to do this♥♥♥♥♥♥ I will say that at least this group moved out of early access before abbandoning the project. But they still abbandoned it within a week of its release, so that isn't much better.

For anyone who's a fan of roguelikes, this game is right up your alley. It's actually got a bit of personality above and beyond many roguelikes that are out there, and the pixel graphics really add charm, if they're your style.
Progression is quick, and every death seems to lead to either a new bit of knowledge, or extra strength for the next run. It also provides a fine amount of replay, incorporating daily realms and other online elements, so if you're looking for another run on a new class, or a new level of challenge, the game is constantly giving you new stuff to contend with.
For whatever reason, the game won't let me play in fullscreen, despite my best efforts to do so, but that's really just a tiny complaint. Same thing for the keyboard-only controls, which thankfully are very simple and intuitive.  All in all, this game provides a remarkable amount of content for under five bucks, and even if it was ten, I'd heartily recommend it to roguelike fans.
Final rating: 8/10

Would I recommend this game? Hell yes, but not to everyone. LISA is an acquired taste. You've gotta have a taste for the weird, the creepy, and the wrong.. and you definitely can't be feint of heart.
Before I start, I'll just say, 10/10, hands down. Dingaling has created one of my favourite games to date. LISA's story is very refreshing and original, and definitely something not anyone could have thought up. There are secrets o' plenty, and the playstyle is very old-school. Of course, there are plenty of perverts, mutants, and substance-abusers as well, but they make it interesting. LISA hits all emotional buttons; you'll laugh, cry, rage, get the weirdest of boners, and most of all, cringe. It's one of the most original, well-thought-out, and intriguing side-scrollers I've seen in a really long time.
The soundtrack is created by Widdly 2 Diddly, which is actually just the same guy who makes up the one man show that is Dingaling. It's perfect; eerie and cheerie. Some of my favourite tracks include "Beehive", "All Hail the Fishmen", "Work Harder" (because of the hilarious area in the game in which it's used), and of course, "Summer Love" (all of which can be found either in the DLC soundtrack on Steam or on Widdly 2 Diddly's bandcamp page).
I found very few bugs. I think I found a grand total of one, and it wasn't even really a big deal. There was an invisible ledge and I somehow got onto it. I doubt many people managed to do it. Some of the caves do lag because of a candle here and there, which use dynamic lighting. That's it. Otherwise, completely smooth. Combat is turn-based and it works like a charm. Really easy to get used to if you're not usually into that.
All-in-all, LISA is a morally challenging game as well. I can't mention anything without spoiling it, though, so you'll have to see for yourself. If you're a pervert, a broken man, or you just appreciate the weirder things in life, this is for you. If you just appreciate a really well made old-school type game and want to support an indie developer, this could be for you too. Like I said, it's an acquired taste, but if it tastes good to you, you'll get the joy.. joy..

Men of War is, in short, the best RTS i've ever played. If I had just one word to describe it, that word would be "Mindblowing". There are four campaigns that put you in the different theatres that were present during the time period. From the sands of North Africa to Sevastopol, you'll be duking it out as the Soviet, German, English, and American forces. I've put in somewhere around ninety hours upon writing this review, and almost 200 into its sequel, Men of War Assault Squad 2. It's worth mentioning that the multiplayer for this installment isn't really its shining point, so if you want multiplayer, you should probably buy Assault Squad 2.
I'll give off a bulletin list and then go a little more in depth on the more important aspects.
So the first one I want to talk about is the fact that your units are almost entirely unique. Their skins are the same, but they can lose their helmets from a stray bullet, lose their weapons in an explosion, or even be shot and wounded, only to be saved by a godly medic. They have their own names too, though a name may repeat sometimes.
The replayability in this game is immense, with each mission having different ways to approach your objective. Will you fall back to a hill and fortify, or will you meet them head on with your T-34s? Will you sneak in with a sniper team, or will you steamroll their position with your panzers? The choice is completely yours.
The mission editor is, as of this review, almost 9 years old. Despite its age, it has held up really well, and i'm proud to say about 75% of my time spent in this game was making battles in the editor.
Alright alright, this game isn't all perfect. It has some major flaws that the later installments tried their best to fix.
The graphics on this game are pretty bad, but considering both the year it came out and the scale of the game, it's forgiveable. The later installments got massive graphical upgrades, although they're not the prettiest things.
Although the multiplayer is dead on this installment, you can play Assault Squad 2 and get into a lobby in almost no time, assuming you have Robz Realism (hahaha funny joke).
The mods have never been that impressive on the first game, but both later installments, Assault Squad 2 and Assault Squad 1, have plenty of mods to play around with.
Good god, the controls are horrendous. If you've never played the other Men of War games, you can forgive them, but they're so confusing and♥♥♥♥♥backwards that you don't know what to press half the time.
Do I recommend this game? Hell yeah. It's, as I stated before, one of the best games i've ever been lucky enough to play, and before I forget, you can make your men climb trees.

Men Of War is an exquisite, visceral game of chess. Each piece, each soldier, each tank and artillery weapon has its special strengths and weaknesses. But our little battlefield avatars, seen from the god-like heights, or joined in the mud, are not fixed, unchanging. They can pick up a bazooka from the hands of a dead grenadier, they can forage amongst the ammo dumps for rifle or machine gun rounds. They can hide behind walls and creep through long grasses to ambush and surprise their enemies. And if their new-found bounty is not enough, they can lob a grenade into a half-track and take control of the vehicle. They can capture tanks and motorcycles, ack-ack guns and rocket-cannons, and repair them if they are damaged, re-fuel them if they are out of petrol. Like no other game before, Men Of War has the dynamics and flexibility to be a classic. Now we need more period warfare (sort out some hand-to-hand animation for medival battles, please) and perhaps it is time to dive into the future. I actually have some pretty polarizing thoughts on this game. Here's a quick summary before I go more in depth:
Pros
+ Authentic portrayal of the late 40's/early 50's
+ Well optimized; very few bugs encountered
+ Great graphics, though character models are notably aged
+ A story ripped straight out of the mobster movie genre
+ Literally the best collectible item I've ever seen in a game ever (Playboy magazines)
Cons
- Terrible open world
- A.I. is wonky most of the time
- Nvidia Physx
The game actually has very few cons, but the cons that it does have seriously hurt.
Let's talk open world, first. To put it simply, Grand Theft Auto 4 is still fun to play after beating the story, Saints Row 3 is still fun to play after beating the story, Mafia 2 is NOT fun to play after beating it. The only reason you'll want to play is for the story, and once it's done there's not really anything else going for it, unless you want all the collectibles, but you can just load up individual chapters from the main menu to do that. Most open world games have fast travel, Mafia 2 DOES NOT. This is horribly, horribly annoying. You literally drive MORE than you shoot at bad guys or experience the story. And get this, driving isn't fun. At all. It's at least somewhat realistic, but it doesn't have a sophisticated damage system so you'll always see the same pre-canned scratches and dents, cops seem to literally spawn around your character constantly and it's very easy to die whilst driving. If there was a fast travel system the time it would take to beat Mafia 2 would be cut in half. Seriously.
In most open world games it's fun to cut loose and wreak havoc. Mafia 2 does not want you to do that. It encourages you to act like a civil person. There are no crazy weapons like an RPG, tank or even a sniper rifle and cops in this game are EVERYWHERE. They literally do spawn around your character, ESPECIALLY when you're wanted. I've watched cop cars (they show up on your minimap) appear right next to me, just around a corner or behind me. They actually do spawn like this, it's very annoying.
A lot of crime oriented open world games have side missions or little activities to do on the side. Mafia 2 does not. Its world feels empty. This makes up most of the reason why it's simply not fun to play after beating Mafia 2.
Now time to talk story. Mafia 2's story isn't the most original thing on the planet. It draws very heavily from mobster movies and while that is intentional the plot itself is fairly contrived, the writers did not try to do anything crazy or ambitious to try and blow your mind, they just made a coherent mafia-themed story set in the late 40's/early 50's. While this is all true, I still found myself wanting to see how the story ended, and what twists would occur. There were twists, there were moments of excitement and I did enjoy the story. Until the ending.
*SPOILERS*
*SPOILERS*
Stop reading if you don't want spoilers.
The ending of Mafia 2 is really bad. I'm not joking. It's downright terrible. You kill the big bad guy once all is said and done, there are some revelations and you're feeling the climax approaching. A happy ending is literally set up, but then that's thrown way out the window and your partner the entire game is killed for no reason. The developers just shoe-horned that classic "oh he made it but at WHAT COST!?!" ending when it didn't even belong. It seriously was very, very unnecessary and actually made me mad as I liked Joe a lot (certainly more than Roman from GTA IV).
Something interesting to note about this game: it may be called Mafia 2, but for the majority of the game you're doing things non-mafia related or doing things FOR the mafia, but never really doing things AS the mafia.
Onto the subject of Nvidia and Physx. This game looks GREAT wtih Apex Physx. Combat is enhanced greatly, slick cloth physics are dangling everywhere, particle effects are flying all over the place, it really is something to behold. HOWEVER, because Nvidia is a greedy company, they deny access to this technology to anyone that doesn't have an Nvidia graphics card. Because of this unfair gimmick, I am placing it as a con and I really hope that one day video games can be experienced AS THE DEVELOPERS INTENDED, and NOT AS GREEDY COMPANIES INTENTED.
So, in short, I can't NOT Recommend this game. It's a well made video game, but what's inside of that video game isn't always good. Play it for the story and collectibles, then shelf it. If you're a fan of the mobster genre and/or the 40's/50's aesthetic this game will be perfect for your tastes.
There's just better open world games out there, most of them blow Mafia 2 out of the water, but for its unique ties to the mobster genre and its time period, I'd say it's still worth it.

I can say that while there are problems with the game; the tutorial is fairly useless, the combat mechanics make no sense, the lack of diversity in the battle system entirely, and the bare bones mechanics of understanding your character's status (and the fact you can't even check other party members aside from level) I can't for the life of me understand some of the other gripes people are making about this game.
It's a fun little game with a unique system. I love the option of making your own Tavern. All I really want is more more more though. I want to be able to modify my character a bit. I want a bit more of variety in gear or at least some more methods of improving my character's abilities. The way to accumulate money only "seems" hard at first but, once you understand a good portion of the mechanics you realize that gathering cash should never be an obsticle ever. It's just not done in the standard way of "kill enemies and watch them drop money". Which to be honest is actually a nice touch in my opinion.
All in all this game could have much much more added to it. but, the unique premise just makes me want to greedily play it more and more and hope for vast additions to the game or just more additions to this type of genre.  8/10

I was given a copy of this game for reviewing purposes. This has is no way altered my review of the game.
Moonstone Tavern is an interesting concept, but very poorly executed. I'll spare lots of details to not be redundant, since many other reviewers have covered them, but it's all true: the terrible game mechanics (combat especially), clunky menus and interface, difficulty in earning money/getting upgrades, and so on and so on.
My personal biggest problem with this game is that it's a blatant ripoff of the developer's previous game, Fortune's Tavern, which is currently no longer on Steam. Supposedly it's a prequel, but having the exact same graphics, music, gameplay, interface, and problems seems suspicious. And lazy. That's something I can't excuse here. I understand these are indie developers and making games are difficult, but this just screams cash grab to me. All in all, I don't recommend Moonstone Tavern. The idea is cool, but it's too frustrating to play and its many problems are very distracting.

You are going to die.

IT's your 30th try, things are going great, you're zipping along, and then you hit an ion storm and a nasty enemy, next thing you know you've got systems on fire, hull breaches (oh, that's right, you pulled your energy from the O2 system to get that extra shield bubble....), a dead pilot.... You know there's an away team causing havoc on your ship, but with your sensors down you can't see them. Everything was going so well, next thing you know.....
There's only one reasonable reaction to this sheer frustration. Start another run, because you know if you only had that weapon preloader things would have been different!
The repeated frustration is tempered by the realization that one small thing would have been the difference. You'll keep trying, you'll keep dying, but then it will happen - the magical run. It's not easy, but things are lining up, your strategy is paying off, and when you finally beat the game you'll know exactly what to do.
Start another run.

At 35 hours, I've yet to win this game -- on easy mode. One of my two forays to the last level was my first game with the ring ship. I swear I saw the boss ship breaking apart when I was suddenly notified it had teleported away. Decided to repair up before taking it on again, miscounted the jumps, lost.
This game is unforgiving, even when luck is with you. Make sure you count the jumps, that the path on the map really won't leave you stranded in a corner with three jumps through the entire enemy fleet, that you understand what principle is behind your ship, that you don't run out of fuel or any resource that your strategy depends on.
It's a game above all about resource control. Don't drop that missile when you can finish off your enemy by slow laser fire without losing more than two hull points.
And then, all the same, all your essential components might evaporate somehow or four tank aliens might auto-teleport onto your ship to bring you to an early end...
So many times I was going to drop the game, but every play gave me another realization to try out...

Dingaling worked ♥♥♥♥ing magic with this title. Puts many big-budget releases to shame. The script is on point, the presentation is charming, the story is twisted and disturbing. It's one of the best RPGs I have ever played, and I've been gaming since the NES. It wears its influences proudly. Think of it as Mother 4 for those who played Earthbound on release, a wonderful, quirky game that hits all the right notes while giving its audience something to think about. Seriously impressive work from this dev. I rank it alongside The Witcher series as the best example of player-driven storytelling in gaming. It's not often you see a game that uses the medium so well to tell a story. Follows the cleverness of games like Streets of Rage, Bioshock, and Metal Gear Solid 3, using gameplay as a storytelling technique. How satisfying to find the rare game that respects intelligence, and doesn't give all the answers, and doesn't rely on exposition to tell another bog standard tale. Lisa is something special. Don't miss out.

LISA is an incredibly engaging homage to the seminal 90s SNES RPG Earthbound. It stays true to its quirky roots, but its setting in a gritty post-apocalyptic world forces you to make some truly harrowing decisions. Are you willing to cut off an arm to save a friend's life? Would you sell out a tiny refugee village to a group of bandits to keep your belongings? Even with many indie releases made in the retro style, it's still quite interesting to me how far devs will go to mimic the exact style of retro games. For me, this is best shown in You Have to Win the Game.
Cons:
-No music whatsoever. I understand that it's going for the style of a Commodore game, but many games for that computer had good music. This is my biggest problem with the game.
-It seems to me as though the developer (who refers to himself as Kyle in the "support the developer" section) tried too hard to exactly mimic the C64. I would love to see this game made more expansive.
Pros
-Metroid-style gameplay. Of course, there are fewer items, you're not a badass Power Suit-wearing bounty hunter like Samus (in fact, as far as I know, there is no weapon) but the combination of player-driven exploration and strong platforming bears a resemblance to Super Metroid or Metroid II.
-Amazing conveyance. Here is how the developer designed the game: You start the game and immediately encounter branching paths. Since the player just started, they want to keep going. They choose a direction and go. As they go along, they find outlines of platforms. They realize that there must be something to create platforms. This gives them the patience to keep going. They eventually find a boss. Having no weapon, they instead figure out the most effective way to dodge the barrage of projectiles. They then will find either the Crimson or Cerulean Aura. Et cetera, et cetera. Short version: the game is good at keeping the player going and teaching them.
-The player is always, always in control.

As of right now, it's exactly what you think a very new multiplayer reboot would be, a series of game crashes and server overloads so frustrating that it becomes barely playable. Then, in a rare case where you get into a server, you remember why we all love this game so much. I have high hopes that Disney (who decided to give this game multiplayer capablilities) will smooth out the rough bits and give us an all round experience that is just as fun as we remember it to be.
