This game is brilliant.
I know that's not a proper review so let's go into more detail: this game is really ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant.
Okay seriously now...
I have just spent 27 hours completing the first campaign with the Soviets, on normal. Yes that is my entire playtime. No I do not suck at wargames. This game is
, and not always for the right reasons. Aside from the fact that I traditionally play as a virtual Montgomery (yes, the WWII Field Marshal known for his caution and methodical attacking strategy), Men of War throws things at you that I guarantee you you've never seen in any other WWII RTS. Let's get the bad out of the way first, so we can gorge on the good for dessert.
If you don't like micro-management of units in an RTS, steer clear of this game. I personally consider this a good aspect of the game, but because it's on such an intense and vast scale, it can be...overwhelming. You may be in command of many dozens of men at any one time and because each and every individual gets their own inventory (more on that later), that's dozens of people whose weapons and ammo loadouts you generally need to keep an eye on.
What really gets on my nerves, and will get on yours, are the small terrain bugs. This is a problem that applies mainly to vehicles and large equipment like anti-tank guns. This may be a tech constraint more than anything else but it seems where they've tried to map out terrain accurately, they've ended up not quite getting it right, so your vehicles/equipment sometimes end up going very, very slowly over pieces of terrain that are not completely smooth. The whole issue is a minor thorn in your leg but it's still bothersome.
Finally, the game is often difficult because you are given barebones assistance in terms of objectives. To be clear, yes you are given objectives and yes there's a red arrow that points to objectives during missions. But it's a thick red ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that really only points to the general region of your objective rather than the specific item or area, and your objectives are not always explained clearly enough. What I mean by that is, the game tells you what to do but it doesn't do it specifically enough. Minor spoiler ahead if you want more of an explanation on that:
Now, if you can at least tolerate all that then please,
, stay for the brilliance.
Anyone who is familiar with games like Company of Heroes will feel right at home with this game. Only you're not at home because THIS. IS. MEN OF WAR. First thing you might notice is how there's no base. Instead you're given a complement of troops each mission. Every single soldier you can click on has their own inventory box. Literally every single one. They can pick up [and use] most anything and everything you can find on the battlefield, ranging from helmets and grenades to ammunition boxes and rocket launchers. You could probably play this game as some kind of Inventory Collection Simulator 2009. Now, the best thing about this is essentially unit customization.
You cannot customize the looks of your men but by ♥♥♥♥ you can customize damn near everything else. Want to go into battle with a squad of bazooka-armed Nazi officers? Done. Want to strip your men to the bare bones and send them into battle as nothing but trained martial artists? You're covered there. Just want to craft a well-armed, well-rounded squad with rifles and a couple of light machine guns? Go for it! The game practically begs you to do this and the system is self-perpetuating because EVERY SINGLE soldier on the battlefield has their own inventory, even your opponents. On a special forces mission and in need of some heavier weapons? Tough luck. Oh wait, I can hear the deep growl of a truck coming this way, get ready lads...
Another highly celebrated feature of this game is the Direct Control system. Using this you can essentially play through entire missions as one soldier or one vehicle. The system does precisely what it claims to do and gives you control over a single entity in the game, thereafter moving it around with the arrow keys and aiming/shooting with the mouse. This is not only massive bucketfuls of fun but it's paticularly useful if you want to accomplish specific tasks or turn the tide in a small tactical skirmish. I can't explain in words how satisfying it is to have one of your squads in trouble, losing men fast, only for their prayers to be answered as YOU turn the corner in a T-34, traverse the turret in the direction of your enemy and BOOM, ♥♥♥♥ YOU. Yes, the game has those moments, providing you want to make them.
You can of course play this game completely as a traditional RTS and it's likely you'll spend more time directing squads and tanks at the strategic level than "on the ground". But it's those "on the ground" moments that really drive home the fun- ahem I mean, brutality of war. Graphics-wise the game is nothing particularly special. It was released in 2009 but it uses a slighly older engine so don't expect too much polish. You can still observe troops getting pulverized into a fine mist by 20mm FlaK fire, let's put it that way.
Another great feature, though more minor in comparison to the others, is the way the game crafts what I like to think of as a "persistent battlefield". In most missions you will be accompanied by AI-controlled friendly troops. These guys all have their own programs and will get on with hurting the enemy wherever they can. They will even accomplish main game objectives for you in some instances. One mission I had, focused on the titanic struggle for the Seelowe Heights (anyone who knows their history will know this is a particularly bloody episode in the book of WWII) in 1945, ended up with me relying on my AI friends to clear out the enemy towards the end of the mission, as every assault I made had been pummeled into near nothingness and I ended up having no reserves left to commit. Instead, all I had left was one squad of tank crewmen.
Now, if there's one thing this game teaches you like nothing else ever will, it's that failure is not the end. Only the beginning. This is where anecdotal value really comes into its own...
You know what I did with that tank squad? Yeah that's right. Instead of giving up I searched the battlefield and, lo and behold, found myself a Mark IV Panzer that still had all its parts on the same vehicle (as opposed for instance to the turret being found hundreds of metres away having been blown clean off). With a heart full of vengeance, I commanded my squad to retrieve a repair kit from the inventory of an earlier destroyed T-34 and set about repairing the Panzer. My crewmen and I looked in disgust at the white cross. "We'll drape a red flag over that cross soon enough brothers", thought I. In minutes, to my deep satisfaction, my crewmen had a fully functioning Panzer, armed with a 75mm main gun on the turret and the deadly MG-34 in the hull and coax positions.
I would love to finish that story (the bulk of it is we unleashed that vengeance) but Steam only lets me type so many letters. Anyway, the point is, if you hadn't already got it, this game is a main course of amazing with a starter of hard and a side order of occasionally frustrating. Do yourself a favour and buy it.

This game is not so much a game as it is a test of twitch reflexes and micromanagement. While technically an RTS, it is very different from Starcraft, Red Alert, or any other game in the genre. You have no base and you cannot create units. So you are stuck with what you get. Therefore you resources in MoW are your limited supply of men.
This game is very very difficult. Even on easy, missions will take you many tries to beat. The learning curve is insanely steep - like Mt. Everest steep. To make matters worse, the tutorial like 5 minutes long and teaches you nothing about how to play the game. So you're left to figure how to play the game yourself by watching YouTube videos and reading online walkthroughs. After all the research, the controls will still bewilder you. There is no reliable way to get your troops to do what you want everytime. After much research and pratice you will still get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked repeatedly by the AI, since the missions are stacked against your favor. In many missions you basically just pray that your soldiers can survive the enemy's assault.
In spite of all this, the game is still fun in a maschostic kind of way(hurts so good?). But I truly suggest, that most casual gamers do NOT buy this game at ANY price - as it won't be fun for you. Only hardcore fans of WWII and RTS games should buy Men of War. Other reviews are funny and witty and make the game seem kind of cool. DO NOT TRUST THEM! They make the game seem much more approachable then it really is.

Moonstone Tavern is a combination of a city builder (or tavern in this case) and an ARPG, similar to Pokemon Mystery Dungeon type games, but in real time and focused on the development of the tavern, which then adds stat bonuses to your character and extra party members.  It has both a main quest line and repeatable quests of various difficulty that strengthen the main character in different ways.
Pros -
Lots of depth to developing the tavern
Enemies are fairly difficult to start
Marriage, familiar system, and hired heroes for a fairly large party (main character + 7 others that I know of)
Crafting system to make most gear, as well as food for the tavern and other things
Cons -
Heavy lag inside the tavern, less in combat but still enough to slow the game down and make fighting more jerky than it should be
While there are many different enemy sprites, there are apparently only two kinds of enemies (melee and ranged) with no real distinction between any of them; higher level enemies sometimes move and attack faster, making them very dangerous, but there's no inherent difference between a dragon and a blob of goo.
Bad follower AI, party members often get left behind or trapped inside enemies and unable to fight
Clunky UI, mouse works in some areas and not in others
A lot of terrain that looks like obstacles but isn't
This type of game is rare for RPGmaker.  It has a lot of bugs but a lot of potential.  The game is unique and the devs are active in responding to and fixing the issues, which is why I gave it an overall positive review.
Edit - this review was written in Mid-May 2016.  There's a good chance patches and updates may have resolved some of the issues listed here since the time of writing.

Imagine if an RPG met The Sims and they wanted to settle down and run a tavern, but didn't want to hang up their adventurer boots just yet. Enter Moonstone Tavern. The gameplay is basic: use your keyboard or mouse clicks to move your avatar around as they quest through friendly villages and deadly forests. You are given quests which help you gather materials to create better equipment and stats, but also ingredients to make meals for your tavern guests, or find a priest to help exorcise your haunted rooms. Fun extra are unlocked as you play, such as the arena where you can place bets, but also challenges like the dreaded tax collector!
Overall I am having a lot of fun with this game. The enemies are challenging but not impossible, there are a ton of quests and assignments so you're never unsure of what to do, and you have a "pet" (I say pet since my current one is a giant blob of goo!) companion that battles with you, and you can gather more with different abilities. There is a clock that gauges day from night so you may collect bills from your guests- I have never played a game before where the lighting in the game fades from light to dark as you play, to signify the sun setting/rising. This little added touch just adds another memorable experience.
The characters are cute, it's fun, and a good combination of RPG and Sims, I like Moonstone Tavern, and I'm excited to continue playing to unlock more!

Pinstripe started out as a passion project for Thomas Brush over 5 years ago, but thanks to some help from the YouTube gamer community and an army of donors on Kickstarter, it became a full-time job.  The game is finally out and, having played it, I have to say I'm so happy that I decided to back the game.
In Pinstripe, you play as Teddy - a preacher who's traveling with his little daughter, Bo.  A greasy antagonist - the titular Pinstripe - kidnaps your daughter and it's up to you to rescue her.  Armed with Bo's slingshot and a pocket full of memories and clues, you journey through actual Hell to save your child.
The art design of the game is beautiful, with Teddy's lithe silhouette evoking Tim Burton's Jack Skellington, and although the game isn't particularly gothic in style, the story and certain elements are certainly very reminiscent.  Most of the game's stages have you bounding about in the snow, fighting various foes, and also traversing dark, damp caves in search of more clues.  There are a number of puzzles scattered throughout the game that are woven seamlessly into the fabric of the story, making it feel highly personal to Teddy and, in turn, to you.  Although some paths and elements might be beyond you at the start, everything unfolds in time, and each new discovery is delightful.
The voice acting in the game is also exceptional - including the likes of Dan Avidan and Ross O'Donovan (of Game Grumps), Nathan Sharp (of NateWantstoBattle) and many more.  Mia Ciscon and Elizabeth Ollier also do incredible work as the adorable Bo and gleefully batty Mrs. Birdy, respectively.
In an industry that's started taking after Hollywood and produces almost nothing but too-expensive-to-fail AAA titles, it's just so refreshing to see such an original, heartfelt work.  This was a labor of love for Thomas and his belief in this project, his love for telling this tale, were easy to see in his Kickstarter videos and updates.  It's what convinced me to donate to the project and keep tabs on it all throughout development.  Although there are countless nightmare scenarios of Kickstarted games never being completed - or, in some cases, never even begun! - I have to say, I'm so glad that we were able to help Thomas complete the game.  I can't wait to see what other amazing stories he has to share!

Metro 2033 is a solid shooter with a good story.  It is mostly a shooter with few stealth elements.  The game objectives and mechanics are not well explained but the game play is flowing, logical and engaging.  I would recommend it to those looking for a good story shooter.
Metro 2033 is labeled as a horror survival stealth game.  It possesses elements of all of these types of games.  However at it's heart is none of these.  What it is, is a solid shooter that follows the main character on a quest to save his home from the "Dark Ones".  This may sound played-out or overdone, but Metro 2033 did it very well.  I know of relatively few games that are based on books and that maybe why it's story is better than most.  The game is complete and flowing from one objective to the next with a sense of purpose.  While much of the game is a corridor style shooter it feels far less mindless because of the goals and progression.
Metro 2033 has some horror elements but it is not what I would call a true horror game.  The horror seems to come most from the sounds which are very well done.  There seems to always be something scratching or walking behind you.  There are most certainly fast moving creatures that pop out of holes to freighten the player...but that just gets more annoying as time goes by.  I found that the simple technique of running into an area, find a corner and wait for the creature to jump out and attack me was the best way to beat most monsters.  A few shells would end the poor little guy and any damage received was normally slight.  If you ran around the level I'm sure the critters would be more scarey as they jump out of whatever hole they're hiding in.
Similarly the stealth portions are a let down.  The stealth is basically optional and some levels are just more fun to mow everyone down Rambo style.  I feel like this is manly due to the fact that I didn't understand the stealth cues until almost done with the game.  I either missed or forgot the portion of the game where the wrist-born tool that tells you about stealth and air is explained.
The game's survival elements are very well done and thought out.  Ammunition, items and weapons are limited.  The supply of gas mask filters add a sense of immersion and desperation that I found deeply rewarding when compared to ammo.  Conserving ammo is a matter of well placed shots and using shotguns when dealing with melee enemies.  But having to complete a level before you suffocate is a clever way to force action.  The desire to search for items is always balanced with survival.  Using ammo as currency is also interesting because as the game states...you are literally shooting money.
I didn't like the navigation/objective setup of the game.  I missed a few optional objectives because I was following the compass which only lead me to the main objective.  I found myself confused a few times trying to figure out what my next task was.  I would follow some NPC and eventually something would flash in the enviroment and I would accomplish the goal.  In one case...a trip to YouTube answered my question.  (In fairness I missed the conversation where the goal was explained)
Finally I didn't like the "moral point" system which was never explained but had a rather large bearing on the ending experienced by the player.  If you want to know more...google it.
Those 2 faults do not detract from a good solid, fun to play, engaging game.  It had enough atmospheric elements to be scarey but not at the expense of the action.  It had enough stealth (if you wanted to) that you could be sneaky, but also allowed for mass shooting.  It had a good story that moved the player along.  Metro 2033 is well worth the money.  I was a big fan of RAGE...until the ending...and I liked this game more from start to finish.  The story is not as good as Bioshock Infinite, but it's better overall as it flows better from start to finish.

FTL is hands down the only rogue-like with replayability that I enjoy. You obviously don't know me so I guess that isn't saying much to you though. The game has a similar feel to XCOM:enemy unknown in its strategy system. If you rush and don't think things through, bad things will happen. And you will REALLY feel it in the long run. Unlike XCOM, playthroughs are shorter and you will learn from each mistake. The UI is beautifully done, and nearly every strategy you can come up with is viable. And it better be, because this game is HARD. I haven't personally even come close to beating the game on anything above the easiest setting. Advanced addition was an incredible update that added more to the gameplay, races, weapons, interactions, soundtrack and metagame. Everything feels even more chaotic, as you truly feel like a captain of a starship navigating in a maze of alien forces coming after your♥♥♥♥♥ One wrong move and you're dead. One wrong move and it will cost you scrap that couldve gotten you that missle to pierce those shields you just didn't have the firepower to break through. One cheap out of repairing your health and you were one shot away from killing that drone and it kills you. One... you get the point. As stressful as it sounds, the one mistake costs you mechanics of the game give it incredible depth and replayability. Did I also mention that Advanced Edition can be turned off if you want to play the legacy version of the game? And oh yeah baby, this game has mods too. If you wanted a whole new campaign and an even bigger update than ADV edition was, Captains edition has you covered. If you just feel like adding a star destroyer as a playable ship, then whatever floats your boat.
In conclusion I'm not sure what else you could possibly ask for this title. The devs have gone above and beyond the standard, and though it likely won't happen, I would absolutely love another update here in 2016 or beyond. This may be an old title, but it's far from dead.

King Arthur's Gold is a multiplayer 2D sprite medieval combat game, like if Terraria and Chivalry had a baby. If you think you'd really like that, that's cool, but I'm personally not too crazy about it from the time I've spent on it and the observations of my friends who've played it more than I have. Caveat emptor applies pretty damn strongly here: the game is neat in conception, but not so much in execution. Unless you're willing to put up with
of the following, I would not recommend this game.
There are three classes: knights, archers and builders. Archers fire arrows, builders are in charge of managing (destructible) team fortifications and catapults to attack the enemy base with. Knights are the front-line class, and...they're kind of overpowered. I
say that lightly. It's entirely possible for a skilled knight to continually decimate a good portion of your team. That's not game-sinking by itself, but it's also entirely possible for said skilled knight(s) to bomb-jump right over your castle and start camping your spawn. By the time they finally die, they've probably earned enough gold from killing your team to buy a good number of base-destroying bombs, and their team's builders have had leeway to set up multiple catapults.
KAG's learning curve is fairly steep, even for me, but that wouldn't be as much of an issue if knights were weaker, and more importantly if the game's community was large and vibrant. It's not. It's
small and pretty toxic, even for a niche competitive game. This is a problem that
also suffers from, but at least that game is relatively easier to understand and very engaging at times.
This game is also rather buggy, but I consider that a minor issue compared to the others I've talked about here. Really, it's more of a combination of all these things that prevent KAG from reaching greatness. At any rate, I hope you are now an informed customer and will decide wisely.

Company of Heroes 2 (CoH2) is a great multiplayer and coop game with mod support. It also offers  good single player campaign(s via DLC) and missions.
The game not just feels like a Dawn of War 2 (DoW2) set up @WW2. The new visuals are outstanding and the new gameplay mechanics like inventory pickups for infantry or the whole view simulation system of your units  are also great. First I missed the hero units from DoW2, but after playing some rounds I overthrow that feeling very fast and get used to the "Generals" very fast.
You will get a lot for your money if you get the Master Collection here or at any retail store. It is containing 3 more factions, 3 more mission packs for the and whole new American campaign with a different kind of mission mechanics.
CAMPAIGNs and Scenario Missions (Theatre of War):
============================================
For the ones, who like to play singple player missions. The main game offers a single player campaign set at the eastern front. You play as the Red Army and fight the Germans back from Moscow 41 to Berlin 45. It is just a introduction to the main game mechanics when playing online as the Red Army. The story is entertaining, has ingame cutscenes but is not that great. The missions are set in a fixed order.
The second campaign is a standalone game, called Ardennes Assault. Here you play as the Americans. It is set in the ardennes with a system, that allows you to select missions from a map, similar to the system Relic introduce in Dawn of War - Dark Crusade. This means, the missions take place on random maps and the objetives are also randomly generated. In addition to this you also got and troop leveling system. So keep an eye on them, cuz the game is using just a single slot to save your progression ;)
Unfortunately by September 2016 there is no campaign for the Brits or both German factions. Not even as scenario missions. But maybe Relic pays attention to my cries and publishes :D Cuz this is the only feature I am mission from CoH1!
The scenarios, you can play solo at the "Theatre of War", are single missions. Their objectives are static. But the objective locations are set ramdomly at the map. There is no fixed order to fullfil them.
Theatre of War and Scenarios are NOT MODABLE!
Coop, PvP and Scenario Missions (Theatre of War):
============================================
The multiplayer game mode "Victory Points" rocks. Great to play and offering intense fightings from 1vs1 to 4vs4 matches. Feels like the conquest mode from the Battlefield franchise, cuz it's almost the same concept. Capture some points and watch the tickets going to zero until you win... or like in most of the first attempts: lose :D
You also have to take care of ressources manpower, fuel and ammunition, which are represented by different points at the map.
There is also another game mode called "Extermination" where you have to kill your enemy to win. Feels like the usual RTS game mode build up, attack, defend connected to hold the ressource points at the map.
If you can't get ennough, the modes can be extended by the workshop. Dont like the unit count and wanna increase your max population, just pick up the corresponding mod...
You also got dozens of scenario missions, which are set at the eastern front. Some of them are ment to be played as solo missions, but a lot of them are available as coop missions.
The above mentioned "Theatre of War" mode also offers a lot of coop missions, you can play with your friends. They are entertaining, but I liked the competitive mode more.
Now the main aspect, why I like this game, its
GAME MECHANICS AND ENGINE:
============================================
+ infantry is organized in squads, except some special units like snipers and captains
+ cover and suppresion system influencing your unit behaviour (e.g. infantry cant move or conquer capture points when suppressed)
+ flanking your enemies gives you advantages, especially when it comes to battle enemy vehicles - hit them at the back or side to increase the damage
+ every unit has a counter, especially infantry dislikes fire very much
+ units gain experience and should be kept alive (by retreating them just in case)
+ every unit has one or more abilities, from supporting ones like healing infantry to defensive ones like putting smoke screens for cover and offensive ones like the use of special ammo
+ abilities can be unlocked by gaining experience levels
+ stealth units like snipers, which can be ordered to cease fire in order to not be detected
+ destroyable and dynamic environment; houses, bridges, walls, even trees can be destroyed or burned down, to destroy cover; if vehciles are destroyed, they offer your infantry a new cover position
+ weather and environment influence your unit behaviour like movement speedand their line of sight
+ winter scenarios offer snow storms, which forces most of your infantry to stay at houses, vehicles or close to fire places (which can be build)
+ winter maps and snow storms offer you the opportunity to pass frozen waters - but consider your units cannot swim in case your enemies wanna do "Explosive Ice Fishing"
+ all mechanics can also be extended by mods, which change the game experience. Even Relic released some extension since the release like special abilites or weapons
+ by September 2016 you got 5 different factions, all differ from each other concerning their units and tactics, you have to use
+ commanders influence your special abillites and usable tactics e.g. artillery or airstrike support
+ special unit boosters can be unlocked by playing the game and gaining new ranks e.g. better precision for your squads
+ great visuals, units, environments and effects have a great detail level
+ soundeffects and musics are awesome, when you zoom in and a Tiger 2 fires its main gun, it feels like you gotta visit your otologist the next day when playing with headset; playing with your speakers will make your whole environment happy :D
Of course the game has its CONs like every product
============================================
Don't buy this game if
- you like massive battles with more than 100 units in your army e.g. Supreme Commander
- you like games with hero units, which gain experience to get stronger
- you dislike AI misbehaviour e.g. navigation and pathing - the main problem of almost any RTS game
- you liked the differentiation in axis and allies in your teams; here you can mix up your teams or play e.g. axis vs. axis. This is some kinda crazy
- you dislike ingame shops - a lot of commanders and units upgrades can only be purchased there - wth?! :O
and last but not least:
- IF you want to see NORTHERN AFRICA or EASTERN ASIA as WW2 scenarios in this great gameplay concept. First one is what I'm waiting for; so Relic do something PLS!!

Basically a rogue-like with a procrastination prevention method.  The Darkness in the game keeps you continually advancing to the right of screen.  Otherwise you die.  This is a consistent play mechanic.  Otherwise the levels, or "dimensions" are randomly assigned from a large specifically coded database, and the game saves your last 2 recent ones.  So, if you played a dimension you really liked, you can come back to it.  If the next random one generates a virtually impassable mountain range, you can go back to the first one.  I'd recommend keeping a list of the favourable dimensions.
You're given a choice of a variety of classes, with more unlockable as you play, with little restriction on equipment.  Nevertheless, some classes are geared to more specific weapons and styles of play than others.  You can also unlock perks that help out in general, and can give that bit of a boost to a class that may otherwise lie outside your usual play style.  You can also save items and equipment to your Dimension Vault to take between playthroughs, but I haven't found anything awesome enough yet to make it worth finding out how to retrieve it.
And fear not, those on lunch breaks, there is a save feature.  It does require either buying a Save Crystal item, or finding an NPC who will save your game.  But if you've invested time on especially the higher difficulties, you can come back to a game you may not have had time to finish in one sitting.
As far as price and gameplay value go, it gets a thumbs up from me.

Personally I do enjoy this game and while this game certainly does have its ups and downs, I am not here to praise or criticize this game. I am here to offer a phenomenal 4 Cheese Ravioli recipe!
Here are the ingredients you will need!
Ravioli Dough: 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 pinch salt, 1 teaspoon olive oil, 2 eggs, 1 1/2 tablespoons water.
Ravioli Filling: 1 (8 ounce) container ricotta cheese, 1 (4 ounce) package cream cheese, softened, 1/2 cup shredded mozzarella cheese, 1/2 cup provolone cheese, shredded, 1 egg, 1 1/2 teaspoons dried parsley.
Pesto-Alfredo Cream Sauce: 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 cloves garlic, crushed, 3 tablespoons prepared basil pesto sauce, 2 cups heavy cream, 1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese, 1 (24 ounce) jar marinara sauce.
1. Mound the flour and salt together on a work surface and form a well. Beat the teaspoon of olive oil, 2 eggs, and water in a bowl. Pour half the egg mixture into the well. Begin mixing the egg with the flour with one hand; use your other hand to keep the flour mound steady. Add the remaining egg mixture and knead to form a dough.
2. Knead the dough until smooth, 8 to 10 minutes; add more flour if the dough is too sticky. Form the dough into a ball and wrap tightly with plastic. Refrigerate for 1 hour.
3. While the dough is resting, prepare the ravioli filling. Combine the ricotta cheese, cream cheese, mozzarella cheese, provolone cheese, egg, and parsley and mix well. Set the filling aside.
4. Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add the crushed garlic and pesto sauce and cook for one minute. Pour in the heavy cream, raise the heat to high, and bring the sauce to a boil. Reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the Parmesan cheese and stir until the cheese melts. Remove the pan from the heat and keep warm.
5. Meanwhile, in a separate saucepan, warm the marinara sauce over medium-low heat.
6. Preheat an oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C). Beat the egg with the tablespoon of water to make the egg wash.
7. Roll out the pasta dough into thin sheets no thicker than a nickel. To assemble the ravioli, brush the egg wash over a sheet of pasta. Drop the filling mixture on the dough by teaspoonfuls about one inch apart. Cover the filling with the top sheet of pasta, pressing out the air from around each portion of filling. Press firmly around the filling to seal. Cut into individual ravioli with a knife or pizza cutter. Seal the edges.
8. Fill a large pot with lightly salted water and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Stir in the ravioli, and return to a boil. Cook uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the ravioli float to the top and the filling is hot, 4 to 8 minutes. Drain well.
9. Grease a baking sheet. Place the cooked ravioli on the sheet pan and bake in the preheated oven until brown, about 4 minutes.
10. To serve the ravioli, divide them among four warmed serving bowls. Drizzle the marinara sauce over the ravioli and then top with the cream sauce.

Having beaten this game once, I feel as if I definitely got my money's worth.  One Way Heroes takes the concept of a roguelike, and twists it here and to create an enjoyable end product that reminded me of 30 Second Hero and Desktop Dungeons.
In the beginning, the jrpg graphics threw me off slightly, as did the premise of a scrolling field of darkness.  The text-based screams of people being enveloped was a nice touch that may both cause cringing as well as a chuckle. After my first death, having made a decent run, I was suprised to see an entire system in which I could not only store items I had acquired, but also purchase new ablities for the next run, as well as extra storage space for my 'dimensional chest'.  Although the procedurally generated structures becoming familiar after a time, the randomness of both the wares of merchants and the contents of containers keeps things fresh, not to mention the occasional mob with a modifier on them, from cheap merchants that can rip you off, to ancient monsters that drop a rare item.
The prices for many items may be steep at times, but a trick I've found is to bring high-priced items like the fox tail into your next playthrough with the dimensional chest, making your next endeavor a bit more comfortable upon reaching a merchant.  Perhaps you might want to bring in a favored weapon, perhaps one with multiple upgrades?  With the scrolls of swordplay and armoring, you can upgrade equipment, and although they have durability, with luck you can grab a repair item to keep that overpowered sword nice and sharp.
The mechanics are complex, but simple enough to pick up on.  You have an hp bar, energy bar, and hunger bar.  The hunger bar continuosly goes down, and you use energy for many of the special abilities.  With hunger being directly tied to your ability to regenerate, similar to minecraft, food becomes a valuable resource, and since potions don't fill hunger, even the slightest morsel becomes important.  Luckily, food is still not incredibly hard to find, and you even recieve some at the beginning, so although you may be led by your stomach, you won't always feel compelled to make mad dashes for food.
A weight limit means you need to make tough choices between grabbing a strong armor or weapon (which by rule of thumb weigh more the better they are) or carrying more of the much needed potions.  If you feel a huge need for a higher weight limit, simply change your character's starting buffs and abilities.
Energy is used for swimming, climbing mountains, and using abilities, paricularly as the force user, who spams the one damage spell in the game with imputiny.  You will often find yourself conserving this, as without energy, ever expidenture eats your own health.  In terms of climbing and swimming, these are desprate measures taken when there is nowhere else to go, and if possible, always find another way.
With a rolling screen at your back, this sidescroller of a rpg may make you cry with frustration as you fail to escape due to a wall. Luckily, the developers added a skill to help you called awakening.  With a cry of "Time, Stop!" you can stop the movement ofeverything for three turns, plus an attack boost.  Although you have limited uses, this can be used to survive almost any encounter, from freezing bandits in place so you can thin numbers without fear of being triple-teamed, or gaining enough time to destroy the afformented wall with your sword and escape the dungeon.
Besides this, each class is varied and unlockable modifiers and classes are accessible, and in terms of classes, unlockable even if you don't fufill their requirement if you use the points gained on your runs.
Of all the things this game reminds me of, the frantic escape reminds me of cutesy 30 second hero, where you get limited time to defeat a level, causing a similar amount of frantic despair as the end of your attempt approaches and Desktop Dungeons, which also can drive you crazy when a forgotten option causes death, although the forgiving mechanics make this game far more accesible, even with both running off a mechanic of unlocking.
This and many more intricities await in this game, and I only have two cons.
1: There could be more force abilities and weapons(especially force abilites), hopefully coming later
2: More randomized structures and new mechanics would be cool, but not a huge deal for a game of this size and price
Overall, I'd say this fun, fast-paced experience was worth playing.

But there's a pattern to everything.  As of this review, all you have to do is remember six dates:  the 5th, 15th, and 25th then the 6th 16th and the 26th. The second set of dates is when the true archvillain of the game shows up, the tax collector.  Seriously?  What tax collector shows up that many times in a single month?  He's pocketin most of your harrd earned cash, no doubt.  But, if you stockpile meals with the cook, open rooms slowly, you can easily deal with these obviously over TRITE obstacles.  Just kill/gather enough to make up the differece and soon you'll be able to wander/kill/gather/kill to your herat's delight.  And as a bonus, please take this into consideration:  At 0600 (the start of the new day with the management screen popping up)  everything resets.  So, if you're in, let's say, a DRAGON HORDE MISSION, and you've cleared everything out  and it's close to 0600, just wait there until afterwards and watch every chest close and refill with goodies. From the title, you can probably guess what you might be engaged with doing in a game such as this, and that's running a tavern in a fantasy setting; one that seems to be rather enjoyable, even with my little time in the game.
The game opens up with having you teleport to this epic, fantasy land, where you're there to claim your inheritance from an aunt; an aunt who just seemed to of owned a tavern and has left it in their will for you. After a few minutes in, you'll discover that the tavern is understaffed and dilapidated, and requires your hard work to return it to its former glory.
Part of the game involves you searching around the rather giant map, looking for ingredients to help feed your guests, as well as repair the tavern itself. Unfortunately, in "RPG-land", there's no such thing as safe, hence why there are monsters for you to battle all over the place. Thankfully, you won't be doing it alone, as the game has a pet system employed to help you protect yourself. This system isn't the type of thing that simply got shoehorned in, as in actual fact there are 50 familiars (pets) for you to take along with you and help train up.
Aesthetically, the game may disappoint some people with the fact that it is an RPG-maker game, but thankfully the developer themselves have opted to implement their own art assets for the game. Ultimately, this has only increased the enjoyment of the game, especially when you spend some time searching around the dilapidated areas in the game.
Overall, Moonstone Tavern does a number of things different from your conventional video game, and breathes a little extra life and hope to the RPG-maker engine, an engine that tends to be linked with laziness, but with this title it makes sure to stay well away from such a feeling!

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Moonstone Tavern is the latest game from Michael Flynn, the developer of other great and original RPG Maker games: Apocalypse Hotel, Star-BOX, and Fortune's Tavern: the Fantasy Tavern Simulator.
I have all of Flynn's other games, lacking only a couple of DLC, and I immediately added this one to my wishlist when I saw it on Steam. So bear in mind that I'm a bit of a fan; Flynn's games have been the most enjoyable RPGMaker games that I've played.
Moonstone Tavern plays a lot like Apocalypse Hotel, but in a fantasy rather than a zombie-infested, post-apocalyptic setting. You play a very green adventurer who inherits Moonstone Tavern from you aunt, whom you've never met. Arriving at the tavern through a portal, you are greeted by your aunt's talking cat, who guides you around the tavern and grounds and introduces you to the basics of the game.
If you've played Apocalypse Hotel then you'll be familiar with the gameplay of Moonstone Tavern as well: alternately manage and improve your tavern, and go out on adventures in search of loot and resources to use on the next round of tavern improvements.
Graphics - Moonstone Tavern is a RPGMaker game, so the graphics are as you'd expect for this engine: generally quite nice low-res graphics, in this case with a fantasy theme. The tavern itself and all of the maps I've seen so far are well designed and nicely laid out.
There have been a number of reports of poor graphics performance, and my laptop has these issues when playing Apocalypse Hotel as well, which I put down to issues with the RPGMaker engine on this hardware. However, I've not run into the same problems with Moonstone Tavern, which is a welcome surprise. The developer has been working with the community to try to identify and resolve these issues, in any case.
Sound - Sound isn't the best. The cancel sound (when pressing escape to close a menu) in particular is grating and too loud, but most of the other sound effects are okay. The music is quite nice, but seems a bit too electronic for the setting; I'd expect some nice classical flutes, rather than the electro vibe I get at the moment.
Gameplay - When you start a new game you get to choose the sprite you'll control for the game, as well as the generic 'class' of your character, based on his or her ability with magic, swords, and guns.
Gameplay is extremely similar to Apocalypse Hotel, but in a fantasy setting. In your 'safe zone' -- the tavern -- you wander around keeping track of stats, talking to guests, and tending to the running of the hotel. You then venture out of the safe zone into the surrounding areas, killing creatures that respawn each time you enter the map and collecting the loot you find, which is hopefully what you want to further your tavern enhancements.
It's a formula that works well and keeps you playing for longer than you mean to, with that "just a little more" feeling dragging you on to the next map, to complete the next quest, or to get enough silver to upgrade the next room. Unfortunately it doesn't include Steam Achievements, which would make this striving feel a bit more worthwhile.
Personally, I've been running into the same problem I had with Apocalypse Hotel, although not to quite the same degree: I keep running out of ammo and other necessary resources. I'm not sure if it's intended to be this way, or if I haven't quite got the hang of it yet, but each time I've played I've fairly quickly exhausted my ammo supplies, relegating me to melee combat whenever I venture out in search of food or other supplies. And I also keep finding myself changing map without intending to.
Pros:
+ A good sense of humour
+ Tried and true formula, polished from Apocalypse Hotel
+ Lots to do! Moonstone Tavern will keep you busy for a long time
+ Responsible and responsive developer, with a proven history on Steam
+ Trading cards
Cons:
- It could use a copy editor: "Choose the character which you'd like play as."
- The cancel sound (pressing escape from a menu screen) is awful
- Hard to get started; not enough ammo, and basic resources are expensive, although the gift of silver near the start helps significantly
- It's sometimes hard to tell when a dead-end pathway on a map is just a dead end, or whether it will lead to another map
- No achievements
I really like Moonstone Tavern. It's a nice fantasy rework of Apocalypse Hotel and although it's not quite as original anymore, it's still a very good game.
The lack of Steam achievements brings it down a little, as do the numerous errors in the writing, but the cat-led tutorial works well and there's plenty to do once you get the hang of how the game works.

There’s some special charm all indie games have, and this one is no different! It’s made as a classical RPG, but with some cute new features and more advanced gameplay. Fans of the RPG genre will find all the familiar features here like loads of quests, loot, the search for different items and a variety of management tasks you’ll have to complete to move through the game. Most of the problem-solving will concern you precious Tavern, which to be fair is pretty beaten up, so you’ll have a lot of things to fix, build and many people to hire. One of the cool features is the ability to change the class of your character after you’ve created him and played for some time. You can change your gaming style and complete more quests this way.
You’ll get to meet and interact with cool characters like elves, funny gnomes, brutal orcs and many others. You can also find, collect and even breed your own pets that sometimes, but not always, come with some useful abilities. In any case, it’s always interesting to see what hatches out of those eggs you find. There’s also an Arena – an interesting way to earn money without doing anything. You don’t need to fight, just place bets and see who wins!
I’m having fun playing the game, it’s witty and has nice graphics. Recommend!

To accurately review this allow me to tell you what the game has and what the game doesn't.
Basically the game provides you a vareity of spaceships each with a particular strategic role. In a team based slaughterfest, you pilot your chosen ship and try to bring down the enemy fleet. The graphics are aesthetically pleasing and the SFX is very authentic, quite becoming of an ideal sci-fi game.
Now that I've pointed out what makes this game look great to take for a test drive, here's where my review looks under the hood and points out what areas need work. First and foremost, it is lacking a tutorial. To know what the controls are, you have to go through the options and then pretty much jot down all the keyboard controls on a notepad and keep it near by for reference as you learn the game through a tedious trial and error process.Secondly, the controls aren't exactly uniform for all the ships either: yes, in terms of mobility they are, but each ship has different weapons, meaning different triggers. Thirdly, the game doesn't have a notification system to let you know when your team is biting the dust or when the enemy is. Quite often I came to the horrific surprise of being this lone bomber against a fleet of 3 large ships with fighters still buzzing around. This ties in to the fourth issue: No communication medium at all. There is no way to plan and strategize with your team. Neither is there a way to call for help.
Now I bet you are wondering, "you just wrote a lengthy parapgraph ripping this game apart for what its missing; how can you still reccomend it?" Simple: I'm aware that the game is still being worked on and I'm willing to bet that all these problems I listed are going to be resolved after a few patches and updates. Who knows: maybe the team behind this is going to go a step further and add in a bunch of stuff (like customization) and completely make this review an ancient record of the game's infancy. I'm an optimist about this game in all respects because I can see it has promise. Overall its actually an original idea: a simple teambased space naval combat game. Just give it a try and you'll see what I mean

Pinstripe's the game that takes you to Hell, but is so charming you don't want to leave.
The atmosphere is what makes the game for me. From Mr. Pinstripe to Mr. Dicky, the characters were all top notch. The puzzles weren't hard, but were a lot of fun. These reasons were enough for me to validate my purchase, but there are a few cons.
To start the games kinda short. I finished in 3.5 hours and from what I've seen new game plus doesn't add a ton of content. The combat was pretty boring. The best way to describe Pinstripe is quality over quantity. But I do recommend you try the game if you are into atmospheric puzzle games.

This was a fantastic game. I've heard complaints about grinding, I assume for the purchase costing 300 frozen drops, but the game teaches you and guides you based on what you learn without holding your hand along the way. It's a beautiful game with a very intuitive way of showing the player what to do. And as I finished the game, I realized there was clearly more to explore, so I look forward to unlocking the secrets of Pinstripe.
The story begins to make sense if you truly take time to play, and pick up the clues. One can easily just rush through and ignore the information, but if you look at what's there, you see the story of the ex-minister, how he died, what happened to him and his daughter, and his wife long ago. I won't give things away, but WHO Pinstripe really is doesn't matter as much as other things you learn along the way. Take your time, smell the roses.

Beautifully haunting, wonderfully whimsical, and deeply enjoyable. Pinstripe is a game that will take you into the macabre, pull at your strings, and drag you into Hell; yet, it also brings a smile to your face as you submerse yourself into beautiful visuals, fantastic game play, amusing interactions, and a terrific soundtrack. Never has anything hellish been so stunning.
Utilizing a witty and often humorous script, the voice acting helps bring to life the dark characters of the game (plus your dog). The story progresses nicely. Your trusty, canine companion will help guide you along the way. The controls are simple, but fluid. The puzzles and interactions are difficult enough to make the game an amusing challenge, but not make you feel like you are in a literal hell. The music is often lighter than the visuals, but they are actually pair perfectly. The combination makes for a game that can actually be relaxing and a pleasure to play. (You should consider getting the soundtrack.)

I love free things.  This is especially true for games on steam that pay tribute to one of my favorite genres.  You Have To Win The Game is a free game and rightly so.  Its not bad but it is quite bland.  It offers a fun little bite-sized adventure but not much else.  Sit down, take about an hour to play through it, then move on and forget about it.
You Have To Win The Game is pretty straight-forward Metroid clone.  You run around from one screen to the next seeking new abilities and switches needed to access more areas.  Sadly, there is no map feature and I often found myself running around like a chicken with my head cut off trying to find out where I could proceed next.  Thankfully, after a half-hour or so the layout becomes quite familiar and its begins to get easier to memorize how to get around.  Once you obtain a new ability you'll already have been by several areas where it can be utilized.
The visuals and sound effects are about as retro as they come.  The backgrounds are pure-black with just a couple specks of light while the foregrounds are often purple with occasionally with a bit of green or white thrown in.  There really isn't much to see.  The sound design is just as bland.  All you hear is your characters beeps every time you jump.  At least the "boss" enemies that come before the power-ups give you some rhythmic beeps for variety.  Did I mention the soundtrack?  Oh wait, there is none.
What this game lacks in aesthetics it makes up for in level design.  This game offers a increasing challenging hurdles but it never feels like its asking for too much.  Learning to navigate the map as you acquire access to new areas is quite rewarding.  The game offers several unique obstacles never repeating the same idea twice.  The learning curve may be fairly steep but it seems to be a pretty smooth.
I enjoyed playing this game despite its short-comings.  The fun gameplay manages to trump the out-dated aesthetics.  I will say however that my experience was nearly ruined in by the ending.  It would appear that as you played you where supposed to find a magic word that you are prompted to enter at the end of the game.  So when I finished without this password it simply reset the game.  It was a very unsatisfying conclusion after all the work but what should I expect at this point.  This is a free download, take it or leave it.

I play FTL when I want to relax and focus on nothing else. The art stye and setting are perfectly fitting for your space quest. You can play it at your own pace, and on easy mode is usually doesn't get too stressful. But if you let it FTL has the ability to overwhelm you and make you panic, and that is when the game is at its best. If you are unprepared you'll come across no-win senarios where you need to deal with a fire running through the ship, crew members suffocating, systems needing repair, missiles and drones bombarding your ship, and no way to comprehend what to do next. And that is before you play with the free expansion that allows you so many more ways to suffer. But with practice and time you'll be able to understand how to overcome the miriad ways your opponents make you suffer and turn it back on them. Burn them, shoot them, control them, invade them, incapacitate them, kill them one by one. Or offer peace and move on to more pressing matters like saving the galaxy from an all-consuming miasma of rebels.
As a PS, I really wish FTL had a multiplayer mode that allowed you to play against other people.

The Bad

- Recycled content
Saints Row IV goes a little too far in powering us up, but it still knows how to show us a good chaotic time.

I just started playing and I’m already addicted to this game.

While obviously an indie game, Moonstone Tavern shines as a very respectable RPG by any standard.
---
Things I liked:
One of the most  pleasantly surprising things about the game is its expanse. The game is HUGE, and has a large, explorable world that you don't often see in indie games.
I like the old school graphics and gameplay - they are reminiscent of old TurboGrafx RPGs like Dungeon Explorer
The combination of a simulator/management type game and a quest-based RPG is genius, and this game pulls it off well.
Many RPGs these days hold your hand through the entire game, with quest markers, etc. - Moonstone does not, and that is a good thing. I like the challenge of actually reading the dialogue in order to figure out where to go next.
There is a fully featured pet system - neat!
When a day ends, a screen appears saying "Day Over" - and you continue playing where you are. I really like this, as I generally find it annoying when games have you respawn in your bed at the beginning of a new day.
---
Some minor suggestions:
There are a few issues with movement/controls - they just require a bit more polishing
I would suggest that items like coins be automatically picked up when walked over, instead of requiring a button press.
Ability to move during dialogue would be nice, but not a big problem.
---
Overall, despite a few issues, Moonstone Tavern is a very good game.

The only thing I would say is, I wish they'd combine the great maps and interesting gameplay with some kind of story and/or more unlockables or goals. To me, this game is a model of the potential unlocked by games like League of Legends or Binding of Isaac, where there is always a reason to try your best during the game, and to be satisfied with losing.
The only thing designers need to do is combine this perpetual effort by its players with some kind of story that works despite the seeming interchangability of the maps.
Recommend this game to a RPG roguelike fans who are slightly on the hardcore side.

Company of Heroes 2 (CoH2) is a great multiplayer and coop game with mod support. It also offers  good single player campaign(s via DLC) and missions.
The game not just feels like a Dawn of War 2 (DoW2) set up @WW2. The new visuals are outstanding and the new gameplay mechanics like inventory pickups for infantry or the whole view simulation system of your units  are also great. First I missed the hero units from DoW2, but after playing some rounds I overthrow that feeling very fast and get used to the "Generals" very fast.
You will get a lot for your money if you get the Master Collection here or at any retail store. It is containing 3 more factions, 3 more mission packs for the and whole new American campaign with a different kind of mission mechanics.
CAMPAIGNs and Scenario Missions (Theatre of War):
============================================
For the ones, who like to play singple player missions. The main game offers a single player campaign set at the eastern front. You play as the Red Army and fight the Germans back from Moscow 41 to Berlin 45. It is just a introduction to the main game mechanics when playing online as the Red Army. The story is entertaining, has ingame cutscenes but is not that great. The missions are set in a fixed order.
The second campaign is a standalone game, called Ardennes Assault. Here you play as the Americans. It is set in the ardennes with a system, that allows you to select missions from a map, similar to the system Relic introduce in Dawn of War - Dark Crusade. This means, the missions take place on random maps and the objetives are also randomly generated. In addition to this you also got and troop leveling system. So keep an eye on them, cuz the game is using just a single slot to save your progression ;)
Unfortunately by September 2016 there is no campaign for the Brits or both German factions. Not even as scenario missions. But maybe Relic pays attention to my cries and publishes :D Cuz this is the only feature I am mission from CoH1!
The scenarios, you can play solo at the "Theatre of War", are single missions. Their objectives are static. But the objective locations are set ramdomly at the map. There is no fixed order to fullfil them.
Theatre of War and Scenarios are NOT MODABLE!
Coop, PvP and Scenario Missions (Theatre of War):
============================================
The multiplayer game mode "Victory Points" rocks. Great to play and offering intense fightings from 1vs1 to 4vs4 matches. Feels like the conquest mode from the Battlefield franchise, cuz it's almost the same concept. Capture some points and watch the tickets going to zero until you win... or like in most of the first attempts: lose :D
You also have to take care of ressources manpower, fuel and ammunition, which are represented by different points at the map.
There is also another game mode called "Extermination" where you have to kill your enemy to win. Feels like the usual RTS game mode build up, attack, defend connected to hold the ressource points at the map.
If you can't get ennough, the modes can be extended by the workshop. Dont like the unit count and wanna increase your max population, just pick up the corresponding mod...
You also got dozens of scenario missions, which are set at the eastern front. Some of them are ment to be played as solo missions, but a lot of them are available as coop missions.
The above mentioned "Theatre of War" mode also offers a lot of coop missions, you can play with your friends. They are entertaining, but I liked the competitive mode more.
Now the main aspect, why I like this game, its
GAME MECHANICS AND ENGINE:
============================================
+ infantry is organized in squads, except some special units like snipers and captains
+ cover and suppresion system influencing your unit behaviour (e.g. infantry cant move or conquer capture points when suppressed)
+ flanking your enemies gives you advantages, especially when it comes to battle enemy vehicles - hit them at the back or side to increase the damage
+ every unit has a counter, especially infantry dislikes fire very much
+ units gain experience and should be kept alive (by retreating them just in case)
+ every unit has one or more abilities, from supporting ones like healing infantry to defensive ones like putting smoke screens for cover and offensive ones like the use of special ammo
+ abilities can be unlocked by gaining experience levels
+ stealth units like snipers, which can be ordered to cease fire in order to not be detected
+ destroyable and dynamic environment; houses, bridges, walls, even trees can be destroyed or burned down, to destroy cover; if vehciles are destroyed, they offer your infantry a new cover position
+ weather and environment influence your unit behaviour like movement speedand their line of sight
+ winter scenarios offer snow storms, which forces most of your infantry to stay at houses, vehicles or close to fire places (which can be build)
+ winter maps and snow storms offer you the opportunity to pass frozen waters - but consider your units cannot swim in case your enemies wanna do "Explosive Ice Fishing"
+ all mechanics can also be extended by mods, which change the game experience. Even Relic released some extension since the release like special abilites or weapons
+ by September 2016 you got 5 different factions, all differ from each other concerning their units and tactics, you have to use
+ commanders influence your special abillites and usable tactics e.g. artillery or airstrike support
+ special unit boosters can be unlocked by playing the game and gaining new ranks e.g. better precision for your squads
+ great visuals, units, environments and effects have a great detail level
+ soundeffects and musics are awesome, when you zoom in and a Tiger 2 fires its main gun, it feels like you gotta visit your otologist the next day when playing with headset; playing with your speakers will make your whole environment happy :D
Of course the game has its CONs like every product
============================================
Don't buy this game if
- you like massive battles with more than 100 units in your army e.g. Supreme Commander
- you like games with hero units, which gain experience to get stronger
- you dislike AI misbehaviour e.g. navigation and pathing - the main problem of almost any RTS game
- you liked the differentiation in axis and allies in your teams; here you can mix up your teams or play e.g. axis vs. axis. This is some kinda crazy
- you dislike ingame shops - a lot of commanders and units upgrades can only be purchased there - wth?! :O
and last but not least:
- IF you want to see NORTHERN AFRICA or EASTERN ASIA as WW2 scenarios in this great gameplay concept. First one is what I'm waiting for; so Relic do something PLS!!

To be honest, the game isn't as bad as it seems. It's really improved, and here is my summary of what the game is like:
Characters
Each character in Genesis has an indestructible spirit, which passes from one body to the next after death. With that spirit, players have many paths to choose from, and can play as race or beast in any one lifetime.
Alignments
There are eight alignments in Genesis divided into two sides: four are aligned with order and four with chaos. Each alignment is ruled by a god that is associated with certain properties.
Races
There are a total of 64 humanoid races in Genesis, eight for each alignment based on size and abilities. Any player can also be a beast instead of a humanoid, taking on a radically different approach to the game.
Classes
There are a total of 32 humanoid classes in Genesis, four for each alignment based on each of the four character stats: Strength, Agility, Intelligence, and Discipline.
Professions
Characters can be one any number of professions in Genesis, and change between them at any time. They work with various resources to create items and buildings.
Political Status
Political power is also an option for those that want it. There are four levels of political status for each alignment, as well as eight military ranks.

What a game!
FTL is a lot of fun.  If you like space adventures with several alien races, a game where you can choose a crew made up of these different aliens, purchase upgrades, explore strange, new worlds, boldly go where no one has gone before, etc, FTL is a great game for you.  Kind of similar to games like Star Control.  Lots of options.  Tons of weapons and other interesting pieces of equipment to familiarize yourself with.  You'll probably play for hundred hours, if the game can get a hold of you.
Oh--but I've gone way ahead of myself.  Because FTL can be absolutely awful to you, time after time after time after time.  It's all dependent on the random number generator.  Even if you're the most skilled player ever, you'll pretty much need to get used to dying, a lot.
Basically, the premise is that you're a ship owned by the Federation, and the rebels--who are apparently the bad guys for about the first time in the history of media (except Star Trek's Maquis, which the rebels are perhaps based on)--are chasing you down, attempting to destroy your ship before you can get back to your base.  You travel through eight sectors in the process, and each sector has around ~20-30 star systems you can go to.  I don't think you'll manage to make it to every start system in a sector even once, but you should try to reach every star system you can, to collect all the scrap resources and weapons and equipment and crew members you possibly can.  Why?
Because the the rebels are never far behind--in that sense, FTL is a time management game.  Should I go to that store right next to me and try to get repairs, since I have barely any health?  Or should I skip the store, go that other nearby system, hope I can pick up some nice equipment or scrap WITHOUT DYING, and then hope I can make it to the store in time to get the repairs, without the enemy catching up with me?  These kinds of decisions grace almost every move you make in FTL.  You're always making tradeoffs.  And that's what makes it so much fun.  But especially early on, you really have to figure out exactly what to do, or else you'll almost certainly die.  The game can be unforgiving early on, and you'll end up having to restart frequently, as you die over and over and over.  Usually if you make it to the mid-game, with at least 3 shields, around 5 crew members and two or three decent weapons, you'll have a pretty good chance to reach the end of the game.
Where your reward will almost certainly be decimation by the extremely powerful rebel boss--unless you know exactly what you're doing, AND have all the right equipment, crew, etc for the job.
Fun.  Unforgiving.  A blast.  Incredibly frustrating.  Lots of planets, lots of adventure.  Lots of unlockable secrets, of which I've only managed to get maybe half myself.  Not too flashy or gimmicky, rather barebones graphics.  That's FTL.

Really wanted to like the game, but the platforming and grappling hook is just way too frustrating. It doesn't seem to follow it's own internal logic for when you can grapple to something and when you can't. After trying a platforming section with spinning windmills about 50 times, I still had no idea why I could grapple to the windmill about one out of every five tries. I wasn't doing anything different on each attempt, yet it would only grapple to the windmill 20% of the time. I was definitely close enough to grapple and the windmills even had the icon that indicates something you can grapple to, yet, it still only worked 20% of the time.
When you have to grapple multiple objects in a row to get to the next platform, about half of my attempts would fail because the grapple would pull me too close to the object I am attached to and throw me off course or stop my momemtum entirely. I get that the grapple will pull you all the way to whatever you're connected to, but they really should have implememented a system so it would know when you are trying to swing from an object and when you are trying to land on an object.
There really should be a Super Meat Boy or Trials instant restart as well. The platforming is frustrating enough, but having to wait upwards of ten seconds for the game to reload every time you fail is just way too long. I lose interest and it would make me want to quit playing even more than I already did.
I really liked the art style and the story seemed at least somewhat interesting, but the frustrating, endless platforming is just too much for me to keep playing or recommend to anyone.

I just finished Awkward Dimensions Redux a few minutes ago, and I think I have to add my two cents to the mix. It feels necessary, when it has impacted so deeply.
The game is a hugely personal insight into the dev's dreams and thoughts. It is very short, and split up into a variety of levels that all have their own structure and 'gimmick'. Quite a few of them involve (not-too-hard) platforming, and some just have the player sit and listen - or watch. I think that as a dream experience, the game meets its goal perfectly. There are lots of abstract ideas and messages going on, and it's very surreal. If you're someone who needs to 'win' games or understand them completely, I don't think Awkward Dimensions Redux is for you.
I think one of the game's biggest strength is atmosphere and design, because even though there are low-quality textures and assets (which is fine, this is a free game, I'm not expecting AAA-levels of graphics), the overall impression I get from the levels through the use of colour and style is vastly more important. As you can see by the store screenshots, there's a lot of bright, constrasting colour that evokes a whole range of emotions and moods. The beautiful music backs that up brilliantly, too, by the way. You really should wear your earphones when you play this game.
Anyway, I consider the visuals of the game to be only second to the narrative. It's a fractured one, with no overall plot or aim, but I think each small vignette (through the levels) has its own impact. There were one or two that really hit me in the heart. I teared up at one point, I think.
I'd recommend this to everyone, unless you fit into the categories I stated above. This game doesn't have a 'point'. It's a stream-of-consciousness (or subconsciousness, I guess) look into the dev's dreams, and if you're a creator, a person who's gone through a breakup, or even a dank memer, you'll find a piece of this game that resonates with you. :)
Have a nice day!

One Way Heroics is like an old Ultima game condensed into a Roguelike. The various classes and goals make the game very replayable, and I think this is a really interesting model for RPGs to overcome the monotony and over-simplification of Final Fantasy style games.
The only thing I would say is, I wish they'd combine the great maps and interesting gameplay with some kind of story and/or more unlockables or goals. To me, this game is a model of the potential unlocked by games like League of Legends or Binding of Isaac, where there is always a reason to try your best during the game, and to be satisfied with losing.

Recently got this game after seeing video of it online and I have to say I'm very pleased already.  This game is deceptively simple, appearing like a normal roguelike in gameplay and presentation, but the more you play the more you learn it has surprising depth of mechanics and writing, getting this for such an astoundingly cheap price is well worth your money.
Starting with two available classes - Swordmaster who's good with combo hits and Knight who starts with a shield for extra defence you unlock more classes either by performing certain actions in game or by 'buying' them with the Hero Points you earn after each playthrough.  Hero Points can also be used to unlock new Perks you can add to your character at the start of an adventure or to expand your Dimensional Vault which allows you to store items from characters you've played then give them to a new character to start off stronger - very helpful for the higher, harder difficulties.
In short I highly recommend this deceptively simple, tremendously affordable and greatly fun game to anyone a fan of RPGs and Roguelikes.

Cracktackular. I picked this up on a sale, and got more than enough of my money's worth out of it. It presents a good amount of challenges, and is just a damned fun game, with a good amount of replay value.

You are a hero.  There's a darkness steadily advancing from the left.  If you get caught in it, it kills you, so you'll be steadily advancing to the right.  There's a demon lord that'll show up at some point to try to kill you.  It's your job to kill him first.  That's pretty much the story.
This is essentially a turn based RPG.  Every step you take, action you make, etc. is matched by both the encroaching darkness and all other creatures/NPCs in the game.  As you progress right, you'll run into friendly NPCs that can sell/buy/give items, enemies that want to end your quest, random items strewn across the landscape...pretty much everything you'd expect from an RPG.
The worlds you'll play on are randomly generated, so you have the option of a new map each time you play, although you also have the option of playing a world you or someone else has already played by inputting a code.  So, if you find a world you like, you can keep returning to it, or you can keep exploring new layouts...although if you return to a dimension already visited, there will still be some things that change, as shops will have different stocks and random item drops will be different.
You start out with two classes available(and a male and female skin for each one), and as you either perform tasks during your attempts(killing an enemy with a bow, for example, unlocks the Hunter class) or spend the points you accumulate at the end of each run, you will unlock more classes and various boosts for your characters, known as perks.
There's something about this game that keeps managing to pull me back in, even after it humiliates me.  This game is not much in the way of being forgiving.  Your character is pretty weak to start out each run, and there's always a good chance that a fairly strong monster will be hanging around a few meters from the start to make you notice just how weak you are, and there are always chances you'll take the wrong path through some terrain and get pinned behind a wall of mountains that you won't be able to cross before the darkness catches you.  But, even with that, there's always a chance the next run will drop off an awesome weapon early on, or the planets will align perfectly and you'll take a golden path through the land and take down the Demon Lord with ease...only to never be able to recreate that run again.
So yes.  I highly recommend this game.
