My "First Play on Launch Day!" Video and First Impressions Review:
This game is definitely different and unique, not quite like any other game I've ever played before.
The goal is start from a blue safe box area and move about a randomly generated level and find prisoners being held captive by the evil doers which aim to kill you and the prisoners.  Once you find them, you can simply press the E key to order them to follow you and you lead them back to the starting blue safe zone.
Movement is made by rotating your direction with the mouse, then holding the left mouse button down to move forward in the direction you face.  You can fire unlimited bullets in a straight path in front of you by hitting the space button.  To me, the movement controls would be much better if they had taken a more traditional approach and made WASD be movement, perhaps using A & D to rotate, W to move forward in the direction you face, and this would allow you to move backwards by simply hitting the S key.  To me, I think this would have worked much better and it made it less awkward because it would free up your left mouse button to fire.
Regardless, the game is pretty fun and has a certain level of addiction to it.  The cutest element of the game comes when you get into a close battle with the baddies and any prisoners following you will run off to a corner and quiver and shake, obviously scared to death.  You'll simply need to go recapture them with the E key if this happens, but it always seemed to get a smile out of me.
The game is not without faults despite its unique gameplay and the fact I love the randomly generated levels to keep the game engaging and different every time you play.
My biggest complaint occurs once you fail a level which happens if your character gets touched by any baddie.  When you fail, you immediately replay the failed level, but it completely generates a new random level, and this is my biggest gripe with this game.  There are many times that I want "another chance" to fix whatever I did wrong on the SAME exact level I just played, not a new randomly generated one - which can be 10 times easier (or harder) just based simply on the procedural generation and placement of your prisoners and the danger zones which spawn the baddies.
My next complaint comes with what definetely feels CHEAP from the baddies when they crawl over walls to get to you and they don't have to work through the maze as you do.  I don't know if this is intential game design or a flaw that needs to be worked out.  Because this game is not "early access", I tend to believe this was left in the game intentionally, and it certainly feels cheap when it happens at certain times.
Add in the awkward choice of controls that takes time to get used to, and you have a very unique game that I just feel could have been done so much better.  I hope that the developers can make some adjustments, add in an option to repeat a failed level rather then procedurally generate a new one, and give us some customization on the movement controls... as well as prevent the baddies from walking through walls essentially by moving over the top of them.
My Scores for this game break down as follows, and sadly this game doesn't seem to break out of the sub-par games that the publisher 'Strategy First" seems to have a reputation for:
Value of the Game: 20 out of 40 - It's not priced too high at $4.99 and the game offers a unique experience, but the game breaking faults I mention above with the awkward choice of controls brings this score down over it could have been.
Fun Factor of the game: 12 out of 30 - Again this "could" have been a unique Indie game if only it was made with a little more pre-planning and if the code made the AI enemies use actual intelligence to work through the mazes rather then just climing over walls and if you could repeat the exact same levels you just failed.
Controls/Bugs: 5 out of 20: Ugh, giving the controls a 5 out of 20 here is giving the game benefit of the doubt and assuming that they actually tried the more traditional control layout
I mentioned above.  Bugs like the mobs climbing over walls lowers this score as well.
Graphics/Sound: 7 out of 10 - The graphics and sound work fine for this style of game and while they aren't anything special, they work just fine.  Unfortunately for this developers of this game, graphics and sound are only 10% of my overall scoring criteria.
--------------------------------
FINAL FIRST IMPRESSIONS SCORE: 44%
As much as I want to like this game based on "what it could have been" and its unique gameplay, I just can't recommend it, even at it's low price point of under $5 USD.  Sorry devs, make some adjustments to fix my above complaints, and comment below my review.. and I will be more then happy to give this game a second look and review.  I DO believe this game could be really fun with just a few tweaks and changes.

You Have to Win the Game is a retro precision platformer that looks like it could have been made for MS-DOS or the Apple II.  The player must navigate through a non-linear subterranian world, completing difficult jumping puzzles and collecting moneybags while trying to find out where the exit even is, eventually obtaining classic staples of the precision platforming genre like the double-jump and the wall grab.  For the pros who laugh in the face of platforming, an Extra Spicy mode offers remixed challenges that are twice as hard as before.
APPROXIMATE LENGTH
1-3 hours to reach the exit, another 1-3 hours to find all the moneybags (Highly variable based on player skill)
PROS
(+) Controls are tight and responsive for maximum precision
(+) Game layout is well-designed and can give even skilled players a challenge
(+) Minimalist visuals look good without looking lazy
(+) CRT monitor emulation (it's the simple things in life your treasure)
CONS
(-) Very easy to get lost (and no map makes it even worse)
(-) Fast screen transitions can be disorienting due to the minimalism of the game
YOUR MILEAGE MAY VARY
(?) Be prepared for maximum frustration on certain rooms (as expected for these style of games)
OVERALL
Win the Game is short and sweet, combining old-school nostalgic visuals and sounds with new-school sensibilities (and unlimited lives).  The difficulty is well-balanced, and an abundance of checkpoints takes away the sting of trial and error.  An enjoyable experience, and it's hard to beat the price.

There's a lot I could say about this game, but I'm pretty confident that whatever I say, some other review has already covered it in depth.
As such, what I can really say from myself is that FTL provides me with an immersive space adventure that's different each time; you never know for certain what's going to happen next. The ability to name your ship and each crewmember only adds to this. Sure, after playing for so long, I've seen almost every encounter type available, but when I'm playing I just feel like I'm in control of my ship and its crew, struggling to get along until the bitter end in this cruel universe. Each action has immediate consequences, and somehow making it to the end and defeating the final boss provides an extreme sense of satisfaction.
Of course, this game isn't about getting to the end; it's about the journey along the way. The possibilities are endless, just like the reaches of space.
... Except for the abrupt ending to your journey, which is
certain you will die a very sudden, brutal, exploding death.

I'm not an expert nor even a big fan of strategy games and yet, FTL was easy to learn and instantly engaging. There are countless number of hours to be had here. Screentshots simply cannot encompass the greatness of this game--it needs to be experienced.

Moonstone Tavern is a game you NEED to try if you are found of traditional RPG maker games. For a indie title it is surprising how very well achieved it is as a product overall and I will start to explain:
The game runs perfectly on me after turning the effects off. Honestly it wasn't impossible with them on, just slightly laggy. It is a smooth experience, and most problems I've read about have been addressed by the developers in a very fashionable timeframe. Always good to know that the game is just not released as is, but a work further developed as bugs get pointed out. As someone already pointed out in a review, Performance Issues seem to be the only issues with the game so far, and that was taken care at most cases.
You get a big Tavern to run, a Hatchery for your pets (yes, a whole pet hatchery system) and a big world to explore. Beside the normal tasks that you will get from running the Tavern, there is much more to be done in-game, and the tutorial day will get you started with pretty much all you need to know. Day and night cycle, and each day will sum up how much you did with your tavern, listing both expenses, taxes and of course, profit.
A lot of the game is set on exploration, so do not expect to be told about everything exactly. Some things you just have to go and give it a try (like Arena fights or promotions where you can get extra currency or special items). A whole lot of the game is based on completing some tasks so others can be unblocked (or used, like most buildings). At all times it will be required that you do your best from a day, and that implies task>exploration>task routine.
Graphically it has a lot of "eye-candy", as everything is done in pixel-art style and always looks coherent with the rest of the scenery elements. From a visual appealing color palette to the little nice animations here and there, pretty much everything adds up to the gameplay itself. The tunes are nice and match the magical dimension you are playing in.
The user interface is very simple and works great too, the only think I would "touch-up" is really how the dialog system behaves. I would add extra smoothness to it, but it turns out to be a detail as they work perfectly as is (and I mean, you can always clearly read what you are supposed to read). I would point out the resolution issue, but it seems the development team is already at it. And maybe a couple of achievements would also add out to the experience and hook up players even more!
So if you are still wondering, I'd say go for it. It's a game you get to love very quickly and for the work obviously put into it the price tag is really low ;)

1: Maybe make it so loot from baddies is auto picked up when walking over/near it.  Sometimes when an enemy dies their loot gets sent flying behind some trees and it can be quite difficult to find.
2: More random events within the tavern.  These travelers and heroes have character and it would be fun to see them interact more, maybe get into bar fights, have a druid accidentally set something on fire, that sort of deal.  I'm not sure if these are already implemented as I'm still pretty early into the game.
3. Customization. Lots of people enjoy personalizing and making something their own.  If possible maybe implement some sort of decorating system. Just a few suggestions, but otherwise its a real solid game so far, just needs some polish.  Keep up the hard work and keep updating the game and it could go far.

I want to start by saying that I certainly didn't hate this game. It was really for an afternoon's session. The visuals are really impressive for an indie game like this,  the soundtrack is simple but works well, and there's tons of fun easter eggs hidden throughout the play. The travel and exploration mechanic is great too, but at the end of the day it just feels like a "proof of concept" game.
The mechanics work, but I found myself falling more than progressing over the course of the 3-4 hour game. Some of the running and jumping controls work, some of them don't, and not being able to cusomize it for a keyboard feels like a bit of an oversight. The ability to grapple onto pretty much any surface was really impressive, and would have been a really good selling point for me if I wasn't getting stuck in-between rocks and being forced to fall back to the save point over and over. Plus the game is VERY liner, which is disappointed given the posiblilites to explore that you start to see after the first hour.
There is a bit of story to the game, which being called "A Story About My Uncle" (a rather poor title if I may say so) but I was expecting a bit more depth to it. You get a bit of narration as you go, but if anything it seems very dry and unenthusiasitc. Story wise it just doesn't rope me in. There are tons of NPCs, but they don't do anything besides just sit or stand in one place. For that reason the world seems pretty empty. For a game with such strong visuals it's really ashame there wasn't more thought placed into the characters.
Again this is far from a bad game, but it just feels too short and too plain of a world to be worth it. Just when I was really starting to get into the game it ended, and I felt like a wasted my money (even if it was on sale).
In the long run I think this game would be GREAT with VR, but as is...it's a "proof of concept" and not enough to call a good game.

There's a lot I could say about this game, but I'm pretty confident that whatever I say, some other review has already covered it in depth.
As such, what I can really say from myself is that FTL provides me with an immersive space adventure that's different each time; you never know for certain what's going to happen next. The ability to name your ship and each crewmember only adds to this. Sure, after playing for so long, I've seen almost every encounter type available, but when I'm playing I just feel like I'm in control of my ship and its crew, struggling to get along until the bitter end in this cruel universe. Each action has immediate consequences, and somehow making it to the end and defeating the final boss provides an extreme sense of satisfaction.
Of course, this game isn't about getting to the end; it's about the journey along the way. The possibilities are endless, just like the reaches of space.
... Except for the abrupt ending to your journey, which is
certain you will die a very sudden, brutal, exploding death.

I'm not an expert nor even a big fan of strategy games and yet, FTL was easy to learn and instantly engaging. There are countless number of hours to be had here. Screentshots simply cannot encompass the greatness of this game--it needs to be experienced.

Where to start... Well, first off, I got this game for free to play, enjoy and do Let's Plays of. When I first started, I started with out a class, which in all honesty, was funny. Other than that, starting out, things worked great! Tutorial was pretty straight forward, (im just an idiot at times XD ), Things start off easy, getting customers and making food and all that. I like how you have to manage things, like making sure you have money to pay any employees you hire, cleaning up sick guests messes, the diversity of the races you have in your Tavern, etc.
A familiar, a great ally that can heal you, once you get a fountain repaired, is a wonderous thing. Even better is when you can repair cottages and have heroes to help you out. Makes things much easier to deal with, so you can gather more resources needed for things, like making food or crafting your own gear. And in the recent updates, you can ride a unipony, though I've yet to find one. And there's new merfolk beds just recently added as well. Combat is pretty fun. I've yet to try other classes, though I've been a Sword Saint since the beginning.
Each weapon has a interesting effect/animation when you attack regularly, like the Fall Sword has a bunch of stars that come out when you hit an enemy. Underworld sword has fire. Even heroes have weapons like that as well. Your allies don't die either, they just get knocked out. You can revive them with revive potions too. When you lose all your HP (if it doesn't bug and transfer control to a allied unit, though you should either let the hp get to 0 or rush the quest, cause if you strike at all with a companion, the game will crash)  you go to your room in your tavern, so there's no game over.
You only lose a small amount of health or magic, which isn't a big deal! There's a few side quests, as well as the main ones and the quests you get from your customers. There's varying difficulties as well, ranging from easy, to impossible. I Suggest you don't take impossible, unless you have a couple allies with you, that being a familiar and at least 1 or 2 heroes. It's a fun, casual RPG. A lot of the time, it's hard for me to quit the game, even after finishing an episode of it, because it's addicting to me. Like all RPG's though, there IS some grinding, but you don't have to grind too much, really. Oh! Also, there's someone that everyone 'loves'. It's the Tax Collector as well! Giving him other things, like food or piety helps reduce the tax costs, though, if you're making enough money and don't want to sacrifice anything else, pay in full.
It's honestly not that much, compared to what you'll be making. Basing the taxes on number of people and rooms and such, can be a pain, but it's nothing you can't fix :D. The music is fairly interesting too. It seems to change after every few screens I think, I couldn't pinpoint the timing on that ha ha. Things only got better with updates/patches. Over all, it's a fairly enjoyable game! Sure, it had some bugs here and there, but most of them weren't game killing. By that I mean, making your game crash. Definitely worth playing!

This game is two things in equal measure: a sandbox tavern sim, and a quest oriented, action RPG.
The first it does well, immersing you in the daily chores of a tavern manager in a fantasy world: mopping up sick, speaking to guests, hiring staff, setting prices, repairing leaks, chasing of rodents, dealing with bandits and hauntings, and generally upgrading the place to make it more accessible to a whole host of humans, gnomes, dwarves, fairies, and so on! As for the quest oriented RPG part it does this fine, not amazingly, but fine. There are plenty of different quests to go on from finding  eggs to hatch to collect new pets, through collecting resources, to slaying dragons. It is let down very slightly by the combat which is basically shoot stuff with guns and wands, or hit them with your sword (depending on your class). Personally I prefer to rely on breeding up a strong accompanying pet, or hiring heroes rather than doing much fighting myself. You still get all the rewards and XP if you let your companions do it, so I just run around foraging the maps as they do all the killing.
One of my favourite parts of the game, as you may have guessed, is the creature breeding. A talking cat has told me that there are around 50 collectable and breed capable creatures. You begin with two working stables although you can upgrade to five (please devs add more I hate sending pets away). You can get new eggs by going on quests and by breeding your creatures using genetimagic (don’t know how to pronounce that). Breeding creatures is simple yet fun, although crafting the magical ingredients can be difficult.
Crafting is a huge part of the game. Alongside cooking there are so many armors and weapons, magic potions, scrolls, and magic gems that it can be, at first, a little overwhelming. Learning where to get all the ingredients from (which there are definitely over 100) is a challenge in itself.
There is of course a story, and although it uses some common fantasy tropes, such as a blight spreading across the land, it does so in a way that is new and interesting. I especially like that the elves seem to be the bad guys, although, as in all games by these devs, the whole world is cast in shades of grey rather than in black and white. The story is also linked directly to your success as a tavern manager which is obviously important. I’ve not finished the main storyline yet but I think I’ve guessed where it is going due to reading some of the books located throughout the world.
 
In my last hour of play I purchased another tavern (you don’t get to manage it but you do get profit).
I went on a quest for some magical ink to write out a scroll but I still need to find a feather before I can craft it. I got killed by some orcs in a mine. I did my daily forage and was annoyed that I got no feather. I spoke to my guests and met some new ones (all guests have a funny few things to say – definitely worth talking to. I tried to get married but there is a curse on my potential husband and need to go on another quest.
Pros:
- So much to do – although can be a little overwhelming.
- Great characters that you can talk to and get quests from.
- Interesting story.
- Can start as one of ten different characters and six classes.
- Beautiful pixel graphics.
- Breeding pets!!!
Cons:
- Simple battle system – although can be mostly ignored.
- I have to turn off weather effects when its blowing as it makes my computer lag. (2009 laptop)
- Sound effects need to be more varied.
- No journal so you have to remember what to do or go back and ask again if you forget. In a normal RPG this wouldn’t be so bad but it’s easy to forget when you’re running a tavern.
- No window mode!?!
Overall I would give this game: 8/10 – However you must be aware this is an RPG Maker game, and not a AAA title.

This game has to rank amongst one of my top most favorite rogue-like RPGS. With the first difficulty already being hard and the other difficulties and scenarios much harder than the previous one, this game makes you carefully plan your decisions (through movements, skills, choosing appropiate stats, and watching your three bars closely) in order to even get close to killing the final boss. All of the classes have a completely different playstyle (besides that most of them require you to use basic attacks to damage) to even get past the 100m mark. And although you start fresh everytime you begin a new character, the game rewards you by allowing you to keep a limit of items from past runs to aid your next. All of these elements combine to create a satisfacting experience that can be enjoyed by any RPG player and can consume time faster than you consume a bucket of KFC chicken. The soundtrack is worth a mention as well, fitting and worthy of rocking your head to the beat at the speed of the tempo. I would highly recommend this game to all RPG fans looking for a fair amount of difficulty, and recommend all casual players to give it a go as well. It's more than well worth its price of $3.49, so try this amazing masterpiece of a turn-based slightly pixelated RPG.

The wanna-be Stalker-game that really didn't quite succeed and here's why.
First of all Metro2033 is a corridor shooter with very few alternative paths or ways to tackle different situations. You mostly just wander after an NPC who talks in broken english (why not just plain english, why?) and dies later. Then the demons/aliens/russian dogs attack and you have to survive.
This is where it all falls apart.
It's basically an aren a fight but in a closed space with not much room to dodge the attacks. Aliendogs are melee only but something feels off with the shooting and it's hard to knock 'em down until they're on your face, munching away. Good thing is that you don't really emotionally connect with the clunky NPC's so you just duck behind them to take cover and conserve some ammo.
Then you follow another NPC until there's suddenly Nazis and Reds (communists) fighting each other. YOu don't care about either and just pump them full of lead and keep walking, doing some poor jumping on pipes etc. to reach the cold overworld aka Moscow which is a huge city and still just one corridor.
Russianwingeddogs come flying and everyone seem to be super afraid of them. You fill it with lead like thanksgiving turkey and forget about it until you get an achievement for doing just that. Gj.
There sort of shops that let you buy ammo and customize your weapons but the latter is ultimately just a waste of resources. You can carry three weapons (all three can be from the same 'class') from revolver, peashooter, assault rifle, nailgun to shotgun. Human enemies use the same weapons and drop them when they drop, so you can keep switching weapons until you get one with desired customizations.
Problem is that you just don't care. Only good thing in this game is the atmosphere as long as no one opens his mouth. The enemies are unsinspired and the gunplay is horrible. Mjetro1952 Reduck might have more ducks but it still can't rival it's opponents.
Buy Stalker instead. And mod it like a boss.

An amazing gem that masterfully mixes game and narrative work of art. Despite the game being short - I strongly recommend it.
Pinstripe is a game about ex-minister who takes a journey through Hell in search of his daughter. If the original plot does not intrigue you, there’s some more to it: you really don’t know why the minister is there and what’s going on, other than your daughter has been kidnapped. Encounter quite eccentric characters, solve puzzles, jump on platforms, and fight enemies. All that in order to reach the wrongdoer who took your daughter from you.
•	Amazing Graphics: the lighting, the particle effects, the backgrounds, the surrounding
•	Responsive controls: if that was a simple puzzler – that would not matter much. But in Pinstripe, you also encounter enemies apart from puzzles and will have to do some shooting. I’ve played the game with the controller and suggest you do the same.
•	The plot is not obvious at first: as you go through hell, you continue encountering some clues that build the full storyline in the end
•	Great Music and Sounds that help you feel the atmosphere of the game
•	The points mentioned above transform it into a spectacular combination of game and art. This is hands-down the most captivating title I’ve played this year. It catches your attention from the first seconds and does not release it until you are done.
•	The game is about 2, maybe 3 hours tops. After you complete it – there’s the “plus” mode, but it’s the same story, only allowing you to buy extra items to make it easier. To counter that: You’ll probably have to play one more time if you want to see all the references and understand everything better.
Despite the short length, the game turns out to be a unique work of art. For some of you, 15 EUR for 3 hour entertainment might seem too much and I can understand. But it turns out to be a rare combination of both solid gameplay mechanics and immersive storytelling: jumping through the platforms and shooting enemies feel good, but this never overshadows the main point of the game: plot. It feels like an experience to live through and the game to play at the same time. Honestly, the game has so much going in these 3 hours that it feels totally worth it in the end. It is what it is: a sequence of breathtaking experiences that does not release you until you figure out the mystery in the end.

The cars, clothes, music, buildings... everything fits perfectly. You also have the ability to obtain a few DLC's as well, which I personally haven't played yet, so I can therefore not express myself when it comes to those. The developers of the game has added a lot of details into this game to make it really special.

You have SweetFX, different types of ENB's and those types of enhancements to make the game look really sick. I think it sucks that there aren't more games in the Mafia series, or that there are games reminding me of- or being similar to Mafia, as this game is one of my favourites of all time. It pretty much outplays the other competitors taking place in the same era, even though there aren't many. At least in my opinion. I'm definately hoping for a Mafia 3 game. Mafia 2 has given me one of the best gaming experiences out of all the games I've ever played. Though, I do suppose this type of game doesn't suit everyone. Great game in my opinion.
The price on steam isn't too bad, but there are places where you can get the game really cheap. I picked up my copy of the game through a game-bundle on Humble Bundle. I would have loved to see more mods to boost the experience even more, though.

A really good game, but like many other 2K products (Bioshock) it feels unfinished, as if the developers simply ran out of money before their final vision had been accomplished.  The city in the game is very well done and its fun to simply drive around and explore, but I wish more exploration had been included in the story missions.  In the Grand Theft Auto games many of the story missions introduce new areas and things to do, but in Mafia 2 all the exploration was left up to the player between missions.  The games story also felt very unfinished to me since it ended when things were just beginning to get interesting and the main character was beginning to realise the type of people he was involved with.  It would have been nice if the game continued and showed us where this interesting character ended up later on in his life.  Maybe thats what the sequel will be about.  If this is the case then I think the cliffhanger ending was acceptable, but if the next game is not connected at all I will be a bit upset.  Overall, though, I thought that all aspects of the game, from driving to fighting to shooting, were all very well done and this is impressive since its a fairly large game.

LISA is one of the most interesting, unique & thought-provoking games I've played in recent memory, and easily the best RPG Maker-based game I've ever seen.
Earthbound's RPG gameplay and quirky surreal humour (though WAY less light-hearted) meets Fist of the North Star's martial arts & post-apocalyptic themes, with a brutally dark & depressing story reminiscient of Nier/Last of Us & characters with similarly questionable morals at best.
It also has an open-ended world & is viciously unforgiving, especially in 'Pain' mode where all save points are one-use only. You'll face unavoidable brutal choices with lasting consequences, and certain powerful enemies which WILL randomly use one-hit-permakill attacks on your PCs (at least there's like 30+ you can recruit).
Not for the squeamish, easily frustrated or those looking for a happy story, but it's definitely an experience worth checking out. You'll laugh, you'll cry, you'll be horrified, you'll have a good time.

I'm writing this review a year of so after playing this, so at least you can be sure everything I'll say about this game has had time to mature and settle in my mind.
First of all: it's an amazing experience and worth every penny.
In Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines you play the digitalized version of the famous World of Darkness tabletop RPG. You become a vampire right at the start and get to learn about a new, undeground world that has been going on for centuries, complete with its own rules and regulations. Just like with the tabletop version, the focus here is dialogue, story progression, mistery and drama. You get your fighting abilities, sure, but the action gameplay is not that great. Where this game truly shines is in its sortyline. You'll be played around like a fiddle by much wiser, older and stronger vampires. You'll be doing several tasks for everybody and by the time you finally understand what you're doing, it will be too late.
Make your own little vampire, dress apropriately, jump into the darkness of nighttime L.A., feed from a ♥♥♥♥♥ and get tossed around by vampire politics and drama. There are scary missions, action missions, story-heavy missions, funny missions and, of course, a sewer stage. It's all there. Soundtrack is absolutely great, fitting perfectly in each moment, and graphics are impressive for 2004, specially people's faces, it improves immersion a bunch. If you enjoy RPGs that say "♥♥♥♥ it" to gameplay and spend time instead polishing the storyline and narrative, then you'll love this game.

I'm giving this game my recommendation only because there are many elements that make it a worthwhile game for the right player. Like others I am not a huge fan of "Thumbs Up" versus "Thumbs Down". This game has both pros and cons; however, I'd rather say "Thumbs Sideways". This is an early review (about 50% in) and I will update if my opinion changes.
Metro 2033 Redux as a short and linear FPS: Thumbs Up
Metro 2033 Redux as a RPG with reasonable character development and open world aspects: Thumbs Down
The Redux version is visually stunning outdoors; no compliants about atmosphere in general above or below ground. Decent weapon selections and modelling without being over the top or rediculous. If you are primarily looking for a run and gun FPS, 2033 is worth the sale price. If you are looking for a deeper set of skills development, crafting, or open world movement, don't look here. Unfortunately this game was tagged with "Open World" by a few Steam players; it is decidedly NOT open world and very linear.
Cut scenes abound but are well done and keep you involved with the story line. I found the best levels to be those where I could use stealth and silently dispatch enemies (I preferred stalking the human foes over the beasts). Unfortunately, there were not that many stealth levels and most require plenty of shooting; especially when restrained by the gas mask (limited time). Perhaps more will come further into the game. No system crashes thus far and the game runs smoothly with very minor jaggies now and then, but overall looks great.
Documentation is slim and you will have to learn some keyboard commands through online guides or trial and error. That became very unappreciated when I could not save in place and test something out. Yes, another serious flaw is the all-to-typical-nowadays "checkpoint system" for save games. Just kill me. So many times I would have liked to try a different approach, or weapon, or tactic, but was not willing to redo a complete level just to try it. For me this is one of the joys of gaming; working through scenarios multiple times to see how well I can execute. In 2033 it is usually more trouble than it's worth.
I got this on sale in a bundle that included both Metro 2033 and Metro Last Light (not yet played) and that made it worth the price. When the need to run around shooting things hits me, I can have some fun with this. For me, I would have been unhappy had I paid full fare for this game.

One Way Heroics is a simple, yet unique and addicting RPG with an interesting spin on a common video game trope. I honestly didn't expect much, but it provides a lot of replayibility for its price; you can beat the game very quickly if you want, but you have to put quite a bit of effort to see everything.

As I've mentioned before and is somewhat common knowledge about a niche genre, every rogue-like is a balancing act between luck and skill to varying degrees. One Way Heroics, to its credit, trends more toward skill from my play time so far. There are moments of failure, but they are logical moments.
"Whoops. Forgot about the scrolling screen of doom."
"Whoops. Ignored the icon above an enemy showing it's a miniboss."
"Whoops. Forgot about my potions."
That's what is refreshing about the game; every failure makes sense. Often, that isn't the case in other examples of the genre. Each game has its own unique learning curve and priorities, of course. But this isn't the kind of game where you decide to drink a potion and roll the dice on it being poison or acid. It's far more structured than that, with information clearly presented to the player. This ensures that any difficulty is genuine, and not just a random number generator. I can appreciate that.
Aside from that noteworthy benefit, One Way Heroics is pretty cool on its own merits. Classic pixellated graphics aren't rare, but the game uses them in a charming way rather than seeming budget-minded. The scrolling mechanic is fairly unique, and adds elements of point-focused gaming such as Cannabalt. It's a simple thing, but executed just right to encourage that "one more run" mindset.
In short: I got this game less than a day ago, and I already feel like I've got my money's worth and then some. Give it a shot.

So no bulls-hit, One Way Heroics is possibly my favorite game of the year so far. It's neck and neck with Banner Saga, and though Banner Saga definitely has a greater immersion factor, the pick-up-and-play roguelike aspects and the replayability of OWH put it over the top.
What you have here is a game with the energy and fun of a classic Japanese RPG on the Super Nintendo, but with the ruthless difficulty and randomness of a roguelike. However, the developer very wisely simplifies the roguelike formula, so that you are not playing an overly complicated survival simulation; you are playing a game that feels both fun and intense; it is demanding of your judgment without being a drain on the limits of your attention span.
It's not perfect; once you've seen the 3 or 4 variations of "towns" and "dungeons" in the game they'll get stale quick. Enemy and landscape variety becomes a little threadbare after a few (successful) playthroughs as well. Also, even in full screen mode, the characters are ridiculously small. Don't even bother trying to play in windowed mode. You might as well go outside and stare at ants.
The achievements are very good as well; they're almost all challenge-oriented, encouraging you to push your skills to their limit, rather than go out of your way to fulfill random garbage achievements (I'm looking at you, Rogue's Tale).
One Way Heroics is a badass game, especially for the price.

I do not normally write reviews, but after playing (and beating) this wonderful game, I felt I owed it to the steam community to share my thoughts on LISA. First of all, if you're thinking about buying this game, but are easily offended and/or cannot handle very mature (and rather dark) content, I would definitely recommend looking elsewhere for a game to satisfy your personal tastes. However, if you are like me, and enjoy a good dose of dark humor with some very solid RPG elements mixed in, this game is definitely for you. To make this a bit simpler, I'm going to break this review down into sections. Oh, and I must warn you, the story section contains some minor spoilers, though I tried to cover up those that you do not find out within the first few minutes of the game.
If you're a fan of dark humor and/or old fashioned RPG style games, I highly recommend giving LISA a try. The story elements come together nicely without being completely overbearing, and the world itself is an incredible (though pretty p*rverted at times) place to explore. If you're on the fence like I was, definitely give it a go. Underneath the humor/grotesque imagery lies a deep and memorable story with very solid RPG style gameplay.
I want to start by saying that, despite the copious amount of humor, LISA manages to weave together a tale that both makes you think, and makes you sad. The game stars Brad Armstrong, who finds a second chance in life in a baby girl he finds one day in an apocolyptic wasteland where females have (supposedly) ceased to exist. Brad,
takes in this baby girl and, with a few of his childhood friends, raises her as his own daughter. But one day, I believe while he was passed out in a drugged up state
Buddy, his adopted daughter, is stolen away by the lonely men of the world (who, having not interacted with a female in many years, are rather hell-bent on real female intimacy, if you know what I mean). The main plot of the game centers around Brad's attempt to rescue his daughter, a daughter who may very well be the only female remaining in the world. Throughout the story you must make many tough decisions and sacrafices, and by the end you're left wondering whether or not your journey is even the right thing to do. The background info is slowly gathered throughout many flashbacks triggered when Brad enters certain areas. All in all, the story is very well done, and by the end, you can't help but feel bad (which, ironically, is what makes the story so good).
Story: 9/10
Honestly, this is the part of the game that impressed me the most. With so much emphasis on story (and the world), I was afraid that the gameplay mechanics might suffer. Boy was I wrong. The game turned out to have very solid RPG style mechanics, with the fights done in the classic RPG turn-based style. The character progression is wonderfully done, with almost every single companion having a specific niche to fill. Also, the companions play very well off of each other, with specific companions fighting very well alongside each other with highly complementing move sets. Being a big RPG fan, this was the part of the game that I was most worried about when originally deciding whether or not to purchase LISA. After playing the game though, I am incredibly impressed at how well this game managed to stick to its RPG roots.
Gameplay: 9.5/10
Overall, the sound helps quite a bit in adding to the atmosphere of the game. The music helps quite a bit in getting into the world of the game. That being said, I was a bit disappointed in the lack of variety, as many times the same few tracks seem to be played in numerous areas with just a slight change in tempo. Even so, I never really got sick of it until the very end of the game, and I never got so sick of it that I muted my game (the tracks were enjoyable, just too often repeated).
Sound/Music: 7/10 (though see general atmosphere section for more on the positive aspect of the music)
This is an area that the previews/store page promised would be excellent, and I believe that the developers delivered quite well on that promise. The mood is set right from the beggining of the game, and the sort of dark and gloomy atmosphere is maintained throughout the entire game without the game trying too hard to achieve it. However, this bleak, gloomy atmosphere is quite often lightened a bit with a touch of humor (usually right as it's needed), as well as numerous references to popular culture that can be picked up on. The humor does tend to be a bit dark and edgy at times, but (at least for me) that's exactly how I like it, and I believe it suited the game very well.
Atmosphere: 9/10
If you're a fan of dark humor and/or old fashioned RPG style games, I highly recommend giving LISA a try. The story elements come together nicely without being completely overbearing, and the world itself is an incredible (though pretty p*rverted at times) place to explore. If you're on the fence like I was, definitely give it a go. Underneath the humor/grotesque imagery lies a deep and memorable story with very solid RPG style gameplay. I would recommend LISA to anyone with a dark sense of humor, those who like a story that makes you think, and all generic fans of RPGs (who can handle or enjoy dark humor).
I highly recommend this game!
P.S. This is one of my first reviews (ever). I hope it was at least a little bit helpful! :)

It's a short free visual novel. It took only 24 minutes to get all endings.
I really don't like to downvote free games, but the problem here is that very little happens, nothing is resolved, and the Steam store description is somewhat misleading.
It's about a down on her luck calligrapher trying to make ends meet. As bad things happen to the protagonist you're given two choices of how to respond. If you choose the lazy/despairing option you invariably get a "BAD ENDING." But if you choose the persevere/hope option the story continues.
So it seemed like the story was headed for a satisfying conclusion where the protagonist's perseverance is finally rewarded. But there never actually is any payoff, instead the story just abruptly stops with another bad ending. It's almost like the story is unfinished, and after looking into it I found that's actually true.
There's two sequels which continue the story but they are not free like this. So this is basically like a first chapter out of a visual novel, a free hook to try to get you to buy the next chapters. I'm OK with this sales strategy, but I feel it should be immediately stated in the Steam store description, perhaps even the title should be changed to something like "Without Within Prologue," because going into it I thought this was going to be a self-contained story with an actual conclusion and it's not.

FTL is a sci-fi strategy game where you manage a ship and it's crew in an attempt to overtake a large interstellar Rebellion. You play as the crew for a ship of your choice. The game has 10 playable ships, with all of them having a second variant, and 8 having a third variant as well. You can take control of the ship's power usage, your crew's placements, the ship's weaponry, shields, engines, and much more. You can purchase upgrades from your SHIP menu or from a Store using a currency known as scrap metal.
Pros
+The battle system is fluent, fair, and satisfying
+The game is difficult all the way through, never being unfair
+Each character race feels diverse and useful
+The ship types provide a large amount of gameplay variety
+The game's procedure generation is usually great
+The game runs buttery smooth in most cases
Cons
-The game begins to feel stale after a while, as you can usually predict the outcome of a situation before you even read it
-The game can get almost too difficult at some points, to the point where it is incredibly hard to complete even on Easy
-The dialouge is a bit generic at times
Overall FTL, in gameplay, is fantastic.
Personal score: 9/10

First off let me say that I first purchased 2033 and Last Light many years ago for my Xbox 360 when they came out, so don't let my (potential) lack of game hours fool you my life is just busier now days. This is the only game I have ever taken the time to write a review for, as I feel it really deserves to be revered as one of the greats. I have also learned that if you click off this review page it deletes all of your carefully crafted ramblings.... boo.
This game is and always will be one of my all-time favourites of any genre, it’s a desert island disc game for sure. It's based on a book which I always think is a good start for dramatic and gripping storylines, no other game (including some of the best open world RPGs Skyrim, Fallout Vegas etc) have ever made me feel so, well I'm struggling to find the right word but connected is the best I can do. I actually cared about Artyom, wanting to succeed in the missions and not become just another forgotten corpse in the frozen darkness. The other characters encountered throughout the game I also felt had just the right amount of depth to feel like there could be more to them, lives lived and stories untold, far deeper than what is able to be presented to you in the brief snapshot that is your in-game interactions.
As you travel through the game you have the opportunity to come into contact with so many different people, not many in great depth but how often when you are passing through an unfamiliar town in real life do you stop and find out people’s life story? The game feels alive, the stations are busy and hum with conversation (if you take your time and eavesdrop there are some great Easter eggs to be found). You can stop outside a house to check your to do list and overhear the couple inside having an argument or children asking their farther questions, the level of voice acting detail is phenomenal in my opinion (this came out in 2010!!). In comparison the tunnels are eerily quiet.... too quiet, the only sounds may be a distant dripping of water and your own footsteps echoing off the concave walls. It feels almost primal, you're on alert listening for the slightest hint of danger lying in wait, just beyond the reach of your lamp, because it knows you're there. A distant roar makes you stop in your tracks and long for the comfort of a station filled with people. But you are alone, and no one is coming. Listening, fervently checking your meagre ammo supplies whilst eyeing up your ratty old gun hoping that today isn't the day it explodes in your face. You'll peer into the inky black... thinking, is that a Nosalis, or something new? Fear the unknown. You have to face it, there's no going back now that's for sure plus you're in a tunnel. So, forwards it is. The surface feels dead, but not completely. The wind howls past your ears, carrying the pained moans of the murdered city, creaking buildings and abandoned playgrounds charred by a nuclear winter. If you thought the tunnels were bad, to be cliché "you ain't seen nothing yet". Being a book worm is not a popular pass time in the endless winter, I wouldn't bother with a library card.
The actual gameplay is brilliant. It is a first-person shooter for sure but whereas others have a loading screen that simply drop you into the next action-packed sequence, in the metro you have to think. If those station gates slam shut behind you and you've only got 3 bullets and a single filter, you gone F&@ked up! Cause they're not letting you back in and the darkness is calling. There are a wide variety of variables that will affect how things pan out. I won't go into them here because discovering how to survive is half the fun! However, I will say don't expect something like call of duty where the only real obstacle to survival is your ability to run as fast as you can from cover to cover whilst holding down the trigger, that just will not work here. I've never felt such genuine concern for my inventory in a game, it’s not like there are 3000 rounds in a convenient ammo dump just around the next corner. Being pleased to have more than one full magazine is a novel experience and really adds to the tension as you anxiously watch each round slip through your fingers and out of the muzzle. You can't afford to shoot at shadows, but hey you've always got your trusty knife...
The story itself is also enjoyable, again I won't give anything away here but it’s not always exactly clear what is coming next or where you might be going. There is a definite feeling of some end goal to be achieved but reaching it by way of your travels, adventures and encounters through the metro lends the feeling that there is far more to this than first met the eye.
So, the crux of the matter, would I recommend this game? Well I think you can probably guess if you've got to this point it is and unequivocal YES!!
Buy 2033 now, just buy it. If it’s on sale be happy, because all must be well in the world! Play it, enjoy it. Then buy the book and read that. Yes, you'll know the plot and what ultimately happens but there is so much extra detail in the books that tie into the some of the Easter eggs that can be found in the game. You might also find yourself getting a bit nostalgic in a weird way for certain places and people, as it almost feels like you've been there. I have played through the campaign multiple times and each time it was different, the choices you make and paths you take through the map can greatly affect how each mission feels. The difficulty levels also add variation to the challenge, think you’ve got what it takes to be a real ranger?
Then buy Last Light and repeat the process with metro 2034 the book, which has now been translated into English!
If you still don't like it, then there truly is no hope.

Greetings Everyone!  Today I will be reviewing Helldivers a twin-stick shooter that has been on my radar for a bit now thanks to my desire for quick games and co-op.  As you may be able to tell I’ve only played the game for about two hours and did request a refund.  But, is this a game you should put your time into?
Become a Legend:  As stated above this game is a twin-stick shooter where you aim with one ‘stick’ and move with another.  These were very popular is old arcades and in co-op circles of the early generations of online consoles.  There is controller support (which I find essential for a game like this) and the replay ability of the game comes from leveling and trying out different combos.  The story is far from forgettable but don’t let that fool you into some epic narrative.  The story is based around humanity basically sending ‘democracy’ to the galaxy at the end of a gun…or a few million of them.  The enemy factions are all characterized as pacifist alien species that are somehow violent.  If you can’t tell it is a very tongue in cheek with a slap of ‘Team America’ and Starship Troopers thrown in.
So lonely:  In my opinion this game lives and dies based off the online community; thankfully this game still has one.  All the players I played with were friendly and at least communicated to some degree; increasing the fun of the game.  But sadly, after a few levels I saw really what the game was:  An arcade twin-stick shooter where the enjoyment was solely dependent on the community but otherwise honestly being rather shallow.  You play one mission you’ve played them all as there are limited objectives and the enemies are not super varied inside each faction and there just doesn’t seem to be much variety in playing styles to choose from as I felt some guns were just objectively better than others and the people I played with seemed to agree by their choices as well.
PC Mastery:  My understanding is this game originally came out on consoles and later on PC, which makes sense as this game feels more at home with a controller than a keyboard and mouse.  With that said they really should have done more to make the controls more refined for the PC as they are a bit of nightmare.  This is almost immediately resolved by simply plugging a controller in but feels this should be stated none the less.  The game didn’t seem to have any bugs that I noticed but I found myself annoyed by the lack of any real innovation, it seems like they just ported a stick shooter for an arcade machine with better graphics.  Finally, a decent amount of the game’s options are locked behind DLCs that admittedly aren’t that expensive but still annoyed me as I felt the game really isn’t up to snuff without them.
So, twin-stick shooters are a lot of fun with people.  If you have a few friends wanting to get this I think it would be a great addition.  However, alone is a no go unless you love meeting new people 10 minutes at a time.  I will say I did have a good time with mine and glad the game at least carried the parties from mission to mission.  Overall, it is really up to you, I requested a refund because none of my friends seem interested and didn’t see myself spending a lot of time on this game verse my other hobbies.  Regardless of what you decided, enjoy as always.

Bought the whole bundle on sale and worth it for $20. At full price with all the DLC, probably not.
Game has a loadout system with different guns, stratagem and perks. Loadouts are effective especially when tailored for specific enemy type/worlds and mission difficulty.
Guns are plenty but most are trash and players will often find themselves sticking to a specific for each of the weapon types. Standard fare of action shooter weapons with lasers and conventional shotguns and auto rifles.
Stratagems are called in via CTRL key and WASD key. Call in fire support from artillery to orbital lasers and personal equipment like shields, anti tank rockets or jump packs.
Perks affect your character's survivability, stratagem cooldown or deployment and equipment like stun grenades.
Friendly fire is deadly and often laughably absurd. Drop pods are a serious threat to both friend and foe.
Very easy to level up and attain mission/planet specific rewards in equipment and stratagems. Thankfully it's only late game cosmetics that are hidden behind the grind wall.
Enemies come in three types. Cyborgs, Illuminates and Bugs. Has both strenth and weaknesses to weapon types and stratagems so adjust loadouts accordingly.
Game has a campaign event targeting one of the specific enemies every few days or depending on how fast the overall multiplayer progress goes. The campaign and game in general reminds the players of introducing "Freedom" to these enemy regions.
Good gunplay and the impact of having the right stratagem, perks and aiming feels satisfying.
Overall, a fun game to be hold your attention for a couple of weeks or so.  Good blend of overly militaristic humors with responsive gameplay.

Company of heroes 2 is one of those games based on world war 2 that really makes you think about the situations created during WW2 and after by giving a indepth expierience on the battlefields of europe. The expansions are a little pricy but they go on sale almost every other week, and i recommend if you do buy this game that you get the add ons. Being a WW2 buff i fell in love with this game the dame i bought and almost got on one knee when i bought the expansion for the battle of the bulge.

For the base game you get to play as either the Wermacht (german army 193? - 1944) or as the Soviet army in all its glory. For starters every weapon and unit that bose sides posses is EXTREMELY accurate with historical means. As The germans you can construct basic pill boxes and sand bag lines.
While the russians only make sand bag lines but make for this by having larger squads of troops.

Thats another thing as well. If you play as the germans you have better trained squads and units but they are in small numbers and rather pricy to be relevent with germany's army size and production capabilities, but thats the boring old infantry side. Now lets jump to germany's incredibly advanced vehicles which range from thier basic mg32 mounted patrol cars to the mighty Tiger Tank from the later stages of the war. The vehicles are your strong point as the germans where you can easily overwhelm the Soviets tanks, but keep in mind the german tanks are rather expensive and slow if you're working with the larger models.

The Soviets on the other hand are capable of building massive infantry and Tank based armies with thier larger troop count per sqaud and cheaper tanks. This is only hindered by the lack of sheer armor on thier tanks in comparison to the germans. Another determining factor for victory for the Soviets is the T-34 medium tank wich is both cheap and fast. Its 76mm cannon is powerful as well, but when faced against heavy armor its not very effective.
That covers the general game so far as id like to rant on about, but now ill og into detail on the campaign expansions where you play as the americans on the ardennes assault. This game also made me realized how royally screwed our ground forces could have been if it wasnt for hitlers incompitance in the later part of the war. As the americans you get rellativly large squuads of troops and vehicles. Namely the Stewart light tank and the M4A3E8 Sherman Bulldozer tank. another great vehicle for dealing with the new german faction The Ober Commandos (Rommels forces) is the M10 tank destroyer which is almost your only method of dealing with tigers because its the only american tank with a powerful enough gun to pierce its armor without the use of dangerous tactics. Back to the troops as the americans you actaully have 3 choices to play. You can play as the infamous Airborne whci lack general utility but make up for in rapid deployment, The armored division which by far is the heaviest of the three in tanks, and finally the U.S. Army rangers the most skilled and infantry focused goup that excells in making your enmey hurt when they least expect it.
Now you're enemy the Ober Commandos are as powerful as its gonna get. They start off with no base because they follow Blitzcrieg(Lightning War). Instead you call in support trucks that convert into buildings with various abilities and troop selection available. As the Ober Commandos you get access to the most terrifying tanks of WW2. The mighty Tiger II and the feared Panther. Both tanks apeared late in the war but had oustanding success little to late to win the war for germany. These tanks have no equal on the battlefield and require your opponent to devise stradigies just to deal with them alone. this alongside of airsupport and large numbers of troops makes the Ober commandos a force to be respected and feared, but enough of me ranting PLAY THIS GAME AND SEE FOR YOURSELF SOLDIER!!!

Honestly, just play space invaders. I'm not trying to be mean because this game does have a few things going for it. First though, the bad. By default the game has an extremely annoying feature where anytime you turn left or right, the screen tilts with you. You can turn this off but it nearly made me exit the game in the first 10 seconds I played it because it was so annoying. In addition, your ship's weapon has so much spread it's nearly impossible to hit anything. That's only compounded by the fact that the enemies take way too many shots to kill on average and it just makes the gameplay boring and annoying. It's not a hard game from what I played, the weapon just sucks. The game also has a lot of flashing, and they did give a proper seizure warning at the beginning, but honestly it's a bit over the top and should probably be toned down anyway.
Now onto the good...the powerups are pretty satisfying in this game. The Quintuple shotgun is fun to use and really makes you feel like you're doing real damage compared to the default weapon. Also, the visual aesthetic is nice with the retro ship and enemies mixed with modern effects. The game overall looks quite nice and I think it was presented well.
It's not a bad game by any means but I think there's a few design decisions that they should've seen were bad ideas before the game came out. Maybe they weren't properly tested, I have no idea. The screen tilt is fine, but it shouldn't be on by default. The flashes are fine, but why are they like half the screen in size? The default weapon would be fine if you could actually hit anything with it. The first boss would be fine, if his attacks were actually telegraphed.
I have to say avoid it honestly unless you get it for really cheap or in a bundle or something. Like I said, it's not bad, it's just kind of annoying to play. It's all stuff that could certainly be fixed too, so we'll see.

Alright, so I'm just going to be honest. I didn't like this game.
I can say I liked the core mechanic, swinging from rock to rock was nice , but it also really gets old after a while.

The writing is sub-par, with simple grammatical mistakes somehow slipping through into the final product. None of the characters were endearing or likeable, with Maddie being the worst. The wonky animations and bad voice acting certainly didn't help either.
I can respect the game for wanting to be peaceful and non-violent, but there really needed to be something else in there to liven up the gameplay. Overall, I wouldn't recommend this game, and I feel like the mechanic would have been better suited a puzzle game or something that requires thoughtfulness instead of just reflexes.

LISA: The Painful RPG is a 2014 sequel to the 2012 RPGmaker game of roughly the same name. Whereas LISA: The First was a puzzle game that delved into the surreal mind landscape of a horrifically sexually abused girl in a suburban neighborhood, the sequel concentrates on a post-apocalyptic world where a phenomenal White Flash has seen every last woman on Earth gone in the blink of an eye.
That only scratches the surface of this bizarre RPG, that has risen instantly to a cult classic status.
First thing to note about LISA is that despite the usual trappings for an RPGmaker game being a watered down clone of an early Final Fantasy or Ultima game, LISA is legitimately fun and novel, immediately bringing more involved mechanics to the table with "dial-a-combos" and an emphasis on status effects so heavy you'd be forgiven for thinking you were playing a Shin Megami Tensei game. The amount of party combinations and varied battles make for engaging fights, and their insanely quick pace prevents the situation from ever getting boring.
Of course, the main draw for the game is the bizarre, grotesque and comedic world, which is incredibly well written in itself. Far from resorting to non-sequitur "quirkiness", LISA manages to explore the sweaty desperation of middle-aged men trapped in a world that doesn't make any sense to its logical (and illogical) ends, with gags that reflect off the world itself.
Thematically, it's not afraid to delve into depressingly material as you play through the story of Brad, a deadbeat trying to do the right thing. Haunted by his past, he searches for Buddy; his adoptive daughter, and the last girl on Earth. An incredibly well-paced story keeps you involved through this 8-15 hour romp, depending on how much of the completely optional content you try to seek out.
It's not a perfect game by any stretch, no cult classic is, but I personally found its flaws to stem not from its status as an RPGmaker game but from intentional design choices.
LISA's touted "character consequences" are complete bull. Having finished the game 4 times, I can tell you that there are absolutely no lasting consequences for any of your actions - most of them are purely superficial or vestigial and do not alter the plot in any way. Your sacrifices matter about as much as a choice in a Telltale game - a line of dialogue is the norm, but even that's pushing it.
The massive amount of party members - over 30, in fact - sounds great on paper, but leads to an incredibly amount of redundancy, with party members being plain better than others. Add to that, that you get the best party members very early on and there's almost no character development whatsoever in the game.
Instead of the contemporary RPG route of taking a few select characters and having them be real characters, most of the recruitable characters in LISA are just pawns, with exactly one line of dialogue after you recruit them that hardly masks their status as disposable NPCs. Whether or not this is actually a flaw depends on your own point of view, the variety is certainly welcome but you could probably cut about half the recruitable NPCs in this game in favour of fleshing out the ones that exist with more varied mechanics.
But perhaps this is the attitude that has lead to the sorely limited party casts of contemporary RPGs.
Despite a linear plot with some obviously contrived elements - especially the main antagonist and the MacGuffin that doesn't react like any other 10 year old ever has - what's there in LISA is fantastic. Having no love for any of the inspirations that it wears on its sleeve or any love for retro-inspired titles, I bought LISA at full-price and haven't regretted a second of it.
I'd recommend this RPG to anyone looking for a title with heart, in a sea of soulless entries.

As a story driven game, LISA has a lot to offer. A fairly large world to explore, a wide and varying cast of characters, and a narrative that will leave the player awestruck.
Another element this game nailed is atmosphere. From the level design that reflects the barrenness of both the world and the emotional state of the main character, to the soundtrack that can go from catchy-funky to sickening, the player can tell that much thought and love went into this project.
The gameplay consists of the average turn-based party combat stuff. It's not frustrating, but not incredibly challenging either. Most puzzles are pretty easy to figure out, and the game seems to be designed so that there's really no "right" combination of party members, it just depends on how the player want to play the game (or which characters the player finds most funny or charming. This game would probably fall under what some may refer to as "casual", but that's not always a bad thing.
All in all, if you are the type of player who love's a great story and a game with atmosphere, LISA is the game for you.

The game has 10 playable ships, with all of them having a second variant, and 8 having a third variant as well. You can take control of the ship's power usage, your crew's placements, the ship's weaponry, shields, engines, and much more. You can purchase upgrades from your SHIP menu or from a Store using a currency known as scrap metal.
Pros
+The battle system is fluent, fair, and satisfying
+The game is difficult all the way through, never being unfair
+Each character race feels diverse and useful
+The ship types provide a large amount of gameplay variety
+The game's procedure generation is usually great
+The game runs buttery smooth in most cases
Cons
-The game begins to feel stale after a while, as you can usually predict the outcome of a situation before you even read it
-The game can get almost too difficult at some points, to the point where it is incredibly hard to complete even on Easy
-The dialouge is a bit generic at times
Overall FTL, in gameplay, is fantastic.
Personal score: 9/10

Personally, I'm not a big fan of this game.
On the other hand, it is one of the best arcade platformers I've played.
The platforming puzzles in this game are absolutely top-notch; they challenge your timing, pixel-precision, and overall mechanical ability without being artificially difficult. The game is also relatively glitch-free. Because the game is made in the style of traditional platformers, newcomers may not be familiar with the idea of 'hitboxes' and 'states'. As such, newcomers will find spikes frustrating because 'they didn't hit it', or because 'they didn't know they could touch it'. Newcomers will also find it difficult to land on some platforms; they assume they can't jump while in mid-air.
I'll be honest, the game is well-designed, well-coded, and definitely worth playing. That said, it is a homage to the platforming genre and carries many of the frustrating game mechanics that turn off newcomers to the genre. The quality is very high, as far as the genre goes. The colour palette is well chosen, also.
If you enjoy games like Mario, Metroid, Ninja Gaiden, and Castlevania, you'll probably enjoy this game.
If you don't, then don't play this game.
And if you've never played a platformer, give this a shot; it's free, and is a great introduction to one of the earliest game genres.

You probably have already read it on the store page, on another review or on a trailer: the world is doomed, and The Darkness keeps coming at you as the world spins its days away until you finally kill the Demon Lord that made The Darkness. Fairly typical hero stuff, really.
Although deviations to the term aply, this game is a rogue-like in most of its aspects. There is a grid system and it's "turn based", as one would expect: strategy plays a role here, if not too deeply, since you should be killing or avoiding any enemy that comes across you. The mechanics are pretty simple too: you can move in eight directions, you can attack, skip a turn, interact with a friendly character near you (or in your party), use the various items you come across, equip equipable stuff and use skills related to your character's class, chosen at the beggining of a session.
If you aren't into rogue-likes, you may consider this one for how forgiving it is: at the end of a session (where a victory or defeat condition activates, I mean,) you will always get some "Hero Points" that you can save up to unlock more features, such as different classes, more starting perks to help you ensure victory and the all-important sink that is your Interdimensional Vault. Simply put, when you get a game over you can stash stuff you had with you and take it out with your next characters. Maybe that sword you picked up last run was actually good? Use it some other time and turn the tide when you most need it, maybe. Winning a session also nets you different items depending on the victory conditions which are significantly powerful, so a win may cause you a streak of wins later if you play your cards right.
Where One Way Heroics (OWH from now on) shines is that even though this is a rogue-like with little depth it is extremely replayable for quite a few reasons.
First, for the achievement-seekers out there, you litterally can't (or shouldn't) be able to get everything in a single day, but only a couple of the hardest challenges will make you gnash your teeth; you will surely think them worth it when you complete them.
Second, even though you can input a seed (ie: the base for how something else spans) for every session you start, OWH kindly gives you a few ones specific to each and every day with incentives to play them. There's a "guaranteed ally" seed, a "special rule" seed and a "hey, this is just another seed, but since everyone knows it there's a bigger chance of finding someone else's ghost to help you" seed. In other words, seeds that will help you be victorious or give you the challenge you need to feel like the game is actually worth playing it for the sake of claiming to be its master.
Third, but possibly not the best reason, is that in a world filled with many things claiming "rogue-like" or some such thing without actually being and where every indie game is more likely to be something you didn't really want before you've realized it, OWH is a genuine rogue-like that is, albeit simple and on the easy side, masterfully done. Unidentified equipment that can be identified, scrolls of enchanting, items of quirky features that let you escape something you surely couldn't face, the traditional "go down to level X" transformed into "hey, if you don't get a move on The Darkness will swallow you" and monsters with randarts such as Tough, Fire-breathing or Crazy... Yes. If a game has a right to call itself rogue-like, OWH certainly qualifies.
The pixel art of the game is pretty good too. Nothing is under or overdrawn or feels out of place. You also get to see some "higher definition" portraits every now and then of some relevant characters in the game, but that's not really the most common of events. The interface may be a little quirky before you get used to it, as it is clearly built to save time while using it intesively, but it's very solid once you're familiar with it. I noticed some people complain about the music: it's entirely optional to mute it, but I advise against it; some themes may be dull or annoying after a while, but others stand out for their inspiring feel. I'd even risk saying that without the music this game would lose all of its mysterious "continue playing me" effect. As for the general sound effects, it doesn't stand out much: it's not bad, it feels natural but it won't make or break the game if that's your tipping point.
Also to consider is that OWH allows saving of the particular run you're going through. With (infinite?) save slots, the only limitation is finding the Save Attendent NPC in a random upcoming village or how much bagspace you can afford to carry save crystals (which, even though also found in the wild, are sold by the afforementioned NPC). I'd advise against saving unless you really want to continue that particular run the next time you come around, as personally I encountered a feature I didn't anticipate in the game that prevents a serious exploit about item duping: an older run won after another run has finished can not save its items into the vault. Live and learn, live and learn...
The last thing I want to mention is the "online features" the game has. Basically, useless info keeps popping up in the interface about the other people that are playing (or have played) in your session's seed. Arguably nothing to write home about, if not for the subliminal knowledge that gets leaked from it now and then: others may have come upon strategies that you can replicate and have an easier time reaching your own goals by using. But of course, the same aplies in reverse: your session's information sometimes gets uploaded and everyone else will see your useful/useless little blurb about how you're doing or how you did. You can even set what message to be broadcast the next time it gets uploaded, in case you care (you should care; your default message is "I've reached NAME OF UNREADABLE RANDOM_STRING #typeOfLand", when you can be saying cool stuff like how many bad guys you've bagged or what you currently have equipped).
By now you should have your own opinion about whether you're interested in this game or not. If you're into true rogue-likes, this is an excellent one to add to your library. If you're not sure if you'd like rogue-likes but would like to know, this game is a good bridge to the vast world of (real and true) rogue-likes with its narrowed aproach. If money is usually the issue, say no more: OWH is just a cent short of being 3€; in a time/money spent ratio, your use time is approaching infinity for the low initial investment you'll pay. If nothing of the previous paragraph urged you to buy this game, let me try the superliminal way.
If that didn't work, I'll even chuck my seal of aproval straight in your eyes. And if that didn't work either, I guess you're one of those people who'll miss out on a true gem because you're more into "CODs" or "Assassin's ExcuseOfAGame" than classic gaming.
