Great game with a fun singleplayer campaign that will keep you occupied for a few hours, endless fun in galactic conquest, fighting for control of all your favourite star wars planets in the galactic civilwar of the clone wars, and instant action for just hoping into an all aout battle. And fantastic mod support bringing so many more hours of fun.
But, most important of all, after so many years, official multiplayer support, is back.

For starters, this isn't going to be a formal review: with the recent return of online servers, I wanted to have my own go at why I think people should play this game. I'd love to do something more formal in the future, but for now, this is something meant to be quicker.
I personally didn't grow up with Battlefront II, but I did grow up with Star Wars. I've played a lot of Star Wars games, but I don't think any capture the tone and feeling of Star Wars quite like this one. Star Wars Battlefront II is, in my mind, the ultimate Star Wars game. It has many of the vehicles, troops, locations, and characters that are most iconic to the franchise, and you can expand all of those even more through modding (though the recent update may stop some from working). Everything feels exactly how I'd expect: The AT-ATs are powerful but sluggish, the starfighters fast and maneuverable, and the Hero characters are all incredibly powerful. You can have massive-scale battles that capture the intensity and excitement of the conflicts from the films, and it's all set to the classic John Williams music.
The campaign, focused on the 501st Legion through the Clone Wars and their eventual fall during the Battle of Hoth, has a fair amount of missions and can last quite a while. Some missions (Operation Knightfall in particular) are incredibly challenging and will test your skill at the game. The AI is pretty decent and offers a good challenge both in the campaign and the normal modes as well. The Galactic Conquest mode, while I've only experimented a tiny bit with it, adds plenty more replay value to the game while adding an element of strategy as well.
The gameplay is incredibly solid for a FPS. There are many game modes, ranging from hunting down local beasts to taking down massive space ships. The ground controls are fantastic, and the game is incredibly balanced: there are many different classes for the four major teams, each with its own playstyle, and the Hero characters, while very powerful, have a health meter to prevent them from staying around too long. Regardless, seeing Darth Vader charge at you is still an incredibly terrifying sight. The vehicles are generally a little tougher to turn and can't aim directly ahead of them for the purpose of balancing, but they all feel and play exactly how one would expect iconic vehicles such as speederbikes or AT-STs to control. The space battles are massive in scale, and it's exhilarating to weave through other starships on your way to the enemy's massive control ship. All in all, this is a game that any shooter fan could enjoy, let alone any Star Wars fan.
The new multiplayer features are tough to talk about given that they were just implemented and there have been server overload problems due to the rush of players trying to get in. However, from what I managed to play, multiplayer is tough but a lot of fun, adding even more replay value. This is a game that's easy to sink a lot of time into, and I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys Star Wars or shooters in general. May the Force be with all the new players joining in for the new update!

Ater 18 or so hours, I'm finally done with my playthrough as a Brujah! This review won't be super in depth, just listing off a few positive and negative things from my experience!
Man, this game had so many high and low points for me. Been on a bit of an open world rpg slog recently, discovering new games or older ones that I may have missed! Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines popped up several times on my search and I found myself drawn to it. So many people praising it as a masterpiece while others called it a bug-ridden mess with potential, Turns out it's a bit of both.
I installed the unofficial patch because apart from fixing some issues the game looked ugly as sin and very low res without it. When I finally did start playing I found myself getting lost several times as this game does very little hand holding, which honestly isn't a bad thing! It gives you an objective, and then it's up to you to figure out how to get to or solve said objective, this leads to a bunch of running around, but helps you quickly become familar with your surroundings.
Despite being an older game, over 10 years old now, it's look and feel has held up remarkably well! The environments are pretty appealing, the npcs have decent voice acting and are fun to engage with, and your character, controls pretty satisfyingly overall.
The combat is where I found myself getting frustrated, it was a tad floaty at times and my character's fighting felt very stiff. I especially struggled with the first "boss" in the art gallery, who gave me the final death a few more times than I'm willing to admit. He actually had me walk away from the game for a while (only to be drawn back because I was already too invested not to continue!).
A lot of boss fights turned into a game of "find the exploit" for me, whether it be a corner they can't hit you in, a particular weapon or ability they are stupidly weak against, or a random glitch that makes them pull the T pose or simply stop attacking you. This fight-stopping glitch helped me beat both the gargoyle and Ming-Xiao (And thank god because she was making me pull my hair out.)
I definitely preferred melee over ranged weaponry and only used them when it made tactical sense. The guns can be very effective, but only with a higher ranged level, it was hard for me to use them at the start because I could barely hit anything. I'd fire my gun all over the place and before I knew it, 5 guys are on top of me beating my♥♥♥♥♥♥into mush.
Fighting did get easier and more enjoyable as time went on and I got used to the mechanics. It was only a few hours before I felt like a bad♥♥♥♥♥♥vampire swinging a sword around through hordes of bad guys and monsters, getting stronger with each fight and loving the feeling of progression!
Vampire TMB was never lacking in things to do, where there are the main story quests, there are also plenty of side quests to get your teeth into! If someone seems to have a lot to say, usually the right response will trigger a quest you can do for them to earn some more experience and cash. One of my more favoured side quests was the club in downtown, and how helping out the owner can give you a nice little income on the side, which is necessary to keep your inventory stocked with ammo and blood bags!
There are even some side quests that are ongoing side by side with the main story that conjunct with each new location you go to, such as the serial kiler quest! I originally let him go when I first encountered him because it seemed like the right thing to do, only to then fail the quest and have the game tell me I'm a donkey. I quickly reloaded a save just so I could kill him off and get the exp, the only reason I spared him in the first place was because I was trying to be the "good guy".
With each first playthrough of a large rpg world, if the option for morality is there, I usually always play the straight good guy first time around. The game didn't make it too easy for me at first though. After getting used to the game and it's mechanics I found my character being cruel to people without an option to do otherwise, it was then I started paying attention to my humanity meter, turns out if its too low (mine was 4 at the time) then you get denied "good guy" options in your dialogue. So I ended up going and dancing in all the clubs because for some reason you get a humanity point once per club if you dance there long enough! Weird but I'm not complaining!
Also there is the matter of The Anarchs, the supposed resistance/protagonists of the game. Naturally with the moral direction I was going in I wanted to side with them as soon as possible, but it turns out they don't really appear to your character very much in the game (At least they didn't for me) so you don't really have time to get invested in them. They had me do like two missions for them and then just told me to "spy on the bad guys", which I guess I did for the remainder of the game (ocassionally telling them what I learned) before siding with them in the last battle because that's what I wanted to do in the first place, but it honestly felt a little lacklustre.
In my humble opinion, this game isn't perfect. But even with all the bugs and broken elements that make it up, I was still glued to Vampire TMB from start to finish! I'm very glad that I've played it all the way through and will have to play as another class some time in the future.
Overall I give this game a 7.5/10 If you're an open world rpg lover, this game is worth a play!

Even though its now many years old, and it was never officially finished, Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines remains (in my mind) the greatest game I have ever played. Of course, now that its vintage, the graphics aren't anything to shout about, but the soundtrack remains as great as ever, and the plot is as dramatic and atmospheric as ever. It is a game of intrigue, deception, violence, and choice. It is one of the few games created that successfully merges the best aspects of several genres: horror, roleplay, action, and adventure, with a few clever puzzles and the occasional comedic relief (especially if you play as Clan Malkavian).
The dialogue is compelling and intricate, and the choices you make have a lasting effect on the storyline. The end game will be determined by the actions you make during the game in a way that most other RPGs don't, without making it feel railroaded, like a visual novel.
But what really makes VtMB stand out leagues above other games, as far as I'm concerned, is how the playing style is optional - whether you choose to focus on melee combat, gunplay, stealth, or diplomacy. Of course you can't talk your way out of every situation, a speech won't save you, when you're staring down the barrel of a gun, but many violent situations can be averted by choosing your words carefully, and that - I think - is a very good message for a game to send. Sometimes, you even get a bonus of experience points, for solving a problem in a specific manner, so think twice before resorting to flamethrowers and ninja swords.
I love the replayability of VtMB - you have 7 different clans, several possible endings depending on your allegience, and a bunch of optional content that is not required to finish the game, but can offer interesting interludes, rewards, or additional experience points.
My advice is to first play the game with any of clans Brujah, Gangrel, Toreador, Tremere, or Ventrue, then replay it as Malkavian, for the unique dialogue (which can on occasion be hard to understand, if you haven't already played the game) and as Nosferatu, with the increased difficulty of having to stay hidden from mortals in public. Whether you play as male or female is largely irrelevant, save for a few gender-specific dialogue options, and whether you are gay, bi, or straight makes little difference when you employ your vampiric talent for seduction - sure some characters will only respond to male seduction, some only to female, but that's life, right?
1) Unless you have the official patch fix, the game WILL crash during the main quest. Always and unavoidably. Easily solved by getting the official patch. Additionally installing the unoffical patches can improve the game significantly, by including content that was always meant to be in the game, but was left unfinished due to budget issues (at least, that is what I heard), but I advise to first play the game without the unofficial patches to really appreciate the game for what it is, in its purest incarnation, before adding all the fanbased content.
2) When you get to the later stages of the game (past the point of the game crashing without the patch fix), it can feel a little rushed - as if the developers had all the intention in the world, to make the later game as content rich as the early game, but simply ran out of time and money, and had to exclude a lot of good content to rush the release. For example, after a certain point, persuasion, intimidation, and seduction doesn't really serve any purpose anymore.
3) Memory Hog: The game is, regrettably ineffectively designed, and as a result it burns on your computer's memory. It's not a real issue if you play for less than 3 - 6 hours before rebooting your computer, but if you like all-nighters in the World of Darkness, you will find yourself confronted by the true horrors of misplaced objects, graphic glitches, excessive lagging, and all manner of unpredictable issues, from falling through solid floor, to being cheated of certain dialogue options.
4) And most grating of all: Every clan only gets a choice of 4 different outfits. Nothing more. You get to choose from one of four possible looks. Sure if you play your cards right, you can get a body armor that looks identical to Outfit #4 but that's it. Of course, since there are seven different clans, each with a unique male and female model with its own unique 4 outfits, there are plently of choices, but its not like you can just up and change your clan any time you get bored with the way you look.
On the plus side, VtMB is one of the few games I know of, where female characters can wear skirts! Actual skirts! And not the sort that just stick to the legs like a pair of pants without inseams, but actual, flowing and waving skirts that move in a semi-realistic manner consistant with your movements. Of course, the complexity of animating the physics of these skirts does make them look a bit clumsy on occasion, as one is periodically confronted by your skirt suddenly getting stuck awkwardly on your hips, but a small jump is usually enough to solve that embarrassing situation.
The fact that the player can choose to play as either male or female, and each clan has a unique model for both the male and the female player, is another point in favor of the game.
In conclusion: despite its many, many, many, many flaws, playing Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is an experience worth paying for, whether its on sale or not. The Alistair Grout's recordings alone are worth at least 5€, the antics of Jack is worth another 5€, and the werewolves, kuei-jin, gargoyles, ghosts, and various other creatures of the Night are worth at least another 10€. The soundtrack alone is easily worth the cost of the entire game, as is the atmosphere and ambiance, and finally the plot itself is worth paying for, even if all the other stuff had no appeal.
If I could only play one game, for the rest of my life, I would want it to be Vampire: The Masquerade: Bloodlines.

Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is quite a mess. There are parts missing, game-breaking bugs and more mistakes than any other game I've played. I won't lie; it's very dated and probably not for everyone. It was one of the first Source engine games to become available, but sadly the companies involved were financially doomed. Thus, the game never really got the attention it deserved.
However, if you fancy yourself as a Source Engine Vampire, you'll be rewarded with this one. There's an unofficial patch, which adds more content and fixes hundreds of bugs - but it still remains quite broken. Putting all of this aside, I'm happy to recommend this title. It may even have replay value to you.
Pros
+ The story is perhaps one of my favourite in a game. It's dark and tries to be adult orientated. Max Payne-like?
+ Reasonable variation between Vampire Clans.
+ Plenty of levels spread across a wide assortment of environments. The explorable areas and buildings are quite varied.
+ Vampire skills, knives, baseball bat or gun - kill at will, however you please.
+ Great character progression.
+ Moderate customisation.
+ Dark humour.
+ In-game actions decide your character's path, skills, items and fate. Play Mr Nice, or Miss Nasty.
+ Faithful to the original "Vampire: The Masquerade - Redemption" and the whole White Wolf thing.
+ Fairly good skill set for the different Vampire Clans.
+ Captivating story of your making.
+ Atmospheric cinematics using the engine instead of full motion video.
+ Graphics aren't terrible for it's age. At the game's release most of us went "Wow!"
Cons
- The dialogue scenes and their "1 - Yes, 2 - No." interaction becomes tedious after the first mission.
- Major flaws in AI. Missing dialogue, broken responses and overall beta quality [at best].
- Dodgy controls, FOV and camera angles.
- My Vampire feels like I'm driving a bus. It's a very clumsy affair when you encounter stairs or obstacles.
- Enemies usually aren't very clever or tough. There isn't much variation. Sometimes they bug too.
- Vampire: The Masquerade - Redemption was a much more enjoyable story, game and overall experience.
Overall, if you give this game some perseverance - you will probably enjoy it. It's not that easy to become fluent - but stick with it. The endings are quite rewarding. It's also very slow to begin with - but picks up pace to be quite an enjoyable challenge. It's not unlike Vampire: The Masquerade - Redemption in that respect.
If you have already played Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines and enjoyed it, you probably want to check out Vampire: The Masquerade - Redemption. It's much, much older - but easily one of my favourite games ever.

My pod touched down with a thud barely audible to me through the reinforced and shielded hull.  The red light on my command console blinked at me. It was ever so subtly speeding up, telling me that in a few seconds the doors above me would open and I would be amongst my Helldiver squad... spreading Democracy at 200 rounds per minute.  I readied my MG-105 Stalwart squad automatic weapon, giving it one last check to make sure it would dispense freedom reliably.  It would be my first line of offence and my last line of defense against the bugs we were here to squish.

The red light was faster now... and slowly turning green.  I knew when the green light lit and the alarm went off, I would be in combat.  My auditory amplifier was coming live and I could hear the muffled sounds of gunfire above me.  Yes, there was Democracy to spread this day.  My heart was pounding at the chance to convert Super Earth's enemies yet again.  At once, the light turned green and the doors flew open.  I pushed up hard with my legs and my rocket assist boots kicked in, propelling me up and away from my pod.

The sound of gunfire was at once deafening and exhilarating.  The world seemed to explode around me.  The dopamine injectors kicked into full forward and my eyes lit up with a lust for blood and violence the likes of which have not been seen since Travis found that box of gerbils back in middle school.  I brought my Stalwart up and trained my sights on a wall of bugs moving towards my position.

As I squeezed the trigger and began to feel the climactic rush of Democracy about to leave the barrel, I noticed a 6-sided shadow around me, growing larger.  I looked up in time to see the bottom of the next Helldiver's pod racing towards me at 1000 meters per second.  I was about to take a full load of freedom right in my face... and it was magical.  I had time only to hit the "max" button on my dopamine regulator and feel the explosion in my veins as the pod crashed through me and into the ground, letting the next Democracy dispenser begin his mayhem.

Gameplay:
Mafia II has some of the best gameplay aspects in a sandbox game, and is by far one of my favourite games. The game features classical cars, weapons, music and a various of other things from the 1940's - 1950's era. The game has a variety of cool features, like feeling your car up with gas, opening and closing windows, robbing stores, modifying your vehicles, stealing cars, lock picking locks, climb through windows and various other things like that nature. Mafia II mainly focuses on the story driven gameplay rather that petty side missions that distract you from the story (like grand theft auto.) so people that love a good story I strongly recommend picking this game up. I love mafia games and mafia films, and this was just perfect and I am hoping they release another one. If you get bored within game you can collect some Playboy posters (which actually show nudity, I think their are 50 of them.) you can also collect wanted posters and other collectable items to keep you interested, I managed to collect and play as it was fun anyway and I did not get bored. I have played the game both on consoles and PC and love them on both, obviously I had a better time on pc since the higher frame rates and better graphics but it was still an awesome experience on console.
Graphics:
Mafia II; now this game just has overwhelming graphical aspects and visuals(especially for the time the game was released.) The game features awesome dynamic lighting, 3D Rendered models and high resolution textures. When playing the game my breath was taken away with the graphics. It included amazing reflections, no frame drops and feels like a solid build. I can't really explain the graphics other than they are some of the best visuals I have seen in a sandbox game; I'll prove that later on when I post some screen shots. The game runs of the Illusion Engine with PhysX, even though I have an AMD graphics card the game still did it's job and created an amazing experience. The game also uses real time cutscenes which are created by the Illusion Engine so they are not pre-rendered cutscenes, so if you have a half broken car, it will show that in the cutscene which is pretty awesome if you ask me. Some scenes are pre rendered such as the hotel explosion.
Ratings:
Gameplay: 10/10
Graphics: 9/10
Controls: 10/10
Plot: 9/10
Overall: 10/10
Conclusion:
Mafia 2 is one of the best game I have ever played; it's definitely worth buying and I would advise you buy it on pc, if you have a good enough pc that is... but console still gives an amazing experience nonetheless.

OWH is like Solitaire: you aren't guaranteed to beat every game, but you can play it off-and-on, learning its ins and outs until you learn how to overcome its many challenges. The presentation is workmanlike, but functional. The music is quaint. Overall, a good entry-level Rogue-like.

Okay, One Way Heroics is not a normal RPG, not by any means. Sure, there are the usual suspects, such as stats, leveling, items, monsters and even a final boss. But that is where the similarities end. Each game is a race against the clock where the encroaching darkness at the left of the screen advances while your heroic character must scramble right in search of experience, items, gold and helpful npc's.
Sound fun so far? It gets better, not only is the difficulty brutally hard and the classes vary in play style, but each world you play in is randomly determined at the start of a game. You can keep the names of these worlds and re-enter them to go back to the same world as before, yet even then the experiences are fresh enough to ensure replayability of the highest caliber.
Like in Rogue Legacy, death is not the end of your efforts. Choosing a new class, and storing items in the dimensional vault makes the next game a little less harrowing if you choose. You can use the Hero points, awarded at the end of the game to unlock more classes and perks.
That being said, I was not kidding when I mentioned the brutal difficulty. In addition to powerful enemies, you might not have the best equipment because merchants do not appear often and you might not have cash at hand then. Or they appear often, but sell basic articles. And if you find a legendary sword? Use it sparingly as all equipment has a lifebar of such, if it runs out they break. Unless you have awesome perks and have gained levels at a crazy rate you can't beat the Demon Lord naked and unarmed.
In conclusion, this game is truly one that gives great bang for so few bucks. So get it!

A seizure-tastic Shmup! Graphic style is strongly reminiscent of the earlier BIT.TRIP games. It also has a great soundtrack if you’re into chipstep – and it’s included as a free DLC with the game!
When Void Invaders first came out, it was more of a Shmup version of Clicker Heroes, making you play through the same set of levels over and over again with increasing difficulty and forcing you to grind for EXP on previous levels whenever the difficulty got too high. Over a year after the game’s release, there came a few new patches which completely overhauled the game progression. With the new version, the upgrade system is still there, but you only have to play through the 30 levels once. The difficulty ramps up quickly, forcing you to grind to max level if you hope to have a chance of reaching the end.
The game’s difficulty is pretty silly – it’s about 50% dodging skills, 50% spray-n-pray. The game takes refuge in its ridiculousness: many levels have huge waves of undodgable bullets. Many levels will give you bombastic powerups which will fill the screen with colorful explosions so you literally can’t see anything for entire seconds at a time. Many levels will troll you with hilariously huge enemy patterns. And to be fair, I feel that the game pulls off the crazy style well. The action is wild and death isn’t too punishing. It works.
Aside from the main game mode, Void Invaders offers a few absolutely awful bonus modes:
“Endless mode” throws a constant mess of random, unsynchronized enemies and powerups at you, and seems fine-tuned to smash you to death with extreme prejudice EVERY TIME just moments before you would be awarded the achievement. (Healing is impossible, and you seem to take more damage from collisions the longer you survive – so the final difficulty spike will usually kill you in seconds regardless of how much HP you’ve saved.)
“Wave mode” throws synchronized groups of enemies at you, but it’s skull-crushingly boring, and random to boot – the enemy hoard is either going to fall straight down on you faster than you can dodge, or decide to move slowly enough to let you kill them. High scores are dependent on getting a random HP refill which may or may not show up.
Finally, “Hardcore mode” makes you play through 10 unique levels on a single life. It’s quite boring and easy until the end of level 9, which throws a (practically) one-hit KO enemy at you near the end of the level, prone to render the last ten minutes of gameplay wasted.
I give Void Invaders a 5.5 / 10. Recommended if you like the BIT.TRIP aesthetic and aren’t prone to seizures. It’s silly, colorful, addictive, and has got some great music. And it’s cheap!
But if you’re an achievement hunter looking for a cheap and easy 100%, I’d recommend leaving this one be. For me personally, the headache caused by the bonus modes has ruined any fun the rest of the game may have provided.

One of the most underrated and unique turn-based roguelikes on Steam. There are many elements that are similar to that of more traditional roguelikes, such as slaying monsters, leveling up, and collecting loot. However, unlike any other game in the genre, there's a looming wall of death that draws closer to you ever turn, forcing you to flee to the right. There's little time to stop for breath and allow yourself to heal; if you don't keep moving, the wall will devour you and end your game. You'll stumble across towns and dungeons where you can buy or obtain items, or slay enemies for experience, but even those will soon be engulfed in darkness. As if things couldn't get any worse, every so often the very powerful Demon Lord will spawn and try to end your quest before you become strong enough to kill him. Early on in the game, you'll have no choice but to run away from him, because luckily he'll be forced to retreat after a pre-determined amount of turns. Either way, it's another unique element of the game that you'll be forced to plan around.
Oh, and there's plenty of other rather spiffy features you might not expect in a game this cheap. There's a decent number of rather diverse classes to play, unlockable perks to customize your character, multiple difficulty settings, daily challenges with unique gameplay twist, limited interaction with other players online, selectable world seeds... oh, and you can post the results of your run to Twitter. There's that. But seriously, there's no reason not to try this game. It has plenty of depth and replayability, and it's only a few dollars. If there was anything bad I could say about it, I suppose the graphics could be better? Who cares, it's a roguelike. Half of those are in ASCII anyway. Get on it, yo!

Great game with a fun singleplayer campaign that will keep you occupied for a few hours, endless fun in galactic conquest, fighting for control of all your favourite star wars planets in the galactic civilwar of the clone wars, and instant action for just hoping into an all aout battle. And fantastic mod support bringing so many more hours of fun.
But, most important of all, after so many years, official multiplayer support, is back.

For starters, this isn't going to be a formal review: with the recent return of online servers, I wanted to have my own go at why I think people should play this game. I'd love to do something more formal in the future, but for now, this is something meant to be quicker.
I personally didn't grow up with Battlefront II, but I did grow up with Star Wars. I've played a lot of Star Wars games, but I don't think any capture the tone and feeling of Star Wars quite like this one. Star Wars Battlefront II is, in my mind, the ultimate Star Wars game. It has many of the vehicles, troops, locations, and characters that are most iconic to the franchise, and you can expand all of those even more through modding (though the recent update may stop some from working). Everything feels exactly how I'd expect: The AT-ATs are powerful but sluggish, the starfighters fast and maneuverable, and the Hero characters are all incredibly powerful. You can have massive-scale battles that capture the intensity and excitement of the conflicts from the films, and it's all set to the classic John Williams music.
The campaign, focused on the 501st Legion through the Clone Wars and their eventual fall during the Battle of Hoth, has a fair amount of missions and can last quite a while. Some missions (Operation Knightfall in particular) are incredibly challenging and will test your skill at the game. The AI is pretty decent and offers a good challenge both in the campaign and the normal modes as well. The Galactic Conquest mode, while I've only experimented a tiny bit with it, adds plenty more replay value to the game while adding an element of strategy as well.
The gameplay is incredibly solid for a FPS. There are many game modes, ranging from hunting down local beasts to taking down massive space ships. The ground controls are fantastic, and the game is incredibly balanced: there are many different classes for the four major teams, each with its own playstyle, and the Hero characters, while very powerful, have a health meter to prevent them from staying around too long. Regardless, seeing Darth Vader charge at you is still an incredibly terrifying sight. The vehicles are generally a little tougher to turn and can't aim directly ahead of them for the purpose of balancing, but they all feel and play exactly how one would expect iconic vehicles such as speederbikes or AT-STs to control. The space battles are massive in scale, and it's exhilarating to weave through other starships on your way to the enemy's massive control ship. All in all, this is a game that any shooter fan could enjoy, let alone any Star Wars fan.
The new multiplayer features are tough to talk about given that they were just implemented and there have been server overload problems due to the rush of players trying to get in. However, from what I managed to play, multiplayer is tough but a lot of fun, adding even more replay value. This is a game that's easy to sink a lot of time into, and I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys Star Wars or shooters in general. May the Force be with all the new players joining in for the new update!

We all have that one person in our lives that reminds us of Brad from LISA, right? A little bit broken, addicted to pain killers, armless and working as a cross dressing hooker named Sexy Boy.

"What is the price of redemption?"
That is the primary question in Lisa, and it is something you will be forced to struggle with throughout your adventure.
Brad, our protagonist, has had a rough life. He also lives in a world where there are no women left. Brad has tried to make the most of this, arguably failing in a lot of respects. This mundane life changes when he comes across a baby girl that he names Buddy. Brad becomes a father figure and protector for Buddy. While his effectiveness is debatable, Buddy is eventually kidnapped by the infamous Rando Army. From here, Brad finds it within himself to try and save Buddy at any cost.
This game, for lack of a better word, is insane. It's ruthless in its attack with heavy subjects, and spares no expense in showing you the worst that humanity has to offer. Its humor is predicated upon the darkest corners of our minds, and forces us to laugh in spite of the pain or be crushed by the unforgiving nature of this world. This game will leave you emotionally weary, and that's exactly the point. The unverise established here is one of beauty yet immense sadness. You need to play this game, if but for the story alone.
Help Brad save Buddy, and see how much of yourself you can keep intact in the process.

LISA is a tough game to describe. Its gameplay is your typical turn based combat. Nothing revolutionary. If you're looking for an absolutely amazing turn based combat game then you should probably turn somewhere else; however, if you want a deeply disturbing and powerful experience this game is for you.
Personally, LISA is probably the most powerful game I've played since the release of The Last of Us on PS3. This is an incredibly engrossing world with some REALLY morally complex characters in it. The world built in this game is an incredibly strange and punishing one. If you're faint of heart or don't like making tough decisions, you should probably avoid this game. This is one of the few games I've ever played where the consequences for your decisions are actual gameplay consequences rather than just story consequences. This makes all the decisions in the game much more powerful and lemme tell you, I was sitting for probably ten minutes just staring blankly at the screen trying to decide what to do at some points.
I don't want to write too much but if you're interested in an adventure with a powerful story and wonderful characters, DO NOT HESITATE. This game is without a doubt one of the most memorable games I've played in years and I would encourage anyone not put off by turn based combat or punishing gameplay to buy this immediately. It's worth it.

One of the most underrated and unique turn-based roguelikes on Steam. There are many elements that are similar to that of more traditional roguelikes, such as slaying monsters, leveling up, and collecting loot. However, unlike any other game in the genre, there's a looming wall of death that draws closer to you ever turn, forcing you to flee to the right. There's little time to stop for breath and allow yourself to heal; if you don't keep moving, the wall will devour you and end your game. You'll stumble across towns and dungeons where you can buy or obtain items, or slay enemies for experience, but even those will soon be engulfed in darkness. As if things couldn't get any worse, every so often the very powerful Demon Lord will spawn and try to end your quest before you become strong enough to kill him. Early on in the game, you'll have no choice but to run away from him, because luckily he'll be forced to retreat after a pre-determined amount of turns. Either way, it's another unique element of the game that you'll be forced to plan around.
Oh, and there's plenty of other rather spiffy features you might not expect in a game this cheap. There's a decent number of rather diverse classes to play, unlockable perks to customize your character, multiple difficulty settings, daily challenges with unique gameplay twist, limited interaction with other players online, selectable world seeds... oh, and you can post the results of your run to Twitter. There's that. But seriously, there's no reason not to try this game. It has plenty of depth and replayability, and it's only a few dollars. If there was anything bad I could say about it, I suppose the graphics could be better? Who cares, it's a roguelike. Half of those are in ASCII anyway. Get on it, yo!

Take (a kinder version of) Rogue Legacy's "death gains you currency to improve all future runs" mechanic, put it in a more traditional turn-based, top-down roguelike format, and remove the ability to head left without risking death massively. Add in the concept of daily challenge worlds a la Spelunky HD, and you have a killer combo - every day, random custom worlds show up for everyone to play in, and the deaths of others can benefit you directly. Find someone's corpse and gain XP/items from it... but be careful, god only knows if what killed them is going to come out for you as a result.
It's a solid roguelike with interesting mechanics and "permadeath" that still gains you progress. Plus it is CHEAP AS HELL. If you aren't interested by this description, dodge it, but I really can't add more to this without going stupidly in-depth on mechanics and I think you should be able to pick out your choice from here.

Pick up loot, kill wild monsters, avoid getting trapped against walls or else it will be game over.
If you don't play rogue games often however expect to die, a lot! Hunger will cripple you, monsters will one shot kill you, walls and other obstacles will always seem to get in the way at the worst possible time, and thieves will spawn while you are already holding on for dear life.
Despite the above however the game is
about cheap deaths! This is refreshing because Rogue like games usually go the 'uber hard' route by killing you for trivial stuff. You know the kind, you didn't drink enough water so died. You didn't see the hidden pit of instant death so you fell in it and died. This game has none of those, if you died, it was your fault and you can learn something from every death. This means the game is more about learning than it is about gruelling difficulty which is what makes it so much fun.
Enjoy the game and watch out for those treasure chests in dungeons, they'll get you killed.

What to say about One Way Heroics? Well, it is an amazing game where the darkness is devouring half of the world and every action/move you make decides the fate of your hero, its people, and the world. One Way Heroics, is a turn base rpg similar to FF tatics (to me) with a new experience with every game play. Some gameplays may be similar than others but with the random drops, enemies, and companions each run. It is a different run each game play. There are multiple different endings in the game and you do get to encounter other players in the muti-dimension worlds as ghosts. The ghosts are fallen players that give half a level and a random item they had on them (sometimes something really good).
With each play through, you are rewarded with Heroic points at the end of the game. Even if you died you are rewarded from your progress. The points can be used for Perks (examples swimming lvl 1, having a pet to fight along side you), the dimensional vault (will explain what this is next), and other classes (the other classes can be unlocked for free by just completing the requirement for the class). The dimensional vault is a place to store your epic equipment, loot, and reward items at the end from each run. You can reuse them in the next play through to start off stronger then you did at first. If you take an item out of the vault, make sure to return it or you will lose that item.
I would recommend One Way Heroics for the price they are offering for it. The game itself has a lot of growth in it and if you like the old school tatical rpg type of games. I am pretty sure you will love this game and get hooked on it.

This is one of those games where I really wish that Steam allowed for a numerical ratings system, or at least a "neutral" option for recommending or not.
If you've played the original Company of Heroes you'll know a lot of what to expect from the gameplay.  Capture resource points, build up your forces, and use them to smash through the enemy lines.
For players not familiar with the first CoH game it is worth noting that the relatively low unit cap does mean that you'll be relying on micro-managing the positioning of your units, where they're taking cover, and which way they're facing far more than in some other RTS games.  Tanks and crewed weapons are particularly notable for this, as tanks have different levels of armour on their different faces and some weapons can only be fired in the direction they are facing.
The single player campaign mixes things up a little with a slightly broader variety of missions, often giving you only limited numbers of troops to complete the mission rather than relying on you being able to build more.
One of the new additions to CoH 2 is perhaps one of the more controversial. Micro-transactions.  Like the original Company of Heroes you can select your commander during a battle, and this gives you access to new special powers or vehicles to call in.  However, in CoH 2 if you want more variety in the commanders you can select from (and, indeed, some of the ones with more powerful abilities) you'll either be grinding for a long time (read 40 hours or more per commander, and there's a lot of them) or you'll be paying out in micro-transactions.  You also won't see this ahead of time as these commanders are not available in the Steam store, only through the in-game shop.
Where the commanders just provide variety to mix up the abilities you have this isn't quite so bad.  Where they're a straight upgrade you can pay for to make you more powerful this is slightly harder to swallow.
The larger DLC available for the title has been a little more of a mixed bag, and it's worth noting that single player and multiplayer content has been split for the DLC.  Where the original CoH tended to have a single player campaign accompanying the new forces as they were released, this one doesn't.  Keep that in mind when eyeing up the DLC; the British forces can only be used in multiplayer and skirmishes, and the Ardennes Assualt pack is single-player only (you need to purchase the US multiplayer/skirmish pack separately).
In the end, my decision to recommend this game was a difficult one. When the game was first launched at a more expensive price, with the amount of content that was locked off, it would have been easy to not recommend it at that time.  However, with the drop in the price of the base game this isn't quite so bad, but with the cost of the micro-transaction commanders not insignificant it still feels slightly like you're buying part of a game to start with, then being nickel-and-dimed for the rest of it.
If you're a fan of WWII RTS games and you see this on sale (or if you're going to be happy playing skirmish or multiplayer with just the limited selection of commanders) then definitely pick up the game.  If you're after the single player content, then you'll want to grab the game and some of the DLC packs.

Great game with a fun singleplayer campaign that will keep you occupied for a few hours, endless fun in galactic conquest, fighting for control of all your favourite star wars planets in the galactic civilwar of the clone wars, and instant action for just hoping into an all aout battle. And fantastic mod support bringing so many more hours of fun.
But, most important of all, after so many years, official multiplayer support, is back.

For starters, this isn't going to be a formal review: with the recent return of online servers, I wanted to have my own go at why I think people should play this game. I'd love to do something more formal in the future, but for now, this is something meant to be quicker.
I personally didn't grow up with Battlefront II, but I did grow up with Star Wars. I've played a lot of Star Wars games, but I don't think any capture the tone and feeling of Star Wars quite like this one. Star Wars Battlefront II is, in my mind, the ultimate Star Wars game. It has many of the vehicles, troops, locations, and characters that are most iconic to the franchise, and you can expand all of those even more through modding (though the recent update may stop some from working). Everything feels exactly how I'd expect: The AT-ATs are powerful but sluggish, the starfighters fast and maneuverable, and the Hero characters are all incredibly powerful. You can have massive-scale battles that capture the intensity and excitement of the conflicts from the films, and it's all set to the classic John Williams music.
The campaign, focused on the 501st Legion through the Clone Wars and their eventual fall during the Battle of Hoth, has a fair amount of missions and can last quite a while. Some missions (Operation Knightfall in particular) are incredibly challenging and will test your skill at the game. The AI is pretty decent and offers a good challenge both in the campaign and the normal modes as well. The Galactic Conquest mode, while I've only experimented a tiny bit with it, adds plenty more replay value to the game while adding an element of strategy as well.
The gameplay is incredibly solid for a FPS. There are many game modes, ranging from hunting down local beasts to taking down massive space ships. The ground controls are fantastic, and the game is incredibly balanced: there are many different classes for the four major teams, each with its own playstyle, and the Hero characters, while very powerful, have a health meter to prevent them from staying around too long. Regardless, seeing Darth Vader charge at you is still an incredibly terrifying sight. The vehicles are generally a little tougher to turn and can't aim directly ahead of them for the purpose of balancing, but they all feel and play exactly how one would expect iconic vehicles such as speederbikes or AT-STs to control. The space battles are massive in scale, and it's exhilarating to weave through other starships on your way to the enemy's massive control ship. All in all, this is a game that any shooter fan could enjoy, let alone any Star Wars fan.
The new multiplayer features are tough to talk about given that they were just implemented and there have been server overload problems due to the rush of players trying to get in. However, from what I managed to play, multiplayer is tough but a lot of fun, adding even more replay value. This is a game that's easy to sink a lot of time into, and I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys Star Wars or shooters in general. May the Force be with all the new players joining in for the new update!

Do you like Earthbound? Now, do you like Mad Max? Drugs? Maybe a bit of surrealism? A bit of Cormac McCarthy? Violence, that's for sure - do you enjoy... pain? Human suffering? Tough choices?
If so, this is your game, dog.
Alright, it's not as crass as it might sound: the human element here is quite well-done. It is also covered in a layer of ambiguity and showing-not-telling that's quite tasty. I don't wanna say more 'cause it is quite worth it to go play it blindly, at least in a first moment.
That was the story - how's the gameplay? It's good too. But bear in mind this is mostly an adventure game, despite its jRPG trappings: it's very easy to break the game, plus I don't think there was that much of a concern, in the making of this game, about balance and whatever. On the upside, it's very fun and kinda inventive. Ok, not that much - but whatevs, chill out and have fun with the game's 20ish characters.
Here are my favorite ones - check them out if you ever somehow screw yourself, which, beliebe me, will happen whether you're a jRPG lord or not - Ajeet Mandeep, the Badass of Bengal; Shocklord, the Shocklord; Bo, the Bard of Bosnia; and a few other ones, that I don't really recommend but hold dear in my heart, such as Terry Hintz, Hint Lord, mostly useless if not for one very good buffing ability; and that halibut lawyer guy I've never used.
Now that's all very nice, but what can be said of negative about LISA: The Painful? There apparently is a Normal Mode of playing and a Painful one; guess which one I inadvertedly played the first time around? It sure wasn't Normal to easily die from falling off a cliff only to have to redo a huge part of the game 'cause my last save was around an hour ago. Yeah: saving is limited in Pain mode, and that, I think, is its' main drawback. You can only use a saving point once, and after that it's gone. It is a bit interesting, as it forces you to strategize around making your saving habits a rhythm: do I save now or do I hold this stupid expendable saving point back for when I'm done raiding all these mutants? Nonetheless, it still seems better to be able to save anytime, as the game is quite unpredictable and can ♥♥♥♥ you over many times, in very gruesome fashions. I'm an adult and I no longer savescum like crazy anymore no sirree I do not.
Also, the saving points seemed oddly spaced. Not good bro.
Still, this was a very magic experience, I find. It is a challenging and unique game - especially themewise - that does not lose itself into its own♥♥♥♥♥ like many other indie games of now. Can't wait for the next installment.

The world we once knew is gone, taking with it our mothers, wives, girlfriends, sisters, and daughters in one catastrophic blinding flash. All that remain are men: powerful alphas, cunning betas, and monstrous omegas.
You are a retired martial artist that indulges in a numbing drug called joy to escape a life lived through past regrets and failures.  One day you stumble upon a crying baby girl, and realize this is your second chance at life, but everybody wants this. Everyone lost something when the world exploded and everyone has nothing to lose in order to get what they want.
There are no dragons to fight, crystals to collect, or worlds to save, just a man who wants to be redeemed and a post-apocalyptic world that thinks otherwise.
The choices will be difficult and the humor will help you through it, but there is no crying until the very end.  Play it.

This game is something special and is unlike any other RPG... maybe even game, that I've ever played. Not because of the gameplay, which is for the most part not that original - 2D side-scrolling RPG with a standard old-school, turn-based battle system.
What makes this game special is partially the story, but mostly the world everything revolves in. It's post-apocalyptic, but hardly hopeful. It's merciless and bleak and the few places there's hope to find it's almost entirely based on desperately clinging onto something to a degree that's it's tragic. And there's tragedy aplenty.
I have to applaud the game for doing something that so preciously few games do these days - provide hard choices. And by hard I mean putting you in situations where there is no right or no wrong - only consequences, and bad ones at that. You have to choose what you believe is the lesser evil while knowingly accepting that the consequence of your choice sets you back in some way.
This is common in old-school RPGs, but I have to give it credit for the amount of small and absurd little secrets there are hidden all over as well. It makes the game that much more entertaining and you really feel like exploring the world, which  is fascinating enough in its own right.
Definitely recommendable if you want to try an RPG that stands out from the rest.

You are Artyom, a young Ranger living in the Moscow Underground along with the rest of the dwindling human population. It is crowded and unsanitary but there's nowhere else to go. World War III left the city above dead and irradiated, but far from empty as vicious, misshapen creatures crawl, swoop and snarl in the toxic leftovers of humanity's self-destruction. Now Artyom must leave the underground and face the horrors that await him above. Welcome to Metro 2033.
Based on the novel penned by Dmitry Glukhovsky (as the game is keen to frequently remind you), Metro 2033 places you into an alien yet somehow familiar world. The first that you notice is that the game is incredibly immersive. A minimalistic HUD and gripping story of an imminent extraterrestrial threat creates a world that immediately pulls you in. Many elements that would be automated in other games, such as blood and grime on your screen that disappear over time, are manually controlled. Artyom must wipe the glass of his gas-mask by his/your own volition. Small touches like this are seen throughout the entire game and they add up to create an immersive and often harrowing experience.
The game's graphics and sound design are nothing to scoff at either. The lighting is stellar and texture work is up there too. Metro 2033's vision of a bombed out Moscow is beautifully realised as wind howls, snow glistens and distant monsters snarl and salivate. Light shining down through glass or fog is especially pleasing to the eye. There is the occasional shoddy texture, usually on rocks and other environmental details, but I rarely noticed it while playing, especially under the gorgeous lighting effects.
Now, here's where things start to get iffy. The game itself is very linear, almost distractingly so. I found myself often growing frustrated at NPC characters who took their sweet time opening the door to the next area. While most of the game is fairly unrestricting in terms of player movement, the times you are restricted are definitely noticeable. Even the best moments in the game, in which you climb above the metro system and explore the decaying city of post-apocalyptic Moscow, seemed to want to railroad you to your destination with obstacles such as crashed cars and collapsed walls, sharp rebar jutting out of them as if warning intrepid players to back away.
Gunplay is serviceable, if not amazing. The firearms themselves are open to practical customisation, like adding silencers, stocks and different optics. One of my most memorable moments was when I swung by an arms dealer and customised my starting pistol with a stock and an extended barrel, only later realising that I had taken what was originally a six-round revolver and created a makeshift carbine out of it. Weapons in Metro 2033 all carry an improvised, homemade look to them and participating in that process was something I found surprisingly rewarding.
The opponents you will go up against vary throughout the game, although some overstay their welcome. Warring extremist factions make up the human threat, in my mind proving to be the game's weakest point. AI in human enemies is average as they rush down staircases, only to meet a headshot from your makeshift carbine as they join their countless brethren who made the exact same mistake. Many enemies will outright not see you if you're crouched, even when standing right in front of them, leading to some unfairly easy kills.
Mutant enemies, on the other hand, are brutally efficient predators, pinpointing your exact location if they so much as smell you. The sheer variety of monsters helps break the monotony of gun-toting goons, from nimble Nosalises to hulking Librarians, even flying Demons that roar and glide around the empty city, always on the lookout for an Artyom-sandwich.
Metro 2033 is a gorgeous, atmospheric and sometimes flawed experience. It combines action-packed shooting, immersive storytelling and even tense moments of horror and dread, all wrapped up in breathtaking visuals and audio design. Despite being rough around the edges with buggy AI and some overly linear moments, Metro 2033 is a game I would recommend to anyone who wants to get truly lost in another world like never before.

Void Invaders is short and sweet and well worth the price. There are 30 levels to get through, with bosses spaced out periodically as you progress. Gameplay is fast-paced and the enemies are relentless. Power-ups make things infinitely easier, but they're often short-lived and are placed strategically throughout the levels, so you have to use them wisely.
There's both keyboard and full controller support, I tried each and definitely preferred using my controller, the controls are very responsive and maneuverability felt much more natural and smooth. To each his own, though.
Achievements are a bit buggy but easy enough to fix (I had to disable Steam Overlay and in some cases restart my game).
There is an epilepsy warning at the beginning of the game and Endless Mode is particularly guilty of ridiculously bright flashing explosions and colors, so that's something to look out for (the regular levels and Wave Mode weren't as bad with this, I don't think).
Always enjoyed games like Space Invaders, Galaga, etc. and this one took those inspirations and did its own thing and was very easy to enjoy. It's colorful and upbeat and a decent challenge, not too easy yet not terribly frustrating, either. Definitely worth checking out!

Was enjoying this for a bit, hoping that it wouldn't fall into the trap that many shoot em ups get into in later stages, but it does. Later on instead of making better units, or continuing with more variety, they start throwing 4-5 entire screen covering shot enemies on screen at once that you clearly can't avoid and have 3 waves in a row of this, and just hope you don't take too much damage. Then more really hard guys later, thus making you get through tons of overly difficult poorly designed parts at once, and if you die you must repeat. Why do designers think increasing repetition in later stages and frustration makes for good game design because it gets "more difficult". At one level, 21, you encounter this guy that stays all the way at the bottom of the screen, who also constantly shoots continuoues never ending streams of shots at you. So since you can't get under him and you can't shoot sideways or down, you have to try and get through his unending shots, and just hope a few bullets hit him on the sides and head. Since you barely get any damage done at all you need to do this forever. If you die its "do this and all those other parts with multiple screen filling attack enemies" over and over again. It's a terribly designed enemy that's lacking in design and just hard for the sake of being unfair and lazy.
Many guys look the same. There's no getting health, except leveling up, which the game decides on, based on how many enemies they give you and where. So it can be annoying how they laid it out instead of medkits of floating health from killing enemies like it should. You level up, but it doesn't seem to do much, and you don't know how it makes you better. There are some cool upgrades, although some can hurt more. Bosses are cool, but later stages also fall into lazy design by having 4 bosses in a row so you have to survive them all, instead of just making 1 boss have more health or design him better.
First 2/3 was good, unfortunately bad design wins out in end.

One Way Heroics is a lot of fun.  It has four difficulties (plus an added setting to make things even harder,) three main endings, as well as several epilogues based on the allies that you manage to recruit along the way, and limitless replay value, thanks to short playtimes, unlockables, and the ability to transfer a limited number of items from one playthrough to the next. As you run, behind you the world is being devoured by the darkness, and you along with it if you dally.  You have to find the best equipment you can, upgrade it, level up, and recruit any allies that might be willing to help, and stop the Darkness from destroying the world by any means necessary.

Pretty incredible game for 3 dollars. But...it's cheapness does kinda rear it's ugly head. Generally, the most interesting part of it is that it pretty seemlessly goes from a side-scrolling adventure to a strategic battle field...of sorts (as discussed below)
In no paricular order:
Let's start with the classes.
To start with, you've got 2 classes available, and up to...6 (?) other classes if you unlock them.
They all are kinda balanced, aside from the fact that bows are incredibly overpowered, because all but two enemy types, that I've encountered in my various runs through this game, lack any sort of ranged attack...and the sword master is really kinda underpowered. Dies too easily, and starts with a poor selection of gear.
CUSTOMIZATION
Visually, you can choose from male and female of each class you unlocked, and when you beat the game with it, you can play as a special visual version of it. These have no non-cosmetic effects, as far as I've noticed.
To start with, you can assign up to 3 perk slots, but eventually unlock more. I'm not sure how, I think by beating the evil wizard boss thing.
And, to start with, you can select from all the stat+ perks, which boost said stat, and give minor side-bonuses, like Str+ gives bonus carrying capacity, and Endurance+ gives bonus damage reduction. You also start off with one specialist perk: Survivalist, which gives a large bonus to health, but nothing else. (Generally, I going full Str+ on all the perks seems to be the most efficient option, as you will probably then kill everything in one shot with proper gear.)
Again, you can unlock more, like a pet, or other specialist perks, like + to carrying capacity, or other things.
ENEMIES
Honestly the weakest point of this game. There is so little enemy variety. There's an imp, dogs, harpies, bats, orc-looking things, lizard men, Druid, skeleton, skeleton champions (they use shields), and the boss. OK, that's actually not too bad, but what was dissapointing was that they all seem to do the exact same thing: walk up to you and hit you with their stick. There is nothing very interesting about the enemies. It's like they are all just reskins of the same creature. And this is most appearant when it shows at the death screen what they used to kill you (pretty much always basic attack).
Now, the imp, and Druid, they have ranged attacks. the imp throws stones. and the Druid launches a level 300 something lightning bolt at you. Thankfully, you only aggro druids if you had killed innocent creatures (which give you stat bonuses), and you can run away with just 1 or 2 uses of your awakening (the game's "oh sh*t" button)
Unfortunately, the boss is basically like the basic monsters, except he is immune to the first 15 hits you land on him, including your pets' hits.
ART STYLE
look at the damned screen shots. I kinda like the style they went with.
COMBAT
Kind of falls into the same trap that the enemies did. You've got 3 equipment slots: weapon, armor, and accessory. Generally, you have swords(basic melee), spears/lances(melee to 2 squares), axes(melee, focused on wall/chest destruction), and bows for weapons. And that's really about it
Depending on the class you selected, you might have an active ability, but they are rarely all that useful, save for the knight's ironwall, which heals her and protects from damage...it's kinda insane. So, it's kinda like combat in D&D 3.5 "I hit him with my stick!" Over...and over...and over again. Thankfully, battles don't tend to last long, if you have a lot of strength...and if you don't, they still won't last long because you'll die.
You can throw objects from your inventory, but unless it's specialized for throwing...like rocks(???) or acid... it's not going to do much. Not to mention, acid does damage over time, giving the enemy that time to kill you. Best just to attack it.
You can beat down walls, so, you can create your own pathing, if you get stuck, or if the side of the building with the door is surrounded by mountains... It's neat.
LOOT
As discussed in the above, there aren't many weapons, but the other types of items you can collect and sell is quite expansive. If you're doing well, you're going to be carrying a sack of gold and goods heavier than an african elephant...mostly for food, and occassionally healing(maybe)...and throwing....if you want. But, although you have tons of gold, you can rarely find upgrades from merchants, it seems. So, you go fighting the boss, letting a couple hundred thousand gold coins weigh you down, after weeks of no sleep. (Sounds like a perfect storm.)
YOU KNOW?
I can't really think of anything to really say this is actually a GOOD game...but it was fun for the first 2 or 3 hours, even if I'm never going to touch it again. And for the price, it was quite worth while.

Even though One Way Heroics is kind of cheaply made in a sense -- being coded in Wolf RPG and somewhat unfortunately prone to crashing now and then -- I find it hard not to recommend. The best description I could give it is that it's a JRPG roguelike that's evocative of "The Neverending Story", a brilliant but bizarre fantasy movie from the 80's. Namely that One Way Heroics is about a hero trying outrun something like the Nothing from said movie -- a darkness slowly creeping and devouring the world -- and confronting evil while also deconstructing certain narrative tropes. I'm not going to spoil anything but while One Way Heroics has a simple story, it's not as simple as it may look and it hints at some deeper and admittedly stirring themes. Again, given all that, it's almost required for Generation Y gamers to occasionally put on the Neverending Story soundtrack esp. if they're playing a Hunter.
I consider it pretty much a must-play for anyone genuinely interested in eventually "getting into" roguelikes, as well for anyone who is interested in designing them. Like any other roguelike, you will die many times and rarely get to keep anything of substance from one run to another. Unlike most of them, One Way Heroics offers detailed feedback about how to improve your future runs and the game over screen NPCs are kind, sympathetic and encouraging. It also strikes a very tight balance between what choices a player has at any given time (especially in character creation) without compromising the unforgiving nature of the roguelike genre. It's also really neat to be playing one that takes place primarily in the great outdoors. On top of all that, the way seeds work lets you share worlds with other players and the game even tracks who is playing what world and when. Defeated players who were playing at the same time as you will even show up in your game to give you random items from their inventory. As I said, it's very novel.
Yeah, this isn't a $3.50 you need to second guess for even a moment if you're in the mood for something different or enjoy (or wish you could enjoy) roguelikes. I salute you, Smoking Wolf!
By the way, while the game does a great job of pretty much giving you all the advice you'll need to optimally play it (which I've never seen a roguelike EVER successfully do before now) I strongly recommend using the numpad to move instead of the arrow keys. Holding shift to change direction without moving is very useful too. Also it's not required, but if you see Queen Frieda please give her a hug for me.

This game is advertised as a real time strategy game, but it's not. It's more like a real time tactics game since you give units specific orders with specific inventories.
Anyway, I can't advise buying this after just playing the first level. I know it's not much, but when:
- Your units won't make decently intelligent decisions on cover fire and throwing grenades at machine gun nests or armored cars while the pause button requires unpausing and selecting new units manually to coordinate orders,
- Your tank randomly doesn't aim or shoot at targets for dozens of seconds at a time while shooting endlessly at other targets until you manually turn the tank a little right before the infantry with a sticky bomb gets right up to the tank (by the way, did I mention that any excess squadmates just sit on your tank while getting shot at and that your tank takes damage just from moving around?),
- The camera angle (not pitch) becomes a pain to handle, and
- Mission objectives require hunting down every last guy in an area rather than those guys engaging you to prevent you from running over their comrades in arms...
...you know this game's bad. People will say that I'm just bad at the game, but the game actually just has really clumsy controls and doesn't respond to them half the time. It reminds me of that stupid Jagged Alliance series.
If you want to play a decent real time tactics game, I'd suggest getting Fallout Tactics.
EDIT: I've played the first mission a second time, and it wasn't as bad. That said, defeating the enemy was rather ridiculous. This time, it didn't respond to my grenade attacks at all, and just let itself get blasted. The enemy had no bazookas, and its AT guns just got wrecked. The hill I had to take was pointless as well since the infantry just rushed my tank which mowed them down with its machine guns, and the convoy either got blasted to bits, or just ran by my tank. It hardly engaged, and the light tanks which did engage hardly damaged my tank even though the tracks got disabled three times. Unlike the first time I played, I was actually able to repair the tracks multiple times as well.
I don't know. The game seems to suffer from black or white thinking with little balance.

and is one that's hard to get over. Leave units unattended, and they lose all of their organization. The units need the player to survive.
's strength comes from
. Direct Control allows the player to use the mouse and kewyboard to move or shoot any of their tanks, troops, turrets, etc. Direct Control can make the difference in any battle because it lets creative combat take place. A well placed grenade thrown by a submachinegunner hidden in the rubble destroys a heavy tank's engine. An armoured car weaves through tight alleys and flanks a set of anti-tank guns. If you want a realistic RTS game that rewards creativity, buy

I did a review on this game on a site a couple of months ago so here we go:
Gameplay:
Mafia II has some of the best gameplay aspects in a sandbox game, and is by far one of my favourite games. The game features classical cars, weapons, music and a various of other things from the 1940's - 1950's era. The game has a variety of cool features, like feeling your car up with gas, opening and closing windows, robbing stores, modifying your vehicles, stealing cars, lock picking locks, climb through windows and various other things like that nature. Mafia II mainly focuses on the story driven gameplay rather that petty side missions that distract you from the story (like grand theft auto.) so people that love a good story I strongly recommend picking this game up. I love mafia games and mafia films, and this was just perfect and I am hoping they release another one. If you get bored within game you can collect some Playboy posters (which actually show nudity, I think their are 50 of them.) you can also collect wanted posters and other collectable items to keep you interested, I managed to collect and play as it was fun anyway and I did not get bored. I have played the game both on consoles and PC and love them on both, obviously I had a better time on pc since the higher frame rates and better graphics but it was still an awesome experience on console.
Graphics:
Mafia II; now this game just has overwhelming graphical aspects and visuals(especially for the time the game was released.) The game features awesome dynamic lighting, 3D Rendered models and high resolution textures. When playing the game my breath was taken away with the graphics. It included amazing reflections, no frame drops and feels like a solid build. I can't really explain the graphics other than they are some of the best visuals I have seen in a sandbox game; I'll prove that later on when I post some screen shots. The game runs of the Illusion Engine with PhysX, even though I have an AMD graphics card the game still did it's job and created an amazing experience. The game also uses real time cutscenes which are created by the Illusion Engine so they are not pre-rendered cutscenes, so if you have a half broken car, it will show that in the cutscene which is pretty awesome if you ask me. Some scenes are pre rendered such as the hotel explosion.
Ratings:
Gameplay: 10/10
Graphics: 9/10
Controls: 10/10
Plot: 9/10
Overall: 10/10
Conclusion:
Mafia 2 is one of the best game I have ever played; it's definitely worth buying and I would advise you buy it on pc, if you have a good enough pc that is... but console still gives an amazing experience nonetheless. I know the review has already been made but I felt like he did not do it justice; also thank you for your feedback and thank you for reading my review, I am really trying hard to achieve that Game Reviewer Badge and I also love playing games and going over them it's really cool to express your feelings on that game.

Do you want to feel like Spiderman? Here's your chance!  In A Story About My Uncle you are settling down with your daughter to put her to bed for the night and she asks you to tell her a story.  So you recount your adventure to find your Uncle.  Your Uncle is a quirky inventor who created a terrific body suit that can grapple and swing from long distances.  He also created a teleport pad to a new and wondrous world, and this is where you went to find him.
This intro gives the game a bit of a "Princess Bride" feel in that throughout the game you will hear conversations between you and your daughter as commentary on the story.  It's very cute, but I can imagine that the appeal of this cuteness is going to be more for adults than younger players.
The game is played through three primary settings.  The first setting will introduce you to the primary mechanic of the game, as well as the population of the world your uncle is adventuring in.  The second setting will augment your primary grapple ability and force you to creatively 'swing' from point to point.  The final stage introduces a new rocket boot mechanic and significantly ramps up the difficulty.  Even with the higher degree of difficulty, save points are plentiful.  You may find a few sections that require multiple sequences of swings before saving, but in most cases you will be rewarded with a save point at each step of forward progress.  In some cases there are multiple ways to move ahead, and you may even find that you traverse some sections by accident.
As I neared the conclusion of the game, I found that I alternated between frustration and joy.  Some maneuvers are truly difficult as you must master releasing the grapple at just the right moment to avoid flying directly into the object you have attached to.  In some case you cannot see the next grapple point until you have already committed to a jump.  The joy comes from the authentic feeling of flight and swinging, of completing a particularly difficult move.  I sometimes found myself, shoulders tensed, 'ducking' to avoid rocks and outcroppings.
A common complaint is that the game is short.  In an age of $3 apps, it can be hard to justify spending over $10 on a game that you may finish in less time than a standard length movie.  Even so, I feel like the experience is worth recommending.

This is one of those games where I really wish that Steam allowed for a numerical ratings system, or at least a "neutral" option for recommending or not.
If you've played the original Company of Heroes you'll know a lot of what to expect from the gameplay.  Capture resource points, build up your forces, and use them to smash through the enemy lines.
For players not familiar with the first CoH game it is worth noting that the relatively low unit cap does mean that you'll be relying on micro-managing the positioning of your units, where they're taking cover, and which way they're facing far more than in some other RTS games.  Tanks and crewed weapons are particularly notable for this, as tanks have different levels of armour on their different faces and some weapons can only be fired in the direction they are facing.
The single player campaign mixes things up a little with a slightly broader variety of missions, often giving you only limited numbers of troops to complete the mission rather than relying on you being able to build more.
One of the new additions to CoH 2 is perhaps one of the more controversial. Micro-transactions.  Like the original Company of Heroes you can select your commander during a battle, and this gives you access to new special powers or vehicles to call in.  However, in CoH 2 if you want more variety in the commanders you can select from (and, indeed, some of the ones with more powerful abilities) you'll either be grinding for a long time (read 40 hours or more per commander, and there's a lot of them) or you'll be paying out in micro-transactions.  You also won't see this ahead of time as these commanders are not available in the Steam store, only through the in-game shop.
Where the commanders just provide variety to mix up the abilities you have this isn't quite so bad.  Where they're a straight upgrade you can pay for to make you more powerful this is slightly harder to swallow.
The larger DLC available for the title has been a little more of a mixed bag, and it's worth noting that single player and multiplayer content has been split for the DLC.  Where the original CoH tended to have a single player campaign accompanying the new forces as they were released, this one doesn't.  Keep that in mind when eyeing up the DLC; the British forces can only be used in multiplayer and skirmishes, and the Ardennes Assualt pack is single-player only (you need to purchase the US multiplayer/skirmish pack separately).
In the end, my decision to recommend this game was a difficult one. When the game was first launched at a more expensive price, with the amount of content that was locked off, it would have been easy to not recommend it at that time.  However, with the drop in the price of the base game this isn't quite so bad, but with the cost of the micro-transaction commanders not insignificant it still feels slightly like you're buying part of a game to start with, then being nickel-and-dimed for the rest of it.
If you're a fan of WWII RTS games and you see this on sale (or if you're going to be happy playing skirmish or multiplayer with just the limited selection of commanders) then definitely pick up the game.  If you're after the single player content, then you'll want to grab the game and some of the DLC packs.

I got about an hour into the game. Got distracted by something else and didn’t go back to it for more than a year. I decided to give it another chance and I’m really happy I did. It really managed to get some hooks in me.
With hindsight one of the things I like a most about this game is that it has multiple endings based off of a morality points system, that is almost entirely hidden from you. I think too many games hold your hand too much when it comes to choices. You may as well be asked, “Would you like the good ending or the bad ending?” Metro judges you silently and gives you what you earned at the end of it.
