There were a couple of levels where I thought the checkpoints were very far apart. Even for the lowest difficulty settings. Finally, for whatever reason, I couldn’t get the game to play nicely with OBS. So streaming it was a headache.
In short. Great game, good quality remaster. Lore and story is super interesting to me. It plays well. Could run better than it does. But overall I would recommend it. I’m looking forward to playing the next one.

This game is something special and is unlike any other RPG... maybe even game, that I've ever played. Not because of the gameplay, which is for the most part not that original - 2D side-scrolling RPG with a standard old-school, turn-based battle system.
What makes this game special is partially the story, but mostly the world everything revolves in. It's post-apocalyptic, but hardly hopeful. It's merciless and bleak and the few places there's hope to find it's almost entirely based on desperately clinging onto something to a degree that's it's tragic. And there's tragedy aplenty.
I have to applaud the game for doing something that so preciously few games do these days - provide hard choices. And by hard I mean putting you in situations where there is no right or no wrong - only consequences, and bad ones at that. You have to choose what you believe is the lesser evil while knowingly accepting that the consequence of your choice sets you back in some way.
This is common in old-school RPGs, but I have to give it credit for the amount of small and absurd little secrets there are hidden all over as well. It makes the game that much more entertaining and you really feel like exploring the world, which  is fascinating enough in its own right.
Definitely recommendable if you want to try an RPG that stands out from the rest.

*WARNING* THIS GAME IS A SEQUEL TO A GAME CALLED 'LISA: THE FIRST', A MAJOR PLOTPOINT WILL BE CONFUSING AND MAKE NO SENCE, SO GO PLAY THAT.
LISA is on the same par as classics like MOTHER 3 and FFVII, and this game is sure to go down in history as one of the greatest RPGs ever made. This game is brutal in every sense of the word, the game can be soul-crushingly challenging, gut-bustingly hilarious, and unfathomably depressing and somber. The game's strongest aspect is the fantastic story that  takes you on a grand quest to save your adopted daughter and shelter her from the cruel and unforgiving world that seeks to use her for its own gain. The game will constantly be throwing very heavy descisions at you, and unlike games like Mass Effect or The Walking Dead, your actions have very serous immediate and long term effects that change gameplay, the story, and the world as a whole. There are over 30 different followers for you to recruit on your journey, and it is incredibly easy to miss out on meeting new allies, and it's also incredibly easy to permanently loose them. Combat in this game is your somewhat standard turn-based RPG affair, but there are plenty of clever twists that make fighting more fun and memorable, like characters that input combos, build up a special meter, and characters who buff and heal the party. This game is somewhat bipolar, and the constant switching between (incredibly funnycomedy and tragedy makes the game a very surreal experience, and the mood whiplash can leave you completley flabbergasted. If i had any real problems with the game it would be the lack of a map, although you gain the ability to warp to and from specific zones, which somewhat help the issue. People who are easily lost or have no navigational abilities what-so-ever will have trouble navigating the world, and will end up very frustrated.
Prepare your feel hole for complete and udder destruction. this is the single saddest experience i have ever felt, and ihave spent long sleepless nights staring into my ceiling, lost in thought. If you are emotionally unstable, this game WILL break you.
TL;DR, I would give this game a 10/10, it is a masterpiece, and nearly every sprite has tiny cute nipples.

It could at least have wrapped up with a feel-good ending, something nice happening to inspire Vinty and help her find a new direction for her life; but instead I can't decide whether the ending is a joke that doesn't work or the developer just got tired of the story.
The funniest part of this is that there are prominent "Q.Save", "Q.Load", "Save", and "Load" buttons for a game that can be played through to the "good" end in less than five minutes and which can be clicked through to the end in less than fifteen seconds.
Extremely short, doesn't really tell much of a story, and the art is only so-so. Even for free, probably not worth your time.

YHtWtG is a simple little Metroidvania. Your only actions are moving, jumping, and falling down through platforms. Later on you acquire a couple new powers, but they're basically just variations on those actions. Run around retro caverns and hop across pixelated mushrooms in order to collect money bags and hearts, find the four power-ups, and make your way to the end.
It appears to have taken some inspiration from Jet Set WIlly, and perhaps also from VVVVVV which was itself inspired in part by JSW. YHtWtG ups the retro by making the default visual style a warped tube TV type deal. Sound effects are also sufficiently retro.
There's really not a whole lot to write here. It's a rather short game. There's an achievement for finishing in under 10 minutes, though that will require some dedication. Expect to finish in maybe around an hour or so your first time. More if you're going for 100%.
You will likely find yourself running back and forth and revisiting areas often on your first playthrough. There's not usually an obvious path forward, but with each power-up many possibilities open and one of them will inevitably take you the next power-up. Once you have all four, you can reach the end which is actually kind of hidden. Once you know where it is, it's actually not so impossible to find. The problem for me was, I walked right past it and didn't even take notice of the route. But hey, that's part of the charm I think.
You Have to Win the Game won't take overly long to finish, but for $0 it won't cost you overly much to play. So it kind of balances out.

Even though One Way Heroics is kind of cheaply made in a sense -- being coded in Wolf RPG and somewhat unfortunately prone to crashing now and then -- I find it hard not to recommend. The best description I could give it is that it's a JRPG roguelike that's evocative of "The Neverending Story", a brilliant but bizarre fantasy movie from the 80's. Namely that One Way Heroics is about a hero trying outrun something like the Nothing from said movie -- a darkness slowly creeping and devouring the world -- and confronting evil while also deconstructing certain narrative tropes. I'm not going to spoil anything but while One Way Heroics has a simple story, it's not as simple as it may look and it hints at some deeper and admittedly stirring themes. Again, given all that, it's almost required for Generation Y gamers to occasionally put on the Neverending Story soundtrack esp. if they're playing a Hunter.
I consider it pretty much a must-play for anyone genuinely interested in eventually "getting into" roguelikes, as well for anyone who is interested in designing them. Like any other roguelike, you will die many times and rarely get to keep anything of substance from one run to another. Unlike most of them, One Way Heroics offers detailed feedback about how to improve your future runs and the game over screen NPCs are kind, sympathetic and encouraging. It also strikes a very tight balance between what choices a player has at any given time (especially in character creation) without compromising the unforgiving nature of the roguelike genre. It's also really neat to be playing one that takes place primarily in the great outdoors. On top of all that, the way seeds work lets you share worlds with other players and the game even tracks who is playing what world and when. Defeated players who were playing at the same time as you will even show up in your game to give you random items from their inventory. As I said, it's very novel.
Yeah, this isn't a $3.50 you need to second guess for even a moment if you're in the mood for something different or enjoy (or wish you could enjoy) roguelikes. I salute you, Smoking Wolf!
By the way, while the game does a great job of pretty much giving you all the advice you'll need to optimally play it (which I've never seen a roguelike EVER successfully do before now) I strongly recommend using the numpad to move instead of the arrow keys. Holding shift to change direction without moving is very useful too. Also it's not required, but if you see Queen Frieda please give her a hug for me.

Key features:
- JRPG look and feel
- No location transition; everything happens on the overworld map
- Shadow pressing you to move on vs stick around longer to explore more of this town/dungeon
- Turn-based
- JRPG style menu system
- Running non-stop, your hero still require sustenance
- Items have limited durability
- With each death (or victory) you gain hero points, which can be used to purchase more options (and thus more freedom) in future games
- Item vault to transfer items to your next characters. Item vault size is expanded by using hero points
- Unlockable classes
- Unlockable perks
- Randomly generated world with a short text-based random seed
- Many features in the world which you can explore. (I found some high-end merchants hidden inside a mountain once. Was too slow to get back out).
- You can replay a world by entering the seed
- Fast paced. You can easily win a game in one sitting
- Online events everyday. There are worlds with special rules which you can play in
- Multiple difficulty levels can be unlocked
- Great attention to details that will make you smile
- Steam cards and achievements
This $2.69 will be the best $2.69 you've ever spent.

I've only just scratched the surface of this game (3 runs so far), and yet I'm already so happy with it.  There's a large variance of items, the character types and skills feel unique from one another, and even though the game is constantly pushing you forwards (it's quite literally "One Way"), I don't feel rushed at all while playing.  It's an excellent game to play for a short break or a long session of multiple games, and the RPG & Rouge-Like elements blend seamlessly.  On top of that, it has a top-notch soundtrack and intuitive scoring system.
I can't even say all of these things about some AAA titles.  This is a small Indie game.  If there's one Indie game under $5 that's worth your time, it's this one.  I would go as far as to recommend it to people who have never even glanced at a Rouge-Like before.

A Story About My Uncle is a game that presented itself to me as quite promising with its amazing atmosphere which sucked me in from the beginning. I was later led to disappointment as I realized just how little story there actually is and that the game relies on using cliffhangers to keep the player going. I was fine with this until I completed the game and was left quite unsatisfied. The game made me very eager to see just what would happen next as I swung from stage to stage hoping that I'd get some dialogue. The ending left me quite disappointed as I saw the developer could've done much more with the game. A lot of players have trouble with this game (refer to the other reviews for this, mostly the negative). I find that this is what gives players their play time. The developer is asking $13 for a game that could take a player 1-3 hours to complete (depending on just how much they die).
-----------------------------------------------------
Pro/Con Version
Pros
- What little dialogue there is can drive your curiosuity enough to keep you playing.
- Amazing atmosphere.
- Fun gameplay.
Cons
- Very little dialogue.
- 1-3 hours of gameplay.
- Monotone narrator/unconvincing voice actors (don't let the narrator's beautiful voice fool you!)
- Massive price tag for how long the game is.
-----------------------------------------------------
Conclusion: I'd say get it on sale, it's a very fun game however its price tag is just quite demanding. For a story based game the story really isn't there; the atmosphere is. You could get something that'll get you more for your buck elsewhere.

In all seriousness, though, this game is a really immersive tabletop RPG. Character sheet is just like the tabletop game, format, appearance, stats, and all. It's welcoming to new players of tabletop and veterans. The scenery was really well done for its time, and with a dedicated fanbase, only gets better. The voice acting (in my opinion) was spot on. I have had one friend that watched me play this that said the voice acting was terrible without excuses, he might've been trolling me, but I feel the opposite. My hours are wonky, but I've been playing this on disc since I was a junior in high school and when I wrote this review, I was in my third year of college, and I've been playing the tabletop games even longer than that. The music, I won't lie, it sets a mood but you kinda wish you could hear nightclub songs better, but maybe that's just me. I'm still looking for where Type O Negative played. As far as the character quiz, it's great for customizing your stats off the bat or if you just kinda wanna play around a bit. As far as clan picking though, I'm 90% sure it's random, so just be prepared ahead of time. The game is not trying to insult you when it says it thinks you're Nosferatu. Also, this can be a scary game, but that isn't the full intention. There are creepy moments, and even a few jump scares, but this game is primarily a mystery game, lots of puzzles, lots of obscure details, be open minded to a lot of "stupid" ideas you might have for the solution, because this game can be very fickle.
(Side note) I don't know about anyone else, but when you get into the lore of this game and White Wolf's world that they created, I feel this is an entirely possible scenario. Vampire society (among others) that blends with human society so well... it's just eerie to think about, you know? All of a sudden, you're checking over your shoulder, looking around for abnormalities at night, all because the World of Darkness seems all too realistic. Keep that in mind.
All in all, this is probably my favorite game of all time. It's content is great, I recommend the game to literally every person I'm friends with, sometimes going as far as buying the game for some of them to encourage they play. No complaints (yet...). Yes, the base game is buggy, and you NEED to find a patch for it starting out, but if that's the worst issue, this game is still worth the money (take notes, No Man's Sky), and is usually on sale anyway.
Are you ready to learn of the World of Darkness? I was.
10/10. White Wolf, please come back and make another.

FTL is a surprisingly entertaining, tough little turn-based game about a starship that tries to reach its destination followed by an enemy fleet. With each turn you get to explore planets along the way and get various events with multiple choice answers. Even the outcomes of the same events may differ. Is the alien refugee really in danger or is he a saboteur working for the enemy (this time)?
As you advance through the galaxy, with each move you make the chasing fleet comes closer. So you don't have unlimited time and have to watch out that they don't catch up to you. The fights are challenging, especially towards the end. It took me 6 hours to get through. More than expected. But you can pause the game anytime to think about the next move and trust me, you will need it.
When the hull breaks, fires start spreading around the ship, systems are getting damaged and intruders knock on your door it can be tricky to react in time. FTL won't give you time to get bored. Unless you land on an empty system with no other events then looking out the window.
I only finished the game once, but the replay value is high. So many different routes, ships, weapons and strategies to try.
The tutorial could be bigger. It covers only the most basic options. You will have to figure out the rest. Learning by doing. Normally that's not the best thing, but it's the whole concept of the game. And it works.
edit: 13 hours of play. My first playthrough was the only one (out of 4) where I managed to finish the game. Funny fact about FTL: It's not whether you finish it or not, but how far you will get before you get killed. Sounds frustrating, but somehow it isn't. It actually motivates you to try again and prevent the mistakes that got you killed last time.
I tried a couple other ships with different races as crew. They all play very different and rely on different weapon systems. So that's one way to learn what every weapon or system is good for ^^

Helldivers is a tongue in cheek mixture of Judge Dread, Starship Troopers, and some Orwellian nightmare made real.  You play a raw recruit that will die, over and over again to fight in the war against the bugs, the borgs, and the squids.  In the 2 hours I have on record so far, the game has made me laugh out loud, sit on the edge of my seat, smile like an idiot, and just about rage quit.
This is not a game for sissy mary's, you are going to die, a lot. especially if you play solo where it always seems like you have to reload at the WORST possible time, where calling in a defensive turret or some other strategem is always going to be an edge of your seat skin of your teeth affair.
This is an unapolagetically twisted and violent twin stick shooter, which works pretty darn well with mouse and keys (I like the controller, but you lose a LOT of accuracy with your weapon).  The action is frenetic and satisfying, and the carnage is everywhere.
In a very real sense, this game plays like a moving tower defense game, at least in the sense that as much as you need to move around and explore to complete objectives, a LOT of the key objectives revolve around defening an object for XYZ time while enemies flock to your location.  This is good, but predictable, and is both part of what is fun, and annoying, because if you are playing solo, or even with a team you will need to use your "strategems" to survive (at the moment the defense turret is my oh S#@t button.   Strategems are these special abilities that range from ammo drops, respawns, air support bomb runs, and defensive turrets etc.
However, you don't simply select what you want and it drops for you... Oh no, the game uses a brilliant mechanic where you need to input an up up down down konami style code to use these special items, and in the heat of battle this can be both infuriating, and brilliantly exhilarating.
Of course what modern game would be complete without loads of unlocks and things to improve your power... Every mission has slews of items you can collect to give you research points you can dump into weapons that you want to improve, and strategems you want to buy.
All of your efforts go toward a global campaign that everyone who plays contributes toward.  The forces of Super earth are at war on three fronts, and as the humans win, or lose, the galactic map changes, offering new worlds to fight on, new environments, and more.  Eventually through community effort, the humans either gain victory points, or the aliens do, and if enough victory points are accumulated by the human players, the humans will advance till they reach the alien homeworld.  Take that, and that part of the war is over.
The war ends when the humans conquer all 3 aliens, or when one of them reaches Super earth.
So there is always incentive to keep fighting. To add just a few more points to the war effort.
In addition the multiplayer has a report/commendation system where good players can get commendations and this ranks them as a good player worth playing with, the matchmaker does it's best to match you with suitably good players, while people who get reported at lot (usually for being a griefer etc), get limited to only being able to join people with a similar bad rep.  This bad rep takes time to go away, and good comendations can repair your standings reasonably quick.  I don't know how well this works to limit griefing, but judging by the community opinion of the game, it must work well enough!
Sadly, I haven't tried the game with a group yet, I want to play it with RL friends more than strangers, and didn't want to be an embarrassment to a team of oher players who might know what they are doing.  So for my first 2 hours I avoided it.  Now I'm about ready to try, and from all accounts, multiplayer (with friends or strangers) is where this game shines.
I already like it a lot, and I expect when I get going with multiplayer I will be hooked.

What makes LISA special is not gameplay but narrative. It is unrelentingly dark. If Cormac McCarthy and Quentin Tarantino got together to write a video game, LISA would be it. You have to make choices that will genuinely upset you. Bad things will happen, sometimes randomly, sometimes because of something you did earlier, and all you can do is face the music. Humor shines like an oil slick on the ceaseless tide of suffering that the game presents. LISA is a study in misery, redemption, sacrifice, and betrayal, and yet it is deeply engaging and worthwhile in a way that few games today manage. It's the game everybody who grew up playing the same JRPG over and over again as a kid realizes that they deserved to be playing all along.
It's just like The Room all over again: Lisa is tearing you apart.
Intensly sad and dark......................but fun :D

One Way Heroics plays like your typical mystery dungeon game, but this time, it's a bit different. Your dungeon is a randomly generated overworld that scrolls in one direction, dotted with enemies, dungeons, towns, and treasure. What I love most about the game is that at the conclusion of a runthrough, you're rated based on your actions and progress which in turn rewards you with points used to unlock new classes, new perks, or expand our dimensional vault(a storage that allows you to bring over items from a previous gameplay).
The game is a great price, only three dollars and it has alot of replay value. Even if you beat normal and hard modes, there are other modes that are updated and added into the mix every so often that challenges you with a new way to play.

Metro 2033 Redux  is a remastered FPS based on a popular novel of the same name. You play a young Russian named Artyum during the year 2033 who lives among others in an underground bunker due to the world around you being eradicated by nuclear warfare. Now there's nothing but destroyed buildings and mutants walking among the lands. Oh and Nazis and Commies , they're there too!
This is a fantastic game , that has a few hiccups that may or may not have to do with the engine upgrade however the storyline and the characters are so interesting and whacky that there's a lot here to be into. The gameplay is pretty great too. For such a small team to create this game , it's impressive and I can see why it has the following now it has.
Pros:
-Story is really great. It's not the most "wowing" story of all time but it's interesting.
-The way things look , the broken buildings , the bunkers and stations filled with people talking to each other and military , the mutants, the way some of the particles look in the dark look really fantastic. Sometimes you'll find yourself stopping to hear full conversations with some of the npcs around the bunkers. Some fascinating stuff that really fleshes out the world, I really wish more games would do this.
-Gameplay kinda feels like an early FPS and it's fun to stealth around a map and take someone out as well.
-AI is very smart in some spots of the game.
-The choice of Survival or Spartan mode before playing. I went Survival just to get the full experience.
-The music is really great too. Lots of acoustic and some piano. Some really spooky stuff at times and a lot of it makes the game.
-A lot of your comrades are real characters and you'll enjoy their parts of the story. One of them is hilarious. Bit*ches!
-Some fun secrets to find if you can get off the beaten path.
Cons:
-At some point of the game you obtain Night Vision. And the game does not explain to you how to get it to work out side of saying "hit the N Key". You get a charger early in the game , like super early. That they ALSO do not explain how to use, this powers up your Night Vision and your Flashlight. Just gotta hold F and click....
-The game also does not explain how to use the
Later in the game. You have to hold R and click to pump it... Very important.
-Since I Played on survival , the ammo etc is more scarse. But for some reason around Chapter 5-6 there's like no ammo , anywhere. Period. You run out , you're screwed. The last chapter or so was a nightmare for me because all I had was my
and no ammo for any of the guns. I even picked up a new gun and it had like 3 ammo. Was very upset by this.
-Keys are like easy to find for the first 3 chapters then it just becomes a mess. You'll end up finding vaults before you find keys...Wish they made this slightly easier, maybe highlight keys more. Things get more dicey when there's 2 keys in a level..
-Wiping your Gas Mask feels useless. Just smears sh*it all across the screen , unless it's blood...that goes away.
Mixed:
*Nitpicking*
-Just wish there were more gun types , more playstales. I feel like every gun even when you fully customize them is super limited and the reloads take forever. It could be because I played on Survival though.
-Some graphical glitches occur throughout the game, I actually noticed this happens in the trailer for Redux too. It's not enough to bother you but they exist. Especially when characters sweat.
Anyways play this game. The libarians are scary as fu*ck. Enjoy. Gonna start Last Light now.

I must say that i have never expected to enjoy a Space Invaders clone as much as this.
So, starting the game, you are confronted with a settings menu that contains everything you need and some excellent music (soundtrack is included when you buy the main game) prematurely filling you with adrenaline that you will need later on. Then there's the selection between gamemodes being:
Jumping into it i admit that i saw nothing but a weak space ship in a take on the classic coin-eating Space Invaders, but it didn't differ from the original enough to keep me interested. That was until it started borrowing some of Galaga's complexity, and classic shmup elements and pacing from the bullet hells such as CRIMZON CLOVER. And that is basically what this is, classic arcade Space Invaders/Galaga with shmup elements thrown into it.
But somehow, Void Invaders succeeds in not feeling like another one of these unoriginal ripoffs as instead of blending different existing games together, it does that and adds more to it. They added
of new enemies and bosses with original patterns and also new shmup-like temporary upgrade pick ups with not only "more bullets in a wider range", but besides that also a handful of unique upgrades that cause different playstyles and pacing, much like Bit Blaster XL.
What also differs Void Invaders from other Space Invaders clones is that the general amount of♥♥♥♥♥♥happening on the screen is not inserted merely for the sake of eyerape. It actually adds to the aesthetic of the game. FTL is a surprisingly entertaining, tough little turn-based game about a starship that tries to reach its destination followed by an enemy fleet. With each turn you get to explore planets along the way and get various events with multiple choice answers. Even the outcomes of the same events may differ. Is the alien refugee really in danger or is he a saboteur working for the enemy (this time)?
As you advance through the galaxy, with each move you make the chasing fleet comes closer. So you don't have unlimited time and have to watch out that they don't catch up to you. The fights are challenging, especially towards the end. It took me 6 hours to get through. More than expected. But you can pause the game anytime to think about the next move and trust me, you will need it.
When the hull breaks, fires start spreading around the ship, systems are getting damaged and intruders knock on your door it can be tricky to react in time. FTL won't give you time to get bored. Unless you land on an empty system with no other events then looking out the window.
I only finished the game once, but the replay value is high. So many different routes, ships, weapons and strategies to try.
The tutorial could be bigger. It covers only the most basic options. You will have to figure out the rest. Learning by doing. Normally that's not the best thing, but it's the whole concept of the game. And it works.
edit: 13 hours of play. My first playthrough was the only one (out of 4) where I managed to finish the game. Funny fact about FTL: It's not whether you finish it or not, but how far you will get before you get killed. Sounds frustrating, but somehow it isn't. It actually motivates you to try again and prevent the mistakes that got you killed last time.
I tried a couple other ships with different races as crew. They all play very different and rely on different weapon systems. So that's one way to learn what every weapon or system is good for ^^

"Just a few hit points on the hull, and these are the final moments of FTL. My sweaty hands press sweaty buttons as the flagship bears down upon the S.S. A-Hole. If only my Mom could see me now."
Let’s start off with the basics — FTL is a Rogue-LITE. There’s permadeath, but that’s about the only thing that really connects it to the classic concept of a rogue-like game. In fact, I think FTL is basically its own classification. I’ve never really played anything quite like it before, and it was refreshing to see a new concept on the market.
Let’s talk about the pros.
FTL’s gameplay is super solid. So far, I’ve come across no bugs at all, everything works as it should. The tutorial correctly explains each mechanic, and they’re each so simple that I thought at first the game would be a dud. Oh boy, how I was wrong. These simple mechanics scale into a huge atmosphere of strategy, where each move you make could decide your life or death in the final battle with the flagship.
Just like in XCOM, you get attached to your crew super quickly, and when one dies it’s almost enough to rage quit. Each race manages to bring a different component to your crew, which again adds to the overall strategy.
The combat relies on your micromanagement of different weapons, and your outfit in general. It’s satisfying to find a weapons strategy that destroys the enemy. Thankfully, there isn’t just ONE strategy to choose from, although they all revolve around your opponent’s shields.
"One by one, my crew members are dead. The shields are down, the weapons turn orange, this is the end. But I know I just need a one more shot. I can do this."
Them cons tho.
FTL does fall short in a few instances, and none bigger than the lore. If FTL could create a real world around it’s fantastic gameplay, the game would be SO MUCH BETTER. Also, the text-heavy encounters try to be physiologically difficult to decide on, but honestly it’s super easy to figure them out.
Another large shortcoming is the lack of weapon variety and quest variety. Even with the expanded universe I find quests that I’ve already done and are super easy to do again with my foreknowledge. I just can’t see myself replaying this with so little variety.

I tried this game on the free weekend it had in October, and then bought it on sale after just a few hours of gameplay.
PROS:
-Rules are simple, and gameplay is straightforward.
-Missions are relatively quick, and other players can join mid mission.  Which can be VERY nice, because there are times you are getting wrecked and need the backup.
-Unlockable and upgradeable weapons, stratagems, and gear.  As you defeat other planets, you unlock more and more gear.  Each mission you can find these little items laying on the ground, and once you collect enough you earn an upgrade point.  Those can be spent to improve all of your equipment/weapons.  It isn't at a grueling pace to get them either, so you will usually be able to improve equipment often enough.
-Teamwork.  This game really leans heavy on playing the harder difficulties with others.  Because otherwise you would be overwhelmed and die.  Some folks may list this in the CON section, but I feel like the company did a good job at making this aspect work really well.
CONS:
-There are 3 enemy races.  You are pushing into their territory and killing them off, etc.  Once a "sector" of planets is conquered, it is locked off.  The game is "real time," meaning all players share that status of the sector locked off, so if you never played that region then you have to wait for the war to "Reset."  And that could be regions to unlock more gear you do not have yet.  Kind of a bummer.  That is pretty much the only real drawback of this game.
OTHER:
-Friendly Fire!  Oh man...this can be upsetting moments, or funny moments.  You can easily shoot a teammate.  Might do only moderate damage, so no big deal.  Or you were firing a rocket launcher and you aim was♥♥♥♥♥♥poor.  Results may vary.  You can also call in a piece of equipment that is a mech, and accidentally walk on teammates and crush them.  OOPS!
-The story/environment of the game is VERY entertaining!  While in the hub area of your ship, there is scrolling news stories at the bottom of the screen.  They are purely for fun/flavor, and can be quite hilarious!  It has a very...Starship Troopers type of feel to it.  You are Helldivers going out to "spread democracy" with your guns!  Your characters even say similarly motivating (brain washed) things while running around during missions.

If you have 3 friends and dont mind blowing them up then this twin stick shooter is for you!

Though the idea of a "time-limited RPG" threw me off at first, I quickly realized that this game has such huge potential, and is a very fun game.
If you can get past the first few playthroughs without wanting to hit a cheatcode button for every monster that chases you, then you have a very playable and fun game. The game is set in the style of an old Japanese RPG but with the twist of the Darkness coming from the left side of the screen, essentially moving roughly 1/3 - 5/12 of a block every turn. You have to continue running to the right and beating off monsters that hunt you down like a wild animal. There are multiple difficulty levels in this game, starting with a Walk in the Park difficulty, which is where the End-Boss appears at 400 km and you get npcs to help you when he appears (basically easy mode).
There are multiple choices of class in this game, each with it's own Steam achievement, and each with it's own unique skill set/passive stats. The 8 different classes are Swordmaster, Knight, Hunter, Pirate, Bard, Adventurer, Force User (Mage), and Hero. Some of the classes are rather overpowered, where they can one hit anything with a sword or axe that has at least 10-15 Attack power, and some of them are very weak, requiring you to play like a coward and run until you can get a Holy item or find equipment that makes you super powered. Although there is a lack of creativity in the active skills of each class (basically just Awakening, and some skill you learn at level 1), the uniques are nice to play around with. For example, the pirate has a maxed out Swimming unique, where he uses only 1 turn to swim instead of 5. In terms of playability with the classes, you essentially master one, usually the Hero class, and run through the whole thing playing strategically.
There is an element of playability where you can transfer over items that you really like or want to use on a different playthrough called the Dimensional Vault. After you die or beat the game, you can place items, up to a limit, in the Vault and access it through your next character. This was a nice idea, but I feel like instead of having a NPC that you have to talk to in order to access it, there should be an option to ask you if you want to access your vault at the very beginning of the game, after you've already started. Another thing the developers added were perks. There is a very limited number of perks, and it's a nice addition. Lastly, there is the Heroics leve ratings, where you get rated from F - SS on how well you did in the criteria of Levels, Battles, Chests looted, and Distance. This was really sweet, and there is also the bonus points that you get for certain actions, like killing no friendly characters. This portion makes you want to play again until you get it right, and I loved it. It could definitely be expanded upon.
I really enjoyed the dimensions, but it feels very plain when using "Create random dimension". When you create a random dimension, it's just a normal dimension with everything placed around differently, no bonuses to equipment, unique NPCs that can join you, or any of that sort. It's just a map with the areas randomized. However, every day, the game updates a few special campaign dimension, about 3-4, and they have unique differences. Some have stronger monsters for more experience, others have a special NPC that you can recruit. Those are nice, but they only change once a day, and though it's a nice catch to get people to play every day, when you beat the game a couple times, it gets very boring and you lose interest of even looking at the list.
That being said, the time you do spend playing this game would be worth it, especially for a low price. It's super cheap, fun for a good amount of time, and you can replay through the campaigns as much as you want. The perks are very limited however, and I do hope they update it to have a comprehensive list of unique skills, and possibly vary the classes more to feel more balanced.

Wow, this game actually got me thinking a lot. When it was on sale, I decided it was time for me to try a new genre (Indie RPG from the store page) and little did I expect it to be one of the best games I've played.
Let's start with the gameplay and content. LISA is a side scrolling RPG with pretty humourous cutscenes and events. Most of these events also have crude references to other games/ TV entertainment shows or just plain irritating (like the _l_ , play it to find out xD). Combat can be pretty tough at times too, but the option to mix and match party members and layer members' skills really make combat unique and entertaining.
However, DO NOT assume that's all LISA offers. There is actually a mindblowing story which is very dark and while confusing at the start, bits of information will be given as you play the game or explore hidden locations. Only halfway into the game did I realise this game was about CHOICES. Your choices have direct impact on your character's outlook, abilities, your friends' survival, and an optional cutscene at the end; choosing to sleep in the open randomly triggers events that may result in abandonment, theft or kidnappings, but you could also be surprised with a gift from a stranger.
To be honest, I did not completely understsand the story until I Googled and found out about LISA the First (LtF in short). From there, things became much clearer and even more mindblowing. For me, I chose to play the game in PAIN mode and I had difficulty winning some crucial fights here and there and I had to replay a large portion of the story. Players who start with normal difficulty could replay the game to recruit as many teammates as possible for steam achivements, but I would still recommend the PAIN mode for the first playthrough. Go PAIN or go home!
10/10

What!? You're giving "You Have to Win the Game" a thumbs down, but you gave VVVVVV a thumbs up!? Where is your logic! I don't see it on you! Are you even human?
Yes, I didn't care for "You Have to Win the Game" as much, yet I still enjoy playformers like VVVVVV. Why? Well, it's very simple. And I'll explain that in a second. YHtWtG is really good on graphics. The purples (or I  guess reds, as the game calls them), are beautiful to look at. The challenge is acceptable, emulating the same fair-checkpoint system that VVVVVV had. But I personally thought that THtWtG was just a little stale. It felt too much like every other platformer I'd played, with the same tight controls as VVVVVV. It just didn't stick out as much to me. I feel like it would've been a lot stronger if the bosses were actually bosses instead of hazards like every other enemy in the world, and that you'd get your powers for double-jump and spider-climb at the beginning and that the whole game was centered around you unlocking new blocks for places for you to explore.
I also don't like the win/lose portion at the end. If I've played through the whole game and gotten to the end, I'd like some form of recognition, but you can only win or lose from some arbitrary secret-word game.
Now, some of my complaints stop very quickly, because the game is free. And, yes, it is fun. But aside from the lack of memorability, or charm, or real humor (besides the VVVVVV-esque way of titling your screen something clever)... "You Have to Win the Game" just doesn't impress me.

This is one of those few games that can be considered a gem. With exhilirating combat, a tragic campaign from the eyes of a 501st trooper, and full mod support, this game is every Star Wars fan's dream. The combat is quite satisfying. Even in the heat of battle, you'll hear troops cracking jokes and saying witty lines on the battlefield. Become a legendary Star Wars hero or villain, from Darth Maul to Anakin Skywalker. Pilot walkers, tanks, anything to cause your dreams of destruction. In space, you have full control of your craft, no assisted flight, auto-lock, nothing. It's another game inside a game. Board enemy ships and wreak havoc. Take part in exhilirating dogfights and show the galaxy who is the best starfighter pilot.
The campaign spans the time between from the fall of the Galactic Republic all the way to the rise of the Galactic Empire. It provides small details that give key information to the overall saga, all from the POV of a 501st Legion clone trooper, later a stormtrooper of Vader's Fist. Take caution however, because this game is considered "Legends" material, which is the title given to any Star Wars media (Other than the movies, Star Wars Rebels, and Star Wars: The Clone Wars.) that was released prior to 2014, since story details don't fit or may contradict the new Disney canon.
Finally, mods. A key player in Battlefront II, it can make or break your game, depending on where you install one from. Tired of playing the same maps over and over? Install the Battlefront II Conversion pack from Moddb, which adds new maps, planets, heroes, and more. Install the Battlefront III Legacy mod, and experience what Free Radical Studio's version of the Battlefront franchise would've felt like before its cancellation. The possibilities are endless.
Overall, Star Wars: Battlefront II is a must-have for any Star Wars fan out there. It provides a quality experience of the Star Wars universe from a soldier's point of view, and is able to play out your wildest fantasies.

My friend recommended Metro 2033, and I decided to try it since I was in search of a single player FPS adventure. What I got was far more than a mere single player FPS adventure. Unlike what I'd expect from FPS games, the focus on Metro 2033 is
on combat, but rather traversing the post-apocalyptic wasteland of Russia on a mission to get somewhere for plot reasons that I won't spoil, and finding ways to get past tense scenarios. There's a lot I liked about Metro 2033, and a lot I disliked, all of which I'll cover in my review with a tl;dr at the end for those who just want the key points of my review.
I'll start with the gameplay itself; there's two gameplay options, "Survival" and "Spartan". Survival mode is the ideal Metro 2033 experience, with resources and ammo few and far between; you have to approach each encounter and scenario wisely and cautiously, even resorting to stealth often to get by. I haven't played many stealth-oriented games (not even Metal Gear), but I really enjoyed how stealth works in Metro 2033 (as it's far more enjoyable than, for example, Payday 2's excuse of a Stealth system). The other gameplay mode, Spartan, is for people who want a more traditional FPS adventure; ammo and materials are more readily provided, so you can approach each scenario guns blazing and rely on your FPS skills to get through the game. There are also four difficulties to choose from that suit the player's skill level for the most enjoyable and/or immersive experience, and
However, the two harder difficulties increase both player damage and enemy damage, so it often feels like the enemies can soak up quite a few bullets and attacks on the easier difficulties.
I played this game exclusively at night with headphones on to maximize immersion, and what I appreciate the most about the game is that the "Horror" tag is just there in-name only. I
horror games
, and Metro 2033 is more tense than scary; there are no jumpscares, and fighting for your life in various parts of the game really gets the adrenaline pumping. I think this game is best enjoyed when immersed in the world and atmospheres it provides.
Another thing I liked about the game was the weapon system; there are several different weapons and ways to modify them, and no two weapons feel the same; each weapon is unique, creative and viable in its own regard, and they all have strengths and weaknesses, as well as attachable weapon modifications to better suit how you wish to use the weapon (such as a regular or zoomed sight, or a silencer). You can carry 3 weapons at once, and I found myself using all 3 weapon slots actively throughout the game. The currency system in Metro 2033 is Military-Grade Ammo; you can either use your money bullets to kill powerful enemies very quickly, or spend them on resources, weapons, weapon modifications and regular ammo.
There were also many things about the game that got on my nerves, primarily due to the trial-and-error nature of some levels. There are occasional tripwires that are difficult to see and can be disarmed, but if you walk over one, you hear a click, a fizz, and boom. You're dead. So you load the previous checkpoint and try it again. There's a level with an occasional but infinite-spawning weak enemy that will sneak up behind you, hit you for small damage, and run away. They're hard to hit, fast, and ultimately drain your health packs just trying to get through the level. Fortunately it's only for one level, but it is very annoying. Sometimes the enemy mechanics are inconsistent as well; to keep it as spoiler free as possible, one of the hardest stealth sections of the game is traversing through a building with extremely powerful enemies that kill you in one hit, but only if you startle them. I was moving through as gently as possible, and when one spotted me, it felt like there was a 50/50 chance he would get startled or just leave me alone (the game suggests they'll leave you alone if you don't move), and it was irritating to have to rely on what felt like luck to get through a portion of the game.
And now, the tl;dr pros and cons list.
If you are looking for a single player FPS adventure, I
recommend Metro 2033. It'll take you for a ride.

A gem among indie games.
You ever played one of those games where you feel like the devs got to make the game they wanted to make?
This is one of those games.  The premise is simple, it's basically Space Invaders on crack and it's absolutely awesome.
The game has three modes - level mode, where you fight fixed spawns (and also fixed weapon powerups) that never change but get progressively harder as you go up in levels.  You have a fixed box fight every 5 levels for a total of 30 levels.  This will be a good 2-3 hours of gameplay as the later stages get very challenging.
Endless Mode, which speaks for itself.  Enemies come at you nonstop in very random fashions.  All types of enemies with different flying patterns.  Later on during the mode it becomes absolute chaos as you try to manage staying alive before the next powerup.  Lots of fun!
Wave Mode, which is similar to Endless Mode but the enemies come at you in Galaxian-style "waves" all clumped up together.  You can get powerups in this mode but only if you kill the entire line (or wave) of enemies.  Otherwise it's just staying alive as long as possible and going for the highest score.
The game has a variety of interesting powerups, from a double, triple and quadruple shot.  A double attack that doubles your current shots and can stack with the previous powerups I mentioned, extra health, a clone that replicates any shots you do (including powered up shots), a "wave" shot similar to the semi-controllable laser in the Raiden series, a tornado powerup, which is essentially a wave powerup but fires in a sine/cosine wave without you needing to adjust it, and lastly, the rotating shotgun, which makes your "ship" (which is a little space invader itself) fire in all directions.
You do not die in one hit in this game.  You have an HP bar and a very limited XP bar, which you gain as you progress through Level Mode which allows you to do more damage and take more hits.  You'll understand in the later levels why an HP bar is needed rather than dying in one hit like most other hardcore shmups, as the bullet patterns in this game are very random and can be tricky to dodge.
The game has Steam leaderboards for its Endless Mode and basic X360 controller support.  Options are limited, but the game can practically run on a toaster because of how simple its graphics are.  There is no story whatsoever to speak of.  Just like the games of yesteryear, your focus is to shoot down the flying alien bad guys.
Oh, one more thing, the music for this game is AWESOME.  Seems to be SoundTrekker style instruments in the form of EDM, or electronic dance music.  If you're a fan of that genre you're going to absolutely LOVE the tracks that this game has.  Sound effects are old school style chips, boops, and blarps.  This game is definitely a love letter to the oldies out there.
I picked this up on a sale for $0.49 and I feel like I ripped these guys off.  Even at full price (which is less than the price of a snack!) it's a lot of fun.  If you see this on sale during the Steam sale, this is an absolute *no brainer*.  Get it.  You won't regret it.
A game simple, challenging, fun and with a awesome soundtrack (if you like electronic music with a 8-bit vibe). I don't regret buying it.

So first off: YES I read the reviews, YES i know this is roughly two hours of my life I will never get back. But I was bored and curious. I wondered how bad the game really was. I wanted to know how my lottery chance wiht the games randomness went out there. So I installed it.
Now I originally said Two hours but it is more like one.
Like many players the game stopped at 85% and stuck there for a while. Instead of pausing i decided to make a game of this instead. How long would it stay that way? Perpetually? So I plugged in my laptop and went to the corner store to get something to eat. I came home, still there. I set the mouse arrow on the edge of the line so I could gauge how long it would take to move between jaunts and set about to do random things elsewhere while I ocassionally checked into the game.
Finally about an hour later I was surprised to find the character creator up and waiting for me. So I made one.
Now the designs aren't that awesome but I can accept that. Not every game will have good character graphics especially something that is meant to be a really poor alpha imitation of Minecraft. I chose something I didn't think was too terrible and went to work through the tutorials. Now I know I could have done other things and in some cases I did. I made a dirt room to live in. It lacked the details of a proper house but i wasn't in the game to build. I was in it because of the sheer number of bad reviews. I'm not trying to prove everyone right I just wanted to see how Right they were.
I successfully found wood (For those who wish to do the same as I, go to the largest area beneath the tundra and use the pick on the leaf brances on top of mountains) and managed to complete several tasks until I came to the wonder machine to make bricks. But sadly that is where my adventure ended. The randomization would not work for me and the game stopped, consistantly sending me back to the loading screen where I decided that an hour wasted on the game was enough to quench my curiousity on how bad the game was.
There you have it. A tried and true test on the fact that the game is as terrible as they say.

Got this game because everyone talked about it, hyped it up, and it's only $10.
This game is not at all for me. Here's my take on things.
Pros:
Nice space look
Different species and interactions
Targetable ship systems a-la Nexus, the Jupiter Incident
Delightful Pews and Razzes (I'm really stretching to find good things about this game)
Didn't notice any bugs (a very important thing in a game with permadeath)
Cons:
RNG: Not a fan of RNG in games in general, since it leads to save-scumming and re-rolling. This section was going to be longer, but then I realized this is a rogue-like, made for fans of the random number generator. Maybe this would be a good description: heads you win a little, tails you lose a lot, if the coin balances on its side you lose a little - the coin usually lands on its side. And if you lose the toss at the shop, you'll have nothing on which to spend your coin. Seriously, this is a 20% skill based game and 80% luck, and I'm generously estimating the skill component.
Story: It's fairly simple, a rebellion in space forces a loyal Federation ship, you, to travel through the universe straight to headquarters to deliver information about a crippling weakness in the enemy fleet, then promptly exploiting that weakness. Along the way you stop at shops, repair your ship, get into fights with the rebels, slavers, and other criminals, rescue people, etc. Curious are the times you find and install upgrades on your ship. The general tone is that you're in a Need for Speed style race to keep the enemy from reaching the main Federation base before you do, while allowing you to paint your car, add spoilers, and even lift out and replace the engine. Of course, in this analogy, the car is driving while these modifications are taking place. And the David-to-Goliath transformation does happen all the time in games; it's just that this one implies you don't have time for it. After reading in the forums a bit, it turns out a large part of the story and gameplay make no sense or are very implausible.
Instead of getting this game, flip 9,998 pennies. If 6,999 or more of them land 'heads', you can proceed to the skill portion. Flip the last one into a cup, normal cup size and on a table within arm's reach. If the last coin lands in the cup and is heads up, you win! If not, you'll have to start all over again. After each game in FTL, you'd be more familiar with it, more skilled. So for games 2-6 remove one penny from the pile and reduce the 'heads' requirement accordingly, so at game 6 and onwards you toss 9,993 pennies and need 6,993 'heads' to get to the final boss. Though, you're not allowed to win your first time unless you've seen someone else play or watched penny-flipping Let's Plays on YouTube. But at least when you're bored of the penny game, you can use your pennies to buy something else.

I'd say this was a good game. It's a great and inventive space roguelike with interesting mechanics and beautifully designed universe. The premise is simple get your ship from one end of the galaxy to the other without being overtaken by advancing rebels so that you can defeat them at a last stand encounter having upgraded your ship along the way to take on the oncoming rebel menace. So far so fun and add to that interesting encounters along the way and plenty of ship and weapon variety for replay value. Combat mechanics are on a surface level entertaining, each ship have different rooms with different systems, such as shields, weapons and oxygen, and you target your weapons onto these rooms to take out those systems. All of this would make for a great game but...
The one issue is FTL just can't seem to win fair, rather it seems determined to up the difficulty by cheating it's own mechanics. Ostensibly the game does a grand job of incrementing the difficulty with your own progress and as long as you fight well you should theoretically have no trouble overcoming harder enemies and reaching the final battle. This however is where the game overcompensates and falls short badly. Firstly the final boss fight is absurd. An unbelievably overpowered ship with incredibly sophisticated systems that consistently overpower all but the most well prepared and perfect ships. This isn't a problem if you can get a well armed ship unfortunately the game decides that stronger enemies  must be accompanied by a sudden downward spiral of your own ship's abilities. It doesn't matter how well prepared or skilled your crew or ship is by the time they get to the later levels you will find yourself captaining a bunch of toddlers inside a tin can in space. Shot chances and damage are somewhat probability based and I have a feeling that the game suddenly loads the odds completely against you by the later stages. No matter what weapon or how well designed the ship you'll suddenly see your deadeye weapons specialist firing wide time after time and any shot that lands seems to do no serious damage to the system inside. Shields remain up whilst the shield room is on fire, weapons remain firing despite a breach in the weapons room the size of a tank. By contrast the enemy, be they the final boss or-if chance doesn't fall your way-some random mid tier enemy that the game decides is your new God now, will blow you to pieces with almost insulting ease. Every shot will land, every missile will break your systems and with a snap of it's fingers the game will decide that you will lose now. It doesn't matter how well planned your strategy, how well designed your ship. Every now and again the game breaks itself if it feels you're doing too well.
At this point fans will probably be dismissing this with comments about engine upgrades and dodge increase, to which I say I've had a fully shield upgraded zoltan cruiser, with top tier weapons and shield guys armed with mark III lasers, pike beams and breach missiles turned to scrap in seconds by a slightly upper tier pirate cruiser simply because not one shot would land and the battle became unwinnable. The thing is this type of game breaking isn't necessarily routine and it is perfectly possible to see that the game is designed to be balanced and challenging without being frustrating. It just happens too often to be fun.
I write this as someone who is very easily frustrated by a game ♥♥♥♥ing up it's own mechanics as a way of building challenge and this game has that in spades. If you're the kind of person who enjoys challenging roguelikes but gets turned away by death via ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t this game is just not for you. In all honesty I'll keep trying to play it because there is enough in here to make it worht your time if the above doesn't get to you but to save on your blood pressure it may be best for you to come into this one prewarned. It's times like these when you wish for a better metric for steam reviews rather than a simple yes/no. I will say no even though it can be fun and engaging simply for the fact that the game can treat your progress with such pathetic disdain. No game that abuses it's own mechanics for the sake of difficulty can get away with a wholly positive review as far as I'm concerned.

So I bought Mafia II around the same time that I bought Watch_Dogs. Despite being 4 years antiquated, I actually much preferred to  play Mafia II.
The driving is probably one of the best I've played on PC. A speed-limiter to go the speed limit was a really good idea, and having it a toggle, so you can have it when you want but not wen you don't, was even better. The driving is pretty smooth, and I like the lock-picking ability, as opposed to indiscriminately smashing windows open.
Customization of cars surprised me. The damage is realistic, and being able to customize color and detail is common, but changing license plates (specific digits to your request, I might add) was a really cool addition. The police are also realistic when it comes to cars. Although they still don't follow you for driving recklessly, they do pursue you for speeding, hit-and-runs, and man slaughter. Also, they only ticket you for minor violations, which you can pay for, like in real life. (Who'd think a speeding ticket would get me so excited about a game? lol)
Even the city itself changes. You go from the early 40's to the early 50's in "Empire Bay", and you watch the city evolve. Everything from the little details like the price of food, or the posters plastered to the walls; to the big things like the cars being driven, music on the radio; and everything in between, like the clothing and speech of the civilians and NPCs
The shooting is good. I admit it falls into the shooter faux-pas, where you can cary like 20 guns on you of various sizes, but I can not complain. But I love the semi-destructible environments. Some places are fully destructible, some are not, but even still, it's fun to see a dinner or hotel in the middle of a fire-fight and actually look like it's being shot up, as opposed to staying pristine. Guys can take several bullets to kill, but that's ok since you do too.
As for the story (Semi-Spoiler Alert), it ends short. I don't know if there's a DLC to  continue, but the ending came suddenly, but it was a wild ride to the end. A wide variety in casting also made the characters rich, and really added to the game. Voice acting was good, and did not sound forced, and the animations were very well done, especially for a game that is 4 years old.
There are gay and racial slurs, but it's to be expected by mob members in the 40's and 50's. It wasn't exactly a Politically Correct era...
All in all, I'd say this is a severely underrated game, and probably in my top 10 if not my top 5 games to play.

Mafia II has you in the footsteps of Vito Scaletta, a rising Italian in the mob. You have to go through multiple tasks to prove yourself to the mob, while helping out buddies. This game was incredible. It is in my top favorites. 2K Games did an absolute fabulous job on this game.
Mafia II's plot is story-rich with the right amount of action. Set in the late 1940's-mid 1950's, Vito Scaletta is trying to rise through the mob to become a "Made Man." His buddy Joe, is there to help him out in the long run. These 2 go on all sorts of jobs together, helping out multiple mob bosses in the city of Empire Bay. During this time, you can see Vito also struggle with which is more important, his hand in the "Family Business" or his real family, immigrants from Sicily. Which one Vito chooses will truly impact who he becomes.
Back in 2009, when the graphics still had a bit of rough edges, Mafia II came out and just blew everyone away. 7 years later, these graphics are still a pleasure to have on your screen. The graphics are wonderful, and they really show the time period very well. The voice acting is also very nice to listen to.
By all means, buy this game. It is truly left it's mark on the gaming industry. If you loved the Godfather movies, then all I got to say is, this game will make you an offer you just can't refuse....

Wowee. This is poetry. And the gameplay always exceeds the boundaries of it's laughably limited game engine. One twist on the formula I like is that it's consistently unfair. One minute you fight a huge enemy, and it cries or shoots itself, and the next a tiny spider takes off half your health with one hit - so you end up starting every fight with high-energy moves just in case. For the few enemies that are *obviously* dangerous you go in chucking one-use fire bombs, as they will probably win if maximal damage isn't inflicted before everyone's health runs out. There is a lot of monotonous wandering around lost, due to the complicated maps and slow movement - but it's your fault if you didn't start drawing a map on some paper when the game started. Some of the unfairness caused me to load saves, but actually not much of it, and I did so feeling a little wiser each time which can't be said of most RPGs. When a character in your party dies, there are so many recruitable characters scattered around that it feels like oh, well let's try this other one now. It's more important to have got the *main* character through the fight. Maybe I'm too much of a jerk, oh well. The game's ethics are ever-present in that nearly everything is a decision with some permanent consequences, but they are also inconsistent - sometimes it makes you feel guilty for killing a small animal, the next the path forward is blocked with loads of unavoidable small animals. So it's meta-unfair as well as unfair!
Edit: the ending is really disappointing but it is only the last 10 minutes where it suddenly stops being interactive. It belongs on a list of worst endings ever. The story doesn't have to have a happy ending - but giving you a depressing ending caused by actions you have no control over is bad. If nothing else you should be able to lose the last boss fight and get the ending credits rather than the game over screen. In my mind that's how I want to remember the game ending.

This is an amazing game. I don't usually write reviews, but after starting this game, I couldn't put it down.
The game is highly reminiscent of Earthbound but it doesn't feel like a rip-off or low quality imitation. The story is very mature and is incredibly emotional. It touches on a lot of difficult themes such as abuse, loss, depression, sacrifice, and selfishness, but all of these horrible things are presented with an off-beat sense of humor, making it palatable. One moment you will find yourself laughing and another you will feel like you were punched in the gut.
I accidentally started the game in "Pain Mode" which only allows you to use each save point once, and frankly I feel like it was the right decision for me because the game forces you to make hard choices that can lead to one of your party members permenantly dying or drastically changing the outcome of a scenario. I'm the type of player who is kind of a perfectionist and would otherwise save often so that I can reload and make the "perfect" choices, but the Pain Mode really forces me to make a decision and stick with it.
Anyways, this game is great. Buy it if you like a good old-fashioned RPG!

Metro 2033 Redux looks impressive. The lighting and textures are great, the stealth mechanics are fun, killing is satisfying, enemies are well-designed, and the ability to customize your loadout allows you to play the game your way. To top it all off, the campaign is of considerable length depending on your playstyle, so there's plenty of content to sink your teeth into.
However, it is also a deeply flawed game. Glitches and game freezes are common in Metro 2033, there's little variation within the environments as everything looks the same, the backstory is poorly delivered, the characters are largely generic, and the plot is incohesive. Metro 2033 doesn't feel like a large quest, but rather a string of missions that are barely connected. I was unable to invest myself with the title's main character and his journey, which sometimes made the game a chore to play.
Metro 2033 is a decent game. That being said, I probably won't ever play through it again.

Overall, this game is fantastic and free, that's a great combination in my view!

When some say the game does not have gameplay, they they probably really mean it does not have a story. I personally enjoyed the game, but even so, I feel I didn't get what I was looking for: story. What I found in this game was a lot of thrown around emotions and random scenes that seem almost like a journal. Some of the graphics are quite decent and have much potential, but in order to get away with having only decent graphics is to include narrative. I played the game twice (once on commentary mode) and still felt cut short, although I found more bits of the creator's life. Since the game is free I would say it is worth playing.
Here are some extra critiques-
Pros:
- Creative/mindful Levels
- Music fits well in most scenes
- Relatable (especially as I am a creator of a type myself)
- Artistic
- Variety
- Levels are skippable (in case you get stuck or bored)
- Free
Cons:
- Music is at times too loud
- Voice is at times too quiet
- Some parts of the game are overextensive (although they are intended to be that way)
- Lacks originality in some levels
- Level transitions are not smooth
I hope the creator can take some criticism and continue to make games - Preferably ones that have stories and consistent style.

Well, what can I say...
First of all, it's a walking simulator so don't expect full blown action. What you can and should expect though is some wacky stuff. Cool stuff nevertheless. It has some good moments, I enjoyed the FMVs a lot, and some moments made me actually think and question myself, which is defenetly a plus. This is a game to think. If you don't like thinking then it probably isn't for you. The only cons would have to be that the ending is very inconclusive. You feel like it doesn't go anywhere even though some kind of story and mindset is built along the game, which is sad and might annoy some people (because there is no conclusion, some may feel they have just wasted their time). Also, and maybe the author doesn't think this way, but I noted a kind of "special snowflake" vibe from the players' point of view, like he felt he was entitled to things, you know the drill.
All in all, I recommend it. I finished it in 70 minutes, and I feel those moments of questioning and confusion were worth my time.
THE FEELS

Got this game because everyone talked about it, hyped it up, and it's only $10.
This game is not at all for me. Here's my take on things.
Pros:
Nice space look
Different species and interactions
Targetable ship systems a-la Nexus, the Jupiter Incident
Delightful Pews and Razzes (I'm really stretching to find good things about this game)
Didn't notice any bugs (a very important thing in a game with permadeath)
Cons:
RNG: Not a fan of RNG in games in general, since it leads to save-scumming and re-rolling. This section was going to be longer, but then I realized this is a rogue-like, made for fans of the random number generator. Maybe this would be a good description: heads you win a little, tails you lose a lot, if the coin balances on its side you lose a little - the coin usually lands on its side. And if you lose the toss at the shop, you'll have nothing on which to spend your coin. Seriously, this is a 20% skill based game and 80% luck, and I'm generously estimating the skill component.
Story: It's fairly simple, a rebellion in space forces a loyal Federation ship, you, to travel through the universe straight to headquarters to deliver information about a crippling weakness in the enemy fleet, then promptly exploiting that weakness. Along the way you stop at shops, repair your ship, get into fights with the rebels, slavers, and other criminals, rescue people, etc. Curious are the times you find and install upgrades on your ship. The general tone is that you're in a Need for Speed style race to keep the enemy from reaching the main Federation base before you do, while allowing you to paint your car, add spoilers, and even lift out and replace the engine. Of course, in this analogy, the car is driving while these modifications are taking place. And the David-to-Goliath transformation does happen all the time in games; it's just that this one implies you don't have time for it. After reading in the forums a bit, it turns out a large part of the story and gameplay make no sense or are very implausible.
Instead of getting this game, flip 9,998 pennies. If 6,999 or more of them land 'heads', you can proceed to the skill portion. Flip the last one into a cup, normal cup size and on a table within arm's reach. If the last coin lands in the cup and is heads up, you win! If not, you'll have to start all over again. After each game in FTL, you'd be more familiar with it, more skilled. So for games 2-6 remove one penny from the pile and reduce the 'heads' requirement accordingly, so at game 6 and onwards you toss 9,993 pennies and need 6,993 'heads' to get to the final boss. Though, you're not allowed to win your first time unless you've seen someone else play or watched penny-flipping Let's Plays on YouTube. But at least when you're bored of the penny game, you can use your pennies to buy something else.

I'd say this was a good game. It's a great and inventive space roguelike with interesting mechanics and beautifully designed universe. The premise is simple get your ship from one end of the galaxy to the other without being overtaken by advancing rebels so that you can defeat them at a last stand encounter having upgraded your ship along the way to take on the oncoming rebel menace. So far so fun and add to that interesting encounters along the way and plenty of ship and weapon variety for replay value. Combat mechanics are on a surface level entertaining, each ship have different rooms with different systems, such as shields, weapons and oxygen, and you target your weapons onto these rooms to take out those systems. All of this would make for a great game but...
The one issue is FTL just can't seem to win fair, rather it seems determined to up the difficulty by cheating it's own mechanics. Ostensibly the game does a grand job of incrementing the difficulty with your own progress and as long as you fight well you should theoretically have no trouble overcoming harder enemies and reaching the final battle. This however is where the game overcompensates and falls short badly. Firstly the final boss fight is absurd. An unbelievably overpowered ship with incredibly sophisticated systems that consistently overpower all but the most well prepared and perfect ships. This isn't a problem if you can get a well armed ship unfortunately the game decides that stronger enemies  must be accompanied by a sudden downward spiral of your own ship's abilities. It doesn't matter how well prepared or skilled your crew or ship is by the time they get to the later levels you will find yourself captaining a bunch of toddlers inside a tin can in space. Shot chances and damage are somewhat probability based and I have a feeling that the game suddenly loads the odds completely against you by the later stages. No matter what weapon or how well designed the ship you'll suddenly see your deadeye weapons specialist firing wide time after time and any shot that lands seems to do no serious damage to the system inside. Shields remain up whilst the shield room is on fire, weapons remain firing despite a breach in the weapons room the size of a tank. By contrast the enemy, be they the final boss or-if chance doesn't fall your way-some random mid tier enemy that the game decides is your new God now, will blow you to pieces with almost insulting ease. Every shot will land, every missile will break your systems and with a snap of it's fingers the game will decide that you will lose now. It doesn't matter how well planned your strategy, how well designed your ship. Every now and again the game breaks itself if it feels you're doing too well.
At this point fans will probably be dismissing this with comments about engine upgrades and dodge increase, to which I say I've had a fully shield upgraded zoltan cruiser, with top tier weapons and shield guys armed with mark III lasers, pike beams and breach missiles turned to scrap in seconds by a slightly upper tier pirate cruiser simply because not one shot would land and the battle became unwinnable. The thing is this type of game breaking isn't necessarily routine and it is perfectly possible to see that the game is designed to be balanced and challenging without being frustrating. It just happens too often to be fun.
I write this as someone who is very easily frustrated by a game ♥♥♥♥ing up it's own mechanics as a way of building challenge and this game has that in spades. If you're the kind of person who enjoys challenging roguelikes but gets turned away by death via ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t this game is just not for you. In all honesty I'll keep trying to play it because there is enough in here to make it worht your time if the above doesn't get to you but to save on your blood pressure it may be best for you to come into this one prewarned. It's times like these when you wish for a better metric for steam reviews rather than a simple yes/no. I will say no even though it can be fun and engaging simply for the fact that the game can treat your progress with such pathetic disdain. No game that abuses it's own mechanics for the sake of difficulty can get away with a wholly positive review as far as I'm concerned.

So for those who don't know what this game is, let me first explain what my impression (and the tldr) of the game is:
Understandably, some people wouldn't call it a roguelike because of the save/load feature or the dimensional vault, but since you do not accumulate hero points after resuming a loaded game (after death), my interpretation has been that saving/loading is only a feature for those who are in it for the story content.  A good compromise imo.
A creative take on this style of game.  I haven't seen anything like it -- the closest comparison would be Shiren the Wanderer.
An objective (the demon lord) that plagues you from the start, but not impossible to vanquish once you have progressed enough.
Party members that serve a purpose, but also have depth.  Like everything else in the game, they are not permanent.
The music is fantastic.
I'm not a fan of visual novels (?), so the abundance of text serving as the beginning and end of your adventure is not something that is fulfilling for me.  It's very well written, imo, so I imagine JRPG / Story-reading fans will like this.
No cursed items.  Unidentified items you can wear, but none of them cursed. :\  The only undiscovered attribute on an item that poses any uncertainty is the durability.
The price is so low, it feels like I robbed some poor hard-working developer that just loves making games like this.  Playism's site says something about letting you pay what you want (donation-based I guess?), so hopefully some people have been more charitable towards this game.
There is no way to isolate the leaderboards to personal social groups - as a result, it's all meaningless information, sadly. :\  It would be great if I could see where I rate among my friends list.
There's no underground -- Yah, it's a pretty big game already, sure.  But fantasy games need dungeons.  An intricate right-way-progressing dungeon would've made the screen edge much more intimidating.
Those are my impressions of this game. :)
