This game....oh God this game is so addictive.
The rule of a lot of RPGs is
A reason why a lot of RPGs are long and tedious. Most people who has a lot of stuff going on with their life doesn't have time to play RPGs straight in one sitting. Even though their playtime only consists of a few hours, it'll still take them days to weeks before they finish it. That's because they can't play in long durations.
One Way Heroics ignores this rule. It's a straightforward RPG with rouge-like elements. You don't need to explore hours in a dungeon. Here it'll only take you seconds. You don't need to grind. As levels are really not much of an importance later on. You don't need to get money, as you won't be spending a lot anyways. You don't need to look for secrets, as with each step you take the every growing darkness will engulf you if you don't keep moving forward(right).
The game is not real-time, not fast-paced, it is turn-based. Which means you have time to pause and think the actions you will make. And that is not noticeable until you play it. With each step you take at every turn, the whole world will move after you do. Enemies, allies, npcs, everything moves as you move. It uses a World Generator. Which means you can have different maps in every game you start. It generates random seeds at every reload of your save, with still keeping the same world and same map, but with different outcomes of enemies, treasures and such.
It is not repetitive as one might think. As with each new game, there will always be new stuff to unlock, and these stuff will make the game more enjoyable with each run.

This game is a very rewarding experience. The thrill of finally beating it on its easiest difficulty was one I haven't felt in a turn-based game in a long time. And then, I just kept taking on tougher and tougher challenges. Dying quickly each time, I had to try as many things as I could. Now, I take on the hardest difficulty setting with no problem. And, One Way Heroic's doesn't just up the stats for its difficulty; It adds in new items and characters, something that needs to be seen more in games.
The easy mode is just a short voyage that ends in a boss fight, but the other modes don't have to be. In other modes, that same boss attacks much sooner, and appears at various intervals. There is a thrill as you run from the darkness, dodging past its summoner as they chase you down with attacks that become more survivable over time. You can feel the progress. And, with the game encouraging you to restart, you can also feel yourself getting better. Dying after three days with your best gear carried over is replaced with surviving for ten days with the default starting gear and what you scum up along the way. Every class becomes a force of destruction, even long after its stats become redundant.
The game also has a major count of stuff you'll miss the first few times playing. There's funny conversations to be uncovered, but that's something every game seems to have. Although often short in words, characters and endings give backstory that matters. The things they mention are in the world, and their tellings are sometimes clues. All the characters that can join your party are somehow linked, and understanding their origins and motivations will teach you how to truly save the world.
This game isn't some cheap let's-make-a-roguelike-because-it's-been-done-several-times. It adds to the formula.
(On a side note, the game used to crash sometimes. It seems to have been fixed in a recent patch. It was never much of an issue for me, though. I only had three crashes that were in-game.)

Don't listen to people who hate on this game. Some complain about the story, or the gunplay, or how
not-so-open-world it is. The problem with this is that they're picking the game apart and judging it on individual merits. Sure they have some valid points, but this isn't a game that excels in any particular area. The key to enjoying Mafia II is to view it as a complete package. I first played this game on PS3 and I wasn't too into it. I played about half the game and really had no interest in finishing it. It was like a hack version of WWII era GTA IV. I didn't care for the vehicle handling, there was nothing you could really do while roaming the city, the missions were bacically cut scenes mixed with a shooting hallway, and at no point did I ever feel pulled into the story.
Then I picked the game up during a Steam sale and started playing it to to see if I could catch up to where I was on PS3. But before I played I looked into some mods. I found a graphics mod, a mod that lets you load by chapter, and the Free Ride mod. It was the graphics mod that really impressed me though. I'm running it on a laptop with a GTX 550, which isn't anything fancy at this point, but oh man does this game look good with the graphics mod. It looks so good that I have to stop while I'm playing to admire the environment. The mod really brought the game world to life. I hate saying this, but it looks better than Watch Dogs on my machine.
Anyway, with the world looking so pretty, my gameplay experience actually improved. I went from looking at the mechanics as mediocre at best to seeing them as not so bad, which brought the game from "Meh" to "Pretty good." The story even picks up after the first half and I started to enjoy it. I'm not big on a game's story so me getting into one is saying a lot.
If you're on the fence about Mafia II, I say that if you can get it for 75% or more and you have an decent machine, it's well worth the buy. With proper mods and an open mind, it's an enjoyable experience.

You Have to Win the Game is a free exploration platformer that at times can be repetitive and frustrating to new gamers. On many of my reviews I like to point out that I am newer to the gaming community, so keep that in mind when reading my reviews.
This particular game reminded me of my Mario days on my GameBoy Advance. Much like that sort of game, you are given the freedom to explore what seems to be a never-ending world of death traps and surprises. Since the world itself seemed to be rather large, I do admit that I had to use a walk-through a few times to help me in some of the tricky puzzle parts of the game. You will have to use your head for some of the situations you may put yourself into at times.
Something that I really enjoyed with this game in particular is the complete goofiness of the development of the game. What I mean by this is, when you get to the end of the game, and you're about to beat it...you are given he option to go through the "win" or the "lose" door. There are sections of the game that you will find some really funny things, but I want to keep them a surprise, so you can find enjoyment in them as well.
All and all, even though this game can be difficult at times, the fun graphics, the silly nature, and the frequent checkpoints make it a very fun and addicting game. I definitely recommend giving it a try; you may fall in love with it at 3am just as I did. Did I mention it is free as well?! Can't beat free.

I'm still waiting for Galaga, Steam. Where are you?
You would figure that with all the arcade remakes ever to be made in this history of the world wide web, we can find a Galaga $15.00 rip-off with pretty colors remake on steam, but we don't live in that future just yet. We, in the modern era of the computerphone technology, live in arcade remakes of Space Invaders, not Galaga.
We have not progressed this far as a civilization to remake an amazing arcade game and continue to rely on the models of the old, conventional alternative (Space Invaders). This is like how we end institutional racism and deem racism socially unacceptable, but racism still persists in our culture in many different facets and never goes away. Space Invaders reboots are everywhere (persist in our culture) and come in many different aspects.
Void Invaders is not Galaga. It is 15% Galaga and 85% Space Invaders with pretty colors and/or seizures. While it is an 85% Space Invaders remake, Void Invaders has three different modes to the game: endless, wave (true arcade), and 'level', which is almost a storyline mode but with a level up system which doesn't really amount to anything. The level system also relies on power-ups to beat the level as the game gets tougher, but it doesn't detract from the experience (fun). Just because there's a clone-power up doesn't mean this game is Galaga. The ways to get powerups is also much different from Galaga because you don't die to get them, nor are their bonus rounds.
Where is my Galaga remake, Steam/Indie Game Developers? Don't you people remember what fun used to be??
tl;dr: It's cheap and great for all but the epileptics and colorblind folks. It's also not entirely space invaders but that doesn't mean it's Galaga. Where is Galaga, Steam?

Got this game because everyone talked about it, hyped it up, and it's only $10.
This game is not at all for me. Here's my take on things.
Pros:
Nice space look
Different species and interactions
Targetable ship systems a-la Nexus, the Jupiter Incident
Delightful Pews and Razzes (I'm really stretching to find good things about this game)
Didn't notice any bugs (a very important thing in a game with permadeath)
Cons:
RNG: Not a fan of RNG in games in general, since it leads to save-scumming and re-rolling. This section was going to be longer, but then I realized this is a rogue-like, made for fans of the random number generator. Maybe this would be a good description: heads you win a little, tails you lose a lot, if the coin balances on its side you lose a little - the coin usually lands on its side. And if you lose the toss at the shop, you'll have nothing on which to spend your coin. Seriously, this is a 20% skill based game and 80% luck, and I'm generously estimating the skill component.
Story: It's fairly simple, a rebellion in space forces a loyal Federation ship, you, to travel through the universe straight to headquarters to deliver information about a crippling weakness in the enemy fleet, then promptly exploiting that weakness. Along the way you stop at shops, repair your ship, get into fights with the rebels, slavers, and other criminals, rescue people, etc. Curious are the times you find and install upgrades on your ship. The general tone is that you're in a Need for Speed style race to keep the enemy from reaching the main Federation base before you do, while allowing you to paint your car, add spoilers, and even lift out and replace the engine. Of course, in this analogy, the car is driving while these modifications are taking place. And the David-to-Goliath transformation does happen all the time in games; it's just that this one implies you don't have time for it. After reading in the forums a bit, it turns out a large part of the story and gameplay make no sense or are very implausible.
Instead of getting this game, flip 9,998 pennies. If 6,999 or more of them land 'heads', you can proceed to the skill portion. Flip the last one into a cup, normal cup size and on a table within arm's reach. If the last coin lands in the cup and is heads up, you win! If not, you'll have to start all over again. After each game in FTL, you'd be more familiar with it, more skilled. So for games 2-6 remove one penny from the pile and reduce the 'heads' requirement accordingly, so at game 6 and onwards you toss 9,993 pennies and need 6,993 'heads' to get to the final boss. Though, you're not allowed to win your first time unless you've seen someone else play or watched penny-flipping Let's Plays on YouTube. But at least when you're bored of the penny game, you can use your pennies to buy something else.

I'd say this was a good game. It's a great and inventive space roguelike with interesting mechanics and beautifully designed universe. The premise is simple get your ship from one end of the galaxy to the other without being overtaken by advancing rebels so that you can defeat them at a last stand encounter having upgraded your ship along the way to take on the oncoming rebel menace. So far so fun and add to that interesting encounters along the way and plenty of ship and weapon variety for replay value. Combat mechanics are on a surface level entertaining, each ship have different rooms with different systems, such as shields, weapons and oxygen, and you target your weapons onto these rooms to take out those systems. All of this would make for a great game but...
The one issue is FTL just can't seem to win fair, rather it seems determined to up the difficulty by cheating it's own mechanics. Ostensibly the game does a grand job of incrementing the difficulty with your own progress and as long as you fight well you should theoretically have no trouble overcoming harder enemies and reaching the final battle. This however is where the game overcompensates and falls short badly. Firstly the final boss fight is absurd. An unbelievably overpowered ship with incredibly sophisticated systems that consistently overpower all but the most well prepared and perfect ships. This isn't a problem if you can get a well armed ship unfortunately the game decides that stronger enemies  must be accompanied by a sudden downward spiral of your own ship's abilities. It doesn't matter how well prepared or skilled your crew or ship is by the time they get to the later levels you will find yourself captaining a bunch of toddlers inside a tin can in space. Shot chances and damage are somewhat probability based and I have a feeling that the game suddenly loads the odds completely against you by the later stages. No matter what weapon or how well designed the ship you'll suddenly see your deadeye weapons specialist firing wide time after time and any shot that lands seems to do no serious damage to the system inside. Shields remain up whilst the shield room is on fire, weapons remain firing despite a breach in the weapons room the size of a tank. By contrast the enemy, be they the final boss or-if chance doesn't fall your way-some random mid tier enemy that the game decides is your new God now, will blow you to pieces with almost insulting ease. Every shot will land, every missile will break your systems and with a snap of it's fingers the game will decide that you will lose now. It doesn't matter how well planned your strategy, how well designed your ship. Every now and again the game breaks itself if it feels you're doing too well.
At this point fans will probably be dismissing this with comments about engine upgrades and dodge increase, to which I say I've had a fully shield upgraded zoltan cruiser, with top tier weapons and shield guys armed with mark III lasers, pike beams and breach missiles turned to scrap in seconds by a slightly upper tier pirate cruiser simply because not one shot would land and the battle became unwinnable. The thing is this type of game breaking isn't necessarily routine and it is perfectly possible to see that the game is designed to be balanced and challenging without being frustrating. It just happens too often to be fun.
I write this as someone who is very easily frustrated by a game ♥♥♥♥ing up it's own mechanics as a way of building challenge and this game has that in spades. If you're the kind of person who enjoys challenging roguelikes but gets turned away by death via ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t this game is just not for you. In all honesty I'll keep trying to play it because there is enough in here to make it worht your time if the above doesn't get to you but to save on your blood pressure it may be best for you to come into this one prewarned. It's times like these when you wish for a better metric for steam reviews rather than a simple yes/no. I will say no even though it can be fun and engaging simply for the fact that the game can treat your progress with such pathetic disdain. No game that abuses it's own mechanics for the sake of difficulty can get away with a wholly positive review as far as I'm concerned.

A perfect definition of the term "flawed gem."
In terms of role-playing, this is one of the very best games available. Your vampire's clan has an immense effect on what you can do, and how people react to you. It's a definite consequence from the outset, with no real right option other than what you want to do. No moral material is pushed on you, unlike several modern titles; instead, the game lets you form your own opinion, based on your own values and ideals, and choose a side that best fits them.
The writing is one of the high points of this medium. I was astonished from the simple tutorial at how real the dialogue sounds, how gutteral and simplistic in a way that near approaches elegance in its construction. Flowery prose is almost non-existent in this title, except for *where it should be,* which is with the aristocrats caught in ASOIAF-like politicking. The Masquerade is rarely predictible, and it's never unenjoyable...
...except for the final act. While the first and second hubs are used perfectly, the third is overburdened with side quests, and the fourth (and final) hub is barely used at all. The game has a strong finale, but the moments spent leading up to it are lacking. Main questlines basically boil down to "Find this so you can get this so you can go here to get this to do it all over again," which, admittedly, doesn't differ to much from the start of the game, but it becomes truly overdrawn and repetitive near the end. You can burn through these boring segments if you're not a completionist, but it does grate on those of us that are, especially if you want the superb passive upgrades that act as rewards for the side quests that bloat this part of the game.
Combat isn't stellar, but it is serviceable, especially when compared to how poor combat usually is in RPGs of this period. The character sheet is big and diverse, which allows for truly different builds when combined with the seven different Vampire clans at the beginning.
I can't recommend this game enough. It's one of my all-time favorites, and probably the best RPG I've ever played.

Helldivers is a skill based twin-stick shooter where you go up against 3 radically different alien factions with up to 4 players with any mix of online or local co-op featuring realistic military themed weapons, tactical strategic options, and friendly fire.
It is set in a dystopian future where players fight to protect
where the Helldivers are the last line of defense to help in the Spread of Managed Democracy. The game doesn't feature a typical campaign story as it follows an endless design where it gives a brief intro and then lets the player play at their pace, picking from 1 of 12 difficulties in up to 3 different war fronts.
It is only by completing proceduraly generated missions and conquering planets that players collectively push back against the enemy factions away from
and towards their respective home worlds. If the players can reach and defeat any of the enemy factions, those enemy factions are out of the game until only
remains. Conversely if players are unable to keep any enemy faction away, they can initiate an attack on
and blow it up. In either scenario, after a brief cinematic and some global war statistics, immediately as one war ends, another begins and the cycle continues.
The progression system used by the game uses both XP earned as well as accomplishment based unlocked and on mission sample gathering to help upgrade various options in their arsenal. Leveling up by XP is based on completing objectives within missions which lead the player through a series of military ranks starting from Recruit all the way up to
. A player doesn't get stronger (so this is not an action-RPG), just gets different ranks keeping with the military theme and has access to some weapons and options that a starting player may not.
Along the way earning new Ranks, the player will unlock additional Primary Weapon options, Perk options, and cosmetic Outfits.
The accomplishment based unlocks have to do with completing planets across the full spectrum of difficulty the game offers. Combined together each Helldiver quickly accumulates a massive collection of loadout options.
The additional options aren't necessarily better as much as just different since there is a strong attempt by the developers to give everything pros and cons in an attempt to keep things generally well balanced. What this does is allow new players to play with more veteran players and the more significant difference between the players will always remain about skill, not progression.
In addition to all the base game content and continued developer support to grant players additional free DLC content, they also released a couple of free major expansions to the game adding in new Bosses (called Masters), a Horde variant mission type (called Retaliatory Strikes), and additional enemy units and objectives that can show up on missions. All these free additions have been complimented with a wide assortment of paid DLC options that provide players even more options for their loadouts. Indeed, many favored items seen in frequent use by players are from one of these paid DLC packs.
For myself, I have found all the paid DLC options to be worthwhile additions. Some more than others, but no regrets on any of those DLC pack purchases. It may seem like a lot if you are just now looking at the game, but I have been playing the game since it first released in March, 2015 on PlayStation and it may help you to know that the wide selection has grown over time as the developers continue to support while players continue to play and enjoy.
I decided to get the game again on Steam from scratch once it became available here and I continue to play on both platforms because I have made different friends I like to continue playing more with on both platforms. Steam and Playstation players cannot play with each other (no cross-play), but the Galactic Campaign of players vs the enemy factions in a global co-op campaign is shared between the two platforms.
Helldivers is the best 4P co-op multiplayer game (local or online) I have played to date. I look for and play a lot of co-op games, and I haven't found anything else that even comes close.

This is a pretty good turn-based RPG for $3. It's short (less than an hour to reach the end) but the replay value is mostly what keeps the game interesting.
You start out with 2 classes and unlock several more as you play through the game's randomly-generated worlds. You can also carry items from game to game, and they'll be available from the start.
As you're forced to keep moving to the right, you have to plan your actions more than you would in something like early Final Fantasy games. You can take things at your own pace for the most part and One Way Heroics isn't too difficult. If you mess up, the game will give you hints, and you have a couple of abilities to make things go easier. If you want a more difficult game you don't have to use them, and there are multiple difficulty settings. Save points can be easy or hard to find, depending on your luck and where you go.
I don't like that weapons and armor have a limited number of uses, but since you can upgrade stuff it would probably be game-breaking to have unlimited uses on things. A couple of playthroughs would give you way-too-powerful weapons.
Overall this is a decent game to get, and the price is adequately low. If you see it on sale for less than $1 you can't go wrong buying One Way Heroics.

King Arthur's Gold has something that few other MOBAs of this type can replicate.
Sheer, utter chaos.
The Terraria similarity only goes skin-deep, as the only things this game has that makes it similar to the popular platformer are the ability to build and the art style. The latter keeps things simple, with enough expression in each of the three classes to make them distinguishable, yet not overly complex, whereas the former is a stroke of genius.
At the beginning of each game, you and your team will have a short space of time to construct whatever you deem effective in staving off the enemy. Teamwork is essential, as a good castle is perhaps more important than good combat skill. Once the match starts, sheer hell is unleashed.
The ground between two bases becomes a warzone. Makeshift wooden structures are built only to be destroyed a second later. Knights use their shields as makeshift gliders to parachute into the midst of the war, archers hang from trees and walls, sniping anything wearing a shirt that isn't their colour, and builders hang back in the base, pixelated faces cackling as they toss a boulder into the enemy or pefect a foolproof deathtrap.
The games are fast and furious, but what elevates it even further from other MOBAs is the drop-in / drop-out feature. Is the other builder overruling your suggestions for a space tower and is nicking all your gold? No big D. Just leave that game and enter another. Are you having trouble fighting, or even surviving more than thirty seconds post-spawn? Fine! I'm sure your skills would be valued in a new game. The seemingly obvious issue of everyone leaving as soon as the tide turns is obliterated by the gameplay, however; fortune never rests with one team for long. As such, this game is often my go-to for fast fun before I need to go somewhere and don't have time to be locked into a thirty-minute game, the threat of my status being diminished should I leave constantly hovering behind the 'quit' button.
In conclusion, this game is fun, moddable and a great long or short term solution to the MOBA hankering. In my opinion, it's worth every penny.

Metro 2033 Redux is simply a masterpiece. It follows the story of the books written by Dmitry Glukhovsky. After a nurclear war that has devastaded humanity and the people of Moscow who live now in the underground metro tunnels, seeking refuge from the high levels of radiotion and from the monsters that prowl above ground... You take the role of Artyom, a young man who seeks his destiny in finding and destroying the Dark Ones. Creatures with supernatural ablities. The gameplay and story is implented brilliantly in the whole game with you, trying to survive on high difficulties, on hordes of monsters on little ammo and health kits. Graphics are realistic and immersive while the snow shaders and volumetric lightning is awesome to look at and appealing to the eye. The enemies are smart and dangerous, unlike the mutated creatures that are deadly and fierce and can kill you in 2-3 hits. Also the atmosphere is one of the best I have seen, you struggling in the dark with your flashlight while monsters are coming from anywhere to feed at your corpse. Overall this game is about 8-12 hours long plus one or two hours more for scavaging goods. I absolutely recommend you to buy this game especially when it drops to 5 bucks during sales. Hovewer the best thing you could do which is economical is to buy the Metro bundle which includes this game and the sequel Metro: Last Light which to some is better than this is one or the same. Whatever you know about these games matters little, it would be a wrong move if you would pass these games so it's a must buy for you.

Let me start off saying that Civ 5 is a great game with a great premise...and a major flaw. Civ 5 is a wonderful game to begin playing, as its learning curve is gradual and improvements feel great. For example, I hopped into Civ 5 only having played 30 or 40 hours of Civ 3. The game felt great, the mechanics seemed strong and fun, and the game was rewardingly difficult. The strategies with the various civs felt numerous and fun, and the game didnt feel like a stomp.
Before I continue, please buy the complete collection if you are going to buy. Its worth it. The game is incomplete without it.
Fast forward 400-500 hours, and I have effectively played every civ. I know their weaknesses and strengths, I know their playstyle, I know map and city strategy. I am finally good at the game. This, however, is where things went downhill for me. Once I began running out of fun ways to win, I decided it was time to move past king-ish (slightly above medium) difficulty, and begin playing the tougher AIs. This was because I had noticed that the AIs in this difficulty were just not good.
Civ 5's major flaw is AI design. Players have 2 actions on most units, and the average turns were "move 2 squares" or "move 1 square and fight". Its simple, easy, and actually pretty fun to design a strategy to break an enemies attack incoming. However, this was where most of the flaws shone through. First: AIs vastly underestimate the number of units they need, bring outdated units, and attack like 12 year olds fighting on the playgrounds. It was sloppy. I discovered I could win 90% of my fights by having walls, and having 1 unit per city, building more when attacked. Im sorry, but catapults aren't useful versus infantry, but the ai Didnt know this. Going back to my discussion of what the average movement of a unit looked like, did you know that the AIs ranged units cant move AND shoot in a turn? this vastly cuts down their strength. Civ AI is horrible at decision making, and will go through all the military techs just to wage a war with 5 old units, or not even attack at all. There is no strategy in their play.
So I moved to the higher difficulties. I figured that they more difficult opponents would have stronger AI and would actually be fun to play against. I was sorely mistaken. The only ai change I could find was that the AI was more aggressive. This equated to a couple more units in a fight that was still easily defeated. War was laughable. Player Victory was inevitable, and cities were always conquered provided you weren't too far behind in military tech and you brought enough units.
This is where the second part of this major flaw kicks off: CIV AI didn't get tougher because they were better and well made. They got tougher because they cheated. Beyond King difficulty, the AI were given free techs, units, and even cities to start with. Now while I will admit that this does make the game more difficult, it does not make it more fun. Remember all those wonders thare are fun to rush? They already have the tech for them and have them 20 turns before you can begin them. Remember that fun strategy of early game warefare? It's impossible now because you are 4 military techs behind. The only strong strategy in immortal/deity play is to rush every single science tech,♥♥♥♥♥♥no one off and hope to get to turn 200 (on quick, most games end between turns 200-300 on lower difficulties), where you are finally caught up and actually manage to work towards a vitcory method. There is no early game. There is no mid game. This is not my definition of challenging. This is cheating at its finest.
I would still recommend this game, but with a huge warning: once you get to 400-600 hours, you will need to decide whether or not you are ok with easy wins, or playing the very un-fun deity difficulty, or if you want to play multiplayer. Multiplayer with friends can be cool if you have some friends who aren't sore winners, or I'd recommend finding a No Quitters Steam group to play with, as that's the only way you'll get real games. Be careful, though, as even multiplayer turns into a♥♥♥♥♥♥show quickly. Have fun!

Lisa is for people who are not looking for happiness or power fantasies. It's for people who want to see just how dark a story can be, how unrelentingly brutal yet fascinating a ficitonal world can be. The game can best be sumarized by a small anecdote: At one point, you wander into a random house to find a man with a fish bowl on his head dancing. Funny enough because of the randomness. But when you come back, the same crazy music is playing but the man has hung himself. Lisa paints a truly bizarre, sometimes funny and mostly sad portrait of a world where hope is the most precious commodity you can have and it's nowhere to be found. Until Brad, a karate teacher, discovers a baby girl. The only female known to exist in the world. Brad raises her as his own until one day she is taken by someone. Brad sets out to get her back and prevent something horrible from happening to her.
This game is essentially a side scrolling turn based JRPG, and while the combat is solid enough, it's the world and story that make this worth playing. I'm trying to think of something to compre it to andI'm failing miserably. I've heard comparisons to Earthbound for just how strange it is, but I sadly need to still get around to playing that game. But here's the bottom line: This game is wholly unique and worth a look for people who can deal with unhapy stories. The humor in the game is used to prvent it from being more soul crushing than it already is.
The ending is bound to be controversial, but one thing is certain: after seeing how everything gets resolved, this game is going to stay with me for a very, very long time. It's darker than hell's deepest dungeon, sometimes funnier than most comedy movies and one of the most thought provoking games ever made. It has some notable flaws, especially serious frame rate issues in a few of the final areas that reduced the FPS to about two (and that's not an exaggeration) but it is so unique, so different and so damn fascinating that it's easy to overlook those flaws.
Don't buy this if you're looking for a happy ending or easy resolution. Don't buy it if you like games that make you feel empowered.
But if you can appreciate something different, something almost endearingly sad, something that will latch onto your brain and refuse to let go, buy this game.

Can you?
Because LISA is worth the pain, if you can.

ADR is a (seemingly) biographical game/walking dream simulator about the developer, Steve Harmon and lets us explore his dreams, thoughts, anxieties of the future and pain in the past by letting us through them.
Even though this is a great premise with lots of potential (evidenced by previous similar games most of us will have already played) , it is bogged down by the fact that this game only cuts skin-deep. Often it simply falls short in conveying his feelings through mechanics and letting us relive his memories does not do anything for me. (e.g. Most people have experienced unrequited love but it does not feel like walking in a big pool of water staring at huge letters) Hints at something bigger are strewn around the entire game but it does nothing with it.
I can relate to his experiences easily but I can't truly empathize because even when he seems to let his walls down, it still feels like a performance, a socially acceptable level of artistic pain but nothing beyond that.
While the game is free as in free beer and I wish more games like these made it to Steam, I'm still giving this a "No" as I wouldn't recommend any of my friends to play it.
However, I'd like to add that I am interested in what Steve Harmon has to offer in the future and I wish him all the best!

Mafia 2 is a good game that could have been amazing.
There is a lot of good, a lot of inexplicably bad, and a lot of wasted potential.
First, the story. It's decent, but there's rarely anything going on, and when there is, it's either near the end or doesn't last very long.
A lot of events have no impact on the story whatsoever, and most characters are pretty bland, particularly the main protagonist, whose only personality trait is his complete lack of care for his actions, he just does whatever he's told until the final missions, and most of what he does before getting into the mafia is just busy work.
Busy work you'll have the privilege to experience for yourself.
This leads me to my next point : the gameplay.
First of all, the missions. Some of them are, as I said earlier, busy work. You drive a cigarettes truck for a bit, park it, give cigarettes to people, go somewhere else, and do it again. Sure, after that you'll get to shoot some greaseballs in the face for burning your truck down, but the first half of this mission is terrible, and stuff like that happens pretty often.
Another problem with mission design is that the game forces you to drive everywhere. And I mean everywhere. Drive to Carlo's, watch a cutscene, drive to get someone, and then drive to the mission zone. When the mission is done, drive back to your place. This is really annoying, despite the game's fantastic physics. Driving is fun, but being forced to drive accross the map quickly turns driving into a tedious task.
Checkpoints are very scarce, but missions are short so this really isn't a problem, except in the DLC, where you have to start all over again (including the lenghty driving sessions) if you fail.
Despite their lazy checkpoints, DLC missions actually fix a lot of the game's issues, and most of them involve you shooting bad guys. A lot of them. The car stealing missions in Jimmy's vendetta can get a bit boring at times, but it makes up for it by having a lot of shootouts, most of which are surprisingly well designed.
Now, one of my favourite aspects of the game. The marvellous physics engine! It makes driving incredibly weighty and fun, and makes shootouts really intense. Wooden crates get torn apart and send wood flying everywhere, bottles explode, glass shatters, lights go out, bullets leave giant holes  in conrete walls and send dust flying everywhere.
Weirdly enough, you can't shoot from your car. Some might see it as a big problem, but the game doesn't need it. Besides, it makes car chases more challenging.
The APEX physics option doesn't seem to do a huge lot, but is completely brokens and halves the framerate of the game (your mileage may vary).
Finally, the best part of the whole game, the gunplay. The game lets you carry a metric ♥♥♥♥ton of guns, and they're all very fun to use. They sound good, they look good, and they feel good. The recoil is very nicely done, and makes automatic weapons particularly fun to use.
The game uses health regen and a cover system. But have no fear! They don't impact the game in any negative way (which is a miracle). Your health only regenerates to about 75% and you'll need food to replenish it. The cover system is extremely basic and only useful to get you out of spicy situations when you're about to die. The game actually lets you run around the place and shoot people without forcing you to hide behind a wall, and doesn't even force you to zoom in (!) to be accurate at medium range!
Mafia 2's big problem is that you don't get gunfights as often as you'd want. Some missions even rely entirely on you using your fists, and the melee combat system is really bad. It's basically impossible to lose as long as you're holding your block key.
Another very good aspect of Mafia 2 is the atmosphere. The cars look fantastic, and so does Empire bay. It's colorful, it's flashy, and the radio is amazing. All the characters naturally have a cheesy mafioso accent, which may or may not be great, depending who you ask. (it's great)
It's nice to have a shooter that doesn't look completely dull.
Despite its open world, Mafia 2 doesn't have anything for you to do in it outside of the storyline.
It serves as a beautiful backdrop, and driving in the streets while dodging traffic at 100km/h is fun, but secondary missions would have been welcome. The cops don't do a whole lot, but will come after you if you exceed the speed limit or bump into another car. They can get mean if you start to shoot at them, and they won't hesitate to pull out the tommy guns.
The game's wasted potential comes in the lack of secondary missions, which could have easily fixed some of the game's biggest problems by adding more gunfights and introduce car races (it's a shame they didn't implement any, because the car physics are some of the best around, and tuning your car isn't very useful).
To sum it up, Mafia 2 is a good game despite its flaws. Sure, some missions are uninteresting, and the story and characters are somewhat disappointing, the melee combat sucks, but it makes up for it with its incredible gunfights and delightful atmosphere.
If you've been looking for a good PC third person shooter, look no further. I heavily recommend it if you can grab it on sale, especially the DLC missions, which fix most of the main game's issues.

Without Within is a Visual Novel that tells the story of a girl who has Calligraphy as her job, and how she manages to live everyday using her job.
This Visual Novel depicts that Reality is harsh. It's not those "Slice of Life" animes that we watch. It's where you have to find a job to earn yourself food and a cozy abode, besides other amenities that you have to pay while using (i.e. Electricity, Computer, Water).
Another factor this VN teaches us is that not everything we like is useful to us that much. This affects us especially on your job if you ever have one. The protagonist's job is a calligrapher, but besides drawing letters and symbols, what can you earn more? This VN tackles that aspect.
As expected of a free game (most of the time), Without Within is short.
But then, since Without Within 2 is out (and also at a reasonable price), I'd recommend you to skip this one and buy the second instead. It has more content and you won't miss out that much.
- Free game.
- Artwork is cute! I really like the Protagonist's art.
- Music is okay. Loops fine.
- There are "Bad Endings" in this game. But it's so underwhelming! It's also instant; choose the bad one among the two choices given, and it will lead into a "Bad Ending". That's it.
- The Protagonist's status is unrealistic. Having a derelict apartment to live in yet having gadgets AND Internet to go with it. I know that communication is a basic right and we musn't miss out but in times of desperation we tend to sacrifice our perks just to eat and afford a decent living space. But to each their own.
- Not enough content in this Visual Novel, but I can't complain. It's a free game, right? But there are other free games that has much more content.
, this IS a free game.
- The DLC offers not so much content besides Digital Artbooks, Soundtracks, and some pictures. I reckon they add some backstory in how the Protagonist got into her apartment, or how she wanted Calligraphy as her job! Maybe add some tension about her parents arguing over her, or something like that. But the DLC is a dollar, and I bought it to support the creator.
- One thing comes to my mind. I think Without Within is an introduction (
) for Without Within 2. I mean, producing a free game to gain enough popularity for the second game, which is not free.
All-in-all, Without Within is a free game, so I encourage you to try it. But I'd suggest you buy the second game, Without Within 2, instead.
Yeah, it's pretty fun, but way too short. I know that it's free, but still, come on.

King Arthur's Gold has something that few other MOBAs of this type can replicate.
Sheer, utter chaos.
The Terraria similarity only goes skin-deep, as the only things this game has that makes it similar to the popular platformer are the ability to build and the art style. The latter keeps things simple, with enough expression in each of the three classes to make them distinguishable, yet not overly complex, whereas the former is a stroke of genius.
At the beginning of each game, you and your team will have a short space of time to construct whatever you deem effective in staving off the enemy. Teamwork is essential, as a good castle is perhaps more important than good combat skill. Once the match starts, sheer hell is unleashed.
The ground between two bases becomes a warzone. Makeshift wooden structures are built only to be destroyed a second later. Knights use their shields as makeshift gliders to parachute into the midst of the war, archers hang from trees and walls, sniping anything wearing a shirt that isn't their colour, and builders hang back in the base, pixelated faces cackling as they toss a boulder into the enemy or pefect a foolproof deathtrap.
The games are fast and furious, but what elevates it even further from other MOBAs is the drop-in / drop-out feature. Is the other builder overruling your suggestions for a space tower and is nicking all your gold? No big D. Just leave that game and enter another. Are you having trouble fighting, or even surviving more than thirty seconds post-spawn? Fine! I'm sure your skills would be valued in a new game. The seemingly obvious issue of everyone leaving as soon as the tide turns is obliterated by the gameplay, however; fortune never rests with one team for long. As such, this game is often my go-to for fast fun before I need to go somewhere and don't have time to be locked into a thirty-minute game, the threat of my status being diminished should I leave constantly hovering behind the 'quit' button.
In conclusion, this game is fun, moddable and a great long or short term solution to the MOBA hankering. In my opinion, it's worth every penny.

A game based off a novel, metro 2033. Is it a good game? Is it scary? Well i am going to review the game in a pro/ con style of the game and finish it off with my final conclusion.
Note: I am currently on chapter 17 and my playtime is messed up since i was offline and steam doesnt keep track of offline play time.
Pro:
The world looks very good. No matter where you are in the tunnel system or on top, the world looks very good. The land up top looks like a land that is under a nuclear winter while the underground metro system looks spooky and dark.
The game has a very nice show not tell segment. I say those moments where you see the civilians in these safe zones talking and interacting with each other and the player sometimes can be very emmersive and tell an underlying story of hope and survival. You cant help but be nice to these guys.
Con:
The story is not well explained. Mind you i didnt finish the game but so far the game is not making much sense. One moment that stands out inparticular is how i just got to this free use safe zone and got arrested for no particular reason and had to run for my life. It made no sense as to what happend. Also spirits? What game are we trying to show off here?
The voice acting is horrible. Now not every voice acting is bad but the way the game is stiched together causes their voice to be drowned out by sound effects and ambient noise or they are using some bad distance and directional audio placement. If you not looking at someone who is talking then you wont hear anything even if your right next to them. All i got to say is thank god for subtitles but it should never come to that. That should not be the only way to understand conversations between characters in the game. Also back to my main point some characters have horrible lines and are annoying to listen to. Mainly all the russian kids in the game have either the same voice actor or present it in a similar way that they sound the same....they all suck.
The frame rate is abnoxious. This is not a big issue that everyone faces but a fair bit of research shows people having similar problems. My thought is the developers got lazy and did not optimize there game. When I was playing, the game would change frames per seconds rapidly. Mostly it was 60 fps but on other times which were pretty often it would drop to 40, 30, or 20fps. It becomes a bother to me when it effects gameplay which it sure does. Mainly these drops occure in those moments when stealth is about to be broken and when I need that throwing knife to hit a guy and the frame rate drops to 20 and I miss. That gets annoying so often, mainly the work around is to skip stealth and go straight to shooting which sucks beacuse I actually would not mind stealthing. Even in fire fights the frame rate drops down to 30s. Needless to say gameplay for the game is in consistent and it is noticable when these frame drops happen.
The main characters are very uninteresting. They are uninteresting because none of them last long enough to care about. If we had more time with some characters to build a bond and understand more about them then there would be some emotional response if they were to die or leave. Many characters except for like one you experience for one or two levels. That is not a good sign for a game, if I can not care for the characters or the story then what is the end goal?
The load times are weird. Now i dont mind if a game has some what longish load times but you need to give me something in return for waiting. Now the loading here is used for the main character to write about the mission in his diary. The issue here is on a large ammount of levels the monologue is too short to ammount to much of a loading time. One monologue is like two sentences long for a loading screne that takes about 2 to 3 minutes. Thats roughly about 2 to 3 minutes of nothingness for the player to do besides wait. Let's compair the loading screen here to say modern warfare 2. In modern warfare 2's loading screen it is a cutscene that shows off details about the mission with dialogue and that cutscene is longer than the loading time but it can be skipped once it is fully loaded. What that game does is has interaction with the player by telling a story through the load time instead of saying a few sentences and then letting them sit there bored waiting for the game to finishing loading the next level.
What exactly are we? Faction wise whose alliance are we. I know there is the redlions and nazis and another group but even the other group does not know what alliance we are in because they stated we are not a redlion and obviously not a nazi. The game through all the time playing did not clarify this question to me.
The game is horribly dark. Now I dont mean dark as in tone but i mean visually dark. The flashlight does not do much in terms of illuminating the area to allow for me as the player to see where I am going or where am I suppose to go. Being dark does help with atmosphere but at the cost of the ability to play the game. With the game being so dark it makes it a huge challenge to see traps. The game would benefit if the maps that are in a dark tunnel were brighter to help the player see.
The game has no sense of direction. The game is nice enough to give us a compass to show us where to go but the problem is that in a fair bit of moments the game does not tell me where to go so instead of fighting the infinite spawning enemies in the map to survive I must run as fast as I can to get to some point to do something. I am running instead of fighting because I am carrying that compass to show me where to go because that is a problem that game fails to do.... guide the player some times. Another moment I got lost was in the building to broadcast the radio message. The map of the building was so poorly designed that where does one go to progress.
Finally some enemies are awful. I am referring to those tiny little monster that come out of those holes. They never stop spawning and they run fast. I dont know what purpose they serve but they seem to exist just to be annoying and something to hurry the player along so they dont get too distracted with exploring in a game that exploring is the key of survival.

This game is amazing. It originally featured a very small development team that worked on the game for something like 6 years. You can tell from the details there is a lot of love put into Metro. The redux is awesome, as they fine tuned the original and put some options to make the game more accessible. You can choose whether to focus on stealth or make it more focused on gunplay. Both are excellent and regardless of what you choose you can still opt towards stealth options which will definitely be necessary.
There are so many good things about this game, and so many details that lend themselves to the immersion. I couldn't fathom playing it on a console because there are so many buttons and little details you use.
You blast a beast, blood spatters on your face. You hit G to wipe your gas mask so you can see, then quickly charge your batteries so your flashlight or night vision doesn't crap out on you in the next fight. You run through a maze of carnage outside, trying not to get picked off by whatever that is flying around, you stumble upon a huge pack of enemies, you grab your shotgun and check that it's loaded.
BEEP BEEP BEEP, SHIIIIT, your filter has expired, you start struggling to breathe. Frantically you start blasting the group of enemies while searching for a spare filter, but you are attacked and broke your gas mask anyway. Your vision goes blurry as you race towards a building for refuge, choking on radiation. You run like a ♥♥♥♥♥ from the last of the enemies, and squeeze inside at the last second before collapsing on the floor.
You feel overwhelmed, damning the fact you hadn't scavenged for a spare filter before going outside. Then you hear a low cry, something you haven't heard before. Uh oh, it's a librarian, I hope you found and read the journal entry on how to control this beast, because you don't have many shells and they aren't doing much anyway. It comes at you and your heart skips a beat. Hard stop.
You pause the game, and remove your headphones. You're safe in your room. "This is too much" you think as you take a breather, pacing down the hall to return to the challenge in 5 minutes. This game is very intense, sometimes unforgiving, and incredibly immersive. I love it. The details all add up to something great.
When the newest metro comes out next year I might just♥♥♥♥♥♥myself!!!!!

Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is an underrated gem and probably the best vampire game ever made. If you're a fan of deep RPG's and have never played this game you're missing out. How I didn't write a review for this sooner I will never know. I have far more hours played then what I have showed here. I use to play it at my friend Alex's house. All the time!
Basically before the newest updates, you had about five base races and around four to five ships. The update added a few more things and made the Crystal people (people who do not use air the way all other races do) and their starting ship, a starter ship.
FTL is a rouge like space sim. You manage a grid based system closed or not closed off by air tight doors. Each room can and will be populated by important subsystems like the engines, firearms, shields and so on. If a room (and it will) gets damaged during combat it will turn orange then red, closing down whatever function it serves until repaired. Your hull also takes a beating here and like most games once it reaches zero, que explosion sound.
You also have to manage fuel consumption as this can only be randomly found or purchased at stores sprinkled along the in game star maps. All the while a swiping armada is ever in pursuit of you meaning you can never visit every star system along the way and choices will be made, for better or for worse.
What cool about FTL is the feel. Space is a static place, combat is handed in real time (unless you pause to que up orders) with two ship layouts suspended by two frames side by side as it all unfolds. Half the fun is trying to rock paper scissor your way out of whatever ship design you’re up against using whatever tools (subsystems can be gained along the way along with new improved weapon systems including drones of all kinds) you have at the moment.
The game is fairly long, there is a point system but you mainly play to unlock new ship types and variants of older ones.
In my humble opinion this is one of the most unique and fun rouge crawlers I've ever seen. And I own and have played many but nothing compares to FTL, it is a lazy Sunday played right in my book. You could sip a beer, smoke a joint and just get lost in it. Oh and the music is exquisite!

One Way Heroics looks really simple and shallow on the surface but it is a gem that wont break the bank! Why should you buy this game?
*Multiple classes, fully customizable with feats and items from your vault and shops.
*Near infinite amount of randomized worlds to explore and attempt to beat.

One Way Heroics has a straightforward but great concept. I was just about to overlook this game and not buy it but brought myself to anyway. Did I regret it? Definitely not. Why? A small price to pay for several hours of game gameplay and replayability. Was it worth it? I don't know about you but if I followed the concept of "$1 = 1 hour gameplay" then this is definitely worth lots more than what it's priced at.
-Overviews and stuff- (
)
You play as the "almighty" hero and continue travelling right to take down the demon lord who is slowly consuming the world in darkness. This darkness will continue following you throughout your travels. The game will also happily remind you that the very left side of your screen is death and despair and you don't want to be caught in it otherwise it'll eviscerate you...

There are several dimensions and special ones every now and then. This means you may share a dimension with friends (though you won't see them, you'll see how they did).
In case you don't know what rogue-likes are, they are basically games that start you at level 1 and if you end up at the game over screen you have to start the game all over again, at level 1. Games like these however will allow you to carry certain 'things' over to your next playthrough. In this case, you'll be allowed to carry a limited amount of items you found across your previous travels (the limit of items can be increased as well).
With One Way Heroics, you'll want to explore as much of an area as you can because you cannot stick around for long, and this is the part I liked best about this game. Exploring dungeons is risky because walls end up being an obstacle (and possibly sandwich you with the darkness if you can't get out). Don't stick around towns for too long as you'll want to do what you need to do then get out so then they can die and you'll continue on your journey.
There's quite a number of items you can obtain in-game, dungeons to explore and as you finish your playthrough, you'll see your "Heroic rating". Depending on your rating, you'll earn certain amounts of Heroic points to use to unlock perks, classes and the cap limit of your dimensional vault. What you do affects your rating (challenging yourself can be rewarding as well).
Perks are upgrades to your hero and you may change them to however you like. Extra perks are unlockable if you earn enough points for them.
As for classes, you may either use your points on buying them OR you can unlock them for free by doing the objective for them.
Dimensional vaults can be used to carry items from your last playthroughs and into your new game. The cap limit can be increased with heroic points and become more costly the more space you have.
-Opinion(s)-
There's a lot to why I find this game enjoyable but I'll tell you the main ones.
1. The concept is pretty simple, and when it comes to concepts, I usually prefer simple ones. It's how you execute the concept is what appeals to me the most. This game actually did a great job at it and you'll be reminded very 'clearly' as well. I personally liked it and of course, this is basically my opinion of it. It'll either be a hit or a miss. Definitely a hit for me.
2. Usually when it comes to RPG, I tend to think that there will be a lot of items that aren't neccessary but are there anyway for the quanitity. Most cases I prefer quality over quantity and in this case, it was the right amount for either two. You won't find many things necessary but they are useful items so it is completely up to you how you want to play and you'll have a variety of items to venture with.
3. The gameplay mechanics are simple but for this top-down it also features diagonals (yes, very strange for a top-down to certain people but this added more of a challenge and I enjoyed it). I enjoy playing with a controller and I'm glad I don't have to actually use my mouse or keyboard at all to play this game.
4. Music. Why? It was great to listen to when I played the game and never thought about turning it off.
5. After you die or finish the game, you get to choose a variety of messages to tell others how you died or survived the struggle in dimensions. Even if the game ends, I'll be left satisfied with these messages (and unlocking more stuff).
6. Bread crusts. You'll understand once you play the game and meet the chefs.
Overall, I was very close to missing out this amazing game. I usually don't play top-downs, rogue-likes and what not but this game, whether you play games like this or not, I recommend you at least give it a go. It's not a grindfest and it's not too hard to pick up as well. It's also a cheap game, whether you get it on sale or not. This game was worth buying for just a few bucks.

Now LISA has all the bells and whistles of a good RPG: plot, characters, solid combat. But that's not what makes LISA special. The sheer amount of enjoyable content that LISA packs into itself is incredable. There's very little padding between the genius comedy, or painful interactions you face.

Expected a throwaway RPG maker game with♥♥♥♥♥♥ironic humour.
Got a very creative game with lots of absurd humour (not obnoxious sorandum jokes), a depressing plot with deep choices (can't think of another videogame from the top of my head that made me feel as bad about my decisions as LISA), simple but solid turn-based RPG gameplay with lots of replayability due to the sheer number of different party members (although I would've wished some of them were a bit more fleshed out) and a little bit of optional content you're bound to miss on your first playthrough, a fitting OST and pretty pixelart.
Must-play if you enjoy NES/SNES-era turn-based JRPGs, but highly recommended for everyone else, too. Don't be fooled by first impressions, LISA handles mature themes very well. Probably the best thematical presentation of drug addiction I've ever seen in a videogame, for example.
LISA: The Painful is actually a sequel to LISA: The First, which is downloadable for free. The First is gameplaywise completely different from this LISA (it's best compared to Yume Nikki, a pure exploration game) and since it's very niche I doubt most people will like it. It's not necessary to play The First prior to The Painful in order to understand the plot, it simply gives a little bit of background information on some of the characters in the game. If it sounds like your cup of tea you might want to check it out before playing LISA, but it's really not a necessity if the game ends up boring you.
Playing through LISA for the first time took me something like 9 hours if you were wondering if it's worth the price.
Oh yeah, and a word of warning: The game asks you if you want to play on Pain mode in the beginning. Pain mode makes it so that you can only use a savepoint one single time, which can probably lead to some frustration for first-time players. I recommend doing the first playthrough on normal mode and a second one on pain mode.

[SPOILERS] [I'M NOT KIDDING]
-The Good-
It's free. The art is very cute. The music is pleasant and usually accompanies the theme of the game fairly well. The only real character (the leading lady) feels more like a character than many in video games lately, so I'll give them points there. The occasional breaking of the 4th wall isn't too bad and I can tell that the developers really *wanted* this game to be charming.
-The Bad-
It tries to make you feel like there are multiple ending and that your choices matter (which is pretty important in this sort of game), but there aren't and they don't. At least, not in the sense that I expected. Any choice that deviates from the ending they want you to get gives you a "bad ending". I'm not even joking. They literally tell you "bad ending".
To make it worse, the "bad endings" are VERY heavy-handed. You didn't help that little boy? Well, guess what, everyone in the world is scum like you and the kid disappears and your life is basically over. Bad Ending. You (depicted as a small girl) hit a large man who was hassling you? Well, the police are now at your door and probably going to throw you in jail. Bad Ending.
But this is the one that kills me- You decide to get some sleep instead of playing a video game you were hassled into buying? YOU'RE ENTIRE LIFE STINKS AND YOU CAN NEVER ACHIEVE YOUR DREAMS, BECAUSE THAT'S HOW IMPORTANT PLAYING GAMES IS.
It just...
It was trying so hard. It wanted to deliver a specific message about how you can get inspiration from the weirdest places and how it's best to do things with a passion instead of half-heartedly, but they were SO focused on that SPECIFIC message that they lost sight of the fact that they could have had other messages. Or, if that's all they wanted to convey, they could have explored the other avenues of how to reach that idea.
-Conclusion-
Playing a game like this, I didn't want to feel like every choice was a "pick the one that will obviously give you a bad ending or pick the other one which will give you the ended we spent time on". I don't know if this decision was based on the development team just wanting to throw out a product to show people that they were around, or if it was just something they did on the side, but unlike a lot of the reviews I saw for this game, I just don't feel like it was done as well as I had hoped.
But, hey, it's free. So, there's that. And I guess it got me talking about it, which is more than I can say for other titles, so, if you want to waste about half an hour or less (depending on your reading speed), go ahead and try it out.

In the mode where you'll have to complete levels, you are trying over and over, finding the best way to complete the level and the tactic to beat the boss.
Overall, certainly worth the low price of 3 €.

SPOILER ALERT!!! THIS REVIEW IS A SPOILER!!! DO NOT READ!!!
During Part 1 of the Battle of Seelow Heights, I was tasked to sneak four Soviet commandos past German lines.
It was night. The anti-day.
Being seen would kill my men.
I crawled one of my commandos close to the Nazis and tried sneaking him across their lines. He died. I reloaded a save file and I tried it again, and he died; I reloaded.
I then tried sneaking across two at a time. They died. Reloaded. I then crawled all of them across simultaneously and reloaded. Then I tried sending them across: one-by-one. And the first made it. Then the second made it. Then the third was found and they died. I then tried sniping some Nazis from afar, saving now and then, adding Nazi deaths. And with weakened enemy lines, I sneaked my guys into a bush, on the other side. Two Germans walked into that bush. Reloaded.
After two hours of reloading saves later, I got them past the enemy lines. And three hours after that, I de-mined a canyon, planted my own mines, planted some TNT, and moved my Ground Hog Day commandos to the Part 2 checkpoint.
Dawn. The Anti-Dusk.
The game tells me we have to take the German positions on the hills, and it tells me I have a limited number of computer-controlled reinforcements, whose bodies are essential to victory. And the battle is a slog. The Germans are dug-in. I see the number of reinforcements ticking down. I see that I will run out of friends long before the main base is captured. So I reload. Many times.

Four hours later, I give up on reloading and on playing the game on “Normal.” But I don’t lower the difficulty. I just wait for the number of reinforcements to tick down. And it does….
They keep coming; allied troops keep coming; an hour later they keep coming; the end of the battle they keep coming.....
7/10

While the gameplay mechanic is fun (grappling hook, etc.) and the art direction is lovely, ultimately this game is very frustrating. In the 2nd half of the game, the checkpoints get unevenly placed, often requiring you to re-do some frustrating platforming.
What's more is that you have to be at a precise range for your grappling hook to be activated. I had a couple of occasions where I missed my intended point by just a few inches which made me plunge to my death. And since the checkpoint was a bit way back, I had to do some sections before I could get back to the frustrating part to retry. If I missed it, it was back to square one.
This could've been avoided if the checkpoints were placed right before the frustrating bits. But nope, it wasn't. And if I failed a certain point it took way too long for the game to restart from the previous checkpoint as you have to waste too much time seeing your character plunge to his death. Sometime you don't even know where to go and you end up just dying and have to watch the overly long plunging animation.. Just make the time before restarting from the previous checkpoint just a bit shorter and place the checkpoints immediately before frustrating parts and this would've been a gem.
The story is nothing to write about and ultimately this game could've done with a couple more play testing and refinements before release to minimize frustration. And it is a bit short for its full asking price. Ultimately, a game's ultimate objective is to make the player have fun and not leave the gamer with a frustrating experience.

This is definitely a game that deserves an HD rerelease.
If you are put off by the occasional bug, such as doors not unlocking properly, you may get frustrated by this game.
Looking past that, however, this game makes you feel like you actually gain something from most of the quests given to you. Like most games of this type, however, your choices don't seem to impact the quest-to-quest style, however you do get a few choices of ending based on what you do throughout, which is pretty cool.
There are definitely characters that feel under-utilised, but for the most part, characters within were fun and interesting, and most left you wanting to help them (and sometimes hinder). The dialogue options for the vast majority of the game were varied and intriguing, though your options are different depending on your clan, and your skills.
Another thing to note is that each clan makes your playthrough different in some significant ways, such as "racial tension" each clan has their own reputation and may be viewed with disdain or awe depending on who you deal with, and the choice of clan you make can change your entire experience in the game.
Further, this game doesn't fall into the usual pitfall of simple race and class mechanics. Sure, some clans excel at certain things that others don't, but for the most part you are able to customise yourself to be able to fill the roles you want, though there are extreme classes that restrict specific aspects of your character. It actually feels like your choice of clan doesn't dictate entirely who you are, merely your initial strengths and weaknesses.
The absolute best part of this game though, is that it doesn't make Vampires boring. Not all vampires are the same, they're given personality. It actually feels like the undead have lives.
(It's recommended to get the Unofficial Patch, to support your gaming experience)

The game is one of the most immersive RPGs' I have ever played, I connected with it's dark atmosphere, gritty settings, well developed characters and the White Wolf License. This game faced disaster when it first came out on the same day as Half-Life 2 back in 2004. Firstly releasing it against one of the most influential games was obviously going to side-line it, but, secondly the game wasn't finished by the time Activision decided to push it out; as a result it went into the wind, unheard of.
I must state that I play games for their stories' and immersion, while some people may find other mediums of entertainment such as TV and Film to indulge in better stories; this game did not disappoint. The story of the Vampire clans vying for control in L.A and the underlying plot about a certain object is well thought out and crafted, supported by top-notch voice acting; all thanks to the Source engine.
Graphically this game may look dated now that we are in 2013, but don't be fooled it still captures the gritty setting perfectly. The gameplay may also be dated, however as stated I mainly play games for their stories' and as a result tend not to focus on 'high' graphics and 'great' game-play. (I'm not saying it isn't integral of course). Speaking of the gameplay, the amount of variations that are found in the different vampire clans is fresh. For example if you play as a mad-stricken Malkavian, this may open up specific dialogue options and immersive events; and that's not even including the different powers and abilities.
The game design isn't open-world, but boy it is fun to explore! The side-quests may not be as numerous as the ones' found in Skyrim or other top RPGs'. However the quests in VTMB are rich, immersive and are genuinely fun to play.
Overall I find this game to be in my top 30, and would recommend this game to anyone who likes fresh, original, and immersive stories coupled with vampire fiction and good but not revolutionary game-play.

The first time I played the original game, not this version, I would literally be sweating in fear at points of the game. The atmosphere was just unbeatable. It's something that Eastern European developers seem to pull off very well, especially in comparison to American devs.
The ever present fear of running out of supplies, the fear of suffocating without another filter to replace your spent one in your gasmask, as well as the creatures lurking in the dark, snarling and barking as they get closer and closer. Smaller creatures yipping and yelping... it's great. Creaking doors and metal, and the general ambient noise in my opinion, really immerses you in the underground world humanity has retreated to, with all the dangers - and protections - that is comes with.
I won't talk about the story because that's best left experienced without any clue beforehand, as to what awaits you.
The redux gets rid of the bugs and some performance issues that were in the original version and adds ease-of-life features from the sequel game. That being said, the original wasn't atrocious, and may not be even too noticeable, if at all, on powerful rigs.
I could gush and gush and gush about this game for page after page, so instead of taking my word for it, buy it and try it out. It usually gets put on sale whenever steam is having one and is incredibly cheap. I think even at the asking price, it's cheap. This game is well worth the cash.

How I didn't write a review for this sooner I will never know. I have far more hours played then what I have showed here. I use to play it at my friend Alex's house. All the time!
Basically before the newest updates, you had about five base races and around four to five ships. The update added a few more things and made the Crystal people (people who do not use air the way all other races do) and their starting ship, a starter ship.
FTL is a rouge like space sim. You manage a grid based system closed or not closed off by air tight doors. Each room can and will be populated by important subsystems like the engines, firearms, shields and so on. If a room (and it will) gets damaged during combat it will turn orange then red, closing down whatever function it serves until repaired. Your hull also takes a beating here and like most games once it reaches zero, que explosion sound.
You also have to manage fuel consumption as this can only be randomly found or purchased at stores sprinkled along the in game star maps. All the while a swiping armada is ever in pursuit of you meaning you can never visit every star system along the way and choices will be made, for better or for worse.
What cool about FTL is the feel. Space is a static place, combat is handed in real time (unless you pause to que up orders) with two ship layouts suspended by two frames side by side as it all unfolds. Half the fun is trying to rock paper scissor your way out of whatever ship design you’re up against using whatever tools (subsystems can be gained along the way along with new improved weapon systems including drones of all kinds) you have at the moment.
The game is fairly long, there is a point system but you mainly play to unlock new ship types and variants of older ones.
In my humble opinion this is one of the most unique and fun rouge crawlers I've ever seen. And I own and have played many but nothing compares to FTL, it is a lazy Sunday played right in my book. You could sip a beer, smoke a joint and just get lost in it. Oh and the music is exquisite!

In case you couldn't tell from the video, the big gimmick of One Way Heroics is that the left side of the map is slowly disappearing, and will eventually kill you if you're not careful.  The game has 8 classes, and each one is unique in a very refreshing way, ranging from the toe-to-toe fighting style of the Hero to the purely utilitarian Adventurer.  In addition, there are four difficulty levels with another major difficulty setting that makes minor changes to the gameplay.  With a total procedurally generated possibility of just over 250 trillion unique "dimensions," this game is very replayable.  And, as in any good rogue-like, you will die in very stupid ways and want to throw your computer every once in a while.
My one big issue with this game is that every once in a while it crashes.  And then it crashes again.  And then it crashes again.  And before you know it, you're losing games more often to crashes than to deaths.  This is supposedly due to a server issue (likely from the massive Steam influx) in the process of being fixed.
Crashes aside, this game is well worth what it's being sold for.  More, even.  I definitely recommend it to anyone with a little bit of loose change lying around.

Minecraft is a sandbox video game originally created by Swedish game designer Markus "Notch" Persson, and later fully developed and published by Mojang. The creative and building aspects of Minecraft enable players to build constructions out of textured cubes in a 3D procedurally generated world. Other activities in the game include exploration, resource gathering, crafting, and combat. Multiple gameplay modes are available, including a survival mode where the player must acquire resources to build the world and maintain health, a creative mode where players have unlimited resources to build with and the ability to fly, an adventure mode where players can play custom maps created by other players, and a spectator mode where players can fly around and clip through blocks, but cannot place or destroy any. The PC version of the game is noted for its modding scene, where a dedicated community creates new gameplay mechanics, items, and assets for the game.
Minecraft received praise from critics upon release, and won numerous awards and accolades. As of February 2017, over 121 million copies have been sold across all platforms, making it the second best-selling video game of all time, only behind the various releases of Tetris. In September 2014, Microsoft announced a deal to buy Mojang and the Minecraft intellectual property for US$2.5 billion, with the acquisition being completed two months later.
