Metro 2033 is a unique title that, despite what it looks like, is a linear FPS. There are some light survival aspects, and resource management is a massive part of the experience, but it's not STALKER if that's what you were expecting. That said, it's also one of my favourite games of all time, there's nothing quite like it. The game does give you options to difference scenarios, but at the end of the day you can't choose the order of events or where you must go.
Allow me to explain:
You take the role of Artyom, a semi-silent protagonist whom lives in what is assumed to be the last bastion of human civilization on Earth. 20 years prior to the game's events, there was a global nuclear war, and the only people who survived were underground, where only a fraction of the original survivors exist to date. We're talking a world where managing to get 20 people in one place is considered a decent sized settlement or large fighting group. Artyom has only ever known this world, having only lived on the surface for at most 3 years before the bombs dropped. His father never having made it to the Metro, and his mother having died to a swarm of rats (We'll get to that in a moment.), he's been adopted by a man in charge of a station near the end of the line in the whole of the Moscow Metro System, or what's left of it.
I will leave the rest unexplained, because story is a big part of this game, and honestly it's a joy. Not in the sense of it being happy, Metro is a game without happiness, but in the sense of being something you can simply get absorbed by. The game almost stands up on it's narrative design alone.
I want to preface this by saying one thing, play the game on Ranger Hardcore for your first playthrough, should you get the game. It removes almost all HUD elements, and also changes how much damage you and enemies take. It also effects how much loot you will find from enemies and lying around, as well as how much ammo you can carry. This is the true Metro experience. One thing I should mention, is it also disables the icon telling you if you can interact with something, so keep that in mind, and click on everything you think you can fiddle with. You'd be surprised how many boxes, crates, and lockers you can open.
Metro is an FPS game, and one of the best at that. One of it's strengths is it's weapon design, no weapon is ever made obsolete, but some are clearly better than others. For instance, one of your first weapons you receive is an SMG, made in the Metro, it's got poor accuracy and is the only weapon in the game that can overheat. But it also is cheap to both upgrade and easy to obtain, while also boasting one of the highest rates of fire in the game. This matters, because it can chamber the legendary Military Grade Rounds (MGR). This will boost the damage of the gun beyong most others in the game due to it's sheer rate of fire, at the expense of firing money, but I will get to that later. The gun also has another very nice feature, in tha the magazine is easily visible, thus you can see how much ammo you have left. This is more important that you think. I've run out of ammo many times without realizing I've just loaded a magazine with only 5 rounds in it with traditional and late game weapons, only to run headfirst into a fight and pepper those 5 to a click.
Metro also boasts a stealth system, one of the best in gaming, with clear indication of visibility and a sound detection system. If you want to survive the Metro, you will be utilizing the stealth mechanic, you simply will not survive otherwise. Unless of course you play on a lower difficulty, like a wimp.
There's also the matter of the surface, still irradiated even 20 years later, so much one cannot exist up there without a gas mask. This means you need to be on the lookout for filters and even new gasmasks if your sustains damage and breaks. This is not as difficult as it sounds however, and a smart explorer will never be without ample filters and masks.
Metro does something a little different with it's money. See, in Metro, the currency is based on a system of barter, with the universal currency being Military Grade Rounds (MGR). MGR are 5.45x39 firearm cartridges that were created before the bombs fell, they cannot be produced in the metro with the rudamentary equipment available, thus they're finite. This means they work great as a currency, this also means you're firing money at the enemy if you use them. Money that hits like a truck and has great accuracy, but money nontheless.
MGR can be used at any shop, and are very expensive, thus you will want to conserve them. Most weapons can be found, especially if you do a lot of exploration, thus I tend to rarely use my MGRs until the later chapters, when I load them in my weapons for a damage boost since there are no more shops after a certain point.
Metro has a large variety of enemies. Mutants who survived the bombs and became something horrid, and humans who decided the apocalypse was the right time to enact the communist revolution/roleplay as the most extreme nazis/become bandits. Most of the mutants are better left for you to observe and learn their patterns, but I will offer two pieces of advice.
Metro is intense, you can feel it with every step you can take. The breeze courses through you, the sounds of distant creatures, the breath of a monster. Every breath on the surface is one less you have until you choke and die. Every step into the damp darkness of the metro is another step to the beasts in the shadows. You will feel every last bullet you use, every last one you find. You will pray that every round you use is enough to finish your enemy, because you're scraping by with tooth and claw to win. It's not uncommon for me to enter a fight with almost no rounds left, and become one with my Kalash as I count down my rounds. Good headphones and a sweet GPU are a must, you will not regret it. Metro also boasts a haunting soundtrack of ghostly guitars and chilling female vocals, characteristically Slavic.
I'm goign to stop here, because Metro is a game best experienced. If you liked Halo CE on legendary and have a thing for post-apocalyptic settings, you will love metro.

Presented in both third- and first-person perspective, the gothic reimagining of Los Angeles features a tumultuous social and political landscape between the various factions of vampires vying for control. You assume the role of the unnamed protagonist thrown into this violent underbelly and join the clan of your choice before being literally let loose in to the new (and often strange) world.
But what happens next is up to you.
The game world is the centrepiece of Bloodlines as it constantly invites the player to really explore the depths of what it has to offer. With the incredible variety of methods and playstyles available within this sandbox-like environment, replay value is immense, as is the sheer enjoyment of exploration. There are plenty of unique abilities to use (and abuse) on the unsuspecting citizen, ranging from the seductive bloodsucking of the Toreador to the animalistic brute strength of the Nosferatu or Gangrels. Each clan has its own particular style and the variety of outfits available to the player reflects this.
Despite associating yourself with a particular clan at the beginning of the game, there isn’t content that is locked off to the player due to the constant political in-fighting of the Camarilla that forms the basis of the game’s narrative. Revealing your presence to the human population results in Masquerade point deductions, which can result in failing the game entirely and your activities depend on keeping up this secrecy. Outside of that however, your journey actively encourages as much havoc as possible and those interested in the supernatural will not be disappointed.
: Technical issues aside, VtMB is the vampire-themed game that you've been dying to play. A great example of the capabilities of the Source engine in it's prime, embrace this flawed gem with lowered expectations or during a sale and prepare for a bloody good time.

.

"The blood of Cain controls your fate"
What a game, what an absolutely amazing cult classic, a gem. Originally an unfinished mess with lots of bugs, the community patch has improved this to a point where you can enjoy it to its full potential. Not to mention you get cut content as well.
The dialogue in this game is very well thought out. Each vampire clan has its own dialogue and intricacies in gameplay that a playthrough is never the same. Malkavians are the crazy ones, talking in riddles whereas the Nosferatu are the monster Vampires that have to hide from society or be shot on sight. There are lots of dialogue options here and the skills you can get for your characters heavily influence the direction of each conversation.
To me graphics in such a game are not very important. It's a game from 2004 running on the source engine, it's expected to look quite aged but make no mistake here, the art direction is beautiful as well as the environments are designed in such a way that almost every quest can be completed in a different way. There are some lightning and texture bugs but that could be an isolated case on my end.
The gameplay immediately pulls you in from the start. Each vampire clan has its own powers and it's up to your choice on how to play and approach each situation, unlike a certain very popular "RPG". Will you try the diplomatic route and talk your enemies to death/surrender, try to make the enemies fight each other, maybe sneak past them because you decided to take a hidden path or will you make them explode in a gory mess of blood and guts as soon as you see them? It's up to you! However, your vampirice powers aren't unlimited, you are expected to feed from humans(or other things...) and drink their blood to sustain yourself, as a proper vampire would!
My only complaint here is that towards the end of the game, you don't get much choice in the matter and you HAVE to resort to combat but that's clearly an indication of the financial problems that Troika Games faced back then. I still have to put it out there though.
What is more, you can't go around town and destroy people with your awesome vampiric powers without consequences. You have to uphold the Masquerade, a set of rules in the vampire community. Betray the Masquerade and face what's to come.
Keep in mind that there's no hand holding in this game. You have to solve the quests yourself, the puzzles yourself, read the quest text and use your brain. Oh that security door is locked huh? What if there's a password around here somewhere or maybe I can bypass it by returning to the apartment and find a clue on my email. The possibilities are endless in this game, I can't stress enough how good the questing is. There is no minimap either, you'll have to remember the layouts of each area. Personally I love this, it's been quite a while since I played an RPG that wasn't a mindless follow the objective arrow simulator and it's been a breath of fresh air.
The music is excellent in this game. It really gives you chills when you hear Cain by Tiamat for the first time, the music immediately immerses you into the depraved, corrupted world of Vampire the Masquerade. Each piece of music and sound is specifically crafted and chosen in such a way as to make you think about what's really going on, if what you're doing is right or wrong. It really fits the vampiric theme and I can't stop listening to the soundtrack of this game.
My complaints here are that the gun sounds are not very good.
I can't recommend this enough to RPG lovers. If you can put up with older graphics and gameplay quirks(no map or magical arrow that points to the quest, you have to do the reading and thinking yourself here), you will absolutely love this. Remember to download the latest community patch!
P.S A certain main quest in the game will remain in your memory forever. It didn't get an award for one of the best levels in gaming for nothing.

Once in a while you encounter a town where you can spend money on new items or food, and sometimes you encounter dungeons with great loot.
An interesting mechanic that helps the game last longer are the perks you can unlock with points you get after an adventure is complete. Before you start a game you can select up to 5 perks (after you unlock the 5 slots) that can help you on your run and you can even carry over items you've obtained to use later.
Overall One Way Heroics is worth the $2.00 asking price and is deserving of any casual-hardcore gamer.

Okay, let me get a few things out of the way here, yes, this was made using the Unity Engine. No, not everything made using Unity is utter crap - there's been some really, really, really, bad things made with Unreal and Crytek, as Jim Sterling points out. Lastly, I have several games that fall into the same criticisms that I have for Chariot Wars, games that are badly designed, unbalanced, and at times glitchy, but are still fun to play such as Plane Crazy, Primal Rage, Hyper Blade, or The 7th Guest - the list goes on and on, but like I said, they're fun to play.
Gameplay: 65/100 D
Chariot Wars is simple, four directions for your acceleration, breaking, and turning, plus a speed boost that can be used after collecting "coins" on the track. The more you collect, the longer the boost. It's simple, the bare basics of gaming and yet there feels like everything is missing. Nothing feels right for a game, instead it feels more like a school project one makes to show off your understanding of basic coding and isn't really meant to be played for entertainment.
Audio: 69/100 D+
The sound effects are nice, the horses sound like horses, but nothing blends or fades together, everything seems to be a full blast, recorded separately, then thrown together. The music is okay for what it is, but what really grinds me gears is the sound the game makes every time I press a button. They couldn't have picked a less annoying sound. And I know these things can be turned off, but that's not the point.
Visuals: 71/100 C-
Unity isn't known for it's graphics, instead it is more known for cheap, poorly made knock offs, and while there are exceptions such as with Max - The Curse of the Brotherhood, games like Chariot Wars is what fills the market. Granted, Chariot Wars isn't the worst looking game out there using this particular game engine, it does look like it's from another time, specifically 2002. The intro cinematic for example looks like something that was made for Age of Empires and goes on for several minutes longer than it should have. The game itself is bland and very static in its animation and is also a prime example of how NOT to use bloom and motion blur effects.
Content: 63/100 D-
There isn't much in terms of actual meat to the game, you race, you play through the story, you race others, you pick your chariot, your horse, and your driver.
Story: 71/100 C-
Yes, there is a story here, starting off with a double murder and a mysterious symbol on a piece of cloth, and well, yeah, it really doesn't have much to do with the actual game as far as I can tell. Presented in comic book style slides that are decently colored and drawn, it seems as though this part of the game was given the most attention and care, which is a bit sad since it also seems to be the most disconnected part of the game.
Multiplayer: 61/100 D-
It's like the single player...just with others. At least from what I was able to play.
Design: 59/100 F
As I mentioned at the beginning, I have a fair amount of games that suffer from, let's say - flaws, that ruin what could be otherwise unique and amazing games. Before doing any research and actually playing the game, I was quite intrigued by Chariots Wars on name alone, thinking "Chariot racing? Tell me more." The emotion instantly brought me back to when I played Plane Crazy heavily, but that was quickly dissipated the moment the game started the "tutorial." The basics of it boil down to the fact that Chariot wars feels like a simple track game with a Roman skin laid over it. Even the names are unimaginative and are rather what someone would think ancient Roman names would be after watching The Gladiator, and that's the unfortunate side. This could easily be a great game in the right hands, and before you blame the Unity Engine, it is just a tool. It is up to the developer to make it great.
Performance: 77/100 C+
Crashed a few times when I first installed the game, but then the first patch came and seemed to fix that along with some other things. Besides that, the game ran fine, but I didn't expect it that it wouldn't.
Verdict: 67/100 D+
Chariot Wars just feels lazy. I'm not saying the developers were lazy, not at all. The game feels more like the equivalent of an animated story board for a film. It's the basic idea, show casing the ideas that you want to have in a much bigger game, but instead becomes the thing that is released, and I feel like it's a shame that things like this is what gives people and gaming a bad name down at the indie level of things.

This is possibly one of the best games I've played on Steam in my 9 years of usage from the service. At least, without a doubt, one of the best titles this year, by far. Let me tell you why that is.
These guys put many AAA Studios that release blockbusters to shame. Simply because these other studios spend hundreds of millions on useless stuff like advertising and marketing, and other unnecessary overhead costs, they probably spend all the money on pizza parties every day for example. But what I’m trying to get at here is that these guys, on a not so high budget, have managed to produce a high quality racer, that is either on par, or above par with a lot of triple A releases. Let’s talk about this in more detail.
The graphics, now I’m going to admit here, this isn’t their best asset for the game, it’s not ultra-realistic, even though it is pretty close. However, if these guys have made Chariot Wars as good looking to most other megaton releases, then not only is OM Entertainment talented, I ask the other developers out there, how in the hell do you get away with spending so much money on new graphical technology, when there is barely any difference from your last game release?
Ok, onto the gameplay. There is a rush of adrenaline when each race starts, you’ll want to ram and make your opponents crash, while you race onwards. The sense of speed and danger of your opponents possibly catching up behind you will have you on the edge of your seat, trying to keep ahead and control of your chariot. Honestly, it’s really hard to put this into words, so I’ll simply say, it’s just amazing.
We also can’t forget about the variety in locations and everything else. You can select multiple characters, and multiple different chariots with nice highly detailed designs to make yourself look more intimidating to your competition.  You can get an extra advantage over others if you choose the right type of horse depending on the map, which leads it into more of a thinking game of what to choose to out-do your opponents. Hats off to the developers for bringing some depth and variety to the selection process before each race including the nice selection of maps to choose from.
Speaking of the maps it’s nice to see highly detailed locations in Ancient Greece Egypt, and Gaul. You’ll actually spot some nice landmarks on some of the maps so you’ll know fairly quickly, where you are if you’re a history and geography fanatic like I am.
Really looking forward to the Multiplayer update, I’ll update this when it’s in the game to talk about it!

Metro 2033 is an interesting enough game, however I feel the flaws may outweigh the things that this development team strived hard to achieve.
For me, the main issue with this game is the frequent and lengthy cut-scenes and 'set-piece' stuff that made me in many cases just bored. Most of the game feels like it is tied to rails, and in several situations literally – with the dreaded rail shooter segments and associated drivel taken from 'Battlefield' and similar titles. Similarly, 'quick time events' pop up from time to time causing me to sigh in dejection… please stop this design in PC FPS games, it is boring and annoying. Overall, whenever you feel pulled into the game world and setting, you get jabbed back out again with QTE's, on rail events, and the like. I was frustrated… but pushed on.
It seems that this game would have greatly benefited from longer more spacious level design where you are left to your devices. Yes in one or two times this happens, but in my mind not frequent enough and the levels are still far too short. These issues seemed to be resolved in the sequel game. Moreover the 'check point' based saving system is a clear example of why it doesn't work in FPS games. Want to redo half a level over again because you didn't anticipate an instant kill scenario… well enjoy this game.
This game departs from the honed and perfected FPS model that Half-Life 2 gave us, and goes towards the Call of Duty and Battlefield 'linear corridor' motif instead. I prefer what DOOM had done last year, by delivering a lot of story though the environment and game-play with splashes of dialogue and interaction. Rather than lots of loosely put together and rushed exposition with a cast of characters that keep dying.
The game excels in set design and world building via the environment, some echos from 'S.T.A.L.K.E.R.' can be seen in the design, however this game never exceeds the atmosphere and world building found in that series of games.
The gun play is good, with an interesting 'home-made' feel to many of the weapons; the upgrade system is OK but nothing special and perhaps a little stale. The health system is arbitrary and confusing, but don't worry just hit a magic button to receive an instant heal to full health in return for one healing item.
This is my second play-through, this time in the Spartan mode, after running both games a few years ago. My first reaction was all the moments that I was anticipating and excited to see again were *actually* from my recollection from the sequel title: 'Last Light'. The sad reality is that game is far superior in every single way to this game, and the only thing I recall from this game is the decent into the D6 laboratory and the ending (or shall I say the lack of one)… a pretty poor showing for ~10 hours of game-play.
Where this game seems to play better is the stealth levels, which are pretty few and far between. Over-all the rest of the game seems add odds with itself, and the developers seem unsure what type of game to present to the player. I feel that most of the flaws in this game arise from this problem, and to note again that from my recollection Last Light solves nearly all of these problems and delivers a better experience.
For those interested in going to this game as the prequel, I suppose you might want to play this. But in reality to answer Steam's question 'would I recommend this game?' – No way.
Get Last Light instead, better in every single way possible. The 'story' in this game can be picked up from a let's play or a synopsis, it's simple and pretty bland, and acutally if I'm honest very rushed.

If you have not played this 12 year old game it ROCKS if you like a Vampire RPG where your character is turned against his/her will (girls are more fun to play ;)) and she is introduced into the Los Angeles vampire scene. I first played it  on Windows 7 and now on Windows 10, neither of which are mentioned as compatible on the game page. IMO Steam or someone dropped the ball on this. You need to install a patch to get proper functionality. There are threads about this in the Community pages.
Find the 9.5  patch here:
.
Runs fine on Windows 10. You may have to use an earlier version of the patch for Windows 7, but I've not looked at which patch.
Some tips: Make sure the patch has the right path to the game (Steam or SteamLibrary to SteamApps>Common>Vampire The Masquerade - Bloodlines)  especially if you have multiple Steam libraries. If it goes to the wrong place, no warnings, ti will happily install it at the path it shows.
After it's installed and you launch the game, the first sign the game is running from the patch, you'll see the game intro splash screens. If it's a black screem, just hit enter several times to get to the game menu and be advised you are not running the patched version of the game.  My understanding it's still possible to run the vanilla game after the patch is installed.
Select Options>Gamepay and if the patch is not listed, that's verified it's running the vanilla game. The vanilla game may seem to run ok, but when you run through the tutorial, you may run into issues, like not being able to select your fists using the default key (F1).
It has been suggested to find the game in in your Steam library list, right click it, select properties, and under the General tab, click "Set Launch Options" and in the blank space type in "-game Unofficial_Patch" without quotes, so the patched version of the game launches. I did this and really don't know if it made a difference, but the  patched version of the game launches. :) Also read the readme with the patch. If you add the "+" plus  content, it says you'll have to start over with a new game. No problem, this is my 4th run through. :):) Good luck, enjoy!

"The blood of Cain controls your fate"
What a game, what an absolutely amazing cult classic, a gem. Originally an unfinished mess with lots of bugs, the community patch has improved this to a point where you can enjoy it to its full potential. Not to mention you get cut content as well.
The dialogue in this game is very well thought out. Each vampire clan has its own dialogue and intricacies in gameplay that a playthrough is never the same. Malkavians are the crazy ones, talking in riddles whereas the Nosferatu are the monster Vampires that have to hide from society or be shot on sight. There are lots of dialogue options here and the skills you can get for your characters heavily influence the direction of each conversation.
To me graphics in such a game are not very important. It's a game from 2004 running on the source engine, it's expected to look quite aged but make no mistake here, the art direction is beautiful as well as the environments are designed in such a way that almost every quest can be completed in a different way. There are some lightning and texture bugs but that could be an isolated case on my end.
The gameplay immediately pulls you in from the start. Each vampire clan has its own powers and it's up to your choice on how to play and approach each situation, unlike a certain very popular "RPG". Will you try the diplomatic route and talk your enemies to death/surrender, try to make the enemies fight each other, maybe sneak past them because you decided to take a hidden path or will you make them explode in a gory mess of blood and guts as soon as you see them? It's up to you! However, your vampirice powers aren't unlimited, you are expected to feed from humans(or other things...) and drink their blood to sustain yourself, as a proper vampire would!
My only complaint here is that towards the end of the game, you don't get much choice in the matter and you HAVE to resort to combat but that's clearly an indication of the financial problems that Troika Games faced back then. I still have to put it out there though.
What is more, you can't go around town and destroy people with your awesome vampiric powers without consequences. You have to uphold the Masquerade, a set of rules in the vampire community. Betray the Masquerade and face what's to come.
Keep in mind that there's no hand holding in this game. You have to solve the quests yourself, the puzzles yourself, read the quest text and use your brain. Oh that security door is locked huh? What if there's a password around here somewhere or maybe I can bypass it by returning to the apartment and find a clue on my email. The possibilities are endless in this game, I can't stress enough how good the questing is. There is no minimap either, you'll have to remember the layouts of each area. Personally I love this, it's been quite a while since I played an RPG that wasn't a mindless follow the objective arrow simulator and it's been a breath of fresh air.
The music is excellent in this game. It really gives you chills when you hear Cain by Tiamat for the first time, the music immediately immerses you into the depraved, corrupted world of Vampire the Masquerade. Each piece of music and sound is specifically crafted and chosen in such a way as to make you think about what's really going on, if what you're doing is right or wrong. It really fits the vampiric theme and I can't stop listening to the soundtrack of this game.
My complaints here are that the gun sounds are not very good.
I can't recommend this enough to RPG lovers. If you can put up with older graphics and gameplay quirks(no map or magical arrow that points to the quest, you have to do the reading and thinking yourself here), you will absolutely love this. Remember to download the latest community patch!
P.S A certain main quest in the game will remain in your memory forever. It didn't get an award for one of the best levels in gaming for nothing.

This is honestly one of the better rogue-type games.
A lot of useful features such as saving the crew station positions and being able to return them at a click of a button ( would like to see send injured to medbay too )
Pros:
- Intuitive / simple ui with a lot of features / clickables to easily control power, weapons, drones, etc...
- Simple / Enhanced mode for new players ( so you can play it without all of the new content, weapons, etc.. )
- Games are relatively short ( 10 - 20 or so minutes if you rush ) and I am able to finish most within 1 sitting ( broken neck and back from mva where someone ran a stop sign and hit me because they were too busy looking at a "going out of business sale" in their passenger mirror to notice I had the right of way - they slammed on the accelerator after I passed the point of no return... I get stuck in bed for days at a time following too much neck movement among other issues ) so having a short / enjoyable game is quite nice...
- Graphics aren't "terrible" like you see in a lot of rogue-style games..  they are simple but not too simple.. And there are weapon animations, they light up as they charge up, etc... npcs are animated, etc..
- I like the idea of ship unlocks because it gives incentive to keep playing ( albeit meh in terms of how long it can take )
- Each ship has 3 different starting layouts ( including weapons, crew, systems, augmentations, etc.. ) but they need to be unlocked...
Cons:
- The bug that didn't make sense... If the enemy had sensors then, yeah, I could buy it not being a bug...
- The ship unlock mechanism is lengthy ( no I don't have 20 hours on "record".. I left the game open when I needed to lay down and was stuck for most of that time; realistic play-time is 1 to 2 hours in multiple sittings )
Bugs:
1 ) The only bug I've encountered so far, is if you defeat an enemy ship and still have an enemy on board, then travel to another location where another ship is present which also has a teleporter.. that ship will "recall" the enemy off your ship which doesn't make a lot of sense because they wouldn't know about the enemy especially since they didn't have any sensors onboard...
Other notes:
I purchased it during the summer sale for $2; I regret not buying it sooner. Because of the clunky unlock system which takes a long time to unlock there is replayability value to get those ships, but because it takes so long it can get annoying fast.
While I do recommend it, I'd recommend it at $5... There is a lot of repetitive gameplay and while the randomization aspect of shop contents is nice, the layout of each "stage" is also random but the same... I really wish this game would've incorporated some mini-games to ease up on the repetitiveness of the gameplay.. What I mean by mini-games is things like the game orbit or those small games which have gravity as an acting mechanic which could work well here....
"Your ship is being affected by the gravitational pull of a dark-planet / black-hole", then you have to sling-shot away by using thrusters at certain angles as your orbit.. this could work for planets, planetary landings such as when you go to the surface... etc etc etc... This would make the game a lot more enjoyable in my opinion...

Well, I just picked this game up a few days ago during the 2016 Steam Summer sale for 3 bucks. The first time I loaded it up, by the time I stopped I had over 13 hours played. That's how quickly this game hooked me. I just couldn't put it down. It's not possible to better spend 3 dollars!
I didn't beat the game until about 19 hours played (on normal difficulty). I pride myself at being well above average at most video games so when this game posed this much of a challenge for me to beat just the one time, I felt a real sense of accomplishment.
For new players thinking of getting this game, you have to understand that this game is very difficult. If you don't want to experience the frustration of dying your way through learning the basics repeatedly, you may want to invest the time to read a few guides, pull up the wiki and/or watch a few Youtube videos giving you some pointers and tips. That being said, I personally refrained from reading/watching any guides myself and while things were frustrating at times, learning the game firsthand this way was an extremely rewarding experience. I just know that not all gamers are like me and I'd hate to see someone quit this amazing game prematurely due to the frustration that learning it can cause.
The game is not without fault though. While it's difficulty is one of it's primary attractions, it's also one of it's most apparent weaknesses. There are times this game is so punishing that it borders on the unfair.
As good as this game is, great even, it requires a fair amount of luck. IMO, this is a fault. It may be better phrased that you have to avoid being unlucky. What I mean by this is, the game hinges on quite a bit of RNG. This RNG can be the difference between you becoming a Space God or you literally being so weak the game becomes unwinnable. Here's what I mean...
Now I'll stipulate that this was fairly early on for me and I was very much still learning, but I played one game where I managed to get far enough into the game without being offered anything in the way of weapon upgrades that I literally could not destroy the enemy ships I was fighting against. With the default arsenal you're provided, it was not possible for me to win. I went through three entire sectors (fairly large chunks of the game) looking for a new weapon and found none. This is what I mean by having to avoid being unlucky, because due to the procedural nature of the game, while this is exceptionally uncommon, it's quite possible for the game to simply not give you the tools to actually win, forcing you to start over. Now while I've had my fair share of unlucky runs, this was the only run where I felt there was literally no chance at all for victory.
Otherwise, expect this game to be like other procedural games where you'll have really great runs where the game gives you everything and bad runs where you're struggling to stay afloat. This is not in of itself a bad thing as it becomes very fun and FTL pulls it of beautifully. So beautifully that it becomes quite addicting. Starting a brand-new game and not knowing what wonders are in store for you this time or what horrors are bound to beset you and your crew is just an intoxicating experience that will enchant you from start to finish. And while this game will be frustrating at times, starting over from scratch almost immediately washes away any lingering adverse emotions the previous run may have left as you set out again, confident that during this new run, things are going to be different!

Despite its ridiculously tiny native resolution (which you can scale up) and its random crashes, OWH is a fantastic take on the roguelike, boiled down to its most simplest form - keep moving, and hack at everything.  Well, that's kind of trivializing it a bit as there are a bunch of abilities, weapons, and generally oodles of lootles to find and methods of keeping them from game to game.  There's also a save system, so it's not entirely roguelike at all, but close to a J-ARPG from the dayes of Yore.
Ahem... the main mechanic of the game is that the world is constantly scrolling into oblivion (the game is turn-based so as long as you stand still, nothing happens) and you need to keep moving right until you meet the boss.  If you make it that far.  If you can survive.  If you brought/found the right gear.
Regardless, success or fail, once you've concluded a run, you earn Hero Points in order to unlock character classes, abilities, perks, and most importantly, slots for your DImensional Vault.  Whazzat?  Easy - it's a safe to store items you've found so you can give it to the next hero you roll.  Pretty simple stuff.
Presentation is great, sounds are perfectly retrofit, and the only hit against it (considering this thing is priced less than a hamburger) is that it's a bit unstable.  Good thing there's a save system.
Anyways, if you have money in your pocket, you could spend it on stupider things than One Way Heroics; don't.  This game will satisfy you more than glitter putty ever could.

I've played RTS games off an on for basically my entire life, eg Command and Conquer, Warcraft, Age of Empires, Starcraft, League of Legends etc. I haven't been able to find a strategy game that has really grabbed me ever since I started League of Legends in 2010. Then I found this game.
I'm 40+ hours in and I've beat the first campaign, learned to win AI skirmishes on hard, won several multiplayer matches and I still have TONS to do and learn. I've still got the second campaign, and all the Theatre of War DLC's to get through. Most importantly, I feel like I am nowhere near mastering each of the factions for multiplayer. I haven't even tried 2 of the 5 factions, because I am making a point to learn them one at a time.
COH2 is awesome if you are a strategy lover, but RTS noobs will be frustrated if they aren't eager to learn. This game is not easy to master. but it's extremely fun after your first hour or 2 of getting owned. The graphis are great, even though I'm writing this review in 2016. The battles are packed with action and are a ton of fun to watch.
In regards to the gameplay, COH2 really redefined how I look at RTS games. Rather than just building a sprawling base and pumping out as many units as possible, this game DEMANDS careful and fast attention to exactly how and where you are using your units. If you want to win, you better learn to group and hotkey your units, and be able to micro manage combat on 3 or more fronts. Once the rifles start to fire, the battle never stops until the game is over.
My biggest complaint is that I didn't get into it earlier when the community was more active.
--
TLDR: Fantastic game if you like strategy. COH2 will take 100+ hours to master.

LISA: The Painful RPG is probably the most rewarding and unique game I've played this year. What drew me into purchasing it was the game's apparent dark humor content and its likeness to Earthbound, one of my favorite RPG's of all time. It seemed like a nice distraction, and at $7.50 for the special edition, I certainly didn't have much to lose.
What I wasn't counting on was this game stealing my heart unconditionally. Behind the absurdist front LISA puts on at first glance, there's a level of depth to this game both mechanically and narratively that I frankly didn't expect. The decisions that have to be made throughout the course of the game have such a strong weight to them. It puts you through hell, and forces you to make game-altering decisions that will leave you emotionally torn to pieces. I felt the weight of my decisions like a pit in my gut, which is something very few games successfully pull off without offering more than just the illusion of choice.
There's such a strong moral conflict between the game's protagonist and antagonist(s) that goes far beyond the mere struggle of good against evil. There are things at stake here, things to lose. I won't go into detail about what these things are for spoilers sake, but trust me when I say you're going to find yourself struggling to make a choice in the face of the brutal adversities LISA brings to the table.
On a more pleasing note, the game's dialogue and comedic value is top notch, and had me in tears on quite a few occasions. The motley band of fighters, monsters, and plain weirdos you run into throughout your journey always have something to say that's worth listening to (you'll be laughing at most of it). On top of the 30 recruitable allies you can obtain (each with a large variety of skills to use in combat), there's an innumerable number of characters you'll cross paths with that will either want to pick a fight with you, or just ramble to you about their problems. I guarantee you'll have a hard time forgetting each moment, because there are just so many worth remembering. You'll definitely have a large handful of favorites by the end of it.
LISA's soundtrack also delivers, with enough trippy, dungeon-like tracks to make any battle in the game feel like an eccentric nightmare (in the best of ways). From the somber, atmospheric noise that fills the dark caverns and heart-stopping flashbacks - to the gritty, yet feverishly catchy battle themes, you'll have a hard time keeping the music out of your head, even after you put it down. I highly recommend buying the OST along with the game, you won't be disappointed.
_ _ _ _ _
What's left to say about LISA? I'm trying desperately to find something negative to say about it, but I'm drawing a blank. It's quite honestly one of the craziest rides I've ever had in my gaming experience, and I can't stress enough how much larger the game is than the way it's presented. Do yourself a huge favor, and buy LISA. Buy it for you, and for all your friends. With a vague but chillingly compelling story, a colorful cast of characters, a gut-busting amount of humor, a soundtrack that oozes cool, and player-driven choices that ACTUALLY make a difference, what's not to like?
Be warned, this game will rip your heart out, but you won't want it back, because you'll be so madly in love with it all.

They dont make games as dark as Lisa. having been stripped of all the "save your feelings" fluff one is trained to expect from anything short of a George R. R Martin Novel.

After Saints Row: The Third, it was hard to imagine how this series of increasingly zany open-world crime games could possibly get any zanier. Rather than attempting to tackle that challenge head-on, Saints Row IV sidesteps it by being an almost completely different type of open-world game. Sure, the core of Saints Row is still there; there are still plenty of absurd weapons, costumes, and activities. But the way you interact with the world has changed. No longer are you an ordinary earthbound mortal. Saints Row IV turns you into a superhero capable of running up the sides of buildings and flinging people with your mind. This isn't a refined game or a challenging one, but it is a sometimes hilarious playground of a game that gives you plenty of fun abilities to use and plenty of opportunities to use them.
How does the game explain your new capacity for doing things like leaping tall buildings in a single bound and zapping enemies with freeze blasts? It's simple. You saved the world from a terrorist threat and became the president of the United States. Then Earth was invaded by aliens, and the evil alien overlord had you placed in a Matrix-style computer simulation of a city where, much like Neo, you can acquire all manner of abilities that break the rules of the simulation.
Saints Row IV mines its goofy premise for all it's worth. When "What Is Love" by Haddaway comes on as you're escaping from an alien spaceship, the juxtaposition of grim sci-fi visuals with '90s dance beats is so unexpected that it's delightful. And there's an infectious joy in the way your extremely customizable character, puckish rogue that he or she is, delights in it all, whether you've opted for one of the male voices, one of the female voices, or the aptly named Nolan North voice.
The simulation in which you spend most of the game is a virtual re-creation of the city of Steelport, and the city's layout hasn't changed much since Saints Row: The Third, but the evil alien overlord, Zinyak, has remodeled a bit, and he likes to keep it gloomy. Because there's no day-night cycle during the course of the campaign and the whole city is shrouded in darkness, Steelport is a drab, monotonous setting. But it's much more attractive on the PC, where objects are sharp and defined well into the distance, than it is on consoles, where objects even a short distance away look muddy by comparison.
Given that this is a game in which you can run around naked shooting people with an Inflato-Ray, you might expect the humor throughout to be crass and juvenile. And, for the most part, it is, but not always in the ways you expect. The game's humor is unabashedly stupid, but it's smart about being stupid, working in references to Shakespeare, clarifications about the distinction between alliteration and assonance, and knocks at those silly people who don't know the difference between a robot and a mech suit. The banter among Saints is consistently sharp and will definitely have you laughing out loud on numerous occasions.
Very early on in Saints Row IV, you acquire the abilities to leap incredibly high and to sprint at superhuman speeds, and by collecting ubiquitous glowing blue clusters, you can enhance these abilities and the others you gradually unlock. Once you can sprint, you'll probably hardly ever use a vehicle again, since you can run faster than any car, which makes all of the car customization options carried over from earlier games feel a bit superfluous. But it's hard to lament the lack of emphasis on vehicles given the exuberance that can accompany leaping 15 stories into the air and gliding all the way across town.
Those collectible clusters are visible from a great distance, so on your way from point A to point B, you're constantly incentivized to divert from your path, zipping up this building or leaping atop that house to collect them. And if you've attracted too much unwanted attention from the authorities, you can wipe out your notoriety by pursuing a golden snitch-like alien computer orb as it zips around the streets of Steelport and destroying it. It's a refreshing take on the common process of wiping out your wanted level in open-world games, and one that makes using your sprint ability a lot of fun.
While sprinting may replace driving as your primary way of getting around, the powerful attack abilities you acquire, like freeze blast and telekinesis and stomp, don't totally replace your regular weapons, but instead just augment your arsenal. Your offensive abilities need a brief time to recharge, so in between each use, you have a reason to switch to another ability or fire a few shots of whatever weapon you have handy. Unfortunately, though enemies may sometimes overwhelm you through sheer numbers, their AI is thoughtless, so the satisfaction of battle comes not from overcoming a challenge, but from reveling in the power fantasy of obliterating them with energy swords and dubstep guns.
Because the game is so good about doling out new weapons and abilities at a steady pace, you often feel like you have some fun new toy with which to torment your puny alien oppressors. However, because you have so many ways of so effectively overcoming them, combat eventually starts to feel rote and inconsequential, and you may often find yourself just freeze-blasting and shattering your enemies repeatedly to be done with a fight as quickly as possible. And it doesn't help that even though many of your weapons have crazy visual effects or other gimmicks associated with them, they lack any sense of oomph.
Thankfully, there are activities that give you a compelling reason to use some of your abilities. In the twisted game show Mind Over Murder (from the mind of returning murderous madcat Professor Genki), you need to use telekinesis to hurl people, cars, and Genki heads through designated hoops, and it's empowering to zip around the city streets, picking up hapless pedestrians and sending them flying for your own benefit. But the best activities are the old familiar standbys. Hopping into a tank to cause as much destruction as possible is a simple, explosive pleasure, and hurling yourself into oncoming traffic is still good for a few morbid laughs.
Saints Row IV definitely recycles plenty of ideas from earlier games in the series, but it's also frequently inventive, not just in its shift from absurd crime game to absurd crime game with superpowers, but in the content of its story missions. You play a 2D beat-'em-up, return to the series' Stilwater-set early days, complete a Metal Gear Solid-esque stealth mission, battle a Godzilla-size can of the Saints Flow energy drink, and get embroiled in all manner of other insanity. Almost every core story mission and optional crew loyalty mission has an entertaining concept or a funny surprise in store. However, these missions often focus on the same ho-hum combat you find throughout the game, so even though the ideas on display are varied, the gameplay feels a bit flat. Still, it's well worth playing through the story missions just because of their outrageous scenarios and sharp writing.
Even if combat sometimes falls into a rut, there are more than enough surprises in the game's story missions to keep you entertained, and as in previous games, you can increase the mayhem by inviting a friend along to do missions and other activities. Saints Row IV owes a lot to games like Crackdown and Prototype, but the absurd humor that infuses every aspect of this game gives it an identity all its own. The simulated city of Steelport doesn't offer deep gameplay or the most satisfying challenge, but it is a great place to mess around.

Travel through a post-apocalyptic 2D wasteland on a quest to save the last female. The story itself is pretty decent, nothing too special,  but I found that the setting and the characters were what brought the game to life. The post-apocalyptic, male only world would generally be pretty depressive, but the constant humor is perfectly juxtaposed against the depressive setting.
LISA's gameplay is very similar to the Earthbound series. Fights are turn based, and every character has their own unique skill set that they bring into combat. And there are a lot of characters to bring to your party. With 30 characters to find and recruit, you can mix and match your four man party to find a perfect match. Fights are pretty fun, with your main character being able to do combos in order to perform special moves.  I found the most fun in this game was exploring the world, never knowing what would happen next. Every area has different set pieces that could range from just being funny to knocking your party down to 1hp to permenantly losing all your items. I found that a little usage from a guide works best, knowing where to go next and what to avoid.
The soundtrack in LISA is amazing. The songs range from creepy and unsettling electic music, to mellow relaxing trumpets. I honestly wasn't expecting too much from this game, but the soundtrack was stuck in my head for days after beating it, and I still occasionally look up songs on YouTube because they are that good. I did have some issues where the music would cut out randomly for about 5-10 seconds, but it wasn't a huge problem.
For a 2D pixel game, this game has really detailed graphics. I'd say the highlight of the graphics would come from the character sprites.  Every character has their own unique sprite, so you don't see "Generic Thug #3" every battle, which is very refreshing. The world itself does get a bit repetitive, with it mainly being mountain-y wasteland desert, but it does change up every now and then. Don't expect to be wowed from pixel graphics, but they do their job in this game.
LISA is a tough game, which is fine, but sometimes in unusually cruel ways. Without spoiling too much, there's a part in the game about halfway through where you are forced to have your party members play Russian Roulette, with permadeath. This event is random, so one time I had almost my entire party wiped out, but after reloading my save several times I managed to pass through with only one death. There were several times were I just would hit a wall and didn't really feel like continuing with the game. Aside from that, there were the aforementioned audio cutout for several seconds, which isn't too bad. And finally, my game would occasionally freeze up for about 3 seconds, but my actions were still being processed, so I would end up jumping off a cliff to my death more times then I would have liked. Overall, the cons are very little nit-picking.
LISA is a wonderful game that I highly reccommend. If you like funny games or turn based RPG's, such as Earthbound, I would highly reccomend you get this gem of a game.

Let me start off saying that Civ 5 is a great game with a great premise...and a major flaw. Civ 5 is a wonderful game to begin playing, as its learning curve is gradual and improvements feel great. For example, I hopped into Civ 5 only having played 30 or 40 hours of Civ 3. The game felt great, the mechanics seemed strong and fun, and the game was rewardingly difficult. The strategies with the various civs felt numerous and fun, and the game didnt feel like a stomp.
Before I continue, please buy the complete collection if you are going to buy. Its worth it. The game is incomplete without it.
Fast forward 400-500 hours, and I have effectively played every civ. I know their weaknesses and strengths, I know their playstyle, I know map and city strategy. I am finally good at the game. This, however, is where things went downhill for me. Once I began running out of fun ways to win, I decided it was time to move past king-ish (slightly above medium) difficulty, and begin playing the tougher AIs. This was because I had noticed that the AIs in this difficulty were just not good.
Civ 5's major flaw is AI design. Players have 2 actions on most units, and the average turns were "move 2 squares" or "move 1 square and fight". Its simple, easy, and actually pretty fun to design a strategy to break an enemies attack incoming. However, this was where most of the flaws shone through. First: AIs vastly underestimate the number of units they need, bring outdated units, and attack like 12 year olds fighting on the playgrounds. It was sloppy. I discovered I could win 90% of my fights by having walls, and having 1 unit per city, building more when attacked. Im sorry, but catapults aren't useful versus infantry, but the ai Didnt know this. Going back to my discussion of what the average movement of a unit looked like, did you know that the AIs ranged units cant move AND shoot in a turn? this vastly cuts down their strength. Civ AI is horrible at decision making, and will go through all the military techs just to wage a war with 5 old units, or not even attack at all. There is no strategy in their play.
So I moved to the higher difficulties. I figured that they more difficult opponents would have stronger AI and would actually be fun to play against. I was sorely mistaken. The only ai change I could find was that the AI was more aggressive. This equated to a couple more units in a fight that was still easily defeated. War was laughable. Player Victory was inevitable, and cities were always conquered provided you weren't too far behind in military tech and you brought enough units.
This is where the second part of this major flaw kicks off: CIV AI didn't get tougher because they were better and well made. They got tougher because they cheated. Beyond King difficulty, the AI were given free techs, units, and even cities to start with. Now while I will admit that this does make the game more difficult, it does not make it more fun. Remember all those wonders thare are fun to rush? They already have the tech for them and have them 20 turns before you can begin them. Remember that fun strategy of early game warefare? It's impossible now because you are 4 military techs behind. The only strong strategy in immortal/deity play is to rush every single science tech,♥♥♥♥♥♥no one off and hope to get to turn 200 (on quick, most games end between turns 200-300 on lower difficulties), where you are finally caught up and actually manage to work towards a vitcory method. There is no early game. There is no mid game. This is not my definition of challenging. This is cheating at its finest.
I would still recommend this game, but with a huge warning: once you get to 400-600 hours, you will need to decide whether or not you are ok with easy wins, or playing the very un-fun deity difficulty, or if you want to play multiplayer. Multiplayer with friends can be cool if you have some friends who aren't sore winners, or I'd recommend finding a No Quitters Steam group to play with, as that's the only way you'll get real games. Be careful, though, as even multiplayer turns into a♥♥♥♥♥♥show quickly. Have fun!

Many compare Mafia to Grand Theft Auto. This is because both have open-worlds to explore, explosive action, and several cars to drive. However, Mafia II has a much more serious tone to it, and this helps to immerse the players in an amazing storyline. Personally this is one of my favorite games, but this is only because of its story. It's gunplay is average and it's open world is not really that open. This brings the game down just a tad, but if you are just playing for the campaign you will find this to be an issue. One of the main points about this game are wonderful driving physics. The roads actually impact the cars handling, the damage models are well done, and the cars have a realistic feel to them. This realism is furthered with the feature that cops are actually responsive to your actions on the road. If you speed, drive recklessly, or drive on the wrong side of the road, the police will try to stop you. If they catch you, you may pay a ticket or run, but running away is not that easy. This is one of my top ten games of all time, but this is only because of the story, if you are looking for great gunplay and an expansive open-world look elsewhere. I'd strongly recommend the Grand Theft Auto series or the Saint's Row series.

Metro 2033 is a decent game. Not great, just...good. It's relatively short, but then again I don't usually care how long a game is as long as it's good. I just feel like not that much happened narrative-wise over the course of the 7 hours it took me to beat the game.
However, what they absolutely nailed is the atmosphere. The green, hazy, radioactive tunnels of the metro are certainly a unique experience to say the least. Those scorpion things are scary♥♥♥♥♥♥ I know it's based on a book, but the post-apocalyptic world feels original and is visually and tonally interesting.
A few negatives now. The enemies feel a little bit overpowered compared to the guns you have to fight them, and how often you have to reload. But it's not enough for me to say 'lol bad game op enemies,' it's just a little bit annoying. Another thing is the resources like ammo and filters. There was one specific time where I ran out of filters and kept dying before I made it to the next cutscene/setpiece-thing. I kept having to replay the sequence, sprinting the whole time, hoping I made it before I just died. I felt like filters were a little bit too rare for how important they are.
While not "bad" per se, a lot of the characters were...forgettable. No one stood out to me as someone I remember, except for the commander guy right at the end of the game (but that's only because it's fresh in my mind). I also took quite a long break about a third of the way through playing it (like, many months long), and found that when I came back I had no idea what my main objective had been or why I was out in the tunnels. I still don't really remember why Artyom (the player-character) set out in the first place. And at the end of the game, I found that that didn't really matter. I'm no expert on stories, but I'm pretty sure that's a bad thing.
Playing 2033 was a perfectly good experience. Unique setting and atmosphere, mildly compelling story once you get into the thick of it, adequate gunplay. It wasn't anything special, but I am looking forward to playing Last Light now, which I got in the bundle with this game. I recommend buying it that way, or just while it's on sale.

Set in a world where women have been brought into extinction, only men with broken dreams, minds and ambitions remain.
A very popular drug called Joy runs rampant  warping people into disgusting mutants after extended use. You are one of these Joy takers, a man named Brad. Brad finds a baby, the baby is a girl. This is where the story and obscenely
difficult choices to protect her innocence begin.
Sounds depressing? It is, this games ending broke me. It was beautiful and left me with many emotions days after playing. Why do I recommend this game? Mostly the fantastic dialogue melded into the story using both dark humour, and weighty choices.
The gameplay is very simplistic but organic enough to encourage multiple playthroughs, sporting a challenge mode and many recruitable followers. The overworld gameplay is platforming, both walking and riding a suprisingly durable bike will help you traverse the terrain, the battle mechanics are the simplistic turn-based battles seen in the Earthbound series. The combat never got old in the 9-14 hours of gameplay mostly due to the imput of certain keys to create powerful combos with certain characters.
The music, while somewhat repetitious in a few places is fantasic, yet it almost feels ill fitting of the game you are playing due to the strangeness of the world; yet at the same time it somehow comes together to create something absurdly beautiful.
The game is stylised in a matter very familar to Earthbound players, yet I would say it works a lot better here. Brad is a warped individual and this is often shown in flashbacks and hallucinations leaving you not knowing for sure if the many characters are always what they seem to be. Colourful, creative and often frightening, they do their job very well.
The game does however have a few minor flaws. The options and key binding menu is a little ugly and unintuitive, some of the bosses can feel luck based at times leading to some frustratiton.
Thank you for reading this review, I really hope it convinces you to buy this fantastic game!

LISA is, without a doubt, of the best, most emotionally-captivating games I've ever played.  From the unique and heartbreaking story, to eclectic cast the characters, to huge variety in party building, to the bizarrely catchy music, to the surprising replayability - everything about this game hit all the right notes for me.  This game is hilarious, morbid, creative, quirky, surreal, sadistic, exciting, beautiful and about a million different other adjectives I just don't have time to list.
I love RPGs - I'd have to say that they're my favorite kinds of games; and somehow this primitive little RPG Maker title made by some weirdo named Dingaling, that I bought for cheap on a whim during the Steam Summer sale, has managed to worm its way into my heart to become one of my favorites.  It's just...wonderful.
When people think of "the best" JRPGs they think of Chrono Trigger, Earthbound (which obviously heavily influenced the development of LISA), Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest and the like - and I do too.  But in a lot of ways, I think LISA does many things better than even those wonderful titles, especially in its storytelling.  No other game I've played has ever managed to tell a story that feels so real and human, while also being so absurd and ridiculous.
I've never 100%'d a game before - I've just never cared to.  But LISA made me want to see and do everything there was to see and do, and now that I've beaten the game 4 times and gotten all the achievements, all I can think about is what I want to do for my next playthrough.
I've got the Joy, Joy, Joy, Joy down in my heart, and if you give this game a chance, so will you.

I've been meaning to review LISA The Painful RPG for a while, but I felt like I couldn't do the game justice. Now that I've completed the game and extracted as much as I'm going to extract without resorting to a replay to watch the additional ending scenes, I feel it's about as good a time as any. (Steam also denied me from posting this review for something like a week, I've went through a handful of versions, so bare with me if it has any errors.)
Let me preface this review saying that I am an experienced JRPG player. Having both played and completed a large amount of them, both in my youth and in recent times, I feel that I can complete any game that decides to follow the format without much difficulty, although LISA does build upon the JRPG genre by adding its own flair to it, which might or might not remind you of Adventure games of old, such as those made by Sierra, as well as a 2D environment where you can go left and right, climb up as well as jump down cliffs (although be warned as falling damage does come into play and is even a fairly interesting and rewarding mechanic).
That said, LISA is a hard game. It will not hold your hand, and it won't think twice about killing the characters you've grown to love. It makes you think about your decisions, and every turn can be the difference between having your party wiped or a glorious victory - save-points being far apart enough that it can be a challenge - and if you want to keep your party intact through loading a previous save, you will likely have to replay content (especially if you've decided to play Pain Mode, the game's hard mode which only lets you save once per point, although the game does give you enough of them that it is not an issue.)
I've played Pain Mode the first time around, and I feel it is the way LISA is meant to be played -- it makes a game that is an already very memorable experience even more so. I recommend it if you're up to it, but you should be warned: it can become very annoying, very fast.
LISA's 'Mad Max'-ian post-apocalyptic world is well-written, full of character and color. It lives and breathes, and through it, the storyline conveyed bit by bit, keeping you guessing until the very end, although it can be cryptic at times, and it's a slow build. The gameplay will often take a backseat to storytelling, which can be a problem, but I was hooked by the story before I could care (this is more noticeable at the beginning of the game, where they set a lot of the ground for the story).
Speaking of character and color, LISA has tons of it. The landscapes while very simple, can be beautiful and moody, which is fairly hard to convey in a 2D game -- although most of the time you'll be looking at dusty mountains and cavern systems which can be a bit daunting at first. What shines most in LISA are the characters: There are tons, and so many of them interesting enough for you to want to know more about them and how they and the world came to be. It can almost be a problem, as they'll leave you wanting, and the game can be very lean on dialogue at times. Most characters will have plenty of lines, but some can join your party without as much as saying a word, and that's a shame.
Now, I've gotten pretty much everything I wanted to say out of the way, but I want to just take a moment just to appreciate the soundtrack. Oh, the soundtrack. It is, excuse the french, abso-♥♥♥♥ing-lutely incredible. I don't think I've ever been as moved by a game's soundtrack as I have by LISA's before. It adds so much to the game, and I don't think it'd be half of what it is without it -- it's comforting, creepy, upsetting, wacky, lovely and just straight-up badass. It can be anything the game needs it to be, and that's fantastic. It makes soundtracks the likes of Silent Hill 2 proud.
In the end, LISA knows how to pull your strings. It will annoy you, it will make you laugh, and it'll probably make you cry. It knows how to move you and break you, and knows how to build you back up. It is absolutely worth its asking price, and will leave you wanting for more if you do manage to complete it, and completing it? Now that's a hell of a journey.

FTL is one of those games that will kick your♥♥♥♥♥97% of the time, and the weirdest part is, you'll actually enjoy it.
The graphics of this game are simple, which means pretty much anything can run it. Even my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop that used to get like 20 FPS in Terraria. Yet, don't be fooled with that, sometimes the backdrops are pretty good looking.
The music of this game is pretty awesome too, from slow, calm songs to stuff that quickly escalates when you're in the middle of a fight. The sound effects are simple, and it's quite easy to recognize different mechanisms or weapons.
The gameplay revolves mostly around micromanaging and strategy. Your weapons, your crew, your bots, they are mostly controlled by you. And sometimes, it's hard to take control of them during the heat of the battle. You also gotta plan your route carefully. Risky, but with a high chance of getting useful stuff? Or not risking it, but being unprepared in the face of danger when a raider ship demands your stuff?
But when you get used to it, and you do it smoothly, it feels good, man. The difficulty of this game is truly remarkable. Everything wants you dead. Everything can go wrong. Is there something that can go wrong? Well, it's going to go wrong for you.
You try to help people just to get backstabbed by raiders, you send your people to help and one of your crew dies to a spider attack or a plague, or you want to trade just to get yourself killed and looted. What's that? You don't want to help anybody? That's pretty good, but the game will find a way to ♥♥♥♥ you up, somehow. Like spawning a huge battleship that's way more equipped than you are, ripping you apart before you manage to escape.
.....And this is on easy difficulty.

One Way Heroics is a fine example of a miniature Roguelike done right. Character building isn't tremendously deep, and the randomly-generated environments are never fiercely different from one another, but the constant pressure from its unique side-scrolling progression affords precious little time to test the boundaries as you press on, resulting in an experience that always feels satisfyingly complex despite its lighthearted presentation.
The premise and gameplay are dually summed up with this statement: The world is being swallowed up by a deadly shadow ever creeping from the west, and your only means of surviving long enough to undo this cataclysm is to travel east with the shadow ever at your heels. You pick your character's name, class, gender, a handful of flavorful perk, and prepare to go right a whole lot.
One Way Heroics likes to keep things light. Classes are differentiated by variations in starting stats, plus one or two spells to break out when the going gets rough. Maps are relatively linear, with occasional obstacle mazes to keep players light on their feet and miniature dungeons and towns to venture into when there are a few extra turns to burn. Not that there often are, of course, as every turn scrolls the screen a bit more to the left, and getting swallowed up by the left side of the screen is fatal. The decision to enter a stone dungeon isn't one to be taken lightly, though neither is anything else. Using an item, equipping a weapon, or speaking to an NPC is just as dangerous as any other action that isn't stepping to the right, but as the monsters grow fiercer the further east you go, deviating from the main path to grab extra equipment or visit a merchant is often prudent.
One would think laying this mechanic on top of an otherwise traditional roguelike would make the experience drastically more difficult, yet surprisingly, One Way Heroics is not that bloodthirsty a game. Actual victory is a completely attainable goal, and not neccesarily all that challenging a task (unless you want it to be). Your character will only last the length of one run, but "horrible, horrible death" isn't necessarily going to be the reason for their retirement. It's a nice feeling.
With comparatively few options for character development, streamlined combat, and limited variety to be found even in the mix-and-match biomes of the extremely linear maps, One Way Heroics doesn't run quite as deep as the games it seeks to emulate, yet unlike many mass-production Roguelikes it still manages to capture pretty much all of the fundamental qualities that make the genre great, all while introducing unique and memorable mechanics to set itself apart from the crowd.
Whether you're a newcomer to the genre seeking something unintimidating but satisfying or a long-time Roguelike fan looking for something simple and unique, One Way Heroics is worth a fortune more than its humble price tag, and should be investigated as soon as possible.

I'm really enjoying this fresh take on the roguelike. One Way Heroics takes the best elements of the Super Famicom classic, Shiren the Wanderer, and makes it more accessible through unlockable classes and perks. Highly replayable and increasingly challenging. I also dig the cheesy MIDI tunes.

Warning: Not to be underestimated.
One-Way Heroics combines turn-based combat, side scrolling arcade style gameplay, limited saves, and a hearty dose of classic RPG nostalgia. It also ranks in difficulty with the likes of Mega-Man, Ninja Gaiden, and Castlevania.
The foundation of Heroics would make it seem like two things that should never go together.
On the left side of the screen, the world fades into a Darkness that consumes men, women,  children, small animals, dungeon bosses, buildings, eveything. It is your job to find out what is causing the darkness by travelling to the ends of the earth and defeating the source (oh, and the final boss has finally attained some common sense, and will randomly spawn in an effort to kill you before you get enough power and equipment to wreck his world.)  It would start to sound as if it's an infinite runner (akin to Temple Run and Flappy Bird).
And then there are the RPG elements.
Randomly generated worlds, item upgrades, exploration, looting, unlockable perks and classes, the element of permadeath between save points (random enemy drops and treasures will not be the same after continuing from a save file), and the random enemy attributes lead one to question their sanity.
Each playthrough is different. You have the option to create a new random world every time that you start a new game, but you can also play through the same world as different classes.
There are 8 different classes in total, (Only the Knight and Swordmaster are available at the start, but with additional playthroughs, the roster expands with Hunter, Pirate, Bard, Adventurer, Force User, and Hero) with very different play styles. Swordmasters are tough, but it comes at a cost to stamina and carrying capacity. Hunters, however, are better suited to stealth, ranged weapons, and have a special ability that allows them to see off-screen enemies before they encounter them.
All in all, it's got great addictive gameplay, the sprite animations are charming, the music is fantastic , and I would give this an 8-8.5
