Metro 2033 Redux is the vastly upgraded and improved version of the original Metro 2033 post-apocalyptic FPS game. First brought to gamers in 2010 by THQ and then given a complete makeover in 2014 by DeepSilver, the title is based off of the novel of the same name written by Russian author Dmitry Glukhovsky. Though I have not personally read the book, friends of mine have stated that the game is very close to its origins, and the few differences are forgivable.
First up, let's talk about the changes that the Redux brings. If you play, and/or own, the original Metro 2033, it's definitely worth your time and money to invest in this edition of the game. The updated graphics are a drastic improvement over the old title, bringing in high quality textures, dynamic lighting, and improved atmospheric effects such as fog, steam, and rain that bring an entirely new depth to the campaign. All of these changes combined make the darkened tunnels of the underground feel more claustrophobic, and the open areas more derelict. There have also been some alterations to a few of the major cutscenes; full side-by-side comparisons can be viewed on YouTube. On the other hand, there has also been notable outcry regarding the reduced difficulty of the overall experience, primarily when it comes to Survival mode, in that scavenged resources are more plentiful.
Now, if you haven't played Metro 2033 before, here's what it's all about: A nuclear war occurred in 2013, wherein Russia was targeted with atomic bombs that caused severe radiation; primarily across Moscow. The devastating impacts caused all survivors to flee into the underground tunnels of the metro stations, where they proceeded to build as much of new 'cities' as they could, each one being housed at a different base metro station, leaving the tunnels to connect them like roads. In the game, you play as a 20-year-old male survivor who was born prior to the nuclear fallout known as Artyom. The year is now 2033, and his home in the northern metro station, Exhibition, is under attack by a group of creatures that are referred to as the Dark ones. Artyom must travel to the main metro station of Polis and plead for help from their rangers to save his home, family, and friends.
Though Metro 2033 Redux is classified as a post-apocalyptic FPS title, it has deep survival elements to its gameplay. The currency of choice are military-grade bullets, which can be exchanged in a few metro stations for ammo, grenades, gas mask filters, med-kits,weapons, and weapon upgrades. The bullets themselves can be found by exploring every nook and cranny of the levels, and also from some scripted events that happen. Likewise, if you're unable to pony up the rounds for supplies, you can find all of the aforementioned things (sans weapon upgrades) by scavenging. However, playing on Survival mode, as opposed to the only other mode that the game has called Spartan, reduces the amount of supplies that you find out in the wild.
While enjoying your 10-13 hours of play time exploring the toxic, snowy wastelands and deep, dark corridors of tunnels, you will find that the game has a hefty arsenal of weaponry at your disposal; assault rifles, shotguns, revolvers, pneumatics, and even a flamethrower all make their appearances, plus a few others. The gun play is good, though the upgrades can be a bit lackluster, and you will find yourself shooting from the hip more often than not, as taking the time to aim can be futile since the enemies are incredibly speedy. It should also be mentioned that most of the guns are old-fashioned, and some of them, such as the flamethrower and pneumatics, require Super Soaker styled pumping to get them to work.
When it comes down to atmosphere, ambiance, graphics, and sound, THQ and DeepSilver thought of just about everything. From the thick fog, to green toxic air, rain that blurs your vision a little, spiders and flies that sometimes land on your gas mask, to downright having to wipe blood and grime off of your gas mask to see; the latter actually becomes rather prominent, as when you are in a heavy firefight, you will absolutely need to wipe the blood off to see where you're shooting. The soundtrack is just absolutely stunning, and as near to cinema quality as it can get. In fact, the entire game itself comes off as cinematic; at some point or another, it houses everything from horror, to action, to drama, to even fleeting moments of comedy.
Metro 2033 Redux can best be described as the lovechild of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. and Fallout series'. Though the levels are heavily enclosed in most cases, there's almost always a ton of chambers, decrepit buildings, and passages to explore. There's also a high level of replayability, as there are two different modes and two different endings to obtain; along with 51 worthwhile diary entries to pick up and read. It's worth standing around and listening to the conversations that people around you are having, as you can gain more insight into the story and it's also really immersing. Everything about this title is as near-perfect as a video game can get, and that means that it most definitely needs to be in your library at some point.

LISA is, without a doubt, of the best, most emotionally-captivating games I've ever played.  From the unique and heartbreaking story, to eclectic cast the characters, to huge variety in party building, to the bizarrely catchy music, to the surprising replayability - everything about this game hit all the right notes for me.  This game is hilarious, morbid, creative, quirky, surreal, sadistic, exciting, beautiful and about a million different other adjectives I just don't have time to list.
I love RPGs - I'd have to say that they're my favorite kinds of games; and somehow this primitive little RPG Maker title made by some weirdo named Dingaling, that I bought for cheap on a whim during the Steam Summer sale, has managed to worm its way into my heart to become one of my favorites.  It's just...wonderful.
When people think of "the best" JRPGs they think of Chrono Trigger, Earthbound (which obviously heavily influenced the development of LISA), Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest and the like - and I do too.  But in a lot of ways, I think LISA does many things better than even those wonderful titles, especially in its storytelling.  No other game I've played has ever managed to tell a story that feels so real and human, while also being so absurd and ridiculous.
I've never 100%'d a game before - I've just never cared to.  But LISA made me want to see and do everything there was to see and do, and now that I've beaten the game 4 times and gotten all the achievements, all I can think about is what I want to do for my next playthrough.
I've got the Joy, Joy, Joy, Joy down in my heart, and if you give this game a chance, so will you.

I've been meaning to review LISA The Painful RPG for a while, but I felt like I couldn't do the game justice. Now that I've completed the game and extracted as much as I'm going to extract without resorting to a replay to watch the additional ending scenes, I feel it's about as good a time as any. (Steam also denied me from posting this review for something like a week, I've went through a handful of versions, so bare with me if it has any errors.)
Let me preface this review saying that I am an experienced JRPG player. Having both played and completed a large amount of them, both in my youth and in recent times, I feel that I can complete any game that decides to follow the format without much difficulty, although LISA does build upon the JRPG genre by adding its own flair to it, which might or might not remind you of Adventure games of old, such as those made by Sierra, as well as a 2D environment where you can go left and right, climb up as well as jump down cliffs (although be warned as falling damage does come into play and is even a fairly interesting and rewarding mechanic).
That said, LISA is a hard game. It will not hold your hand, and it won't think twice about killing the characters you've grown to love. It makes you think about your decisions, and every turn can be the difference between having your party wiped or a glorious victory - save-points being far apart enough that it can be a challenge - and if you want to keep your party intact through loading a previous save, you will likely have to replay content (especially if you've decided to play Pain Mode, the game's hard mode which only lets you save once per point, although the game does give you enough of them that it is not an issue.)
I've played Pain Mode the first time around, and I feel it is the way LISA is meant to be played -- it makes a game that is an already very memorable experience even more so. I recommend it if you're up to it, but you should be warned: it can become very annoying, very fast.
LISA's 'Mad Max'-ian post-apocalyptic world is well-written, full of character and color. It lives and breathes, and through it, the storyline conveyed bit by bit, keeping you guessing until the very end, although it can be cryptic at times, and it's a slow build. The gameplay will often take a backseat to storytelling, which can be a problem, but I was hooked by the story before I could care (this is more noticeable at the beginning of the game, where they set a lot of the ground for the story).
Speaking of character and color, LISA has tons of it. The landscapes while very simple, can be beautiful and moody, which is fairly hard to convey in a 2D game -- although most of the time you'll be looking at dusty mountains and cavern systems which can be a bit daunting at first. What shines most in LISA are the characters: There are tons, and so many of them interesting enough for you to want to know more about them and how they and the world came to be. It can almost be a problem, as they'll leave you wanting, and the game can be very lean on dialogue at times. Most characters will have plenty of lines, but some can join your party without as much as saying a word, and that's a shame.
Now, I've gotten pretty much everything I wanted to say out of the way, but I want to just take a moment just to appreciate the soundtrack. Oh, the soundtrack. It is, excuse the french, abso-♥♥♥♥ing-lutely incredible. I don't think I've ever been as moved by a game's soundtrack as I have by LISA's before. It adds so much to the game, and I don't think it'd be half of what it is without it -- it's comforting, creepy, upsetting, wacky, lovely and just straight-up badass. It can be anything the game needs it to be, and that's fantastic. It makes soundtracks the likes of Silent Hill 2 proud.
In the end, LISA knows how to pull your strings. It will annoy you, it will make you laugh, and it'll probably make you cry. It knows how to move you and break you, and knows how to build you back up. It is absolutely worth its asking price, and will leave you wanting for more if you do manage to complete it, and completing it? Now that's a hell of a journey.

FTL is one of those games that will kick your♥♥♥♥♥97% of the time, and the weirdest part is, you'll actually enjoy it.
The graphics of this game are simple, which means pretty much anything can run it. Even my ♥♥♥♥♥♥ laptop that used to get like 20 FPS in Terraria. Yet, don't be fooled with that, sometimes the backdrops are pretty good looking.
The music of this game is pretty awesome too, from slow, calm songs to stuff that quickly escalates when you're in the middle of a fight. The sound effects are simple, and it's quite easy to recognize different mechanisms or weapons.
The gameplay revolves mostly around micromanaging and strategy. Your weapons, your crew, your bots, they are mostly controlled by you. And sometimes, it's hard to take control of them during the heat of the battle. You also gotta plan your route carefully. Risky, but with a high chance of getting useful stuff? Or not risking it, but being unprepared in the face of danger when a raider ship demands your stuff?
But when you get used to it, and you do it smoothly, it feels good, man. The difficulty of this game is truly remarkable. Everything wants you dead. Everything can go wrong. Is there something that can go wrong? Well, it's going to go wrong for you.

I bought this game on the steam summer sale for $2.59. There are a couple things that you have to know about this game before you buy it.
1) The story is very short. I was able to complete the game in a little over two hours.
2) The character animation (other than your hand's) is very basic. not horrible by any means, but when you see an npc running towards or away from something, you can easilly see that they're "slipping" on the ground they're running on.
3) At times the narrator can seem bleak, and toneless (the daughter was great in my opinion).
4) The gameplay was fun as♥♥♥♥♥♥ i dont think i've ever played a game where i had this much fun with the movement. being able to charge up your suit and jump really high/really far, then use the grapple hand thing (which is also totally awesome) to grab onto a floating rock only to fling yourself higher is just amazing!
5) The story (short as it was) was very enjoyable to me. it gave you just enough to keep you interested in what was being said, but not too much that you contemplate turning your speakers off.
6) i don't know if it was because they're wasn't that much happening on the screen at one time or what, but the game not only looks great, but ran at a smooth 60fps the entire time (it's not a huge game so you would expect that, but i've seen simpler game's get worse framerates).
Overall this was (in my opinion) an amazing game. the story was a little short, and the character models/animation could use a little more work, but the amazing graphics, decent story, and unbelievably fun gameplay make up for the imperfections that this game has. I had a hell of a lot more fun than I thought I would playing this game. I really hope the developers take the hint, and make this into something huge. knowing how much i would enjoy the game, I would have gladly bought it at full price.

There is a lot that is good about the game.  Style, atmosphere, overall concept.  At first it is very engaging and fun.  Then it gets challenging and there are some easter eggs.  Then suddenly it gets nearly impossible.  The minor glitches in the mechanics become crippling, and the game becomes repetitive and frustrating.  When you spend 10 minutes trying to make the same series of "jumps" 40 times before you make it, that's just not fun to me.  The fact that there is an auto save after every single one of these is a clear indication the devs knew how insanely hard it was, so once you got lucky enough to make it you didn't want to have to try again.  Now if that type of game is fun for you, this game is fantastic.  Personally it burned me out real fast.  What you see in the trailer is the best it has to offer, and those moments are great.  Unfortunately for every one of those there are 5 that make you lose you mind.  By comparison Mirror's Edge and Portal 2 that had similar "die a few times to figure it out challenges" and a similar game feel were great games.  This falls just short of that, and as a result falls into the abyss like you do so many times playing it.

I really wanted to like this. I loved the concept and the whole idea of travelling through the dreams this dude had. But it falls really flat. I know it shouldn't be judged as a game and more as art - and art is subjective. But it's really not that great. The controls feel sluggish, the rooms are incredibly dark and hard to manouver - the "levels" are incoherant and they give you an objective but with nothing to go on. I saw some weird graphical tearing, like the chicken on the tutorial dream passing through the wall unintentionally, being able to see through some walls and being able to scale areas, that I assume should have been unaccessible.
I admittedly thought the level with the paintings was cool and had a really neat mechanic of seeing things in art that you don't see around you - or whatever. That was neat. But then you get levels like the self destruct clock - this seems like it was some dude complaining about getting critique on his work - and a straight up 5 minute video of some kid punching himself and tearing up paper. Then it rolls you into an angsty "I want to love" "I miss her so much" situation - it ends up feeling really awkward and honestly a little cringey. Even more so when the audio is just the developer saying over and over again of how good his art is and how good of a game dev his is.
In the end it all feels sorta forced and feels as if the developer is pushing your face into his work and going "see! See how good it is? It's great! It's so great!"  when in reality it's just simple attempts at trying to be emotional and failing.

tldr Version:
Simple and challenging at the same time! you take a basic sandbox idea and put it into an 2d-shooter enviroment.
It makes a lot of fun either in small groups capturing holds or in big groups building huge defenses and then conquering each other for the flag! Modding support as well (yet i haven't used that by now) so alot of fun mechanisms to play around with :)
Long Version:
I had this game on my wishlist for roughly two years, and now in the summer sale of 2015 i bought this little fun bomb!
I really liked he tutorials, though they were short, they showed you everything you need to know.
The Story mode is fun as well as you can train basic movements and actions for combat.
When it comes to multiplayer there are a feqw gamemodes, which all are extremely fun!
CTF: classic gamemode, but with a twist in this game, as you get to build your base and defensive structures in the first 3-4 minutes of the game (of yourse you can and should keep building all the time!!). after that time has passed you are able to attack your opponent team which, of cousre ahs build their base as well. the rounds can be very short (when one team has a huge error in their defense) or it can take very long ( an hour or more) to a point where the lpayers are going to vote for a map change
Conquer the Holds (wor whatever its called XD): 2 to 4 Holds per map and the teams get roughly 2 minutes to fortifie their first one. after that it is time to get to the others, get inside and stay inside for a short time to capture the Hold or your team. again a very nice twist on a classic shooter gamemode.
Team deathmatch: very classic gamemode, yet i haven't played it by now.
then there are multiplayer variants of the singleplayer missions which i find really nice :)
In a nutshell this game is very open to a lot of playstyles and NEVER underestimate the importants of offensive Builders!
!!Big reccomendation!!

My overall rating for Without Within: 95/100
This visual novel is very cute, I think it deserves its chance. Made by small team of developers, yet it still has humour, wishes, expectations and all emotions, which are present in our lives. Lets see in detail this short lovely game.
GAMEPLAY
+ Cute animations
+ Good story design
- Short time
- Fullscreen is clunky
Animations and story was perfect. There were choices, I think my most favourite part was playing the Sunflower War (that joke was hilarious, I like, when authors are able to make fun of themselves).
Only negatives were a little short time and fullscreen resolution is not optimized well. But this negatives are just a small scratch on a perfect facade of the game.
CHARACTERS
+ Vinty
+ Good actions are rewarded
I think everyone of us is a bit similar to Vinty. We desire for success, fame and respect, but we have to fight our everyday struggles. I like, that when I gave a chance to good action, I got rewarded. Thanks!
VISUALS
+ Decent
By the visual side, game has no faults. Enjoyable, childish shoujo style. Suits this title well.
SOUNDTRACK
+ Limited, yet fine
There are only few tracks, but they complete and enhance the atmosphere. Good work, even better, than some big studios.
SUMMARY
Without Within is a humble title, that deserves its score. Made by a small team, perfect idea from Invetmouse, other members did well too! Do you want to live one day as an artist or calligrapher? Well, here is your chance.
Strongly recommended.

Well I was pleasently surprised. I really wasn't expecting much but actually, it is quite good. First thing to understand is that although the game has an open-world it is not an "open-world game". It is not 1950s styled GTA. It is 1950s GTA paired down to just a series of missions. You can ignore the checkpoints and go and drive about if you like but at the end of the day you're always in a linear a mission that will automatically progress to the next when it finishes. This might sound a bit rubbish but actually it allows for greater focus and a far better narative experience.
Open-world games, later GTA games in particular, suffer from the contrast in having a character get up to whacky highjinks in between missions and then be expected to act like they live in a serious world in mission. Saints Row tackled that by making the missions just as rediculous as the open-world. Mafia II goes the other way and takes out the whacky highjinks. For example, I think I must have run over about five innocent people during the course of the entire game.
If you go into it expecting a sandbox you're going to be disapointed. On the other hand if you don't particularly want yet another open-world driving sandbox and want a good set of story missions to plow through then this is pretty good. Okay, the plot gets very confusing in terms of the various crime bosses and their relationships to one another but if you just let that go, accept that you'll be doing things you don't fully understand and concentrate on Vito's story then it works just fine.
Mechanics, graphics, sound, all that stuff. It is all fine. Little of it is really great but it is all fine. The 1940s music drags but even that draws you into the story and gives you a taste of the thrill of the introduction of rock 'n' roll. The best is probably the look and feel of everything. The feel and stylings evokes the period perfectly.

You see there is no side missions or anything that would involve requiring you to really go out of the linear path from Mission A to mission B. The game would have done better if it took a bit of extra time to flesh out the city with side missions like assassinations,racing, and other activities.

Like I've been trying to tell everyone for years, it's not the size that matters, it's what you do with it that counts!
Without Within is a very short, free, visual novel about a young woman called Vinty who dreams of being the world's greatest calligrapher whilst trying to get by in her day to day life and not totally suck at it, too. Yeeaaahhh... world's greatest calligrapher...
OK. Sure. Why not?
You'll follow her and her innermost thoughts over a couple of days as she tries to sell her works, hold down an unfulfilling job and deal with her crotchety, old landlady to boot. Oh, and depending on the choice you make, also prevent a small boy from being bummed to death. I like the way the game gives you choices at a handful of points throughout, making the right one will eventually deliver you to the final, good ending, while making the wrong choice will result in something bad happening and end the game. It adds a little something extra to what could easily be a very linear experience, being a visual novel. Or at least that's what I've found with what's admittedly so far been a very brief flirtation with the genre. Though games like this make me want to try more.
The art style is kinda minimal but still pleasing, and the character design beyond adorable (I especially love her eyes which appear to be two thick lines made of brush strokes. A really nice touch to the character). Vinty could probably have come across as a little entitled or maybe even a tad petulant were she not so lovable, thanks in no small part to the clever and astute writing. I guess these games largely live or die based on the quality of the writing (at least if it's not relying on drawings of boobs and weird squealing audio, as this one isn't), and this game most definitely blossoms from it. It's self-aware and referential without beating the player/reader over the head with it, and is funny and interesting enough to keep them engaged 'til the end, which will only be about 15 or 20 minutes, even seeing all the endings.
So if you have some time to spare and want to have a brief, pleasant read of something cute and whimsical, then it's well worth giving this freebie a shot. Even though it's only the story of a small time chaligrapher, you brush off this stroke of inkredible genius at your own peril.

I don't know what to say about this game, so here is a recipe for pancakes,
Ingredients:
4tbsp plain flour (about 100g)
1 large free range egg
½ pint semi-skimmed milk + water (about 300ml - ¾ milk ¼ water)
Pinch of salt
Butter for frying
How to make pancakes:
Sieve the flour and salt into a large bowl and make a well in the mixture.
Break in the egg and stir to make a breadcrumby mix.
In a jug add 1/3 of a pint of milk and top up with water to make 1/2 a pint (200ml milk, 100ml water) - this makes a lovely light batter.
Add the milk and the water mix bit by bit, beating constantly to avoid lumps.
Tip:*If you have a food processor just throw all the ingredients in and zap until smooth!
Pop a large frying pan over a medium heat.
Add a large knob of butter (roughly 50g) and melt.
Pour the excess butter into a small bowl and reserve it for later.
Using a ladle pour a spoonful of the pancake batter into the hot pan and swirl to get a full covering - cook for about 1 min each side (it's ready when it's easy to flip over).
Serve immediately with sugar and lemon or other exciting toppings. We love cheese and Marmite for an extra British twist! Delicious!!

Honestly I regret spending that 20€ I payed for CoH2 during a sale until today. Not because I did not get a proper “value” out of that money but rather because I don’t like it one bit to have supported this kind of half arsed, crappy game developening style that Relic & SEGA pulled off.

The sad thing is, the majority of people who seem to play this game are really into CoH. I rarely see anybody who has not put 900h+ playtime into coh2. So that is a dead-set fan, which would indeed explain the just way, waaay to good ratings this game has. But then again, CoH1 has 95% positive ratings and coh2 around 75%, so that is at least somewhat of a statement.
In theory CoH2 is a "ok" RTS, nothing outstanding or new, just simply an ok game.
In reality however, it’s a half-arsed game that is an obvious money-grab, with tons of bugs, incredibly bad performance overall, micotransaction and a mind baffling amount of RNG.
Honestly after 230H of playtime, I’ve seen enough that I can say with certainty that this game plays & feels like a alpha or beta version, but sadly that’s indeed the finished product I’m experiencing.
I can only recommend anybody to go and find any other RTS. I'm serious, any other RTS will do better than this sheit.
Warcraft, Starcraft, AoE, Codename Panzers... just look around. If you seriously can’t pick any of those X other RTS games that are around and are dead set on getting CoH2. Please for the sake of everything, only pick it up on a sale.
Even if you want to buy CoH2 only for the singleplayer. Just don’t, it sux.
First thing you need to know: this game is Pay2Win.
There are 5 armys, each army should have 3 commanders.
Commanders cost 3 - 4€ each. The commander’s you get by default are mostly garbage & the good ones you need to buy for € or grind with ingame currency. Grinding a single commander will take you around 80-hours, yes eighty hours, for a single one. And yes, commanders have enough impact on the game to be the decision between a win or a loos.
Second thing you need to know: this game is heavily RNG based and even if you outplay your opponent and are winning by quite a lot, a single bad RNG outcome can turn the game right around. Now before you stop reading here and think: “that guy is probably a noob”, here are my ranks at the time of the review:
those are worldwide ranks btw. (more to that later)
Anyhow, I could easily write an entire review just on how stupid the RNG in this game is, but I’ll just give this short example:
You let 2 tanks fight against each other, exactly the same unit, no micromanagement. They just stand there and shoot each other. The outcome can variate from close call up to one tank wins with 60% HP left.
Almost every single unit in this game works this way. They have % chances to hit/miss and then armor (vehicles) or cover (infantry) adds additional modifiers.
It’s like a slot machine, you pull the lever you win, you pull the lever you loose. Enough to make even the worst kind of players win some games from time to time. Which is especially cancerous in team modes, when you get to play with/against people who are just in your “skill level” because they got lucky a bit in the last games.
As the active player base is small with an average of 5k people online at all times, worldwide, this is a legitimate problem.
Also to note, this game does not work, at all. Performance wise.
It has:
-memory leak (which will also make the game crash if you don’t restart all 3-5~ games played)
-Random disconnects of players at the beginning of a match.
-lots of players do have incredibly long loading times for no reason at all.
-FPS drops no matter your hardware. (every DLC made the game worse apparently)
-stutters at always the same time / “thing happening” in a match.
-Graphic settings don’t do anything on “good” PC’s: ingame benchmark all settings maxed: 43FPS minimum, all settings on lowest: 50FPS min. - and all that while never seeing my CPU go above 30% and the GPU above 75% usage on either of the benchmarks (I7 3770 @4.3ghz, GTX 970 @1450mhz, 16GB Ram, game on SSD)
Look at this cancerous performance:
-the menu, due to extremely poor background design, is capped to 30FPS and sometimes will drop as low as 10FPS (some people do report 5FPS and less)
-everything in this game takes forever, changing your loadout, opening a menu, switching game modes, waiting for a game to start, waiting for a game to end. You need to wait a good 15~ seconds until the game will display you the match overview for example after you have seen the victory screen.
Pathfinding of units & how well units respond.
Command & Conquer from the ‘90s is laughing at how f*ing bad CoH2 is in this aspect.
Units will ignore commands from time to time and not move at all, they will constantly block each other if vehicles are involved. Even if you order them to do something, like to go behind “this” cover in “this” formation, they sometimes won’t do it properly as you did order.
Vehicles are even worse, they are.... let’s just say a 10 year old is driving a tank, that’s the amount of “intelligence” you can expect from an vehicle. They need to be microed constantly, into the tiniest detail. Which is may or may not appealing to some. Reality is, the AI is so brainded, that they will, instead of reversing back as ordered, just do a 180° spin because the other tank behind them didn’t move away fast enough, so instead of waiting or slowing down a bit and continue to reverse, a 180° spin it is, which takes like 10seconds to execute.
This game, honestly, has the worst AI I have ever seen in any RTS game, ever.
Bugs..
CoH2 is full of them. Units getting stuck behind fences or buildings in sandbags or such and can’t move anymore.
Vision bugs giving you vision on enemy units you are not supposed to see.
In every patch relic farts out they manage to bug a unit, which in turn will become OP and it takes weeks to be fixed.
Games will get “sync errors”, so everybody looses and gets a loss counted to they’re stats.
Visual bugs ranging from soldiers not being animated up to random “artifactcs” of your screen.
Vehicles will warp backwards a few meters if they go full-speed and get a new order.
Random crashes, random errors, random delays....
Surrender sometimes gets bugged and you cant fix it.
Well what else is there… let’s finish a short list.
-One server for everybody. EU, US, Asia.. all will be teamed together happily. Performance or proper ping? Nah, f* that.  - Remember when I said “more to that later”? That’s why ranks are worldwide.
Its also utterly fun to get teammates who dont speak a word english.
-Chat censorship, this game is 18+. The units in the game curse. The chat replaces F*ing with “gardening” and does the same with other curse words. Because adults of legal age need monitoring.
-Matchmaking is crappy most of the time. There are barely any close games, it’s mostly stomp or get stomped. Also the game does not give a f* if you are a premade or random team.
-You can not make your own keybindings in this game or even rebind any keys. These are the controls you have, get used to them.
-There is no report and/or punishment system for cancerous players. Like trolls, teamkillers, leavers, people who are just AFK or kids who tell you to get cancer and wish that your family would die. Good thing we at least have chat censorship, right?

I've had a lot of fun with Helldivers, whether i'm grinding missions with friends or helping out random people, this game has kept me entertained. Still just as fun now as it was when I first picked it up.

I want to be able to recommend Helldivers. I love the co-op squad setup, and the variety of useful gear. I even like the strange little minigame you play to activate abilities which is harder for stronger abilities. The three enemy factions are cosmetically and mechanically interesting. As a basic concept, I loved it.
Unfortunately, the game suffers from a few absolutely critical problems.
First, there is virtually no content. If you've seen a mid-level planet from a faction, you've basically seen everything that faction has to throw at you other than a "endgame" few holdouts. You can experience all the content in the game in at most three sessions.
Second, the game never progresses other than weapon unlocks. Let me explain: Helldivers doesn't have a plot (or story of any kind), characters, or even a setting other than space and fight stages. Since there's no story, the game cannot progress or evolve, and no matter how much you play the game, the universe stays the same. You can go through the same three stages over and over at various difficulties with very slightly altered objectives, but that's it.
Third, the entire online mechanic is awful. This is the most confusing thing, because it seems like it's the result of a weird marketing idea gone wrong. This is how it works: in this basically unchanging world, everybody who beats a level contributes to this online overall war against the enemies of Earth. Of course, nothing really changes other than a graphic depiction of the galaxy divided into territories under various factional control. Everybody who plays the game shares the map. If you buy the game today, you'll enter the game at whatever point it has currently progressed to in the community. At certain critical thresholds, the progress map resets for everyone in the world simultaneously, and you start back at the starting planets. Of course, you can't tell the starting planets from the others, so this is a meaningless event.
Unfortunately, Helldiver revolves around a static world where the only "progress" is a map controlled by the world at large. There's no real sense of progress, and weapon unlocks don't count. So maybe one day someone will make it into a real game, but it feels half-baked to me.

Well I was pleasently surprised. I really wasn't expecting much but actually, it is quite good. First thing to understand is that although the game has an open-world it is not an "open-world game". It is not 1950s styled GTA. It is 1950s GTA paired down to just a series of missions. You can ignore the checkpoints and go and drive about if you like but at the end of the day you're always in a linear a mission that will automatically progress to the next when it finishes. This might sound a bit rubbish but actually it allows for greater focus and a far better narative experience.
Open-world games, later GTA games in particular, suffer from the contrast in having a character get up to whacky highjinks in between missions and then be expected to act like they live in a serious world in mission. Saints Row tackled that by making the missions just as rediculous as the open-world. Mafia II goes the other way and takes out the whacky highjinks. For example, I think I must have run over about five innocent people during the course of the entire game.
If you go into it expecting a sandbox you're going to be disapointed. On the other hand if you don't particularly want yet another open-world driving sandbox and want a good set of story missions to plow through then this is pretty good. Okay, the plot gets very confusing in terms of the various crime bosses and their relationships to one another but if you just let that go, accept that you'll be doing things you don't fully understand and concentrate on Vito's story then it works just fine.
Mechanics, graphics, sound, all that stuff. It is all fine. Little of it is really great but it is all fine. The 1940s music drags but even that draws you into the story and gives you a taste of the thrill of the introduction of rock 'n' roll. The best is probably the look and feel of everything. The feel and stylings evokes the period perfectly.

For Press Radio News, I'm Lol Harris, recommending you give this game a shot.  Let's talk Pro's & Con's.
PROS:
-Incredible story
-Fantastic voice acting
-Well written characters
-Fun gun/driving gameplay
-Great soundtrack, many classics that help immerse you in the time period.
-Beautiful world to be a part of, sightseeing in this game is a blast.
CONS:
If I'm going to be honest, there's really only one Con for me, and that is the open world.  Mind you, I did say it was a beautiful world, and that is because it is.  But the thing is, this world is only useful for getting from Point A to Point B and progressing the story.  Besides bringing cars to the junkyard and starting commotions with police, there's really nothing to do in here.  That's quite a shame, because the world is so beautiful and well replicates the 40's/50's era, and after the story is finished it feels wasted.
Long story short, if a Mafia III is ever made, I hope they take advantage of their ability to create an immersive world, but this time add more content to give the game more depth.

This game absolutley took my breath away. Easy to learn, but hard to master this game can be a fantastic two-hour romp for the casual or a twenty hour treck for the completionist. A throwback to old-school dungeon crawlers execpt each dungeon-world is randomly generated.
The objective of this game is simply to go on a sidescrolling adventure without being caught by the "darkness" (which you will always have to out-run.) and defeat the "demon lord", a powerful foe who will infrequently visit you for short periods of time where you can either attempt to run away from him defeat him. And as you make your way through this world, you will encounter grottos, towns, and all sorts of surprises. You may even find an extra party member or two, who each have thier own side story and indivdual abilities.  You first start a game with only two classes, which grasually expands to a nice collection. The music that plays along your Journey is also cathey, and never gets all.
All in all - espicially considering its price - I would not hesitate to give this game a 10 out of 10.

As a rule, when a game is so poorly made that it almost doesn't work without a fan patching it, I normally consider it a failure. When the last half of a game is just a maze with enemies that you kill while feeling lost and confused and the combat system is pretty sub-par, I consider it a waste of money...
... But the first half of this game is So Bloody Good! It has story! It has characters! It has non-violent solutions if you're a social character! It has sneaking solutions if you're a stealth character! It has hacking and knowledge solutions if you're an intelligent character! Remember how everyone praised Deus Ex for having all these things? Multiple solutions to problems that allow your character to focus on things other than shooting and stabbing? This was like that, only you drink blood!
Then there's the last half of the game... You can almost feel the moment that the money runs out and Activison come knocking at the door, demanding the alpha build be put in stores tomorrow. There's a perceptible shift from multiple solutions, story focus and character driven conversations into: "Go to this place and kill everyone. Enter this 5 x 5 room. You see 3 orcs, roll to hit the nearest one!"
This game was almost something very beautiful but, like a relationship with a shallow woman, it just needed more money thrown at it! Like heating a microwave dinner, it really needs more time than they gave it.
Buy it on the cheap, patch the game, play the first half... If you reach the part where you have to start just running around and killing enemies constantly and you're invested, see it out, otherwise maybe use a cheat or something and just skip the boring, endless corridors of mooks.

This certainly is a great game. It's pretty much a GTA set in the 1940s and 1950s, but much better optimized for the PC. Considering it was released two years after GTA IV, this game runs smoothly at the highest settings while GTA IV to this day does not seem to allow us to do that. Granted, GTA's world is bigger and you have more to do overall, but the detail that  went into the New York based city "Empire Bay" you find yourself in here is astonishing. Beautifully modeled cars and environment, rich story (albeit the somewhat stereotypical characters) and the atmosphere is certainly pulling you in.
It's the nice little details that make this game so awesome. The cops react to minor infractions such as speeding, but you can actually bribe them. Saying that, your cars actually have a speed limiter which prevents you from going over the current speed limit; finally someone thought of that - it can make things much more enjoyable if you just plan on cruising around.
In other features, you need to get gas for your car now and then. You can't just take a car that's parked and find it unlocked, no, you have to actually lock pick it (or smash the window which draws more attention). You can have a wanted level on your person AND/OR your car and you have to change clothes or your car respectively; that does not only mean your car's color, but also license plate.
The look, feel, radio stations, prices (gas, goods) and overall behavior of NPCs is very realistic given the time this game plays in, and so are the attitudes. It may be offering overall less freedom than the GTA series, and it is more story driven and linear in that sense, but between missions you can still drive around freely and all I can say is that I'm having a lot of fun playing Mafia II; to the point I'm actually regretting not ever giving it a try sooner.
You like open world, sandbox, and GTA type games? Get this. You won't regret it.

A superb tactical inventory management simulator.
Men of War is at its best when it is exploring the intricacies of men carrying things.  Gripping shuffling-crap-back-and-forth action is, however, occasionally interrupted by other soldiers with different uniforms who show up at random and shoot at your own troops.  The only function of this feature, as far as I can tell, is to deplete your own ammunition; if one of your units dies it's either entirely shruggable or a nigh-mission-failure anyway, so it doesn't matter much.
And ammunition micromanagement is what Men of War excels at.  It's enthralling to send a truck scurrying around the map to scrape up spare machine gun ammunition for your tank which is locked in combat with a large number of enemy soldiers who are unreasonably insistent upon its demise.  There is also tons of pixelhunting fun to be had trying to click on the thing you want to click on, with tension provided by the ever-present possibility of accidentally telling a soldier to take cover on the wrong side of a wall or do something similarly bat-guano stupid.
(I'm not sure why Steam says I don't recommend this game; honestly, it's the best man-to-man cartridge-counting game around.)

With the Unofficial Patch, this game is absolutely amazing!
It's everything you'd want in an RPG: great characters, unique locations, alternate endings which stem from a terrific storyline.
All in all, VTMB's take on the folklore of vampires is the selling point for me personally, perfectly encapsulating the western perception of vampires. However, VTMB doesn't limit you to the usual sneak, seduce and feed vampiric stereotype, it allows you to choose between several races of vampire, each with unique abilities called Disciplines which fill a whole range of playstyles and simultaneously increase replayability.
I'd definitely recommend it, and I wish I had stumbled upon this game sooner.

Reading through the negative reviews here, most of them have the same complaint: they can’t get the game running. It’s true the game won’t run on a modern OS without the unofficial patch, which is shameful on Activision’s part, especially since the creator of the patch offered it to them for free.
But despite the annoyance of getting the game running, it has a 94% approval rating here on Steam. Indeed it seems nearly everyone that actually managed to play the game liked it. That speak volumes of the game.
Apart from getting the game running is it flawless? Not entirely, the gameplay leaves a lot to be desired. While the combat isn’t quite as clunky as the first Deus Ex, enemies with fully automatic weapons will kill you in about two seconds, though these enemies mostly appear towards the end of the game and thankfully stealth is preposterously easy.
So why play this game? Simple: Atmosphere and Characters. This game has such wonderful way of making you feel like a creature of the night.
The graphics are obviously dated, but there are nice touches such as animated facial expressions. The original soundtrack is great. The licensed music ranges from pretty good to really awful.
What really keeps me coming back to this game is the characters. Though most of them are clinically dead they are more alive the character in any other game I’ve played. The dialogue is brilliantly written and voice acted. It’s just a delight to talk to people in this game. The Vampire Politics at the heart of the game are also really fascinating and how you treat the different factions affects which endings are available to you.
Despite the problems with getting it running and the rather poor gameplay this is a must play if you like good writing in games. If, however, you only care about gameplay this game is not for you.

The game made for a fun experience where I felt like a bloodsucker stalking the streets of hollywood, caught up in a battle with multiple choices and vital decisions that could change the world. Overall, the great story wrapped me up in a web and I thought about the moral and fatal conse qunces of every action, from decisions that could shake the world, to where to spend my experience so that i could spend another night breathing, VTMB had me thinking about every action, and their consequences. 10/10

I always imagine this must be how ants engage in combat when they steal human technology. Terraria combined with the combat from castle crashers, in multiplayer with Capture The Flag. Although fights doesn't feel satisfying, the element of building your 2D makeshift castlefort (for the team?) brings a grin to my face for every spike-impaled kill I earn. Friend or foe, if you falling through that trap door that took me 5 minutes of clicking on a potato-video sized pixel to gather and build, I earned the right to make you respawn again.
There are 3 classes you can switch to, in base and with no appended respawn time. Archers, for artillery support, knights for frontline infantry, and builders for defense and utilities.
Knight combat on its own, without limited items like bombs to aid you, feels like a samurai duel, where if you swing first you better do more consecutive damage on the follow up, to kill him before he kills you.
Archers feels like Benjamin franklin kiting away from the inevitable lightning from Zeus, however if you sneeze at the right time, you might hurt the sky, I just shoot up and hope it lands on someone, cause knights just raise their shields and I can't really do much on this guy.
Bob the builder (my favorite class), has the power to build a series of workshops that introduces the little tribal village of your team to mercantilism. Think of it as a tech tree class for your civilization, except you, the urban planner won't get paid for the layouts, nor the progression of your tribe's conquest. You are a humble servant that fills his needs by serving the land for your team. Scavenging the rocks from the ground, and the berries in the trees, wishfully thinking maybe one day your team might meander far enough to bring home the flag of the enemy.
This is medieval soldat, but a balanced complete 2D destructibility, where players actively repairs and grow the base, this is a game for you. For 3 bucks it's a steal.

I totally love this game. For me, it is a dream come true, and the best entertainment I have experienced in years! That may be partly because I've always been a fan of the 18th century days of sail. I've done some real life sailing and navigation and really appreciate the remarkable authenticity of many aspects of the game. Just as in real life sailing, you have to keep abreast of wind direction, weather conditions, compass headings, sail control, water depth etc. This is an exceptionally good game of tactics, strategy, and skill - skill that you develop as you progress.
The reviewer who claimed that you are effectively forced to buy powerful ships with real money, is completely wrong. I completed the two ultimate objectives, including defeating a fleet of 1st rate ships of the line, without spending a penny of real money. You can develop your assets and accrue in-game 'gold' to acquire bigger and better ships without paying real money.
The graphics are superb. The sea looks and behaves like real sea, including the wake that the ships create. You could easily be watching a movie. Likewise, the cannon fire looks and sounds authentic and dramatic. I like the music score too, which for me, captures the spirit of the era. There is an amazing selection of ships, all beautifully crafted and proportioned. They rock and roll on the waves and lean in the wind with great realism. The sails of the ships fill out with the wind and gibe as you turn. If you have ever fancied trying a bit of real sailing, this game is a great way to gain some valuable skills!
As soon as I started getting into this game, I was hooked. I was having so much fun sailing the open seas in my ship of choice, salvaging wreckage, rescuing survivors, dodging attackers, trading with smugglers and exploring coastlines, that I tended to ignore the regular missions that popped up in the game. Luckily, this was during the festive season, so I had a lot of free time. I was playing it for about 16 hours a day on some days, because I was so captivated. I like the fact that it can be a single-player game - so you can exit the game and carry on later from where you left it.
I think a lot of deep thought and creative work went into this richly intriguing game. I found it a totally absorbing adventure of discovery - partly because the in-game help file is skimpy, so you have to figure many things out for yourself. There are a lot of neat features that aren't covered in the skimpy help menu. So you may need to resort to some trial, error and experimentation, and follow your hunches to some extent. That's another thing I love about the game; it made me think for myself. If you approach the game intelligently, use your wits and manage your assets judiciously, you may fare well.
For my tastes, this is the best game I have yet discovered. It has given me the best 200 hours of totally absorbing adventure I have experienced for years. Total kudos to the developers! I so hope they continue developing it for years to come. There is a sequel ('Plague of the Dead') - but that game has fantasy elements, such as wildly stylized pirate ships and sea monsters, which are not really my thing.
I actually didn't particularly want to be a pirate, and it turned out that I didn't have to act like one in order to succeed. Most of all, I just wanted to sail those beautiful ships, explore the open world, and develop my assets. And there is plenty of scope for that. Now that I've conquered the Pirate Confederacy and the West India Company, I still open the game freqently, because the challenges keep coming, and I just love sailing those utterly gorgeous ships and honing my battle skills!

Loading this into a visual novel engine was overkill; like many other indie free visual novels I've played, the save and load functions provided by the engine were never utilised. It would've been far better as a story or a short manga composition.
The story is still funny and charming, nevertheless, with a hint of admiration for memes. I got the good playthrough in one try (maybe because I'm a good person and picked the good option for each decision, lol); trying out the other options showed me that there was only one path to succeed in the game. Not much effort in terms of building a plot. Picking a bad option rewarded you with a few blocks of text and a trademark "BAD END" (thank goodness with no gruesome imagery; 'tis a cheerful and innocent VN).
I recommend it because it's free, is well drawn and is a nice 5-10-minute treat to enjoy in our otherwise rather depressing world. The plot itself ultimately serves only to preach moral values, probably Chinese in origin: Be patient, be pacifist, be optimistic, be good, do not commit prejudice... and ultimately, to always put your heart into your work and remember the reason why you do the things you do; that if it was born out of love, keep that love first and foremost, never to be forgotten.

This game is honestly one of my favourite games. Of all time. Most people would immediately look past it due to it's seemingly "outdated" graphics. Those people, are what we call a fine shade of "wrong". The graphics, joined with the music, are a spectacle to behold (Especially, especially, the intro theme, I love the main part), and fit so well together. It has something about it- Kindof like saying "It's so Synthesized, it sounds a little bit instrumental". Maybe that's my imagination, maybe it's not.
But onto the review.
In this game, you pilot one of ten ships (Unlocked either by beating the final boss on the ship before, or doing a special quest you find in the space of each of the respective races (Aside from one...)) that are with the Federation (Just like Star Trek!), who are under attack by the "Rebels" (Just. Like. Star- Wait, nevermind), and are going to be destroyed. This is where you come in. You're the pilot of one of said ships on a mission to get back to federation space, destroying Space pirates, and Rebels, along the way, all while being chased by the rebel forces. Now, from that description, one might think this is an action-shooter. That is extremely wrong. at times, there is a lot of action, but it is nowhere near your Asteroids or Side-scroll shooters. This is a game of Strategy. You must use different types of weapons (Bought, found on ships, sometimes found floating in space, from time to time given to you at the end of "sectors" (More later on that)) working together to bring down the enemy ships (My general tactic is to primarily disable weapons, then shield as they reestabilish weapons, and so on), with different weapon types doing different things.
Weapons. There is lots of weapons. They divide into 4 (5?) categories: Laser, Missile, Beam, Bomb, and (in Advanced edition (Free with the game)) Chain weapons= Chain Vulcan= Laser. Machine gun.
But the LaserMachineguns aside, they all have different purposes: Lasers are your standardized weapon: Cannot pierce shields, having to go through them, dealing damage to systems and ship and crew; Missiles are for more... "Assassination" They pierce all shields, and unless destroyed by drone, are going to mess up the enemies (Or your) day. Beam weapons are a little like Lasers, in the fact that they have to go through shields, with each layer they have to go through removing one damage from the laser on hitting the ship itself, and will hit multiple rooms. Bombs are essentially missiles that incur different status effects on the enemy ship, like lighting it on fire, stunning crew, both, etc.
The events. From finding ships encased in crystal to freaking giant spiders on space stations, there's a lot of them, which can happen within different sectors, and have different outcomes if you have a specific type of crew member (Of which you can only have eight, but you can place them anywhere on the ship you want), sometimes you'll stumble upon something that even unlocks you a new ship!
tl;dr - This game is a strategic masterpiece, the difficulty ranging from "Why does it have missiles?!" to "OH MY GOD IT HAS FOUR SHIELDS AND MISSILES" and requires to think more than most other games I can name. Recommended.

, developed by Russian developer SmoleVN, is a visual novel that uses its colorful characters to share a collection of ghost stories told by friends that get together on an evening of eerie adventures. It's short and composed by 9 chapters.
As I said above, the VN tells about a group of friends who are waiting for the strike of midnight to summon the Queen of Spades. As they wait, they decide to share their scary stories with each other. Most of the girls know each other’s stories but the two guys, Stas and Styopa who join in, don’t. Made by Russian developer SmoleVN, they use the character, Queen of Spades, inspired by a popular story by Alexander Pushkin which has supernatural themes about human greed.
isn't a gaming experience but more of a viewing experience with clicking to progress the story and read the next passage. Personally, I wish the stories had some kind of user interactiveness, in other hand, becomes annoying. The characters are of various age groups and these girls are quiet and stylish, sporty and flirty, even grounded and mature, add in the younger little girl cutesy and they have it all covered in personality. Plus, there are also two guys that show up and they are quite distinct as well.
The story isn't about horror, at all. The game has a big side directed for fun and not is as the start looks like. The characters are telling you 'scary' stories but to be honest, they aren't scary at all. I found the story extremely boring, that I needed skipp some scenes. The story is lackluster, characters forgettable and there is really not a whole lot going on in here. Categorizing this as horror is dumb. The game's story line has some sexual allusions, so, the game seems to be targeted at an adolescent audience, though this will vary depending on cultural and sub-cultural norms. Overall, the story is bland and uninteresting. There are some issues in the English translation, but nothing really important.

(I commented these points on another person's review, when I was actively playing the game, in response to some questions that other people had asked. Hopefully this adresses any questions people might have after reading other reviews of the game. It's not much, but it's something.)
This game has a great multiplayer aspect. There are often many people online at a time to play with if you don't have friends on your own. You can join another person's game midway and get right into the action, or you can start your own game, send out an SOS beacon, and wait for someone to join you. Everyone shares a screen (no breaking off into different directions), and there's a max of 4 players per game. If someone dies, the screen will adjust to fit the others. The screen does not change size whether or not a group is close to each other, so you need to stick together to see what you're aiming at (the game is top-down).
Multiplayer isn't server-based, it's player-hosted (meaning there are no dedicated servers, but there are also no queues to get into a game). Players can join or start a mission whenever they want to, and they can dictate whether or not they want other users (friends/otherwise) to be able to join them. There's a system where players can commend or report players based on how they worked with (or hindered) the team. If a player gets enough commendations, they'll be more likely to play with others who have been commended (same idea with reports).
(As I was about to post this review, I just remembered something important about multiplayer: COUCH CO-OP is a thing. If you've got extra controllers to hook up to your computer, you and your friends can use anything you've unlocked/bought, including all of your upgrades for guns/stratagems, I believe.)
Solo is pretty brutal, especially without any DLC or playing on the higher difficulties. As someone who, while playing, didn't have any DLC, I struggled to keep up with my friend who was new to the game and had all-terrain boots for the snow map we were in. As you raise the difficulty, the enemies get tougher. You MUST defeat patrol enemies (weak, but pop up frequently), or they'll sound the alarm and send multiple large and tanky enemies that can only really be defeated with anti-tank guns/missiles. Conveniently, there are machines players can summon which fire rockets (in one of the DLC packs).
Personally, I never tried to play the game with a mouse and keyboard. I used my controller (Logitech F710), and the controls felt very fluid. A friend I'd been playing the game with told me that, as he was using kb/m, aiming felt a bit slow. If you end up buying/playing the game, I recommend using a controller.
I haven't played the game too long (as you can see by my hours), but near the end I was feeling a slight burnout. That's probably a combination of playing it for many hours at a time with my friend (We really enjoyed the game's humor - every time a player kills/blows up some enemies, hearing something along the lines of "For Democracy!") and of having played a few Hell Dives (highest difficulty) and completing them relatively easily (there's not much challenge once you get used to defeating patrols and walking as a group).
I'd say the game's good to get during a sale, if you're unsure. There are great possibilities if you enjoy multiplayer games and maybe have some friends who would enjoy working together (or blowing each other up), but you might need to get some DLC to fully enjoy everything the game has to offer. I probably wouldn't buy the DLC at full price, though.

Helldivers is what you get when you take the unyielding friendly-fire mechanics behind Magicka, put guns in your character hands and launch them down on planets inhabited by critters, cyborgs, aliens and a lack of democracy.
It's a fun, tongue-in-cheek experience where you can always return to play with friends, that is easy to learn but relatively challenging to master, that makes deaths seem like a minor inconvenience (and most of the time, thoroughly funny.
It plays well both with keyboard/mouse or controller (originally being a console game) and even after so long, it is still populated with enough players to have a good time.
It's the kind of game you can drop an hour in here and there or spend an evening on. Both sweet and spicy but always delightfully right.

Vampire: The Masquerade is a very atmospheric game, with gameplay very reminiscent of Fallout 3 but without the scrounging mechanics. The lore of the game is quite fascinating, most likely because it comes from a bunch of D20 nerds who really love the game, and if you're a fan of movies like Blade, Guillermo del Toro's The Strain, and 30 Days of Night, as well as the late 90's/early 2000's club culture, you're gonna love this game and the world it crafts.
The gameplay, much like the dice-based game it's based on, is split between combat and puzzle solving. The combat is adequate, but be sure to specialize in at least something because, like reality, a guy can't just pick up an uzi or a knife and be a mass-murderer. You're gonna die plenty, so make sure to save scum like a scumbag who saves. As for the puzzles, you got a plethora of stealth, clue solving, and genuine investigations that ought to stretch your brain muscles more than the standard fair.
Is the game worth the price? Absolutely, especially if you can get it on sale, because you're liable to spend at minimum 5 hours on the game because it's kinda hard to look at some dude with bizarre pustules spouting about genuinely convincing religious philosophy and just let it pass by, and interesting things are everywhere that you're gonna WANT to explore everything you can, and a few things you can't.
Oh, and a small note. I began my first playthrough as a Malkavian because I did the personality test. If you get saddled up with that, prepare to get even more immersed.

I`ve always had a thing for sailing games ever since I bought Pirates of the Carribbean (the precursor to Age of Pirates) a long timeago. With Naval Action getting less attractive by the minute and the Age of Pirates series being dead (and not having changed a bloody thing over the last 3 games) I was really looking for something new. Now this game is free to play but I`d totally be down to pay some money for a good game in the genre.
With that said, the game has a few MAYOR flaws which are literally appearant within the first few minutes.
1. The game is for PC and Mobile. which means 2 negative things. a) the controls are just not that good, as everything needs to be clicked on the way a touchscreen works. b) The graphics justarent up to par. The game looks more than 10 years old. now I`m not a huge graphics-nerd but these just look too dated for a 2016 release.
2. The game is "free to play" which means that it  wants real money for ingame things.  Now,  I don`t like this in any game in the same way that I don`t like casinos: If I want to play something its because I`d like to relax and for once NOT think abbout how much money Im spending. However in this game it`s worse as the prices are REALLY high and the game constantly nags you to buy something.
3.The game is extremly shallow. The first 10 (!!!) missions or so are literally "sail  here and pick up cargo" with the odd "fight one ship" mission  in between but neither  is a challange! Sailing is as basic as it can be. You set sails with 2 clicks and wait, theres wind but unless youre sailing straight into it, its nothing to worry about and shooting literally consists of pressing spacebar when the gigantic white indication-line is on the enemy ship. There are tradegoods, but no interface for trading and across-the-entire-map-teleportation means trading isnt a fun thing to do.
All in all, I think its worth a look, since its "free" but at the end of the day, I wont be coming back to it.

Without Within is a pretty short novel with a funny story but also a pretty deep message.
Vinty is the main character and she seem like a very famous and respected person in the beginning, but no, it was all a dream. I did not like Vinty in the dream, she seemed like a real D-bag to be honest. When she woke up, we get to learn more about her normal, poor and pretty miserable life. She's struggling with money, she has one job that pays the rent. But her true dream and passion is to work with Calligraphy. She has been working with that for a very long time and she never seems to suceed. Of course she starts to reflect about how this dream is probably never going to live up to her hopes. As she sits on the train station, she hears a little boy crying and she finds out that he has lost his mom somewhere in the crowd. You get the options to eitehr go to the job or help the boy out and be late for work. Of course the majority of people (I,m not sure though, knowing the people of the internet today) and this of course an act that will help her out later on. I will not go too deep into the story, though I'd like to mention that the story is very original. It has some incredibly hilarious jokes and parts. It has a lot of elements from our present day techonlogy and such which made me giggle a few times throughout the novel.
The ending is very sudden and you get a little suprised, but knowing there's a sequel makes you feel good again.
I'd give this a 9/10.
Overall the novel Without Within is a must for people who likes Visual Novels (which is by the way a thing in the actual novel). The story is great, it has a lot of humor and cute artwork. The only thing that makes this game a 9/10 instead of 10/10 is the UI and the menu. It's a boring font with a pretty boring chatbox and boring buttons. Though this is a little issue, it does not change the acutal novel in any way. Again, it's a must have for people who enjoy Visual Novels.

After more than 150 hours on this game, i really have to pay it the homages it deserve.
FTL is a Rogue Like game set in space where you have to micromanage your starship system and crew durring fights. This structure is both it's greater strength and major disavantage.
Know that you will live the same story each game: escaping the Rebels fleet chassing you in order to reach the Federation. But the journey will  never be the same.
As you jump from strars to stars, you will meet dozens of different encounters (enemy ships to fight, people to help...) creating an unique adventure.
The dificulty can be a bit harsh at the beginning, but with time, you will learn about the different mechanics and grow stronger of every defeat. Their is enought variety in the weapon and systems available to allow you to build you own play style.
With a dozen of different ships to unlock and play with, each of them having they own starting gears and achivements, this game will last a long time to the most completionists of you.
The univers of this game, even if it's never clearly explain is also really rich and complexe. At least, complet enought to feel real.
What else can i say? Oh yeah! An awsome soundtrack and a nice retro looking design.
FTL is defintly a game worth your time if you can dive into it.

Metro is a linear FPS (which is one of my favorite types of games), and it does it greatly.
Gameplay- Shooting feels absolutely great, almost as good as Half-Life 2. My only real complaint is how slow it feels to aim. Weapons could have been done better, I thought the silenced guns would be a lot more useful than they really where, but when they were used were some of the best moments in the game. Ammo management is great, being forced to either use an incredibly weak weapon on an enemy or use the special bullets (the game's currency) was a good dilemma that would have to be made fast. Although it didn't add too much in the end, it makes the hectic nature of battles even more worrying.
Story- The story follows one man through the underground Metro on a journey to kill off the race that is trying to kill off you. The story isn't deep, you go from one place to another, then to the next. But the best part is the bits with characters as you make your path through the Metro. As you meet new friends, and watch old ones die, you have little time to mourn or react to their death, which some people like about a game, while others believe is too rushed. This reminds of how The Last of Us treated deaths, although it wasn't as good, it definitely left an impression on you as you pushed forward. After you manage to fight your way to the end though, you are treated to a good, but rather rushed ending. That feels a little bit sudden, although it's still incredibly enjoyable and a satisfying conclusion to the game.
Who Should Play This- Any fan of linear games, whether it's shooters such as Halo, or survival horrors like Resident Evil, this game would entertain anybody who decides to pick it up.
Number Score- 8/10

This game is surprisingly good. It succeeds in sucking you right into the setting and its story with solid gameplay and some memorable levels. The game is practically oozing atmosphere and is guaranteed to give you the creeps now and then. This is an AAA from a relatively small developer and publisher and leaves most of its competitors in the dust.
The game allows you to run stealthy or guns blazing and offers rewards for both styles, instead of railroading you into one particular style. Levels are fairly linear with not much room for exploring or optional objectives, but this is no problem - the story and unfolding events tend to suck you right in.
Style, setting and atmosphere will be familiar for veterans of the Stalker series, and Metro 2033 is certainly on par with those, although it is way more linear and smaller in its setup.
If you have any love for shooters and don't mind an occasional scare - you'd be doing yourself a favour by adding this to your library.

HELLDIVERS, A game that is come a long way, For the type of game it is.
Right off the bat, Your given a pretty in depth tutorial, And i know this game has been out for a long time, Trust be been there with the game as it was first on consoles all the way, The game has a moderate amount to offer in terms of content.
There are plenty of weapons,strategems, And other neat gadgets at your disposal.
Though most of the items you use ingame, Many are shrugged off in a series of they can't or don't do enough damage end game 10 Plus or higher leveled missions.
Here are my pros and cons for the game
:PROS:
+Fun solo but to about 8 leveled missions, I managed to push 9.
+Insanly fun with friends always a good laugh.
+Indepth teamwork mechanic
+Heavy Friendly Fire based game (can be a con)
+Report/Commendation system (So you can get an idea of who joined you)
+Diverse tools ingame
:CONS:
-Diverse tools ends up falling off endgame.
-Hefty on the grind side(Doesn't bother me though)
-Can get repetitive quickly
-You can't always use what you want, There has to be some compremises in your team(Doesn't Bother me)
-Most DLC isn't worth it and poor DLC practice, All Terrian boots the player HAS to buy them to do ice planets, And most of the items in the DLC packs offer very little for any real pay off, Fun here and there, But at level 11-12 end game missions, you'll barely use any of them if even a single one at all except drone boots and maybe a few others.
All in all the game is going threw time rather well, I still love the game after the several years it has been out but i hate the DLC practice in games that developers choose to take.
Without DLC this game is still amazingly fun, By yourself for a few hours but even better and funnier with other HELLDIVERS.
I give it 8/10

Vampire: The Masquerade is a very atmospheric game, with gameplay very reminiscent of Fallout 3 but without the scrounging mechanics. The lore of the game is quite fascinating, most likely because it comes from a bunch of D20 nerds who really love the game, and if you're a fan of movies like Blade, Guillermo del Toro's The Strain, and 30 Days of Night, as well as the late 90's/early 2000's club culture, you're gonna love this game and the world it crafts.
The gameplay, much like the dice-based game it's based on, is split between combat and puzzle solving. The combat is adequate, but be sure to specialize in at least something because, like reality, a guy can't just pick up an uzi or a knife and be a mass-murderer. You're gonna die plenty, so make sure to save scum like a scumbag who saves. As for the puzzles, you got a plethora of stealth, clue solving, and genuine investigations that ought to stretch your brain muscles more than the standard fair.
Is the game worth the price? Absolutely, especially if you can get it on sale, because you're liable to spend at minimum 5 hours on the game because it's kinda hard to look at some dude with bizarre pustules spouting about genuinely convincing religious philosophy and just let it pass by, and interesting things are everywhere that you're gonna WANT to explore everything you can, and a few things you can't.
Oh, and a small note. I began my first playthrough as a Malkavian because I did the personality test. If you get saddled up with that, prepare to get even more immersed.

This game seemed like a great concept to me.
That's why I originally bought it.
I'd been wanting the game for months, and decided to finally purchase it during the Summer Sale.
I launched the game, signed in, and completed the tutorials.
The game's athestics are very nice, and while not ultra-realistic, they are polished.
The game is executed well, too.
IN SINGLEPLAYER.
Build things, fight things, destroy your enemy.
However, when in a Multiplayer enviroment which for me was the highlight of the game, things start to go wrong.
I could not last more than 1 or 2 minutes while playing as the Knight or Archer class.
Any attempts made by me were futile, as the other members of my team refused to provide any sort of help and essentially all tried to do their own thing. This led to me getting killed. A lot.
That's when I turned to the Builder class.
I was great at staying behind our front defenses, and helping to build more defenses aswell.
HOWEVER, if one of your teammates doesn't like the way you set up a fort, or placed traps, they will take it upon themselves to destroy what you built, and place their own structures. If you are new to the game and don't have a lot of experience with setting up traps or building defenses, I suggest you STAY AWAY from Multiplayer for at least 30 minutes of gameplay. Familiarize yourself with how this game works, or you will be called an idiot in Multiplayer.
This was my experience, and I hope you learn not to make the same mistake I did.

Unforgiving World War II Real-time strategy game. What could be better! The genius of the game is it's frangible/breakable environments and the ability to strategically attack a situation in a variety of ways. Are you gonna take out that entrenched 88 with an infantry attack? Attack it head-to-head with a tank? Try to flank it with multiple tanks? Try an air strike? Drop behind it with a paratrooper? Or just run it over with a lightning tank manuever? Time can be slowed down, paused or sped up. Single-player campaigns are historic and fun. Keep in mind that the game is difficult and frustrating at the best of times - but each play-through creates all kinds of random options. Animations, sounds and explosions are top-notch. Micro-management is highly detailed. My favorite modern RTS!
