Hands down, the best game I've ever played. It's dark and gritty without taking itself too seriously, filled with atmopshere and world-detail without playing like a fantasy encyclopedia. and you can roll around town dressed up as a pimp or a stripper. What more could you want from a game?
The best testimony of how fantastic this game is is undoubtedly the fans; Even though this game came out in 2004, there are still unofficial patches being developed and released as you read this. Never has a game been more loved, cherished, or enriched by its community. We're just lucky to be able to play it now, when all the bugs have been fixed by dedicated fans, compared to its initial release.
The game play is fairly simple and easy to access, though the variety of levels mean it never gets dull. You can shoot, tear, or bite your way through your enemies, and look like something straight out of a bondage fever dream/nightmare whilst doing it. The plot is genuinely gripping, with twists and turns I never saw coming, and the ending? The ending is just... f*** me. Well played, Bloodlines. Well played.
Storyline? Basically, you wake up a fledgling after a passionate night with your fanged lover, only to end up becoming a glorified slave of a grumpy french nobleman with a Napoleon complex and a damn nice suit. Be his ♥♥♥♥♥ for what feels like eternity. Blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up. The ranges of choices you're given are actually pretty impressive, and DO make a difference, unlike some franchises I can think of (*cough*Mass Effect*cough). Be sassy. Be crazy. Be sexy as hell. It's one of those games where you can truly be whoever you want.
Aside from appropriately dressed. No mod will ever give you that.

This game is a successor to Soldiers: HOWW2 and Faces of War, some brilliant games that rewarded detailed planning, fast reflexes and initiative. They were not made for casuals. And this is why casuals hated them. Too buggy, too hard, uncomprehensible etc etc. Do not hear their whinning if you do not like to just faceroll a stupid AI, but instead you prefer having a challenge. I remember loading same spot like 20 times trying different things so the AI does not steam roll me. Having 3-5 soldiers and having to clear whole bases, kill/capture/disable tanks, escape etc is not something offered by many games.
This is continued in Men Of War. From 2nd mission and on, you will have to face MANY enemies more than you. I checked the end game stats and saw that I was facing like 1000 enemies in defensive missions...and you have like 50 at most. Not to mention the tanks. AI has some nice ability to kill your tanks easier that you can kill its. Yeah this can be frustrating. So, just be more careful. And save often.
Even if you are a veteran of S:HOWW2, some missions can be tough. Although there is no tactics mode like in Faces of War, you can still die easily by some direct shots. I cannot say much about...replayability. Playing 1 mission for 4h +, makes you feel relieved when  you finish it. One thing that I disagree with is that you cannot do as much as you could do in S: HOWW2 when in pause. Having to command MANY squads, resupply their ammo while the AI launches attack after attack is sometimes very demanding. When you have 3-5 soldiers it is easy...no time pressure etc. But the game and its objectives are still viable, and I have screens where I lost like 10 soldiers/0 tanks in defenses. On normal. So, if you plan carefully, think, reload and try different ways to win, you will make it.
Again...it is not for casuals. If you are one, you will cry. If you like tough challenges, then you will love this difficult ♥♥♥♥♥. Graphics are nice. Enough to make take screens of the environment. Voiceovers and sound I do not care. I am muting all games so I can listen to music. Storyline. Again, I do not care much. I just like killing stuff. From what I saw it was there just to exist. Who really cares...
Physics and realism. The stuff I like: explosions, bodies launch at every direction, bullets fear the brave, they disperse, and they change direction when  they hit hard surfaces. Cannon shells...2 types: explosive, armor penetrating. Self explanatory. Now the spotting dot shows you the area of dispersion, the possibility to penetrate and ofc the distance. All this changes according to angle, vehicle armor, its speed, your speed, and other factors. It is the detail that makes the difference, and in this factor the game is a diamond.
8.8/10 just because I wanted better pause tool, voiceovers and storyline that are there just to exist and sometimes AI kills your tanks too easily to make it even competitive.

I came to my wits end with this game recently. Perhaps it was my fault, but even after asking on the game forums about problems I still have not found a solution to my woes which I will get to after I actually talk about the game.
I can't really recommend this game at all. The first reason is the balance issues plaguing this game. It seems to favor both German factions and British Forces while telling US Forces and Soviets to fall in a ditch. Germans get better units earlier in the game and at reasonable costs while Allied factions are usually underpowered and expensive. New commanders are made obsolete when new ones are available for purchase (yes, for purchase) or you can find them, if the game decides to give you drops. Which after the past few times I played with my friend never happened where I never got EXP or drops after a match was finished. There really feels like there is no incentive to play as Allies when their armor is almost completely outclassed by anything the Germans can throw at them.
Now for the technical issues. There are plenty.
For a while I had a problem launching this game properly. I never feel you should have to go into the game files and disable functions and files just to launch it with no issues.
I don't have the best video card but I was able to get playable framerates a year ago before I switched my mobo and CPU. COH2 hates these for some reason as I am not able to decipher why all my other games work with minimal problems but this game lays an egg when I try to play online. Things start well until about fifteen minutes into a match when I get told my settings are too high and I become victim to input lag. By the time I get to the end game, I suffer input lag of upwards of twenty minutes before I see my units respond to my orders.
Twenty. Minutes.
Even after following all the advice I was given I still experience trash like this. My friends told me they just use my idle units as a barricade to build up their forces before wiping out the enemy. It makes me feel good when my pals tell me "You make a great wall." Really makes me feel like I'm part of a team. For a game exclusive to the PC it doesn't work very well on a rig that at the time of writing this is passable.
After everything I've seen and experienced in the game I can safely say you can skip this. I only bought this to play against AI because I never felt good enough to play against others. Some people are probably already reading this review and calling me a dumb noob for such reasons, but I don't care. I feel that until Relic focuses more on trying to balance the game (and maybe trying to discover the root of these issues I face) instead of farming money out of me, I put this as not recommended.

Solid, intuitive tactics based RTS. The devs focus on trying to make CoH an e-sport type game helps continue refining the balance of the game, and keeps common problems from being an issue for long, for the most part.
On the bad side, CoH2 AI cheats to get an advantage, with unit speed, armor, damage, and resource buffs. This shows the lack of focus on those who want to skirmish the AI with friends as opposed to hectic human based opponents. No improvements to AI decision making, only how well they handle making bad decisions and getting away with it. The unit depth and commander variety can be anywhere from nearly identical to hardly the same faction depending on the commander, which is obviously both good and bad.
On the other hand, putting in a lot of hours, the game is stable, has many community maps, some of which automatically spotlighted in the game, solid replayability, fun with friends, and one of few modern RTS titles that has the player base to force a good showing by devs.

This second installment in the Labyronia series will be much appreciated by fans new and old. Our story continues where the first game left off, as you begin play as Garric, one of the original heroes of the first game. The world has changed into a wintry nightmare filled with demons and undead, and its up to you and your allies to locate Arres in hopes of finding a solution.
The graphics are much improved over the first, and the music is a little tighter as well. Gone are the most frustrating aspect of the game, those darned labrynths - they've been pared down to a more reasonable difficulty. There's plenty of puzzles to be found too and there seems to be a lot less of a need to endlessly grind out levels than there was in the first. One of the things that I appreciated the most was how quickly I found a second party member; who ironically, was the father of the hero of the first game. Fans of the first game will recall that you only found the next member of your party quite close to the end of the story, so locating Windir early on was a relief.
I would definitely recommend this game to friends interested in the genre, and have done so. It's so cheap that it's practically a steal, and furthermore, your entire party of heroes are all middle-aged or older, something that you hardly ever see in a game. If you want to save the world and give horrible monsters an elderly smackdown, this is the game for you!
+Graphics, sound, and puzzles better than the first game
+Continuation of an amazing and original storyline
+Fantastic use of a somewhat limited game engine
+Geriatric smackdown!
+Could have used some better editing

Fantastic game, the RPG element makes it VERY replayable,(I think) the game dynamics because of this are enjoyable and very diverse. There does appear to be room to choose who to work for etc, but I have not tried yet(to turncoat(*see edit)) , so can only speculate whether an alternative story line exists, or if the alternative NPCs are just quest givers(which is very standard for your AAA trashy RPG/open world Botchventure).
EDIT: This game's plot is 'guided' or linear, so there are only added quests alongside the main story, therefore not allowing you to travel alternative story lines(which to be fair, is not surprising)
Level design is nice and there is decent incentive to investigate, scout around and hack into terminals, or look for ventilation systems.  Some things are for the hell of it like silly humour that is in the email systems and the odd pick up, although, the energy system gives you a good incentive to keep in the dark and look for *prey*.
EDIT: In saying that  the game design is good, and most of it is!  But it feels as if the devs were 'slowing down' a bit at the end of the game and felt the need to wrap it up quickly.
Combat is a bit clunky at first, though you get used to it, though it is not as elegant as something like Jedi Knight, for example, I still have great difficulty blocking with respect to a specific attack on this, but its not too bad....  There is plenty of room for takedowns, so throughout the game you are given the opportunity to avoid confrontation, by hitting the enemy when they dont see you, or of course (sometimes) by avoiding confrontaitons altogether..
Talking about takedowns: There is stealth in this game, and it appears like (at least with the class I am using) that you can get through most of the game without being seen, which almost makes it feel like 'Dishonoured', or perhaps 'Thief' with added stuff, which I would count as a definate compliment,  On the other hand I dont think you *have* to go in with stealth, if you have the right class; as there are sweet talking ' half-human' classes and there is definetly room to blow stuff up!
Music is nice, very varied depending where you are and what you're doing.  There are smoother bits, to the gothy bits, to the bluesy bits, to the almost tension/horror bits when you are in a mission area.
It is easy to consider that this is very similar to Deus Ex, with most of the game design choices, though what with the energy system, some skills, and the choice of classes, this game seems to have a bit more to it.
One word of warning though, you may find bugs at first, I downloaded  the VTB Ultimate patch from the RPGscrolls, and I got no issues  since.  They even introduced modern system compatibility, such as high res blah, excellent mod/patch.
Grab the unofficial patch to clear up the bugs and this is a fantastically good RPG. Atmosphere, voice acting, story and characters are all top notch.

Labyronia RPG 2 is a turn based RPG game which is a sequel of Labyronia RPG. The story sets in several years after the first series, in a land which has become frozen due to the events happened before. In order to enjoy this game fully, it's better for you to finish Labyronia RPG first. I will explain some differences between both series later on.
Upon starting a new game, you'll be presented with a prologue which basically explains whatever happened between the first and the second series. Unlike the first series, your main objective is stated clearly from the start. However, although this series is using some characters from the first series, Garric's characteristic changed to be more talkative, and i'm sure that Ann's hair somehow changed (unless i forgot that her hair is changed by the end of the first series). The party talks become merrier, although the jokes seems forced to me.
The story itself isn't delivered smoothly imo, although i can understand what the dev is trying to deliver. It's quite funny seeing that people can change their opinion in just a few dialogue/battle
. Some dialogues need some words to polish up its atmosphere before delivering the final blow.
Most of the maps used in Labyronia 2 are modified maps from the first series. The modification is including the addition of walkable body of water (or platform), the color change of the environment (to darkish blue color), and (or) the destroyed parts of the area.
There are some graphic changes in the main character, such as Garric which is using blue bandanna instead of brown. However, most of the art seems blurry (although it can be because of the snow effect). I also got confused by the mapping of the walkable water and the sea. I tend to thought that you can't walk on both. The same goes with Carallan (third town) with its transparent platform and the "pit".
I'm not that impressed with how the lighting is done. Most of the lighting are lazily done by changing the tile floor. It should be done like in Hall of Madness (third dungeon) where the light looks like glowing/shining.
Some of the mapping looks bland and empty, such as the "almost-nothing-room" in Ann's place.
Lastly, the NPC in the shelter is blocking the path because the path is only using one tile. Perhaps the dev can change the NPC movement area or making the path bigger.
I know that it's kinda hard looking for an appropriate BGM for an area, but i think that the dev doesn't need to force it. Although i can stand that some of the music doesn't suitable with the area, there is an additional music playing in Hall of Madness (third dungeon) in each area of the dungeon, which sounds ridiculous. I even heard Harry Potter's sound when he spoke to snake.
Some music, like the overworld map, is using the same music as the first series.
The first thing that needs to be mentioned is that you'll have 4 party members in the game. The other good thing is that you'll meet your first party member very fast, unlike the first series. However, the party composition looks ridiculous with 2 wizards and 1 priest which need MP to survive. Guess what? There is no MP regen equipment in the game like how the first series is.
Because there is no MP regen equipment, resting (in the inn) has become necessary. However, there is lack of healing spot in game, which forces you either to return to the city or use item to restore MP. I did the first option, and i think that a significant amount of my gameplay is spent in doing so.
There is a learnable skill outside of the level up skill in this game (by using a spell book). However, learning the learnable skill in bulk can be quite a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because you have to access menu screen in order to learn it and it always closes whenever you learn a new one.
This game has more puzzles than the first one. However, most of them requires timing and quite unforgivable, and one of them can take you to the game over screen if you fail.
The dungeons in this game are smaller and easier compared to the first one. The dungeons tend to make up for it by using a small lighting in it. I have tried creating a map for Labyronia's first dungeon before and it's very big. I doubt that the maps in this game is bigger than that (except in the area with a very large maps, of course). Speaking of very large maps, there are two very large maps, although one of them is very easy with no monster in it. Luckily, there is no time limited maps like the desert in the first game. There is a time limited room though.
I don't think you need to grind in this game, but there is no random encounter in the areas of the map. However, there is a random encounter in the overworld and you'll spend a lot of time walking over there before you get an airship.
Some enemy buffs are not shown in battle, which make it hard to check (especially in the last battle). I don't know that the enemy is buffed before i check it in a guide. You also can't defeat the final boss without a certain additional spell.
Lastly, you can't continue the game after you clear the game.
Pros:
- 4 party members
- 2 types to learn skill from: level up and skill book
Cons:
- Blurry images
- No MP regen equipment

Labyronia RPG 2 is a RPG developed by Labyrinthine and released Aug 28, 2015.
synopsis: It's an RPG maker game, you can tell the developers care a great deal about the lore within their game, most people won't read the literal books in it, the sequel has minor improvements which I appreciated being added, like seeing sprites attack in the battle screen. I missed seeing people swing at monsters before numbers pop up.
Welcome back to Labyronia, the story for this series is one of it's strengths
The story is a continuation on Labyronia RPG 1, this makes writing a review a bit sticky, because I first played through the first game before playing this
.
My point is, I'm familiar with these characters already, and the game kinda expects you to know who the heck "Arres" is, because they're going to talk about Arres alot, because he's kind of a big deal, he's the protagonist in the first game!
Basically crap has hit the fan, as the Starks from Game of Thrones warned everyone "winter is coming", but it was too late the land was covered in a white blanket faster then you can say "wait what". ...I guess that's note quite true because Labyronia RPG 2 takes place 10 years after the original game, but that's not funny to say.
You must assemble your party again, and confront the darkness to put an end to this infernal winter. Why did it take them 10 years to do that? I dunno, that wasn't very well explained, or my brain fell asleep. Regardless that's your job now!
Okay, RPG wise, there's not much new which you'll be surprised about. You have gear, you have levels, you have magic, you have elements which are super effective, you have defensive stats, get and equip the right gear before a boss and you'll have minimal trouble. Expect slow progression, some grinding, and random bosses to be hard for no real reason.
Oh yeah, pro tip: Equip your gear when you start the game. Because I went against the monster sieging the wall in pretty much my underpants. I won, because I'm Atratzu... but after realizing I took on a huge monster in my underpants I did blush and ask the Captain-of-the-guard to forgive the noobish mistake and promptly restarted the game  and didn't use any items on the first fight my second time through.
Other then the regular RPG elements, I don't want to go over all the same details my review for the first game did, so really quickly about the mechanics: You attack, use special abilities which use a secondary source (and depending on the type of character, builds up, or uses like magic), defend, or use items.
You can use these to come up with different strategies, yada yada yada blah blah blah... if you don't know how to play an RPG already just google "best JRPG" and buy one of those, you'll be an expert in a few hundred hours.
I noticed a few big changes from Labyronia RPG 1 and 2, aesthetically speaking these weren't necessary to play the game, but made the game actually feel like I was playing an RPG rather then a no-budget-1-man-first-project
You can now see your characters attack! Originally you would chose an attack and you'd just see a swiping animation on the screen to indicate sword attacks, or a particle effect to indicate magic. Now you get to see your cute little sprite walk up to the middle of the screen and then see the animation swipe or sprite attack.   ...Yeah, it's not much, but to gameplay it's a huge improvement! Feels like I have characters fighting, instead of picture frames fighting.
Additionally it's worth pointing out you can see your whole party trailing behind you, the more characters you get, the longer your Snake train gets. Not even Final Fantasy 7, Legend of Dragoon, or Pokemon (or other JRPG's I've played and forgotten the title of) did that. Probably because of hardware limitations... but I digress! a cool feature, I liked it... but very much aesthetic.
Everything else though...? Pretty much the same as the first game, except for starting out at level 20 or 30 and with Garic (if that's how you spell his name. Truth be told I will forever read his name as "Garlic", and so he's endearing to me, my little cranky old-man-vampire-repellent)
Well that's probably more words then anyone actually needs to know weather this is a skip or a buy.  Labyronia RPG 2 goes on sale regularly, you can pick it up at a reduced price. There's not much to the game, I highly recommend playing through some of the first game before jumping into the second game. But as far as RPG's go, you could choose a worse RPG maker game.
I recommend this game to anyone who misses playing classic JRPG's, and just needs to fill that hole in his or her heart. Have fun and may Garlic be with you.

While I did go in expecting something completely different, the straightforward story did have a sense of pure creative passion in a very limited work. I got the only good ending on my first run, as the rest of the story's choices are all purely anecdotal bad endings. That being said, the core story is genuinely sweet, and the art is of a much higher caliber than most independent attempts in the same genre. It doesn't waste your time, and while it doesn't come away presenting anything specifically new or engaging, I came away wanting more, which might've been the point.
Given how the news page is filled with talk about the sequel, I have no doubt that what is lacking here will be resolved in the following game. There is something endearing about stumbling upon a short piece of unadulterated passion, so I have all the faith in the world that the sequel will offer something great. I'll definitely be looking forward to it.
So yeah, if you're looking for something sweet to pass a lunch break or something, give this a go. Free is great, and I probably wouldn't of checked it out otherwise, so I'm definitely glad I did.

Fantastic game, the RPG element makes it VERY replayable,(I think) the game dynamics because of this are enjoyable and very diverse.  The story is quite enjoyable and I have enjoyed playing through...  It is genuinely entertaining, lots of memorable characters and things going on.  There does appear to be room to choose who to work for etc, but I have not tried yet(to turncoat(*see edit)) , so can only speculate whether an alternative story line exists, or if the alternative NPCs are just quest givers(which is very standard for your AAA trashy RPG/open world Botchventure).
EDIT: This game's plot is 'guided' or linear, so there are only added quests alongside the main story, therefore not allowing you to travel alternative story lines(which to be fair, is not surprising)
Level design is nice and there is decent incentive to investigate, scout around and hack into terminals, or look for ventilation systems.  Some things are for the hell of it like silly humour that is in the email systems and the odd pick up, although, the energy system gives you a good incentive to keep in the dark and look for *prey*.
EDIT: In saying that  the game design is good, and most of it is!  But it feels as if the devs were 'slowing down' a bit at the end of the game and felt the need to wrap it up quickly.
Combat is a bit clunky at first, though you get used to it, though it is not as elegant as something like Jedi Knight, for example, I still have great difficulty blocking with respect to a specific attack on this, but its not too bad....  There is plenty of room for takedowns, so throughout the game you are given the opportunity to avoid confrontation, by hitting the enemy when they dont see you, or of course (sometimes) by avoiding confrontaitons altogether..
Talking about takedowns: There is stealth in this game, and it appears like (at least with the class I am using) that you can get through most of the game without being seen, which almost makes it feel like 'Dishonoured', or perhaps 'Thief' with added stuff, which I would count as a definate compliment,  On the other hand I dont think you *have* to go in with stealth, if you have the right class; as there are sweet talking ' half-human' classes and there is definetly room to blow stuff up!
Music is nice, very varied depending where you are and what you're doing.  There are smoother bits, to the gothy bits, to the bluesy bits, to the almost tension/horror bits when you are in a mission area.
It is easy to consider that this is very similar to Deus Ex, with most of the game design choices, though what with the energy system, some skills, and the choice of classes, this game seems to have a bit more to it.
One word of warning though, you may find bugs at first, I downloaded  the VTB Ultimate patch from the RPGscrolls, and I got no issues  since.  They even introduced modern system compatibility, such as high res blah, excellent mod/patch.
Grab the unofficial patch to clear up the bugs and this is a fantastically good RPG. Atmosphere, voice acting, story and characters are all top notch.

This Review is on the Game known a King Auther’s Gold (also known as KAG).
KAG is a 2D, “tidal styled” multiplayer war game with elements of sandbox added to it, the common mode played in it is Capture the Flag, but there are other modes such as Zombie Survival, and Deathmatch variations, Capture the Flag mode is the most commonly played mode pitting two teams fighting on different sides of the map, with each team given a number of team lives and one base with a flag on a pole. The enemy has to fight to the other’s base and steal their flag or kill the entire enemy to deplete the life counter of their team and finish the rest off. Deathmatch is the classic one life per player, duke it out to the death, PvP. And Zombie Survival mode has a small team of players surviving against zombie AI enemies which get steadily harder each night in the game that passes. The game is Free to Play, but most features are premium based, meaning that, for the most fun, buy it.
There are three different classes in this game, these are, knight, archer and builder. The knight; uses his shield to defend himself, and a sword to slash at others, this class also has thrown bombs. The archer is a ranged class; they can climb trees and fire from a fair distance. The last class, the builder, is where the sandbox elements come to play. To defend their base builders will build traps and defensive structures and also create siege weapons to use against the enemy structures, they also use their hammers and break enemy structures but are super weak offensively. I believe the addition of the builder was due to the popularity of games such as Minecraft and Terraria, and this has not hindered the game in any way, but has made it much more fun and open to other players who enjoy this type of genre. KAG has some decent balancing to the game design. It was mainly developed by a small company called Transhuman Design. The game has some “Mods” released but no full support as of yet. The game has been developed since 2011.
The main graphical design behind the game was based on the small title on the SNES,”King Arthur's World”. This is the reason the game is set in a pixelated 2D setting. I also believe this keeps the game simple in terms of Graphical User Interface. As such the game does age quite well, I’m sure I will be playing it for years still to come, so long as there are online players.
I played this game during the late alpha phase, it was fun and decent, I often enjoyed hours on end slaying the enemy or even participating in “Clan Wars” on the PvP elements in the game. I was in the Best Australian clan, “[AOE]” until a few patches ruined balance and the clan broke apart. And from experience, I can say this game is worth it.
Fun Relaxing gameplay. Easy to pick up and play but at higher difficulties provides good challenge for adept gamers.

The premise behind King Arthur's Gold is a good one. A mixture of sandbox, player versus player action, set in a 16-bit medieval pixel world. The result could have been better, but it could also have turned out to be much worse.
First off, even though this game has been out for at least two years at the time of this writing, the developers have always been extremely active in patching and updating their creation. With that said, their software is prone to crashing often at the end of matches for whatever reason. Besides that, the game performs well enough. The pixel art is cute and fun to look at, while the sound design also provides a nice experience. All the maps available are by design, and the only variety will come from the role of builders, as they will carve through and add to the already existing landscapes. The team deathmatch mode is the least exciting game type I tried, and I've never gone into a sandbox only server. The most fun I had was playing Capture the Flag mode.
The main problem with King Arthur's Gold comes from its small player-base. Finding a server to play on has not been a problem in my region, but there are usually no more than four. Most of the player-base seems to be from Europe. Playing matches in a more distant server is doable, but of course, there will be much lag, which will hinder your gameplay experience significantly. The other problem that comes with the small player-base is that most people playing are King Arthur's Gold veterans, likely with 50 or 100 hours or more of experience with the game. This means that for newcomers, being killed quickly and easily will occur quite often. Someone just starting out is no match for the majority of the opposing team. This uneven playing field does not make for a very enjoyable experience. With that said, there are some helpful and friendly players to be found. I asked some questions a few times and at least one person answered me without making a rude or useless remark. In addition, I've noticed that many of the players know each other, and are familiar with one another, as they often post greetings as soon as joining the server. This made for a warm and welcoming environment to be a part of. Being that King Arthur's Gold is a multi-player online game, you should also expect some annoyances to come from immature and rude players in the chat, but it really does not happen that often, from what I've experienced in about twelve and a half hours of playing. If there were more players, and If there was a more even environment in relation to player skill, King Arthur's Gold would be a much more enjoyable experience. It's a shame that a game with so much potential has such a small, but dedicated player-base. It's probably too late for a revival.
King Arthur's Gold is okay.

Time is limited however, the screen will continuously scroll to the right and if you are caught in this "Darkness" you will die. This is not an open world RPG where you can take things slowly and explore, your destination is eastward and the game will happily remind you of that.
At the end of the Dimension (win or lose) you are graded and given Hero Points. Points can be spent to unlock additional classes or skills, called Perks, but also to expand your Vault. Your Vault allows you to transfer over items you have collected to a bank so that any new characters you make will have access to these items before beginning their level.
The game also comes with achievements and cards. For the asking price I couldn't recommend it enough!

My feelings about this visual novel are a bit mixed, mostly because I didn't pay too much attention to the description. Let that be a lesson, folks: reading is fundamental! This a kinetic novel, so there are no choices that cause the story to branch out into multiple different endings. Second, this is more of a collection of children's horror stories, along the lines of Are You Afraid Of The Dark? Once I understood what it was I was actually reading, I can say that I was able to enjoy the KN for what it was: a cute and comedic story of a bunch of kids telling scary tales. The artwork was lovely, with the sprites conveying emotions using the full range of body language that also helped convey the personalities of each character. I thought that the sounds and music fit the mood of each scene well, and while the translation definitely needs polish, I've seen worse. This being said, I'm thinking that the KN would definitely benefit from some polish, in order to help make the stories told a bit more coherent. But in all, I thought that this was a very cute children's horror tale, and if you are in the mood for cute children's horror stories, there's no reason not to try this out. It's free, after all!

I had already logged in about 70 hours before the Steam release, so let me say that, for a price this small, this is definitely a game worth checking out.
The game's big gimmick is that the world's slowly getting gobbled up from the left side, which means you gotta keep on going to the right, which adds an element of urgency since you gotta plan your moves ahead of time or you're getting screwed over. And with eight different classes to choose from, each actually requiring you to play differently (like, you wouldn't head in solo with a bard or keep your backside exposed with a hero) and a whole bunch of perks to apply and combine in whoknowshowmany ways, in addition with too many possible worlds to traverse and daily campaigns AND a bit of writing here and there that, while often rather generic, still has a couple bits that might make you go "oh, I didn't expect that" the first time you encounter them, you'll more likely than not spend a lot of time on this, provided you're into games experimenting with the roguelike concept.
Presentation wise, it's a bit eh, though that's more of a personal issue. The music got annoying very quickly, so I turned it off. And the character portraits look rather amateurish and sketchy, but you don't see them too much, so they're easy to skim over.
Still, if you got the cash to spare, give it a shot.

The early to mid game can seem a bit bland but it's all worth it when the industrial revolution comes.

A fun, simple, co-op twin stick shooter with a nice amount of mechanical "crunch" that doesn't require some meta-knowledge and rewards experience via faster muscle memory of strategems. The "liberate planets = get strategems/rewards" mechanic encourages play and allows you to decide what strategem to pursue next. Using them is fun, upgrading them is rewarding, and it is simple to activate. Just make sure the landing zone is clear...
As for plot, it's fairly bare-bones. You are a Helldiver, an ODST/Space Marine by another name, sent to pre-emptively liberate the galaxy from the terrorists at Cyberstan, the robots of the Illuminate, or the bugs of... the Bugs. Each enemy has their own ideosyncracies for fighting (cyberstani terrorists remind me a lot of the Orkz from 40k, the Illuminate are effectively "control" fighters who either summon big metal monsters or use forcefields to control the board, bugs are extra tough but have weaker points). Your goal is to defend Super Earth and our VERY WAY OF LIFE... before the enemies decide to one day attack Super Earth itself. By spreading managed democracy, you can ensure that Super Earth will be safe today, be safe tomorrow, and be safe forever.
The hyper-militarized fascist backdrop serves perfectly for the violent extravaganza of drop-pod deaths, friendly-fire turrets, and brutal sniping enemies. It may sound like a lot at first, but the mechanics are simple and the difficulty curve is nicely paced out from "walk in the park" to "oh God why are there so many bugs and why can't I get 10 feet without dying". It's truly optimized for a party of 4, and the drop-in system works wonderfully; I rarely have to wait long to have someone join my game, or I can hop into someone elses. The fact that it takes 2-3 missions to capture a planet goes a long way to ensure players stick together between missions, which helps keep party size up while also helping to ensure a degree of coordination and teamwork. When teamwork fails, the game lets you get back into the fight quickly provided your team mates actually call for reinforcements. I rarely wait more than 10-15 seconds to get back into the frenzy.
I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes cooperative shooters, "last stands" of any kind, and people who like to call in CAS every 10 seconds like an A-10 pilot owes you his daughter's life. If you want a fun "pickup and play" game for the fall season, this is a very casual game that can't really be matched for $10.

I can't really say much about the campaign as I have only played one mission of each. I'm not gonna lie; these missions are pretty hard. You can't go Call of Duty-style run-and-gun across the battlefield! YOUR MEN WILL BE SHOT TO DEATH!! It requires strategy. The same goes for multiplayer.
This game is unique as you have plenty of aspects under your command such as what the soldiers and vehicles carry. Yes, it can get a bit annoying when you have to micromanage everything. I just deal with it. Another neat thing is 'Direct Control' where you can take control of a soldier's or vehicle's main weapon. But this game is not without its cons. The game looks very dated. It looks ugly, but that doesn't affect the game itself.
To close, I recommend this game to anyone who's looking for a challenge. If you need a good strategy game to play on the side, here it is.

LISA is my new favorite RPG, let alone one of my favorite games on steam, and it pierces your heart with a painful story, disturbing imagery, and emotionally manipulative sacrifices.
LISA takes place in a world heavily inspired from Mad Max. The world has become an unihabitable wasteland, clans and barabarians roam the plains searching for blood - and worst of all, all female humans have gone extinct.
LISA starts off with a man named Brad Armstrong, who was traumatized by his sister Lisa's death and his abusive, drunk father, Marty Armstrong. Brad has resorted to the drug Joy to ease his emotional pain, but soon he finds something that would change the world forever; a baby. And not just a baby, but a baby girl. Brad raises the child under the name Buddy and keeps her a secret from the world. One day, after meeting Terry Hintz, Brad finds out that Buddy has run away and the whole world is after her.
LISA's gameplay isn't too unique, but it it still pretty fun to play. It's an RPG that is heavily inspired by Earthbound. Some people confuse it for a platformer, but it barely is a platformer. Some of the mechanics are quite unique to gaming, that can be a tassle to deal with. For example, one of my favorite mechanics is Joy Withdrawl in which Brad performs poorly in withdrawl, but if you don't give him Joy his withdrawl goes away and his addiction starts to diminish. On the other hand, if he gets Joy, he would perform significantly better than in withdrawl or stable, but his addiction becomes heavier and harder to handle since Joy isn't found around every corner.
LISA takes the cake for RPGs on Steam. Its emotional hardships and sacrifices make it ruin you, paired up with great humor that is often well-cued. Disturbing creatures, gory imagery, and lands crawling with perverts make this a diamond in the rough that doesn't get enough attention. Its soundtrack can be menacing, upbeat, or eerie. It can pair up perfectly at some point, but not at all points. I believe this is a
for all people who love RPGs, emotional stories, Mad Max fans, or all in between.
TL;DR: It's like Mad Max and Earthbound had a child, But the TWD games took it and raised it themselves.

Hmm...not sure what to say, the new atmosphere is great, but this installment in the series is considerably shorter than the first game, somehow with far more spelling errors littered throughout, the game threw away balance and most monsters give basically the same amount of exp and gold per battle, the first random encounters you run into give like 1800 exp, second to last area has big creatures with far more devastating attacks and hp, making for a tougher and longer battle...and ~3000 exp as a reward. Even the special leveling island returns from the first game but the fights there only give 10,000 exp per fight, there's no incentive not to powerlevel in the vicinity of the first town, as there's no risk and its much quicker.
The most annoying part is that you can't clear the last boss battle without having gotten a spell in a chest within some little island's cave, I wandered the world map for over and hour and didn't see it, why do this? Seriously.
Considerably worse than the first game, but still interesting for the story, hope future games learn from the mistakes made in this one.

It takes a while to get into, but this is one of the best games I have ever played. You have total freedom to build whatever you want, and there are multiple game modes (Although CTF is by far the best). The community is generally welcoming to new players, so don't be afraid to ask for help. You start with a couple of minutes to build up your castle, and then the game starts and everyone rushes to the center. You could build a tunnel to the other side, or a bridge, or try to rush them head on! Every match is different, and each server has different rules and maps. I had this game before it was on steam, and my hours are in the hundreds. The meta game constantly changes, as does the game. Sadly, the player base is only about 100 now, but there is never a problem finding a match, there are at least two full games running all the time. If you join, you can fix that problem! There is even a roleplay server! If you are on the fence about this, buy it, you won't regret it :D And you will make this awesome community grow!

This game is a really good topdown shooter.
a few caveats though :
- shared screen, in multi you'd better all go in the same direction while fleeing or you can all die for it.
- multiplayer war state means if a race is defeated nobody can play against it. It's great for immersion, though it forces to wait for days potentially weeks if the war doesn't end quickly
-player customization/colors are too similar, it's sometimes difficult to distinguish each comrade from others.
- also I wish there was a bit more modes of play, for example modes where friendly fire matters more, as it is you kill your comrade but incur no penalty whatsoever. Mistakes do happen but as it is people can just troll whenever.
-rushing is also a bit too advantageous.
-and finally DLC to ease your game, that's really too bad in a multiplayer game (even coop, it's still an unfair advantage)

Where do I even begin with this game. First off ive been playing this game for about 7 years now and every playthrough ive had of it was exellent. There is alot of variety when it comes to builds. There is the obvious Light/Dark or Grey option for the game but there is also Force user builds, Ranged builds, Pure combat focused guardian, etc. I find the combat to be enjoyable (In my opinion) since its tactical and you can really plan attacks and things of that sort. Take DA:0 for example. Its pretty much the same system. You can start with 3 beginning classes: Guardian (Combat focused), Sentinel (Better skill progression), and Consular (Force powers). You then later in the game get different set of prestige classes depending on your allignment. Now, lets get to the writing of the game. This game has one of the best stories I have ever seen. You'll see once you play it for yourself. The reason I prefer this game slightly over the first is just because I prefer the darker, philosophical, grey aspects of the atmosphere and story a bit better (Kotor 1 is also one of my favorite games). Anyways, this game presents the idea that Dark is not necessarily evil and Light isnt nessesary good and you really get to see the Flaws of both sides. For example, you play as the Jedi Exile, who was exiled from the Jedi order for rusing to war to protect innocents. The Jedi were lazy and waited to "evaluate the threat". The dialouge and voice acting in this game is absolutely fantastic (Especially Kreia). For this game, you dont even need to be a fan of Star Wars. A non Star Wars fan would look at this game and just play an RPG. However a Star Wars fan would look at this and play an amazing Star Wars RPG. The reason for this is because the game is set in an era wayyy before the Movies. One flaw however, would be the cut content presented this game. Obsidian (The developers) were rushed to release this game by lucasarts, resulting in them needing to cut out content for the game. Luckily, a group of community modders managed to get into the games files and restore alot of the content that was cut. You can find the mod on the steam workshop. Anyways, hurry up and buy the game! You wont be dissapointed.

And you may be thinking... ok yeah so what?. Well, the point is that this game offers all of that OR you can zoom out until infantry are the size of ants and control a column of tanks and armored vehicles in real time... then slow down time and zoom in to the drivers seat of one of your jeeps and make the driver get out and man a machine gun nest whose previous occupant was killed AND if you really think it through you can make that driver pull his jeep up to provide soft cover from one side to protect him from being flanked.
Once defending against a wave of german armor I barely survived until reinforcements came, when they did I was allowed to call in heavy tanks and I did... when I took them to chase the germans accross a frozen river one of my largest tanks cracked the ice and fell in - then I realized I could break the ice to prevent their lighter armor from crossing.
I was instructed to take a fortified position with a wave of infantry.
I broke from the main group to comandeer a truck so I could hopefully pick up enough speed to make it over the trenches and then ram into the machine gunners sandbags with hopefully enough force to dislodge or kill him (this in itself says a lot as this isn't a canned animation or a suggested tactic, or a button - it's just something you figure out because the game apparently has a fairly robust implementation of object physics; destroyed vehicles sometimes explode and sometimes dont depending on what happened to them but if they do explode the pieces land wherever the force of the explosion takes them and then can be used as cover).

Men of War is certainly unique. In no other true RTS have I been able to (and indeed required to) manage the inventory of individual soldiers. Each soldier must carry a specific weapon which they may or may not be proficient at using, ammo, a helmet, bandages, and even knives or entrenchment tools. Each vehicle has fuel and ammo which can be replenished, and each seat must be manned by an individual soldier. Combine this with a fairly realistic ballistics and penetration model (infantry are REALLY vulnerable, and certain tanks simply cannot be penetrated by small rounds) and you have some very micro-heavy gameplay with a good degree of realism.
The problem is that the AI is absolutely terrible in single player, and the game pits you against laughably sized hordes of them to compensate for it. While as a history nut I loved the amount of detail and flavor in the vehicles and weapons that were available, the AI and level design undoes almost all of this. The result is a massive amount of save whoring and gamey behavior to exploit the AI. In multiplayer, the variety of units and weaponry is much appreciated, but the gameplay itself is directionless. You can capture points, but nothing you do in game can change the steady stream of points you receive which allow you to unlock more units. The variety of units and size of maps means that there is a hugely wasted opportunity here, because as long as you have the points, you can buy the most advanced tank or infantry unit from the start. There's no hierarchy or sense of progression, and points are seemingly randomly scattered throughout the maps.
Ultimately, Men of War has an appealing level of micro, but fails in terms of direction.
After more than five years, I ended up playing Soldiers: Heroes of World War II, and replaying Men of War pretty extensively. Below are my thoughts.
- While pretty much all of what I said regarding Men of War's excessive micromanagement is still true, I've come to see the insane level of detail as more of a positive. Especially after playing Soldiers first, I've come to appreciate the potential for creating your own narrative within Men of War's detailed sandboxes. I think you have to be the right kind of crazy to like this kind of thing, but once you do, its very addictive.
- Sandbox gameplay increases replay value and encourages creativity.
- Environmental destruction is impressive. I'd say it's actually more detail than Company of Heroes' system, even if it looks less cinematic at times. For example, walls can be destroyed in smaller chunks, and when buildings collapse they remain a part of the environment, providing cover instead of just becoming a giant obstacle.
- The variety of historical vehicles is insane. As a history nerd, this pleases me enormously.
- Campaigns are focused on lesser-known battles in WWII.
- Using Direct Control is still a requirement to beat most single player missions, when it should be just a neat feature. This is because of the incompetence of the AI - you simply can't leave your units unattended for very long, or expect them to make that crucial shot. You have to do it yourself.
- The micro intensive nature of the game means that its easy to feel overwhelmed by the larger defense missions. This series feels most in touch with its roots when you are in control of just a squad or two.
- Extensive save-whoring is still required to beat most missions.
- The voice acting is horrible, and other RTS titles (Company of Heroes, Starcraft 2) are much better at using voice acting and cinematics to further the narrative.
- Multiplayer modes pale in comparison to contemporaries such as Company of Heroes.
Overall, I'd say the Men of War series is unlike any RTS I've played, and as I said, you have to be a certain kind of crazy to enjoy it. But it can be a lot of fun.

One of my all time favorite strategy games.
First, THE BAD:
The Voice Acting - Id rather be listening to Nickelback.
Learning curve - Second mission puts you in control of over 50 men. It's not noob friendly. This is a drawback for some but it's rewarding succeed in this game.
Minor Gliches - Nothing game breaking but it's no StarCraft 2.
Here's The Good:
Direct control - allows you to take control of a specific unit (anything from a tank to a sniper).
Realistic Tank Combat system - Seriously... it's amazing. The shot penetration depends on the angle, armor thickness, round size, and distance. This makes for some awesome in game moments where you can take out multiple Panzer III with a single KV-1.
Old School Inventory system - This is a downside for some but I love having to drop ammo into each soldier, loading up tanks by dragging Shells from one unit to the other. It would be nice it there was a more steamlined way of doing this but being able to salvage higher teir weapons with extra riflemen can make all the difference in a mission.
Dynamic Destruction - Huge explosions as well as craters and fully distructable buildings. What more do you need?
Mission Veriaty - From huge frontline assults to night raids, this game has something for all.

Alright, for real though, this is a game that has aged very well. It was a golden RPG for 2004, and today is still Golden. With Troika dead, and before Paradox bought out the rights to White Wolf and WOD, CCP didn't do crap with this series including updates, letting other people remaster it, etc. Luckily this game still has a somewhat active, but small, community, and came out with amazing patches even after a decade of death and silence. There was a project to remake/remaster the game called Project Vaulderie, but unfortunately it got shut down by CCP even though CCP had been doing nothing besides working on Eve Online.
The best:
-The music is A1. Introduced me to some good gothic metal bands, and the soundtracks for a lot of the hubs are very pleasing.
-The dialogue is hilarious most of the time, and it changes depending on what clan you are.
-While there was some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ voice acting, there was also a lot of good voice acting from well known voice actors.
-Clans: There are several you get to choose from, each one has its own special abilities, appearance, and ways you run through the game.
-There is no leveling up, you gain experience points and then assign those earned experience points to certain skills you want to increase, which is a simple and nice.
-Kind of has it's own karma system to put it basically, you kill innocents, you lose humanity, you lose all your humanity, you go into a frenzy which isn't always the prettiest. So most of the time you have to be conscious of your actions.
-The atmosphere was greatly crafted; to be a dark gothic setting. Everything is eerie, not especially scary, but eerie and dark really no matter where you are.
-You get to dance like a maniac.
-You get paid good for a lot of quests.
-A ♥♥♥♥♥ON of lore.
The Bad: A lot of this can be excused because of the time it was released, but still mentioning,
-The map is absolutely tiny. There are only 4 hubs you can go to, which all are pretty damn small and will take you like 10 minutes to run through all the buildings.
-The bugs. Of course, this has to do with the state it was released in, problems with the devs and Valve, etc. But if you don't install the patch that was wonderfully made by fans, then you're going to have a hard time playing because this game is bug heaven.
-A lot of the NPCs are the same, there's probably like 5-7 differen't types of NPCS in one city, with 3-4 repeats.
-The AI is awful. You can have a decent sneak level and be crouching in front of a group of cops that are on a hunt for you and they wouldn't see you.
-The game is fairly short. I think the first time I played this I completed the main and side quests within at least 14 hours.
-You don't really get a choice in who you side with. Throughout the game, you are working for LaCroix no matter if you don't like him, but at the end you do indeed get a decision.
-You can't really replay this game much differently than a last playthrough mainly because in terms of storyline, there isn't too much you can choose differently, besides minor decisions.
-It really doesn't show too much or hint at the enormous amount of lore the WOD and VtM series has. The first time I played this I had no idea that there was a crap ton of books belonging to this series. But luckily, once I found out, I bought all of them.
-Because the environment is small and all the work went into the quests, you really can't do much in terms of just exploring. There's not much to interact with.
-LOOT. There is rarely any loot throughout the entire game. Which any loot you find is sold for dirt cheap and you get barely any $$$.
Overall, a lot of the flaws of this game I can look past because of the age. Lets all hope Paradox does a good job dealing with this series, because it can either go absolutely horribly or incredibly wonderful. And lets hope they don't make a MMO.

From what I'd heard about this game I was expecting a diamond in the rough, a cult classic from yesteryear.....Hmnn, not quite....
People talk about this game like it's Deus Ex with vampires - a world where you can pick and match gameplay styles, be stealthy or be brutal, or influence things through conversation. And maybe it is those things, but if you look at my playtime it will be obvious I don't care to find out!
First of all: it looks incredibly ropey. Graphics aren't everything, but beyond the ugly looks it's also hard to take the stealth seriously when your character's stealthy walk animation seems like they're desperately holding in a poo....
Second problem: the combat is pretty woeful, and consists of you either (a) directly fighting the enemy, which basically involves flailing about until the enemy drops dead, or (b) doing sneak attacks where the enemy gives you all the time in the world as they gaze at their shoes, or at an interesting speck of dirt on the floor, or are mentally distracted as they  wonder if they left home without turning the oven off. For whatever reason they spend a huge amount of time not paying any attention to their surroundings - most stealth games choreograph their AI behaviour in this manner upto a point, but it's pretty simply implemented here.
Though this may improve over time it still leaves a bad impression. Having said that...at least that helps with stealth, except it doesn't because the stealth is crap.
I only managed to get through that part of the  tutorial (!!) thanks to the AI doing something stupid. It took about twenty attempts just to sneak past some vampire who absolutely refused to look at anywhere but the spot I had to go past (which was the only possible route!)....until for some inexpicable reason he didn't notice me, despite doing exactly the same thing on the previous nineteen attempts....
If stealth is a gameplay choice, then I choose not to, thanks! Because it totally sucks here! And that was just the tutorial...
Third problem: To hear about this game it sounds brilliantly told, with amazing dialogue and an intriguing take on vampires. I certainly didn't experience anything like that - it was passable stuff, but nothing particularly special or gripping. To be fair though, the voice acting is pretty decent.
Overall I got the impression that to love it in this day and age you have to have nostalgia from playing it before - as someone who only just played it I found it to be somewhat overrated. Yes it's old and is therefore understandably not as slick as modern games, but that's not a problem so much as the fact it just doesn't seem very good.
I played System Shock 2 fairly recently and that's old, and not much of a looker, yet it still deserves it's status as a classic. I know Bloodlines was an ambitious title released by a developer that maybe lacked the talent and / or budget to do it justice, but knowing that doesn't change the fact I don't want to play it anymore after an hour and a half.....

I really enjoyed this game, it is a nice follow-up to Labyronia and the melancholic atmosphere is an interesting twist on the original word.
Pros: a nice traditional JRPG experience for fans of the genre, little to no grinding, straightforward progression, continuity of the main storyline, and hardly any in-dungeon timing fiascos (remember the original game's water temple?).
Cons: weaker dialogue than the original, occasional grammatical mistakes, a little linear, and not quite as challenging as the original game.
Overall, I'm really pleased with this game and I think fans of this genre would like it as well. I hope Labyrinthine keeps developing more games, I look forward to playing the Legend of Mysteria!

Helldivers is a great game! Though its probably not for everyone.
First of the graphics which are good for what it is. In my opinion it doesnt look terrible but actually has a lot of details.
The shading and the lighting are all great and very sharp with only a few times where the shadows look like cubes on high settings. But the detail in this game is also beautiful! Depending on what kind of biome you are on you will leave footprints or if you use laserguns and overheat them small canisters eject from the gun leaving a trail of smoke. It may not sound very great but its fun to watch that happen. Even better are all the bullets that lie on the ground after a big confrontation with hostiles. Such a joy to watch what happens on the screen if something goes wrong.
The sound is great with enemies haveing unique sounds that really set them from others appart. But the soundtrack is rather boring. It follows the simple dramatic horn and violin format most of the time. The tracks sound all pretty much the same at least most of the time. Also I wish there would be some more lines for the Helldivers. At first it may be fun to hear the things characters say when they kill but at some point its quite annoying. Also having to hear a RELOAD voieline everytime you hit reload is especially annoying with shotguns or weapons that have generally small mags.
The gameplay in this game is increadibly fun and addicting! Beeing a twinstick shooter you obciously to the usual things like running arround and shooting everything but the unique thing about this game are it stratagems. They are supplies or airstrikes that can be called down to you on the surface of a planet if you enter their activation code correctly. This is done by using WASD as arrowkeys. Putting them in a specific order will give you a beacon to call down whatever you want! This is something that may be challanging at first but gets more fun to do over time and once you can enter the Reinforcement code under a second you ll feel like a pro player. What keeps me playing this game is the need to be able to play the highest difficulty mission with no problems. This game has a neat learning curve. Depending on how good you are with games you ll be able to get good at the game quickly and have a lot of fun with it.
But untill that happens you shall die from your own supplies. this game has friendly fire enabled at all times and cannot be disabled. Its a part of games which makes you have to play carefull at all time. Dont shoot your friends on ´accident´ or stand beneath the rescue shuttle when it arrives and get crushed.
The progression is something that is nice and also not nice. There are 50 levels in totall and they ll take you more time to get as you go on ... obviously. But at some point you ll be able to notice the grind in this game. Ranking up after 25 can already take quite some time especially if you are not a good player yet. Weapons and stratagems are also upgraded by so called Research Points that can be acuired by collecting a certain amount of samples or ranking up. Getting these is simple and not difficult to do but you ll notice that you will have to grind for them if you want to upgrade more and more as you go on. Both the xp rewards and the research points will make this game feel like a grind that can or cannot be enjoyable because mission always are kind of same with diffrent maps and random objectivs. The only times it get somewhat diffrent is with bossbattles and capital defence missions.
Unfortunately this game has dozens of DLC of which some are undeniably good for the game. Which is why the Digital Deluxe Edition should be bought instead of the standart version of the game.
Generally is this game worth it? Yes I would say so but beware of the grind. Its a game where you have no story whatsoever and you ll be doing things over and over again.
I also do not recommend to buy the standart edition of this game. !! Buy the Helldivers Digital Deluxe Edition!! It will give you all the DLC that have been released so far. It will give you a much larger arsenal of weapons airstrikes etc. Should the Deluxe Edition be on sale its most definately a good idea to buy that instead of the standart edition

One of the only F2P games I've personally played that is genuinely F2P. I'm one of the few Westerners in the world that loves the game Uncharted Waters Online and the ridiculous grind associated with it. Unfortunately, I can't get it to run anymore, so this game scratches that itch.
The Pirate: Caribbean Hunt is really "point and click, collect resources and win" disguised as an open world game. Calling it a sandbox is a bigtime stretch but being able to sail the open world to explore and discover a few things is a nice touch. Combat is a little too easy and borderline exploitable and once you get your bases established (which happens very quickly) the need to trade goes right out the window as you'll have more gold than you know what to do with. Unfortunately, there really is nothing to do with it other than fill your ports with top of the line ships that you don't need (you can solo the entire campaign with a corvette, at least I did). I just wish there was more content for it. Maybe some unique items or discoveries or crafting would make it more interesting. I can't believe I'm saying this but I seriously feel the developers are missing out on a lot of in-game purchases by making in-game currencies so easily attainable, which in the end I guess gives me all the more reason to recommended it.
Sail around, trade a bit, upgrade your ships, discover some hidden ports, kill some pirates and most importantly..  Collect the booty.
Do it. It's free.

I really love the gameplay of this game, and had a blast with friends during the free weekend.
However, the game's serious flaw is the lack of depth. This feels like a demo of a fantastic game. Everything feels like it is 20% of what it should be; you can see everything there is to see in a few hours. Replayability is all in the arcade-style skill improvement, not necessarily progression in the game. This is a great game to couch-cooperate when someone's visiting.
For the experience offered, the game is way too expensive. I would purchase this game for $5, but given the lack of content I would not feel justified spending any more than that. Another thing is much of the content that is there is DLC locked, which isn't too big a deal if there's a good discount, but I still think a fair price for the whole thing plus DLC is $5.
The only other big flaw is the community-driven war campaigns. It could be a cool idea to have the community affect enemy factions in a war, but it's executed horribly in my opinion. It amounted to locking me to one or two planets for most of the free weekend (the homeworld assaults on 2/3 factions - the third faction was dead). The lack of mission selection can be a little frustrating. Didn't get to try any boss battles. Ah, and a minor thing that bugged me was the amount of enemies who are invulnerable to all but highest tier missiles or rocket launchers et al. Also, the player character callouts... Be prepared to hear the same few lines dozens and dozens of times... you can probably hear them all in a single mission. I probably have enough "liber-tea" to start Boston Tea Party Part Two.
Overall, I loved playing the game, but can't justify purchasing it, because it is way too shallow (I'm very sad to say). I really wanted more from this game because I enjoyed it a lot, but after the first couple of hours I said, "Wait, that's it?"

This isn't a bad game by any means, but it's not very good either, especially as compared to Men of War 2: Assault Squad 2.  It's not that any one element of the game in particular is lacking, it's that there are a hundred little things that MoW: AS 2 does much better.
- The latter runs much better/more smoothly, even on my low-level laptop, whereas CoH 2 runs fine, but it doesn't seem "smooth" or crisp somehow.  That might also have to do with the difference in graphical styles between the two games, too.  MoW AS 2 has a tighter, somehow sharper graphical style, whereas CoH 2 has sort of a bumpy texture set.
- Unit designs look generic in CoH 2.
- Units firing at each other oftentimes run right up to each other; cover or lack thereof and distance to enemy don't seem to be overly important factors for how quickly units get killed.  Doing the same will get your units completely mowed down in MoW AS 2.  Sandbags and defensive emplacements do seem more extensive and easier to place in CoH 2.  Fire from a flamethrower unit doesn't lay waste to enemies at close range, at least not very realistically.  In MoW AS 2, you see animations of soldiers aflame and running around for a bit until they finally collapse as charred corpses.
- The unit cap in CoH 2 is dumb and not really necessary; while there might be a limit in MoW AS 2, I've never reached it, and there isn't a formal unit cap visible.
- The Havok engine has somehow been downplayed, so that not only MoW AS 2, but also the original CoH and its first expansion, Opposing Fronts, are games that feature more interactive, deformable terrain, i.e., they're better games in that respect.
- Veterancy exists in both CoH 2 and MoW AS 2, but it functions a little more straightforwardly in the latter, and units that aren't yet veteran units aren't completely slow and bumbling in MoW AS 2 (which they are in CoH 2).
- There is more of a variety of maps and skirmish customizability in CoH 2, and the levelling system and goodies/skills you unlock seem a little more extensive in CoH 2, as well.
- Ammunition counters, inventories, personal soldier stats and names, the ability to swap out weapons and scavenge ammunition and grenades, items, etc. from fallen enemy soldiers is completely absent in CoH 2.  MoW AS 2 plays like a light RPG in that sense, whereas CoH 2 has none of those features.
- There is a carry-over in experience points in both games, but I did prefer how CoH 2 handles that: you accumulate so many points for a match, plus potential bonus points, and that goes towards level increases and all kinds of skins, goodies, and other unlocks.  It's right on the line between cluttered and cool, but I still think that's a point in CoH 2's favor.  By way of contrast, there is a levelling-up that occurs after battles in MoW AS 2, but it doesn't do anything.  It also gives you fewer statistics in the after-battle summary than CoH 2 does, which I think is another point in CoH 2's favor.
- Soldiers seem to move sluggishly in CoH 2...this could actually be an element of realism (since soldiers are freezing to death in the Russian winter!), but I sensed it was more of an unconscious design choice.  In MoW AS 2, each soldier has a stamina bar that recharges pretty quickly, but which is depleted by sprinting vs. the normal quick jog that units default to.  Certain units even have more stamina than others (e.g., elite infantry units as opposed to tank crews).  Health is managed by unit medics and how many med kits the squad has stockpiled [in MoW AS 2].
- Ballistics is more nebulous and sloppier in CoH 2, and doesn't seem to matter as much to actual damage values compared with MoW AS 2.  As others have already noted, components in tanks and light vehicles can be knocked out in MoW AS 2, and it won't necessarily stop the unit from functioning, although it will decrease its utility and efficiency; that's not the case in CoH 2.
- Sound effects and design is one area in which I didn't notice a significant difference in quality, although I did notice the basic design differences - machine gun chatter for a Russian tank-mounted Degyetarev sounds different in CoH 2, though not necessarily worse.
- Somewhat tied in with the ballistics issue, shots from tanks and AT guns seem more "solid" somehow in MoW: AS 2: you often will see shells bounce off of tanks' hulls if they were poorly aimed or didn't penetrate, and every shot carries this sense of weight with it, lent to it by elements like crisp sound design, tight recoil animations, spectacular pyrotechnics if the shot really connects and the enemy vehicle cooks off.
- There were a few elements that seemed potentially interesting in CoH 2, but which I didn't really play around with, like damage to units from the cold (frostbite).  Also, the long-standing doctrine system is still present in CoH 2, but I also didn't play around with it much or care to, honestly.
Overally, MoW AS 2 is just a better game in most respects.  It runs more efficiently, even on low-end systems, it has nice graphics for all of that, and it has a much more in-depth and tighter design.  It's not the CoH 2 is bad, but that MoW AS 2 is more realistic and much better.  Having said all of that, there are a few things (which I've mentioned) that I'd like to have seen borrowed from CoH 2, since they would make MoW AS 2 an even better game.

A neat little game made for folks who enjoy micromanagement, and like bit more realistic stuffs. You can group your soldiers into groups, but can direct them independently of course. Ah, and all of them have their own inventories with ammo, weapons, grenades, and so forth. So, your average Joe can hold an SMG, an LMG, a rifle, and buttloads of grenades. Okay, it might not be entirely historically accurate, but gives the game some enjoyable moments as you can pick soldiers that will be assigned to special tasks as you take direct control of them - yep, this game has direct control. Press End, and your dreams can come true. It doesn't really work when you have multiple platoons to take care of, but on missions where you have just a small group of soldiers at your disposal, it's awesome. Also, direct controlled tanks are awesome - take aim, and disable enemy tanks' turrets. Enemy soldiers will leave the vehicle, and your MGs can easily take care of them. And then...Grand Theft Wehrmacht happens. Hop in with a single soldier, drive the tank back behind your lines, repair it, put some additional bods into it, and bam, you have a fully functional tank to crush your enemies and see them driven before you. Also, it saves reinforcements - if you are lucky and have some skills, you can finish maps without losing your own tanks and using only looted enemy vehicles.
And, it's challenging. Even on Normal you'll have some hard times, if you are not too much into micromanagement, and you aren't a really freakin hardcore strategist. But if you learn the basics, you'll have really good times with this game, and feel growing desire to get each and every one of them. Sadly it lacks proper skirmish where you get a map and battle the AI, but there are enough missions to counter this. Sadly this game was supported by GameSpy, and I'm not sure if you can get it working with Hamachi, but it's worth a try if you and your friends are looking for some WW2 carnage. Especially recommended for wargamers.

Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is considered one of the classic PC RPGs. I've seen nothing but positive things about it, but to be honest, the cover art and the concept kind of warded me off of it. After all, vampires suck now.
Now, after 30 hours and having beaten the game, I can safely say it's one of the best games I've ever played.
It has a unique atmosphere, gothic without feeling forced, gritty and stylish. It takes what the modern take on the modern vampire is and makes it well... good. Great. Apparently, this is the norm for VTM (which I haven't played at Tabletop before). I would say its the best depiction of a modern vampire out there.
It's not all rosy, of course. This game doesn't pull any punches if you're not being careful and keeping aware. I couldn't even get the game to run on Steam. However, VTM-B has a very active, very devoted fanbase that creates custom content and mods so I was able to get a 'true to game' patch that simply made the game run in no time at all.
I only beat the game a few hours ago, but I am already thinking of second play throughs, with new mods and new choices. This game gives the player a ton of opportunities to alter the story, too. I felt like, at most every juncture, that my decisions mattered. That I wasn't just plodding through the developer's story but that I was writing a story of my own.
Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines manages to hold together a beautifully crafted environment, with some satisfying combat and evocative NPC interaction and story telling. It borders on perfection and a standard that other RPGs should be held to.
Pros:
+Amazing Atmosphere
+Cool and gothic without feeling forced
+Likeable/multidimensional NPCs
+Lots of choices and approaches to both build and story progression
+Satisfying, high-impact combat (at least in melee)
+Active fanbase producing extra content
+Very addictive once things get going
Cons:
-The first half hour or so of the game are slow and fail to grab attention
-The unmodded/unpatched game was not playable for me (but this is not such a big issue)
-Character building and numbers can be unintuitive
Overall, I would say it's completely worth the purchase, even at non-sale price.
Great story, brilliant atmosphere, and solid gameplay. A must for anyone with an interest in VTM.

A Story About My Uncle is a great game and is basically Spider Man without the dead uncle and crime-fighting.
Mechanics are great, Voice acting could use some work, and the story is short/sweet.
Now, there are some downsides.
-The voice acting is good, but with the thick accents, it kind of messes up the flow of things.
-Only one section, which is in part of the Ice Cave is actually frustrating, but it stilltakes entirely too much to cross the gap.
-There are a few minor bugs, but nothing too bad, so only .5 of a con.
-The ending was too short. You only see the person who is the focus of the game for about a minute before never seeing him again. I know they say "It's not about the desination, it's about the journey." But this was f---ing insane.
-He's your uncle and refers to you as his nephew the entire time you see him, but as you launch away from the crystal pad, he says "Good luck, son!" or something along those lines. Just a minor continuity error. Could have said "My boy" or "Nephew", or anything like that, but there was a bit more emphasis on "Son", so I was confused by it.
Overall, it's a great game with only minor problems, and I would love to see more of this. Not like people jumping on a bandwagon, but just Coffee Stain doing a longer, better-voiced game like ASAMU. I'd recommend it.
