- The AI is as dumb as bricks, made up of smaller dumb bricks. Ships will happily sail into one another, get stuck in the wind, get stuck on the shore, and just stop shooting (even though they have a thousand rounds of ammo)
- Interface is absolutely terrible, just see how much clicking is involved to repair your measly four ship fleet and re-crew them. Repair and ship sell buttons are side by side, have fun mixing them up when youre really tired and with no way to undo the sale

Have to sail alone as your ships will not keep up with you and get lost and return to town. Oh and you cannot fast travel back to the town you left, you have to fast travel somewhere else and then back to that town
- Game plays like a visual spreadsheet. Everything spawns in X or Y location, always. Very rigid, very little variety
- Happy spawning with you facing the wind and the enemy 1st rates right behind you, with their broadside facing you. By the time you turn around youre already half dead
- Enemy ships will raise sails and start fighting right away. Yours can sit there for 15 seconds not moving at all. Spamming attack/flee commands sometimes gets them moving sooner, otherwise they can get half dead before they even raise their sails
Overall its promising, and could be way better with just a tiny number of changes, but otherwise its a huge let down. Yes its free, but more like a free kick in the balls.

This isn't a bad game by any means, but it's not very good either, especially as compared to Men of War 2: Assault Squad 2.  It's not that any one element of the game in particular is lacking, it's that there are a hundred little things that MoW: AS 2 does much better.
- The latter runs much better/more smoothly, even on my low-level laptop, whereas CoH 2 runs fine, but it doesn't seem "smooth" or crisp somehow.  That might also have to do with the difference in graphical styles between the two games, too.  MoW AS 2 has a tighter, somehow sharper graphical style, whereas CoH 2 has sort of a bumpy texture set.
- Unit designs look generic in CoH 2.
- Units firing at each other oftentimes run right up to each other; cover or lack thereof and distance to enemy don't seem to be overly important factors for how quickly units get killed.  Doing the same will get your units completely mowed down in MoW AS 2.  Sandbags and defensive emplacements do seem more extensive and easier to place in CoH 2.  Fire from a flamethrower unit doesn't lay waste to enemies at close range, at least not very realistically.  In MoW AS 2, you see animations of soldiers aflame and running around for a bit until they finally collapse as charred corpses.
- The unit cap in CoH 2 is dumb and not really necessary; while there might be a limit in MoW AS 2, I've never reached it, and there isn't a formal unit cap visible.
- The Havok engine has somehow been downplayed, so that not only MoW AS 2, but also the original CoH and its first expansion, Opposing Fronts, are games that feature more interactive, deformable terrain, i.e., they're better games in that respect.
- Veterancy exists in both CoH 2 and MoW AS 2, but it functions a little more straightforwardly in the latter, and units that aren't yet veteran units aren't completely slow and bumbling in MoW AS 2 (which they are in CoH 2).
- There is more of a variety of maps and skirmish customizability in CoH 2, and the levelling system and goodies/skills you unlock seem a little more extensive in CoH 2, as well.
- Ammunition counters, inventories, personal soldier stats and names, the ability to swap out weapons and scavenge ammunition and grenades, items, etc. from fallen enemy soldiers is completely absent in CoH 2.  MoW AS 2 plays like a light RPG in that sense, whereas CoH 2 has none of those features.
- There is a carry-over in experience points in both games, but I did prefer how CoH 2 handles that: you accumulate so many points for a match, plus potential bonus points, and that goes towards level increases and all kinds of skins, goodies, and other unlocks.  It's right on the line between cluttered and cool, but I still think that's a point in CoH 2's favor.  By way of contrast, there is a levelling-up that occurs after battles in MoW AS 2, but it doesn't do anything.  It also gives you fewer statistics in the after-battle summary than CoH 2 does, which I think is another point in CoH 2's favor.
- Soldiers seem to move sluggishly in CoH 2...this could actually be an element of realism (since soldiers are freezing to death in the Russian winter!), but I sensed it was more of an unconscious design choice.  In MoW AS 2, each soldier has a stamina bar that recharges pretty quickly, but which is depleted by sprinting vs. the normal quick jog that units default to.  Certain units even have more stamina than others (e.g., elite infantry units as opposed to tank crews).  Health is managed by unit medics and how many med kits the squad has stockpiled [in MoW AS 2].
- Ballistics is more nebulous and sloppier in CoH 2, and doesn't seem to matter as much to actual damage values compared with MoW AS 2.  As others have already noted, components in tanks and light vehicles can be knocked out in MoW AS 2, and it won't necessarily stop the unit from functioning, although it will decrease its utility and efficiency; that's not the case in CoH 2.
- Sound effects and design is one area in which I didn't notice a significant difference in quality, although I did notice the basic design differences - machine gun chatter for a Russian tank-mounted Degyetarev sounds different in CoH 2, though not necessarily worse.
- Somewhat tied in with the ballistics issue, shots from tanks and AT guns seem more "solid" somehow in MoW: AS 2: you often will see shells bounce off of tanks' hulls if they were poorly aimed or didn't penetrate, and every shot carries this sense of weight with it, lent to it by elements like crisp sound design, tight recoil animations, spectacular pyrotechnics if the shot really connects and the enemy vehicle cooks off.
- There were a few elements that seemed potentially interesting in CoH 2, but which I didn't really play around with, like damage to units from the cold (frostbite).  Also, the long-standing doctrine system is still present in CoH 2, but I also didn't play around with it much or care to, honestly.
Overally, MoW AS 2 is just a better game in most respects.  It runs more efficiently, even on low-end systems, it has nice graphics for all of that, and it has a much more in-depth and tighter design.  It's not the CoH 2 is bad, but that MoW AS 2 is more realistic and much better.  Having said all of that, there are a few things (which I've mentioned) that I'd like to have seen borrowed from CoH 2, since they would make MoW AS 2 an even better game.

The Men of War games are like Company of Heroes' weird cousin. They put more emphasis on depth and realism, but are also less polished. At one moment you'll be frantically defending against a massive enemy assault while armor-piercing shells ricochet from your realistically modelled tank armor, at another moment you'll assume direct control of a soldier and go on a wild machine-gun rampage.
This particular game features a long and challenging single-player campaign, which is highly enjoyable if you can endure the worst voice-acting in video game history (No seriously, it's that bad). If you want to play multiplayer or co-op, you're better off playing the sequel, Men of War: Assault Squad.
Overall, I would highly recommend this if you're into WW2 strategy games.

HELLDIVERS is an isometric shooter. Think of Alien Swarm on a more zoomed out level and you'll have HELLDIVERS. It's a game where the objective is to land on planets, complete objectives and then extract. It's a repetitive process with very little to offer. I played till level 10 to see if anything interesting opened up but it was just another grindfest.
Gameplay-wise, it's very simple. WASD keys, Spacebar and the mouse clicks. It's going to be a major grindfest trying to level up to unlock the Weapons, Perks and Strategems but if you love the repetitiveness, this is the game for you. It's not for me.
Conclusion, there isn't enough content to justify playing HELLDIVERS for long. It's a great idea to try but you'll find that Alien Swarm would give you far greater content than this game. I would rather play Alien Swarm since it's free while this is paid material and grindy.
1. Cool Name
HELLDIVERS sells well.
2. Simple to Pickup and Play
Move with WASD keys, Prone with Spacebar, shoot and aim with the left and right mouse buttons.
3. The Toys
You have a mech, vehicles and a lot of different weapons. Sadly, the weapons function the same, it's only whether they fire bullets, lasers or plasma. No fancy♥♥♥♥♥♥like hyper-laser beams that can destroy landmarks.
1. Repetitive Gameplay
There is no real change from 1 stage to another. You just land, go to point A, press arrow combos there, then move onto point B and press arrow combos there. There are a few variations like defusing mines and nuking locations but those don't really vary much.
2. Nothing to Explore
Your base is just the bridge of one starship and you can't really do anything much. All you can do is upgrade weapons, Strategems and Perks at the Armoury, Choose your missions (Single or Multi) and Launch. The Encyclopedia is pretty dull.
3. Lack of Content
4 stages per planet for a total of 12 stages. There are supposedly 3 planets that you have to fight on but the only difference is the terrain and type of units spawned. While it sounds like a lot, most of them look the same and play out similarly.
4. No Special Unit Classes
Every single one of you is just a generic soldier with perks. There is no Sniper class, Officer class, Heavy Weapons class, Scout class, Spy class, Medic class, etc.
5. No Story Campaign
You would expect that game companies would use a story campaign so that the game "sticks" with their audience but no. HELLDIVERS is another one of those generics with no characters.
1. Work with Alien Swarm
You have a similar concept to Alien Swarm but you are missing engaging stages. You have more tech toys, aliens and a perk system. HELLDIVERS might be able to continue Alien Swarm. Work together and I'm very certain you could create a wondrous series. If you build another 20 levels of Alien Swarm, I'm certain you can gather a following.

A simple but fun pirate game. Yes it looks like it was used as an app phone game, cause it was. Yes the graphics are not its best but there are far worse games out there. Interface is simple and easy to understand. The game play is great but adimitfully its hard to play hours on end.
Gameplay- Start off on a smaller raiding ship with few coins in your pocket and a ship that barely keeps you sailing. Pick up missions, level up, buy or steal your next ship. Rinse and repeat until your sailing giant 1st rate ships. Conquer towns, kill other pirates to steal their flags and fly it as your own banner. OR. Become a privateer for a nation, unlocking more missions and allied nation ships to help you in some combat situations. Such as said nations port has been attacked by an another nation, the govener will send you and your fleet as well as his own to break the siege. and pay you handsomely.
Customization- A bit bland until you purchase the DLC to unlock every color possible but it costs just as much as a simple burger at a burger joint.
DLC- mainly just a couple of ships of history such as the black pearl, HMS Victory etc. Faster, more heavily armed and such. Only a few are worth getting do to theres no other ship that looks like it in the game. One being a town upgrade letting you build more buildings to help your economy, but near end game you have a ton of towns as is constantly lining your pockets. Unless you plan on sailing 4 1st rate ships in your fleet I wouldnt bother getting this one.
Endgame/free roam- Once you beat the final missions the game will let you know, but even then you can sail the open world, capture ships and towns, do more missions for your nation, capture every ship class just cause you can, search for the smuggler ports, its endless of what you can do after you beat the game. The devs are constantly adding new ships, new features, new missions, new everything. The games free, not like your getting throwing yourself in a hole here.
Conclusion- 9/10 Only cause like i said before, its hard to play for hours on end. especially once you beat it. The new content keeps me coming back. Such as a new ship, ill spend the next 2 hours searching the open world for it. Or if i work the next day but wanna play somthing simple before i go to bed. Its fun, Its simple, its full of stuff to do, trade, raid, destroy, pilage, burn to your hearts desire.

Disclaimer: I gave up on this game after 3-ish hours of the single player experience, so it would be more fair to call this my "first impressions."
TL;DR: This feels like a poorly-done port of a mobile game that was mediocre at best to begin with. I don't know why anyone would bother with it even at a price point of free.
The overwhelming lack of polish in terms of player experience and quality of life undermined any enjoyment I could find in this game.
The user interface and menus are inexcusably bad. Many of the prompts are confusing or don't apply to the current game state. The quest system lacks any discernable depth. The economy and which affect it are rudimentarily explained at best (if it isn't completely random). Tooltips are painfully infrequent - far too much experimental button pressing occurs during the first couple of hours
The skill system is inconsistent and quite possibly bugged. At one level up I took two skills, one that was supposed to open up quests for ferrying passengers and one that was supposed to allow me to do some type of smuggling quests. I only ever received quest prompts for ferrying passengers. The disparity of the impact of different skills also feels quite poorly-tuned. One skill allows the grappling and boarding of enemy ships - seems like kind of an important gameplay mechanic that shouldn't be optional in a game about being a pirate.
While generally microtransactions are undesirable, some games at least handle them with some degree of nuance and subtlety. This is not one of those games. At most menu screens it's quite easy to inadventently wind up on the transaction page (which, like the rest of the menus, looks like garbage and doesn't even scroll with the scroll wheel). I feel like most of the game is designed to frustrate the player so that they wonder if perhaps spending money on the game would make it more tolerable. As suggested in the previous paragraph, it would be quite easy for a player to find that their skill choices were perhaps not very impactful or appropriate for their stage of the game - well, there's a button at the bottom of the skill menu which doesn't say "Store menu screen" but if someone clicks on it, thats where they wind up.
I didn't find an in-game glossary, useful help screens, or any other way anticipate what ramifications my actions would have. The story quest / tutorial (?) was not helpful at least up through the second pirate fight.
Another TL;DR: Confusing, not at all polished, frustrating.
Few of you will appreciate what follows:
Finally, my favorite bizarre gameplay mechanic. Pirate ship crew costs money, there is an initial hiring fee and they get paid wages periodically (I'm not sure how often because I don't think it was ever stated). This makes sense. Conveniently, however, if you capture a ship carrying slaves, all of the ships in your convoy as well as the captured slave ship automatically get their crews filled to capacity - because the freed slaves join your crew with no sign-on bonus and without being asked. The game actually lists this as a side-reward when browsing for possible mission (yeah - that menu is bad as well). I don't know what kind of developer thought that this was a good gameplay mechanic or a remotely sensitive idea - additionally no mention of what happened to any women, children, or excess adult male slaves ever occurs. If one doesn't have the skill for grappling and boarding, the only way to eliminate the enemy crew is with a lot of cannon balls and grape shot - I don't think that the best way to address this unsavory part of North America's history is to assume that any slaves lucky enough to survive that maelstrom would have been jumping at the opportunity to sign up to be on the side of the people who just indiscriminately slaughtered everyone else just to get a free fully-crewed boat. Then again, piracy was pretty awful too; perhaps the developers were folding in multiple layers of social and historical commentary with their profoundly insensitive approach to the slave trade. I doubt it.

This game.
This story.
This world.
It has soul.
From the crafted atmosphere, to the polished combat, between the integrated HUD, through the honed voice acting, and all the way to the fabricated story, I love this game. The developers put so much love into this game they probably called it their son/daughter during it's creation.  Without going into a synopsis of what the game is, let me just give a few details on what makes this an enthralling experience that sets the gold standard of what a videogame can truly be.
The world FEELS real. The destitute inhabitants of the Metro, their clothes, and how the grimy nature of everything will send a chill down your spine. As if the safety, and warmth of home is truly rare in this world. The desperation of your survive adds to this. Scavaging for air filters, bullets, first aid, isn't a way of life, but merely terrified survival. The great beasts of this game, refusing to bow to death until bludgeoned with repeated blasts of shotgun shells will make you feel utterly fragile. As you scrap by, kill your enemies and fell these abominations, eventually you too feel like those venerated veterans. You learn how badass, and grim they are by becoming one of them. You are not some great hunter, or glorified golden child amongst a group of 'could-be's'. You are one of them. Another hallowed soldier that was both lucky and strong enough to survive in the metro, the surface, and the atrocities that man will still create while facing their own oblivion.
Play this game exactly how you feel and understand the balance/price of your play style. Guns blazing with high adreniline is an amazing feeling. But ammunition is not plenitiful, and a bullet in the right place is your grave.  Slow, stealthy, and meticulous is exacting and safe. But beasts can smell you, air filters do not last forever, and there are worst things than the traps of men lurking in the darkness.
tl;dr
To new gamers out there, let the frustrations be part of it's appeal, and to the old gamers, let it's flaws be part of it's charm; I'm sure you will fall in love as well.

I've played a lot of this game as of late as I plunge into my Steam library and give the games I own a go, and it's stuck with me for awhile now even though I've only played through the main campaign once. This game is incredibly good, perhaps even more so than Last Light because, above all else, the Metro series has consistently nailed its atmosphere. This is especially competent in Metro 2033, and, in my opinion at least, this can be attested to the way the game juxtaposes the environments of the surface and the Metro.
The Moscow Metro is not a happy place, and many would be hard-pressed to call it hopeful, and yet, the developers at 4A have made it a far more welcoming and enjoyable place to be than the frozen ruins of Moscow. A claustrophobic and rank hole in the ground, built upon the strong foundations of worldbuilding established by Dmitry Glukhovsky, is framed as the sanction it truly is, and in a rare case of genius, a player that hasn't spent a day in the pits of the Metro can feel more at home in even the most dangerous of places in the Metro (take Hole Station and Black Station for instance). For a player that has no stake in the world of 2033 to feel the same relief that Artyom does descending back into the Metro after his first excursion is simply amazing.
Upon leaving Market Station, Artyom and the player are both experiencing the alien world of Moscow for the first time. For both, it is a familiar yet skewed image of the world before the war, and it carries with it a deeply dark and dangerous air (no pun intended). It is no coincidence that their time with Bourbon is cut short, leaving the player to experience the world alone, absorbing each detail with Artyom. By the end of the first visit and descent into Dry Station, it is likely that both will have had their fill of post-apocalyptic Moscow and recognize that any hole in the Metro feels more homely than anything offered by the surface. Not only does the environment play into this, but gameplay features like mutant frequency and especially the use of the gas mask all serve to frustrate and scare the player back underground.
I feel as though this speaks for the rest of the game's qualities more than I ever could. The first rendition of Metro 2033 was already superb, but I believe 4A really outdid themselves with this Redux. Not only does the game feel much more fun and smooth to play, but most importantly, the Metro and Moscow above it have never looked more real and unwelcoming. It is truly, utterly unnerving to play this game, and the artists and level designers responsible have done such a fantastic job that this game deserves nothing less than an outstanding reception and rating.

This is a very strange wargame. You see, You can't make a game without having abstractions. Like You don't ask a player to spend 10 years in training for a single battle to die in 10 minutes and then be happy because of realistic permadeath feature. We have abstractions everywhere in every game. Now how does this go with Company of Heroes 2? Well, here developers have created a whole new game around the abstractions. They are now called features. And while each side of conflict in CoH2 has the very same goal and very similar means to achieve that, the CoH2 developers have decided that they will throw in completely different mechanics for game abstractions for each faction.
For example: there are completely different mechanics for research tree for each faction:
The simplest solution is for Russians - You just ask Your engineers to build a respective building and You have new hardware unlocked.
For Germany You have to gather resources to "unlock battle stages". Then build as Russian faction does.
For other German faction (OKH) it is different - here You build special construction "halftrack" and drive to the location of Your preference to set up one of three different types of "forward base".
Now Americans have again their own way - they have to build an officer unit who will unlock the corresponding units.
And at last for the British You have to choose for two different research branches - depends if You plan to attack or defend.
Then how each faction deals with repairs?
The most reasonable feature is for US faction - they can disembark their vehicles and crews turn in to the repair engineers. A nice touch to that mechanic is that You can crew Your tanks with any type of infantry squad. But with a twist: You can't disembark squad equipment. Like You want to abandon Your own mortar and crew that nice Russian 120mm, but ... You can't. You have to call other infantry squad for that and they will stick to that crew weapon until they die. And while US crews are still able to board and abandon every vehicle from other factions, they get their hands on (because sometimes badly damaged enemy hardware can be repaired and captured), their own crews are totally glued to their hardware. Even if You have a "repair by crews" perk available, Your troops will not exit their hardware to do maintenance the way American faction does but they will do it "sitting inside". For god's sake .... why?
Well I do have some clues why this have been done - I am afraid that down behind the visual images all pieces have very similar defence/attack attributes for each tier of equipment and probably it is done to achieve better "multiplayer balance", so that in the end - each faction would probably become almost identical beneath cosmetic appearances unless developers have mixed around mechanics of abstractions for features like tech research, hardware repair and troop customisation.
Do I like it? No.
Personally I would prefer a mix of Russian reinforcement features (Many Russian troop types can merge to reinforce others, American crew mechanics, extended to the crew hardware, American/British style of weapon racks where You can pick up LMG or Bazooka, and German mechanics for engineers who swap their mine detector for another Stg assault rifle. Other engineer troops can't do that. I would prefer to get rid of mobile reinforcement from APC's for because it is silly and have a complete redesign for static defences because these are dumb in this game. The best are "trench house" for German OKH Faction and I think American and British can also build them (with right type of commander) I would only leave winter mechanics as they are, except that every troop type should have an ability to make a fire and hardware should have to be prone to "mechanical faults" during winter too.

I have mixed feelings about this sequel. First of all, the gameplay is still turn-based RPG, which is exactly what I wanted. The world is the same as the first game, but far more bleak and hopeless (this is not a drawback to me). I got additional party members early on, and I can use one joystick for both movement and menu selection, so those improve on the original! However, I feel like the writing was weaker in the second game, possibly due to the increase in "zany" characters, who came off as irritating and not funny at all. I noticed more grammatical errors and exclamation point spam as well, which could mean I'm just being more picky with the sequel. That said, I still enjoyed the gameplay, and most of the puzzles (a few were not intuitive at all, and one made me rage-quit for a day), and I'm curious to see where the story goes from here. If you liked turn-based retro JRPGs, liked the first game, and are willing to put up with some mediocre writing, I'd say you'll like this.

All in all casual or passionate player you'll enjoy this game.

It's not a bad game, but it's pretty mediocre overall, the gameplay formula doesn't really ever change while playing, you often end up going through the same missions over and over again, there's no real objective to the game and for the most part you'll find yourself just grinding for no real reason, most of the game is just you running around for a while and trying to not die, while completing some pretty dull side missions which range from escort missions, moving an item to a certain location, blowing some sh*t up, pushing some buttons to turn some more stuff on and tediously picking up some glowing items in order to get research material, which is needed in order to upgrade any of your equipment.
There's no real end game, you are supposed to be conquering a galaxy or something along those lines, but what really happens is that you get to pick from four different levels in each sector, which set the difficulty level you'll play with, and the overall goal is to get the biggest possible number until the sector is conquered and that's about it, you get to the homeworld and you do the same, no real changes here, problem is that the whole score thing updates in real time for everyone, if one of the factions is ever defeated before you can ever manage to play against it, then you are sh*t out of luck, you need to physically wait, entire days, for the whole galaxy to be conquered as a whole, then, you need to play BEFORE the faction you wanted to play against gets defeated, again, otherwise you are locked out of that part of the game, forever. Until the galaxy gets conqured again.
There's nothing you can do about this, if you want to play with your friends against a specific faction then good luck.
I never really felt like I was really conquering much of anything, you are mostly just messing around with some abbandoned buildings and doing some random sh*t on some boring *ss planets, but other than that number there's no real visual representation of your progress, you are just making some digits go up and that's about it, it feels very artificial.
Nothing overly interesting is done with the research system, certain upgrades are far too expensive and they are outright begginer traps, some of the most expensive upgrades in the game are downright useless in most cases. With enough grinding however this doesn't really matter, but there's no real sense of progression, none of the upgrades really make anything feel better, for the most part they are just simple stat upgrades, which means that you still end up playing the game in the same exact way as you already used to. Vehicles overall feel inefective, shooting the turrets doesn't do much and in most cases they blow up as quickly as they arrived. They are just garbage considering that 99% of the game involves you just running around from most threats, fighting for too long or against too many though enemies means that you probably f*cked something up.
Most enemies are overly bullet spongy at higher difficulty levels, making them pretty unsatisfying to fight, unless you managed to grind for the right equipment, some enemies are straight up annoying, and you might often find yourself stun locked or just dead after one hit, some unique enemies can also invert your controls and some other bullsh*t, but these enemies only appear once per level and only under a specific mission type.
I think that most people will quickly find the first two difficulty levels almost unsatisfying, but there's this stupid spike once you hit the third one, suddenly there's tanks and horribly bullet spongy enemies everywhere, all your equipment feels like sh*t, you quickly realize that there are only a few specific loadouts which are really efective in such situations, most weapons are straight up useless and if you don't have the right equipment you need to rely on your higher level team mates to take down the tanky enemies. You only get some sh*tty *ss air strike, which needs to be upgraded just to even be able to scrape some of these enemies. You are just going to be stuck grinding your *ss of on the first two difficulty levels, until you can get your hands on the proper equipment needed to more reliably handle those level three and four enemies.
Levelling quickly comes to a halt, and it's fairly easy to feel like you wasted your research points, with how long it ever takes to gain any once you get past level five. This game is best played with either a full group of friends or with whatever random people you can find online, otherwise playing it solo really brings out the some of the worst flaws in the game.
In most cases you are just trying to kill the scout parties before they can spot you, if they do see you, then they'll sound an alarm which spawns reinforcements out of nowhere. You either, kill everything while more and more scouts keep flooding in, or you just run away far enough for all the enemies to dissapear. This game features infinite enemy respawns, there's no real way to stop that from happening, you can clean an entire area and fill it with bodies to the brim, come back to it and suddenly, all the enemies you previously killed are already back and they are all over the place, so much for conquering the planet. I've had tanks spawn in front of me and you can often see the shadows of your enemies just pop up out of nowhere as they spawn next to you and it really reminds me that I'm just playing a videogame, any progress you do make at the end of the day feels completely meaningless, nothing of what you do really matters at all, you just run past most enemies, complete your objectives and then you leave the planet.
There are some missions where you are supposed to capture territory, but really all you do is, you stand near some flag, the flag goes up while some bar goes up or down, once you are done with that, you complete the objective and that's it, nothing cool happens, like some turrets get dropped down, or you get some supplies, or the aliens get bombed to hell, nothing at all.
You just complete the checklist, get to the end, and repeat for 20 hours. That's the whole game, that's it, just getting some numbers up just so that we can all feel accomplished. Like what's the point? I don't really get it.
I wouldn't mind buying this game but, it really isn't that great if you ask me. If you like grinding then go for it I guess. You can reset your level in the options menu, get to level five or something, reset your level and stack up on like 100 research points and then never waste your time with the upgrades ever again. By the time you've done that you'll probably realize how there's really not a whole lot to the game, I think it's a shame, this could be an amazing concept for a game but I do feel like there was a lot of wasted potential.
Maybe I'm just stupid and I don't get it, I had some fun with it but, there's isn't much else to it.

the first 3 minutes of the intro caught me like no game before, it´s heartbreaking, deep, shows a person in deep conflicts making hard decisions and makes you see how deep their emotions are.
the main character is a guy who grew up with an alcoholic mean and cruel father who destroyed his self-esteem so he starts taking a drug ("love") which makes him numb and makes the father disappear.when he´s grown up ( it all takes place in a post-apocalyptic world ) he suddenly finds a baby, no idea where it came from or who it belongs to so he takes it with him back to the camp where his friends live and they find out that it´s a girl. there don´t seem to be any women around so first they think about selling it to the local gang leader, all their problems would be solved. but he says no, he wants to keep and protect here. his friends aren´t that happy with this at first but you see how they change from "what the hell is a baby good for" to a deep love, they start digging another room in their cave so she´s got a room for herself, they look after her and so on. you often see the "father" at the edge of a cliff with "love" in his hand and with time he throws it down cause the girl makes the pain his father inflicted go away. but there are also days where he runs down to get them back cause he can´t take it.
first he tries to lock her in to protect her but as he sees that she´s not happy he decides he has to take the risk and take her out with him, this turns this small group into a happy family for a short time and is a beautiful moment in the story. then one day he returns and finds his friends dying, the girl gone and again he decides to find her and throws away "love".....so much for the story by now :)
the game itself is very funny and interesting in many ways, the combat system is sort of a round based weird roleplaying system with funny and crazy options and an amazing combo-system. exploring the world, deciding what to do in situations where you have to choose to kill a friend or lose all your stuff and also an interesting way of moving around (you cant really climb, only when there is a rope or when the height isn´t too high.....same with climbing down. so often you need to fall down and take damage to get to some points) make it really a game that leaves an impression, in my case one that makes this game (by now, didn´t have that much time to play) one of the best i ever played. its a post-apocalyptic rpg with a very important social factor which is just great, the people who did it managed to transport the emotions perfect with such simple graphics....
my rating : get it. if you have to rob a bank or sell your family to do so : get it :D

An excellent game for cooperative play, as the game allows you to join up with 3 other of your buddies to battle thru every single mission from the single-player campaigns. There's a great deal of call for strategic and tactical teamwork, timing and use of wits. You may think this game is good at first. You may think that me having clocked in over 200 hours means it must be good. But really, this game is like cocaine. You'll use it once, think it's interesting, then keep going. Soon you'll know it's bad, and that it's just constantly killing you, but you'll keep going, hoping it'll go back to the good it once seemed to be. If you're lucky like me, you'll escape and never play this again.
Let me explain my opinion a little more. This game is essentially an RTS with guns, tanks and artillery. That's fun and fine in itself, at least on paper, but it necessitates a few things. For example, if you have troops with guns, you expect that they'll be able to shoot enemies, and generally get things done without your constant aid. Not in Men of War. Your troops will frequently throw grenades into their own squads, waste ammo shooting at nothing (yeah, you have to keep track of every troop's ammo), miss enemies at point blank range, stare at the last sighted enemy even if they're miles out of range, stop running in favor of standing in a field trying to shoot an invisible sniper, or just flat out do something that makes no sense. This is only the beginning.
Your tanks fare even worse. There is literally no way to use them apart from taking direct control of the tank, the AI for it is that useless. This limits you to having pretty much one tank on the battlefield at a time. This would be reasonable, except that the game's terribly designed engine starts to really kick in now. Even while you desperately try to aim at an enemy vehicle, your shots will typically bounce off, or just flatout prove useless, while later, while not even trying, a .50 cal will destroy the same tank with ease. The game is just littered with inconsistencies, all the while trying desperately to cling to realism. And once again, this is just the beginning.
In trying to move away, so as to hopefully avoid some shots, you'll find that the terrain is just as poorly built. Tanks will simply stop at steep inclines, and will actually become a physics object upon colliding with a rock, juttering out of control for a crucial second or two, regardless of how hard your brushed against it, while it will have no problem pummelling through a block of buildings. Speaking of buildings, some, and it seems more or less entirely random, will never be properly broken and will stay standing even after you've barraged the area with artillery, while some will crumble after a few grenades come near it.
There's also a huge issue with balance, with the Soviets (possibly in accordance with reality) getting not only the best tanks, but also getting them the cheapest. Forget what you've heard about American tanks being cheap, they are the most expensive to field. Germany is the only nation that can compete; Japan and Britain might as well not be playable. In theory, the American infantry is better than the Soviet, but in practice this is only true for basic infantry. Elite infantry finds home with the Soviets again, who pretty much decimate all other units, until you bring in tanks, where once again, the Soviets take the cake. You'd think maybe some artillery would take out them out, but it proves rather fruitless, because they also get very good light vehicles, which will take out whatever artillery you have.
This is all without even getting into the abomination that is the single player mode. The voice acting is cringeworthy; nearly on par with Zelda CDI. The difficulty curves make no sense, ranging from Niagra Falls drops, to brick wall inclines, and there's an extremely shallow learning curve, with the tutorial teaching you only a quarter of what you actually need to know to play effectively. On top of that, the singleplayer AI is completely insane, relying more on fielding impossibly large amounts of units than actually being able to control any.
But I could go on forever. I'm going to cut my time spent with this game short and now try my best never to think of it again. Do yourself a favour and don't ever touch this game.

Disclaimer: I was generously given a free copy of Labyronia RPG 2 with the understanding that I was expected to review the title after spending some time with it.
So I must admit that my view of Labyronia 2 is tainted before I even began playing; I had quite the negative experience with the original Labyronia and dove into the sequel only a couple days later. To my surprise, however, it appears that the developers learned a lot from their first title and polished up the sequel accordingly. Kudos on that guys!

Upon launching the game, by default it ran fullscreen and while the resolution was rather unappealing, the assets appeared to be improved enough that it wasn’t unplayable on a 1080p display. Sadly the select button is still inexplicably mapped to the O(PS4)/B(360) by default. Unlike the first Labyronia though, I was actually able to easily fix all the mappings and get a grasp of the games controls before setting off into the world. The opening itself feels like the devs learned a lot from the first game because there was a lot better guidance and exposition in the early game to direct the player. The story was no less generic (the main boss introduced at the beginning was the Father of a thousand evils) but I don’t feel that I have the right to judge much about a direct sequels narrative when I was unable to play the first game.

Overall, Labyronia 2 feels like a great application of lessons learned, but this is where my big picture judgment takes a turn. Yes, most of the originals issues were fixed, but that only brought this game up par with every other RPG Maker title. Die-hard fans of this style of RPG may get some enjoyment out of it, but there’s not that “wow” factor to distinguish it from the thousands of other games just like it flooding Steam.

What's to say? I just really really liked it. It's free and it's short. The story is humorously written and the art is adorable at times if not downright beautiful at others. Did this little visual story need sound effects? No, but they're a pleasant touch. Did it need a soundtrack? It might've gotten by without, but the musical accompaniment is lovely. While we're at it, that's a surprisingly convenient interface! :P
Point being, this work is truly a labor of love. No, it's not the next indie sensation, and you might even say it's easy to overlook. If you made it this far though, you owe it to yourself to install and play this little jewel and see what it looks like when somebody combines passion and determination with the will to tell a sweet little tale.
I think we can all see a little of ourselves in the cute little protagonist "Vinty". She's fun and easy to connect with, and like most of us, she's got big dreams about carving out her own special place in this world. Like most of us, too, she struggles with self-doubt and is faced with little choices that will change her life in a big way.
For such a short little game, there's a lot of messages for us here. To avoid spoiling the experience, I'll let you figure them out. Rest assured though, that they're not delivered in some pretentious art-house way. They're humanly understandable, if not inspiring. I see "good art" as a way to let others get a glimpse into the soul of its creator. By that definition, "Without Within" is certainly good art.

I couldn't
give this a look, what with how people have been tearing this apart in the reviews section. Unlike RotMG, where I had expectations going in due to prior experience, and was hoping that the skeptic reviews were just hyperbole,
I knew was a descent into madness at minute one.
After I made my character, the game unceremoneously throws me into my home plot, a 15x15x15 cube populated with only grass and dirt. After 20 seconds of immediate shock, laughing and thinking this was just the tutorial map, that good spirit immediately died when I realized the game's not joking; no matter where I went, I always had to come back to that worthless patch of grass.
Before I went adventuring, the first thing I did was attempt to jump off the side. Sadly, I discovered I wouldn't be escaping this game so easily, as every time I'd be jolted back. No size of jump can possibly kill you, either, to my dismay when I built a hole to the bottom of my plot and then leaped into it. After that, I decided to do 'quests' the game had in store for me. I start off on the first quest....and quickly lose interest, opting instead to dig out my entire plot into an empty husk; rather, emptier than it was. But as I was, maybe, 1/50th of the way done, I realized I didn't want the game to think I was putting in more effort than it took to make it, and just gave up. Then again, I did clock 2-1/2 hours on this, so you can't say I didn't spend more time than the developers spent on QA.
The second lie, with a trip to the shop, is that you won't be
the 'house of your dreams.' No, that would require creativity, something this game would like to discourage as much as possible! Instead, you PURCHASE actual houses for, roughly, $30. Ah yes, this game is far from free; It's loaded with what I now like to call 'macrotransactions,' cluttering every corner of it. Want a blueprint for a table? money, please. Want seeds to grow in your garden? Money, please. Want a noose and a chair to end the suffering? WHAT SUFFERING? YOU'RE HAVING FUN, RIGHT? GIVE US MORE MONEY. To a very minute credit, there's a normal currency you can earn off the quests, but it won't buy you much, and the economy is so ♥♥♥♥ed, you'll never earn another coin off whoever may still play this.
After dealing with the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥y involving the shop, I decided to go on my first real trek, thus finally beginning the grand adventures of HELPME. No shock to anyone, the first thing you ever see when entering public instances is a shop where you can buy all you like but sell sweet ♥♥♥♥ all; opposite that, a bulletin board with advertisements for overpriced♥♥♥♥♥♥you can make with zero effort. You'll learn quickly that all the realms you enter are just as empty and barren as your homestead: the best you'll be able to find in terms of value would likely be crystals, which're rare, and a couple attempts with the RNG-fueled smelter later, I had no idea what to do with. So my wandering a barren land yielded me more ♥♥♥♥ing dirt, a handful of rocks, and some coal. I guess fun is also in the shop as well, I wonder how much I have to pay for fun?
I'd also touch up on dungeons, but I could never enter one! The community is barren, to the surprise of no one; I only saw one other person logged in at the same time as me, and dungeons required 3 people, in some sort of desperate requirement to drum up more players; I guess you can tell how well that worked?
After strip-mining an entire server of all its leaves in a desperate search for planks, since this game has a problem with servers being empty of critical resources due to the fact they never regenerate (ergo no wood,) I made some useless furniture, built a useless well, planted some useless seeds I bought from the useless shop, and then, just as I was experimenting, almost certain I was onto something with the smelter...the game chunked me into a loading screen...then promptly crashed. No better excuse to stop playing, I guess!
In short, this 'game' is the highlight of the worst of free-to-play; it strips itself down to the barest minimum, shoving everything behind a paywall. Its existence is solely as a ♥♥♥♥ing cash grab; a milking of people's yearn for a Minecraft fix they can get free, but it's never that simple. I'm glad nobody plays this; hell, I think I might just have spent more time playing this than anyone, maybe even the developers of this! Because it's obvious, after one look at this abomination, the best place for it is a recycle bin.

Don't run away just because it's a "quirky, artsy rpgmaker game"- it's one of the best, and it sticks to its guns.
You play as Bradley Armstrong, a drug-addled and regretful former karate instructor living with his friends in a post-apocalyptic world where women have apparently gone for good. He finds a baby girl in the wilderness, and chooses to raise "Buddy" in secret to keep her safe, and to give himself a second chance to do something right. He comes back from a guiltful night of drinking and drug usage to find his home occupied by bodies, and Buddy gone. FIND HER.
The game primarily is played as a sidecrolling 2D overworld with some platforming elements- mainly falling off of cliffs to reach items and secret areas. There are three central hubs with their own branching areas that lead to various environments, characters to meet, and dip♥♥♥♥♥ to fight off. It is surprisingly easy to get lost or at least to forget where certain locations are in relation to others, which is my only real gripe. Luckily the game paces itself well by having a smattering of one-off silly vehicle sections, all of which are certainly memorable. Also, hallucinations that certainly spice things up.
As for the combat, it's pretty much your average turn-based RPG, but with a few twists to keep you engaged. Brad's main move is KARATE with the WASD keys, with a limited number of inputs- and all-important combos. Other party members have a variety of skills that range from mostly useless to entirely overpowered, if used in conjunction with certain other members. It's enough of a challenge, especially in Pain Mode. There's also a few joke fights, as this is of course a Mother-inspired game.
Speaking of Mother, though I still have much of that series to play myself, the sound design in the game seems to have a lot in common there as well, with a lot of odd sampling sources for the music andUH-HUH.     UH-HUH.     UH-HUH.
...Well, I feel it adds something, anyways.
Really a must play if you enjoy both pitch black drama and comedy, as this game successfully jumps between the both realms without muddling its thematic goals- even its most hilarious moments contain various undercurrents of hopelessness, dread, and horror. The games personality shines brightest in the wide variety of party characters, many of whom will likely die or be lost one way or another throughout the course of the story. And there's more to lose than just party members. The unreliable narrator and protagonist, Bradley Armstrong, risks loss of limb, loss of possessions, loss of masculinity, and more. This game is harsh, and subversive in both story and mechanics, and full of surprises.
Expect daddy issues, monsters (in every sense of the word,) loss, emasculation, failure, and a lot of pro-wrestling.
I suppose it might not be for everyone, but if you like a good story full of what's been discussed above, then it's well worth the price.

The best way for me to describe Faster Than Light is that it's like Oregon Trail in space.  You choose a ship, you can name your crew, you make decisions but don't always control the outcome, and you try to survive sector after brutal sector.  This game is hard, like really hard, even on the "easy" setting.  However, once you start to develop strategies for each portion of the game and certain scenarios, you'll notice your success rate steadily rise.
One of my favorite aspects of FTL is that it's an easy game to jump into, play for a bit, save for later, then jump back into.  It really doesn't get old very quickly, probably because of the difficulty, but also because there are plenty of ships and types of crew to keep it interesting.  You might think at first that a certain configuration is the only way to achieve consistent victory, only to realize later that trying other things can also yield positive results.
While FTL is most certainly unforgiving and can be frustrating when your ship, which you feel really great about, is destroyed prematurely, it's also very rewarding.  Unlocking new ships is exciting, and it's impossible to anticipate every possible scenario, so each playthrough feels fresh.  You can expect a deep, unique, and fun experience, just don't expect to win immediately.

Men of War is one of the gaming industry's biggest accomplishments, settling once of for all the debate of whether games can be considered to be art. Men of War is one of gaming's first autobiographical games which follows the heavy metal band Manowar from their inception during the 1980s. The game has a beautiful opening scene wherein the player controls bassist Joey DeMaio while he snorts the biggest line of cocaine in his life while backstage at a Black Sabbath concert, and neglects to fulfill his duties as a sober fireworks manager. In this sequence the player must complete a series of quick-time-events in order to guide a stumbling Demaio into correctly setting off the fireworks in order to not burn the stage down. During this sequence the quick-time-events get harder to the point where the player cannot complete them, which reveals that Ross the Boss is right beside you and like a true bro, covers over for DeMaio and succeeds in not causing the death of Ronnie James Dio. DeMaio and Ross the Boss become best bros at that moment and start legendary metal band Manowar.
The rest of the game is a re-tooled version of Activision's Guitar Hero, but all of the songs are from Manowar.

Without Within is a short visual novel about a struggling calligraphist named Vinty trying to survive with what she viewed as talent. The story was pretty good; the writing allowed you to get into her mindset, making it a really cute short story. The graphics, or rather, art, was pretty good. It wasn't anything in particularly noteworthy, but I'll probably remember it anyway, as it was one of the few visual novels that I've finished at this point. Overall, Without Within was a good visual novel.
Looking back on it, it seems that I prefer visual novels that are short and sweet, as I don't particularly like the idea of replaying the same scene over and over again... which I think is a bigger pain if you don't get achievements. At least with achievements, you can look back and remember how annoying it was or how fun it was to get, and then say "Well, I have little to no reason to do that again." With that said, I do wish it had achievements, but I don't really care... because there's going to be a sequel!
I recommend this if you want a quick and cute read that is pretty relatable for the artistic people (unless you're insanely lucky and were immediately successful and never struggled... in which case, I must thank you for reading this. It's an honor!) Seriously though, I see no reason to not read this, so jump over to Steam and get it; it is a free, after all!

I play a lot of platformers, and the most common complaint I make is "floaty jump physics."
The player character doesn't accelerate upwards into the jump or downwards after the jump enough that the jumping motion jibes with your natural expectations on how things should climb to or fall from a certain height.  It's not usually a deal breaker, but it sticks out as something that should have been universally solved a long time ago.
is not one of those games.  It might, in fact, be the game with the most perfect jump physics ever.  It might even have the best controls ever.  Movement is unbelievable fast and accurate.  There will be moments where you are playing when you start to wonder if you are in fact playing, or watching a tool-assisted speedrun.  It's that good.
You've all seen retro-throwback graphics before, but how often do they throw back to EGA PCs?  Retro graphics with an Amstrad CPC color palette are probably more common.  The other thing notable about them is the sheer weirdness of the enemies.  When was the last time you got killed by a giant prawn?  Just do yourself a favor and turn off the simulated low-res CRT monitor (replete with scanlines).  It's cute, but ultimately the graphics stand on their own.

Labyronia RPG 2 is a direct sequel to Labyronia RPG taking place roughly 10 years after the incidents of it's predecessor. Thus most of the main cast, many locations and references both cosmetic as well as story wise will make a more sense to players who have completed the first game. At the same time it has to be mentioned that it is possible to play and enjoy this one on it's own without any prior knowledge. A newcomer will make sense of the story and the relations among it's characters.
Gameplaywise is where the major differences between Labyronia RPG 2 and 1 will be noticable. Most and foremost is a more streamlined and focused approach in Labyronia RPG 2. While the first game saw the fere leave his house in the beginning and thus threw the player into an open world without any clue where to start and what to do next; as such requiring the player to call the "oldschool" ability of being able to explore on there own without any guidance.
Here in hte sequel the path forward as well as the objectives are always clear to the player. You will always know where to go to next and what to do!!!
The battles however are still dificult, expecially in the beginning and require a careful and strategic approach. Simple attack spamming won't get you anywhere, just as in the Labyronia RPG 1.
Overall I can recommend this game to everybody who enjoyed the first one and to fans of the genre who can get past the fact that this is an RPGMaker VXAce game using many default graphics, simply because there is a very nice oldschool style JRPG  beneath it's surface that I enjoyed very much.
---
Quick First Look!
I really like the first Labyronia game, but I still haven't finished it and that is the reason why a quick first look at Labyronia RPG 2 will have to do (at least for now!).
Labyronia RPG 2 is still Labyronia!! Everybody who enjoyed the first one will feel right at home.
However there is one major change and that is a more focused approach to the game. This time around you will not just be thrown into an open game world without any clues; this time you will be pointed into a specific direction once the short opening sequence that functions as a basic tutorial has been finished.
However this doesn't mean that the game has become linear. Whether you are following the directions or just wander off exploring, is still up to you, the player.
The game world is still open and once again, careless rushing out will get you into trouble easily and simple attack spamming without any strategy will get you killed as fast as possible (the very first enemy got me, again XD - This is  Spar....errr...Labyronia!!!).

I love Labyronia 2 !!!! (some spoilers)
I just finished Labyronia 1 and started playing Labyronia 2.
I loved it.
Originally I was worried that L1 characters might be overpowering and less challenging, but I love the design of L2 especially the starting scenario which was carefully thought out to present a sense of challenge.
What makes L2 fun was:
a. 2 starting characters have no healing spells. This makes it necessary to spend money on rations and make money really precious. It also require some planning to drop by a town to stock up ration, else we will just die.
b. The starting characters are challenging because they cannot hurt certain monsters and have to flee from them. This both add a sense of urgency and a need to survive in the game. Wonderfully done.
c. Several things add to the challenge. Getting lost running in endless circles without the compass, running from monsters in the dark, etc make the game a lot more fun and time critical.
d, I also love the fact that there is no choice of difficulty level, otherwise I would have just played the game on EASY and that would have spoilt the sense of challenge in the game.
So developers --- very well done for Labyronia 2 and I would love to immerse my entire weekend in the game. I look forward to providing you more feedback when I finished L2.

One of the best games humanity has ever created , personal favorite , and probably the only actual first-person RPG (role playing game, not just a game where you can level up your character) that was created in 2000s.  Notoriously buggy, yes. However, Unofficial Patch by Wesp fixes ALOT of stuff , and i DO MEAN alot of stuff. And pay no mind to youtubers who play this game.... Honestly guys , being a huge fan, i tried waatching ALOT of youtube stuff about VTMB, just to.... you know, get a fresh look on the game. And oh my god... I dont know whats the problem, but it seems like the IQ of youtubers who play it (atleast those that i watched) is just below 20 or something. They dont understand simple stuff, they mash buttons, etc etc , then they blame the game's engine, buginess and mechanics. Just ignore them. Install this game (and Unofficial Patch , its just a must) and form your own opinion, and trust me - you will not regret spending a single penny on this title.
Pros :
- You can actually role-play different characters
- Rich story with cool plot twists
- Amazing voice acting
- Witty/entertaining/interesting/immersive dialogues
- Variety of options to get the job done (stealth, dialogues, bribes, intimidation, killing, etc etc)
- One of the best horror-themed levels in the gaming history (some say THE BEST) - Ocean House Hotel
- Very thought-through and well-designed character leveling mechanic
- Awesome soundtrack (not just my own taste , but also the way the music fits the environment)
- Variety of clans (Two of which, Nosferatu and Malkavians actually have ALL THEIR DIALOUGES REWRITTEN and basically make for absolutely different game experience)
- Tons of easter eggs, hidden secrets, etc etc.
- Community is still alive and making mods till today...12 years.. gotta mean something , right?
- Honestly , im just tired of going through the Pros , too many of em , lets move on to Cons
Cons :
- Controls. Movement and combat will feel and look wrong. Yes, they will. BUT. Just try to adapt to it, not whine. If you set your mind towards adapting isntead of blaming - it will feel natural to you in 20-30 minutes of playing.
- Bugs. Yes. ALOT. You can get stuck in doors (if youre impatient), prompts can refuse to appear hence rendering the mission impossible to complete, visual bugs, etc. Actually , the raw version of the game was unplayable at some point, because storyline wouldnt proceed because of the bug. Remember theese words : UNOFFICIAL PATCH BY WESP. Got it? Good. Download it. And ~70% of the bugs are dealt with. Dont mash buttons , dont spam USE on opening doors, trying to make it go faster , like alot of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s i saw on youtube , etc, and you will be fine. In fact, when i play this game, i rarely experience a single bug that would make me reload my save or something.
- Biggest con in my opinion - this game ends , sooner or later... Unfortunately ,because of pirating, this game was leaked, forced to launch earlier than planned , hence - it was financially unsuccessful, despite it being an absolute masterpiece. 12 years have passed and there is still no hope to continuation of the story... /sadface

It's hard to explain the appeal of LISA because it's something that's become better than the sum of its parts. The combination of tight, simple gameplay, excellent writing and varied encounters have created a deeply engaging world, and difficult choice and realistic consiquence excel the player engagement that much more, while never feeling frustrating or jarring. I like to compare LISA to Fallout 3 because along with the obvious comparisons like being a post-apocalyptic world with a variety of strange and scary inhabitants, all with their own motives and reactions to different scenarios, it's also a game where a large spread out world has been designed first, and a great story has been laid softly on top afterwards, which means players will get a lot more or less from the story and world based on what they put into it, and that works really well.
One of the great things about LISA is the fact that the game is so simple that all the design elements are clearly assertainable and you can identify why the developer has chosen to do certain things, and what they've added to gameplay as a result. As well as a great players game it's also a reviewers dream.
There are honestly things that are mediocre here. Combat, for example, is fair, it adds a bit of strategy and works well, but I'd be lying if I said it hadn't been done better elsewhere. Platforming too, has some very well designed intuitive learning and progression moments, but otherwise isn't anything special or better than in stand alone competitors titles. But they all do their job pretty well, and they serve the core design principles which are where the meat of the game lies. The characters throughout the world are all unique, interesting and fun to interact with and the progression system is particularly well made because it doesn't rely on grinding, in fact it's nearly impossible to kill more than a couple of the same enemy types, and even those occurrances are rare. Instead, you progress by exploring and defeating everything in an area, which not only adds to your desire to explore and interact, but even rewards you with new items and party members.
Then there's the story, which has been dusted over the game afterwards, and while no means is easy to ignore, doesn't add as much as it would to any other game. This is because, regardless of what the story was going to be, the world and gameplay would serve it from the start and only the writing and art style would have needed to been changed. But the story fits well and when bolstered by the weight of realistic choice rather than the usual black and white Good/Bad system other games tend to have, brings out the desperate nature of this post-apocalyptic world full of horrible human nature. It forces you to invest emotionally into the game, and then to sacrifice to progress. It's often troubling and downright heartwrenching.
The majority of annoyances with this game come from its use of the RPG Maker engine, which both limit its capabilities and cause a few annoying problems. Cliffs, for example, are often very easy to walk off after entering a new screen area, text boxes can cut off text, etc.
There are also plenty of technical issues, particularly in early releases. Fortunately the developer is still extremely active and proactive, which serves the future of this game. There's also a legacy release which, while it has some issues, helps to reduce the scope of technical problems.
Available for £6.99/9.99€/$9.99 on Steam, and with a good 12 hour play time on the main story, this is a very fairly priced title and should probably be played by almost everyone at least once. Completionists and achievement hunters can expect at least another 6 or 7 hours of gameplay and the personal choices and alternative story approaches give this some great replay value too.

I've played some Helldivers before on the PS4 but finally bought it now on the PC... so, a few thoughts on the game (which is absolutely awesome) that might be usefull for some.
- The tutorial is kinda boring/bland and WILL put you of but it's necessary. Then when you play the first mission you might feel a bit lost and at first the game might feel too simple... but don't give up yet. It shouldn't take long until the game starts unraveling it's charms and complexities to you. It took me till the third missions (with randoms online) until the game clicked with me and when it did it became like crack.
- If feels and looks like Warhammer 40,000, specially when you start unlocking the awesome mechs or the armored veichles where all 4 members of the team can get in, with 1 driving and the others using the side guns.
- Besides Warhammer, the game universe also feels alot like Starships Troopers, particularly the cynical sence of humor.
- The gameplay is challeging as hell and good team work is essencial to sucess, except maybe on the very lowest dificulty missions.  Mission dificulty can go from level 1 to 12 with 4 being medium (which can often be very hard).
- You will die a lot and everything is trying to kill you. Even your team mates since friendly fire is always active. When you call in supplies the pod that brings them can kill you if you stand on it's landing zone. The sentry guns you setup to defend the team will also kill any player standing on their line of fire. Even the environment can kill you.
- What makes the game so challenging (ridiculously so for some) is also what makes it so fun. Some times you will laught at some of your cheap deaths rather than feel angry about it.
- The gameplay is the very definition of simple to learn, hard to master. There are lots of diferent strategies that can be achieved depending on what loadout each player is using regarding weapons, perks or strategems. Stratagems are basically drop-ins that you can call during the mission and they can be things like ammunition, sentry guns, vehicles, weapons, drones, reeinforcements (used to ressurect dead players), etc.
- When the action gets going things can get a bit chaotic but if you manage to keep calm and work together the feeling of achievement when you and your team mates survive what looked like impossible odds is trough the roof. Plus, those intense moments feel like you're in a middle of a sci-fi action movie.
- From my experience the online comunity is generally friendly. So far I've only played with randoms and I've mostly had great experiences with some nice team work going on.
- Lots of content, lots of unlockables, lots of weapons, stratagems, randomized missions... there's enough content here to keep you entertained for dozens or hundreds of hours, providing the community remains active.
- All said, it's one of the best co-op multiplayer games I've ever played, so I definetely recomend it. However, some of it's more challeging elements might put some people off.

In short, it utimately depends on whether or not you liked Saints Row The Third or not, but if you did, you will most likely enjoy IV. If not, you're gonna hate this even more than Third.
It's just as whacky, if not, more than Third. None of the Saints Row games ever struck me as hilarious, but I appreciate that the series doesn't take itself very seriously. I'm not joking when I say this game is more fun than Grand Theft Auto V. GTA V may overall be a better game, but it's nowhere near as fun as Saints Row IV.
Story
The story gets the job done. You're in a simulation, yes it takes place in Steelport still, and you interact with the same characters throught out the Saints series. You have to save all your friends like Pierce, Shaundi, Matt Miller, etc, and defeat Zinyak, the alien ruler who destroyed earth and controls the simulation. There's a lot of nods to Saints Row and Saints Row 2, and there's a lot of familiar flashbacks to the Third game too. You also meet several new characters along the way, though not many.
Second weakest story out of the five games. Gat out of hell takes the cake for being the worst.
Gameplay
I think the gameplay is where SR IV shines. You get super powers in this game like super jumping, flash-like running speed, shoot fire/ice, etc. The jumping and running makes all vehicles completely useless, but I still prefer it and it even makes it hard for me to go back to Saints Row The Third.
It makes the game real fun though. The gunplay has always been weak in Saints Row, so adding other forms of combat is better. You can also upgrade these powers by collecting data clusters. The data clusters are littered throughout Steelport, and for most of the game, you will not go without seeing at least one on top of some building for the longest. Collect a certain amount and you can spend them on upgrades. I believe there's 1500 total.
You can also upgrade other things just like in Saints Row The Third. Hell, the entire game is honestly just a reskinned SR3, which is fine. Everything you could possibly think of in SR3 is in SRIV.
Missions are nothing to write home about. They're all pretty similar. Save a character, do side missions for characters, rinse and repeat. The side missions are structured in a way to get you to complete the random activities throughout Steelport like taking out flashpoints or hacking all the stores. I will give it to them for making the side missions like that. In any other open world game, I probably wouldn't have done half the stuff I did in this game. More games should do this.
Overall, gameplay is really fun, and I can see myself 100%ing it, or coming close before I get bored.
Overall, it's extremely similar to SR3 with a superhero-like spin to it. Story is nothing special, gameplay is really fun, and graphics are okay I guess.
7/10. Worth it if you like Saints Row and games like Prototype, Infamous, and superhero games.

What made me see the greatness was picking clan Malkavian on my second playthrough. All i needed to see was the very first conversation before the tutorial and I thought to myself "oh, so that's what it's all about".
What's the big difference between Malkavians and other clans you ask?
Malkavians are a clan of insane vampires and it's not just an empty description you read when picking a character.
EVERY single line you can pick in conversations is written differently from other clans and other characters have additional or altered lines to react to your madness(other clans seem to have much less of those).
It doesn't actually change the course of the story, but it definitely ups the fun factor.
Other than that it's just an all around solid game although a bit buggy(unofficial patch helps with that a lot while adding extra content, balance and whatnot). Nothing we haven't seen before, but with vampires.
TL;DR - great if you pick Malkavian, download the unofficial patch

If you loved the original Mafia game you're going to be quite disappointed.
This is not a bad game, it's a decent third action shooter with some well written moments, but the main core of the first installment in the series was the great story, the awesome characters and, of course, the whole city of Lost Heaven. It had a unique identity and perfectly fitted for all the drama in the first game.
Delete these fundamental aspects and you have Mafia II. The characters are too much stereotyped, the story is practically linear like an average gangster movie set in the 50s/60s and the Empire Bay city is well built but anonymous. It is quite big indeed with few interesting spots, but there's nothing to do there.
Even the secondary quests are useless. It feels like an incomplete game, which is a shame because the developers are great. The only thing that I personally liked was the gunplay. Every weapon feels different and it is satisfying to kill some spaghetti-mobsters all around.
And the DLCs? Jimmy's Vendetta and The Betrayal of Jimmy are pointless. You perform the same actions and approximately the same missions on both DLCs. If you like to score in the Leaderboards go on, otherwise pass.
Joe's Adventures instead tries to add something to the main game, but it's definitely too short and weak. I would not recommend the DLCs for this game. The base game is sufficient if you want to take a ride.

Company of Heroes 2, much like the first game, while it can be good for competetive play, is amazing for casual play.
If you just want to have fun in a WW2 RTS, simple comp-stomping in CoH is just that. You don't need to have a perfect build order and on-point micro for everything on the map. Just load up a map vs CPU, preferably with a couple of friends, and have fun telling your toy soldiers and tanks to shoot each other.
And for an even more laid back experience, load up a bridge map vs expert CPUs and watch the meat grinder.
For those in a more competetive mood, the game has an auto-match feature that is based on your ranking.
There is a progression system, not the greatest ever, but you'll get intel bulletins (small buffs to ingame units or abilites - max 3 at a time), skins, decals and (rarely) commanders that offer unique abilities. Any duplicates are converted into in-game currency that you can spend on said items of your choice.
I recommend this to any WW2 enthusiast, and it's a good "first RTS". If you are not into the WW2 setting you can probably skip this.

I've seen a lot of comments about the game being repetitive and a grindfest; to be honest, if there is a grind, it's not at MMO levels.
The game itself is fun in multiplayer, it's even exciting when you join a party (or someone else joins you) due all the chaos on the battlefield. The main problems I see, that would make it less attractive to anyone are the facts that it has friendly fire (which also applies to the enemy), and that almost anything can kill you amidst the chaos.
Also, the game has basically 4 map types (snow, desert, volcanic and jungle), this sounds terrible in paper, but they are just a template to generate your mission. Basically, you can have a snow map where you have to rescue survivors, activate a communication tower and capture a zone or two, and after that it could be a mission about nuking  a nest or facility, retrieving a pack and disabling some mines.
In the end, the point of the game is not to run and gun, if you stay and fight the enemies won't stop spawning until you either lose them or manage to avoid triggering any alarms while dealing with the current army. Basically, the game is more of a stealth game than a shooter, and what makes it shine is the teamplay and chaos.

Great RTS. Seriously, this game will make you♥♥♥♥♥♥Zhukov, it's so micro-intensive. Games like Company of Heroes, Starcraft 2, RUSE or Command & Conquer are all babby mode compared to this thing.
The game is actually an RTT (Real Time Tactics) at heart and completely removes the base-building component you'd find in a lot of contemporary strategy games.
This leaves you to completely focus on per unit resource management, like equipping each individual soldier with a gun (or even multiple guns), ammo, helmets, grenades, special equipment, and sometimes armour.
There's also a whole host of World War 2 vehicles that include: light vehicles, tanks, self-propelled guns, and weapon emplacements.
Be warned! Cinematic voice-acting is horrendous while unit voice-acting is pretty good.
