This game sat in my wishlist for a long time before I decided to play it.  My main concern was that I couldn't be impartial.  I love the World of Darkness games, and was seriously worried that despite the many recommendations this game has recieved, I couldn't help but be disappointed.
I was not disappointed.
Truely, I felt as if I were in the World of Darkness.  The game is a little crowded with WoD lore, but it was fun to see a little bit of everything from hunters to hengeyokai.  The leveling system is almost straight out of the WoD role playing system, which made it easy for me to know what was going on right away.
The game's controls never got in the way of gameplay, but sometimes the camera would get a bit confused when crawling through sewage tunnels.  It was all worth it though.  The first time I let loose with Celerity 5 in a room full of ninjas, all was forgiven.
I've seen a lot of mention of issues getting the game to run well on Windows 7, but I had no real trouble.  I did get the "not enough RAM" error, but going in and changing the compatibility to XPsp2 fixed that right away.
All in all, this is a fun action RPG.  While some of the programming shows it's age, the gameplay has aged very well.  I feel that most people will find this game enjoyable, but if you are a World of Darkness RPG series fan, then Bloodlines is absolutely not to be missed.

1. Player skill is the SINGLE biggest factor in whether or not you will have a good run.  And by a huge margin.  If you think otherwise, you need to play this game more, watch some videos of more experienced players, and see some of the excellent tricks you can use to play more effectively.

From the cold, dark, and unreal ruins of Moscow, to the cinematic gameplay, Metro 2033 Redux has remastered the original masterpiece to expand the graphics to improve the game's atmosphere. It's rare for games to immerse you heavily into the world, however 4A games has done that well. Without spoiling too much, this game will make you wary of your supplies, caring for your allies, and doing all you can to survive in dead Moscow.
Pros:
•Unique world from both the surface ruins of Moscow to the safe havens in the metro
•Amazing storyline and narration
•Great graphics (The lighting is amazing)
•Interesting characters
•Cinematic controls make for a unique experience
Neutral:
•No manual save. Not too bad, but some deaths force you to rewatch the same cutscene.
Cons:
•All the children seem to have the same voice actor (IMO, their voice doesn't seem to fit)
•Occasional bugs, such as NPCs clipping through walls and freezing
I recommend this game for any player that loves amazing storytelling and world building.
Also, playing in Survival Ranger (Hardcore or not) is the best way to play the game.

I really came away from Helldivers impressed. While I don't have the cash to purchase now, I think I will in the future for sure.
Helldivers is really a quite intuitive game. The gameplay is easy to grasp and solidly entertaining. but that's more the foundation than the meat of it.
Through a combination of its matchmaking and unlock systems, Helldivers manages to cultivate, seemingly thorugh design decisions, one of the best public co-op experiences I've ever seen. I found myself constantly helped along by more expereinced players. And upon unlocking some new things, I think I know why. Completing missions you've already gathered the reward for gives you bonus XP instead. So there's an incentive to go back to things just under your level and help lower level players. Let alone that the unlocks you've gathered make you feel like a save-the-day badass when you drop into a lower level game.
A lot of abilities to deploy equipment are single-use, but can be stacked in your four slots. And I found myself actively wanting to be the guy dropping into games with people who had no access yet to say, the exosuit walker and handing them out. It just feels damned good to be the ice cream man delivering extra firepower and new toys.
Everything about the game seems polished to inspire teamwork, and the relatively forgiving respawn mechanics mean slip-ups and accidental TK's are often more a source of laughs than frustration or screaming. (It helps that such is talked up in the marketing too.)
I wound up coming away from Helldivers feeling like I met some friendly people and had a good time, instead of having been put under a performance microscope and berated for playing poorly like is the case in so many more competetive team play experiences. And I feel like the mechanics have been designed expressly to foster that sort of positive public experience.  For that alone, I really can't recommend it enough.

so first of all great game, ive been playing this for 13 hours and for a free game theres alot in here.

the map:

-if you wish to you can just sail in real time towards your destination and engage ships on your way like in assasins creed black flag which i'm super happy about.
ways to get from A to B:
-you can either choose to use fast travel or you can just sail in real time and sail in the open world
the AI:
-the AI is.. well.. it's not good but also not bad, maybe needs improvements when it comes to behaviour and when to engage and when to run. combat itself they are actually quite good.
graphics:
-the graphics don't look that great but then again it's a free game, and the main focus goes clearly into making the gameplay great so kudos to that.
my experience:
so when i started you get your usual tutorial, aside a few missions your are free to do as you like once you bought your first map, you can even just go upgrade your town and make tons of money with the goods it produces or just go out and start hoarding ships like you are planning to start a huge naval invasion >.>
but there are things that need some changes in my opinion, during my play trough ive noticed i often got attacked by small ships which just run of as if they only now in battle realised my ship could easily sink them, aside that prices to sell ships are unsatisfying, you may only sell ships for a third of the buying price and it's not even worth repairing them before sale as you would just lose money on it.
ive also noticed that while i looked at the ennemy ships, the cannon hatches are closed, now.. if there werent any cannons there that would be ok.. however cannons are infact there and shoot trough the hatches as if they arent there making it hard to judge if it's worth engaging or not, this also ruins emersion a bit as i want to see the cannons sticking out to look fearsome towards your ennemy while you tell your men to open fire and release a big smoke cloud.
other cons:
-microtransactions even tho the game might rely on this to exist, but the way it's done is like a android game which kinda upsets me a little.
-the sounds of the game are really cheap, it sounds like a 2000 game and it kinda breaks emersion, great examples are the cannon and thunder sounds.
score and final note:
i actually enjoy the game, i would especially recommend this to people who liked the age of pirate series, but keep in mind this game is probably not for everyone, you need patience and a bit of strategy to kinda not end up with a tiny ship and no crew because you cannot afford to pay their salery.
overall i would rate this game 7.2/10 for what it is right now, it just needs a bit of fixing and a bit of polish but other than that it's a awesome game.

King Arthur's Gold is a multiplayer battle game, formatted similarly to a simple Terraria style. Meaning, it's 2D, smallish characters, swinging/stabbing, etc. KAG is a lot more hectic, though, and it's not uncommon to see groups of little knights swimming or digging toward another's base, while trying to kill each other. There's different classes, last I played there were three; Knight, Archer and Builder, basically.
It's pretty fun, but I have a few sticking points that kind of keep me from recommending it. One is the netcode; it's workable, but when you have so many players, it's going to be tough to keep it from being a bit laggy. And, when everything is so small on the screen, it's easy to get a little mixed up (and killed while trying to work it out).
The other bit is that building in the game can be an exercise in patience under pressure. You're meant to build up your defenses (as it's a King of the Hill-like capture game, in the main modes) while your more warrior types mix defense and offense in the game. Personally, I found building to be too annoying to bother, and generally just stabbed at whatever enemy players I could.
As with other MP games, too, it's better with friends to play with. But, with the playercount so high, it won't really be too much of an advantage, especially if you're different classes. That's not a bad thing, exactly, but it can feel a little less like playing with friends if you're on opposite sides of a large map.
Generally, games will grab me, or not, and KAG didn't. It's fun as a new experience, but that experience hasn't really pulled me back. I just haven't felt inclined to play more then those couple times.
In short, I love shotgunning Pepsi, and KAG is an okay game.

The quality and hilarity of the writing does indeed extend to the game itself, and so much more really. This is easily the best story I've ever seen in a tower defense game, and indeed it ranks among the best stories I've read in a game period. The journal adds a ton of depth to the characters, and the game has made me gasp, worry about the characters, and at one point at least openly weep. The writing is AMAZING. I cannot hammer this home enough.
"But I don't care about all that namby pamby story and characters and emotion and stuff, how's the GAME play!?" I hear you say, as I slowly reach for the lever on the makeshift guillotine poised precariously over your head. Fine. You want to know about the gameplay? I'll tell you about the gameplay. It's excellent. Tower/Hero defense games will never be earth shattering when it comes to innovating mechanics, but this is a very solid, tightly balanced tower defense game, and the most fun one I think I've ever played. Placement and tactics can make all the difference, but in true RPG fashion, you can always go level up and unlock some new skills or upgrade your equipment if your strategy of choice isn't -quiiiiitttee- cutting it.
(A word about difficulty: if you play the game on normal, it's pretty easy, possibly distressingly so if you want a challenge. Play on advanced if you want the challenge, though you may want to come back later with new classes for certain enemies.)
It's the RPG side of the gameplay that really has me hooked, trying to move the story forward to unlock new shops for better gear and then using that gear to go back and try the expert level which lets me get some extra scrap for new gear or even better unlock a new UNIQUE ITEM (oooh, aaahhh) which, in new game + can be upgraded with delicious magic skulls for extremely epic unique items that have unique abilities as well. The gameplay loop is so engaging I have more than once looked up and noticed that 6 hours have gone by without me realizing.
TL;DR: It's great. buy it. If you want to wait for a sale go for it, but seriously, buy it. amazing writing, excellent tower defense gameplay, and excellent RPG gameplay.

This is one of the best sci-fi films I've seen in years.  There's no flashy graphics, alien invasions, or apocalyptic scenarios.  It doesn't spend a bunch of screen time ratcheting up false tensions, piling on mountains of expository dialogue, or following predictable movie tropes.  The "hook" is presented with an unapologetic lack of explanation.  The viewer is thrown into the chaos alongside the characters trying to piece it all together.  This is smart sci-fi and a great character-driven thriller.
Multiple viewings are encouraged and rewarded.  I've seen it several times and I've loved it more each time.  There are lots of little details that might be missed on a first viewing which have profound implication upon subsequent viewings, such as one character's quick glance at an object in the room or a line spoken off camera that is barely registered the first time around.  I won't ruin the plot in this review and suggest going into this film knowing as little as possible.  It's interesting piecing it all together and if you love it as I did, you'll want to watch it again and again to pick up on all the subtle details.  I had a bunch of "oh sh-t!" moments on my third viewing once I started paying really close attention.
The way it was filmed is also really interesting.  This is an indie film with a $50k budget shot on Canon 5D's.  It was filmed at the director's own house over the course of 5 nights with only pair of cameras, a skeleton crew, and completely natural lighting.  The most interesting thing is that the acting is entirely improv.  The actors had no scripts.  They didn't know the story ahead of time.  It was filmed like a mystery dinner party, with the actors staying in-character, and the director as master of ceremonies pulling strings behind the curtain.  Before each scene the actors received a small sheet of notes directing them as to what their character should accomplish.  He left it in the actors' hands to craft the scene, only pausing to "right the ship" when they started veering too far off course.  What we get from this are natural conversations and genuine characters while the actors work together to craft a coherent story.  They're figuring it all out as they go, just like the audience.  It's a fun way to create a film, certainly too risky in the big-budget space, but it really works here to create a compelling, refreshing experience.
I have a couple gripes with the Steam version.  It appears this film is only currently available at a maximum of 544p resolution.  The store page suggests 720p and proper 1080p options are available, as listed in the recommended system requirements, but these options were not present at my time of viewing.  I've also viewed this film on Amazon Prime Video and it has a 1080p option, so it shouldn't be a matter of availability of a "full HD" version.
Also, some scenes are particularly dark due to filming outdoors at night and using only natural lighting sources.  Due to the low-light conditions and digital compression there are occasionally color banding and artifacting issues.  Despite these technical issues, this is one of my favorite indie films of all time and I look forward to see more from this director in the future.

When they got bored I spent some more time farming for upgrades and doing bosses, but I didn't really get too far solo.
An important thing to mention is that in multiplayer, everyone sees the game from the same perspective. The camera focuses on the average position of all the players in the squad and you can't leave the field of view which makes running long distances while fighting off enemies a hasle.
The game has a server wide metagame where the missions you do contribute to the ongoing war by helping capture territory. This means that you get a new selection of random missions to do every time a territory is captured, but it also locks you out of fighting a faction if the war against them has been won. This can lead to only missions for one faction being available for as much as a couple real time days if they're the last one standing.

Vampire: The Maquerade - Bloodlines was developed by Troika, who went bankrupt in 2005, only a few months after the game's release.
The strongest points of this RPG are without any doubt it's fantastically dark atmosphere and the charm of the NPC's. By using the Source facial animation the developers have surpassed themselves by providing lively expressions for each meaningful characters, an extra surplus being the great voice acting. What characters say is impressive too, you're gonna laugh with guys like Jack or Fat Larry or you just feel that a person is trying to win you over (what doesn't necessarily needs to be done with speech, Jeanette's and VV's 'attributes' on their own may be enough ... for some of you). Rest assured that these dialogues will keep you busy for a long time without getting boring. The people on the streets and in buildings aren't worked extensively and usually don't do much more than just walking around, you can't even talk with them. They're just dumb, moving bags of blood.
This game is a masterpiece and Wesp's Basic Unofficial Patch actually fixes every bug in the game, while the UP Plus also restores content (maps, quests) that was dropped by Troika for various reasons. VtMB has a high replay value and there are also mods like Clan Quest, Camarilla Edition, Final Nights and Antitribu to increase that.

Now that I can analyse it in hindsight years after first having played, it is clear that Civilization V, while looking prettier than predecessors such as III and IV, was painfully dumbed down in comparison to them. That isn't to say that it's without its merits, but it just isn't deserving of that "grand strategy" tag it has in the slightest – both because it isn't even in that genre and because it's severely lacking genuine challenges.
Even when one places the game on its hardest difficulty setting – that being "deity" – it remains easy for anyone with the mind to figure out how the rather simplistic AI works and that ranged units are generally the way to go from the start to achieve a victory. This is because the only real change in "difficulty" on higher levels are various handicaps for the AI, which is completely incompetent in naval warfare might I add.
If Steam had a number rating system, I could be more generous here, because this game did provide me with some fun times regardless. However, this was only possible thanks to mods, and between a thumbs up and a thumbs down, I simply cannot with a straight face recommend a game that requires mods to make it enjoyable to anyone. Mods are not a part of the purchase as-is.
Perhaps some will find it enjoyable anyways, and that's good for them, but I see no reason to play an unmodified Civilization V over its predecessors. It is simply not a challenging game, although with that said, it remains leagues above VI, which is shaping up to be a DLC-laden mess (among other questionable decisions). Hopefully the developers will have learned from their mistakes with V and VI when the time comes to make VII.

I'm really sitting on a 'Maybe' recommendation, leaning towards recommending it.
Other reviews will tell you about the pros; I'll tell you about how "accessible" it is.
And it's not that accessible.
Sure, the tutorial tells you what you need to know, but that's as far as it goes.
It doesn't teach you about some of the cooperative mechanics like loading someone else's rocket launcher.
Nor does it tell you (read: only in loading screens, rarely) how calling down 'Stratagems' and being near objectives will attract unwanted attention - and (I haven't read this anywhere yet) how you sometimes ought to just run away.
That, and there's a strong emphasis on momentum and equipment choice. If your team keeps having friendly fire mishaps and/or they're having to call down 'Stratagems' at objectives, things can go downhill fast. Really fast.
But if you can get past the hidden quirks and work with the tactical gameplay, you'll do alright.
Overall, I recommend either reaching out to existing players in the community, or to buy an extra copy or two for close friends.
Also dedicate some time to reading gameplay guides.
Trust me. If you can't be bothered, and just want to throw yourself into a high-level mission expecting others to drag you through it, that just won't happen in Helldivers.

1. Player skill is the SINGLE biggest factor in whether or not you will have a good run.  And by a huge margin.  If you think otherwise, you need to play this game more, watch some videos of more experienced players, and see some of the excellent tricks you can use to play more effectively.

The starting ship is actually quite strong (unwinnable runs simply don't exist with this ship, IMO), but many of the ships you can unlock are just bad, giving you quite a challenge. The world Troika built is fantastic, and absolutely oozing with the kind of atmosphere you want in a Vampire RPG. At one point in the game, you'll appear in a room in Santa Monica. I personally sat there for like an hour just listening to the news on the tv, and then listening to Deb of Night on the radio. it's the kind of thing that really brings the game to life. I tuned in every so often to check if there were any new stories. There's also a lot of really memorable characters in Vampire: The Masquerade. All of whom are wonderful to meet, good, evil, or in between. I really liked the setting as well, the game world you get to explore has a really interesting aesthetic that channels gothic horror. From Santa Monica to Chinatown, all the locations have a wonderful look to them. Some with a run-down 80s aesthetic to them that reminds me of The Terminator (1984) and Escape From New York. The asian locations feel like something out of a John Woo movie. They're all great. A lot of the businesses and buildings have really interesting or funny names too, that I just love. The OST is mainly different genres of rock, and is pretty cool, I definetly enjoyed it as well. That's not to say that it is without problems though. While the characters are all mostly well written, and well voiced, a lot of the voices seem to suffer from some audio issues, like some characters randomly talking way too quietly, or sometimes seeming to be talking into a tin can. The character progression isn't stellar either. You only gain experience from completing quests and objectives, and instead of levels, you directly use experience to purchase points in various skills and abilities. Which doesn't sound all that bad, but you don't get to use a skill point that often, and most the changes are negligible. Another thing annoyed me was doors. Walking through doors is a pain. You have to wait for the door to open completely, and it opens very slowly. If you try to go through while it's opening, you'll get stuck in the door way. The combat in this game is action based, and isn't that good either. In fact you'll probably try to avoid it in your playthrough using stealth and the social mechanics. This game is very bittersweet, on one hand the setting is really amazing, and the characters and places in this game are lovely. On the other, Troika being forced to publish the game before it was finished makes it suffer from bugs that make it unplayable (Unless you have Wesp5's Unofficial Patch), and lack of content. It seems like the city zones could have potentially been bigger and better, if Troika had enough time. As they are, they're still great, but in the back of your mind you won't be able to help thinking what could have been, with more npcs wandering about, more places to visit, and more to do. Do I recommend this game? Yes. Even with all its problems, I'd still say that it is an absolute classic and there isn't really another game like it.

"You know, I think it's important to keep a balance in things. Yeah, balance, that's the right word. Cause the guy who wants too much, risks losing absolutely everything. Of course, the guy who wants too little from life, might not get anything at all." - Thomas Angelo - 1951
This game. This game is one of the best story driven open-world games I have EVER seen. Sweet Jesus I could spend days playing the story of this game and never get bored, never lose the feeling of awe at some points, never not enjoy this beautiful game.
You take up the role of Vito Scaletta, a man who seeks to better himself one way or another, if that means a life of crime then does he care? Nope, but he holds moral values and a sensible mindset that clash brilliantly with his lifelong friend Joe Barbaro, and thats where this game has some of its best story, two lifelong friends as they finally get what they dreamt of as children, but as Thomas Angelo said, they risk everything.
Mafia II brings amazing old music from the 40's and 50's and delivers a gritty experience which I would happily play through again again. Any fan of Mafia: The City of Lost Heaven should definetly play this, and so should any fan of a good plot.
It has little flaws, but these literally only matter if you play this game for the open-world, not the story, which is simply a pointless thing to do.
10/10

Not many games cover this period at all and it was werid since probably my favorite part was just driving around in classic cars listening to the classics on the radio. Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines, is Role Playing game released in 2004. You can play in both First or Third-person Mode, as one of several vampire clans each with their own abilities and gameplay style: Playing as Nosferatu, are especially challenging. You start the game as a fledgling vampire who has to find your way through the streets of Los Angeles. Along the way you learn about the Various Vampire clans, as well as investigate a recently discovered relic that is supposed to bring an end to all vampires. The story takes you through Santa Monica, Downtown Los Angeles, Hollywood, Chinatown, as well as the Underground.
I don't want to go into the story to much, due to spoilers, but I will say the game has varying levels of difficult depending on what clan you choose to play as. You have the ability to create ghouls, which are humans who are fed Vampire blood, giving them powers, and binding the ghoul to you. I have had the opportunity to play a multitude of great FPS titles over the last two decades.  This, however, is not one of them.  I had high hopes given the posted reviews.  I ran down my checklist:  FPS, check.  Survival horror, check.  Post-apocalyptic environment replete with humans of questionable moral fortitude and beasts derived from the repetative and erroneous cell replication cycles of a former intact genome that is now subject to the random DNA strand damage induced by the ionizing radiation of radioisotopes released into the atmosphere as the result of nuclear war...check!  Unfortunately, despite the contents of the recipe card looking as though once combined, the whole would provide a palatable multi-course meal fit for the most uncompromising of gamer gadflys, the final result was more akin to boxed mac and cheese...with powdered cheese.  The storyline was dull and haphazard, the cut scenes were protracted beyond reasonable tolerance, the level design was  wrought with beautiful but invariabley boring and laborious transitions and the persona of the main character seemed less developed than the career goals of a 15-year-old boy with the attention span of a rabid squirrel (I contend redundancy on that last analogy).  I rarely write reviews on games.  And this is really only a superficial opinion as I could go on and on...and on.   I just couldn't let this one sink gently into the Marianas Trench of my Steam Library without giving it a little kick to help it on its way.

Metro 2033 Redux is a very meat and potatoes game, in terms of actual gameplay. Everything you've seen in the average shooter, you'll see here. The typical variety of weapons, mechanics, stealth, all the typical ingredient that make a shooter a shooter in the modern day. You'll see an annoying amount of point of no return ledge drops and such, and you will learn to search thoroughly. If you came here looking for a spiritual successor to S.T.A.L.K.E.R., you won't find it in the mechanics.
What makes it different from every other shooter is the setting. Metro is a very tense game, with good plot, light enough for the more run and gun fanatics, but enough present for those who enjoy their plot. It's one of those games that keeps your attention. Whilst the gameplay itself is very basic, the features draw you in. Artyom's movements feel quite natural, the ability for your gas mask to get spattered upon, and the ability to wipe it off was an interesting touch, the visuals are quite good even on my low end machine,
Overall, I'd say the game is worth a look, especially for those who enjoy a touch of the survival, and thoroughly enjoy their post-apoc games. Ideally, I've love to see the Metro team and original Author work on a S.T.A.L.K.E.R. title. If you're looking for an atmospheric shooter, definitely get the Metro series. And if you enjoy this one, get Last Light too.

Tower Defense games used to be a bit rare. Now they're a dime a dozen on Steam. The real question is "which ones are worth a damn?" and in my opinion, Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten is one such worthwhile TD. Why? Well, let's see...
It has a cartoon-like look to it, and has a smooth design, in my opinion. It's nothing visually jaw-dropping, but it gets the job done, and I feel like the characters' facial expressions and body language did an excellent job emoting and making me like the characters more. I won't say more on that until the story section, though.
I really liked the music in this game. I wouldn't compare it to memorable tracks from a Final Fantasy game or a SuperGiant game (Bastion, etc.), but it's still good stuff that fits in well and was enjoyable while it played.
Your protagonist summons different combat characters into a maze-like pre-established battle map, and as per the typical TD, you can place the characters where you want. The protagonist is locked down in a pre-set starting position and is the "core" or "lives" you're trying to guard. Each of the characters you summon can be "boosted" (i.e. leveled up per battle) up to five times, unlocking new abilities for use in the fight which will help out.
I played this game twice: once something several years ago...a little while after it first came out and got a discount, and again just last night and tonight. The first time, I hired recruits, and the extra unnamed characters deteriorated my interest in the game and I stopped playing for a couple of years because I didn't like the recruits. This time, however, I was compelled to complete the game, as a "hero mode" setting (new, I think) was available where you only use story characters in battles, meaning a maximum of six combatants plus your spell-slinging protagonist.
Each level has different rewards and star ratings with various difficulties to play them at. You can get unique gear that can't be bought in the game's various shops that is often better than what's offered in shops lby doing the tougher difficulties on maps. When you complete the game, new game + is unlocked. You can either go back to your first playthrough and try to get more stars/items unlocked, or you can start over in new game + with your gear and XP, and try to take the game on again. That said, I got my butt handed to me badly on new game + so I went back to the first playthrough. Unfortunately, despite my best efforts and doing a respec on my protagonist, I was not good enough to get the higher-star scenarios done in the latter part of a cave system onward. I could have tried the second hardest difficulty, but I didn't really want to bother with that.
I know I'm being redundant here, but this is a tower defense game...with a
that's not awful. In fact, the good ending (there are two endings!) was rather satisfying and felt like a better conclusion than I've seen to a lot of movies, and certainly better than I've seen in most games. The dev kept the number of characters small enough to be fairly memorable and give different characters screen time, and the aforementioned facial expressions and the characters' dialog are bursting with charm. He enjoys being silly, and I found myself smiling many times throughout the game's storyline, thanks to the more entertaining characters' lines.
I even really liked the lead protagonist. Leaders of groups are often very uninteresting, portrayed as perfectly balanced and level-headed, not doing anything exciting or interesting, and lacking fun dialog. With Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten, this was handled well in my opinion.
Azra, the lead character in Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten, is fairly straight-laced externally, but does have some playful dialog with different characters, and you can read her journal which has tons of updates, both lore-filled and incredibly silly. It makes her a far better character than most group leaders I've seen in entertainment, and I cared about her and the other team members.
NOTE TO DEV: In the "bad" ending, I can't recall it perfectly, but a word was missing in the text across the screen when it's dark. They're talking about a length of time that passed, and a word is missing on the screen. It may have been "to" or "for" or something like that. It was a brief word that was missing.
Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten is graphically simple, yet attractive in a nicely-drawn cartoon fashion, with enjoyable tower defense gameplay, and perhaps the deepest storyline I've seen in a tower defense game, at least from a character depth and lore depth perspective. This game obviously comes from a developer who was very into what he was making. Many people can be developers these days, put out a garbage game, and put no effort into it. Defender's Quest: Valley of the Forgotten couldn't be further from that. It is one of the TDs I have enjoyed the most. I came for the gameplay, but I stayed for the storyline/characters. It's bizarre, but I'm okay with this. :D

If you loved playing Final Fantasy, Legend of Zelda, or other such games on the early Nintendo systems you will love this.
There were always two things about particularly Final Fantasy type games that I didn't like as much (that I've heard plenty others complain about as well):
1. SO MANY RANDOM MONSTER BATTLES OH MY GOD. They are less common in this game and there's a Pokemon-esque item that keeps monsters away for a bit. Inexpensive to buy in the shop and makes my life so much better. Even better, once you've played a bit, it gets BETTER. Eventually you will receive an item that allows you to turn off random encounters until you wanna turn them back on. Amazing. Perfect. Wonderful. Yes. This makes me particularly happy because there are a lot of fun hidden things in the big world and it's nice to be able to go looking for them without having to go through all those encounters!! (I would say, definitely turn encounters back on enough to level up, but it's amazing to have the choice.)
2. If you stop playing for too long and don't take copious notes while playing, you'll come back and have no idea what you were doing. Sojouner gives you a fun Telepathy Ring to contact the queen at any time to remind you about what you were trying to do. I haven't had this issue anyway because I have been binge-playing this because it is a load of fun and not so frustrating (thanks largely to the ability to turn off encounters when I don't feel like battling a load)... so I guess that's another feature that helps with that issue!
I'm at the very end of the game (I'm pretty sure) and have played for about 13.3 hours total (not in one go). I feel like there's a bit more to be done and this boss battle is kicking my butt, BUT when I get frustrated with that, I can go on a fun SOJOURN (heheh) to another place to train up, explore, do a side quest, and/or get more fun items.
I used to (and really still do) love those old RPGs, but they really did frustrate me so much. Sojourner fixes a lot of what frustrated me while lovingly poking fun at the flaws and quirks of old games. It has some really lovely messages put in, loads of fun extras to find, and a wonderful sense of humour. Plus it's only $4.99, y'all! You can't beat that pricing! Seriously though, you guys should play this thing.

Since the game first appeared, lots of people have asked and discussed how KAG relates and compares to games like MineCraft and Terraria. I haven't actually played either of the two, but I've watched enough trailers and gameplay videos, I think, to say something about the differences. Firstly, KAG is more oriented around hectic team-versus-team combat in a couple of different flavors. Secondly, it features different classes with different abilities that really requires practice to master. The graphics are also 2D, with very crisp, blocky, cheerful sprites. Oh, and there are physics, effects and different player head costmetics. The crafting system is more shallow and simple; you harvest/mine resources or gather coins that you trade in for buildings, other materials, weapons or tools.
The game features several modes. Some of them I've mentioned. There's also a sort of obstacle course mode and a sandbox mode (single player). Sadly, that's all there is of official content (apart from a weird mod example). Previously, the game featured other modes such as a zombie survival mode. The good thing is, the game has a relatively good mod support, which people have taken advantage of to bring the zombie mode, amongst others, back to the game. There are also various other custom modes. Lately, I've mostly played theese mods.
I love the action in this game, and I love building stuff. There's plenty of humor in the crazy battles and accidental deaths (sadly, there used to be more of those, but anyway). Graphics-wise it's top notch. Music is alright, but I wouldn't say no to more variety. There are some annoying quirks to building that I really had hoped they would sometime fix, but they have not. Some latency problems on certain servers (might especially apply to some modded servers). All in all though, it's just a lot of fun.
If the gameplay videos doesn't convince you, trying it should. Of course, it might not be everyone's cup of tea, fair enough. But I, at least, have had heaps of fun with this. It's quite addictive, and even after being away from it a long while, I fell a bit in love with it all over again. Well worth the price.
2015.10.05: The game is still being updated, but not like it used to. Sadly, the people who worked on the game initially have stated they are "done" with it. Instead, they are working on other projects. Fortunately, they've hired someone to add some new things. That said, the game still has some issues that have really never gotten fixed, but they do occational fixes, so I hope some day they will address it. I think this game still has a big potential, even considering how good it already is.

King Arthur has a huge gameplay.
You can see the vids and the store page to be interrested like me.
There are tons of things to do.
But in multiplayer... oh god... this is so frustrating to be overwhelmed like that ! [Long review]
3 classes: Builder, Knight and Archer.
Quite simple to grasp the basics with few tutorials.
You build a castle with tons of elements in few mins (2 or 3) and go fight the enemy and test its own defenses.
So where is the problem ? If this rich gameplay has been implemented it's for a good reason, right ?
It's because there is too much to handle and the game is absolutely unoptimize.
Take a look at the following....
BUILDER:
You try to build simple defenses. Wood, the weaker, Stone, the strongest. The main  problem is directly link to this class: King Arthur's Gold is not a Sandbox game !  As an example you can't move soils such as dirt. There is no editor, so every maps are design by the developpers. An other problem is you have no wooden traps. The only availiable a retractable spike. It can kill your friends and  you have to build a special block that makes enemies fall through instead of you team. The fact is that you have to spend a huge amount of stones to build a simple trap system. Securing a flag or an entrance is horribly long and quite often you get blocked by the "trap block" because you can't pass through... Even aiming the blocks to build and even digging is hard. You will rant when you will see this little red arrow with a horrible sound to show "you can't build here" (thanks we haven't noticed !!).
Add to that the fact that when you missed your clic you can't deconstruct your block.
Very nice to endure when you are in the fire of the action and a trap needs to be finished in a hurry ! (in general a guy from the opposite team is coming at you...).
And it's really, REALLY, annoying to be rushed all the time by "Airborn" knights carrying bombs (Knight after droping a bomb can use his shield to propels him in the airs and glide anywhere holding the shield above him like a hang-glider). And the situation is absolutely obvious when you see a lone guy exploding the walls you put so long to build.
People will tell you, you have siege weapons!
But you can be propelled with a catapult and again it's a huge boost of mobility. For the non rushing team it's a sentence of death because building siege weapons needs a lot of stone, A LOT (Wood can respawn but it's not the case for stone). And when you die few times in a desperate attempt to repair or rebuild the structures previously destroyed by few kamikaze... you start to be angry.
Considering the fact that you just can't store the materials you've found for the rest of the team, can't fight correctly as a builder (because you only score points when you kill someone) or even building a decent base at the start (around 3 mins to do it !). You can buy items for the Builder, such as a drill, but like all aspects of the game, nothing mentions that the drill overheat and is unavailiable for few mins. So nobody use it. You can understand how frustrating this game can be as a builder.
KNIGHT:
Exhausted of building stuff that won't last more than few mins, you try your luck as a close combat fighter [Not a Kamikaze Knight of course].
But it's delightfull to fight and being unable to chain few blows without being overwhelmed by characters and explosions (bobies are persistent and can be picked up, so if someone dies it will block the line of sight of everybody and instead of taking valuables you will take a corpse ...). In general you click in the mass of pixels and hope to reach your target. In the fire of the action you will be unable to see the small hearts of the ennemy (his health of course). Note that if you died you won't have enough money to buy the bombs (you can throw it even before dying to blow everything... Kamikaze Style !).
So you go to range fight when you have enough of getting killed. If you look deeper on the forums, you will find that some dudes has mouse mods so they can burst you in melee if you are a regular player like me [translation: a fair play man].
ARCHER:
You have a bow, you shoot, simple enough ? No.
Consider the fact that you have a long time to load the arrow, the low damage it does and the fact that you can't see correctly if you damaged the target. You have a special attack wich throws 3 arrows, but the way to use it is so much complicate that you won't us it. Only in close combat if you have luck to land one or two arrows on the target and in general you have a knight in front of you (whe can use the same shield to glide to protect him... yes sir).
You can use a grappling hook to reach higher locations (by the way it's very hard to build high towers) but this tool is so unaccurate and with a very limited range that quite often you will loose your life in a desperate way to aim/evaluate the distance/ and dodge the incoming foe.
Bomb jump is much better in terms of efficiency and power.
Add to that ammunitions, because you have basic and special arrows like the fire one to burn wooden structures or the bomb arrow for stone. An other great way to reduce to ashes the work of Builders...
So like all players you won't stay long as an Archer and go Knight.
Again if you die you will drop some gold the enemy can use to buy ammunitions,
and if you rush and place shops on the way to the enemy base you will win quickly with continuous Kamikaze Knights...
IN GENERAL:
The concept is appealing but frankly the learning curve is horrible and there is too much content.
I never thought i would say something like that...
You rarely understand why something didn't worked especially during a fight where 2 or 3 secs determines the fate of your character.
You have so many game mechanics that you can't handle everything at the same time. As, again, for a Builder you can't extinguish the fire on wooden structures. You have to take an other class and buy a water bomb/ water arrow. So you can't even defend buildings yourself except if you build a balista or a catapult.
But like many other games the community doesn't help and explains nothing (the text window is bad, even the dozens of emote icons: players just uses smileys to laugh in front of your death, only one guy used it correctly to say to build a tower on a location).
There are many cheaters (without any protection against them) and even if some players are really good, we don't know if they use mods.
Things are quite often unfair like when the maps puts you to the worst location or the overall design is bad.

King Arthur has a huge gameplay.

But in multiplayer... oh god... this is so frustrating to be overwhelmed like that ! [Long review]
3 classes: Builder, Knight and Archer.
Quite simple to grasp the basics with few tutorials.
You build a castle with tons of elements in few mins (2 or 3) and go fight the enemy and test its own defenses.
So where is the problem ? If this rich gameplay has been implemented it's for a good reason, right ?
It's because there is too much to handle and the game is absolutely unoptimize.
Take a look at the following....
BUILDER:
You try to build simple defenses. Wood, the weaker, Stone, the strongest. The main  problem is directly link to this class: King Arthur's Gold is not a Sandbox game !  As an example you can't move soils such as dirt. There is no editor, so every maps are design by the developpers. An other problem is you have no wooden traps. The only availiable a retractable spike. It can kill your friends and  you have to build a special block that makes enemies fall through instead of you team. The fact is that you have to spend a huge amount of stones to build a simple trap system. Securing a flag or an entrance is horribly long and quite often you get blocked by the "trap block" because you can't pass through... Even aiming the blocks to build and even digging is hard. You will rant when you will see this little red arrow with a horrible sound to show "you can't build here" (thanks we haven't noticed !!).
Add to that the fact that when you missed your clic you can't deconstruct your block.
Very nice to endure when you are in the fire of the action and a trap needs to be finished in a hurry ! (in general a guy from the opposite team is coming at you...).
And it's really, REALLY, annoying to be rushed all the time by "Airborn" knights carrying bombs (Knight after droping a bomb can use his shield to propels him in the airs and glide anywhere holding the shield above him like a hang-glider). And the situation is absolutely obvious when you see a lone guy exploding the walls you put so long to build.
People will tell you, you have siege weapons!
But you can be propelled with a catapult and again it's a huge boost of mobility. For the non rushing team it's a sentence of death because building siege weapons needs a lot of stone, A LOT (Wood can respawn but it's not the case for stone). And when you die few times in a desperate attempt to repair or rebuild the structures previously destroyed by few kamikaze... you start to be angry.
Considering the fact that you just can't store the materials you've found for the rest of the team, can't fight correctly as a builder (because you only score points when you kill someone) or even building a decent base at the start (around 3 mins to do it !). You can buy items for the Builder, such as a drill, but like all aspects of the game, nothing mentions that the drill overheat and is unavailiable for few mins. So nobody use it. You can understand how frustrating this game can be as a builder.
KNIGHT:
Exhausted of building stuff that won't last more than few mins, you try your luck as a close combat fighter [Not a Kamikaze Knight of course].
But it's delightfull to fight and being unable to chain few blows without being overwhelmed by characters and explosions (bobies are persistent and can be picked up, so if someone dies it will block the line of sight of everybody and instead of taking valuables you will take a corpse ...). In general you click in the mass of pixels and hope to reach your target. In the fire of the action you will be unable to see the small hearts of the ennemy (his health of course). Note that if you died you won't have enough money to buy the bombs (you can throw it even before dying to blow everything... Kamikaze Style !).
So you go to range fight when you have enough of getting killed. If you look deeper on the forums, you will find that some dudes has mouse mods so they can burst you in melee if you are a regular player like me [translation: a fair play man].
ARCHER:
You have a bow, you shoot, simple enough ? No.
Consider the fact that you have a long time to load the arrow, the low damage it does and the fact that you can't see correctly if you damaged the target. You have a special attack wich throws 3 arrows, but the way to use it is so much complicate that you won't us it. Only in close combat if you have luck to land one or two arrows on the target and in general you have a knight in front of you (whe can use the same shield to glide to protect him... yes sir).
You can use a grappling hook to reach higher locations (by the way it's very hard to build high towers) but this tool is so unaccurate and with a very limited range that quite often you will loose your life in a desperate way to aim/evaluate the distance/ and dodge the incoming foe.
Bomb jump is much better in terms of efficiency and power.
Add to that ammunitions, because you have basic and special arrows like the fire one to burn wooden structures or the bomb arrow for stone. An other great way to reduce to ashes the work of Builders...
So like all players you won't stay long as an Archer and go Knight.
Again if you die you will drop some gold the enemy can use to buy ammunitions,
and if you rush and place shops on the way to the enemy base you will win quickly with continuous Kamikaze Knights...
IN GENERAL:
The concept is appealing but frankly the learning curve is horrible and there is too much content.
I never thought i would say something like that...
You rarely understand why something didn't worked especially during a fight where 2 or 3 secs determines the fate of your character.
You have so many game mechanics that you can't handle everything at the same time. As, again, for a Builder you can't extinguish the fire on wooden structures. You have to take an other class and buy a water bomb/ water arrow. So you can't even defend buildings yourself except if you build a balista or a catapult.
But like many other games the community doesn't help and explains nothing (the text window is bad, even the dozens of emote icons: players just uses smileys to laugh in front of your death, only one guy used it correctly to say to build a tower on a location).

More Details:

Been looking for a card game since trying Gwent and enjoying it (Card game noob here).  Was intimidated by the scale of Magic and such (I will go that route at some point though).  Took a chance on this game and played it for 9 hours straight.  Very fun and easy to get into but with some real stategy on card placement.  A few bugs here and there but hopefully devs will keep refining the game.  In short, I really like this game and recomend it.

"Trading card game" is not an appropriate description for this one - a better name would be "Tactical card game". Decromancer differs from most of the card titles out there in that it's much less random and focuses more on placement.
You don't have a "hand" from which to play cards, instead - you have a grid on which to place them.
All the cards you have are available from the start of a battle, but you're limited to only 3 creatures per turn.
The resources you have to summon cards do not grow with time (only with your character level), so plan wisely
Creature cards have attack patterns on the grid, so their placement matter a LOT..and of course many also have special abilities, but that's not so novel.
The game is a port from mobile devices and so one should be prepared for some characteristic elements that are more suited to mobile, but the developer is still working on implementing some additions to make use of what PCs have to offer - like hotkeys. There's still traces of microtransactions here and there, but honestly - you never needed to make those in the first place - all the game has to offer is avalable through normal play. Sure it does mean a bit of grinding, but  not an awful lot and the grind itself is not a a boring thing you just keep doing over and over - replaying some known battles actually lets you try out some different tactics and polish up your skills.
There are of course some bad sides - biggest of all is that the game is mostly singleplayer. The only mp element is a hotseat skirmish. Decromancer doesn't make use of network connections, sorry. At least you can play it when you're out of range without losing anything.
There are some bugs of course, but that's what we - the players and community testers are here for to find them and the developer takes our reports seriously, plus the bugs we find so far aren't something gamebreaking so it's quite a job well done so far. Mind you that's a small developer without a big marketing department so it might take time to react and long periods of silence, but that only means they're focusing on getting the game right instead of flinging empty words.
to sum it up (TL;DR ?)
pros:
-Focus on tactics and planning - in battle, not just in deckbuilding
-No microtransactions to access every element of the game
-Well-made consistent single player campaign
-The usual stuff that makes a game playable
cons:
- only hotseat multiplayer

They have 2 versions of the game; a classic version and a standard version both with slightly different controls and very different options.

I tried windows borderless gaming and it wouldn't work. There's a supposed fix using windows magnify to zoom in on the window to make it look full screen but that was a horrible fix to what should be a non-issue.
Secondly the controls. I assume because the game is so basic they assume, somewhat correctly you will figure it out - which you do but if you bring up the options menu, there's no resolution settings and the control settings have things like a = c, j1 = c , no jump, run, talk, just letters for letters on the keyboard or letters for joystil keys. It makes absoulutely no sense.
I get from all the praise that a lot of love went into the story but it's packaged in such a poor way I just couldn't bring myself to play it any longer.

Defender's Quest is not your average Tower Defense game, but what it does, it does really well. It has a nice story, good cartoon art design, whacky characters and a simple to learn yet hard to master core mechanic of tower placements and upgrades as well as about 40 different maps counting all bonus levels and challenges, all of which have an alternate harder version in NG+. Complexity wise it's on the smaller end of the spectrum with only 6 different hero (tower) types and a maximum of 36 towers in total. It also requires to shift heroes (towers) on demand during a map which makes the whole game also a resource management game under great pressure, although it is always possible to completely halt the game while being able to issue commands as well as to up to speed up the game by a whopping factor of 16.
All in all: Great accessibility, time well spent and a good game to recommend to fans of the genre.

There is a reasonable amount of strategy involved, as some levels will take a little trial and error to complete without taking any damage, and the unit cost and unit limit are well balanced in this regard.
Shortcomings are mostly that the game could have had much more depth on the RPG side - equipment is fairly limited in variety, and characters and units have relatively low skill/level cap compared to most games. This game has a more gradual progression to character power as you play rather than some games that ramp up quickly or more dramatically.
Overall a perfectly enjoyable tower defense and certainly worth playing for fans of the genre.

This is not a run and gun game (on Hard (the hardest difficulty, and the only one I played it on)), if you try to, you will be shot dead if they have anything but melee weapons or pistols.
Despite this not being a run and gun game, you still take on hoards of enemies, but consider your deadliness more of luck and skill rather than dumb enemies, for I died many a time, especially on the last mission, for the enemies are not bad shots at all, you just have to time it right for when you decide to shoot and when you decide to duck and cover... you have the "advantage" of being in 3rd person mode
The vehicle AI's in this game are impeccable; they drive feasibly... meaning they will attempt to avoid crashing into you, but not via oversteering. Only once in the entire game did a vehicle turn into me and that is because I did a hard swerve at high speeds around a vehicle onto the wrong side of the road and back over the right side of the road, the vehicle braked a bit and turned to its left (of which anyone would do who sees a vehicle swerving over into its side of the road at height speeds angled towards its side of the road sidewalk). The people can be run over, but are usually smart and dodge out of the way at a realistic rate.
MINOR SPOILERS FOLLOW:
The story has one vehicle race absurdly fast away from you (you feel like you are keeping a good pace with them then they just take-off), which is realistic since they are in a  hot rod and just had to shift up, but it is unfair you have no option to actually catch them.
On one mission one can be stealthy and kill guards methodically... or one can just shoot them all and engage in a massive firefight that is realistically hard (the cops/guards know how to shoot, but can miss (makes them feel human)). No-one just haphazardly runs out, the AI's are tactical in positioning, and tend to pop out at the same time to shoot you. Only one time in the entire game did I see AI's have an issue, and that was with a closed door in a drug acquisition shootout of which the AI's couldn't open and would teleport through after a fashion about 8 feet on the other side of the door (they teleported behind me).
The game has various alternate outcome situations... for instance, in one car chase you can disable a guys car and run him down, push him off the road so he has to back up, get out while he is doing so, and shoot him, chase him to his destination and have a shootout, or lose him and go back to Joe's (your friends) apartment.

There lurks a dark in-game purchase store, a stain on the otherwise clean image of this game, but I don't think enough people use multiplayer for anything that can be used there to be a problem. I have fond memories of crappy pirate webgames from my childhood, much, much worse than this, so that may be biasing my review a bit, but all in all this deserves a 7.5/10. Not a fabulous work of art, but not garbage either. In a world of half-baked free games that occasionally pester you to give them money, this one stands out in a good way.

King Arthur has a huge gameplay.
You can see the vids and the store page to be interrested like me.
There are tons of things to do.
But in multiplayer... oh god... this is so frustrating to be overwhelmed like that ! [Long review]
3 classes: Builder, Knight and Archer.
Quite simple to grasp the basics with few tutorials.
You build a castle with tons of elements in few mins (2 or 3) and go fight the enemy and test its own defenses.
So where is the problem ? If this rich gameplay has been implemented it's for a good reason, right ?
It's because there is too much to handle and the game is absolutely unoptimize.
Take a look at the following....
BUILDER:
You try to build simple defenses. Wood, the weaker, Stone, the strongest. The main  problem is directly link to this class: King Arthur's Gold is not a Sandbox game !  As an example you can't move soils such as dirt. There is no editor, so every maps are design by the developpers. An other problem is you have no wooden traps. The only availiable a retractable spike. It can kill your friends and  you have to build a special block that makes enemies fall through instead of you team. The fact is that you have to spend a huge amount of stones to build a simple trap system. Securing a flag or an entrance is horribly long and quite often you get blocked by the "trap block" because you can't pass through... Even aiming the blocks to build and even digging is hard. You will rant when you will see this little red arrow with a horrible sound to show "you can't build here" (thanks we haven't noticed !!).
Add to that the fact that when you missed your clic you can't deconstruct your block.
Very nice to endure when you are in the fire of the action and a trap needs to be finished in a hurry ! (in general a guy from the opposite team is coming at you...).
And it's really, REALLY, annoying to be rushed all the time by "Airborn" knights carrying bombs (Knight after droping a bomb can use his shield to propels him in the airs and glide anywhere holding the shield above him like a hang-glider). And the situation is absolutely obvious when you see a lone guy exploding the walls you put so long to build.
People will tell you, you have siege weapons!
But you can be propelled with a catapult and again it's a huge boost of mobility. For the non rushing team it's a sentence of death because building siege weapons needs a lot of stone, A LOT (Wood can respawn but it's not the case for stone). And when you die few times in a desperate attempt to repair or rebuild the structures previously destroyed by few kamikaze... you start to be angry.
Considering the fact that you just can't store the materials you've found for the rest of the team, can't fight correctly as a builder (because you only score points when you kill someone) or even building a decent base at the start (around 3 mins to do it !). You can buy items for the Builder, such as a drill, but like all aspects of the game, nothing mentions that the drill overheat and is unavailiable for few mins. So nobody use it. You can understand how frustrating this game can be as a builder.
KNIGHT:
Exhausted of building stuff that won't last more than few mins, you try your luck as a close combat fighter [Not a Kamikaze Knight of course].
But it's delightfull to fight and being unable to chain few blows without being overwhelmed by characters and explosions (bobies are persistent and can be picked up, so if someone dies it will block the line of sight of everybody and instead of taking valuables you will take a corpse ...). In general you click in the mass of pixels and hope to reach your target. In the fire of the action you will be unable to see the small hearts of the ennemy (his health of course). Note that if you died you won't have enough money to buy the bombs (you can throw it even before dying to blow everything... Kamikaze Style !).
So you go to range fight when you have enough of getting killed. If you look deeper on the forums, you will find that some dudes has mouse mods so they can burst you in melee if you are a regular player like me [translation: a fair play man].
ARCHER:
You have a bow, you shoot, simple enough ? No.
Consider the fact that you have a long time to load the arrow, the low damage it does and the fact that you can't see correctly if you damaged the target. You have a special attack wich throws 3 arrows, but the way to use it is so much complicate that you won't us it. Only in close combat if you have luck to land one or two arrows on the target and in general you have a knight in front of you (whe can use the same shield to glide to protect him... yes sir).
You can use a grappling hook to reach higher locations (by the way it's very hard to build high towers) but this tool is so unaccurate and with a very limited range that quite often you will loose your life in a desperate way to aim/evaluate the distance/ and dodge the incoming foe.
Bomb jump is much better in terms of efficiency and power.
Add to that ammunitions, because you have basic and special arrows like the fire one to burn wooden structures or the bomb arrow for stone. An other great way to reduce to ashes the work of Builders...
So like all players you won't stay long as an Archer and go Knight.
Again if you die you will drop some gold the enemy can use to buy ammunitions,
and if you rush and place shops on the way to the enemy base you will win quickly with continuous Kamikaze Knights...
IN GENERAL:
The concept is appealing but frankly the learning curve is horrible and there is too much content.
I never thought i would say something like that...
You rarely understand why something didn't worked especially during a fight where 2 or 3 secs determines the fate of your character.
You have so many game mechanics that you can't handle everything at the same time. As, again, for a Builder you can't extinguish the fire on wooden structures. You have to take an other class and buy a water bomb/ water arrow. So you can't even defend buildings yourself except if you build a balista or a catapult.
But like many other games the community doesn't help and explains nothing (the text window is bad, even the dozens of emote icons: players just uses smileys to laugh in front of your death, only one guy used it correctly to say to build a tower on a location).
There are many cheaters (without any protection against them) and even if some players are really good, we don't know if they use mods.
Things are quite often unfair like when the maps puts you to the worst location or the overall design is bad.
Even voting is a pain and disturbs you quite often because there is no timer and you have to vote even if you don't care of it. You can't see if someone has done something wrong, the chat window is small and you have to click on it to enlarge it for few seconds.
TO CONCLUDE:
You have better multiplayer games for free with much more balance and interrest.
King Arthur's Gold is not a sandbox and it's a game where gameplay goes too far and makes the multiplayer messy. You can't manage everything and your team doesn't act with you, in general Builders stays behind away from Knights and Archers, the only classes that can work together naturally.
You endure many crashes and latency is often very high. This is related to a bad optimisation of the game and you will need more than an average computer to run it !
Maybe a major update on the solo mode where you could control you're team or  better stability and more scenarios in multiplayer.
Actually, this game is the only one i've uninstalled after only 5 hours on it...
N.B: I will update this review if the game changes but actually i just can't recommand it.
And be ware, some players are ruining bad reviews to keep the overall good rating of the game.
But fact are here: the game is unoptimized, the gameplay clumsy,ect... So buy it at your own risk.

Now, this isn't a great hindrance, as you can find the guides to help you right here on Steam.  There are even guides that will aid you in getting the graphic-enhancing mods to work that come with one of the patches (I chose Wesp's Unoffical Patch since it seemed to contain more goodies).
Yeah, yeah, I know the game's developer's are out of business.  I know it 'only takes five minutes to install the patch'.  Doesn't really matter.
Someone is asking people to fork over $20 for a decade-old game (as of the time of this writing, you can get it for $5 though!), and someone is getting that money.  That 'someone' could at least update it with a patch of their own that is included in the purchase.  Whoever is getting paid for this game is relying on the cult status this game has achieved to put money in their pockets and giving their fans the middle finger as they do it.
Which is a shame because, what I've played so far, it's a great game.  Not top-notch, but pretty good for its niche.
Graphics:  They're a decade old and even with enhancements, it shows its age.  Animations are kind of stiff and clunky, and everything is sort of reminiscent of the way the original Blood Rayne looked.
Voice-Acting:  Some of it is Grade A, some of it is Grade F.  Pretty hit or miss, as usual with most games, your protagonist stays silent.  Nothing wowing here, except for how terrible some of it is.
Gameplay:  Pretty basic.  Forces you into third-person view whenever you do melee fights, which I find irritating.  I'd like it a lot more if I didn't have to see my own character's awkward flailing strikes.  There are some nice elements, such as your ability to be a silver-tongued rascal, or computer-hacking nerd, or lockpicking sneak really coming into play.  I also like how faithful they are to the source material, with Nosferatu having to stay hidden from humans, the rivalry war between Sabbat and Camarilla, etc.
Story:  It's nothing to sneeze at, but it's not quite as great as some people claim.  Your dialogue choices are often clunky and ridiculous, but the whole thing weaves together fairly well.
TL;DR:  Get it while it's on sale.  KNOW YOU WILL HAVE TO MANUALLY PATCH IT TO GET IT TO WORK.  DO NOT IGNORE ALL THE REVIEWS TELLING YOU THIS, THINKING IT WILL WORK ON YOUR RIG.
If whoever is making money off of selling this game would patch it themselves, I would give it a positive recommendation.

I am strongly biased towards the idea that everyone who enjoys Italian style music, quality AI Vehicles, old car fans, 10 car garages (with one being able to repair ones' cars in the garage itself (for $ of course)), making vehicles blow up, non-run and gun shootouts, melee combat (it teaches you slowly but steadily), car chases/escapes, customizing paint/license plates, quality pedestrian AI's, (dumbed down) lockpicking, scraping cars for money, or I suppose if you enjoy holding up stores and/or causing mayhem, then this is the game for you.
It feels like an authentic Italian experience with what I cannot attest to, Mafia integration... although the lack of (Italian) food on tables in the restaurants in conjunction with not being able to purchase any, has the immersion a bit removed... although you can use a jukebox and/or have some alcohol/coffee with a hot dog, then purchase some sleek or casual suits.
This review entails: Some minor spoilers
AI Drivers are smart
The game truly makes you feel like you’re in the mafia (although it is more or less a streamlined open world (aka mission 1 to mission2 to mission 3), although one can lockpick cards, tune, paint, change rims & license plates.
If you do die, checkpoints are usually not more than a few minutes gameplay of a setback.
This is not a run and gun game (on Hard (the hardest difficulty, and the only one I played it on)), if you try to, you will be shot dead if they have anything but melee weapons or pistols.
Despite this not being a run and gun game, you still take on hoards of enemies, but consider your deadliness more of luck and skill rather than dumb enemies, for I died many a time, especially on the last mission, for the enemies are not bad shots at all, you just have to time it right for when you decide to shoot and when you decide to duck and cover... you have the "advantage" of being in 3rd person mode
The vehicle AI's in this game are impeccable; they drive feasibly... meaning they will attempt to avoid crashing into you, but not via oversteering. Only once in the entire game did a vehicle turn into me and that is because I did a hard swerve at high speeds around a vehicle onto the wrong side of the road and back over the right side of the road, the vehicle braked a bit and turned to its left (of which anyone would do who sees a vehicle swerving over into its side of the road at height speeds angled towards its side of the road sidewalk). The people can be run over, but are usually smart and dodge out of the way at a realistic rate.
MINOR SPOILERS FOLLOW:
The story has one vehicle race absurdly fast away from you (you feel like you are keeping a good pace with them then they just take-off), which is realistic since they are in a  hot rod and just had to shift up, but it is unfair you have no option to actually catch them.
On one mission one can be stealthy and kill guards methodically... or one can just shoot them all and engage in a massive firefight that is realistically hard (the cops/guards know how to shoot, but can miss (makes them feel human)). No-one just haphazardly runs out, the AI's are tactical in positioning, and tend to pop out at the same time to shoot you. Only one time in the entire game did I see AI's have an issue, and that was with a closed door in a drug acquisition shootout of which the AI's couldn't open and would teleport through after a fashion about 8 feet on the other side of the door (they teleported behind me).
The game has various alternate outcome situations... for instance, in one car chase you can disable a guys car and run him down, push him off the road so he has to back up, get out while he is doing so, and shoot him, chase him to his destination and have a shootout, or lose him and go back to Joe's (your friends) apartment.

I played through the normal game mode in around 13 hours, completeing the highest difficulty on about half of the levels.
Defender's Quest plays in a rather novel way, where the 'towers' placed to defeat the incoming waves of enemies are actually characters with health, items, levels and individual abilites. Some of these characters take part in the story, which is surprisingly not as awful as in most other Tower Defense games.
Leveling up, getting new items and some hilariously written dialogue lines make for a very addicting start of the game.
However, about half-way through the repetitiveness of the gameplay really shines through.
Moving down hordes of enemies is highly satisfying and thankfully levels can be sped up and slowed down any time, significantly lowering the time where you wait for your next action.
I enjoyed my time with this game a lot. The 13 hours I put into the game over the course of a few days. It sets itself apart from the vast majority of Tower Defense games by giving the towers some actual life.
Ultimately I did stop after one playthrough, forgoing the New Game+ mode, as I have become tired of the repetitiveness.
But I rarely ever go for a NG+ mode in any game, so you might actually revel in grinding through some more of the levels.

Addictive tower defense game with a twist: the turrets are characters who can be equipped, trained and taught new skills/attacks. Each stage can be cleared in different difficulty settings for different rewards, or just to farm EXP/money.
The game is strictly 2D with nice little sprites during battle and good-looking art during cutscenes.
There's a "new game plus" feature with stronger enemies, more unlocks and a dev diary containing both making-of entries and a diary of the main girl, which gives more insight on the characters and how they get along during the main campaign.
Definitely a great game, with tons of replayability.
