The moment I fell in love with King Arthur’s Gold is a moment that I have never been able to repeat, and likely never will. My team, red, was at the gates of the blue team’s home base for nearly 20 minutes, stuck in a stalemate that never seemed to go anywhere. The blue team had constructed a massive tower, complete with spikes and platforms for archers that made it impossible to ascend. To make matters worse, it was on the edge of a lake, meaning there was no easy way for us to dig under their tower and attack from behind. I was at a loss as to how we would be able to win, until someone had the bright idea to construct a boat.
It wasn’t just any boat mind you, for it was a war boat designed for ramming enemy fortifications that could also double as a spawn point. I, along with 12 others, hopped on the boat, and sailed towards the enemy stronghold. Arrows bounced off the hull, and someone was in the proper mind to shout “RAMMING SPEED!” through chat as we slammed into the base of the tower. It collapsed with one blow, and it killed around 20 people, defenders and boat people alike, in the ensuing chaos. But it didn’t matter, for within the next minute my team stormed into the enemy’s last stronghold and secured victory.
I encountered several similar moments throughout King Arthur’s Gold, each different from the last. Yet they all had one quality in common: insanely ridiculous action. And that is what this great multiplayer experience is really about.
King Arthur’s Gold is a two-dimensional side scrolling multiplayer game that pits two teams of 16 players against each other across several game modes. While each game mode differs in terms of goals, they all focus around building fortifications in your teams base and assaulting your opponents in return. The three classes that one can choose from and switch between at any point in the game are the knight, who focuses on stabbing and slicing the life and limbs out of his opponents; the archer, who has a wide variety of arrows for any situation alongside a handy-dandy grappling hook for climbing; and the builder, who can harvest resources and build epic structures that will make medieval castle designers blush upon first glance.
Each class works well in most situations. Knights are for when you feel like suicide bombing an enemy’s front gate, or want to not die as often as everyone else. Archers are for when you get tired of dying as a knight and want to rain death on whatever patch of ground takes your fancy. And builders, my personal favorite, are when you want to bugger off and construct elaborate traps and structures that someone will hopefully appreciate one day. It’s a healthy trio that allows for one to never get too bored, as you could just as easily change your style at a moment's notice.
As a general rule in multiplayer games, I tend to like it when there is a certain order to how the game operates. Objective is to kill the enemy team? I’ll grab a rifle, walk forward and start shooting. King Arthur’s Gold is an exception to that, in more ways than one. While a match will always start with some semblance of planning in effect, within five minutes utter chaos will descend upon the map. Suddenly the enemy is digging a tunnel under your capture point, and you forgot to place spikes around the pit of death you just constructed. Your teammates are imitating kamikaze pilots as they march to set off bombs at the enemy gates, and the catapult someone just constructed has just fallen over and killed a builder. And to top it off, you just discovered that not only do sharks exist in the water and that they can eat you, but they can also be ridden like a horse at the rodeo.
The amount of crazy that occurs in any given match never ceases to produce laughter and keep me entertained. Seriously, I discovered shark riding on accident. The simplicity of the game, combined with the number of possibilities that can be exploited, make for one hell of an entertaining ride.
That’s not to say that there are not any problems with King Arthur’s Gold. There is a singleplayer mode included within the game, along with a genuinely helpful tutorial that brings you up to basics quickly. The singleplayer is bland as a whole, lacking any of the chaos that is present throughout the game’s multiplayer portion. The AI is a pain, mostly because the archers have a godlike aim to them and the constant pursuit by them does not help ease the pain in singleplayer. In fact, one could skip out on the singleplayer portion entirely and not miss out on a single important concept that is necessary to know for the multiplayer.
And this may be minor nitpicking, but there are several bugs that are found in multiplayer that I have come across several times. For one, I occasionally was unable to respawn after dying, forcing myself to disconnect and rejoin a server to gain the function back again. And after several matches, I and several others I was playing with had to leave a server because the game was convinced that the new match would not start for half an hour. TLDR; get it, difficult and satisfying combat with a great story.
This game took me 7.5 hours to complete, and I got it on sale for $5.
This game is a steal, I would have gladly forked over $20 to play this game.
Let me start with the combat. I wanted an authentic and difficult experience so, I went for the more difficult one out of the two provided, hardcore mode. The combat is very fun an satisfying, and has high emphasis on stealth and should be taken when given the option. There were several opportunities where stealth was an option, and I took them. The combat is very slow, and it indirectly shows you that every bullet counts, and it isn't smart to spray and pray. The game doesn't constantly throw ammo your way unless you're in a section where you're fighting other humans, which in that case you'll find plenty of ammo, assuming you take your shots well.
The hardcore mode had me killed a few times, where I had to restart the spot of the level and figure out what I'm supposed to do in order to beat it, who to kill first, where to hide, etc.
This game does not hold your hand very well, and as a lover of difficult games, that had me fall in love with the combat very quickly. There was this one level where I had to fight on a bridge and there had to be maybe 15 enemies, most of them with rifles and armor, so when I peeked it was a must that I hit them in the head and then got back to cover. Sounds pretty easy right? Well, there were lights in my face the entire time, and this made shooting them insanely difficult as I was practically blinded, I had to shoot out the lights first before I could actually do anything, and it was satisfying and rewarding when I finally did, as I found several weapons that were better than the ones I had, which made the game more fun to go through and complete. I love this aspect of the game, and if you love challenging yet rewarding combat, then the combat will have you in love with it in no time.
Next up is the story, which was fairly vague and took a lot of thought to understand what exactly was going on. This is a blessing and a curse, I had a lot of "a ha!" moments when I was thinking about the story in the down time, like "oooohhhh- thats why this guy said this one thing about that thing I didn't completely understand! It all makes sense now!" The story is satisfying, and once you put a bit of thought into it, makes sense.
Conclusion: For $20, this game is more than worth it. If you enjoy story driven games with some great combat, this is a good game for you.

I'd rate the various aspects as such:
NOTE: Gunplay feels... weird. I think there's forced mouse acceleration which would explain the weird aiming, and aiming down sights feels clunky (think Fallout: NV clunky). However the gunplay is still good. There are lots of modifications for weapons and enemies can drop mods too. It's a bit of a challenge to get your gun to actually hit something, but you get used to it and adapt your playstyle (this may be an intended effect!). Also, don't try to melee. Bad.
NOTE: Bullets are your currency, which I found to be a nice touch. However you can only carry a certain amount of ammo so you'll be running low either right before or right after reaching a station (places where you can trade, upgrade and modify your weapons by paying NPCs with your bullets).
NOTE: The game is linear (i.e. not open world) so exploration is rather limited. However every side path and corner will most likely hold something of use.
NOTE: This is probably the game's lowest point. Friendly NPCs have very basic walking paths and often make precise 90 degree turns to get somewhere (you can see this if you pay that kid a bullet to lead you to Bourbon early on in the game). Voice acting could be better, especially since every single child uses the same voice lines (according to gender of course). There is only one model (including face) for male children and female children, so it gets awkward when two kids are standing next to each other and they look the exact same. There is also a limited number of adult faces, so the same things happens, albeit to a slightly lesser degree.
NOTE: To be fair you've gotta give credit to the book for this.
NOTE: You can wipe your visor when blood splatters on it, you see your character swap oxygen filters, your visor cracks when you get damaged there, your character makes realistic sounds according to the actions he performs, exposure works well outdoors, the graphics are beautiful overall... the only issue here would be the NPCs and enemies, coupled with some wonky camera, taking you out of the zone.
NOTE: You can edit basic options like graphics quality and control scheme, but two central options are gone: Mouse acceleration and FOV. I actually got nauseous when playing this game because of the tiny FOV (I think it's 65 or something).
The AI is about what you'd expect in terms of aim, but I don't think they ever flank you. They react weirdly to sound and the death of their comrades, often shouting "Alarm! Alarm" but never actually doing anything about it. I once shot a resting enemy with a shotgun and missed, but he didn't do anything despite looking straight at me (this was in the middle of a battle). Often when you kill them their voice lines will continue or their mouths will move as if they're speaking. However most of the enemies aren't human so it's alright. It's easy to pick up enemy behaviours but they still pose a challenge in the end.
The story and atmosphere save the game's average gunplay and limited adventuring capabilities. Bad AI, limited options and seemingly rushed NPCs can be overlooked due to the bigger picture. When you're actually playing instead of trading for items, the game's story unfolds and you can look past the errors. I like the game a lot despite the problems listed above.

An art in making a RPG grind fun.
Imagine the game where your typical RPG party become towers in the typical Tower Defense game and you have Defender's Quest in a nutshell. The game consists mostly of mowing down a conga line of various enemies that constantly move towards your main character as an end goal. Place your Knights, Berserkers, Druids and Ice Mages like buildings beside the highway and enjoy the fireworks, swords and arrows flowing. Recruit more units and upgrade them while spending experience points or buy them better equipment.
While looking at the bare game, RPG and Tower Defense mechanics aren't that much complicated. There aren't that many character classes, statistics and different weapon types like in a classic RPG game and Tower Defense parts aren't that much complex either. It's quite a simple game in reality, but this doesn't deter me from stating the fact that the game can be very enjoyable when you get the right flow for it, which is quite important and enforced by one of the weirdest difficulty curves I have ever seen in gaming period.
While attending the battle, you have a choice between several difficulty levels. You level up and get cash after the fight, but even playing on Normal, you will find yourself struggling with keeping up with the enemies. Eventually you will hit that unmovable roadblock which might be very frustrating if you don't know what to do.
Every time you hit that unreachable challenge, go back to the previous missions and play them on higher difficulties. You will find your team extremely overpowered while gaining wind in the sails back again. At this point the game starts becoming a task of choosing the right battles, backtracking and creative grind, while still getting meaningful progress with it by obtaining unique equipment, experience and skill points. You will be constantly switching back and forth between story progress and grinding to stack up. Your team will meander between being very powerful and unable to advance in this endless circle until the end credits, and truth be told, this somehow ends up as a satisfying experience. Because of those constantly shifting roadblocks, you will often times witness your party taking on previously unimaginable tasks and it is very cathartic to experience those situations. Mowing down tons and tons of zombies that previously were relentlessly biting your back? Those moments drive straight home.
While this system creates a game where experience grinding is fun, it isn’t without its flaws. This whole circle of  progress, backtracking and shifting difficulties is quite hard to notice and tune in to, making beginner’s experience quite frustrating. People are conditioned to stick to one difficulty for a singular playthrough of a game. Break from that habit may come only after a few “quits” that I personally experienced. It takes some time to get the right clue and to find the flow. There is also that problem of New Game+ which basically extends the whole cycle for “another round”. Unfortunately, staying ahead of the difficulty curve becomes a real challenge, resulting in more roadblocks than I would wish for, putting progress to a crawl. This can be mitigated a little bit by using the punishment-free experience gain modifiers in options menu, but it kinda feels like cheating to me.
Liking everything so far? That’s very good, because the presentation sure wouldn’t win you over. Even after the Deluxe update, sprites don’t really look that good and story parts remind me of Newgrounds with its below-mediocre art and music. This is a big shame because the story itself isn’t half-bad and also fits the gameplay in the sense that it also likes to flip-flop between several states: the
mode with the serious, classic fantasy shtick and
mode where interactions between characters are so hilarious that you can be sure that writers had some real fun writing those. In both modes the quality stays on a decently high level, so I cannot really complain on that department. Those humorous moments can feel a little out of place, but most jokes hit that sweet mark leaving a positive impression.
Overall, I’m recommending Defender’s Quest. If you like building your little snowballs of death, constantly tripping out while climbing the mountain and getting even bigger snowball in the process, then I invite you to put some dosh to dev’s pocket. It is a curious little title which doesn’t like to be put in a single niche and those looking for something different yet familiar to their tastes will definitely appreciate that.

Company of Heroes 2 is the second in a renowned RTS series of the same name. The game is developed by Relic Entertainment who, if you remember, were the masterminds behind the phenomenal Dawn of War series as well as other RTS successes. The game was published by Sega and releasesd in June of 2014 with a generally positive reception, although muddled by a bit of controversy about the portrayal of the Soviets. The game includes a single-player campaign and two multiplayer modes: Co-op scenarios and competitive versus. The main campaign has 15 missions and should take you about 12-16 hours depending on what difficulty you choose and how experienced you are with RTS games as a whole. The whole of the game is superb, if a bit cliche in some places, and was clearly made with quite a bit of love on Relic's part.
Company of Heroes 2 is a different kind of RTS more in the vein of Dawn of War II than more standard games such as Starcraft and Grey Goo. In Company of Heroes 2 there is one main campaign and one DLC campaign, seeing as this is a review for the base game I will only be talking about the main campaign. The story starts you off with a mission to retake Stalingrad with a very Enemy at the Gates feel to it. After that point you go through many other missions through mostly snowy environments, with some exceptions towards the end, and even a forest mission or two. The problem is that most of the levels are designed to clearly use much of the same tileset so half the game is set in very typical wintery forests and towns with very little in the way of unique map design. However, this makes the maps that aren't wintery feel a lot more fun as they're your only chance to break from the mold. Seeing as the main campaign is completely focused on the Soviets i'll talk about how they work as a faction.
So every faction in this game has different abilities they can use on a little hotbar above the UI. These abilities include actions such as calling in a stuka fighter to do a strafing run or bringing in a squad of poorly-trained conscripts depending on the faction. These abilities are key to the campaign and can be the difference between victory and defeat in some missions. I feel the game could have some more interesting powers that affect the game in a bigger way other than just adding units to the fray or doing a basic strafe. As the soviets the gameplay is focused on the typical mentality of quantity over quality which I feel works incredibly poorly seeing as the Company of Heroes 2 as a game is meant to make every unit feel important. This directly counters the Soviet style of play and makes them incredibly hard in multiplayer and in some singleplayer situations because you end up trying to make miracles happen with infantry who's main use is to be disposable. The units are all insanely boring and begin to blend together between factions as they all pretty much have either the same units or very close copies. The co-op scenarios are just too slow and seem to be built around setting up ambushes and really playing strategically with your units but that's practically impossible against a cheating AI.
As a whole most of the campaign is very boring and repetitive but there are just enough moments where a true RTS peeks out for me to recommend CoH 2.

This is not like any other RTS you've played, but damn is it worth it. Your units are your backbone, so treat them right becasue they aren't disposable.

2007 was an earnest, blissfully ignorant year. As the US economy was gearing up for an epic real-estate crash J.K. Rowling was wrapping up Harry Potter, the first iPhone was announced, and the internet collectively turned its attention towards one thing: demonstrating inarguably, with so many blurry off-screen videos and well-worn plastic guitars, that they could indeed finish Guitar Hero 3’s (2007) unofficial anthem, DragonForce’s “Through the Fire and Flames,” on expert.
One could argue that Guitar Hero 3 was the last true hurrah for the series before it choked to death on so many ill-fated sequels and spin-offs, but more than just a great game its most challenging song elevated it to pop culture infamy. “Through the Fire and Flames” was the sort of thing you called your friend over to witness, strum bar clicking and gasping for breath as your fingers worked overtime on shoddily manufactured color buttons. This was the truest example of what Guitar Hero was as a game and for so many people. It brought rooms together and became a defacto party game alongside Wii Sports (2006) as something your whole family and friend group could enjoy.
This is all a roundabout way to segue into talking about Stikbold! A Dodgeball Adventure (2016), a dodgeball party game by way of Denmark studio Game Swing that is neither a 2007 vintage or music game, but nevertheless conjured comparisons to Guitar Hero 3 as my girlfriend and I pummeled the devil with projectiles. Why we had ended up in hell facing off against the devil to win back the girl of our dreams isn’t important. What matters is that the devil is a bloody pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and far better at dodgeball than he has a right to be.
Perhaps it was the lava or the horns or the chugging guitars, but for the entirety of this sports battle all I could think of was “Through the Fire and Flames” and how agonizing it was as well. This is Stikbold incarnate, a ridiculous pseudo-sports game at one moment, and a death metal migraine the next. When it is not causing you to chuck controllers at the screen in frustration, Stikbold is a riotous multiplayer game that channels the best elements of so many unfortunate sports comedies, from Happy Gilmore (1996) to, appropriately, Dodgeball (2004).
Another pre-recession artifact, the sports comedy has been resurrected by indie developers in recent years with the likes of Sportsfriends (2013) and Videoball (2016), and Stikbold fits marvelously beside them as an asses-to-elbows couch co-op gem. A few unfortunate run-ins with Satan give way to extreme difficulty spikes, but there really is nothing quite like throwing a beehive at your best friend only to have them retaliate with a barrage of bunless hotdogs. Stikbold is the buddy-cop dodgeball epic I didn’t know I needed, and best of all Vince Vaughn is nowhere in sight.

My love for this game was unexpected but a welcome surprise I went into the metro series blind through a bundle.
Pros:
> Amazing immersion gripping world that you learn to care about
> Great assortment of weapons that feel great
> Linear story that allows the game to maximise its assets >Somehow is able to make the outside far more terrifying the inside
>minimal to no hud and believable hits taken
>truely beautiful, stunning environments
>Stealth is less broken than the original and relies on your eyes and observation not a map making it too easy
>Gripping and investing lore with socio- political ramifications
>The Gas Mask system looks and feels fantastic! (although not quite as good as the original)
Cons:
>Random pointless quick time events that add drama but push incredulity. Mate you're a human not some super mega solder who always gets out of the last minute! A game with stealth horror elements is bettered with a sense of fragility
> Still pretty buggy at points
>Auto save function is tedious. Both taking away tension as well as saving at inconvenient points. Had to restart a chapter because I would get instakilled after a point it decided to autosave. Also autosaves include stairs and stuff also wasting your time post death
>You are a massive Mary Sue. Again an apocalyptic games benefit by fragility
> Some missions feel a bit like filler and feel like shooting corridors
Overall its immersion makes this a great game. Play with no HUD (ideally in ranger mode) and it becomes a unique and engrossing game. It's not a masterpiece by anymeans but its an impressive shooter that is far more than the sum of its parts. Higly recomended if you like good stories, are interested in russia/russian culture, like apoclyptic scifi, or just a game that takes you to a diffrent world. Had a lovely time with it.

Despite its quirks (graphical hiccups, repeated NPCs, wonky combat) and the absolute NEED to mod V:tM-B in order to run it on modern systems, Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines is, hands-down, one of the best RPGs - and possibly the best vampire game - ever made. Simply put, LA does not give two hoots about you, and events are only driven forward when you begin to interfere. Nevermind that vampires have generally fallen out of favor amongst gamers - this is one that should be played through at least once. Lust, hunger, betrayal, and hard decisions - its all here.
Expect to die at least a couple of times; the game doesn't pull its punches, and will backhand anyone thinking they're running on rails. The game's world may seem small, but given that the game is over 10 years old now it has quite a bit of space to roam. Maybe not Witcher levels of freedom, but very few of the game's quests are (or really feel like) fetch quests. The things you do change how the game plays, and each Family has their own oddities to them - both good and bad.
If there ever was a game that needed a graphical (and gameplay) overhaul, though, it would be this one. The visuals, while striking, are severly dated, and you'll see the same bums/hookers/random people begin to repeat over and over after a while (although it does give the feeling that the city is beginning to mess with your head). As well, the combat system feels severely tacked-on, and while functional, it is almost ALWAYS preferable to go in with a gun rather than a bat or blade, as melee combat suffers the worst. While it only becomes troublesome in a few areas, those can be the places that make one throw the keyboard in disgust.
Finally, as mentioned, the game will NOT run unpatched, so picking up an unofficial patch is necessary to run it on a system with a Windows 7 or newer OS (not sure about Vista; it might work, but it definitely doesn't on W7). Attempting to run the game unpatched causes many issues, so don't even think about it.
Overall, though, it is worth picking up (especially when it goes on-sale), as it was Troika's last game before they went bankrupt, and while buggy their games have managed to pick up cult classic status over the years. Beyond that, its a damn good convoluted tale featuring the children of the night, and certainly deserves praise for making the player FEEL like they're a bloodsucking monster.

You get a pen and paper-like character customizer where you get to pick your gender, and vampire clan along with a backstory about before you became a vampire. Everyone burned to death. Then everyone suffocated to death. Then, a few runs later, everyone was burned, suffocated, and blasted to death.
Giant spiders ate my crew, strange monoliths evaporated them, and asteroids turned them into fine, dehydrated powders drifting through the void.
Then I started getting better. I stayed away from the spiders, I vented the oxygen out of burning rooms, rather than sending a single hapless insectoid to fight the flames. And then, one glorious day, after so much blood, sweat, and tears, I destroyed the rebel flagship and won the game.
That was 40 hours in. There was still much to be done. This was before Advanced Edition came out, of course, so the unlock quests were the only ways to unlock all of the ships. And how long did it take me to obtain the Crystal Cruiser? 100 more hours.
That brings us to the present day, when I'm 450 hours in, and still banging out a game every week or two. And so, if you're still on the fence about buying FTL: Faster Than Light, ask yourself this: do you want a game that you'll play once and never touch again, or do you want a game that still has tons of replay-value after a frankly embarassing amount of time?

This is one of my favorite games. And Yes, I've actually played it for hundreds of hours. There was a time when every day while I was winding down I'd put youtube videos on and just play this game, for hours. It's hard to pinpoint what exactly about it is such a draw to me. I think that the gameplay is super satisfying, the story is well-written and actually interesting, and the progression of equipment and levels feels fair and gives you a lot of choices.
Beating the game is really only the beginning and throughout your entire first playthrough the game won't be too challenging, your main strategy choice is where to put your archers, which are easily the best class early on. In New Game +, the enemies have various strengths that go beyond just "more health and damage" which is nice. Stuff like 50% ranged damage resistance to make you switch up tactics, fading in and out of targetability to make it harder to clump units into a death zone, etc.
You also get a new type of reward: in the first playthrough, you accumulate legendary weapons and armor by completing the levels on harder difficulties, which is great but has two issues. They don't feel very unique since it's just high stats, and eventually the stuff you can buy becomes better than the legendary stuff so they're useless. NG+ gives Skulls as a reward for beating higher difficulties that you trade in to upgrade the legendary items, and the upgrades fix both issues. The upgraded legendary items are better stats-wise than the stuff you buy, and they get unique abilities like extra bleed chance, higher crit damage, etc.
Another cool thing in NG+ is the addition of several levels where you can only use certain classes, so you might have a level with only berserkers and healers. These levels also introduce a new character who is cool.
Basically if you like tower defense games this game is perfect for you, or if you just want a game to relax and wind down with it's been prefect for that for me.

"You Have to Win the Game" is a simple, well done old-school hardcore platformer offered for the low, low price of FREE. I've gotten about 8+ hours of enjoyment out of this game so far, so it's emphatically been an incredible value. If you like games like Super Meat Boy, hell even if you don't, download this game. It's free, so what have you got to lose?!
[GOOD]
+ Plenty of presentation options. Play in the old school looking default settings, or if that doesn't tickle your fancy, set it up the way you want with the multitude of display options available. 8-bit color, 16-bit color, fullscreen, monitor border, there's a lot there.
+ Tight controls. A game like this NEEDS spot on controls, and "You Have to Win the Game" delivers. I was able to comfortably play only using the keyboard, something that's very difficult to do with other hardcore platformers.
+ Simplistic gameplay. No health bars, attacks, scores, timers, lives, map screens, inventories, etc. It's just jump past obstacles and collect the 4 powerups you need to advance in the game. Very simple, very clean.
+ Challenging. FACT: You will die a lot in this game. But if you keep at it you'll eventually move past difficult obstacles and subsequent run throughs will become easier and easier.
+ Incredible replay value. "Won" the game? Great, now try the extra spicy mode. Then try and go for 100% completion on both maps. Or beat it as a cat. Or try and beat it in under 10 minutes. Or without dying. Two maps (the original and then the remixed and more difficult 'extra spicy'), a cat mode, and YOLO mode, plus going for 100% completion, gives you a lot to do after your first go round.
+ Style is well done. YHTWTG looks and plays like it came straight out of an 80s arcade machine.
+ Good time waster. Play for 5 minutes or 50, either way you'll feel like you're advancing well enough. Can play in chunks or long sessions.
+ FREE!!!
+ Exploration. The game plays kind of like a metroidvania where there are certain places you can't get to until you get the powerup that will allow you to access it. This leads to a lot of exploring and backtracking as you collect powerups.
[NEUTRAL]
= No music. Didn't bother me at all.
= Sound effects consist of blips and bloops. True to it's nostalgic roots.
[BAD]
- Backtracking through areas can get tiresome.
- Confusing to know where you're at at times. A map feature would have been great.
- Some screens require pixel perfect placement to beat. Not for the faint of heart.

Let me say right now, that I played this game for about an hour and a half, and I reached one of the endings. It was the bad ending, by the way, which came after having to get through challenges such as "hardcore Prawn", "I never could look the other way", and "swimming upstream" to name a few off of the top of my head.
This game tested me, and not necessarily in a good way. I enjoyed parts of it immensely; the graphics were nicely done, and the general atmosphere of the game is fantastic, and the difficulty is all because of level design that is difficult, not psuedo difficulty like one might find in, say, "I wanna be the guy".
And yet, there are places in it in which I felt like hurling my monitor across the room, or like I was taking my head to a wall that was also a cheese-grater.
The game's difficulty spikes at a certain point not too far after the start, remains increasingly difficult throughout, and in the end, the game's ending (the bad one, anyway) didn't make me want to continue playing; It made me want to give up, more than anything. And  after reaching the ending, the game restarted; you return to the beginning, without upgrades, and are forced to start again, going through every little arduous challenge over and over, dying again and again and again ad infinitum.
I know people like games that are difficult. Platformers like VVVVVV and Super Meat Boy are two examples of games of a similar difficulty standard. You WILL die, repeatedly, and you will do the same thing over and over again until you finally get the timing just right, or a platform or an enemy is just so, and then you can make it.
If you are into games that sound like what I've just described, feel free to pick this game up (literally; it IS free). However, if you want a casual platformer, or something fun but not altogether rage-inducing, you might want to seek entertainment elsewhere.

I'm a fan of the franchise and bought this one not to purchase Civ6 yet. Am almost done with my first actual full game (marathon mode, prince difficulty level, two continents and a few island). I currently fully occupied a continent and plan on nuking all the cities of the other one. Am taking my time to see the full potential of the game. But overall I dont think that my opinion would change much once i get to the end.
Compared to Civ4, they took out several things that I kind of miss and that are “ideologically” a bad choice. First of, war per se does not make people unhappy as far as I've seen. You have some kind of penalties for fast expansion, but they are easy to overcome. Also,there is no religion...!? Really makes no sense.... Diplomacy is basically crap as usual but worse in terms of visibility of relationships between the players. UI in this field is weird and uneasy to read and consult. And you cant stack units. Never really abused of stacked armies but it changes a lot the feel of the whole thing and makes it hard when moving units.
Tecnology tree at first glance seems a lot "shorter" than in Civ4. At least in the late part of the game, where by the way, pollution seems not to exist?! But the thing I dislike the most is the policy system.... Makes no sense, at least if you consider the names and effects of the different policies. Overall really bad and dumb.
On the other hand, apreciate the exagons finally. But the game overall is basically an easier and prettier version of the Civ format. So, if you are a fan and did not play it yet, not sure its really necessary. At this point will not go further in the franchise. Kind of sad that new games are getting better looking as hell but really washed down to the bone in terms of strategy and depth.

BALANCE SITUATION:
This game gets a lot of hate form a lot of people  and some of it for a good reason .
the dev tim had some really bad decisions concerning balance in the past , but now things are looking better than ever.
So don't listen to trols  ,haters and 0.2 hour reviews that say the game is crap and that coh 1 (I am a huge coh 1 fan)  is batter because they are all full of crap . As far as strategy games go this game is really well balanced now and the dev team (such as it is) still pumps updates and new content very often . Most of the butt hurt Imo comes from new players who go online first game knowing nothing of gameplay mehanics of which there are many here , and get their butt handed to them .Not one faction or unit is op ,almost  everything is in the hands of the player .This is not Starcraft or C&C game where apm or spaming units wins games , its all about combined arms , flanking and conserving units, losing just one unit can spell doom for you. Go read up on some beginner tips before you go aginst other players .Also the matchmaker gets the job done fine , only the first 10 games will you go aginst players of diffrent skill until it determines your skill level.
DLC/PAY TO WIN SITUATION:
I spent around 20$ on this game during diffrent sales , bought base game and two aditional armies. Almost EVERYTHING  else I wanted I got form in game loot drops .The drops are random and you wil get something every 3 to 4 games. None of the stuff I got gave me any kind of an adventage and I have gotten and continue to get my butt handed to me by people who play with base game stuff (I consider myself an ok player and I sit around 60% win ratio in 1v1 games), the stuff you can get for 8$ when the game is on 75% sale and the game and most of the dlc are on 75% sale arount 4  to 5 times a year. Company of Heroes 2 is easily one of the best multiplayer strategy games i ever played (I played almost every strategy there is). If you love WW2 and strategy games get it .The game is light years in front CoH 1 in terms of gameplay and balance , just take  your time read a few treds on army you want to play and on mechanics of the game before you go online aginst other players ,this game is very easy to get a grasp of but hard to master . Defender's Quest is an excellent tower defense game that, while not perfect, is one of the better offerings in the genre.
The pros (+) and cons (-) are as follows:
+ Solid tower defense gameplay. It follows a typical X unit is good against X enemy type formula, and for the most part this works well.
+ The story in this game is much better than you'd ever expect from a game of this type. You can more-or-less ignore it if you don't care, but if you take the time to read the journal entries, you'll find that the world and characters are very fleshed out. A lot of the characters and situations are very tongue-in-cheek, which relieves some of the tension a game like this can inspire. :)
+ Level design constantly pushes  you out of your comfort zone. You often find that you can't quite use units in the way that you'd want to because of the limitations on the terrain. Things don't get as monotonous as a result of this.
+ For a tower defense game, it's pretty long. If you're a veteran of the genre and can breeze through tough fights with effortless tactical accumen, you'll find that getting maximum stars on each level takes about 10-15+ hours.
+ New Game Plus (NG+) adds sidequests that aren't available in the normal game, which includes new story and cutscenes. The behind-the-scenes journal entries are also really interesting.
+ Hero Mode makes for an even more challenging game (you can only use the 6 story characters).
+ Lots of customization for loadouts, units, etc. Branching skill trees make the customization feel a little more fleshed out, although some options are clearly better than others.
+ The DX version of the game vastly improves the graphics. The biggest mark against the original game was that it was in SD and the art looked very amateur. With this update, the game supports HD/Widescreen resolutions, and all sprites/cutscenes look 1000% better.
+ You have the option of increasing the amount of XP and Scrap (money) you get after each battle by up to 300%. Scrap isn't all that useful, but XP is mana from heaven. This is great, because if you left it at 100%, it'd take a metric ♥♥♥♥ton of grinding to get to the end of the game. See cons for reasons why even this feature doesn't save NG+ from grindiness, unfortunately.
- In the normal game, Rangers are by far the best unit. You can win almost every fight by just using them, even on Expert. It seems that the developers were very aware of this, which is why --
- In NG+, the Ranger (the only
ranged unit in the game) is the subject of immense nerfs. Many enemies that appear in large numbers and have high speed either have 50% resistance to ranged damage, or 60-70% ranged
. These are the kinds of enemies you'd want an archer for because they can slip past your melee, but your archers can't hit them. This really hurts the unit's viability in a lot of fights. I feel like the challenge could have been increased without this frustrating change. There are some enemies that the Ranger is still really good at dealing with, but mostly you'll be relying on melee in Expert modes.
- Most of the added difficulty in NG+ is artificial. Inflated HP and stats, enemies that phase out so that you can't target them, etc. You're often forced to spam global spells to deal with certain situations because your units simply can't no matter how you have them set up. This mode just isn't very well done in my opinion. It's frustrating and tedious, not fun.
- The super sheep levels are tedious and not fun at all. You kill a slow moving sheep (that you can slow even more) that has about a bazillion HP and takes optimal tactics and resource management to kill before it reaches the end of the level. It is a very boring, very long fight even with the game sped up to 16x speed, and you have to do it TWICE in order to get all the achievements. If you're a completionist, you'll be subjected to several grindy annoyances, which brings me to the final gripe:
- If you complete the game in Hero Mode (can't recruit units), once you've finished those achievements (after finishing NG+), you'll want to recruit units because there are some levels that are impossible to get 3 gold stars on with only the main 6 heroes. Unfortunately, the recruited units at that point will be so low level that even setting the XP to 300% is an unbearable grind to get them to 60. Battles take a long time to fight, and the XP from a battle -might- give your units half a level. You can imagine how long this would take. This was originally a community challenge that the developers put into the game later (along with associated achievements), but they didn't really balance the post-achievement gameplay for it. I actually gave up with only a few achievements left to get. Not worth it.
Overall, if you're interested in a tower defense game that's challenging and satisfying in the base game, and aren't too concerned with unlocking every last achievement, then this game is for you. If you love punishing grinds, NG+ has you covered.

In this era, there are very, very few games considered "New", or "original", without taking key gameplay elements/codes/graphics/other from a different, more popular game.
Thankfully, King Arthurs Gold (KAG) is one of those few.
In no other game I have played can you
As you can see, this game truly is unique- It carries graphic styles and building mechanics from previous games such as Terraria, without actually "Stealing" what those games already have done.
This game has many strong points, but unfortunately many weak points, however small. Like every other multiplayer based game in this era, it is expected that the community is terrible (which is very, very sad), and KAG is no exception- With incompetent allies, moronic chat-spammers, and annoying griefers, this game has its fair share of community troubles.
But that is not something the developers can control.
Some other main complaints about this game are things that the developers CAN control, such as useless kegs (update months ago caused them to be virtually unusable outside of getting shot out of a catapult, but even that can go haywire after a simple arrow can shoot the keg off your back), and weakend ballista bolts- Seriously, 2 shots for 1 bolt? Now that I think of it, though, these really are my only complaints- everything else is generally balanced.
As for the good things, A lot of them I didnt list- For example, you can do things such as launching your best friend straight into enemy territory via catapult, crashing down enemy towers (Just for the awesome physics of this game you should buy it),  and taming sharks- thats right. TAMING. SHARKS.
1 last thing before I sign this review off- There is seriously a lack of players in this game right now- What happened to the 5-or-6 full servers ay any given time? now hardly anyone plays Take the Halls, and when someone does it rarely exceeds 10 people.

This game is very challenging, play it if you like that and don't if you hate a challenge in reflexes and
.  Especially don't try to do a 'Let's Play' like I did the week a paper is due or something like that; doing an extra college class during the summer while recording my impressions of this game was excruciating.  This game is best played when everything you have to do in real life settles down and should be especially enjoyable if you have plenty of spare time and friends to watch you fail (I'm assuming). If you want a hard platformer that's more stimulating, and actually has challenges you can remotely solve on your own, try Eryi's Action (also available on Steam) instead.  Let me warn you that you can only win the game if you can descipher the markings in some of the stages and figure out what the magic word is using the code, so good luck trying to figure that out before googling it like everyone else (if you must know the magic word is 'super,' because you have to be supremely patient and determined to win this).  It was worth every penny, which is to say it's worth nothing at all and that's not just because the game is free.  I'm sorry if I sound harsh, I just expected better from the developers. Everyone burned to death. Then everyone suffocated to death. Then, a few runs later, everyone was burned, suffocated, and blasted to death.
Giant spiders ate my crew, strange monoliths evaporated them, and asteroids turned them into fine, dehydrated powders drifting through the void.
Then I started getting better. I stayed away from the spiders, I vented the oxygen out of burning rooms, rather than sending a single hapless insectoid to fight the flames. And then, one glorious day, after so much blood, sweat, and tears, I destroyed the rebel flagship and won the game.
That was 40 hours in. There was still much to be done. This was before Advanced Edition came out, of course, so the unlock quests were the only ways to unlock all of the ships. And how long did it take me to obtain the Crystal Cruiser? 100 more hours.
That brings us to the present day, when I'm 450 hours in, and still banging out a game every week or two. And so, if you're still on the fence about buying FTL: Faster Than Light, ask yourself this: do you want a game that you'll play once and never touch again, or do you want a game that still has tons of replay-value after a frankly embarassing amount of time?

I have enjoyed the game, but it lacks a serious amount of polish that would make me rate it higher. There are glitches, and serious problems with AI (your own guys not shooting at enemies or enemy soldiers not reacting to me trying to shoot them in the head with an unsilenced revolver). Sometimes it feels like the AI was made terrible because some parts of the game would have been much more difficult without game exploits and dumb as rocks enemies.
More positive aspects are the varied guns and equipment. many assault rifles and shotguns and scavenged weapons actually help define the aesthetic of the Metro world, letting you know that these weapons were made by a people trying to scrounge together a means to defend themselves against a terrifying mutant horde and dangerous humans. The setting is well defined through the living quarters and interactions with people in the many stations that really help push the idea that things are desperate for those who inhabit the metro.
The combat is nothing to special, and while varied in its setting it often just feels like a call of duty where it is harer to tell whether that mutant is dead or just recoiling from a shot. The game just falls a little flat due to its limited AI and sometimes clunky glitches, but regardless I can honestly say it has its fun moments .

I see a lot of reviews that are one sided, so I will try my best to give this game a fair review with: What I like and what I don't.
What I don't like:
1. In the game's multiplayer, there is free reign to choose one general. That is not a problem, but people can buy these generals. this gives some people a "pay to win" feel.
2. This game is not for children under 15. Units, both in campaign and multiplayer, use an incredible amount of cursing. Some images in the campaign can be disturbing(nothing sexual, but a lot of blood).
3.The game's population cap limits the use of large scale warfare.
4.The Campaign is limited to USSR and USA.
Now for the thing I enjoy about the game.
1. The game is the Halo to men of war 2's call of duty. The Game has an outstanding campaign for the USSR, providing historical accuracy behind things like The Battle Of Stalingrad and Order 227. The campaign seems to glorify no one (including the player's faction) and has a very neutral tone on politics.
2. The game is constantly growing( though it does require payment for DLC). What  started off as Whermacht and USSR became Whermacht, Oberkommando west, USA, USSR, and British commonwealth.
3. The amount of time put into the voice production. I was Playing as the Whermacht,  and my ally had his stug stolen by our enemy. I ordered my Pak 40 to destroy it, and I heard, "Destroy that captured stug". The voices will change depending on the map, and unlike most strategy games, When a unit captures another unit(infantry crewing a tank), Their voice sticks to that of their unit, though slightly altered for the new role they serve, rather than changing the voice to that of the original vehicle.
4. Every battle is rewarding. After any match, whether it be skirmish against AI or players, one recieves a loot crate containing generals, buffs, and other goods.(The Loot crate is free to open).
My personal opinion of the game is that, while it is not perfect. it is a very fun game to play on your down time, and even more so with friends. Many people cry out that the game is unbalanced, but thats not entirely true. the factions are also based on time. the length of the battle can determine who wins or loses. People who say the game is unbbalanced may simply not know how to play their faction to its fullest. I played OKW, not knowing anything about it, and thought it was underpowered. I didn't realize that the faction gained power as the battle dragged out.
I hope my review of the game has helped new buyers make a decision.

CoH2, to this day, is still a downgrade from CoH in most ways as far as I'm concerned. The DLC system is kind of 'okay'- you can acquire every commander in the game randomly as a drop (or craft it after disenchanting drops, which is massively inefficient, the ratio is 30:1), but if you want the best available to you right away in multiplayer, you'll have to spend more.
I've always loved (1v1) CoH for its slow early- and mid-game where there was lots of room for tactical play like using barbed wire, shenanigans involving HMGs in buildings, cap-points were contested for several minutes at a time, it was great. I feel like this was lost a bit with CoH2, the game definitely seems a lot faster to me, even playing classic maps like Angoville (10 more years!). Maybe it isn't even so much a question of speed in teching, but rather that there are more hard-counters, I'm neither sure, nor an expert.
Performance is, sadly, shocking. Running the game on win7/10 x64 (couldn't tell a difference in performance), i5-4670K (auto-OC), 8mb, r9 290 (4gb), and while this certainly isn't the most up-to-date rig, it should be able to positively destroy this 2012-released-yet-2008-looking♥♥♥♥♥game. Instead, my CPU is vastly under-utilised, my GPU is at 100% load at all times and I don't even get stable 60 fps in 1v1- that's pretty preposterous. Mafia II
Mafia 2's strength comes from its realistic gameplay and thrilling, blockbuster story. Ironically, its realism also leads to some weaknesses.
+ Mafia 2 has to have one of the greatest storylines I've ever played in a video game. The content could be adapted to a film, it's that good. Set in the 1940s and early 1950's, there are many twists in the plot, with unexpected events and dramatic scenes.
+ This game has fun, realistic shooting (at least when played on hard). You must use cover effectively or you'll die quickly. There's a mix of firearms to use, like tommy guns, pistols, the MP40 and shotguns. Many environments are destructible.
+ The driving mechanics are also realistic. If you hit another car or concrete pylon at high speeds, you will be killed on impact. The handling on vehicles reflects the time period well, the cars are slow, difficult to steer but still enjoyable.
+ The police react properly to crimes, they are far more responsive than any Grand Theft Auto game. If you're speeding, the cops will try and pull you over. If you hit a pedestrian or even another car, the fuzz will attempt to apprehend you for a hit and run. The police keep tabs on your appearance or wanted vehicles, so you need to change clothes and ditch your car to remove suspicion.
+ Mod shops can change your licence plates to legalise your car if it's on a wanted police list, again a realistic addition to the game. You can paint automobiles with many colours and upgrade the engines.
- Mafia II is quite short. It will take 15-20 hours to finish, depending on your difficulty setting (not including DLC).
- There are some moments in the game where the realism can be frustrating. There's a lot of cool features, but it can be annoying when you're driving along and happen to hit another car. Oops, you died. Re-load to the checkpoint and you'll need to repeat everything you just did. Same deal applies to the police, they can be a real nuisance sometimes.
Overall Score: 8.5/10

Greetings as always!  The short of it is that if you like tower defense this is a good addition to your collection.  Even without a sale the price is worth it, though this game could have been more appropriate for a tablet I didn’t feel cheated and was left satisfied overall.
Graphics and Audio:  The art is basic, no way around that, but it gives a certain charm with that understanding.  Unlike many games this one understands that the core is gameplay not graphics and audio.  Instead of doing a poor job I feel that the developers made the most of they could without cutting quality or requiring a tripple A budget., can’t really complain and the second game looks like they are bringing it to the next level without cutting that charm.
Tower Defense:  The game is simple enough, you ‘build’ towers by summoning characters and level them during the match which dramatically increases their power and unlocks a new attack (assuming they know the skill).  The combination of skills needed (like piercing armor or slowing) along with the unique pathing of each unit type gives a lot of strategy.
RPG:  The leveling system is decent but a bit shallow; this really isn’t an issue as the game’s leveling mechanics do exactly what is intended.  Along with some gear (weapons, armor and books) and a small bit of color customization for your characters it certainly could be better but I left the game content.  This small addition gives you something to work towards, a reason to 'grind' levels over and a method to make levels harder wtihout require silly levels of micro or creating a game that simply overrun with templates and walkthroughs that anyone can copy.
Story:  The narrative is good, the background and story told is very interesting in the premise although it could use a bit of work in the telling.  The mix of silly humor and playful tones keeps the game light without undermining the games overall serious story (looking at you Slak!), no, you aren’t getting BioWare story telling, but you aren’t getting generic forgettable story arc A either.  I’d definitely read a novel based around this fiction.
I’m not really sure what else to say, it is a solid game, especially for the price.  Even more so if you are looking to scratch that tower defense itch that seems to be dried up for now.  I hope you manage to enjoy it as much as I did.

This game is of the few RPGs that I've actually completed. I'm not a big fan of the genre in the first place, but this one looked unique enough to give it a shot. Even early on I could tell that biggest draw for me was going to be the writing and music. All the characters feel like they have a unique personality, even if all you have to go by at times is one line of dialogue and a sprite. The story isn't your typical "save the world" boringness. A downside for me, however, was that some of the serious moments weren't written in a very believable manner. Hopefully Dingaling will improve this aspect in their next game. Music ranges from abstract to extremely catchy and does a really good job of setting the mood. There's a good number of battle tracks as well, so you won't get annoyed by the same music every time you fight.
As for the structure of the game, there are basically 3 central areas, all of which have a good amount of branching paths. The sidescrolling perspective keeps traversal from one area to the next interesting in the form of some light platforming. You can even ride a child-sized bike! Combat is turn-based and you have your typical special moves and items. Some characters can also use a neat combo system to get extra damage out of special moves.
If I could summarize the game in one sentence it would be "Earthbound for grown ups". It's darker than Earthbound at times and uses stronger language, but you can still feel some of the silliness and surrealism that was abundant in that game.
Get it!

This game is not as awesome as it looks. The graphics are appealing, but that's as far as it goes. Here's a list of things that annoy me:
-Jump is up. Why? Because you travel vertically when you jump, of course!
-Ladders are climbed by jumping. It makes sense with the default controls, up to jump, but I changed them. Because pressing up to jump is stupid.
-Everything is overcomplicated. If you want to pick stuff up, you hold the pick up key, click on the item, then it sort of floats in front of your character. From there, you open your inventory and drag the item in.
-The sound effect for an enemy warrior dying is the Wilhelm Scream. Every single time.
-The sound effect for picking up a large coin (which, mercifully, is automatic) is the same exact sound used for picking up a coin in Super Mario World.
-Chickens drop nothing. Cows drop nothing. Sharks drop steak.
-Don't bother trying to stay on a ladder while swordfighting, because the ladder breaks when you hit it with your sword a few times.
-It seems buggy. In the "Save the princess" mode, I went into a castle and every enemy randomly exploded into blood and body parts for no reason whatsoever.
Of course, lots of people say this game is good. Maybe I'm just nitpicking. But I really, really, wanted to like this game. And I don't.

This is hands down one of the best shooter experiences I have ever had.
The gameplay itself isn't really anything spectacular or unusual. It's exactly what you'd expect a common shooter to feel like. Don't fix what isn't broken, is how this felt. It combines stealth mechanics with FPS in a very fun and sometimes challenging way. But to top it off, this game gave me legitimate feelings of anxiety. I full felt afraid at more than one part and I struggled quite a bit in others. I've done three playthroughs for Metro: 2033. I usually don't find much replay value from most games, but this one doesn't get old.
The characters are all fairly complex, the environment itself is hostile more often than not, but what really made this game so good was the ending. What a fantastic conclusion for this part of the story. In a lot of ways, it's a little better than Last Light, but that isn't to say I didn't love them both.
The enemies are all super interesting as well. There's just so much going on and you get a very good taste of what it would feel like to live in this kind of world. The only real drawback to this game is the silent protagonist aspect. I've never been a big fan of that, but it still does its job. The story would have flowed better with more dialogue between the protagonist and main characters.
Metro: 2033 is extremely well done, with an atmostphere that really pulls you into what's happening and a story line with twists and turns and so many completely unexpected events that I don't see how anyone could not love this game.
It is scary, engaging, and all around fun. Each chapter will have you wanting to play more.
I highly suggest this game and Last Light. Easily my favorite shooter of all time.

Having put a little over five hours into this game, I have to come to realize what prevents this "good" game from becoming a "great" game.
"Then why the hell did you give this a thumbs down if it's a 'good' game?" You might ask.
Well, i've yet to find any bugs, and the gameplay is for the most part pretty solid. I'd even say the gameplay if pretty quick. However, i'd also have to say it is a little too quick at some times, and this drive to have "fast gameplay" seems to me to be pretty ironic at times.
How battles start in the game is pretty straightforward; all the ships spawn in a "coastal arena" type of setting, with all the ships being within sight of eachother. What's wrong with this formula however, is how close this spawn in can be. Sometime's you'll spawn facing eachother at a fairly far distance... sometimes they'll spawn to the side of you at approx. double cannon distance.
Oh, and they'll also spawn directly behind you, and even in between your ships.
What kind of captain would, before starting a battle, allow the enemy to sail BETWEEN his ships and then PUT HIMSELF AGAINST THE WIND, while having five other enemy ships within a cannon shot of one another. I mean, for god's sake, i'd swear the pirate that sailed into battle during the loading screen was hammered out of his mind. I kind of get the feeling of getting "quicker into the action" but for gods sake, the wind negates this! For example, when you're chasing an enemy into the wind and it causes you to spend five minute chasing them before you're in cannon shot range: It's at these times that the wind mechanics go from "cool additions" to "aggrevating annoyances" And when it comes to your friendly AI ship intelligence; you can tell they're hammered as well. "AVOID THE ENEMY" = "Sail into the land, get yourself stuck, and then continue to take broadside bombarbments untill you sink". It's rage inducing!
To summarize, the trading, sailing, and leveling mechanics are fun. Overall this game is pretty good. What ruins it for me however, is the purely mindblowing battle spawn locations, and the aggrovating chase into the wind that serves no purpose. It's at moments like these that all other aspects of the game are forgotten, and you feel nothing but a sense of dissapointment with what WAS a good experience.

It's one of these cases where Steam's binary review system forces me to give a 'thumbs up' rating followed by a long text with all the caveats.
If you're looking for a relaxed, not-to-deep tower defense with colorful graphics, thematic music and some tongue-in-cheek dialog you might try this out. If you're looking for the best-in-class tower defense game, this is not it.
The game has us accompany Azra, the royal librarian of a fantasy land, through her journey across the land where she must overcome various evils. You wouldn't play this game for its story per se but the dialogs and well crafted scenery and overworld make for a compelling reason to keep playing. Via overlay tutorials the player is introduced gently into the actual gameplay of placing and managing your figthers. While the start is great you soon realize that there isn't a lot of depth to the gameplay. I've played Warcraft 3 custom maps that had more mechanical variety in their tower defense than this game.
The mechanics merit a closer look because they are the Achilles' heel of this game really. There just isn't a lot to do other than the basics : placing your figthers (towers) and upgrading them, using your global hero powers now an dthen. There's no option to call a wave early for extra cash, no towers that teleport mobs to the beginning of the maze, no flying units that ignore the ground paths altogether, no possiblity to send your own troops against the enemy, etc., etc.
Mostly you'll be fighting against zombie like creatures which is justified by the story but it gets stale fast. There's a missed opportunity here for including a much more diverse set of enemies that challenge the player to adjust their strategy and tactics.
Outside of combat you'll have the opportunity to manage your party by purchasing equipment, acquiring new fighters up your fighters by assigning points in a talent tree. The game limits itself to 6 classes of figthers (towers) all of which are nicely integrated into and justified by the story. Every figther has a unique role and there's little possiblity of straying from that role via the talent tree. You want your archers exel at ranged combat and your freeze mages to excel at slowing down foes. That is that. I dare to say that this game suffers from a mild sort of RPG syndrome: the inclusion of RPG elements (experience bars, talent trees, interchangeable equipment) for the mere sake of it.
The developers have included many interface features that are very useful in this type of game, like being able to slow or speed up time at will or being able to reuse your previous tower layout if you failed a mission. Being able to control the game's speed at will makes for relaxed play sessions and there's even the option to scale experience points and loot rewards if you feel the pace is to slow or to fast.
One of the decisions that astonishes me is that the developers decided to hide away some content like side missions and additional dialog in new game plus (ng+) mode. Since this game's story and presentation are on the strong side (for this genre) this baffles me. I've tried my fair share of ng+ and In the way of difficulty or mechanics there isn't much that varants a second playtrough. Defender's Quest is rather the kind of game that you play through once to see the plot come to its conclusion and then move on to something else.
This game supports the Steam controller ouf of the box and the layout is quite sensical. When using it though, the game would often hang in dialog scenes or null pointer crash. No such issues presented themselves however when playing with well though out keyboard layout.
All in all, I've had my fun with Defender's Quest and I'm looking forward to see the devs expand upon it with Defender's Quest 2 which is currently in development.
Edit: the game supports modding via the Steam workshop. While there aren't very many modifications available as of writing (February 2017) this is certainly a big plus!

I've never been a fan of the Saints Row series. I gave the first three games shots, but never found the games interesting enough to continue playing on past the first few hours. When I heard that Saints Row IV had a lot in common with Crackdown, one of my favorite games on the Xbox 360, I was a little skeptical. The idea of a Crackdown-esque game on the PC intrigued me, but I felt I had given the series more than enough of my time. During the fall sale I finally decided to take the plunge.
I was happy to discover that Saints Row IV is a lot of fun in almost every aspect. The open world had a lot to do, and the superpowers and collectable data clusters reminded me of my favorite moments in Crackdown. All the activities in the open world are a lot of fun, and give you creative ways to create chaos and I never got bored with these activities, as I can towards the end of most open world games.
The biggest issue I had with Saints Row IV is the main story missions. When compared to the excitement of running around in the open world, these missions feel incredibly boxed in and are used as ways to parody other game series.  These missions are very linear, and almost every one I had to restart at somepoint because an NPC didn't show up or I had  done something out of the strict confines of what the level wanted me to do.
I highly recommend Saints Row IV if you are looking for a fun open world game or are a fan of Crackdown, and it's a game I desperately want to complete 100%, it's just a shame that the main story missions lack any of the excitement and fun of running around in the open world.

I see a lot of reviews that are one sided, so I will try my best to give this game a fair review with: What I like and what I don't.
What I don't like:
1. In the game's multiplayer, there is free reign to choose one general. That is not a problem, but people can buy these generals. this gives some people a "pay to win" feel.
2. This game is not for children under 15. Units, both in campaign and multiplayer, use an incredible amount of cursing. Some images in the campaign can be disturbing(nothing sexual, but a lot of blood).
3.The game's population cap limits the use of large scale warfare.
4.The Campaign is limited to USSR and USA.
Now for the thing I enjoy about the game.
1. The game is the Halo to men of war 2's call of duty. The Game has an outstanding campaign for the USSR, providing historical accuracy behind things like The Battle Of Stalingrad and Order 227. The campaign seems to glorify no one (including the player's faction) and has a very neutral tone on politics.
2. The game is constantly growing( though it does require payment for DLC). What  started off as Whermacht and USSR became Whermacht, Oberkommando west, USA, USSR, and British commonwealth.
3. The amount of time put into the voice production. I was Playing as the Whermacht,  and my ally had his stug stolen by our enemy. I ordered my Pak 40 to destroy it, and I heard, "Destroy that captured stug". The voices will change depending on the map, and unlike most strategy games, When a unit captures another unit(infantry crewing a tank), Their voice sticks to that of their unit, though slightly altered for the new role they serve, rather than changing the voice to that of the original vehicle.
4. Every battle is rewarding. After any match, whether it be skirmish against AI or players, one recieves a loot crate containing generals, buffs, and other goods.(The Loot crate is free to open).
My personal opinion of the game is that, while it is not perfect. it is a very fun game to play on your down time, and even more so with friends. Many people cry out that the game is unbalanced, but thats not entirely true. the factions are also based on time. the length of the battle can determine who wins or loses. People who say the game is unbbalanced may simply not know how to play their faction to its fullest. I played OKW, not knowing anything about it, and thought it was underpowered. I didn't realize that the faction gained power as the battle dragged out.

Battlefront 2 is an overrated game.
With that being said, lets get into it. Battlefront 2 is a great game, no doubt about it. But it is far from perfect. What has kept the game alive for so long is the modding community. But if you did a direct comparison between Battlefront 1 and 2 for the vanilla experience. Battlefront 1 is vastly superior. Battlefront 1 had bigger maps, better AI, air vehicles during land maps, you could go prone, battles felt a bit more intense due to better AI, as well.
Battlefront 2 added playable heroes, a story (albeit a very mediocre one), some really fun game modes like hunt. I'm not sure what happened during development but AI is HORRENDOUS in BF2. Ive never seen so many bots get stuck in the map on a game before. Battlefront 2 also added in space battles, which before the game was released development articles described how attack umbilicles would go onto ships and you would have squads that took the ships section by section, with a call back to x wing vs tie fighter. The space battles are very poor. The ships are just a tiny little section that you just go into small rooms hat are connected to each other and blow em up. Or go into space and dogfight in a system that is ok.
Battlefront 2's strength lies in its active mod community. From new maps to campaigns to Galactic Conquests to new units and gamemodes, this is where the game really shines! Modders for this game are very talented and have added some gorgeous custom maps, units and made the fun a lot more fun than vanilla is.
While a lot of people look at this game through nostalgia goggles and think it's one of the best games ever, it's probably one of the worst games during the age where Lucasarts was making great games.
Many people compare EA BF to this and they should. While I do agree the new BF's have been bare bones, the token system is stupid, simply because they didn't want Battlefront to be a Battlefield clone again, since the first 2 originals are. And some content is lacking. I do have to say the gunplay in the new Battlefronts are vastly superior.
If you plan on modding the game, then it's worth a buy, if you come expecting the absolute pinnacle of gaming in 2005, then it really isn't going to feel as great as a lot of kids make it seem like it was. Definitely a fun game, but a flawed one at that.

CoH2, to this day, is still a downgrade from CoH in most ways as far as I'm concerned. The DLC system is kind of 'okay'- you can acquire every commander in the game randomly as a drop (or craft it after disenchanting drops, which is massively inefficient, the ratio is 30:1), but if you want the best available to you right away in multiplayer, you'll have to spend more.
I've always loved (1v1) CoH for its slow early- and mid-game where there was lots of room for tactical play like using barbed wire, shenanigans involving HMGs in buildings, cap-points were contested for several minutes at a time, it was great. I feel like this was lost a bit with CoH2, the game definitely seems a lot faster to me, even playing classic maps like Angoville (10 more years!). Maybe it isn't even so much a question of speed in teching, but rather that there are more hard-counters, I'm neither sure, nor an expert.
Performance is, sadly, shocking. Running the game on win7/10 x64 (couldn't tell a difference in performance), i5-4670K (auto-OC), 8mb, r9 290 (4gb), and while this certainly isn't the most up-to-date rig, it should be able to positively destroy this 2012-released-yet-2008-looking♥♥♥♥♥game. Instead, my CPU is vastly under-utilised, my GPU is at 100% load at all times and I don't even get stable 60 fps in 1v1- that's pretty preposterous. The load-times are absolutely horrendous except on SSDs (where they're just long) and the campaign is...calling it
would be generous (I've owned the game since 2012, still haven't finished it, doing 2-3 missions at a time is enough for about 9 months). I don't buy RTS games for the singleplayer component, but after the first game had such a fantastic campaign, this just feels like a pisstake.
Still, it is the newest CoH, and there is only one franchise that offers what CoH does, and that's CoH (DoW is close, but it's not the same). I still love the unique gameplay CoH offers, there is nothing else like it. I don't care for the lategame, I don't like what teching has become in CoH2, but it is still the closest thing to the game I fell in love with almost 10 years ago, and it's still way more fun than games where pathing isn't the third opponent in a 1v1.

The well-developed cautionary tale (similar to the movie Godfather) with its poingnant end can get you choked up even the second time through the game. Of course, there's also enough mindless mahem to delight any inner child.
As I write this on March 1, 2014 (the 60th anniversary of the largest US nuclear explosion that was 1,000 times the power of the first atomic bomb of just 9 years before which ended WWII) I realize how significant the decade of this game setting was. It was the loss of innocence at the start of the nuclear era. Buy this game and in a small way you are there.
