I think I picked a good time to play Defender’s Quest: Valley of the Forgotten (Deluxe Edition). The graphics are much better, the game has improved performance, a x16 speed is included, and much more. The smart changes and relentless support make this an extremely good and content rich tower defense game. I didn’t care much for the main story though, but more on that later.
I rather start with the gameplay where this game shines its brightest. As you progress through the 6-hour campaign, you unlock different heroes that function as your towers. Each hero you plop down on the field has four boost levels that can be purchased. You can only place heroes on predesignated spots as the game isn’t about mazing as much as thoughtful placement in a level’s limited space. Each hero has a distinct role to play such as Knights being able to pierce and destroy armor or Healers keeping everyone alive since some creeps attack and casting debuffs on enemies that amplify your damage. There are six hero types in all – Berzerker, Archer, Priest, Ice Mage, Knight, Dragon – that can be used to defeat the Revenant horde.
Heroes and the player character, Azra, can also be equipped with items. Azra can equip two different books that can enhance spells or affect the stage such as heroes having a free Frenzy buff when placed. Books are earned from bonus stages which are unlocked via the perfect stars earned from completing levels without letting Azra receive damage. Heroes can either equip a weapon, armor, or nothing at all. You can purchase equipment and recruit more heroes at towns. You can also earn unique items from tackling the higher difficulties for specific stages. The unique items are worth it as they can also serve a purpose in NG+
New Game Plus adds a significant amount of content for both the reading type of player or TD lover and does more than make the enemies tougher and stronger. You’ll run into new side-quests that provide additional story content or jokes and run into a couple of new characters. One of them is the Hermit, a crazy person who can upgrade all the unique items you’ve earned and give them new, powerful properties. There are also new developer journal entries that can be unlocked by playing if you want even more things to read. Those entries can be surprisingly interesting to read since you can see the thought process behind some of the decisions made for the game. You can also read about what the different inspirations were for other parts including the names of the unique items or the Ash religion. Both the side-quests and dev entries came with the Deluxe upgrade.
Running back and forth between the standard game and NG+ to perfect all the levels, collect uniques, and upgrade the items will probably take a bit more than 20+ hours for players if the standard settings are kept. Keep in mind that you can alter the experience, scrap (currency), and penalty rates in the accessibility menu which is a great thing indeed. Don’t forget about if you ever start to feel as though the game is becoming grindy as you go back and forth between stages in order to level up or earn more money to overcome the later levels. I had my fill of the game around the 20 hour mark and have no desire to go back for the time being.
Now we come to the main story. I did not enjoy the story told through the cutscenes for almost 90% of it. I thought the main antagonist, Zelemir, had some interesting qualities that were revealed during the later levels, but then there’s also Slak, the Berzerker, with his loud and wacky personality that felt really forced or possibly not meant for my age group. He came off as pretty lame with his style of humor and insatiable need to murder things. Maybe I just disliked how he spoke with Capslock. I thought the writing in the journal entries were better and more interesting as were some of the side-quests in NG+. Some of the journal entries explained the main characters in more depth and made certain events much more meaningful due to understanding the significance of certain actions. Some were tainted by Slak’s handwriting and jests which didn’t make me laugh.
Finally, I’d like to cover some other parts of what this game has to offer. The game saw heavy usage of the speed multiplier from me. I didn’t use the x16 multiplier very often, but man, what a time saver for when you have a solid strategy prepared for a level. You can also go in the other direction and slow down time, but I used the Pause feature instead with Spacebar. B, for boosting, is also another good hotkey to know. In addition to the x16 and performance optimizations, the game runs in 60fps which makes fast forwarding very pleasant. There is also the HD art style version of the game which is on by default now, but you can go back to the older graphics if you wanted to when you’re in the overworld map. The drawings for the cutscenes are vastly improved and I wouldn’t want to go back to the original. The retro aesthetics might be preferred by some people though, so it’s nice that you can switch whenever.  The game is very good with all the options it offers in general. Oh, also Steam Cloud and Steam Workshop are there now.
Defender’s Quest is an incredibly solid TD game with enough content to keep you entertained for a while. That’s assuming that the gameplay sinks its hooks into you as I don’t think the story is the major draw for players, unfortunately. The accessibility options can also make the experience friendly to newer players. DQ has been one of the better Tower Defense experiences I’ve had in recent memory so I hope the sequel turns out well too.

Ok, let me start with by saying this is an enjoyable time killer. I binge played this game while being forced to stay indoors because of a flu and tooth removal. It literally erased 2 days of my time and now I have to go back to work.
The game in general is very solid tower defense game. Mechanically it's flawless, and the RPG feature which lets you build your characters and upgrade them definitely adds the charm. Overall, if you enjoy tower defense type games and have nothing better to do for few hours/days, I highly recommend trying this game. It also has a good demo, which lets you play good part of the game for free. So there is no cost of initial admission.
However the best part of this game is the active developers. After the devs being almost dead-silence for 2 years (prepping for a next game/sequel), they returned with HD version and constant updates and patches, which are really nice. Considering the game is over 4 years old, it's nice to see dev sticking to their games. So I recommend the game.
But, I have to nitpick few things before I leave. While none of these were deal breaker for me, your mileage may differ. The story arc is generic, the characters are not really new (by which I mean you saw all of these character archetypes somewhere), and humor in game are at best reddit /r/jokes level. The game is an infinite grindfest unless you change the reward level to 200~300%, which then lets you play a fair game that allows you to progress through all levels. I like the fact that devs included option to choose your own difficulty, but why the default values so low just boggles my mind. Finally, the default graphics option is not very optimized and you should turn off some graphical settings and sprites to prevent the game choking your CPU.
All in all, it's a solid tower defense game you can enjoy for few hours/days. I recommend the game to anyone who likes this genre.

Beautiful game! Rich with a dark atmosphere and a haunting audio design. This game is like playing The Road, if The Road had giant mutants and post-apocalyptic Nazis! It’s as every bit as bleak, grey, sad, as you can imagine. The experience of traveling through an incredibly detailed post-WWIII Russia is too good to pass up.
Pros:
>---Great visuals
>---Haunting sound design (great jump scares to)
>---Decent gunplay
>---Story leaves you wanting more from this world
Cons:
>---Short game, can be finished in 2days. You will of course see longer play time on harder difficulties.
>---Easy to get lost in on the surface word unless you’re a series veteran. The levels are very linear so you should make use of your compass to help guide your way.
>---Enemy encounters can sometimes be overwhelming (having 6-8+ enemies charging you at once is rough)
>---Ammo is scarce, you’ll run out fairly quickly. Forcing you to try and not engage enemies unless your playing on the easier levels.
>---Enemy AI can be a bit…dense. Nazis don’t see/hear a pal getting their skull sniped open from 10ft away. Mutants will just b-line through a crowd of your friendlies and try to eat you (can also be real bullet sponges on easier difficulties).
>---Experienced some stuttering in 2-3 areas of the game, it also crashed to desktop 2-3 times during my run.
>---Game playes better with a controller because there are SOO many items that you need to utilize every other minute or so and unless you are an octopus…you probably won’t have the dexterity to press a certain key in the heat of a fight. The controller layout fixes this issue greatly.
Overall: Despite its slight technical issues, it’s surely an experience you will never forget. Give it a try, it’ll leave you shivering for days.

I have heard much of the Metro series and its much praised atmosphere and story-telling. So I went in there with relatively high expectations, and despite the original game being really old, I can most definitely say that Metro 2033 still stands true to the test of time.
Before we proceed further, one should note that Metro 2033 has two prominent modes - 1.) the Spartan mode and 2) the Survivor mode. Spartan modes makes ammo plentiful, turning the game into a more relaxed-and-shoot-everything-in-sight type of game. Survivor, however, makes the game more grounded, harder, with ammo being much rarer, and environmental dangers are much more lethal.
I should also note that ammo, or more specifically - a specific type of ammo, is the main currency used thorough the game. I will spoil a bit of intrigue that you can get from exploration the game yourself, but to save you the trouble of reloading a chapter - do keep in mind that you might accidentally start using the 'currency' ammo if you are not careful. Pressing and holding the 'R' key will change the ammo from the usual Junk ammo that you might have, to the more rarer and more powerful 'currency' ammo. You can check which ammo you have on the game by checking the ammo on the gun itself. Red tips means currency ammo, while blue tips are dirty and disposable ammo that you can buy in vendors.
From there on, there's another additional difficulty called Ranger, where on-screen tips are limited or downright disabled. The usual normal and hardcore difficulties that you might expect to find in single player FPS games are also present.
Jumping into Survivor with Ranger mode means that you must figure out things as you go by, all the while trying to make sure you have just enough ammo and air as you transverse through the mutant infested tunnels or alleys and streets.  When I bought the game, I had thought that the game's highly rated atmosphere was due to a combination of well-made sounds and visuals. Yes, well-made sounds and visuals are in the game, but even the game mechanics contribute to this feeling of dread and danger in the game.
The story of the game is relatively linear, but its main addition to the fun of the game lies not only in its singular narrative value. As you progress through each level, you see more and more of this post-apocalyptic society of humans living deep underground in the metro, and how they have established themselves, how they continue to marvel in human pettiness still, and how they strive against the unrelenting monstrous tides of mutants and other post-war dangers.
Metro, with the correct mode and difficulties, is a Survivor Horror game that takes place in one hell of an interesting universe, with one of the most dark and cramp settings in video games. Just be sure to save up on the air filters and the ammo.

A simple dodgeball arena game. Decent music and graphics, colorful world and uses the blocky human style similar to games like Minecraft and Thirty Flights of Loving. A decent lighthearted nonsensical story and voices are only in (although subtitles are available for multiple languages).
Rules are pretty simple: Game starts with the single ball dropping in the center of the arena. You can throw, pass, dodge, or catch the ball. You can also do a melee shove to make an opponent drop the ball. Two hits within a couple seconds knocks you out (permanently in harder modes or until your partner revives you in easier modes). And there are often random objects in the environment that can be thrown (only for the first hit; the ball is needed for the second hit).
The campaign is 12 missions with three optional challenges per mission (such as eliminating an opponent with a curving long shot). While the first-to-three regular dodgeball matches were fine, I had more fun with the bosses (which are less dodgeball and more action game). The AI companion is good enough as medium-skill partner (it almost always passes the ball to you to make the shot and can dodge decently) but it's not good enough to handle the harder AI or well coordinated humans. Sometimes it'll make a terrible mistake and randomly get knocked out or pass the ball to the enemy but I've made mistakes just as bad. Just don't rely on it and treat it as an extra life/a ball collector.
In the higher difficulties you have to keep your eye out for incoming projectiles and use your dodge roll perfectly. Otherwise the enemy will just hit you once your roll ends. It can just become a series of throws into catches/dodges until one side gets a lucky hit.
While I had my x360 controller plugged in, it became the sole method of control. No option to switch controls. While fine for me (I don't keep my controller plugged in all the time), may be annoying for those who do. Controls are remappable for keyboard but not controller. The diagram showing controller controls didn't show the pass button (RB for me).
Unfortunately, there is only local coop (no online multiplayer). At least you can do the campaign as coop.
Some things I'd like to have:
While playing I saw some visual bugs but nothing too severe. There were some model clipping issues in cutscenes and a random scratch line across the dialogue box. Thought the scratch might have been on my actual screen but it followed the window when I moved it.
Worth a look if arcadey/gamey dodgeball interests you and you don't mind the presentation/silly theme. It allows you to skip cutscenes (hold space on keyboard) if you find the story/characters grating.

Do I sell the ion cannon to replace my dead crew or save up to upgrade my weapons? Do I accept their surrender when we're both almost dead but I desperately need scrap? With the announcement and early access release of Descent Underground, I thought I'd take a moment to review this forgotten gem and it's amazing sequel.
Imagine a first person shooter, in a space ship, with 6 degress of freedom, meaning you can move forward, backward, up, down, right, left, pitch up, nose down, roll right, roll left, and whatever other direction there is.  It doesnt matter.  For 2 games that came out in 1994 and 1996, that's absolutely amazing, incredibly ahead of it's time.
It's made by Parallax Software, and published by Interplay, the same guys who did Fallout 1 and 2.
You're a space fighter, your objective is simple, go into every mine and shoot and kill infected robots.  Every robot has different abilities, strengths and weaknesses.  You're given a variety of weapons ranging from lasers to missiles to even Fusion Cannons!  Every level is a maze and dark forboding mines, little to no open spaces.  Think Doom but with 3D polygons and 6 degrees of freedom, as it is an oldschool FPS, you're main objectives are to basically find colored keys to get to each area until you reach the boss/reactor room, kill the boss/reactor, find the exit, AND BOOM!  You beat the level!  Simple and very fun gameplay.  It's a classic that I hope and pray gets more exposure!
Note to self: Get a joystick, then play great game.

For todays gamer this game may appear crude and the gameplay somewhat cumbersome, but this title did more to advance the technology and art of 3-D gaming then anything that had come before it. Interplay hit it out of the park with this one and many man hours of work, family time and cuddling with the signifigant other were lost to this game. When this game launched it was a phenom, then came the sequel and well you can guess the rest (all has to do with money of course). Yes its old. Yes the graphics on high seem only slightly better than Mario Bros (they are way better btw). Yes it will defy your logic and not work as you think it should with your fancy shmancy joystick. Suck it up. Jump into the history and let it overtake you.
You know a game is old when in the logout screen there is a phone number for their "BBS"!

I love the change of the seasons within the story mode, and the attention to detail. They missed out on including the Free Ride feature from the original Mafia, but the overall look and feel of the game is top quality. The makers simply needed to focus on designing the game to meet the gamer's mindset, without forcing them to consider spending $10 on an expansion that may or may not bring them more gaming satisfaction. Discount please.
